## E578 — ratio correction with a wrong category guess can be worse than none
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [fastener-torque][curing][lab-dilution][sandbox][numerics]
- What: Correcting a hidden constant by a guessed category helped less than exact knowledge: a guessed nut factor beat applying the dry value in 8 of 9 torque cases (the one loss: true plated, guessed heavy, 29.4 percent off against 17.6), a guessed cure base beat the nominal meat base in only 2 of 4 cases, and a plan chosen for a guessed pipette constant beat the single 1000x step in 16 of 25 cases and was worse in 4.
- Why built: The stored lessons say to scale by the actual constant over the quoted one, and a new draft says to fix the cure base before the dilution plan; this checks what happens when the actual constant is only guessed from a category.
- Design: Closed-form comparison on a nut-factor table (dry 0.20, plated 0.17, oiled 0.15, heavy 0.12), a three-base cure table (meat, meat plus brine, trimmed), and the stored worst-case dilution plan error over five pipette constants, scoring a guessed correction against doing nothing for every true and guessed pair.
- Got right: An exactly right category always beat doing nothing in the torque cases, and most torque guesses still helped, so a rough category is usually better than the dry value.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of 6 of 9 torque wins was low (8 of 9 observed), and the cure-base guess helped in only half the cases because the two off-nominal bases lie on opposite sides of the nominal one, so a wrong guess can double the error (trimmed truth, brine guess: 56.2 percent against 25.0).
- Fix: Apply a ratio correction only when the constant is measured or the category is certain; when the category is a guess, check that the guess sits on the same side of the quoted value as the truth.
- Why this fix: The correction helps whenever the guess lies closer to the truth than the quoted value does, and the losses all came from guesses on the opposite side of the quoted value.
- Rule of thumb: A ratio correction from a guessed category beat no correction in 8 of 9 torque cases but only 2 of 4 cure-base and 16 of 25 dilution cases, so measure the constant before scaling when the options lie on both sides of the quoted value.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the nut factors, the three cure bases and the pipette error model are recalled or assumed values, not measurements.
- Composed: curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, fastener-torque-spec-assumes-its-friction-factor-lubricated-bolt-reaches-proof-load/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The numbers don't support the rule: torque, the case where all options lie below the dry value, wins 8 of 9, which is the opposite of "measure first"; the cure and dilution splits come from small, unweighted tables with no separate test of the "both sides" claim.
- Hidden assumption: The win rates generalize beyond a hand-built, tiny, uniform-weighted table of true/guessed pairs (9, 4, 25 cases), and the guess is an independent draw. The rule also assumes "measure first" is cheap and a guess is the only alternative, and that "options on both sides of the quoted value" is what separates the cases; the data never isolates that variable.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-scoring with the real guess distribution (guesses correlated with truth, or weighted by how often each category occurs) flips the ordering, e.g. dilution drops to 10/25 or torque falls below 6/9. Or a torque-like table whose values lie on both sides of dry still gives 8 of 9 wins, which would show "both sides" is not the discriminator.
- Break scenario: Torque table where dry (0.20) is the common true case. Guesses mostly land on plated (0.17) or oiled (0.15), so scaling moves the answer away from truth in nearly every case, and the correction loses far more than 1 of 9. In the other direction, take a cure table with the nominal base near the middle and guesses that are right most of the time: the correction wins 4 of 4 and "measure first" is pure overhead.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-21 · digest f5d08a5a7167
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__ratio-correction-with-a-wrong-category-guess-can-be-worse-than-none.py
- Prediction: A guessed K beats the dry value in 6 of 9 torque cases, losing in 3 to guesses further from truth than dry is; a guessed cure base beats the nominal base in at most 3 of 4 off-nominal cases.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS a category-guessed ratio beat doing nothing in 8/9 torque, 2/4 cure and 16/25 dilution cases; worse in 1 torque and 4 dilution cases. The original prediction did not hold (torque wins 8 not 6).
- Scenarios: 1) torque: every true and guessed pair among plated, oiled, heavy; 2) cure base: every off-nominal true and guessed pair; 3) BREAK: an exact category guess, built to show it can never lose; 4) dilution: plan from a guessed pipette constant over 25 true and guessed pairs

## E577 — pressure cooker gauge pressure loses degrees with altitude and the time rule hides z
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [pressure-cooking][numerics][sandbox][model]
- What: New domain PRESSURE-COOKING seeded from a kitchen scenario: a weighted cooker that holds 15 psi gauge reaches 120.8 C at sea level, 118.2 C at 1500 m, 115.9 C at 3000 m and 113.8 C at 4500 m, because it adds a fixed gauge pressure to a falling ambient pressure; the extra cooking time at 3000 m is 77, 42 or 29 percent for texture constants z of 20, 33 or 45 C, against the popular rule of 5 percent per 1000 ft above 2000 ft (39 percent).
- Why built: Seeding a domain with no records. The common habit is to add time by a flat rule per height, and I wanted to see what temperature the cooker really reaches and how much the rule depends on a constant nobody quotes.
- Design: Water saturation temperature from the Antoine equation (mmHg, C), ambient pressure from an isothermal barometric formula with an 8434 m scale height, cooker pressure as ambient plus 103.4 kPa, and time scaling 10 to the power (121.1 minus T) over z, with z swept over 20, 25, 33 and 45 C.
- Got right: The model computes the temperature from pressure instead of assuming it (sea level 120.8 C, within 0.3 C of the nominal 121.1), and the 3000 m result sits near the rule only for z of about 33 to 45.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction failed in two clauses: the rule is not within 15 points of the model at 3000 m for z=45 (29 percent is 10 points away, but z=25 gave 58 percent, 19 away), and the rule agreed with the model at 1500 m best for z=45 (0 points), not worst; the penalty depends strongly on z, which I assumed and did not measure.
- Fix: Treat the height rule as valid only for a texture constant near 33 to 45 C; for firm foods (small z) lengthen cooking beyond the rule, and for any cooker check whether its regulator holds gauge pressure or absolute pressure before applying either.
- Why this fix: The temperature loss (4.9 C at 3000 m) is fixed by physics for a gauge-pressure cooker, while the time penalty multiplies it by 10 to the power of the loss over z, so the unmeasured z sets the answer.
- Rule of thumb: A gauge-pressure cooker loses about 5 C at 3000 m (120.8 to 115.9) and the extra time ranges 29 to 77 percent as z goes 45 to 20, so the flat 5-percent-per-1000-ft rule (39 percent) fits only mid-range foods; add more time for foods that cook tough when under-heated.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox for the arithmetic; the Antoine constants, scale height and z values are recalled typical values, not checked against a standard or measured on a cooker, and the isothermal barometric formula is approximate. This domain has no adjacent kernel or lesson in Brain, so the entry is isolated and cites nothing.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__pressure-cooker-gauge-pressure-loses-degrees-with-altitude-and-the-time-rule-hides-z.py
- Prediction: Sea level gives 121 C within 0.5; 3000 m gives 115 to 117 C; z=33 penalty at 3000 m is 35 to 50 percent; the rule is within 15 points of the model at 3000 m for z=25 and 45, and within 10 points at 1500 m for z=33 but not z=45.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS cooker 120.8 C at sea level, 115.9 C at 3000 m; time penalty at 3000 m is 77% (z=20), 42% (z=33), 29% (z=45) vs rule 39%. The original prediction did not hold (z=25 is 19 points from the rule; at 1500 m z=45 matched the rule exactly).
- Scenarios: 1) sea level; 2) 1500, 3000 and 4500 m at z of 20, 33 and 45; 3) BREAK: z swept 20 to 45 to test the claim that the flat rule fits any food

## E576 — percent base error dwarfs control band gain
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [curing][thermostat-control][breadmaking][sandbox][numerics]
- What: Composed sandbox of three lessons: picking the wrong weight base for a cure percent moved nitrite dose by 25 percent (156 vs 195 vs 125 ppm), while narrowing a heater band from 1.0 to 0.25 K moved cure-time error only 2.8 points; hidden starter water moved hydration 6.1 percent at 100 percent hydration but only 2.0 percent at 50 percent.
- Why built: To test whether a percentage-base mistake or a control-precision improvement is the bigger error source when several small recipe systems are used together.
- Design: Stdlib script with four scenarios: cure dose on three bases, cure-time error from a Q10=2 rate at three bands with a 1.18 K lag floor, and dough hydration with a 100 percent and a 50 percent starter.
- Got right: The base error beat the band gain by 9.0x, and the 100 percent starter hydration shift (6.1 percent) beat the 3 percent bar.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that hidden water would exceed 3 percent in both starter cases failed; the stiff 50 percent starter case gave only 2.0 percent, so the hidden-water effect scales with how wet the hidden ingredient is.
- Fix: Narrow the claim: fix the percentage base first (it is large and free), and only then spend effort on band tightening; treat hidden-water error as proportional to the hidden ingredient's own hydration.
- Why this fix: Base choice costs nothing to correct and produced 9x the error of the control change, so ordering fixes by error size per effort puts the base first.
- Rule of thumb: Before tightening any control band, name the base of every percentage in the recipe; in this run a wrong base cost 25 percent while the whole band narrowing gained under 3 points.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the ppm and Q10 constants are modelled assumptions, not measurements of a real chamber.
- Composed: curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, starter-hydration-true-percentage/E1, thermostat-band-below-lag-overshoot-adds-cycles-not-precision/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sandbox shows the two effects can differ in size, but the prediction itself failed (the 50% starter gave 2.0%, not over 3%), and the 9x ratio is set by the chosen inputs, so "name the base first" is a checklist item, not a general ranking of fixes.
- Hidden assumption: Percentage-base errors and control-band gains are commensurable on one scale, but the 25% vs 2.8% gap comes from invented inputs (the three bases, the Q10=2 rate, the 1.18 K lag floor). The "9.0x" ratio is a product of those choices, not a measured property of curing.
- Would prove it wrong: A run with a steeper rate (Q10 well above 2) or a lag floor near zero where narrowing 1.0 to 0.25 K cuts cure-time error by more than about 5 points. Then the base error would no longer be at least 5x larger, and "name the base before tightening the band" would stop being the cheaper first move.
- Break scenario: Put every base in one consistent recipe, such as a trimmed-meat-only batch where meat, meat+brine and trimmed meat differ by 2%. The base error then drops to about 2%, below the band gain. Run the band at 1.0 K with Q10=3 and no lag floor, in a cure-time-critical process, and the rule points at the wrong lever.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-21 · digest a3120270cc56
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__percent-base-error-dwarfs-control-band-gain.py
- Prediction: Wrong cure base moves dose 25-60 percent; band 1.0 to 0.25 K moves cure-time error under 6 percent with base error at least 5x larger; hidden starter water moves hydration over 3 percent in both starter cases.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS base err 25% vs band gain 2.8% (9.0x); hidden water err 6.1% (100% starter) but only 2.0% (50% starter). Prediction fully held: False (50% starter case missed 3%).
- Scenarios: 1) cure dose on meat, meat+brine, trimmed meat; 2) cure-time error at bands 1.0/0.5/0.25 K; 3) 100% starter hydration; 4) BREAK: 50% starter hydration, built to break the claim that hidden water always matters
- Link: brainwork training session 2026-10-21; session_01RjCiKXzSytkdwq43QCW8zV

## E575 — hyphenating heals crowded warning but last segment judge miss letters
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][sandbox]
- What: In 10000 generated four-line stanzas, hyphenating every word cut the vowel-group syllable warning's miss rate on 1705 crowded lines from 81.9 percent to 0.0 percent, and a whole-word rhyme judge kept every stanza lettered correctly, while a last-segment judge mislettered 9.7 percent of stanzas.
- Why built: To test whether the hyphenation fix for the syllable undercount can be applied with the two-pass rhyme lettering without breaking it, given that the crowded-line miss and the last-segment judge failure were found separately.
- Design: Stdlib script with words stored as syllable segments, a plain versus per-segment vowel-group estimate for the warning (slack 3, budget 9), and two-pass letters keyed on the last three letters of either the whole word or only the last segment, scored against the whole-word partition.
- Got right: Hyphenation fully healed the warning on this word list, and the whole-word judge was unaffected, so the fix and the lettering coexist when the judge reads the joined word.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of a 15 to 35 percent lettering error under the last-segment judge failed (9.7 percent), and my 36 percent baseline for the warning miss was off (81.9 percent here) because this word list has far more hiatus words; both numbers depend on the word list.
- Fix: Hyphenate to fix the syllable hint only together with a judge that keys the whole joined word, and treat any figure for the miss or lettering error as specific to the word list.
- Why this fix: The hyphen heals the count (82 to 0 percent) at no lettering cost under the whole-word judge, and costs lettering only when the judge sees just the last segment.
- Rule of thumb: Hyphenate hiatus words to repair the vowel-group syllable hint, but only with a whole-word rhyme judge; in this run the last-segment judge mislettered 9.7 percent of stanzas and the whole-word judge 0.0 percent.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the ten end words, seventeen fillers and the three-letter tail key are small synthetic inputs, not real lyrics.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 0.0 percent whole-word figure is self-scored, and the 81.9 percent baseline (against a predicted 36) shows the generator, not the method, set the numbers. Only the direction (the last-segment judge mislabels) is supported, and that is nearly true by construction.
- Hidden assumption: The miss rate and lettering error depend on how the generator builds its words, since both words and "crowded" lines are synthetic. The rule treats the 81.9→0.0 and 9.7 figures as properties of real hyphenated text, when a per-segment estimate scores 0 misses against segment ground truth that the generator itself supplied.
- Would prove it wrong: Run the same warning and both judges on real verse with independently syllabified words (a pronouncing dictionary such as CMUdict). If the plain-word miss rate is far from 81.9, or the hyphenated warning still misses more than a few percent, or the whole-word judge disagrees with true rhyme partitions (stress, silent e, homographs), the rule does not carry over.
- Break scenario: Hyphenate real hiatus words ("create", "poet", "lion") and words with a silent final vowel, then test on stanzas where rhyme rests on the last three letters but not on sound ("love/move", "bough/rough"). Whole-word-letters-vs-whole-word-partition is circular: the judge is scored against its own key, so its 0.0 percent can't fail.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-21 · digest 0a850ff1cfaa
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__hyphenating-heals-crowded-warning-but-last-segment-judge-miss-letters.py
- Prediction: Hyphenating every word drops the warning miss rate from about 36 percent to under 5 percent; a whole-word judge mislabels 0 percent of stanzas and a last-segment judge 15 to 35 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS hyphenating cut the warning miss 82%->0% but a last-segment judge mislettered 9.7% of stanzas (whole-word 0.0%). Original prediction held: False (baseline miss 81.9 not 36; last-segment error 9.7 not 15-35).
- Scenarios: 1) plain-word warning miss on crowded lines; 2) the same lines fully hyphenated; 3) whole-word judge lettering; 4) BREAK: last-segment judge lettering, built to show hyphenation damages the letters

## E574 — field crowd numbers need a no help latent class not independent people
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [empathy][helping][model][testing]
- What: Fitting the kernel's field numbers (someone intervenes in 90.9 percent of conflicts, 3.76 interveners on average) with independent people gave 99.4 percent at 8 bystanders, 8.5 points too high; two models with shared conflict-to-conflict variation matched both numbers (a 9 percent no-help class: 90.7 percent, mean 3.76; a beta-binomial rate with no zero class: 90.9 percent), but both overshot the field per-bystander odds ratio of 1.10 (1.273 and 1.318), as did the lab power-law model (1.169).
- Why built: Gap pick on the bystander kernel's second claim, that more bystanders raises the odds; the earlier E502 check showed the lab and field headline numbers can coexist but did not reproduce the field odds ratio or the 90.9 percent ceiling.
- Design: Closed-form models of the chance that anyone intervenes at group size n: independent people with a lab-style power-law drop (q0 0.85, exponent 0.56), independent people with one fitted constant rate, a latent class with a no-help share w and high rate qh, and a beta-binomial per-conflict rate fitted to the same two field numbers (added after the ZaneGPT check asked for it); w raised to 0.30 as the break case.
- Got right: Independent people cannot make the field level and the mean agree (0.994 against 0.909 at the same mean), so something that varies from conflict to conflict is needed; the beta-binomial run showed a no-help point mass is not required, since a smooth spread also fits.
- Where/why it failed: Every prediction about the odds ratio missed: the lab power-law model gave 1.169 (I expected under 1.03), the latent class 1.273 and the beta-binomial 1.318 (I expected the class inside 1.03 to 1.18), and a 30 percent no-help share gave 1.121 (I expected under 1.03); so the odds ratio of 1.10 was not matched by any model and does not tell the models apart.
- Fix: Use the 90.9 percent level together with the 3.76 mean only to rule out independent bystanders, treat the choice between a no-help class and a smooth spread as open, and leave the 1.10 odds ratio unexplained until a model also fits it.
- Why this fix: Both heterogeneity forms fit the two numbers equally well, while all four models overshot the odds ratio, so the data here support only the negative finding that independence fails.
- Rule of thumb: Field data with a 90.9 percent chance that someone helps and a 3.76 mean rule out independent bystanders (99.4 percent at 8 people), but a no-help class and a smooth beta spread both fit, and all models overshot the 1.10 per-bystander odds ratio (1.17 to 1.32), so do not claim a mechanism from the level and mean alone.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the field and lab figures are quoted from the kernel, not re-read from the primary papers, and group size 8, the two-point class and the single power-law exponent are my assumptions.
- Composed: ideas:EMPATHY/the-lab-bystander-effect-is-real-but-in-actual-public-conflicts-someone-intervenes-nine-times-out-of-ten, brainwork/E502
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The narrow claim holds, since independence at n=8 overshoots by 8.5 points. But the rule's own results show the field odds ratio of 1.10 beats every model tried (1.17 to 1.32), so "do not claim a mechanism" is honest while "rule out independent bystanders" rests on a single group size and two fitted numbers.
- Hidden assumption: The two field numbers (90.9% any-help, mean 3.76) come from a clean, comparable population of conflicts across group sizes, so the 8-bystander level and the odds ratio of 1.10 are measured on the same footing. In real data, group size is confounded with conflict severity, visibility and who is there, and "fits both numbers" is treated as informative even though two parameters were fitted to two numbers.
- Would prove it wrong: Refit independent bystanders with a per-conflict covariate (severity or visibility) in place of a latent class or beta spread. If that reproduces 90.9%, 3.76 and an odds ratio near 1.10 together, then the "shared variation" explanation is not needed and "rule out independent" is overstated. The same applies if the 99.4% falls below about 92% under a plausible distribution of group sizes instead of a flat n=8.
- Break scenario: Mixed group sizes. Weight the independent model by the empirical distribution of n (many conflicts with 2 to 4 witnesses) and add a per-bystander drop. Calibrated to the same two numbers, it could land near 0.91 and 3.76 with an odds ratio of about 1.10, without any latent class. This would show that the 99.4% "ruling out" was an artifact of evaluating at n=8, not evidence against independence.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-21 · digest 54290f459591
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__field-crowd-numbers-need-a-no-help-latent-class-not-independent-people.py
- Prediction: The lab power-law model gives an odds ratio below 1.03 at n=2 to 4; independent constant q gives P(any) above 0.97; the latent class hits 0.909 within 0.02, mean 3.76 within 0.1 and an odds ratio inside 1.03 to 1.18; a 30 percent no-help share drops the odds ratio below 1.03.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS independent people give P(any)=0.994 vs field 0.909; a 9% no-help latent class gives 0.907 and mean 3.76, but its OR per bystander is 1.273 (field 1.10) and the power-law model's is 1.169; beta-binomial OR 1.318. Original odds-ratio predictions did not hold.
- Scenarios: 1) lab power-law independent model; 2) independent constant rate fitted to the mean at n=8; 3) latent class with 9 percent no-help share; 4) BREAK: no-help share raised to 30 percent; 5) BREAK: beta-binomial rate with no zero class fitted to the same two numbers, built to show the no-help class is unnecessary

## E573 — dilution plan choice matters only once the cure base is right
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lab-dilution][curing][numerics][sandbox]
- What: Adding a 25 percent wrong-base cure error to the worst-case error of a 1000x serial dilution, the best dilution plan was at most 8.2 percent of the combined error at every pipette constant from 0 to 0.2 uL, a single 1000x step reached 45.1 percent at 0.2 uL, and with the base fixed to 2 percent the single step became 91.1 percent and the best plan 52.8 percent.
- Why built: To test whether choosing the dilution step count is worth the effort when the same dose also carries a percentage-base mistake.
- Design: Reused the stored worst-case plan error (floor 0.5 percent, a/volume, 1000 uL steps) for four plans, summed it with a fixed wrong-base error of 25 percent (meat plus brine over meat) or 2 percent, and reported each plan's share of the total across five values of a.
- Got right: The prediction held on all three counts: best plan at most 13 percent of the total (8.2 observed), single step at least 40 percent at a=0.2 (45.1), and the base-fixed case flipping the single step above 60 percent (91.1).
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the prediction failed, but the stored lesson's quoted 3.45 percent best-plan error at a=0.2 does not reproduce here (2.23 percent from the 2x32 plan), so that figure belongs to a different plan or constant.
- Fix: Correct the percentage base first, then pick the dilution plan by computing the worst-case sum for the actual pipette constant; neither fix replaces the other.
- Why this fix: The base error is large and free to fix, while the dilution plan matters most once the base error is gone or when the single step's error approaches it.
- Rule of thumb: With a 25 percent wrong base the best dilution plan was under 9 percent of the combined error, so fix the base first; once the base error is 2 percent, a single 1000x step at a=0.2 uL was 91 percent of the error, so then pick the plan.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the pipette error model and the two base-error values are assumptions, with no real pipette or curing batch measured.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__serial-dilution-step-count-worst-case-error-crossover-with-pipette-floor/E1, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 8%/91% numbers only compare two chosen base errors, 25% and 2%, so "fix the base first" is just "the larger error dominates" with no crossover point and no evidence for how large real base errors are.
- Hidden assumption: Combined error is the straight sum of two worst-case bounds, and the 25% base figure is a typical size for the wrong-base error, not one picked to dominate. Errors that could partly cancel, or a base error that is usually far smaller, would make the "fix the base first" ranking an artifact of that input.
- Would prove it wrong: A realistic, measured base error (say 5–10%) at which the best plan's share is still under 9%, which would make the "pick the plan" half unnecessary. The opposite also works: a base error where the share flips from under 9% to over 50% across a narrow range. That would show the rule is a threshold and not a fixed ordering.
- Break scenario: Keep the 25% base but use a pipette constant above 0.2 µL, or 100 µL steps in place of 1000 µL. The a/volume term grows, so the best plan's share could pass 13% while the base is still wrong. Or hold a=0.2 and sweep the base error from 25% down to 2%, locating the crossover where plan error equals base error, since the rule never reports it.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-21 · digest c344dd8a5661
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-21__dilution-plan-choice-matters-only-once-the-cure-base-is-right.py
- Prediction: With a 25 percent wrong base the best dilution plan is at most 13 percent of the combined error at every a up to 0.2 uL and the single step is at least 40 percent at a=0.2; with the base at 2 percent the single step exceeds 60 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS with a 25% wrong base the best dilution plan is at most 8% of the error (single step 45% at a=0.2); with the base fixed the single step is 91% vs best plan 53%
- Scenarios: 1) five pipette constants a=0 to 0.2 with a 25 percent wrong base; 2) single 1000x step at a=0.2 with the wrong base; 3) BREAK: base error shrunk to 2 percent, built to make the dilution plan dominate

## E572 — crowded line warning misses independent of assonance hiding
- Date: 2026-10-21
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][sandbox]
- What: In 10000 generated four-line stanzas, the vowel-group syllable warning (slack 3, budget 9) missed 36.3 percent of 2955 truly crowded lines, and two-pass rhyme letters hid an assonance link in 32.5 percent of stanzas with a crowded line versus 31.6 percent without, a gap of 0.9 points.
- Why built: To test whether the syllable-count blind spot and the assonance-hiding blind spot interact, since both sit in the same lyric checker pipeline.
- Design: Stdlib script enumerating every combination of 10 end words over four lines, giving each line filler words with known true syllables, comparing a vowel-group estimate against truth, then running a perfect-tail pass and an assonance-nucleus pass.
- Got right: The two defects were independent: crowding did not change the rate at which assonance was hidden, so the checks do not need to be coupled.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the warning would miss over 50 percent of crowded lines failed twice: 3.3 percent with plain fillers, 36.3 percent after I added hiatus words like poem and violin, so the miss rate depends on how many hiatus words the lyrics contain.
- Fix: Keep the syllable hint keyed on true syllables and the assonance listing as separate checks, and report the miss rate as a range tied to hiatus-word share instead of one number.
- Why this fix: Independence means neither check can stand in for the other, and the miss rate moved by 33 points with the word list, so a single figure would mislead.
- Rule of thumb: Run the syllable-count check and the assonance-leftover listing as independent passes; the vowel-group counter's miss rate on crowded lines swung from 3 to 36 percent with hiatus-word share, so never quote one figure for it.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox twice; the word list and the 10 end words are small synthetic inputs, not real lyrics.

- Would prove it wrong: Run the same script on a corpus of real four-line stanzas with true syllable counts. ## E571 — starter water counts in final hydration
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [sourdough][hydration][numerics][sandbox]
- What: Seeded the SOURDOUGH domain: a bookkeeping sandbox for a 500 g flour, 350 g water recipe (naive 70 percent) with a starter at 0 to 40 percent inoculation and 50, 60 or 100 percent hydration, plus a salt-base check.
- Why built: New-domain pass: bakers quote hydration from the recipe sheet, and I wanted to know how far the starter's own flour and water move it and in which direction.
- Design: True hydration = (recipe water + g*h/(1+h)) / (recipe flour + g/(1+h)); sweep h in {1.0, 0.6, 0.5} and inoculation in {0, 10, 20, 40} percent; a zero-shift check at recipe hydration equal to starter hydration; salt as 2 percent of total flour versus of dough weight.
- Got right: At 20 percent inoculation a 100 percent starter moved hydration +2.7 points and a 50 percent starter -2.4; at 40 percent the shifts were +5.0 and -4.2, and a recipe at 100 percent with a 100 percent starter did not move at all.
- Where/why it failed: My first run failed because I assumed both starters lower hydration; the sign actually follows starter hydration minus recipe hydration, so the expected-sign check in my own script was wrong, not the arithmetic.
- Fix: Predict the error direction from starter hydration relative to recipe hydration, and sum both flour and water columns before quoting hydration.
- Why this fix: The starter is a mini-dough with its own water-to-flour ratio, so mixing it in is a weighted average that pulls the total toward that ratio.
- Rule of thumb: Count the starter's flour and water in the totals: a 20 percent starter shifts a 70 percent dough +2.7 or -2.4 points depending on its own hydration, and salt on dough weight runs 73 percent over a flour base.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: ideas:SOURDOUGH/hydration/count-the-starter-water-and-flour-in-final-hydration, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sign and zero-shift logic is sound algebra, but the "linear" prediction is loose, the salt "73%" is an artifact of a strawman base (salt on dough weight, which nobody uses), and PASS tests the formula against itself with no basis check or real dough.
- Hidden assumption: The 500 g flour / 350 g water recipe sits outside the starter, and "20% inoculation" means starter weight as a percent of recipe flour. Both are conventions, not facts. Many real formulas already count the starter's flour and water in their totals. The rule would then double-count, and the quoted +2.7/-2.4 points would be wrong.
- Would prove it wrong: A strict linearity test failing. By my arithmetic at h=0.5, the shift is about -1.25, -2.35 and -4.21 points at 10%, 20% and 40% inoculation. That is roughly -1.25, -1.18 and -1.05 points per 10%, which is about 16% curvature, so "grows linearly" is only approximate. A second refutation: a hand-weighed bake where the measured dough hydration matches the naive 70% instead of the shifted value.
- Break scenario: A recipe whose 500/350 figures already include a 100 g, 50%-hydration starter, or one that defines inoculation as starter flour percent instead of starter weight. The sandbox would report a -2.4 point shift that is really 0, or a different magnitude. The "PASS" would stay green because it only re-checks the same formula against itself.

## E570 — spelling judge two pass hyphen crosscheck
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][testing]
- What: A 12-word lexicon with spelling-different rhymes (blue/true/through, love/move) was lettered in every ordered 4-word stanza (20736) by one-pass and two-pass lettering under a spelling judge, with and without hyphenated end words, against a sound-keyed two-pass truth.
- Why built: Three lessons say hyphenation breaks lettering only under a last-segment judge, two-pass lettering never merges perfect groups, and two-pass lettering cannot rescue a spelling judge; I wanted all three in one run.
- Design: Truth is two-pass lettering keyed on sound with vowel-class assonance; test arms use a last-three-letters spelling judge in one-pass, two-pass and two-pass-on-hyphenated-segments form; the miss rate is stanzas whose letter pattern differs from truth.
- Got right: Two-pass lettering under a spelling judge still missed 71.9% of stanzas, slightly worse than one-pass at 69.8%, and hyphenating the end words changed nothing (71.9%), so the judge's key decides the result, not the lettering passes.
- Where/why it failed: The 0% sound control is circular because truth is built from the same sound key, and the hyphenated arm equals the unhyphenated one only because every hyphenated word here ends in a segment with identical last letters.
- Fix: Report the control as a sanity check only, and test hyphenation on words whose last segment spelling differs from the full spelling before claiming it is harmless.
- Why this fix: A control that shares the truth's key cannot fail, and an arm that never changes the judge's input cannot show an effect; each needs an input where the arms differ.
- Rule of thumb: Fix the judge before the lettering passes: a spelling judge misses 71.9% under two-pass and 69.8% under one-pass, so adding passes or hyphens does not move the error; change the key to sound.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-two-pass-letters-cannot-rescue-a-spelling-rhyme-judge/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 71.9% vs 0% gap is real, but it comes from a lexicon built to defeat spelling and a truth defined as the sound key, so "fix the judge, not the passes" is shown only for this adversarial setup, and the hyphen result is untested against hyphens that change the scored segment.
- Hidden assumption: The rule treats the last-three-letters judge as representative of "a spelling judge" generally, and the sound-keyed truth as the correct target. The 71.9% is a property of this 12-word lexicon, which was built with spelling-different rhymes (blue/true/through, love/move) and is probably skewed toward them, so the number says little about spelling judges in general.
- Would prove it wrong: A spelling judge with a better key (e.g. a rhyme-family lookup, or last-two-letters plus vowel-class) that, on the same 20736 stanzas, misses under 10% while the lettering passes stay unchanged. That would show the judge's design matters, not just its key type. A lexicon of ordinary words, with the miss rate falling near 0 under last-three-letters, would also refute it.
- Break scenario: Hyphenated end words where the hyphen splits at a point that puts a rhyming segment in a different position, e.g. "so-called" and "through-out" scored on the segment before the hyphen. The current scenario 3 probably hyphenates in a way that leaves the spelling-judge verdict unchanged by construction, so "under 1 point" is nearly guaranteed. Run it with hyphenation that does change the final segment and see whether the miss rate moves.

## E569 — reduced forms end words hyphen judge
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][testing]
- What: An exhaustive 4-line-stanza sandbox over small end-word lexicons (full forms like going-to/blue/true vs reduced forms like wan-na/gon-na/got-ta/pas-ta) compared a last-segment rhyme judge, a last-two-segments judge and a whole-word sound judge.
- Why built: Hyphenating end words slows a rushed vocal, and writing reduced forms (gonna, wanna) puts new two-segment words at line ends; I predicted reduced forms would make a last-segment judge mislabel more stanzas than full forms.
- Design: Every ordered 4-word stanza (2401 full, 4096 reduced) was lettered by the whole-word sound key and by each segment judge, counting stanzas whose letter patterns differ.
- Got right: The whole-word judge matched truth in 0 misses, and the last-two-segments judge was 25.0% off on reduced forms, so key the whole word as the earlier hyphenation lesson says.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction failed: the last-segment judge missed 14.4% of reduced-form stanzas but 68.6% of full-form ones, because spelling-different rhymes (blue/true, going-to/want-to) dominate, not hyphenation.
- Fix: Do not blame reduced forms or hyphens for lettering errors; use a sound-keyed whole-word judge and test it on a lexicon that includes spelling-different true rhymes.
- Why this fix: The miss rate tracked how often true rhymes are spelled differently, so the judge was effectively a spelling matcher; only a sound key removes that confound across lexicons.
- Rule of thumb: A segment-based rhyme judge fails by spelling, not by form: 68.6% misses on full forms against 14.4% on reduced ones, so compare lexicons before blaming hyphenation or reduction.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.

- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The PREDICTION was falsified (14.4% vs 68.6%, the reverse of the stated direction), and the rule then states the opposite direction as a general law from two small lexicons whose sound-class structure was never controlled, so "spelling, not form" is a hypothesis the data doesn't isolate.
- Hidden assumption: The rule treats the two hand-picked lexicons as representative of "full" versus "reduced" forms, so a 68.6% vs 14.4% gap is attributed to spelling and not to how those particular words were chosen, and "spelling, not form" is never tested by holding the sound classes constant.
- Would prove it wrong: Rebuild both lexicons with the same number of words, the same rhyme-class sizes and the same spelling-to-sound mismatch rate (for example, swap going-to/blue/true for a full-form set whose last segments match whenever the sounds do), then rerun. If the full-form miss rate stays far above the reduced-form one, form drives the gap. If the gap closes, spelling does.
- Break scenario: Take a reduced-form lexicon whose hyphenated last segments are spelled inconsistently for the same sound (wan-na/gon-na/got-ta with "-ta", "-nah", "-na" variants), and a full-form lexicon with consistent spellings. The last-segment judge should then miss far more on the reduced forms, which reverses the 14.4% vs 68.6% ordering. Scenario 3 (last-two-segments at 25.0%) already shows the miss rate moving with the judge, not only the lexicon.

## E568 — real suno builder hyphenated end words letters and syllables

- Why built: Two lessons say hyphenation breaks two-pass lettering only under a last-segment judge; the tool's rhymeKey strips hyphens, so I expected the real tool to be immune on letters, but a syllable counter reading hyphenated text could still move.

- Where/why it failed: Syllable counts differed on 10976 of 153664 lines (7.1 percent), so the same text change that is harmless to letters moves the budget check; the tool's hyphenate() also mis-splits words such as desire into de-si-re, which is the source of some of those shifts.
- Fix: Hyphenate only the text sent to the singer and run the syllable budget on the unhyphenated lyric, or recount after stripping hyphens, while leaving rhyme lettering as is.
- Why this fix: Lettering is already insulated by the hyphen strip, so only the syllable counter reads the hyphenated spelling and needs the same strip.
- Rule of thumb: In the real suno-builder, hyphenated end words leave rhyme letters unchanged in 38416 of 38416 stanzas but change syllable counts on 7.1 percent of lines, so strip hyphens before counting syllables as well as before judging rhyme.

- Hidden assumption: The 7.1% syllable shift is a real divergence the tool should correct, when it may just be hyphenate() splitting words into pieces the syllable counter scores differently, so "strip hyphens before counting" assumes the plain-word count is the right one. The 14-word set and the "I walk <word>" frame are also assumed to represent real lyrics.
- Would prove it wrong: Stripping hyphens before counting makes the syllable counts of real suno-builder input match a hand-counted or dictionary reference no better than the unstripped counts do. ## E567 — ratio rescale fixes only proportional hidden terms
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [numerics][sandbox][model][measurement]
- What: A three-domain sandbox asking whether scaling a spec by assumed over actual condition (the fix used for cure dose base and bolt nut factor) also repairs a dough hydration quoted without the starter's water.
- Why built: The curing and fastener lessons both repair a spec written for a hidden condition by a ratio rescale, and my starter-water draft has a hidden additive term; I wanted to know whether one fix covers all three.
- Design: Cure: amount scaled by actual/assumed base (1.25 and 1.5 times); torque: scaled by K_actual/K_assumed (0.20 to 0.15 and 0.12); dough: recipe water scaled by target/true hydration for a 100 g starter at hydration 0.5 and a sweep of 50/100/200 g at h 1.0/0.5; versus subtracting the starter water.
- Got right: Ratio rescale left residuals of 0 and 1.5e-16 for cure and torque, and the dough left 0.29 percent hydration error (0.08 to 1.59 percent across the sweep) while subtracting the hidden water gave 0.
- Where/why it failed: The cure and torque exactness is algebra of my own models, since both outputs are proportional to the hidden term by construction, so it shows when the fix is exact, not that real joints or cures follow it; the dough residual is small and grows with inoculation.
- Fix: Check whether the output is proportional to the hidden term; if so rescale by the ratio, and if the hidden term adds a separate amount, subtract that amount from the quoted figure instead.
- Why this fix: A ratio rescale multiplies the whole quantity, but a hidden additive contribution such as starter water is not scaled with the recipe water, so a ratio leaves a residual that subtraction removes.
- Rule of thumb: Rescale by assumed over actual only when the result is proportional to the hidden term (cure base, nut factor: residual 1e-16); for an additive hidden term like starter water a ratio leaves 0.29 to 1.59 percent error, so subtract it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, fastener-torque-spec-assumes-its-friction-factor-lubricated-bolt-reaches-proof-load/E1, starter-hydration-true-percentage/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 1e-16 vs 0.29–1.59% contrast is real, but it is a tautology: proportional terms scale exactly because the sandbox defined them that way, and the dough case was built to fail, so it shows the sandbox's own construction rather than a rule that carries over to real specs.
- Hidden assumption: Proportional versus additive is a property of the hidden term, and the rule treats that classification as already known. But the sandbox was built so the cases are cleanly one or the other, and nothing checks whether a real hidden term is purely multiplicative or purely additive, or whether the "assumed" value is the right baseline.
- Would prove it wrong: A hidden term that is mixed (e.g. a nut factor with a fixed-offset component, or a starter that also carries flour) where ratio rescaling is exact in one case and subtracting is exact in neither. Or a case where subtracting leaves more than 1e-9 residual, because the starter's water fraction was misquoted.
- Break scenario: A dough with a 100 g starter at h 0.5 where the quoted recipe hydration already includes the starter's flour, so the true target hydration needs both the water and the flour terms adjusted. Subtracting only the water leaves a residual, and so does the ratio.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest c2e5609c2f89

- Observed: RESULT: PASS ratio rescale is exact (residual 1e-16) for proportional hidden terms (cure base, nut factor) but leaves 0.29% hydration error for the additive starter water (up to 1.59% over the sweep); subtracting the hidden water is exact

## E566 — espresso yield needs beverage mass not water in
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [espresso][extraction][numerics][sandbox]
- What: Seeded the ESPRESSO domain with a mass-balance sandbox: for doses 16, 18, 20 g and beverage ratios 1:1.5, 1:2, 1:2.5 at a true 20 percent yield, extraction yield computed from TDS and beverage mass versus TDS and water in.
- Why built: New-domain pass: shot logs often record the water put in, and the extraction-yield formula needs the mass of the liquid in the cup, which differs by what the wet puck retains.
- Design: Beverage out = water in - retention*dose + dissolved solids with retention 2.0 g/g (assumed typical); TDS = solids/out; yield from out must return 0.20 and yield from water in is compared; a ratio rescale by out/water_in is tested as a fix; a 1:1 ristretto arm is the extreme case.
- Got right: Yield from beverage mass returned exactly 0.200 in all nine rows; yield from water in read 0.344 to 0.440, inflated 1.72 to 2.20 times, and 2.80 times at 1:1; rescaling by out/water_in restored 0.200 exactly.
- Where/why it failed: The retention of 2.0 g/g is an assumed value and the model has no channeling or grind effect, so the inflation range is a property of the mass balance, not a measured error on real shots; exact recovery is algebra of the same balance.
- Fix: Weigh the beverage in the cup for the yield calculation, log it beside TDS, and if only water in was recorded, rescale by out over water in rather than reusing the TDS blindly.
- Why this fix: TDS is a share of the beverage, so only the beverage mass converts it to dissolved grams; water in includes water that never left the puck.
- Rule of thumb: Extraction yield equals TDS times beverage mass over dose; using water in instead inflates it 1.72 to 2.20 times at 1:2.5 to 1:1.5 recipes (2.80 at 1:1) because the puck keeps about 2 g water per gram of coffee.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: ideas:ESPRESSO/extraction/extraction-yield-uses-beverage-mass-not-water-in, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, starter-hydration-true-percentage/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The formula EY = TDS × beverage mass / dose is standard and holds as stated, but the inflation range and "exact" restoration are self-confirming outputs of an assumed retention figure and prove nothing about real espresso.
- Hidden assumption: The sandbox's own model (out = water in − 2.0 g/g × dose + solids) is treated as reality, so the rule is circular. The 2.0 g/g retention is assumed rather than measured, the "true" 20 percent yield is an input, and the 1.72 to 2.80 inflation factors fall out of that choice. The prediction passes by construction, and the rescale "restores" 0.20 only because it is the same out/water_in identity run backwards.
- Would prove it wrong: Weigh real shots (dose, water in, beverage out) and measure TDS by refractometer. If retention varies across dose, grind, basket, or pressure profile, or if the puck-to-dose mass balance doesn't close, the inflation factors would differ from 1.72 to 2.20. Evaporation, crema and gas loss, and refractometer error on espresso-range TDS would also show a gap. A measured retention near 1.0 or 3.0 g/g would change the factors by a large margin.
- Break scenario: Rerun the 3×3 grid plus 1:1 with retention swept from 1.0 to 3.0 g/g, and with retention that changes with dose. Hold the true yield at 20 percent and add 0.3 g of loss, plus a ±0.2 TDS-point refractometer error. Then check whether "inflated by more than 1.5 times everywhere" and "restores 0.20 exactly" survive. At retention 1.0 the 1:2.5 inflation should drop to about 1.3 to 1.4 times, which violates the prediction. At retention 3.0 the 1:1 case would give a negative or near-zero beverage mass.

## E565 — empathy gap vs level crowd helping
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [empathy][helping][model][testing]
- What: A deterministic 10x10 grid of in-group/out-group empathy scores was run through three harm-generating worlds (gap-driven, out-level-driven, in-level-driven) to see whether the gap predicts passive harm better than either level, then pooled into a crowd.
- Why built: The kernel says the gap between in- and out-group empathy predicts harm, not a lack of empathy, and a sibling kernel says more bystanders raise the odds someone helps; I wanted to know when each holds.
- Design: Population = every (in,out) pair on a 0..1 grid; harm probability = logistic of the gap, of out-level or of in-level; correlate harm with gap, out and in; then P(at least one of n helps) for n=1,3,10 in the gap world.
- Got right: In the gap world r(gap)=0.95 against -0.67 for out-level, so the gap is the sharper predictor; crowd help rose 0.617 to 0.783 to 0.891 for n=1,3,10, matching the bystander kernel.
- Where/why it failed: In out-level and in-level worlds the gap still correlates 0.70 with harm because it contains each level, so a high gap correlation alone cannot prove the gap is the cause.
- Fix: Compare gap against both raw levels (partial comparison), and treat a gap win as evidence only when it beats the better single level by a clear margin.
- Why this fix: The gap is a linear mix of the two levels, so it is a proxy in any level-driven world; only a margin over the best single level separates the worlds.
- Rule of thumb: A difference score correlating with an outcome is not evidence the difference matters: it must beat each of its components, since it inherits 0.70 correlation from either one alone.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: ideas:EMPATHY/it-is-the-GAP-between-in-group-and-out-group-empathy-that-predicts-harm-not-a-lack-of-empathy, ideas:EMPATHY/the-lab-bystander-effect-is-real-but-in-actual-public-conflicts-someone-intervenes-nine-times-out-of-ten, brainwork/E502
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__empathy-gap-vs-level-crowd-helping.py
- Prediction: Gap r above 0.9 in the gap world; in level-driven worlds gap r stays near 0.7; P(someone helps) rises monotonically with n.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS gap r=0.95 vs out -0.67; level worlds gap r=0.70; crowd help 0.617->0.783->0.891
- Scenarios: 1) gap-driven harm; 2) out-level-driven harm; 3) in-level-driven harm (built to BREAK the gap claim); 4) crowd size n=1,3,10

## E564 — cot order reliability threshold and correlated votes
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [prompt-engineering][reasoning][model][testing]
- What: A closed-form toy of a 6-step problem: a model does k serial steps per forward pass with per-step reliability r (sizes S,M,L,XL), comparing answer-first, reasoning-before-answer and reasoning-after-answer, plus 5-sample majority voting with independent versus shared-root errors.
- Why built: The chain-of-thought kernel says reasoning must precede the answer and that gains scale sharply with model size; I wanted to see which parts a minimal compute model reproduces.
- Design: Answer-first accuracy = r^min(d,k) times a 0.1 guess for each unreachable step; reasoning-before = r^d; reasoning-after equals answer-first; sizes (k,r) = (1,.55),(2,.80),(4,.93),(8,.99); voting uses exact binomial majority, with 30 percent of chains inheriting one shared wrong first step.
- Got right: Order mattered exactly as the kernel says: reasoning written after the answer added 0.0000 at every size, while reasoning before it gave +0.03, +0.26, +0.64 and 0.00 for S, M, L, XL; independent 5-vote majority lifted L from 0.65 to 0.76.
- Where/why it failed: The scaling claim failed in this model: gain is a hump that falls to zero once a single pass holds the whole chain (k at least depth 6), and shared-root votes reached only 0.68; the hump follows from my capacity cap, so it shows a boundary, not real model behaviour.
- Fix: Phrase the rule as order first, size second: put reasoning before the answer, expect the largest gain where the chain exceeds one pass, and count votes only from independent chains.
- Why this fix: Extra reasoning tokens help by adding serial steps, so the benefit is bounded by the shortfall between chain depth and per-pass capacity; correlated samples repeat one root rather than adding evidence.
- Rule of thumb: Reasoning before the answer helps only when the task needs more serial steps than one pass holds (+0.64 at L, +0.00 at XL, depth 6), and votes help only when chains are independent: shared-root 5-votes gave 0.68 versus 0.76.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session.
- Composed: ideas:PROMPT-ENGINEERING/reasoning/chain-of-thought-reasoning-must-precede-the-final-answer, brainwork/E130, brain/E178
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__cot-order-reliability-threshold-and-correlated-votes.py
- Prediction: Reasoning-before gains grow with model size from S to XL, reasoning-after adds nothing, and shared-root voting falls short of independent voting.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL kernel claim of gains growing with size does not hold: gains S +0.03 M +0.26 L +0.64 XL +0.00 at depth 6; order claim holds; 5 votes lift L 0.65->0.76 independent but only 0.68 with a shared root
- Scenarios: 1) four sizes at depth 6 answer-first; 2) same sizes reasoning-before; 3) reasoning-after-answer (built to BREAK the order claim); 4) 5-vote independent; 5) 5-vote with a shared root
- Link: scheduled brain train auto session; session_018vkktVQxraRdjDDGahsw1j

## E563 — syllable warning misses follow the words not the rhyme letters
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][suno-prompting][testing]
- What: Composed the vowel-group syllable warning (budget 9, slack 3) with two-pass lettering on one toy lexicon. On lines of 13 to 15 true syllables the warning missed 48.4 percent (1451 of 3000), and 57.9 percent when the end word was an undercounted word such as poem or quiet; the miss rate depends on the words, and the stanza's rhyme letters did not depend on the flag.
- Why built: The new path pairs two-pass lettering with the syllable-slack lesson; the open question was whether the crowded-line warning and the rhyme letters share a failure source, such as end words.
- Design: Lexicon of 17 words with true counts, eight of them undercounted by a vowel-group counter; 3000 seeded lines per scenario at 13, 14 or 15 true syllables; a lettering function on 4096 four-word end-word stanzas with and without the counter flag.
- Got right: Splitting the miss rate by whether the end word is undercounted showed the warning's blind spot is word-specific and larger at line ends.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that the end-word miss rate would be at least 10 points above the overall rate failed narrowly (57.9 against 48.4, a gap of 9.5 points). The scenario showing letters ignore the flag is true by construction, because the lettering function never reads the flag, so it is not evidence.
- Fix: Do not count the letters-versus-flag scenario as a finding; rely on the miss-rate split, and take the stronger count of true syllables rather than the vowel-group warning when deciding which lines to hyphenate.
- Why this fix: The counter's blind spot comes from hiatus words that the lexicon undercounts, so a count that knows those words fixes it, while the rhyme lettering never reads the count.
- Rule of thumb: A vowel-group warning with slack 3 misses about half of 13 to 15 syllable lines in a lexicon rich in hiatus words and about 58 percent when the end word is one of them; the miss follows the words in the line, so check a few undercounted words before trusting a silent warning.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run; the lexicon is hand-picked with eight undercounted words in seventeen, so the absolute miss rates are toy-model figures and only the gap direction is the finding.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, sandbox-syllable-slack-and-undercount-hide-crowded-lines-from-hyphenate-rule/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The finding that the miss rate follows the words is supported, but the headline numbers depend on an arbitrary toy lexicon, the end-word gap prediction failed (9.5 against 10 points), and the letters-unchanged claim is true by construction, so it adds no evidence.
- Hidden assumption: The 17-word lexicon, with eight of its words undercounted (about 47%), is representative enough that the 48.4% miss rate says something about real text; the rule is really a measurement of the lexicon's hiatus density, and the "about half" figure moves with that mix, which the rule never states.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-running the same warning on a lexicon with 1 or 2 undercounted words in 17, or on real verse samples, and getting a miss rate near 5 to 15 percent or an end-word gap above 10 points. That would show the "about half" and "about 58 percent" figures come from the toy lexicon and not from the vowel-group warning itself. The run already failed its own prediction: the observed 9.5-point gap is under the 10-point threshold, yet the rule of thumb states the 58 percent figure as if the prediction held.
- Break scenario: Build lines in which every word is undercounted (or none is) and plot the miss rate against the undercounted-word share, at slack 3 and at slack 0, 1 and 2. If the miss rate is roughly linear in that share, the rule is a restatement of the lexicon's composition. Also run it at 12 and 16 syllables, because the 13 to 15 band may sit where the slack-3 cutoff happens to bite hardest.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 594b02975267
- Distinct from: sandbox-syllable-slack-and-undercount-hide-crowded-lines-from-hyphenate-rule/E1 found the warning silent at true 12; this measures the miss rate on 13 to 15 syllable lines and how much the end word adds (9.5 points).
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__syllable-warning-misses-follow-the-words-not-the-rhyme-letters.py
- Prediction: The counter misses at least 30 percent of 13 to 15 syllable lines; letters are unchanged by the flag; the miss rate with an undercounted end word is at least 10 points higher than overall.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL miss any-end 48.4%, undercounted-end 57.9%, letters differ 0/4096 (FAIL: gap 9.5 points is under the 10 point threshold; letters scenario true by construction)
- Scenarios: 1) true 13 to 15 syllable lines, any end word; 2) letters with and without the flag (true by construction); 3) BREAK: end word always an undercounted word

## E562 — stutter hook title matcher and end word lettering share one hyphen split fix
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing]
- What: Tested whether the hyphen-split fix for a stutter-hook title matcher also protects two-pass rhyme lettering on the same 8 stutter hooks. It does not carry over: the matcher needs the split (hyphen-kept finds 2 of 8, split 8 of 8), but whole-token and last-segment lettering gave identical letters in 8 of 8 stanzas.
- Why built: The kernel path pairs two-pass lettering with the stutter-hook matcher lesson but they had never been run on one input set; the guess was that hyphenated stutter text breaks both consumers the same way.
- Design: Eight stutter-hook lines with a rhyme partner each; three title matchers (hyphen-kept tokens, hyphen-split tokens, plain substring); a two-pass lettering (perfect rime first, then assonance to resolved groups) under whole-token, last-segment and first-segment end-word judges; a plain-end-word control.
- Got right: Keeping the matcher check and the lettering check on the same hook lines separated the two failure sources cleanly; the first-segment judge was a useful extra contrast, differing from last-segment in 2 of 8.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction (hyphen-kept matcher finds 3 of 8; whole-token lettering differs from last-segment in 6+ of 8) was wrong on both numbers: matcher found 2 of 8, lettering differed in 0 of 8, because a rime read from the end of the string is the same whole or last-segment.
- Fix: Treat the two as separate fixes: split on hyphens in the title matcher; for lettering only guard against a judge that reads the first segment of a hyphenated end word.
- Why this fix: The end-anchored rime already ignores earlier hyphen pieces, so splitting there adds nothing, while the matcher compares whole tokens and needs the split to see the title inside the stutter chain.
- Rule of thumb: Do not assume a hyphen fix transfers between consumers: split hyphens in a title matcher, but test the end-word judge separately, since only a first-segment judge changes the letters on stutter ends.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run (8 hooks, 4 scenarios); the toy rime rule and eight lines are hand-made, not a real lexicon.
- Composed: two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-stutter-hooks-break-a-token-title-matcher/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the matcher half is well supported (2/8 vs 8/8), but the "judge is separate" half rests on a null result over repeated-syllable ends, and the prediction was already off (3/8 predicted vs 2/8 seen, 6/8 lettering difference predicted vs 0/8), so the rule's narrower claim about first-segment is unproven beyond 2 of 8.
- Hidden assumption: Eight stutter hooks with a "last-segment" judge are representative of all hyphenated end words, so identical letters in 8 of 8 means the end-word judge is insensitive to hyphens, when it may only mean these ends share a final segment whose rime already equals the whole-token's rime (e.g. "ba-ba" vs "ba").
- Would prove it wrong: A hyphenated end word whose last segment differs in rime from the whole token (e.g. "run-away" vs "away", or "x-ray") where whole-token and last-segment lettering produce different letters, or a larger sample where the 0/8 difference rate climbs above zero.
- Break scenario: Add a stanza whose stutter end is non-repeating, like "bo-peep" paired with "deep" and "sleep-ing" paired with "ring", so last-segment, whole-token and first-segment judges diverge; the rule's "only first-segment changes letters" claim dies if last-segment also diverges there.

## E561 — reduced form ends keep rhyme but hyphenating them collapses a last segment judge
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing]
- What: Ran reduced-form end words (gonna, wanna) through hyphenation and two-pass lettering together. Reduced ends rhyme as AABB under whole, last and first-segment judges; spelled-out ends (going to) fall to AaAx; hyphenating the reduced ends (gon-na) stays AABB for whole and first-segment judges but collapses to AAAA under a last-segment judge.
- Why built: The reduced-form kernel and the hyphenate-to-slow kernel both rewrite end words, and the two-pass lettering path reads those same words; nobody had run all three on one stanza.
- Design: Four toy stanzas (reduced, expanded, hyphenated reduced, interior-hyphen control) lettered by a two-pass assigner under three end-word judges using a small rime rule for two-syllable -a endings.
- Got right: Writing the prediction first including the AAAA collapse; the interior-hyphen control proved the collapse comes from the end word and not from hyphens elsewhere in the line.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the prediction failed; the limit is that the rime rule and four-word stanzas are toy, so real phonetics could shift the expanded case from AaAx.
- Fix: Write the reduced form you will sing, and when hyphenating to slow a line keep the end word whole or judge rhyme on the joined word, never on the last hyphen segment.
- Why this fix: The collapse comes only from the judge reading the final piece (na) of every hyphenated end, so joining the pieces restores the distinct rimes.
- Rule of thumb: Reduced forms keep a rhyme that the spelled-out words lose; hyphenate them for pacing only if rhyme is read on the joined word, because a last-segment judge turns gon-na/Don-na/wan-na/An-na into AAAA.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run on 4 stanzas and 3 judges; the rime rule is a toy, not a pronunciation dictionary.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — PASS only confirms the toy matches its own rime rule (and the "any judge" claim is untested beyond three hand-picked ones), so the collapse under a last-segment judge is true by construction and the advice "hyphenate only if rhyme is read on the joined word" is a tautology until validated against an independent rhyme source.
- Hidden assumption: The "rule" generalizes from a hand-built toy: the two-syllable -a rime rule and the three judges were authored by the same hand that wrote the stanzas, so "reduced ends rhyme AABB" restates the rime rule's definition rather than testing any real rhyme behavior, and "last-segment judge" is assumed to be a judge anyone would actually use.
- Would prove it wrong: Run it on real or independently written stanzas (e.g., gonna/wanna paired with non-reduced -a words like "Donna" vs "gotta"/"wanta") or with a different rime rule (stress-sensitive, or one that treats -nna vs -na differently), and see reduced ends fail AABB or expanded ends stay rhymed; or show any plausible judge where reduced ends are not AABB, which contradicts the prediction's "under any judge."
- Break scenario: Mixed stanza where reduced ends sit beside near-misses and unreduced -a words (gonna / wanna / sofa / comma / gotta / lotta) under the same three judges, plus a hyphenated end whose last segment is a bare syllable shared by unrelated words (gon-na vs. ba-na-na vs. ca-na), to see whether the AAAA collapse is about hyphenation or simply about the last segment being "na" for everything.

## E560 — join view alone letters stutter and timing hyphen ends while the title matcher needs both views
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing]
- What: The title matcher needs both hyphen views (split for stutter, join for timing hyphens). I tested whether rhyme lettering needs both too. A join-view end-word judge lettered 8 of 8 stanzas as intended (4 stutter, 4 timing-hyphen); a last-segment judge got stutter 4 of 4 but timing-hyphen only 2 of 4. The break case is the exception: a laugh stutter (ha-ha-ha, ho-ho-ho) lettered ABCD under join and AABB under split, because a two-syllable rime rule reads across the repeated pieces.
- Why built: The new path pairs the end-word hyphen lesson with the matcher lesson that stutter and timing hyphens mean opposite things; the open question was whether lettering inherits the matcher's two-view need.
- Design: Eight hand-built four-line end-word stanzas (4 stutter, 4 timing-hyphen), two judges (join, last-segment) with a spelling-based rime rule that reads a final vowel after the coda, and a laugh-stutter break stanza.
- Got right: Splitting stanzas by hyphen kind showed the last-segment judge fails only on timing hyphens, and the break stanza exposed the one place the join view loses.
- Where/why it failed: Three first-run stanzas had intended letters that did not match the spelling rime rule (blue and new, summer and winter, fire and higher), so they were fixture errors that I corrected before the final run; the rule is spelling-based and two-syllable-aware, so the result belongs to this toy rime rule.
- Fix: Judge rhyme on the joined word for ordinary end words and timing hyphens, and strip repeated stutter pieces down to the last piece when the chain repeats the same syllable before applying a multi-syllable rime rule.
- Why this fix: Join is right when the pieces are parts of one word, split is right when the pieces are separate repeated words, and a laugh chain is the second kind that looks like the first.
- Rule of thumb: Unlike the title matcher, rhyme lettering mostly needs the join view (8 of 8 against 6 of 8 for last-segment), but a repeated-syllable stutter chain (ha-ha-ha) breaks the join view under a multi-syllable rime rule, so collapse repeats first.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run; eight stanzas and a toy spelling rime rule only, and three fixtures were corrected after the first run.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, sandbox-title-matcher-stutter-split-vs-timing-hyphen-join/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 8/8 vs 6/8 margin is 2 stanzas from author-built fixtures, the break case contradicts the prediction and its fix ("collapse repeats first") was never tested, so the rule of thumb is half-supported at best.
- Hidden assumption: Eight hand-built stanzas, authored by the same person who wrote both judges and the spelling-based rime rule, are representative of real lyrics, so 8/8 vs 6/8 measures the views and not how the fixtures and rules were tuned to each other.
- Would prove it wrong: Run the same judges on stanzas that someone else wrote or that come from real lyrics, with the rhyme scheme labeled blind. If last-segment matches join on timing hyphens (for example 4/4 once the rime rule is adjusted), or join drops below 8/8 on common cases like "-in'" dropped-g endings, "la-la-la" refrains, or "oh-oh" interjections, the "join mostly wins" claim fails.
- Break scenario: A stanza that ends on a repeated-syllable chain in a position where the rhyme does not hang on the final syllable: "ba-by / may-be / la-la-la / ha-ha-ha". Join gives the chain a single long rime, collapse-repeats then erases the difference between "la-la-la" and "ha-ha-ha", and a real timing hyphen like "i-ron-ic" (to "sonic") must not be collapsed. Run the "collapse repeats first" fix against both. If it merges the laugh chains but also mangles legitimate repeated pieces like "bye-bye" or "no-no", the rule of thumb has no safe form.

## E559 — hyphenating end words leaves letters and syllable warning unchanged so the hint never fires
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][suno-prompting][testing]
- What: Put hyphenated end words through a whole-word two-pass lettering judge and a vowel-group syllable counter (budget 9, slack 3). On 200 twelve-syllable lines, hyphenating the end word left the count unchanged in 200 of 200 and the warning silent (0 before, 0 after); whole-word lettering did not change in 2963 stanzas, while a last-segment judge changed letters in 299 (10.1 percent). A hiatus word was the exception: diamond counts 2 plain and 3 as di-a-mond.
- Why built: The hyphenate-to-slow idea is meant to fix crowded lines, the syllable-slack lesson says the warning stays silent on them, and the end-word lesson says hyphens are safe for lettering only under a whole-word judge; the three had not been run on the same lines.
- Design: Lexicon of 16 words with true syllable counts and hyphenated forms (including gon-na/Don-na/wan-na/An-na); 200 seeded 12-syllable lines for the counter; every seventh 4-word stanza of the lexicon for lettering; a hiatus word as the break case. Three iterations: the counter first stripped hyphens (hid the hiatus effect), the rime rule first ignored a final vowel (hid the last-segment collapse); both were fixed in the script before the final run.
- Got right: Counter and lettering were checked on separate inputs so each effect was seen cleanly; reading the raw hyphenated token in the counter exposed the hiatus count change that stripping had hidden.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that a last-segment judge would differ in at least 20 percent of stanzas failed: it was 10.1 percent, because only the na-ending reduced forms collapse in this lexicon; the sandbox RESULT line is therefore FAIL against that threshold although the main claim held.
- Fix: Keep the hyphenate-to-slow hint keyed off true syllables, not off the warning, judge rhyme on the joined word, and recount any line where a hyphen splits a vowel pair.
- Why this fix: A vowel-group count on a hyphenated token changes only where the hyphen splits adjacent vowels, so for other words neither the warning nor whole-word letters can see the hyphen, and a hint that waits for the warning never fires.
- Rule of thumb: Hyphenating end words does not move a vowel-group warning (0 to 0 on 12-syllable lines) or whole-word letters (0 of 2963 changed); only hiatus words shift the count and only a last-segment judge shifts letters, so key the hint off true syllables.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run; the 16-word lexicon, counter and rime rule are toy models and the 10.1 percent figure depends on how many reduced forms the lexicon holds.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, sandbox-syllable-slack-and-undercount-hide-crowded-lines-from-hyphenate-rule/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The null result on 200 lines is real but was built to be null; the hiatus exception is the only variable that matters, it was tested once on one word, and the FAIL on the 20 percent last-segment threshold means the "last-segment judge" half of the prediction was never confirmed as stated.
- Hidden assumption: The test lexicon and seeded lines stand in for real lyrics, where end words are mostly non-hiatus; the lexicon has about one hiatus word and the 200 lines were built so none had one. "Unchanged 200/200" is partly true by construction. Hyphenation is also assumed to insert only hyphens, never a vowel-group split, and the 12-syllable lines were generated at the budget, so they never test the near-threshold range where a +1 shift matters.
- Would prove it wrong: Run the same comparison on real lines with a natural share of hiatus endings (idea, quiet, poem, real, fire, being, create, radio) at 8 to 10 true syllables, where budget 9 plus slack 3 puts the warning on a knife edge. A warning flip (0 to 1, or 1 to 0) in even a few percent of lines, or any hyphenation that shifts the count by ±1 outside the stated exception, refutes "key the hint off true syllables" as a safe rule.
- Break scenario: A 12-syllable line (the warning is silent at 12 under budget 9 plus slack 3) that ends in a hiatus word such as "diamond", "ocean" or "violet", and is hyphenated as di-a-mond, giving a count of 13 and tripping the warning. The same line ending in "quiet" or "being" with a hyphen is a second case. Add a pair like "gon-na" or "wan-na" that hyphenates to one vowel group per segment, so the count shifts the other way. The rule's own exception is large enough to flip the warning at exactly the length it was tested on.
