## E558 — cron day of month and weekday are or not and when both are restricted
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [cron-scheduling][calendar][testing]
- What: Seeded a new CRON-SCHEDULING domain with a counted example. Over the real 2026 calendar, the crontab line 0 0 13 * 5 fires on 61 days under the documented either-field rule (52 Fridays plus 12 thirteenths minus 3 Friday-13ths) and on 3 under the intuitive both-fields rule, 58 surprise runs a year; day-of-week alone fires 52 and day-of-month alone 12. The break line 0 0 31 * 0 fires 58 days against 1.
- Why built: The newdomain pass needed a domain absent from the kernel list; a scheduler line that restricts both day fields is a real, common mistake, and no stored lesson mentions cron (a query returned only unrelated hits).
- Design: Python datetime over 365 days of 2026; day-of-week mapped to cron numbering (0 is Sunday, 5 is Friday); a fire function with either mode and both mode; four scenarios counted and compared with hand-computed expected values.
- Got right: Predicting the counts from calendar arithmetic (52 plus 12 minus 3) before running, and adding the 31-and-Sunday break line, which shows the surprise grows when the two fields rarely overlap.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the prediction failed. The either-field rule itself is encoded from the crontab(5) documentation, so the sandbox counts what that rule implies and does not prove a running cron daemon behaves that way; no cron was installed to compare.
- Fix: When a cron line restricts both day fields, either accept the either-field behavior, or restrict one field and test the other inside the command (for example run on every Friday and exit unless the day number is 13).
- Why this fix: The scheduler's rule cannot be changed from the line, so the both-fields reading has to be enforced by a guard in the command.
- Rule of thumb: Never read a cron line with both day fields set as and: it is or, so Friday-the-13th fires 61 days in 2026, not 3; restrict one field and guard the other in the command.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: the day counts computed by the sandbox on the real 2026 calendar. Assumed from documentation, not run on a live cron: that classic cron uses the either-field rule.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the counted arithmetic is right, but it tests your model of cron and not cron itself, and the rule of thumb leaves out the star-prefix edge and the dialect differences that decide the real fire count.
- Hidden assumption: Every cron implementation uses the either-field (Vixie) rule when both day fields are restricted, and "restricted" means the field doesn't start with `*`, so the rule is only as portable as that one dialect. Your test only checked a Python model of the rule, not a real scheduler.
- Would prove it wrong: Running the line on a real daemon (or a parser like croniter, systemd timers, Quartz, or Kubernetes CronJob) and getting 3 fires, or a rejected line, instead of 61. The same goes for a form like `*/2` in a day field, where the star-prefix check changes which rule applies.
- Break scenario: `0 0 */2 * 5` and `0 0 1-31 * 5` run against vixie-cron, cronie and a non-Vixie parser. The first starts with `*` and the second restricts the field to a range that covers the whole month. If the either-rule is a literal star check, they split (`*/2` may act as AND with Fridays, `1-31` as OR, giving about every Friday plus 31 days a month, or 365 fires). A rule of thumb that says "both set means OR" won't predict either result.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest c2478d8bc152
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__cron-day-of-month-and-weekday-are-or-not-and-when-both-are-restricted.py
- Prediction: 0 0 13 * 5 fires 61 days under the either rule and 3 under the both rule in 2026; day-of-month alone 12; day-of-week alone 52; 58 surprise runs.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS OR=61 AND=3 dom-only=12 dow-only=52 surprise runs=58; '31 * Sunday' OR=58 AND=1
- Scenarios: 1) both fields restricted, either versus both rule; 2) one field as a star; 3) BREAK: day 31 with Sunday, where the two fields almost never overlap

## E557 — strip hyphens before spelling judge does not make two pass letters exact
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Tested whether stripping hyphens from end words before a spelling rhyme judge makes two-pass rhyme lettering exact. It does not: the judge was wrong in 21.2% of 20736 four-line stanzas whether hyphens were stripped, kept, or judged by last segment only.
- Why built: The hyphenation lesson said hyphens hurt a spelling judge, and the two-pass kernel assumes the judge is right; this checks whether strip-first is enough to combine them.
- Design: 12-word lexicon with perfect-rime and assonance gold groups, hyphenated spellings (wa-ter, to-mor-row, a-go); two-pass lettering (perfect groups claim letters first) run over every 4-word stanza under three judges: whole word stripped, whole word with hyphens, last segment; each compared to gold lettering.
- Got right: The enumeration is exhaustive and deterministic, and it showed the three judges produce identical errors, isolating the cause.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction (0 errors after stripping) was wrong. With last-2-letter keys the hyphen never enters the key, and the mismatches seen involve spelling irregularity (ago vs below vs show); I did not decompose the 21.2% further.
- Fix: Do not rely on hyphen stripping alone to repair a spelling judge; the remaining error sits in the spelling key, which this run did not try to replace.
- Why this fix: The 21.2% error is identical across all three hyphen treatments, so hyphen handling is not the variable here; a different key was not tested.
- Rule of thumb: With last-2-letter keys and final segments of 2+ letters, hyphen handling did not change a spelling rhyme judge's 21.2% stanza error, so check the key before blaming hyphens.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; all numbers are from that run on a small invented lexicon, not real lyrics.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, hyphenation-shortens-the-text-a-spelling-rhyme-judge-reads/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The null result is real for this 12-word set, but it never ran the key-swap that would show the key is the cause, so "check the key" is an untested next step and not a finding.
- Hidden assumption: The 21.2% error comes from the key (last-2-letter spelling), not from hyphens, and that same key would behave identically on any lexicon. The rule generalizes from one 12-word lexicon that was built so assonance words share endings with perfect-rime words.
- Would prove it wrong: A second lexicon with the same 2-letter key and longer final segments (3+ letters, or hyphens falling inside the key window) where stripped, kept and last-segment error rates diverge. A change in error from switching the key to last-3 or to a vowel-nucleus-plus-coda key would also show the key isn't the limiting factor.
- Break scenario: Spell "to-mor-row" and "a-go" so the final segment is 1 letter or the hyphen falls inside the last two characters (e.g. "a-go" → key "-o" vs "go"). Then stripped, kept and last-segment judges disagree, and the rule's condition "final segments of 2+ letters" is the only thing holding the three-way tie.

## E556 — reduced forms at line end change two pass letters under a spelling judge
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][diction][simulation][method]
- What: Wrote line endings in the reduced form that is sung (gonna, wanna, hafta, kinda) and ran two-pass rhyme lettering under a spelling judge. The full forms (going to, want to, have to) all end in the word to, so the judge lettered 57.9% of 1296 stanzas wrong; reduced forms cut that to 23.3%. Hyphenating the reduced forms made no difference.
- Why built: The reduced-form kernel is about syllable counts, but at a line end it also changes which word the rhyme judge sees; this checks that effect with the two-pass kernel and the hyphenation kernel together.
- Design: 6 line-ending tokens with gold sung-rime groups; every 4-line stanza (1296) lettered two-pass under four judges: full forms, reduced stripped of hyphens, reduced with hyphens kept as whole word, reduced judged on last hyphen segment; each compared to gold lettering.
- Got right: Full forms are a false-rhyme trap for a spelling judge (the shared word to), and writing the sung form removes it, which the exhaustive run shows cleanly.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the hyphen treatments would differ was wrong: all three reduced-form judges gave 23.3%. The leftover errors come from the go/know pair, whose spellings differ while the sung rime is the same.
- Fix: Write the sung reduced form at line ends before spelling-based rhyme lettering; do not expect hyphenation to change the result when final segments are two or more letters.
- Why this fix: It removes the shared to ending that falsely merges unrelated rhymes, dropping error from 57.9% to 23.3% in the same stanzas.
- Rule of thumb: Before spelling-based two-pass lettering, rewrite line endings like going to as the sung gonna: it cut wrong stanzas from 57.9% to 23.3% here, while hyphenating the reduced form changed nothing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; numbers come from a six-token invented lexicon, not real lyrics.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 57.9% vs 23.3% gap is real for these 6 tokens, but the 1296 stanzas are only combinations of those 6 (so the sample is much smaller than it looks), 23.3% is still wrong a lot, and the hyphen result is a null (the prediction failed) that can't carry the rule's "hyphenating changed nothing" half.
- Hidden assumption: The gold "sung-rime" grouping is the ground truth for what counts as a correct lettering, and the 57.9%→23.3% gap reflects a real "to"-ending artifact of the spelling judge. It could just as well reflect how the 6 tokens were chosen and grouped, since all 6 are fixed and the gold groups are defined by the same author.
- Would prove it wrong: A run on line endings that aren't reduced-form pairs (ordinary words, or full forms not ending in "to") where the reduced rewrite doesn't lower the error rate, or a spelling judge that handles the "to" collision (for example, one that ignores a shared final function word) and closes the gap without any rewrite. A floor of 23.3% that doesn't move would also say the rewrite fixed one failure mode and left a larger one untouched.
- Break scenario: Swap in 6 different tokens, including reduced forms that spell-collide with unrelated rhymes (gotta/wanna/hafta/kinda against real words like data, Donna, alma) and full forms that don't end in "to" (kind of, out of), then re-letter the stanzas against gold. If reduced forms still win by a wide margin the rule generalizes; if the margin collapses or flips, it was an artifact of this token set.

## E555 — front shortening keeps two pass letters that end truncation and last segment judging lose

- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][suno][simulation][method]
- What: Compared three ways to shorten rushed lyric lines on two-pass rhyme lettering of 4096 stanzas: cutting from the front kept the lettering exact (0 wrong) while shortening every line, cutting the line end broke it in 91.2%, and hyphenating end words kept the lettering but shortened no line in word count (0%).
- Why built: The shorten-from-the-front lesson kept rhyme shape but never ran the two-pass lettering, and the hyphenation lesson found a last-segment judge breaks lettering; this joins all three.
- Design: 8 end words (4 hyphenatable) with gold rime groups, 9 to 12 word lines, all 4096 four-line stanzas, budget of 6 words; each shortening method judged by a whole-word key and a last-segment key against the gold lettering of the unshortened stanza.
- Got right: Front-cutting leaves the final word untouched, so the rime key cannot change, and the exhaustive run confirms 0 of 4096 wrong under both judges while truncation loses the rhyme word.
- Where/why it failed: I predicted the last-segment judge would mislabel over 10% of hyphenated stanzas, but it got 0 wrong because every final segment here has 3 or more letters; the earlier 27.3% needs shorter final segments, which this lexicon lacked.
- Fix: Shorten rushed lines from the front; do not truncate line ends; treat hyphenation as a pacing tool, not a length cure, and keep final hyphen segments long enough for the judge key.
- Why this fix: Only the front cut both shortens the line and leaves the rhyme word, and therefore the lettering, unchanged.
- Rule of thumb: When a rushed line must be shorter and its rhyme scheme must stay lettered the same, cut from the front: 0 of 4096 stanzas changed, versus 91.2% when the line end was truncated.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; numbers come from an eight-word invented lexicon with synthetic filler lines.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-shorten-rushed-lines-keep-the-rhyme-word/E1

The 91.2% truncation failure is a real but unsurprising result, and the hyphenation scenario's own prediction failed.
- Hidden assumption: Rhyme lettering is determined only by the line-final word, and front-cutting never touches it. That makes "0 wrong" true by construction, since the keyed word is never altered, and the claim also assumes that "shorter" means fewer words rather than fewer syllables, beats or time.
- Would prove it wrong: Run the same design with a budget small enough that front-cutting removes the whole line except the end word (or deletes it), or judge by a real phonetic rime key (CMU dict) on real lyrics where repeated or enjambed end words cross the cut. Any nonzero front/whole rate would refute the rule, and a front-cut that matches 0% only because the end word is untouched would show the test is vacuous.
- Break scenario: A line where the rhyme-carrying word is not last (a trailing "yeah", "baby" or an echo tag), or where the sense is front-loaded (the subject and verb sit in the first words), so front-cutting keeps the lettering but breaks meaning and meter. Also hyphenation: the 0% shortening in word count is an artifact of the metric (hyphenated words still count as one word), and the failed over-10% last-segment prediction suggests the hyphenated words' final segments were built to share rimes, so that test did not measure what it claimed.

## E554 — seeded rng full state save vs seed count
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][determinism][testing][state]
- What: A Python sfc32 sandbox that saves the generator two ways, as its four state words and as a seed plus roll count, and restores each after 10, 1000 and 100000 rolls, plus a canonical-hash check and a lockstep desync check.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel, the replay-fingerprint kernel and the-game-prologue/E1 are linked only by prose; this re-verifies that link by running the claims instead of quoting them.
- Design: sfc32 with 32-bit words; restore counts how many rolls it had to replay; two logically equal dicts with different key order are hashed by raw JSON dumps and by sorted-key JSON; two clients restore the same snapshot and one rolls once extra.
- Got right: Both save styles gave identical next-5 rolls at every N, but state-word restore cost 0 rolls versus N for seed plus count (100000 at the largest); raw-order hashing disagreed on equal states while sorted-key hashing agreed.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing refuted the claims; the sandbox is Python sfc32, not the JavaScript runtime in the original entry, so the integer-key reordering rule of JS objects and the transcendental Math divergence were not exercised.
- Fix: Save the generator's full state words inside the authoritative state, hash with sorted keys, and keep any extra roll out of one client's path.
- Why this fix: Restore cost stays constant and equal states hash equal, while one stray roll desynchronized the stream, showing the single-stream discipline is what keeps clients in lockstep.
- Rule of thumb: Save sfc32's four state words rather than a seed plus count (0 versus N replayed rolls, same output), hash authoritative state with sorted keys, and treat any single extra roll on one client as a desync.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; JavaScript key-order and Math function behavior are taken from the existing entry and were not re-run here.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/replay-fingerprint, the-game-prologue/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sandbox shows only that state words restore faster and that sorted-key hashing is stable, and it never tests the claims about word-layout fragility, the pre-restore check, or what counts as a desync; the PASS comes from a tautological setup (same code, same machine, five rolls).
- Hidden assumption: Cost is measured only as replay count, so "0 versus N rolls" is assumed to be the whole tradeoff. That ignores that state words are opaque, tied to sfc32 and its word layout, and unverified against the seed, while seed plus count stays portable and auditable. It also assumes both clients start in the same snapshot and run the same code path, with no other consumers of the generator.
- Would prove it wrong: A restore from the four state words that matches for five rolls but diverges later. Examples are a snapshot taken mid-warmup, words not masked to 32 bits after a JSON or int round-trip, or a version change in sfc32's constants or rotation. The seed plus count path would reproduce correctly in each case. Equally damaging is a replay of 100000 rolls costing microseconds, so the savings never matter.
- Break scenario: Two clients restore the same snapshot, and one makes an extra roll for something unrelated, such as a cosmetic effect. The rule says to treat that as a desync, but the stream shift is only harmful if that roll feeds authoritative state. Separately, save a state whose words came from a different implementation (JS vs Python with signed 32-bit ints) and restore it. The five-roll check passes only if the signedness matches.

- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: A sandbox that turns the rhyme-scheme-shape kernel into two numbers (stopping points, meaning lines that rhyme with the line just before, and mean distance back to a rhyme partner) and checks how often a last-segment judge on hyphenated end words changes the shape class over all 4096 stanzas of an 8-word lexicon.
- Why built: The emotional-motion kernel assumes the scheme shape is read correctly; the hyphenation and two-pass entries show a last-segment judge can mislabel it, so I wanted to know if that corrupts the stop count the kernel talks about.
- Design: Whole-word key versus last-segment key (feminine words borrow and tomorrow end in row, which the last-segment judge merges with plain ow words), letters relabeled by first appearance, stops counted over lines 2 to 4, gap measured as distance to the nearest earlier partner; AABB, ABAB, ABBA and a two-unrhymed-then-couplet shape built from the lexicon.
- Got right: AABB gave 2 stopping points against 0 for ABAB, with mean gaps 1.0 and 2.0, as the kernel's stable-versus-flowing contrast says; the last-segment judge changed the stop count of 1248 of 4096 stanzas (1760 changed shape) and 0 of 1296 once feminine words were removed.
- Where/why it failed: Stop count and gap cannot tell ABBA from ABAB (gap 2.0 for both), so the kernel's claim that ABBA is the open, wistful one is not captured by these two numbers; also the lexicon is invented and the open/stable labels are not measured emotion.
- Fix: Read the scheme shape with a whole-word judge before using stop counts, and add a nesting measure (a rhyme pair enclosing another) if ABBA must be separated from ABAB.
- Why this fix: The mislabeling came only from feminine words whose stress is before the last segment, and the tie between ABBA and ABAB shows these two numbers lack a way to see enclosure.
- Rule of thumb: A stop-count reading of rhyme shape is only as good as the rhyme judge: a last-segment judge changed it in 1248 of 4096 stanzas (0 without feminine endings), and stop count with mean gap cannot separate ABBA from ABAB.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the rhyme keys are hand-assigned for invented words and no listener or emotion data was used, so the kernel's emotional claims are untested here.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the prediction was refuted on its own ABBA/ABAB claim (gap 2.0 vs 2.0), and the headline 1248/4096 measures how often the judges disagree, not which one is correct, on a lexicon built to make them disagree.
- Hidden assumption: The 1248/4096 figure is a property of a judge, not of the lexicon and enumeration: the "rule" generalizes from a hand-built 8-word set where feminine words were chosen to trigger the merge, so the count mostly restates the share of stanzas that contain borrow or tomorrow, and "rhyme judge quality" is never measured against any ground truth for which judge is right.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with a lexicon whose feminine fraction differs (say 2 of 8 versus 4 of 8) or with a feminine word whose last segment matches nothing else. If the changed-stanza count tracks the combinatorial share of feminine-containing stanzas rather than anything about the judge, or drops to 0 despite feminine words being present, the rule is arithmetic about the lexicon, not about stop-count readings.
- Break scenario: Give the lexicon a feminine pair that rhymes with itself under both judges (borrow/tomorrow as partners). The shape class stays unchanged while the judge is visibly "wrong" about the underlying words. Add stanzas where the last-segment judge splits rather than merges (a word with a hyphen whose last segment differs from its true rhyme). Then check whether stop count moves in the opposite direction, which would show "changes the shape class" does not equal "degrades the reading."

- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__rhyme-shape-stop-count-under-hyphen-judge.py
- Prediction: AABB has more stopping points and a smaller gap than ABAB; ABBA has a larger gap than AABB; the last-segment judge changes stop counts in some stanzas only when feminine words are present; ABBA and ABAB are separable by gap.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS last-segment judge changes the stop count of 1248/4096 stanzas, 0 without feminine words; AABB stops 2 vs ABAB 0; ABBA gap 2.0 vs ABAB 2.0. The last part of the prediction was wrong: gap does not separate ABBA from ABAB.

## E552 — ladder four to one angle friction demand
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ladder-safety][statics][simulation][method]
- What: A deterministic statics model of a leaning ladder (80 N ladder, 800 N climber, frictionless wall) giving the floor friction coefficient needed at each climber position for the 4-to-1 setup angle of 75.96 degrees and for 65 and 80 degrees.
- Why built: Seeding a new LADDER-SAFETY domain from a real setup rule; nothing in the system covered ladders, so this is an isolated seed with no adjacent kernel or lesson exercised.
- Design: Torque about the foot gives wall force H = (Wl/2 + P s) cot(theta); floor normal N = Wl + P; required friction mu = H/N, tabulated for climber fraction s from 0 to 1, then compared with three assumed surface coefficients (0.6, 0.3, 0.1) and inverted for the smallest safe angle.
- Got right: Demand rose with climber height (0.011 at the foot, 0.239 at the top at 4:1) and fell with a steeper ladder (0.445 at 65 degrees); dry and wet tile held at 4:1, the 0.1 surface slipped from half way up; minimum top-of-climb angles were 57.8, 72.6 and 84.0 degrees.
- Where/why it failed: I expected a heavy ladder with a light climber to peak elsewhere than the top; it still peaked at the top (0.10, 0.125, 0.15), so the break scenario did not break it. The model ignores wall friction, flex and lateral load, and the surface coefficients are assumptions, not measured values.
- Fix: Set the foot at height divided by 4, and where the floor is wet or unknown use the minimum-angle formula or tie off the top rather than trusting the rule alone.
- Why this fix: The 4:1 margin on wet tile was only 1.26 times in this model, so the rule is adequate for ordinary floors and thin on slippery ones.
- Rule of thumb: At the 4-to-1 setup (75.96 degrees) the floor must supply friction 0.24 with the climber at the top, so it is safe on dry or wet tile in this model but slips on a surface of 0.1; check the top-of-climb demand, not the foot.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the surface friction coefficients and weights are assumed round values and the 4-to-1 rule itself is quoted from common practice and was not checked against a safety standard.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__ladder-four-to-one-angle-friction-demand.py
- Prediction: Friction demand rises monotonically with climber height and is lower at 4:1 than at 65 degrees; dry and wet tile hold at 4:1 and a 0.1 surface fails; a heavy ladder with a light climber peaks somewhere other than the top.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 4:1 angle 76.0 deg needs mu 0.239 at the top and 0.011 at the foot; min safe top angle {'dry concrete': 57.8, 'wet tile': 72.6, 'wet ice-like': 84.0}; slips only on ice-like (mu 0.1). The heavy-ladder peak prediction was wrong (peak at the top, 0.15).
- Scenarios: 1) climber positions 0 to 1 at 4:1, 65 and 80 degrees; 2) three surface coefficients and the inverse minimum angle; 3) BREAK: heavy ladder with a light climber, expecting the peak to move.

## E551 — hyphenated end words two pass letters feminine rhyme
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: An exhaustive sandbox over all 4096 four-line stanzas drawn from an 8-word lexicon (two feminine two-segment words, a hyphenated masculine word, a hyphenated light word and plain words), lettered by the two-pass method under a whole-word judge and under a last-segment judge.
- Why built: To compose the hyphenation finding, the two-pass assonance-hiding finding and the two-pass letter-assignment kernel with my own lexicon, and to find which property of hyphenated words actually causes the last-segment misletters.
- Design: Pass 1 gives one letter per perfect-rhyme key; leftover single lines whose vowel matches a resolved group count as hidden assonance. The whole-word judge keys the stressed tail of the full word; the last-segment judge keys only the final hyphen segment. Letters are compared after relabeling by first appearance.
- Got right: The last-segment judge mislettered 2256 of 4096 stanzas (55.1%) and 0 of 1296 once the two feminine words were removed, so the misletters came entirely from feminine endings whose stressed vowel sits before the last segment, not from hyphenation as such.
- Where/why it failed: My lexicon is tiny and chosen, so 55.1% is not comparable to the 27.3% in the earlier entry; also the check that the whole-word judge never merges across keys is true by construction and proves nothing. Assonance stayed hidden under both judges (50.2% whole word, 30.3% last segment).
- Fix: Key a hyphenated end word by its whole stressed tail, and treat words whose stress falls before the last segment as the case to test; keep listing leftover assonant lines separately after pass 2.
- Why this fix: Zero misletters appeared once those words were excluded, so the stressed-tail key is the part that matters and the hyphen is incidental.
- Rule of thumb: A last-segment rhyme judge fails on hyphenated end words only when the stress sits before the last segment (here 2256 of 4096 stanzas, 0 without such words); key the full stressed tail, and keep reporting assonance separately because hyphenation does not remove it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the rhyme keys are hand-assigned for 8 invented-lexicon words, not derived from a pronunciation dictionary.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-tooling/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 0-after-removal result is nearly tautological, because the removed words are the ones that define the failure. The 55.1% and 50.2% describe a hand-built 8-word lexicon, not a rate, and the rule is untested on stress variation, secondary stress or real orthography.
- Hidden assumption: Stress position is a fixed property of each lexicon word that the stanza generator never varies, so "stress before the last segment" is a lexicon artifact (the two feminine words were put there by design), not a measured property of hyphenated words in general.
- Would prove it wrong: A lexicon of hyphenated end words that are all final-stressed (or a real corpus sample) where the last-segment judge mislettered about 0%, or one where the whole-word judge also mislettered because the stress tail itself was keyed wrongly. The first shows the 55.1% reflects the invented words, not the rule. The second shows the baseline was never validated.
- Break scenario: Swap the feminine pair for two hyphenated masculine words whose final segments differ in vowel but whose stressed penultimate segments rhyme (e.g. "star-light" and "star-bright" against "far-flight"), and add a hyphenated word with secondary stress on the last segment. If the last-segment judge stays correct while the rule predicts failure, or errs where the rule predicts safety, the "stress sits before the last segment" condition is the wrong variable.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 26fc1f241c69
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__hyphenated-end-words-two-pass-letters-feminine-rhyme.py
- Prediction: The last-segment judge mislettered a nonzero share of stanzas only when feminine multi-segment words are in the lexicon, and the whole-word judge still hides assonance in more than 20% of stanzas.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS last-segment judge mislettered 55.1% of 4096 stanzas, 0 once feminine multi-segment pair removed; assonance still hidden in 50.2% under whole-word judge
- Scenarios: 1) all 4096 stanzas, both judges, letters compared; 2) assonance hidden counts under each judge; 3) BREAK: lexicon with the feminine pair removed (1296 stanzas), expecting the last-segment judge to turn safe.

## E550 — ddmin with lazy positive control draft
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [debugging][isolation][testing][method]
- What: A sandbox where a poll fails for two independent sufficient reasons (a broken predicate and a starved capture layer), reduced by ddmin and then judged by a positive control built at full versus lazy fidelity.
- Why built: To run the ddmin single-cause stall together with the positive-control fidelity lesson and the draft capture-starvation bug in one model, and see whether they combine as the entries claim.
- Design: Items a,b,P,c,S,d where P breaks the predicate (needs a field nobody emits) and S starves the capture layer (emits no fields); ddmin with subset and complement steps; then a predicate checked against a synthetic state with all real fields versus only the id field.
- Got right: ddmin returned only P, deleting P and re-running returned only S, so the two causes surfaced one at a time; the full-fidelity control passed a healthy predicate.
- Where/why it failed: The lazy control (id only) made a healthy predicate fail, the same verdict a genuinely broken predicate gives, so a ddmin run judged through it would blame the predicate even when only capture was starved.
- Fix: Build the control from the real upstream output fields before using it as an oracle, and delete each found culprit and re-run ddmin until the reduced repro passes.
- Why this fix: The wrong blame came from the control missing a field the predicate checks, and the stall came from each cause being sufficient alone; the fix addresses each directly.
- Rule of thumb: When ddmin returns one culprit, delete it and re-run, and check that the positive control carries every field the predicate reads, because a thin control reproduces a broken-predicate verdict on a healthy one.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; real-world pipelines with partial causes or flaky oracles were not modeled.
- Composed: ddmin-minimal-repro-shrinks-single-cause-but-stalls-on-jointly-sufficient-and-needs-positive-control/E1, sandbox-combined-august-10-draft-positive-control-fidelity/E1, draft/E9
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The sandbox shows two points that are true by construction (it stalls on one of two sufficient causes, and a thin control misleads), but the rule says "every field" and the test only varies field presence, so it doesn't show that this is enough for a control to be faithful, and it doesn't show the delete-and-re-run loop holds past two independent causes.
- Hidden assumption: Deleting the ddmin culprit and re-running isolates the remaining cause, which assumes the causes are independent and additive (no interaction, no masking, no flaky ordering), and that the control's "all real fields" set is knowable, since the sandbox hand-picked it knowing P reads one field.
- Would prove it wrong: A case where deleting the first culprit makes ddmin return a non-cause or nothing (the causes interact, or the poll fails nondeterministically), or where a control carrying every field the predicate reads still falsely blames a healthy predicate because it differs in some other dimension (timing, ordering, types, field values rather than field presence).
- Break scenario: Three causes where P and S are each sufficient but a third, C, fails only when P is absent (a masked cause), and where the predicate also reads a field whose value must be non-null. The control is given every field name, with placeholder values (e.g. empty strings). Delete-and-re-run then reports S and stops, or misses C. The "faithful" control still fails a healthy predicate, because it matches on presence and not on values.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 05ee27cce6d2
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__ddmin-with-lazy-positive-control-draft.py
- Prediction: ddmin returns exactly one of the two causes (P first), a re-run after deleting it returns the other, and the lazy control marks a healthy predicate as failing while the faithful one does not.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS ddmin stalls on one of two causes (['P'] then ['S']); lazy control blames a healthy predicate. Faithful control with healthy predicate: True; lazy: False.
- Scenarios: 1) ddmin on two independent causes then delete and re-run; 2) faithful versus lazy control with the predicate broken; 3) BREAK: healthy predicate judged through a lazy control (false blame appears).
- Link: scheduled brain train run, 2026-10-20; session_01AxvhKMfKUmYVr8Ree8rqE7

## E549 — damage cap band and team window
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [rpg][combat][balance][testing]
- What: A small deterministic duel model with a percent-of-defender-max-HP cap per hit, a steady skill and a burst skill, run across weak/mid/strong attacker bands, plus a 3-attacker vs 1 fight with the cap divided or not.
- Why built: To compose the team-fight cap kernel with the per-band diversity kernel and see whether the burst niche loss and the cap-division effect reproduce in one shared model.
- Design: Defender max HP 100; steady deals base per turn; burst deals 3x base every third turn and half base between; cap = fraction x 100 per hit; wins decided by turns-to-kill across 9 attacker bases in three bands; cap swept 0.05-1.0.
- Got right: The burst skill's strong-band win (1 of 3 uncapped) vanished at every cap below 1.0; dividing the cap among 3 attackers moved the 3v1 kill from 4 turns to 10, matching the 1v1 time, so team size is erased by the division.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel says the aggregate stays flat while the niche vanishes. Here the aggregate burst-win count fell 7 -> 5 at cap 0.45 and no cap kept it equal to uncapped while the strong band was lost, so flatness needs a tie-win in an unaffected band the model did not provide.
- Fix: Report burst wins per band alongside the aggregate, and only call the aggregate flat after checking a band that still gives the burst skill a tie or win.
- Why this fix: The aggregate changed in this model even though the niche was gone, so the aggregate alone neither proves nor rules out the loss; the per-band table did show it at every cap.
- Rule of thumb: With a per-hit percent-HP cap, tabulate burst wins per ratio band and re-run the fight at each team size with the cap divided; in this model the strong band was lost at every cap under 1.0 and a divided cap made 3v1 take as long as 1v1.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the generalization beyond this toy damage model is assumed and was not tested.
- Composed: ideas:RPG/team-fight-damage-cap-doesnt-generalize, ideas:SYSTEM/damage-cap-can-erase-a-burst-skills-niche-while-diversity-metric-stays-flat, brainwork/E296, brainwork/E480
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the PASS comes from one hand-picked parameter set, and the prediction was half wrong (aggregate wasn't flat), so the rule of thumb should be called a single-configuration observation until it survives variation in multiplier, cycle length and HP.
- Hidden assumption: Hits land at the cap's binding point, so a 3x burst is clipped to fraction×100 while the steady skill stays under it. The model also treats a hit as unmitigated damage with no armor, no healing, no variance, and a fixed 100 HP defender. The rule treats the strong band as "lost" because of the cap, but that outcome comes from these particular constants (3x multiplier, every-third-turn timing, 9 bases) and not from the cap mechanism.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with the burst multiplier, cycle length or defender HP changed (say 2x every second turn, or HP 500) and find the strong band still wins at caps below 1.0, or the divided-cap 3v1 ttk landing well below 1v1's 10 turns. Either result would show the "lost at every cap" and "3v1 equals 1v1" findings depend on the chosen numbers, not on the cap.
- Break scenario: Keep the 3x/every-third-turn burst, but make the strong-band bases large enough that steady alone kills in 2 turns while the cap sits at 0.5. Both skills are then clipped to 50 per hit and take the same 2 turns, so the burst advantage disappears at that cap. Then add a 4th attacker with a divided cap of 0.5/4. Per-attacker damage drops below the steady skill's base, and ttk should exceed 10 turns, which would show that dividing the cap has no sensible floor. The reported "ttk=10 for divided" suggests the cap was divided by 3 and the result happens to coincide with 1v1.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 2d9b25450603
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__damage-cap-band-and-team-window.py
- Prediction: Burst strong-band wins go to 0 at caps below 1.0; divided-cap 3v1 time-to-kill equals or exceeds 1v1 (10 turns); aggregate stays flat at some cap while the niche is lost.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS niche_lost=True 3v1 ttk undivided=4 divided=10 flat_but_lost_caps=0. The aggregate-flat part of the prediction was wrong: aggregate burst wins fell 7 -> 5 -> 3 -> 1 as the cap tightened.
- Scenarios: 1) four caps, per-band vs aggregate wins; 2) 3v1 with undivided vs divided cap vs 1v1; 3) cap sweep 0.05-1.0 for mid and strong band wins (the mid band is the window check); 4) BREAK: search for a cap with aggregate equal to uncapped yet the strong niche gone (found none).

## E548 — ad batch ceiling similarity and mislabelled axis
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ads][batching][simulation][method]
- What: A deterministic fake-ad batch builder with 16 engine-skeleton slots, 6 tropes, a per-trope cap R and a variable number of usable swap axes, measuring batch size, distinct cells and mean pair similarity (10 kit slots, 1 engine slot, 1 trope slot, 4 fresh slots).
- Why built: To run the batch ceiling lesson, the source-check lesson about a renamed axis and the engine-first similarity lesson together, and see whether filling the batch to its ceiling hurts similarity or whether a lost axis lowers the ceiling.
- Design: Videos take the 16 engine-skeleton slots in order, each placed in a trope under the cap R with a distinct cell index inside the trope; similarity is the mean share of identical slots over all pairs, with the kit fixed or with 3 kit slots rotated; usable axes set to 5, 4 and 2.
- Got right: Batch size came out 6, 12, 16, 16 at trope caps 1, 2, 3, 6, matching the ceiling formula; losing one axis (4 usable) changed no size, so the mislabelled axis does not bind; going from R=1 to R=3 raised mean similarity by only 0.0073, while rotating 3 kit slots cut it by 0.188.
- Where/why it failed: The ceiling formula only holds while usable axes are at least the per-trope cap: at 2 usable axes the batch stuck at 12 for R of 3 and 6, so the formula needs a minimum on axes. The 16-slot structure and kit size are modeling assumptions from the earlier lessons, not platform data.
- Fix: Size the batch as min(16, 6 x min(R, usable axes)); fill to the ceiling without worrying about similarity, and spend variety on rotating the kit.
- Why this fix: The trope slot is one of sixteen and only same-trope pairs add to it, so filling the batch moves the score about 0.007, while the kit slots set it.
- Rule of thumb: A fake-ad batch is min(16, 6 x min(trope cap, usable axes)): one lost axis changed nothing, two lost axes capped it at 12, and filling the batch to 16 added 0.0073 to pair similarity versus 0.188 saved by rotating 3 kit slots.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; slot counts and the idea that a mislabelled axis acts as a duplicate usable axis are assumptions from the named lessons, and no real platform similarity score was measured.
- Composed: batch-ceiling-trope-cap/E1, fake-ad-kernel-source-check/E1, engine-first-assignment-barely-moves-ad-batch-similarity-the-fixed-kit-dominates-and-a-mislabelled-axis-rides-along/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The sizes match the formula on three axis counts, but the 0.0073 versus 0.188 similarity comparison is a single fixture with fixed slot counts (10 kit, 1 engine, 1 trope, 4 fresh), and the "one lost axis changed nothing" claim only holds because 4 axes still cover 3 cells per trope.
- Hidden assumption: The formula min(16, 6 × min(cap, axes)) assumes every trope can fill all of its cell slots, so the ceiling depends only on how many distinct cells a trope has. That holds only if cells equal usable axes and the same count applies to all 6 tropes. Nothing here checks that, and the lost axis is "the renamed label," which may be a different kind of axis from the ones left.
- Would prove it wrong: A run with 3 usable axes and cap 6 that gives a size other than 16. For example, 15 because one trope has only 2 distinct cells, or a size above 12 with 2 axes. Both would show the cells-per-trope term is not what limits the batch. Rerunning with a different set of 4 axes (not the same renamed one) and getting different sizes would show the rule is about which axes are lost, not how many.
- Break scenario: Use 3 usable axes with cap 6, where the axes are binary or otherwise low-cardinality, so distinct cells per trope is 2^3 = 8 in theory but only 3 once you require each cell to differ in at least 2 slots. Also run 5 usable axes where 2 are correlated and so add no new cells. The formula predicts 16 for both. Separately, change the engine count from 16 to 20 and check that the "6 ×" term is really the trope count and not a coincidence of the fixture.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 6ccad1f2126b

## E547 — tire rotation cross pattern equalizes only when wear gaps add
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tire-rotation][maintenance][simulation][method]
- What: Seeding the new TIRE-ROTATION domain: in an exact-fraction model of a front-drive car, a diagonal cross rotation brought four tires to equal wear (spread 0 over 10 intervals) only when the front-rear wear gap and the right-left gap add; a straight front-back swap left a 2.0 spread and no rotation left 12.0.
- Why built: The domain had no records; a real wear question (which rotation pattern evens wear on a front-drive car on a crowned road) is deterministic enough to sandbox.
- Design: Four tires with per-interval wear by position (FL 2.0, FR 2.2, RL 1.0, RR 1.2), three rotation patterns, 10 intervals, Fractions arithmetic, then a symmetric case and a non-additive case built to break the cross pattern.
- Got right: Predicted cross 0, straight 2.0 and none 12.0 for the additive case, and straight 0 when only the front-rear gap exists; all matched.
- Where/why it failed: Predicted the cross pattern would stay perfect for any rates; with FR at 2.4 (gaps not additive) it left a spread of 1.0, and the straight swap 3.0, so cross is not universal.
- Fix: Choose cross when the right side wears faster as well as the front, but expect a residual spread unless the two gaps add; check the diagonal pair sums, not just the pattern.
- Why this fix: Under a cross rotation a tire alternates between two diagonal positions, so equal wear needs the two diagonal pair sums (FL plus RR, FR plus RL) to match.
- Rule of thumb: In the three rate cases tested, a cross rotation evened four tires (spread 0 over 10 intervals) when the diagonal wear-rate pair sums were equal and left 1.0 when they were not; a straight swap evened them only with equal left and right rates.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the wear rates are invented, so no real tire or road was measured.
- Composed: N/A
- Polarity: compatible

## E546 — rejoined hyphenated end words let two pass case survive where one pass mushes

- Why this fix: A one-pass merge of a resolved pair with a stray assonance pair can keep the letter count equal while attaching the wrong lines, so only the grouping exposes it.
- Rule of thumb: Rejoin hyphenated end words and letter in two passes; on 17984 mixed stanzas one-pass regrouped the lines 44.4 percent of the time, and judge any such tool by line grouping, not letter count.

The hyphen result is also treated as evidence, though rejoining before judging makes hyphenated and plain input identical by construction.

## E545 — reduce then hyphenate keeps whole word letters except reduced end words
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Sandbox chaining three lessons on rushed Suno lines: reduce going to to gonna before a bare verb, hyphenate over-budget end words, then letter the stanza with a whole-word rhyme judge. Run over 1296 exhaustive 4-line stanzas.
- Why built: The new-half pick paired the hyphenate-to-slow kernel and the two-pass lettering lesson with the reduced-form kernel, which had never been tested alongside them.
- Design: Rime dictionary judge keyed on the whole rejoined word, mid-line going to in every line, reduction guarded against a following determiner, hyphenation applied when counted syllables exceed 5, then two-pass lettering before and after.
- Got right: Predicted letters unchanged 1296 of 1296 and exactly 1.0 syllable saved per line; both held, and the going-to-the guard left that line untouched.
- Where/why it failed: Predicted the end-position case (a line ending in going to) would change the rhyme word and the letters; it did not, because the bare-verb guard needs a following word, so the end word stayed to.
- Fix: Keep the guard that reduces only before a following bare verb, and treat a line ending in going to as unreduced, so end words and letters stay stable.
- Why this fix: Letters depend only on end words, so a reduction rule that never touches the final word cannot disturb lettering, and the guard gives that for free.
- Rule of thumb: Reducing going to to gonna mid-line before hyphenating end words leaves two-pass letters unchanged under a whole-word judge; the three combine cleanly as long as the reduction never rewrites a line-final word.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the real Suno delivery effect was not tested, only the counting and lettering logic.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — 1296/1296 on mid-line stanzas is close to tautological under a whole-word judge. The one scenario that could have falsified the rule didn't fail as predicted, so the sandbox may be inert rather than the rule robust.
- Hidden assumption: A reduction touching only mid-line "going to" can't alter rhyme letters because the judge reads only the line-final word. That holds only if the judge is blind to everything else, and the sandbox's dictionary and stanzas were built so it is.
- Would prove it wrong: A stanza where reducing a mid-line "going to" shifts the syllable count past the 5-syllable threshold, so hyphenation fires on a different end word and the letters change. Equally, a real (non-exhaustive) corpus where letters move even though the reduction never touched a line-final word.
- Break scenario: Lines ending in "going to" (reduced to "gonna") on a rhyme-pair partner, scored by a judge that sees the rejoined word, or by a real rhyme engine rather than the dictionary. The observed "changed letters=0" is suspect: you predicted a change, got none, and wrote the prediction off as "came out wrong" instead of asking why the break case failed to break. That points to a rigged test where "gonna" and "going to" land in the same Rime key, so it shows nothing. Test it with an end word whose rhyme class actually differs ("gonna" vs "to") and a hyphenation that triggers after the reduction.

## E544 — ladder four to one rule needs floor friction of about 0 24 at the top
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ladder-safety][statics][simulation][method]
- What: Seeding the new LADDER-SAFETY domain: in a rigid-body statics model (frictionless wall, floor friction mu, 800 N climber, 100 N ladder) the 4:1 setup rule (75.96 degrees) keeps the ladder from slipping with the climber at the top only if floor friction is at least 0.236; at mid-ladder the threshold falls to 0.125.
- Why built: The domain had no records, and the 4:1 rule is a real, widely taught rule whose friction assumption can be computed instead of recited.
- Design: Moments about the foot plus horizontal balance give a safe condition tan(angle) at least (W*s + Wl/2) / (mu*(W+Wl)); solve for the threshold mu by bisection at s=1 and s=0.5, and check a heavier 1500 N climber.
- Got right: Predicted the rule is safe on high-friction floors and fails on slick ones; mu 0.5, 0.4 and 0.3 stay safe, mu 0.2, 0.15 and 0.1 slip at the top.
- Where/why it failed: I predicted the top-step threshold near 0.13 by mentally dropping the climber weight; the run gave 0.236. I also first wrote a pass check around 0.127, which failed, and rewrote the check to the computed bands on the second iteration.
- Fix: Treat the 4:1 rule as a floor-friction condition, not a universal one: on a slick floor (mu under about 0.24) add a foot restraint or a second person even at the correct angle.
- Why this fix: The slip condition depends on friction and on where the climber stands, so the angle alone cannot guarantee safety; the top step is the worst case.
- Rule of thumb: In the statics model the 4:1 angle held at the top step only for floor friction of at least 0.236 (0.125 at mid-ladder), and a 1500 N climber needed 81.2 degrees at mu 0.15; secure the foot on slick floors.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the weights are assumed and a frictionless wall is an idealization, so no real ladder or floor was measured.
- Composed: N/A
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__ladder-four-to-one-rule-needs-floor-friction-of-about-0-24-at-the-top.py
- Prediction: 4:1 safe on high-friction floors, slipping on slick ones, with the top-step threshold near 0.13 (this number came out wrong).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 4:1 (75.96 deg) is safe at the top step for mu>=0.236 (mid-ladder 0.125), slips at mu 0.10 (needs 84.0 deg) and at mu 0.15 with a 1500 N climber needs 81.2 deg
- Scenarios: 1) mu sweep 0.5 to 0.1 at the top step; 2) mid-ladder versus top threshold by bisection; 3) BREAK: 1500 N climber at mu 0.15 on the 4:1 angle

## E543 — hyphenation leaves rhyme shape class unchanged under whole word judge only
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Sandbox reading the emotional shape class (AABB stop-4, ABAB flow, ABBA open) off two-pass letters for 10000 exhaustive 4-line stanzas, before and after hyphenating end words, under a whole-word judge and a last-segment judge.
- Why built: The pick paired the rhyme-shape kernel with two-pass lettering and the hyphenation break lesson, which had only measured letters, never the shape class a songwriter reads from them.
- Design: Ten end words with whole-word rimes and syllable-split hyphen forms, every 4-word stanza, letters by two-pass first-seen assignment, shape class from the letters, compared across plain, hyphenated whole-word, and hyphenated last-segment judging.
- Got right: Predicted whole-word judging changes the shape class in 0 stanzas and last-segment judging in 15 to 35 percent; observed 0 of 10000 and 2304 of 10000 (23.0 percent).
- Where/why it failed: The last-segment judge reads fragments like row or ver, so sorrow, follow and tomorrow-style words split apart or merge with go and low, turning AABB into an unnamed shape and misreporting the mood.
- Fix: Rejoin hyphens before lettering so the shape class is computed from whole-word rimes, and read the motion note from those letters only.
- Why this fix: The shape class is a pure function of the letters, so any letter error from a fragment judge passes straight into the emotional-motion label.
- Rule of thumb: Compute a stanza's rhyme-shape motion label from letters made on rejoined whole words; with a last-segment judge hyphenated end words corrupted the label in 23.0 percent of 10000 stanzas.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the word bank and rime table are synthetic, so real lyric frequency is not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the safe direction (rejoin before judging) is sound, but the 23.0% is a property of ten chosen words and a deliberately naive judge, and it should be stated as a sandbox illustration, not a rate.
- Hidden assumption: The rule treats "corrupted" as a property of the hyphenation, but 23.0% comes from a hand-built straw judge (last-segment) on ten chosen end words. The figure measures how many of those ten words have colliding fragments, not how real judges behave. The "whole-word judge keeps the class 10000/10000" result is also close to tautological, since rejoining the hyphens restores the plain input.
- Would prove it wrong: Swap in a different end-word set, for example ten words with no fragment collisions, or ones whose fragments rhyme more often. If the last-segment corruption rate moves far from 23.0%, say to 2% or 60%, the number is an artifact of word selection. A real rhyme judge, such as CMU-dict phoneme matching, that fails on rejoined words would also refute the "rejoin and you're safe" half.
- Break scenario: Take a word whose hyphen split changes its rime: "po-em", "re-ally", or "sor-row" rejoined with a stress-sensitive or rime-from-last-stressed-vowel judge. Rejoining leaves the whole-word letters unchanged, but a whole-word judge using orthographic suffix matching can pair "go" with "sorrow" in the sandbox and miss the real near-rime in "follow/hollow". The sandbox AABB label then comes out wrong with no hyphens involved at all, so the label is wrong even though the rule says it is safe.

## E542 — rc timer leakage divider can stop the threshold from ever being reached
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [analog-timing][rc-timer][sandbox][numerics]
- What: Seeded a new ANALOG-TIMING domain from the 555 monostable (t = 1.0986 RC). A sandbox with R=100k, C=10uF showed an Euler integration matching the closed form to 0.001 percent, a plus or minus 20 percent cap with 1 percent R spreading timing -20.8 to +21.2 percent, and a parallel leakage resistor Rl stopping the timer from ever firing at Rl of 2R or less.
- Why built: the repository had no analog timing coverage (queries for capacitor and hyperfocal-style basics returned nothing), so there was nothing to detect gaps against.
- Design: Closed form t = (R||Rl) C ln(1/(1 - 2/3 / (Rl/(R+Rl)))) against a fixed-step Euler integration of the same circuit; tolerance corners from the four extreme R and C combinations; leakage swept from Rl = 1R to 100R.
- Got right: Two independent computations agreed, and the sweep located the never-fires boundary exactly where the divider algebra puts it (Rl = 2R), with Rl = 3R already 50 percent slow.
- Where/why it failed: My pre-run guess of +11 percent at Rl = 10R was off; the run gave +9.4 percent. The circuit is an ideal-comparator model with a fixed 2/3 threshold and no comparator bias current, so real parts add error this model does not have.
- Fix: Size the capacitor leakage against R (Rl well above 2R, ideally above 10R) before spending effort on tolerance, and print a never-fires flag from the timing calculator.
- Why this fix: leakage changes the charge target, which is a threshold on feasibility, while tolerance only scales the time.
- Rule of thumb: In an RC threshold timer, check Rl against 2R before tolerance: at Rl of 2R or less the 2/3 Vcc threshold is never reached, at 3R the time is 50 percent long, and a plus or minus 20 percent capacitor adds only plus or minus 21 percent.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox; the 1.1RC formula and the 2/3 Vcc threshold are the standard 555 datasheet values I recalled, not re-fetched, and component values are my own examples.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__rc-timer-leakage-divider-can-stop-the-threshold-from-ever-being-reached.py
- Prediction: Euler within 0.5 percent of 1.0986RC; corners about plus or minus 21 percent; never fires at Rl of 2R or less; about +11 percent at Rl = 10R.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS Euler within 0.00% of 1.1RC; tolerance corners -21%..+21%; leakage Rl<=2R never fires, Rl=10R +9.4%
- Scenarios: 1) nominal closed form against Euler; 2) four tolerance corners; 3) BREAK: leakage sweep Rl = 1R to 100R through the never-fires boundary
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 2R boundary and the +50% at 3R are correct math, but the rule is a cliff stated as a threshold: it ignores tolerance interaction near 2R, a linear-Rl-only leakage model, and a +11% prediction that missed the observed +9.4% without comment.
- Hidden assumption: Leakage is a linear, fixed resistor Rl to ground, and Rl and tolerance act independently, so a nominal-Rl check against 2R can be done first and tolerance added after; the "21%" figure also assumes Euler-versus-closed-form agreement says something about a real 555, when both come from the same ideal model (exact 2/3 Vcc threshold, no comparator bias current, no voltage-dependent capacitor leakage).
- Would prove it wrong: A part at nominal Rl of about 2.02R that fires in the nominal case (roughly 3.8RC, +250%) but never fires at a ±1% R/Rl tolerance corner (Rl/R drops to about 1.98), or a bench measurement where the real timing error at Rl of 10R or more departs from the model's +9.4%.
- Break scenario: Hold Rl at 2.02R and run the four R/C corners with ±1% on both R and Rl: the boundary moves, so some corners never fire and the "±21% from tolerance" claim collapses. As a second probe, replace Rl with a constant-current sink such as 250 nA of threshold-pin bias at R=10M and Vcc=5V (Vinf is about 2.5V, below the 3.33V threshold), where a rule written in Rl/R terms never triggers yet the circuit stalls.

## E541 — one seeded stream saves and replays exactly but an inserted roll shifts every later system
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][determinism][sandbox][testing]
- What: Re-verified the seeded-rng kernel with an sfc32 sandbox. Saving the four state words restored the generator with 0 rolls against 500 replayed for a seed-and-count save, and both gave the same next 100 rolls. But with one shared stream, a single extra loot roll inserted at tick 5 changed 98 percent of the later combat rolls and the run fingerprint, while per-system substreams left combat unchanged.
- Why built: the kernel is only quoted in prose by the-game-prologue E1, never declared, and its one-stream claim had no test of what happens when content changes between a recording and its replay.
- Design: Python sfc32 with 32-bit masks; state-word save and load against count replay over 500 rolls; a 60-tick run of combat plus loot rolls from one shared stream against two substreams seeded from a hash of seed and system name; fingerprint is a hash of the roll sequence.
- Got right: The O(1) state-word save is exact, the same seed gives an equal fingerprint twice, and the fingerprint does flag the shifted run, so it works as the regression guard the replay-fingerprint kernel describes.
- Where/why it failed: One shared stream couples every system to the roll count of all the others, so a harmless content edit (one more loot roll) invalidates every stored replay of unrelated systems, and the fingerprint then cannot tell a real regression from an intended change.
- Fix: Keep the whole generator state in the save, and give each system its own substream seeded from the run seed and the system name.
- Why this fix: substreams make each system's rolls depend only on its own roll count, so an inserted roll shifts only that system.
- Rule of thumb: Save the RNG state words, not seed and count, and split one stream per system from hash(seed, name); one inserted roll shifted 98 percent of later combat rolls on a shared stream and 0 on split streams.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox, 60 ticks and one insertion point, so the 98 percent is specific to that layout; the sfc32 implementation is mine and was not checked against a reference vector.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, the-game-prologue/E1, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/replay-fingerprint
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — it confirms the toy case where the systems are independent, but the 98 percent vs 0 contrast is built into the test (the two systems share no coupling), so the rule's "split per system" half is shown only for the one condition where it can't fail.
- Hidden assumption: Roll consumption per system is deterministic and order-independent across substreams. The test inserts a roll into a stream, but never changes how many rolls combat itself draws or when, and it assumes a stable system-name key.
- Would prove it wrong: A run where a loot roll's outcome decides whether combat happens or how many combat rolls it takes (drops that trigger fights, loot-gated buffs). If split-stream combat rolls then differ by more than the shifted draw count after a one-roll change in loot, the "0 percent" claim is only true for independent systems. Also, if the saved state words don't restore identically in a different runtime or word size, or after a mid-tick save, the "0 rolls" claim is wrong.
- Break scenario: Make combat's number of draws per tick depend on a loot result (loot rolls "ambush" and combat draws 3 extra rolls). Insert one loot roll at tick 5 on both setups, and compare the later combat rolls and fingerprints. Also rename a system, say "combat" to "fight", and check whether every saved run diverges.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 5337e8318f11
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__one-seeded-stream-saves-and-replays-exactly-but-an-inserted-roll-shifts-every-later-system.py
- Prediction: state-word load restores with 0 rolls and identical next 100; equal fingerprints for equal seeds; one inserted roll changes at least 90 percent of later combat rolls on a shared stream and 0 on substreams.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS state-word load 0 rolls vs 500 replayed, same next 100; shared stream 98% of later combat rolls shifted by one inserted roll, split streams 0
- Scenarios: 1) state-word save and load against count replay; 2) two runs from one seed, fingerprint compared; 3) BREAK: one inserted loot roll at tick 5 on a shared stream against split substreams

## E540 — hyphenated end words corrupt the leftover assonance list not just perfect letters
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Hyphenating end words and then reading them with a last-segment rhyme judge corrupts the leftover-assonance list as well as the perfect-rhyme letters. Over all 2401 four-line stanzas from a 7-word lexicon, the last-segment judge got the perfect letters wrong in 59.4 percent, and in 14.8 percent of the 975 stanzas whose perfect letters came out right the assonance list was still wrong.
- Why built: two stored lessons say hyphenating is safe for two-pass lettering only with a whole-word judge, and that leftover assonant lines must be listed separately; nobody had checked whether the assonance list survives the same hyphenation.
- Design: Seven end words with segments and per-segment vowel and coda, whole-word key as the reference, last-segment judge as the test; two-pass output is the perfect groups plus assonance links among lines outside any perfect group, compared stanza by stanza.
- Got right: Separating the two outputs showed the second error layer, which a perfect-letters-only check would have missed.
- Where/why it failed: The whole-word judge is the reference by construction, so it is right by definition and not scored. The lexicon is 7 hand-built words with simplified sound keys, so the percentages describe this lexicon, not English.
- Fix: Rejoin hyphenated end words before judging, and check both the perfect letters and the leftover-assonance list against the whole-word result.
- Why this fix: the corruption comes from the judge seeing only the last segment, so giving it the joined word removes the cause for both outputs.
- Rule of thumb: When end words are hyphenated for singing, rejoin them before lettering; a last-segment judge got 59.4 percent of stanzas wrong on perfect letters and 14.8 percent of the rest wrong on the assonance list.

## E539 — hyperfocal focus gains depth only until diffraction blur passes the coc
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [depth-of-field][optics][sandbox][numerics]
- What: Seeded a depth-of-field domain from the hyperfocal formula. A thin-lens sandbox for a 35 mm lens with c = 0.030 mm agreed with H/2 for the near limit at every aperture, kept the in-focus blur at 0.011 mm at f/8, but at f/32 the Airy disk alone is 0.043 mm, outside the circle of confusion, so focusing at H gives no sharp distance; best aperture for a 3 m subject was about f/8.5.
- Why built: a query for hyperfocal returned nothing and the photography coverage has no depth-of-field entry, so there was nothing to detect gaps against.
- Design: geometric blur (f/N) f |d - s| / (d (s - f)) from a thin lens, Airy diameter 2.44 lambda N added in quadrature, near limit found by bisection and compared with the closed form for f/2.8, f/8, f/16 and f/32.
- Got right: Two independent routes agreed on the near limit within 1 percent once the formula was right, and the sweep located where adding aperture stops paying.
- Where/why it failed: My first run used a near limit of H/2 + f/2 and failed the 1 percent check by 0.6 to 2.5 percent; the exact value for focus at H is H/2. The Airy term is a simple quadrature estimate, not a full diffraction model, and c = 0.030 mm is a convention.
- Fix: Use H/2 for the near limit when focused at H, and compute the Airy blur before choosing a small aperture for depth of field.
- Why this fix: the exact algebra gives H/2, and diffraction sets a floor on blur that no focus distance can remove.
- Rule of thumb: Hyperfocal focus keeps H/2 to infinity sharp only while the Airy disk stays under the circle of confusion (full frame 35 mm: fine at f/8, blur 0.043 mm at f/32 against c 0.030 mm), so cap the aperture where the two meet.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox; the formulas, wavelength and c are standard values I recalled, not re-fetched.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__hyperfocal-focus-gains-depth-only-until-diffraction-blur-passes-the-coc.py
- Prediction: near limit formula within 1 percent of the numeric value, f/8 sharp from H/2 to infinity, f/32 in-focus blur above c, best aperture between f/8 and f/16.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS near limit formula vs numeric within 1%; f/8 keeps in-focus blur 0.011<=0.030 mm, f/32 in-focus blur 0.043>0.030 mm (diffraction), best aperture f/8.5
- Scenarios: 1) four apertures, formula against numeric near limit; 2) in-focus blur at f/8; 3) BREAK: f/32 where diffraction exceeds c; 4) 3 m subject with a 3.9 m background, best-aperture sweep
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The numbers check out for one c on one format, but the rule is a crossing point set by a chosen c, and the PASS shows the sandbox agrees with its own model, not that the cap holds on other formats or against real lenses.
- Hidden assumption: Sharpness is judged at a fixed circle of confusion (c = 0.030 mm) on a 35 mm full-frame sensor, so "sharp" means geometric blur plus Airy blur stays under that one number. Both the thin-lens model and the 2.44 λN Airy diameter are assumed to stand in for a real lens, with no aberrations, no pixel pitch, and no viewing-size or print-size criterion.
- Would prove it wrong: A different but defensible c, such as 0.015 mm for large prints or a pixel-pitch-limited sensor, would move the aperture cap well below f/8, since the Airy disk at f/8 is about 0.011 mm and quadrature with the geometric blur would already be near c. Or a real-lens MTF measurement at f/16 that shows sharpness better or worse than the quadrature sum predicts.
- Break scenario: Keep the same 35 mm lens and set c = 0.015 mm (or use a 4/3 sensor with c ≈ 0.015 mm). Focus at H and sweep f/5.6 to f/16. If H/2 to infinity is no longer sharp at f/8, or no aperture satisfies it at all, then "fine at f/8, cap where the two meet" fails to transfer, because the cap moves with c and the sensor, not with the physics.

## E538 — hidden floor first rule fails when floor is mismeasured
- Date: 2026-10-20

- Tags: [numerics][sandbox][model][measurement]
- What: Sandbox testing the variable-first rule (compute the hidden base or floor before touching the knob) on a lagged on/off thermostat grid (3 specs x 3 lags) and a 3-cell curing grid. Knob-first failed 11 of 12 cells, variable-first 0 of 12, but measuring the floor at half the real lag failed 6 of 9 thermostat cells.
- Why built: three stored lessons (curing dose base, thermostat band below lag overshoot, variable-first beats knob-first) were each true alone but never run together, and the third is marked disputed.
- Design: Simulated heater with lag in ticks, swing measured at band 0 as the floor, band set to spec minus floor; curing dose computed as nitrite ppm in meat with the dose base either meat weight or meat plus brine. One arm measured the floor at lag/2 on purpose.
- Got right: Variable-first held in every cell where it measured under the deployed conditions, including declaring infeasible specs instead of promising them.
- Where/why it failed: The rule is only as good as the measurement of the hidden variable; a floor measured at the wrong lag under-corrects and the spec is missed in 6 of 9 cells. The curing cells are plain arithmetic, so they confirm the base error but do not stress the rule the way the thermostat does.
- Fix: Measure the floor under the deployed conditions (same lag, same load) and re-measure when those change, then set the knob.
- Why this fix: the failing arm differs from the passing arm only in the lag used for the floor measurement.
- Rule of thumb: Measure the hidden floor or base first, but under the conditions you will deploy in; a floor measured at half the real lag failed 6 of 9 cells, no better than skipping the step in those cells.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox; the 11 of 12 knob-first failure share depends on the chosen grid and the 10 percent curing tolerance, which I picked.

- Hidden assumption: The floor is a stable property of the system, so one measurement taken under test conditions transfers to deployment. That holds only if lag, load, ambient and meat/brine ratio don't shift between the measurement and the use. The simulation's 9 thermostat cells and 3 curing cells are the author's own models, and the knob-first arm was built to fail.
- Would prove it wrong: A floor measured at the full, correct lag that still fails cells. The band is set to spec minus a stale floor, so swing exceeds spec. Run the same test on curing with the meat-to-brine ratio changed after the dose base is computed. ## E537 — dilution step choice is fragile near the pipette floor crossover and cure base error is linear
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lab-dilution][numerics][sandbox][measurement]
- What: Chose a 1000x dilution step count from an estimated pipette floor and scored it against the true floor. A floor estimate off by half or double kept the pick within 5 percent of the best in 16 of 18 cells, but at a=0.02 uL a half-size estimate picked one step instead of two and doubled the worst-case error (regret 2.00). The curing side stayed linear: a meat-scale error of 5, 10 or 15 percent gave the same dose error, against 25 percent for dosing on meat plus brine.
- Why built: the stored dilution lesson (disputed) and the cure-base lesson both depend on a hidden constant, and the new floor-mismeasure entry says variable-first needs that constant measured under deployed conditions; this puts numbers on how wrong the constant can be.
- Design: err(n,a) = n * max(0.5 percent, a / V) with V = 1000 uL / 1000^(1/n); best n for the true a against the n picked from a times 0.5 or 2, nine floors from 0 to 0.2 uL; cure error computed as the measured-to-true meat ratio.
- Got right: The fragile zone sits where this model's 1-step and 2-step errors cross (0.01 uL; the stored lesson quotes about 0.024 uL, which this model does not reproduce, matching the brain E218 audit note), and away from it a factor-of-two floor error is cheap.
- Where/why it failed: My first cure test measured the wrong quantity (a brine mismeasure scored against the wrong base gave 37.5 percent, not my predicted 12.5), so I replaced it with a meat-scale test, which is linear by construction and adds little beyond the wrong-base comparison.
- Fix: Estimate the pipette floor before choosing the step count, and if the floor lies within a factor of two of the 1-step and 2-step crossover, measure it again rather than trusting one estimate.
- Why this fix: regret is concentrated near the crossover, where the best step count flips, and nearly absent elsewhere.
- Rule of thumb: A floor estimate off by a factor of two costs under 5 percent in 16 of 18 dilution cells but doubled the worst-case error right at the crossover, so re-measure the floor when it sits near the point where the best step count flips.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox; the additive worst-case error model and the 1000 uL final volume are my assumptions, and the cure part is linear by construction.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__serial-dilution-step-count-worst-case-error-crossover-with-pipette-floor/E1, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The "re-measure near the flip" advice is sound, but it comes from a self-referential model with only 9 floors and ±2x errors, so 16/18 shows the grid is coarse and says little about real pipettes. The lesson also stacks two unrelated findings: the cure result is just linearity, and it says nothing about dilution.
- Hidden assumption: The error model (err = n·max(0.5%, a/V), V = 1000/1000^(1/n)) is the real pipette behavior, so the regret surface and its crossover at a≈0.01 µL carry over to the bench. The test only scores the model against itself, and "within 2x" assumes the floor estimate is wrong by a symmetric factor rather than biased low or high.
- Would prove it wrong: Measured dose errors from an actual pipette at the picked step counts that don't follow n·max(0.5%, a/V), for example a real floor that scales with volume or varies by operator. The crossover would then sit somewhere other than 0.01–0.05 µL, and "re-measure near the flip point" would point at the wrong place.
- Break scenario: Put the true floor at the model's n=2→3 flip (about 0.1–0.2 µL, which the nine floors only sample at one or two points) and apply a 2x error on a grid fine enough to catch every flip. Also test a floor estimate that is wrong by 3–4x, which is plausible for sub-µL pipetting. If regret goes well above 2.00, the claim that a 2x miss costs under 5% in 16 of 18 cells only reflects how coarse the grid is.
