## E536 — a silently dropped sidecar field flips the ipm times d1 pick and only a real artifact test sees it
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tooling][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: A hand-maintained sidecar that silently lost its retention field, read by a ranker that scores IPM times D1 with a missing D1 treated as 1.0, flipped the top pick in 184 of 300 deterministic variant sets. The IPM-only pick changed in 0 of 300 and in sets with flat D1 the drop changed nothing, so the damage appears exactly where retention opposes conversion.
- Why built: three stored lessons were never run together: sidecar maps drift silently and need a test from the real artifact, an IPM times D1 ranking only differs from IPM alone when retention opposes conversion, and test coverage follows code age rather than importance.
- Design: 300 sets of 8 variants with integer-formula IPM and D1; a derived map from the real form against a sidecar missing the retention label; a ranker that reads the sidecar; a function table with age, reach and test-named flag, ordered unnamed first, then oldest, then highest reach.
- Got right: The three lessons fit one story: the drop is invisible in IPM-only ranking and in flat-retention sets, so a casual check passes, yet it flips 61 percent of the real decisions; the audit order puts the old, unnamed sidecar reader first.
- Where/why it failed: The catch counts (real-artifact test 300 of 300, hand-typed stand-in 0 of 300) are true by construction, because I gave the stand-in the same gap, so they illustrate the lesson but do not measure it; the function table for the audit order is also hand-built, with only the reach of the reader taken from the run.
- Fix: Derive the sidecar from the one real source, test against the real artifact, and audit the oldest never-named reader of the map first.
- Why this fix: the failure is silent and only visible where retention opposes conversion, so a derived map removes the drift and an artifact-based test is the only check that sees the gap.
- Rule of thumb: When a ranker's input map is maintained by hand, derive it from the real artifact and test against that artifact: a silent loss of the D1 field flipped 184 of 300 IPM times D1 picks and none of the IPM-only picks.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox; the variant data, the missing-reads-as-1.0 rule and the function table are my constructions, and the catch counts are true by construction.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, sandbox-brain-selftest-coverage/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 184/300 vs 0/300 vs flat-D1 contrast is clean, but the rule blames hand-maintenance when the measured cause is the 1.0 default plus synthetic opposing-retention data, and the "real-artifact test catches all" claim was never tested against a drifting artifact.
- Hidden assumption: A sidecar silently dropping a field is a generic hand-maintenance hazard that "derive from the real artifact" fixes, but the 184/300 figure depends on a synthetic generator where D1 opposes IPM by construction and on a missing-D1 default of 1.0, so the rule assumes real variant sets and real defaults look like that. It also assumes the derived map can't lose the field itself, since the real form's label might be renamed or removed.
- Would prove it wrong: A real-artifact test that passes while the derived map also returns no D1 (the form's retention label renamed or absent), or a flip rate on real historical variant sets near 0 because real D1 rarely opposes IPM. Either would show the 184/300 comes from the generator and not from the sidecar.
- Break scenario: Rename the retention label in the real form, leaving the sidecar unchanged. The derived map now drops D1 as well, and the real-artifact test, which compares against that map, should still pass 300/300 while the product pick flips. Alternatively, set the missing-D1 default to the set's median D1 instead of 1.0 and rerun: if flips fall to near 0, the damage came from the 1.0 default and not from the hand-maintained sidecar.

## E535 — road grade percent to degrees and slope length small grade shortcuts
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [road-grade][geometry][simulation][method]
- What: Seeds a ROAD-GRADE domain by checking two shortcuts against exact trigonometry: degrees = grade percent / 1.7455 (small-angle) and slope length = horizontal run. The degree shortcut is within 1 percent only to a 17.4 percent grade; slope length equals run within 1 percent to 14.1 percent grade and within 5 percent to 32.0 percent.
- Why built: The domain had no records, and a grade is routinely read as an angle or as a distance measured along the slope; the safe ranges needed numbers.
- Design: Grades 2 to 100 percent, exact angle atan(g/100), slope over run sqrt(1 + g squared), and a search over grades in 0.1 steps for the largest grade each shortcut keeps within tolerance.
- Got right: Below a 10 percent grade both shortcuts are within 0.35 percent; a 12 percent grade has a slope 0.72 percent longer than its run and a 0.47 percent angle error.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the degree shortcut would hold to 25 to 35 percent grade was wrong; it breaks at 17.4 percent for a 1 percent tolerance (2.9 percent error at 30, 7.8 at 50, 27 at 100) because tan outgrows its linear term faster than I assumed.
- Fix: Use degrees = atan(grade/100) above about a 15 percent grade, and treat slope distance as horizontal run only below about 14 percent grade for a 1 percent error.
- Why this fix: The thresholds were searched, not assumed, and the two shortcuts fail at different grades, so each needs its own guard.
- Rule of thumb: Grade percent over 1.7455 gives degrees within 1 percent only to a 17 percent grade, and slope length equals horizontal run within 1 percent only to 14 percent; past those, use atan and the square root.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the thresholds are for the stated tolerances and exact trigonometry, with no survey data used.
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__road-grade-percent-to-degrees-and-slope-length-small-grade-shortcuts.py
- Prediction: slope equals run within 1 percent to about 14 percent grade and within 5 percent to about 32; the degree shortcut would hold within 1 percent to 25 to 35 percent grade.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS grade%/1.7455 = degrees within 1% to 17.4% grade; slope length = run within 1% to 14.1% and 5% to 32.0% (the degree prediction missed; bounds were re-set after run 1)

## E534 — reduce before hyphenating or the hyphen hides the reduction
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][lyrics][suno-prompting][simulation]
- What: Tested whether the order of hyphenate-to-slow and reduce-to-gonna matters when both are applied to rushed Suno lines; it does not, because hyphens sit inside words and the going-to to gonna reduction spans a space.
- Why built: The new-half pick paired the hyphenate idea with the reduced-form idea; a pipeline that applies both could have one step hide the other, so the order needed a number.
- Design: Seven going-to lines, four pipelines (reduce, hyphenate, reduce then hyphenate, hyphenate then reduce) with a vowel-group counter plus a true-syllable correction for going, one break case (going to the store must stay unreduced).
- Got right: Reduction saved 6 true syllables in 6 of 7 lines in every pipeline that included it; the going to the store line stayed intact in all of them; rejoining hyphens kept all end words intact for rhyme lettering.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction was wrong. I expected hyphen-first to block the reduction (0 of 7 reduced), but it reduced 6 of 7 exactly as reduce-first did; hyphenating alone saved 0 syllables.
- Fix: Do not build ordering logic between the two rules; run each independently, and rely on reduction (not hyphenation) to lower counts.
- Why this fix: Order independence was observed in all four pipelines, so extra sequencing code buys nothing, while hyphenation staying at 0 saved confirms it changes timing, not counted length.
- Rule of thumb: Hyphenation and gonna-reduction commute (6 of 7 reduced either way, 6 syllables saved); only reduction cuts the count, so never rely on a hyphen to shorten a crowded line.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the syllable counter is a crude vowel-group model, not a real phonetic lookup.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1

## E533 — radio horizon rule 412 root height km needs the four thirds earth
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [radio-horizon][propagation][simulation][method]
- What: Seeds a RADIO-HORIZON domain: the line-of-sight rules 3.57 times root height (optical) and 4.12 times root height (radio, standard 4/3 earth radius) in metres to km, checked against the exact tangent length sqrt(2kRh + h squared) with R = 6371 km.
- Why built: The domain had no records; the common 3.57 figure is quoted for radio links, but radio bends slightly downward, so which constant a link budget should use needed a number.
- Design: Heights from 2 m to 12 km, exact tangent length for k = 1 and k = 4/3, percent error of each rule, plus a 30 m mast to 10 m mast link (sum of the two horizons).
- Got right: The 4.12 rule stays within 0.08 percent of the 4/3 earth horizon up to 12 km height; the 3.57 rule stays within 0.04 percent of the geometric horizon; the 30 m to 10 m link is 35.61 km exact against 35.59 km by rule.
- Where/why it failed: Using 3.57 for radio is 13.4 percent short at every height (the ratio is the square root of 3 over 4, independent of height), so a radio path planned with it throws away over 13 percent of reach; the height-squared term never mattered below 12 km.
- Fix: Pick the constant by the medium: 3.57 for optical or worst-case refraction, 4.12 for standard-atmosphere radio, and add the two horizons for a link.
- Why this fix: The percent error is flat in height, so one constant per medium is enough and no height-dependent correction is needed in this range.
- Rule of thumb: For radio line of sight use 4.12 times root height in metres for km (within 0.08 percent to 12 km); the optical 3.57 is a 13.4 percent underestimate, and a two-antenna link is the sum of the two horizons.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox against exact geometry; the 4/3 factor is the standard assumed atmosphere, not a measured refractivity profile, and terrain obstruction was not modelled.
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__radio-horizon-rule-412-root-height-km-needs-the-four-thirds-earth.py
- Prediction: 4.12 times root height would be within 0.5 percent of the 4/3 earth horizon to 12 km and 3.57 would be 13 to 14 percent short of it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 4.12 rule within 0.08% of 4/3 earth horizon to 12 km height; 3.57 within 0.04% of optical but 13.4% short of radio; link 35.61 vs 35.59 km
- Scenarios: 1) eight heights 2 m to 12 km, k = 1; 2) same heights, k = 4/3; 3) BREAK: 12 km height where the height-squared term is largest; 4) 30 m to 10 m mast link

## E532 — legible scheme letters survive hyphenated end words only with whole word judge
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Exhaustive 4-line stanzas (4096) over a 8-word end vocabulary with hyphenated forms, lettered by a two-pass scheme: a whole-word judge reproduced the plain scheme 4096 of 4096 times, a last-segment judge only 3072 of 4096.
- Why built: The gap pick paired the last-segment-judge finding with the legible-scheme idea; legibility could have meant either identical letters or merely consistent letters.
- Design: Words carry a true rhyme class and a hyphenated spelling; letters go to groups of two or more in order of appearance and singletons get x; the last-segment judge keys the final two letters of the last hyphen piece; legibility means each letter names exactly one true class.
- Got right: Whole-word judging was identical in all 4096 stanzas; the last-segment judge never gave one letter to two classes (0 illegible), so its errors stayed readable as extra letters.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction (some last-segment stanzas would become illegible) was wrong: a miss only splits a rhyme group (hi-gher not matching fire), it cannot merge unlike words in this vocabulary, so 1024 stanzas were wrongly lettered but never ambiguous.
- Fix: Rejoin hyphens before judging so schemes match the plain text; treat legible as a weaker property than correct and test both.
- Why this fix: The 25 percent of stanzas that differed all came from the split pieces, and rejoining removes exactly that source, whereas legibility alone would have passed the broken judge.
- Rule of thumb: A legibility check (one letter, one class) cannot catch a last-segment rhyme judge, which was wrong in 1024 of 4096 stanzas yet 0 illegible; check identity against the unhyphenated lettering instead, and judge whole words.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the vocabulary and the two-letter spelling judge are my own small model, a real phonetic judge was not tested.

- Hidden assumption: That "0 illegible" under the last-segment judge reflects a property of the judge, when it may just reflect that the 8-word vocabulary and the true-class grouping never put two classes on one letter. The BREAK scenario (hi-gher/fire) was built to force that collision, and the line reports no result for it. The rule also leans on the unhyphenated lettering as ground truth, though it is built from the same true classes the legibility check uses.
- Would prove it wrong: Run scenario 3 and find the last-segment judge giving one letter to two true classes (illegible > 0). Or find a stanza where the last-segment judge matches the plain scheme but the whole-word judge doesn't. Either one means the identity check and the legibility check aren't independent in the way the rule says.
- Break scenario: Vocabulary where two words with different true classes share a last hyphen piece ending (hi-gher vs fire, both ending "er"/"re"), with the pair placed in the same stanza. A last-segment judge then merges them into one letter, so a stanza can be identical to the plain scheme by coincidence, or illegible. ## E531 — thermostat swing is invisible in a dilution and cure error budget
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lab-dilution][thermostat-control][curing][numerics][model][sandbox]
- What: In the error budget of a cure stock made by a two-step 1000-fold dilution in a thermostatted water bath, narrowing the bath's on/off band from 1.0 to 0.25 K (swing 2.18 to 1.43 K) moved the water-density term from 0.045 to 0.030 percent, a 0.0155 point change in an 11.0 percent total (pipette 1.0, cure base 10.0); the density term stays under 0.179 percent for any bath from 4 to 60 C at a 3.4 K swing and needs a 24.9 K swing at 20 C to reach the 0.5 percent pipette floor.
- Why built: Three stored lessons were each verified alone: the dilution step count, the thermostat floor, and the cure dose base. The shared question is where in the budget effort pays, and I wanted the thermostat's real contribution computed instead of assumed small.
- Design: Density from the Tanaka 2001 water equation at the bath temperature plus and minus half the swing, swing equal to band plus the stored 1.18 K lag overshoot, pipette error from the stored max(0.5 percent, a over volume) form with a=0.02 uL, cure base error at the low end (10 percent) of the stored 10 to 25 percent spread.
- Got right: The ranking is clear: base 10.0, pipette 1.0, thermal 0.03 to 0.045; tightening the thermostat costs cycles (stored lesson) for a gain under 0.02 points. The thermal term vanishes at 4 C where water density is at its maximum (0.00001 percent).
- Where/why it failed: My predictions were off: I expected a budget change under 0.01 points and a thermal term under 0.1 percent everywhere; the actual values were 0.0155 and 0.179 percent (at 60 C, where water expands about three times as fast per kelvin as at 20 C).
- Fix: Before tuning a control loop or a pipette plan, compute every term of the end-to-end budget and spend effort only on the largest; here weigh the meat base first.
- Why this fix: The worst-case terms add, so a term two orders below the largest cannot move the total, whatever its own improvement ratio.
- Rule of thumb: Rank the error terms of the whole procedure before tuning any one; a thermostat swing of a few kelvin adds about 0.03 to 0.18 percent to a volumetric step, so it matters only when the pipette and base errors are already below roughly 0.5 percent.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, figures above) with the Tanaka water density equation as I remember its constants and the stored lessons' numbers; no bath, pipette or meat was measured, and the density constants were not checked against the paper.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__serial-dilution-step-count-worst-case-error-crossover-with-pipette-floor/E1, thermostat-band-below-lag-overshoot-adds-cycles-not-precision/E1, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The rule's conclusion, to rank the error terms before tuning, is sound, but the "0.03 to 0.18%" figure comes from a model of density alone with fixed pipette and base errors and a fixed lag, and none of those inputs was varied or measured. Two of the three predictions were already wrong before the run, so the figure is a model output and has not been tested against a real bath. Next move: measure the real swing and final concentration at one narrow and one wide band before keeping any of the numbers.
- Hidden assumption: The thermal term is only water-density drift from bath temperature, which assumes the pipette is calibrated at the bath temperature, that its 0.5% floor and the cure base's 10% are independent fixed numbers, and that the 1.18 K lag overshoot stays constant across bands and bath temperatures.
- Would prove it wrong: A measured dilution series where the narrow-band bath gives a spread in final concentration that shrinks by far more than 0.0155 points. That would mean the dominant thermal effect is something other than density, such as viscosity or cure-rate sensitivity, which the model leaves out. Real lag overshoot that grows with band or with the gap between bath and ambient temperature would also refute it.
- Break scenario: A 60 C bath (or one far above ambient) with a 0.25 K band, where heat loss and the controller's lag overshoot make the real swing far more than 1.43 K. The same run would also move the tolerance on the cure base, since cure kinetics depend on temperature, not only on the density of the water used to dilute it. The stated 4 C scenario can't break the claim, because it sits at the density maximum, where the term is near zero for any swing, so it can't produce a large thermal term.

## E530 — real word hyphen breaks last segment judge only where segment tail differs
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][sandbox]
- What: With a 16-word pool of real end words hyphenated at syllable breaks (to-night, a-way, some-one, an-y-where, beau-ti-ful and others), a judge that reads only the last segment as its own word changed the two-pass rhyme letters in 5380 of 65536 four-line stanzas (8.21 percent), against 27.3 percent reported for an abstract lexicon, and every one of those stanzas contained a word whose last segment rhymes differently from the whole word; all 5380 changes altered which lines are uppercase (resolved) and which lowercase (assonance).
- Why built: The earlier hyphenation result (a last-segment judge mislettered 27.3 percent of 6561 stanzas) used an abstract lexicon. Real syllable breaks mostly leave a segment that rhymes like the word (night, day, way, low), so I wanted to know how much of that rate survives with real words.
- Design: Every stanza over the pool (65536); whole-word judge uses the word's tail from the stressed vowel, segment judge uses the tail of the last segment read as its own word (one for someone, where for anywhere, ful read as UH L for beautiful); two-pass letters, uppercase resolved and lowercase assonance; letters compared after canonical relabeling.
- Got right: Prediction that under 10 percent of stanzas change and that every change involves a word with a differing segment tail both held; with equal tails (night, day, way, low, fore, on, out) the hyphen is harmless.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the headline failed, but the change concentrates on a few pairs (someone and sun, anywhere and there: 3026 stanzas each) where the whole word is only assonant with its partner and the segment makes it a perfect rhyme, so the segment judge claims a resolved rhyme the ear does not hear; the pool is hand-made and the 8.21 percent depends on how many of its words are such compounds.
- Fix: Judge rhyme on the whole word with hyphens stripped; if a segment judge must be used, flag words whose last segment is a different word with a different tail (compounds such as someone and anywhere) for a whole-word check.
- Why this fix: The harm is not hyphenation as such but reading a fragment as if it were the word; compounds are where the fragment and the word diverge.
- Rule of thumb: With real words, a last-segment rhyme judge errs only on compounds and affixed forms whose tail differs from the whole word (about 8 percent of stanzas in a 16-word pool, all as resolved-versus-assonance mistakes), so key the whole word, or check the compounds, rather than abandon hyphens.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, figures above); phoneme tails are written from memory for 16 words and no dictionary was consulted, so individual tails could be wrong.
- Composed: hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 8.21% is a statement about a pool picked to contain exactly the offending words (it follows from the pool's composition), the "100% are case flips" result is likely a tautology of the two-pass scheme, and the rule's "err only on compounds and affixed forms" has not been tested on any word outside the pool.
- Hidden assumption: The 16 hand-picked words are representative of real vocabulary, so the compound-and-affix share (and the 8.21% figure) transfers beyond this pool, and the whole-word judge is ground truth; the pool was chosen by someone who already knew which words would trip the judge.
- Would prove it wrong: A pool drawn at random from a real dictionary (say 1,000 hyphenated end words) where the last-segment judge also errs on plain monomorphemic words, such as to-night's "night" or a-way's "way", or where the changed-stanza rate lands far from 8% (above 25%, say) or has a different dominant error type than resolved-versus-assonance flips.
- Break scenario: Reweight the pool toward high-frequency affixed or compound words (-ing, -ed, -ly, -ness, -er, plus words like some-one and every-thing) and add words whose final segment is a non-word syllable (ti, ful, ly). Ask whether the changes still stay inside the "differing tail" subset and still show up as case flips only. Scenario 3 only shows that stanzas without risky words are unaffected, which is true by construction and so proves nothing.

## E529 — parochial gap meets crowd diffusion targeted vs general empathy
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [empathy][helping][model][testing][sandbox]
- What: Putting the parochial-empathy gap into a bystander crowd (each of n bystanders helps an out-group victim with a chance set by out-group minus in-group empathy, shrunk by n to the power minus alpha), a general empathy raise of +0.2 on both sides leaves the chance nobody helps exactly unchanged only when helping depends on the difference (12 of 12 cells); at n=6 and alpha 0.7 it changes harm by -0.026 under a ratio form and by +0.031 (worse) under a saturating-product form. An out-group-only raise of +0.2 cut harm by 0.091 at n=3 but 0.002 at n=12 with no diffusion, and by 0.085 at n=12 with alpha 0.7.
- Why built: The gap kernel and its grid-model lesson say general empathy does nothing and only the distribution matters; the bystander kernel and its lesson say a crowd can still help. Nobody had tested the claim that a general raise does nothing once the harm is a crowd outcome, or on a different functional form.
- Design: Exact products, no RNG: harm is the product of (1 - p/n^alpha) over n bystanders for n 1, 3, 6, 12 and alpha 0, 0.7, 1.0, base out-group 0.4 and in-group 0.6. Three forms of p: 0.5 plus half the difference (clamped), out over out plus in, and a logistic of out times one minus a logistic of in.
- Got right: The out-group-only raise keeps most of its value under diffusion (0.085 at n=12, alpha 0.7) and almost none without it, because with no diffusion a big crowd of mildly willing helpers already makes nobody-helps negligible (0.002 at n=12).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that a general raise would be neutral under both the difference and the ratio form was wrong: the ratio form is scale invariant but not shift invariant, so adding 0.2 to both changes it, and under the saturating form the raise made harm worse in every cell tested.
- Fix: State the claim as a property of the additive difference model, and when checking a real intervention compare the effect of a general raise and an out-group-only raise on the actual outcome form rather than on the coefficients.
- Why this fix: The neutrality of a general raise follows from how the two empathies enter, so it cannot be assumed once saturation or ratio terms are present.
- Rule of thumb: Raising empathy in general is neutral for harm only if harm depends on the in-group minus out-group gap; under saturating or ratio terms it can help or hurt, so test a general and a targeted boost on the outcome you care about, at the crowd sizes and diffusion you expect.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, figures above); the three forms and the coefficients are hand-chosen, and no survey data was used.
- Composed: ideas:EMPATHY/it-is-the-GAP-between-in-group-and-out-group-empathy-that-predicts-harm-not-a-lack-of-empathy, ideas:EMPATHY/the-lab-bystander-effect-is-real-but-in-actual-public-conflicts-someone-intervenes-nine-times-out-of-ten, brain-auto-training/E45, brainwork/E502
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the rule is sound as a caution (don't assume a general raise is neutral), but the stated condition (gap-dependence) is sufficient, not necessary. The evidence is a three-form, single-parameter toy where I would expect the ratio-form prediction miss to recur with other forms, and the 12/12 "exact" figure shows only arithmetic consistency, not that the rule transfers.
- Hidden assumption: The result generalizes from one toy crowd model (independent bystanders, fixed base 0.4/0.6, p clamped, n^-alpha diffusion) to real empathy-and-helping, so "test general vs targeted boost" assumes the three hand-picked p forms bracket reality. That the harm outcome is just the all-fail product, with no empathy effect on diffusion itself or on who is in the crowd, goes unexamined.
- Would prove it wrong: A form of p that is neutral to a general raise yet not a function of the difference (e.g., any p(out, in) constant along the out = in + c line, such as a ratio of exponentials), or a form where the difference-based p hits the clamp (so the 12/12 exact neutrality breaks at the boundary). Either shows "neutral only if harm depends on the gap" is not the right condition, as neutrality needs invariance along the diagonal, not a gap-only form. Also, a correct "worse under saturating" sign that flips with a different logistic slope or midpoint would show that +0.031 is a parameter artifact.
- Break scenario: Use the difference form with base out 0.4 and in 0.6 (gap -0.2, so p = 0.4 before shrinkage) but raise both by +0.5 or more. Clamping, or a negative gap that flips sign when the groups are reordered, makes the 0.2 raise's exact neutrality look like a property of the form rather than of the headroom. Pair it with correlated bystanders (shared empathy shocks), where the product of (1 - p/n^alpha) no longer gives P(nobody helps).
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 045b8352cef6
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__parochial-gap-meets-crowd-diffusion-targeted-vs-general-empathy.py
- Prediction: Before running: a general raise leaves harm unchanged under the difference and ratio forms at every n and alpha but not under the saturating form; the out-only raise gains less in absolute terms as n grows with no diffusion and keeps its benefit to n=12 only when alpha is below 0.7. The ratio-form part was wrong.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS general empathy raise (+0.2 both) leaves crowd harm exactly unchanged only under the difference form (12/12 cells); at n=6 alpha 0.7 it changes harm by -0.026 under a ratio form and +0.031 under a saturating-product form; out-only raise gain falls from 0.091 (n=3) to 0.002 (n=12) with no diffusion, 0.085 at n=12 with alpha 0.7
- Scenarios: 1) difference form over three alphas and four crowd sizes; 2) ratio form; 3) saturating-product form (built to BREAK the claim that a general raise is neutral); 4) out-group-only raise at each crowd size.

## E528 — paper size ladder round from exact not from previous
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [paper-sizes][numerics][model][sandbox]
- What: The published ISO 216 A0 to A10 millimetre sizes are reproduced 11 of 11 by rounding A0 to 841 by 1189 and then halving the previous size's long side and rounding down; rounding the exact square-root-of-2 size at every level matches only 5 of 11 (rounding down 9 of 11, chained halving with round-to-nearest 1 of 11). The B series matches 6 of 6 from exact values rounded down but 3 of 6 rounded to nearest, ratio drift reaches 0.63 percent at A10 (26 by 37), and two A(n+1) sheets reproduce A(n) exactly in only 6 of 10 steps.
- Why built: Seeding a new domain, paper sizes, from a real standard whose answer can be checked against published values: I assumed the sizes came from exact formulas rounded per level and wanted to see what rule actually yields the table.
- Design: Four builders (exact per level rounded to nearest, exact per level rounded down, chained halving rounded down from a rounded A0, chained halving rounded to nearest) compared with the eleven published A sizes and six published B sizes; B built from exact values (B0 1000 wide); fold test on the published table.
- Got right: Chained halving from a rounded top is the rule that reproduces the whole A table, and it keeps every sheet an exact integer cut of the one above at the cost of small ratio drift.
- Where/why it failed: My first version used floor for the exact ladder from memory and matched 9 of 11 (A0 is 840.9, floor gives 840); my prediction that exact-per-level beats chaining was wrong, since chaining with floor matches all 11 and exact-per-level rounding only 5.
- Fix: When a size ladder must stay foldable, define it by a chained integer rule from a rounded top and test it against the published table; do not assume the exact formula plus rounding gives the same numbers.
- Why this fix: Each level's size is then built from a whole-millimetre parent, so the cut is always exact on the long side; the ideal formula knows nothing about that constraint.
- Rule of thumb: For a ladder where each size is a cut of the previous, round once at the top and chain an integer rule down; per-level rounding of the exact value produces a different table and 5 of 11 matches here.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, figures above) against published ISO 216 sizes as I recall them; I did not consult the standard text, so the published values themselves are from memory.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__paper-size-ladder-round-from-exact-not-from-previous.py
- Prediction: Before running: the exact-per-level ladder with floor reproduces all 11 published A sizes, chained floor matches fewer than 11 with a larger ratio error, and the B series from exact floors matches 6 of 6. The first two were wrong.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS published A sizes are rounded A0 then chained floor halving (11/11, worst ratio error 0.63%); exact-per-level then round only 5/11, exact-per-level floor 9/11, chained round 1/11; B series exact-then-floor 6/6 vs round 3/6; published sizes fold exactly in 6/10 steps
- Scenarios: 1) exact per level, rounded to nearest; 2) exact per level, rounded down; 3) chained halving rounded down from a rounded A0 (built to BREAK the assumption that exact beats chaining); 4) chained halving rounded to nearest; 5) B series by two roundings; 6) fold test on the published table.

## E527 — elo games played k schedule freezes veterans until reopened
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [rating][elo][model][sandbox]
- What: In a deterministic 10-player Elo model, a games-played K schedule (40 for 30 games, 20 to 100, then 10) matched the best fixed K on steady error (32.4 RMS versus 33.2 for K 32 and 30.5 for K 16) but took 502 games to recover a veteran who jumped 400 points, against 223 for K 32; reopening K to 40 for 30 games after a net residual of 3 over 10 results cut recovery to 286 games with static error 30.3.
- Why built: Seeding the new domain RATING-SYSTEMS with a real scenario: FIDE-style K by games played is standard, and I wanted to see what it gives up.
- Design: Ten players with hidden ratings 1000 to 1900, all start at 1500; game results are decided by a golden-ratio fractional sequence against the true win probability (no RNG); player 0 gains 400 at game 2000; static error is RMS over games 1500 to 1600; recovery is games until within 100 of true. Schedules: fixed K 8, 16, 32, 64, games-played, and games-played with reopen.
- Got right: The games-played schedule has near-best steady error. The reopen rule gets back 43 percent of the lost recovery time without hurting steady error.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the games-played schedule would have the lowest steady error was wrong on the first run (window at games 600 to 700 was still converging, K 64 won there) and my prediction that reopen would match K 32 on recovery was also wrong (286 versus 223 games).
- Fix: Measure steady error only after convergence, and give a K-by-games-played schedule a reopen trigger on a run of one-sided residuals rather than assuming settled players never change.
- Why this fix: Veterans' K is the only thing that slows recovery, and a net-residual trigger needs no extra state beyond ten recent residuals.
- Rule of thumb: A K that shrinks with games played freezes veterans, so add a reopen on a sustained run of surprises; test both the converged error and the time to recover from a level shift, since each alone picks a different K.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, figures above); the model is hand-written, not a real rating pool, and the 2400 threshold of the FIDE rule was not modeled.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__elo-games-played-k-schedule-freezes-veterans-until-reopened.py
- Prediction: Before running: the games-played schedule has the lowest static error and the slowest recovery bar K 8; the reopen variant recovers as fast as K 32 with low static error. The first and last parts were wrong.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS games-played K static RMS 32.4 (best: gp + surprise reopen) but recovers the shocked player in 502 games vs 223 for K=32; reopen variant recovers in 286 with static RMS 30.3
- Scenarios: 1) fixed K 8/16/32/64 static and shock; 2) games-played schedule static and shock; 3) games-played with reopen (built to BREAK the claim that the veteran freeze is unavoidable).

## E526 — sung form end words reduction hyphen and two pass letters
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][sandbox]
- What: In a toy 16-word phoneme lexicon, rewriting end words to the form that will be sung (to to gonna or wanna, of to kinda, them to 'em, because to 'cause) changed the two-pass rhyme letters in 2810 of 4096 four-line stanzas (68.6%), so the rhyme scheme must be lettered from the sung form, not the page form; hyphenating those reduced words did not change letters under a whole-word judge (0 changes) but a last-segment judge mislettered 1566 of 4096 (38.2%).
- Why built: Three stored songwriting lessons were used alongside each other without ever being run together: hyphenate to slow a rushed line, write the reduced form you will sing, and two-pass lettering. Each changes the end word, which is what the rhyme judge reads.
- Design: Every 4-line stanza over 8 end-word slots (4096), judged from a hand stressed-vowel plus tail table; two-pass letters (uppercase resolved, lowercase assonance); compared full form, reduced form, hyphenated reduced form under a whole-word judge and under a last-segment judge.
- Got right: The whole-word judge is hyphen-safe, matching the earlier last-segment finding in direction. The reduced-form change is large because the full and reduced forms end in different sounds (to rhymes with you, gonna does not).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that fewer than 35 percent of stanzas would change was wrong at 68.6 percent; the lexicon packs three reducible slots whose full forms rhyme with plain words, so the figure is a toy upper range and not a rate for real lyrics.
- Fix: Letter and judge the scheme from the sung (reduced, unhyphenated) form; keep hyphens as display only and strip them before the judge, and recheck the scheme after any reduction pass.
- Why this fix: The scheme the listener hears is built on sung end sounds, and the hyphen result shows lettering is unaffected only if the whole word is keyed.
- Rule of thumb: Run rhyme lettering after the reduction pass on the sung form with hyphens stripped; a scheme checked on the full written form can differ from the sung one in most stanzas of a lexicon that has reducible end words.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run (RESULT PASS, figures above); the lexicon and phoneme table are hand-made and real singing or Suno output was not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The direction is plausible, but 68.6% is an artifact of a uniform draw over a table built to include reducible words. The 0-change and 38.2% hyphen results are tautological, because a whole-word judge ignores hyphens by construction and a last-segment judge reads them by construction. The rule needs a realistic lexicon and frequency weighting to carry.
- Hidden assumption: The hand-built 16-word table, where reducible words were picked and given a reduced vowel and tail, stands in for a real lexicon. The 68.6% is mostly a property of that table, and the "most stanzas" generalization never leaves the toy.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-running on a real pronunciation dictionary (CMUdict) with a corpus-weighted end-word distribution, where reducible end words are a few percent of slots. If letters changed in under about 10% of stanzas, "most" fails. The same result would follow if the 68.6% fell sharply once reducible words were drawn at realistic frequency instead of uniformly.
- Break scenario: Hold the reduced forms fixed and add a "sung form" that differs from the reduced form: "gonna" held as "go-ahn-uh" or "wanna" sung as "wahn-ah". Also run reductions where full and reduced forms share a stressed vowel and tail ("them"→"'em" under a tail-only judge). If the letters shift or stay put contrary to the rule, then "sung form" is not one canonical form and the lettering depends on performance choices the table never modeled.

## E525 — stale fail tag turns ipm times d1 back into ipm only
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: When two 7 s cut-downs of a fixable-fail ad are ranked on IPM times a D1 predicted from a hand-copied fail-ending tag, the tag copied from the parent is stale on the clock cut (it lost the fail beat), both variants read as having it, the D1 term cancels and the ranking equals IPM-only in 441 of 441 grid cells, wrong in 213 of them; a tag derived from each cut's beats matched the measured IPM times D1 pick in 441 of 441, and with no fail effect on D1 all four rankers agreed.
- Why built: Three stored lessons meet in one workflow: rank variants on IPM times D1, cut by beats not clock because truncation drops the fail ending, and a hand-kept sidecar drifts silently. A cut-down pipeline would use all three at once.
- Design: Parent hook 2 s, gameplay 5 s, fail 3 s, end card 2 s; cut B by beats and cut C by clock. IPM is a sum of beat weights (gameplay weight swept 1.0 to 3.0), D1 is 0.18 plus a fail bonus (0 to 0.20) when the fail beat is present. Four rankers: IPM only, measured IPM times D1, stale copied tag, beats-derived tag; 21 by 21 cells.
- Got right: The derived tag removes the error completely, and the IPM-only versus measured gap opens as soon as the bonus is positive (first at gameplay weight 1.9 with bonus 0.01).
- Where/why it failed: The stale tag does not give a noisy estimate, it gives none: with the same tag on both variants D1 cancels, so a retention-aware metric silently degrades to the conversion-only one, which the earlier sandbox warned about only for the case of no retention signal. The result is close to true by construction once the tag is the only D1 input; the figure shows the failure shape, not a rate.
- Fix: Compute the fail-ending flag from each cut's own beat list (or measure D1 for the cut) every time a cut-down is made, and refuse a copied flag; check that the D1 input differs across the variants being compared.
- Why this fix: A derived flag cannot drift from the beats it describes, and a difference check catches the cancel case at once.
- Rule of thumb: A ranking metric that multiplies in a retention factor is only as good as the factor's per-variant input; if the input is a copied tag it can be identical across variants and turn the metric back into the one it was meant to fix, so derive it from the cut or assert it varies.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, counts above); IPM and D1 are made-up linear models, no real ad data was used.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, fail-ad-cutdowns-keep-the-gap/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the rule of thumb (check that a multiplied-in factor actually varies across variants) is sound, but the experiment is circular: the stale tag is stipulated to be constant and the derived tag reads the same feature that generates D1, so 441/441 shows the code is consistent, not that the failure occurs in practice.
- Hidden assumption: The "stale tag" failure is a property of copied tags in general, but the simulation hard-codes it: the stale tag is defined as "parent's tag, always says fail beat present", so cancellation of D1 is true by construction and 441/441 is a tautology, not evidence about how often real copied tags go stale (or whether real D1 depends on the fail beat the way the toy bonus does).
- Would prove it wrong: Run the real pipeline on actual cut-down pairs with their hand-copied tags: if the tags differ across variants in most pairs (cutters re-tag, or the clock cut keeps part of the fail beat), or if IPM-only already matches measured IPM×D1 on held-out ads with real D1 data, the "cancels to IPM-only" failure rarely occurs and the rule guards against a non-problem.
- Break scenario: Make D1 depend on something other than the fail beat (e.g., the end-card or hook length) with the fail beat still cut from C: the derived-tag ranker, which only reads fail-beat presence, then disagrees with measured IPM×D1 while the stale tag and IPM-only do no worse, so "derive it from the cut" stops being sufficient and the 441/441 match was an artifact of the D1 model being a function of exactly the tagged feature.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 5ffd58723e07
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__stale-fail-tag-turns-ipm-times-d1-back-into-ipm-only.py
- Prediction: Before running: the stale-tag ranker equals IPM-only in every cell, the derived-tag ranker equals the measured one in every cell, IPM-only is wrong in a positive share of cells, and a flat D1 makes all four agree.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS stale sidecar tag made IPM x D1 identical to IPM-only in 441/441 cells (wrong in 213) while a beats-derived tag matched measured in 441/441; flat D1 all agree=True
- Scenarios: 1) IPM-only versus measured IPM times D1 over the grid; 2) stale copied tag; 3) beats-derived tag; 4) flat D1 with bonus 0 (built to BREAK the claim that the retention factor matters to the pick).

## E524 — rng save migration new stream name keyed state words
- Date: 2026-10-20
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [determinism][rng][state][testing][sandbox]
- What: Loading an old save of per-stream PRNG state words into new code that inserted a stream in the middle keeps every old named stream exact (3/3) when streams are keyed by name, but the new stream restarts from its seed while the rest sit at tick 50, so it is out of step with a from-scratch run of the new code; index-keyed saves keep only 2/3 old streams; counter-based (name, tick) draws keep all and match from-scratch with 0 words saved.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel says save the state words, and the substream lessons say key streams by name; neither says what a save written by an older build does when a later build adds a stream. I wanted the migration case checked.
- Design: sfc32 streams seeded by FNV hash of master seed and name, three old streams A B C run 50 ticks then saved. New code has A B D C. Scenarios compare continuation over 20 ticks against the old code's own continuation and against a from-scratch run of the new code.
- Got right: Name-keyed load is exact for old streams, and index-keyed shifts C into the wrong slot (C diverged, A and B did not because the insert sat after them), which is why a partial check on early slots passes.
- Where/why it failed: My first expectation was that name-keyed state words fully solved migration. The new stream D diverged from the from-scratch run: a migrated world and a fresh world are different timelines for D even though no old stream moved.
- Fix: For streams that must agree between migrated and fresh worlds, draw by a counter key (master, name, tick) with no stored state; keep state words only for streams where a one-time timeline break on a new stream is acceptable.
- Why this fix: The counter form made the migrated D equal the from-scratch D (20 of 20 draws) and old streams unchanged, at the price of needing a tick or event index every draw.
- Rule of thumb: Name-keyed state-word saves protect old streams across an added stream but not equality with a fresh run for the new one; test migration against both the old continuation and a from-scratch run, and put cross-version-comparable streams on counter keys.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run (RESULT PASS, numbers above); real engines with floating or buffered state were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/a-shared-rng-stream-is-an-ordinal-space, brainwork/E259, name-keyed-substreams-survive-reorder-index-keyed-do-not/E1, sandbox-kernel-system-determinism/E3
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 3/3 vs 2/3 finding on old streams is solid, but "new stream differs from from-scratch" is a property of the unstated expectation and not of name keys, and the counter-based "0 words" advantage was tested only with one draw per tick.
- Hidden assumption: "From-scratch run of the new code" is the right ground truth for a migrated stream, so divergence counts as a defect. That assumes the new stream was meant to have existed since tick 0. A stream added at tick 50 has no history to match, and seeding it fresh at load is arguably correct, not a failure of name keys.
- Would prove it wrong: Fast-forwarding D by 50 draws on load, with no extra saved state, gives match=True under name keys. Then the divergence comes from the loader and not from name keying, and the rule's "put cross-version-comparable streams on counter keys" is unnecessary. Equally damaging: counter-based draws shown to be non-comparable once a stream consumes a variable number of draws per tick, since the tick key then no longer lines up.
- Break scenario: Draw counts vary per tick (stream B draws 0 to 3 values depending on state). Rerun scenarios 2 and 5. Name-keyed words stay exact for old streams, but counter-based (name, tick) draws now need a per-stream draw index that is itself saved state. The "0 words saved" claim fails, and the comparison with from-scratch for D changes with the fast-forward fix.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-20 · digest 1aaddbbac0cd
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-20__rng-save-migration-new-stream-name-keyed-state-words.py
- Prediction: Before running: name-keyed old streams 3/3 exact, index-keyed fewer than 3/3, counter-based all exact; I did not expect the new stream to differ from a from-scratch run.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS name-keyed save keeps 3/3 old streams exact but new stream D diverges from a from-scratch run (match=False); index-keyed keeps 2/3; counter-based keeps all and D matches (16 words saved vs 0)
- Scenarios: 1) same code name-keyed load; 2) new code with inserted stream, name-keyed; 3) migrated new stream versus from-scratch run (built to BREAK the claim that name keys fully solve migration); 4) index-keyed load into new code; 5) counter-based draws.

## E523 — two pass shape names cover few stanzas and one pass renames many
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Across 4096 four-line stanzas from an 8-word end pool, two-pass lettering fits one of the four named shapes (AABB, ABAB, ABBA, XXAA) in only 1010 (24.7%), and a one-pass any-rhyme-counts labeller names a different shape for 308 (30.5%) of those 1010; on a pool with no stray assonance the two labellers agree on all of them.
- Why built: The shape kernel reads emotional motion off the scheme, and the two-pass kernel and its exhaustive entry fix lettering, but nobody had measured how often a stanza even has a named shape or how often the labeller choice renames it.
- Design: Hand-built pool of perfect and assonance keys; two-pass (uppercase perfect groups, then lowercase assonance among leftovers, else x) vs one-pass (any perfect or assonant partner joins a group); shapes canonicalised by letter pattern with unrhymed lines as X; scenarios: full pool, no-assonance pool (built to BREAK the claim that the labeller always matters).
- Got right: Prediction held on three counts: coverage inside 5 to 25 percent (24.7%, at the edge), disagreement at least 15 percent (30.5%), and 0 disagreements on the no-assonance pool.
- Where/why it failed: Coverage landed right at the upper bound, so the band was barely met and the pool, not the method, drives it; the pool is small and hand-keyed, so the percentages do not transfer to real lyrics.
- Fix: When reporting emotional motion from a rhyme scheme, say whether the stanza matched a named shape at all, label with the two-pass rule, and do not rename a stanza using a one-pass label that lets assonance steal letters.
- Why this fix: A stray assonance pair gives one-pass groups that two-pass would leave open, so the same lines get a different named shape; the shape kernel only means something on the labelling the two-pass kernel defines.
- Rule of thumb: Only about a quarter of stanzas here (24.7%) fit a named shape at all and a one-pass labeller renames 30.5% of those, so read shape from two-pass uppercase letters and treat unnamed stanzas as unnamed rather than forcing a shape.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox over all 4096 stanzas; the pool and its phonetic keys are my own, the shape-to-emotion mapping itself is quoted from the kernel and not tested here.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 0-disagreement control only shows the labellers differ when assonance is present, and the 24.7% and 30.5% figures are artifacts of a hand-built pool, so they can't support a general rule of thumb.
- Hidden assumption: The 8-word hand-built pool, with its chosen mix of perfect and assonance keys, stands in for real verse. The 24.7% fit rate and 30.5% disagreement rate come from how many assonance pairs the author put in, not from anything about stanzas or labellers in general.
- Would prove it wrong: Rebuild the pool with a different assonance density, or sample from a real rhyme dictionary. If the fit rate leaves the 5–25% band, or the disagreement rate falls under 15%, the rule of thumb is a property of the pool and not of the method. The 24.7% is also 0.3 points under the band's ceiling, so one extra word could push it out.
- Break scenario: Run an all-perfect pool, where every end word has a perfect partner and assonance is absent or fully redundant. Then check the opposite pool, where every word has an assonance partner and few have perfect ones. The 0-disagreement scenario already shows the effect vanishes when assonance does. It doesn't show the 30.5% means anything outside this pool. The "treat unnamed stanzas as unnamed" advice is also untested, because no scenario checks whether forcing a shape does worse than leaving stanzas unnamed.

## E522 — reduced forms flip end rhymes and need whole word hyphen judge
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Writing reduced forms (gotta, lotta, wanna) before two-pass rhyme lettering changed the letters in 84.6% of 4096 four-line stanzas built from an 8-word end pool, while hyphenating those reduced forms was lettering-neutral under a whole-word judge and broke 45.8% under a last-segment judge.
- Why built: The three kernels were each tested only with their own neighbours; reduced forms at line ends had never been run through the hyphenate-to-slow step and the letter pass together.
- Design: Hand-built phonetic lexicon (perfect key plus assonance key) for 8 end phrases in full and reduced form; exhaustive 4096 stanzas; two-pass letters (perfect groups first, then lowercase assonance to a resolved group, else x); compare full vs reduced, reduced vs hyphenated-whole-word, reduced vs hyphenated-last-segment.
- Got right: Predicted reduction flips at least 10% (got 84.6%), whole-word hyphenation breaks 0 (got 0), last-segment breaks at least 10% (got 45.8%).
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the prediction failed, but the whole-word zero is partly by construction (the judge ignores hyphens), and the lexicon is hand-written, so the percentages depend on the pool, not on real lyrics.
- Fix: Letter the lyric as it will be sung (reduced form), strip hyphens or key the whole word before judging, and re-letter after any reduction pass instead of reusing letters from the full-form draft.
- Why this fix: Reduction changes the sounds the rhyme judge sees (got to ends in u, gotta in ota), so letters computed on the full form are stale; hyphen handling is a separate, solvable judge-scope issue.
- Rule of thumb: Letter rhymes on the written reduced form with hyphens stripped, and re-letter after every reduction or hyphenation pass, since reduction alone flipped letters in most stanzas of this pool.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox over all 4096 stanzas; the lexicon is my own simplification and real-lyric prevalence is untested.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 84.6% and 45.8% come from keys the author wrote by hand, so the test mostly checks that the lexicon differs between forms, and the hyphen result depends on which judge you choose rather than on anything about hyphens.
- Hidden assumption: The hand-built lexicon, with its perfect and assonance keys for reduced forms, matches how real rhyme judges treat "gotta/lotta/wanna", and the 8-word end pool is representative; the 84.6% is a property of that pool and the key assignments, not of reduction itself.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with a different or larger end pool, or with reduced-form keys assigned independently (a second annotator, or a pronunciation dictionary), and find the flip rate falls under 10%, or find that "hyphens stripped" lettering on the reduced form disagrees with the judge the pipeline actually uses.
- Break scenario: Build stanzas where the reduced form's key is identical to its full form's key (e.g. "gotta" and "got to" both end in the same vowel and consonant), so reduction should flip nothing. If letters still change, the lexicon is manufacturing the effect. Also run the last-segment judge on hyphenations that split inside the rhyming syllable, so the 45.8% is separated from the placement of the split.

## E521 — hyphen position decides whether a last segment judge breaks two pass letters
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: In 6561 exhaustive four-line stanzas from a 9-word end pool, a last-segment rhyme judge broke two-pass letters in 0 stanzas when the hyphens were word prefixes (re-turn, dis-turb) but in 3600 (54.9%) when they were suffix tails (burn-ing, morn-ing), so where the hyphen falls decides the damage.
- Why built: The companion entry showed a last-segment judge mislettering 27.3% of stanzas without asking which hyphen positions cause it; the lettering kernel and its exhaustive-stanza entry gave the baseline to compare against.
- Design: Hand-built lexicon of perfect and assonance keys for 9 end words, with segment keys for the pieces; two-pass lettering (perfect groups uppercase first, then lowercase assonance to a resolved group, else x); baseline letters from whole words; judge variants: whole-word, last-segment on prefix-hyphenated forms, on suffix-hyphenated forms, on both.
- Got right: Prediction held on all three numbers: prefix 0.0%, suffix at least 20% (got 54.9%), mixed pool equals the suffix result because prefix words add no breaks.
- Where/why it failed: The whole-word judge result of 0 is by construction (it ignores hyphens), so only the last-segment numbers are evidence; segment keys and the pool are my own simplification, not real lyrics.
- Fix: Before judging rhyme, rejoin hyphenated end words to the whole word (or confirm hyphens are only prefixes), and treat suffix-tail hyphens like -ing, -er, -ly as the dangerous case.
- Why this fix: A suffix segment such as ing carries a different rhyme from the word it ends, so a last-segment judge groups unrelated words, while a prefix leaves the rhyming tail intact.
- Rule of thumb: A last-segment rhyme judge only survives hyphenation that leaves the stressed rhyming tail in the final segment, so rejoin end words before lettering rather than trusting prefix-only hyphens in real lyrics.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox over all 6561 stanzas; the phonetic keys are my own hand-built lexicon and real-lyric prevalence is untested.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 0% vs 54.9% contrast is real inside this lexicon, but a PASS against a prediction the author set with their own hand-built keys doesn't show that hyphen position, as opposed to key assignment, causes the damage. The rule also overreaches by calling prefix-only hyphens safe in "real lyrics" when the test never used real lyrics.
- Hidden assumption: The result comes from a hand-built lexicon where the author chose the segment keys, so "prefix survives, suffix breaks" may just reflect how those keys were assigned. It also assumes real lyric hyphens fall at the same points as in the 9-word pool, and that the last-segment judge is the only way a hyphenated word gets judged.
- Would prove it wrong: A prefix-hyphenated word whose last segment loses its rhyme key, such as a hyphen inside the stressed syllable or a multi-prefix word like "un-re-turn-ing". If the last-segment judge breaks lettering there, or a suffix hyphen sits after the stressed tail and doesn't break it, then the rule is about key assignment and not hyphen position.
- Break scenario: Take a different 9-word pool, ideally one drawn from real lyrics with the lexicon built by an independent annotator or a pronunciation dictionary. Include suffix-only words where the stressed tail stays in the last segment (e.g. "turn-ed", where "-ed" is silent). Also include prefix words where the final segment is an unstressed stem. If prefix breaks come out above 0% or suffix breaks below 20%, the rule fails.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 012ac44da455
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__hyphen-position-decides-whether-a-last-segment-judge-breaks-two-pass-letters.py

- Observed: RESULT: PASS prefix last-seg 0.0%, suffix last-seg 54.9%, mixed 54.9%, whole-word 0 (3600 of 6561 stanzas).
- Scenarios: 1) prefix-hyphenated end words, last-segment judge; 2) suffix-tail hyphenated end words, last-segment judge (built to BREAK the claim that any hyphenation harms the judge); 3) mixed pool; 4) whole-word judge on both

## E520 — hidden parameter error budget is tightest for solder then bolt then cure
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [numerics][sandbox][model][tolerance]
- What: Measuring how much relative error the hidden parameter behind a quoted spec can take before the spec fails gave solder 2.8% (pad conduction fraction at a 350 C tip, steady state 187.5 C against liquidus 183 C), bolt torque 6.2% (nut factor, before an 8.8 bolt at spec torque reaches yield), and cure dose 28.0% (weight base, before nitrite passes a 200 ppm ceiling); a 400 C tip widened the solder budget to 15.7%.
- Why built: Three entries each show a spec hiding a parameter; none compares how forgiving each is, which decides where a bench check is mandatory versus optional.
- Design: Closed-form margins: solder (frac - need)/frac with need = (183-25)/(tip-25); bolt 1 - proof/yield for a 600 over 640 MPa bolt; cure 200/156.25 - 1. Scenarios: solder at 350 C, solder at 400 C (built to BREAK the claim that solder is always the tightest), bolt, cure.
- Got right: The ordering solder < bolt < cure and the 28% cure margin held; the budget is a single number per system that ranks where to verify first.
- Where/why it failed: The 200 ppm ceiling and the proof and yield strengths are my assumed figures, so the absolute budgets move with them; only the ordering was tested for sensitivity to the tip change, not to the other assumptions.
- Fix: Compute the error budget of the hidden parameter before trusting a quoted spec, and spend verification effort on the smallest budget first (preheat or a bigger tip for solder before anything else).
- Why this fix: A spec fails when its hidden parameter drifts by more than its margin, so the margin in relative terms is the common currency across unrelated systems and the smallest one is where drift is most likely to bite.
- Rule of thumb: Rank specs by the relative error their hidden parameter can absorb (solder 2.8%, bolt 6.2%, cure 28.0% here) and verify the tightest first, but recompute when a knob such as tip temperature moves the margin (15.7% at 400 C).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the closed-form sandbox; the liquidus, yield-to-proof ratio and the 200 ppm ceiling are recalled figures I did not check against a standard.
- Composed: curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, fastener-torque-spec-assumes-its-friction-factor-lubricated-bolt-reaches-proof-load/E1, solder-joint-steady-state-decides-not-dwell-time/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The arithmetic is sound, but the ordering is set by the chosen inputs and the 5.6x swing from one knob already shows it, so "verify the tightest first" only helps if the budgets are recomputed for each case, which the rule's own caveat concedes.
- Hidden assumption: The three "hidden parameters" (pad conduction fraction, nut factor, weight base) are comparable as relative-error budgets, which also assumes each model's own inputs (tip temperature, 8.8 yield of 640 MPa, 200 ppm ceiling) are fixed and exact. The ranking is then a property of three hand-picked parameter values, not of the specs themselves.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-running with a different but equally defensible operating point reorders the list. Examples: a 380 C tip (solder budget about 10%) with a 12.9 grade bolt, or a measured nut factor spread of ±25% against a cure base with a ±5% weighing tolerance. Any ordering that flips without a design change would show the rank reflects the chosen inputs, not the specs.
- Break scenario: Hold solder at 350 C and move the bolt to a 10.9 grade, with torque still set for 8.8 (proof/yield ratio unchanged, so budget is about 6.2% or wider), then make the cure ceiling 160 ppm, so the cure budget is 160/156.25 - 1 = 2.4%. Cure becomes tighter than solder (2.8%) and the order is cure < solder < bolt. The 400 C case already shows a knob can move one budget by 5.6x, so the same can happen to the others.

## E519 — counter keyed rolls survive extra consumers but collide on reused keys
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][determinism][testing][sandbox]
- What: Counter-keyed rolls (hash of seed, entity, tick, purpose) changed 0 of 200 attack outcomes when an extra cosmetic consumer was added and the evaluation order was reversed, where a shared sfc32 stream flipped 48.5% (about chance for a fair coin); but leaving the purpose out of the key made attack and crit rolls identical, so joint hit-and-crit was 49.0% instead of 29.0% with purpose-keyed rolls.
- Why built: The seeded-RNG kernel and its entries say to split streams per mechanic; this tested the stateless alternative of addressing each roll symbolically, which the ordinal-space kernel recommends, to see what it fixes and what it breaks.
- Design: 20 entities by 10 ticks; shared stream (sfc32 with 12 warmup draws, extra consumer every seventh entity) vs a keyed FNV-style hash with avalanche mixing; scenarios: shared stream plus extra consumer; keyed with extra consumer and reversed order; keyed with the purpose omitted (built to BREAK the claim that keyed rolls are always independent); save size 4 words vs 1.
- Got right: Keyed rolls are order- and consumer-independent (0 flips) and need only the seed saved; the shared stream really is coupled.
- Where/why it failed: Run 1 predicted at least 50% flips on the shared stream and got 48.5%; a boolean outcome at p 0.5 flips about 50% under full decorrelation, so the threshold was wrong, not the stream, and run 2 used 40 to 60 percent. Run 2 passed; two iterations.
- Fix: Key every roll by entity, tick and a purpose name, never by order, and give each distinct decision its own purpose string; keep the seed as the only saved word.
- Why this fix: Independence of rolls comes from distinct keys, so a missing key component silently correlates rolls (49.0% joint against 29.0% when purposes differ), while order and extra consumers can no longer matter.
- Rule of thumb: Counter-keyed rolls fix extra-consumer and order coupling (0 of 200 flips against 48.5% on a shared stream) only if every distinct decision has its own key part; omit the purpose and two rolls become one.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox twice (the first run failed its own threshold); the hash is a toy mixer, not tested for statistical quality, and outcomes were 200 rolls in one fixture.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/a-shared-rng-stream-is-an-ordinal-space-address-it-symbolically, local__sandbox-seeded-rng-state-words/E1
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__counter-keyed-rolls-survive-extra-consumers-but-collide-on-reused-keys.py
- Prediction: Shared stream flips 40 to 60 percent of 200 outcomes; keyed rolls flip 0 under extra consumers and reversed order; an omitted purpose gives joint hit-and-crit near 50 percent versus under 35 percent keyed.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS shared stream flips 48.5% of 200 rolls, counter-keyed 0, reused key joint 49.0% vs 29.0%
- Scenarios: 1) shared stream plus extra consumer; 2) keyed rolls with extra consumer and reversed order; 3) keyed rolls with the purpose omitted (BREAK)
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 1, session_014pWETJKxgid7E3P5KtDPoT

## E518 — cheese yield forecast moves more with moisture than with milk fat
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [cheesemaking][sandbox][numerics][model]
- What: New domain CHEESEMAKING seeded from a cheddar yield forecast with a Van Slyke-style formula, Y = (0.93 F + C - 0.1) x 1.09 / (1 - M): 100 kg of 3.5% fat, 2.5% casein milk at 37% cheese moisture gives 9.78 kg, one more point of moisture adds 1.61% yield, one more point of milk fat adds 16.45%, so a moisture point is worth only 0.10 fat points, and in fresh cheese (75% moisture) one moisture point adds 4.17%.
- Why built: Seeding a domain with no records; a cheesemaker forecasting yield needs to know which hidden input (moisture of the finished cheese versus milk fat) dominates the forecast error.
- Design: Closed-form formula with F, C and M as parameters; scenarios: baseline cheddar, plus 1 point moisture, plus 1 point fat, and fresh cheese at 75 to 76% moisture (built to BREAK the claim that moisture is a small effect everywhere).
- Got right: The model computes yield from composition, and the break scenario confirmed the sensitivity to moisture grows steeply with moisture (4.17% per point at 75% against 1.61% at 37%).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction missed twice: I expected a 9.2 kg baseline (the formula gives 9.78) and that a moisture point equals about 0.25 fat points (it is 0.10), so the sandbox printed RESULT: FAIL; I kept the original prediction rather than rewrite it after the run.
- Fix: When forecasting cheddar yield, put effort into measuring milk fat and casein first and treat moisture as a second-order input, but reverse that for high-moisture cheeses where moisture dominates.
- Why this fix: The formula divides by one minus moisture, which is nearly flat near 0.37 and steep near 0.75, so the same one-point error costs 1.6% yield at one end and 4.2% at the other.
- Rule of thumb: In a Van Slyke-style yield forecast a one-point moisture error is worth 0.10 milk-fat points for cheddar (1.61% yield) but 4.17% yield for a 75% moisture cheese, so measure fat and casein first for hard cheese and moisture first for fresh cheese.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the closed-form sandbox; the formula's coefficients are recalled published values I did not re-check, and the model is a hand-written estimate, not tested against real cheese yields. No adjacent kernel or lesson in Brain, so this entry is isolated and cites nothing.

- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__cheese-yield-forecast-moves-more-with-moisture-than-with-milk-fat.py
- Prediction: Baseline about 9.2 kg per 100 kg milk; a one-point moisture rise adds about 1.6% yield and equals about 0.25 milk-fat points; at 75% moisture one point moves yield over twice as much.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL base 9.78 kg/100kg; 1pt moisture 1.61% = 0.10 fat points; fresh cheese 4.17% (baseline and fat-equivalence predictions missed; moisture sensitivity and fresh-cheese break held)

## E517 — rejoin all hyphens lettering breaks stutter end words
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][lyrics][simulation][testing]
- What: Rhyme lettering over end words that carry both hyphen meanings (timing marks inside one word, stutter repeats of a word). Three views of the token were lettered against a lexicon judge: last fragment, rejoin all hyphens, and rejoin after collapsing repeated fragments.
- Why built: The hyphenate-to-slow kernel says hyphenate crowded words, the two-pass lettering lesson says rejoin hyphens first, and the title-matcher lesson says hyphens also mean stutter. Nobody had run the three together on one stanza set.
- Design: Lexicon judge with rhyme keys (unknown strings get a unique key, so no false rhyme). 3 stanza pools in AABB and ABAB orders: timing-only (192 stanzas), stutter-only (96), mixed (72). Truth is the real word (timing hyphens joined, stutter repeats collapsed).
- Got right: Rejoin-all was perfect on timing hyphens (192/192) and the last fragment was perfect on stutter (96/96). Collapse-then-rejoin was perfect on all three pools (192/192, 96/96, 72/72).
- Where/why it failed: Rejoin-all lettered 0/96 stutter and 0/72 mixed stanzas correctly, because run-run-run becomes runrunrun, a string the judge does not know, so the rhyme with sun vanishes. The last fragment lettered only 48/192 timing stanzas correctly (ba-by read as by).
- Fix: Collapse a token whose fragments are all identical to one word, then rejoin the rest, before lettering.
- Why this fix: The two hyphen meanings are told apart by structure (identical repeated fragments versus distinct syllable pieces), so one cheap rule serves both views. Lexicon limit: with a phonetic judge the rejoin-all failure may be smaller.
- Rule of thumb: Before lettering rhymes, rejoin timing hyphens but first collapse identical-fragment stutter tokens; a blanket rejoin kept 0 of 168 stutter stanzas and a last-fragment read kept 48 of 192 timing stanzas.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script. Limit of the test: the judge is a small lexicon, so a real phonetic rhymer was not tried.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-title-matcher-stutter-split-vs-timing-hyphen-join/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 360 stanzas were built so that stutter always means an exact repeat and timing never does, so the 100% result confirms the generator's convention rather than the rule, and the 0/168 and 48/192 figures only show that each naive view fails on the pool made to defeat it.
- Hidden assumption: A token's hyphens can be told apart by form alone (identical repeated fragments mean stutter, anything else means timing), so a timing split like "ta-ta" or "pa-pa-ya" is never mistaken for a stutter, and a stutter is always a clean exact repeat.
- Would prove it wrong: Collapse-then-rejoin scoring below 100% on a pool where a real word has identical adjacent fragments ("tu-tu", "bon-bon", "mama" lettered "ma-ma") or a stutter has non-identical fragments ("w-wa-water"). Either one would show the form test misclassifies real tokens.
- Break scenario: A timing-hyphenated word whose true spelling repeats a fragment ("bon-bon", "tu-tu", "pa-pa-ya"), plus stutters that differ from their word ("s-s-sun", "w-wa-water") and stutters of a multi-fragment word ("sun-sun-set"), all placed on rhyme-bearing end words in AABB and ABAB.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest ae37a8111016
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__rejoin-all-hyphens-lettering-breaks-stutter-end-words.py
- Prediction: Rejoin-all perfect on timing and wrong on every stutter stanza, last fragment the reverse, collapse-then-rejoin perfect on all three pools.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS rejoin timing 192/192, rejoin stutter 0/96, last-fragment stutter 96/96, smart ['192/192', '96/96', '72/72']
- Scenarios: 1) timing-only hyphens; 2) stutter-only repeats; 3) mixed timing plus stutter pools, built to BREAK the rejoin-all rule from the earlier lesson
