## E516 — reduced line ends need the sung form before two pass rhyme lettering
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][lyrics][simulation][testing]
- What: Two-pass rhyme lettering of 495 four-word stanzas whose end words may be sung reduced forms (gonna, wanna, gotta, kinda). A spelling judge reading the sung form was wrong in 95 stanzas (19.2 percent), the same judge reading the written full form (to, of) in 364 (73.5 percent), and a last-segment read of the pacing-hyphen form (gon-na, ba-na-na) in 465 (93.9 percent). Rejoining the hyphens gave back exactly the sung-form figure, 95.
- Why built: The reduced-form kernel says write the form you will sing, the hyphenate kernel says add pacing hyphens, and the two-pass lesson says letter the rhyme. Untested together: which form of a reduced end word should the lettering read?
- Design: 12 end words with hand-set true rime and assonance classes; spelling judge with a feminine -a rule (rime from the stressed vowel) and four irregular words overridden; truth is the sung class; four views fed to the same two-pass lettering, compared by canonical scheme shape.
- Got right: Rejoin equalled the sung form (95 and 95), the written full form was perfect on unreduced words (0 of 70 wrong), and the ordering sung < written < last-segment held.
- Where/why it failed: I predicted the sung-form judge would be wrong in under 15 percent of stanzas; it was 19.2 percent because wanna is spelled -anna while it rhymes with gonna and Donna (-onna), a spelling gap no hyphen handling can fix. Earlier runs also failed (99.4 percent everywhere) until I fixed the judge's rime rule, so the first figures were a judge bug, not a finding.
- Fix: Letter on the sung (reduced) form rejoined from any pacing hyphens; never on the written full form or on the last hyphen segment; keep a small table for spellings like wanna that the spelling rule gets wrong.
- Why this fix: The full form puts a different word (to, of) at the line end, so the judge reads a rhyme the singer never delivers, and a last segment (na) merges every -a word into one group.
- Rule of thumb: Judge rhyme on the rejoined sung form: for reduced line ends the written full form lettered 73.5 percent of stanzas wrong and a last-segment hyphen read 93.9 percent, against 19.2 percent for the sung form, which a wanna-style table can lower.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the 12-word lexicon, the toy spelling judge and the sung classes are my own hand-set choices, not measured vocals.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, ideas:SONGWRITING/write-the-reduced-form-you-will-sing
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the ordering holds in the data, but 19.2 percent wrong is far from reliable, the under-15 prediction missed, the 12-word design and the truth-equals-sung-class setup make the "written form is the problem" claim partly circular, and the 0/70 control shows only that unreduced words are fine, not that rejoining generalizes.
- Hidden assumption: The sung-form judge's 19.2 percent error is a property of judging on sung forms, when it comes from 12 hand-set classes and a spelling judge with four patched irregulars, so the ranking (sung < written < last-segment) may only hold for this word list and says nothing about real lyrics or other reduced forms.
- Would prove it wrong: A held-out set of reduced end words outside the 12 (gimme, lemme, c'mon, ya, outta), with sung classes set before any judge is run, in which the written full form errs no more often than the sung form, or the sung-form error rises past the written-form error.
- Break scenario: Stanzas whose end words are reduced forms that rhyme in the sung class and also share spelling with their full forms (gotta against "got a", wanna against "want a"), run with the feminine -a rule switched off and the four overrides removed, to see whether the 19.2 percent is leftover judge patching that the rule of thumb then credits to the sung form.

## E515 — last segment judge damage lands in the perfect pass not the assonance link
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][lyrics][simulation][testing]
- What: Whether a last-segment rhyme judge breaks two-pass lettering depends on where the timing hyphen falls. With hyphens before the rime (to-night, a-way) the last segment lettered all 8855 four-word stanzas the same as the whole word; with hyphens inside the rime (fi-re, lo-ve, star-t) 4989 of 8855 (56.3 percent) came out different, 4440 of them in the perfect pass and 549 only in the assonance link.
- Why built: The kernel says hyphenate to slow a rushed line, the two-pass lesson says perfect groups never merge but assonance can be hidden, and the end-word lesson says only a last-segment judge breaks it. Question: is the damage in the perfect pass or the assonance link, and does it need a hyphen inside the rime?
- Design: 22 end words with true rime and assonance classes; spelling judge (rime from the last vowel group, silent e skipped); all 4-word combinations; lettering pass 1 uppercase perfect groups, pass 2 lowercase assonance link to a resolved group; whole-word view against last-segment view of identical tokens in two hyphenation styles.
- Got right: The first iteration compared both views to a hand-written truth and showed an identical 18.0 percent error for whole and last (1593 of 8855), which exposed that the spelling judge itself errs on leave versus believe; comparing views of the same tokens removed that confound.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction (a last-segment judge costs 20 percent or more, mostly in the perfect pass) was wrong on the first run: the damage was zero because the boundary hyphens left the rime intact in the last segment. It only appears once the hyphen splits the rime.
- Fix: Judge on the rejoined word (or on the segment containing the rime vowel), and treat the hyphen position, not the hyphen, as the risk; hyphenate at syllable boundaries ahead of the rime where the line allows.
- Why this fix: A last-segment read keeps only the text after the final hyphen, so it keeps the rime exactly when the final hyphen falls before the last vowel group and loses it when the hyphen falls inside the rime.
- Rule of thumb: A last-segment rhyme judge broke 0 of 8855 stanzas with boundary hyphens but 4989 (56.3 percent) with hyphens inside the rime, mostly the perfect pass, so rejoin end words before judging whenever pacing hyphens may split the rime.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the lexicon is 22 hand-classed words and a toy spelling judge, so real phonetic judges are assumed, not tested.

## E514 — hidden base error dwarfs dilution step choice in a cure dose
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lab-dilution][curing][fastener-torque][sandbox][numerics][model]
- What: A cure dose prepared by serial dilution carries two stacked errors: the pipette floor error of the dilution plan and the hidden base of the quoted percent (meat versus meat plus brine). The sandbox ran the dilution step count against the base mismatch, then applied the torque lesson's fix of scaling the spec by assumed over actual.
- Why built: The dilution lesson says pick the step count by a pipette-floor crossover, the curing lesson says the percent needs its weight base, and the torque lesson says scale a quoted spec by the ratio of its assumed condition to the real one. Untested together, someone could spend effort tuning steps while a 25 percent base error sits unnoticed.
- Design: 1000x dilution, 1000 uL bulk per step, pipette error max(0.5 percent, 0.02 uL over pick volume), worst case multiplied over steps; 1000 g meat plus 250 g brine; tolerance 10 percent on the dose judged against meat mass; plans of 1, 2 and 3 steps.
- Got right: With the right base the plans cost 2.00 percent (1 step), 1.00 percent (2 steps), 1.51 percent (3 steps), all inside tolerance. Ratio-scaling the spec took the wrong-base case back to 2.00 and 1.00 percent.
- Where/why it failed: With the wrong base the total worst error was 27.00 percent (1 step) and 26.00 percent (2 steps), so no step count rescued it; the base shift (25 percent) was 12.5 to 25 times the pipette term. Step choice only decided the outcome at a 1.5 percent tolerance, where only 2 steps passed.
- Fix: Settle the weight base first and scale the quoted dose by assumed base over actual base, and only then choose the dilution step count by the pipette-floor crossover.
- Why this fix: The base error is systematic and large while the pipette error is a small random-bound term, so fixing the larger one first is the only order in which the step choice can matter.
- Rule of thumb: With picks of 30 uL or more and a 25 percent base gap, fix the spec's hidden base before tuning dilution steps: a 25 percent base error left 26 to 27 percent total error under every plan tried, while step choice moved the total by only 1 point.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the pipette model parameters and the 250 g brine figure are my chosen values, and real pipette specs are assumed, not measured.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__serial-dilution-step-count-worst-case-error-crossover-with-pipette-floor/E1, curing-dose-base-meat-weight-not-total/E1, fastener-torque-spec-assumes-its-friction-factor-lubricated-bolt-reaches-proof-load/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — it holds only inside the tested regime (picks of 30 uL or more, 10% tolerance, worst-case error stacking), and the sandbox never swept pick volume or tolerance enough to show where the base-first ordering flips. The 1-point spread is a property of those parameters, not a general finding.
- Hidden assumption: Pipette error is the same size in practice as the worst-case spec (max of 0.5% or 0.02 uL over pick volume), added linearly over steps, and the 25% base gap is a fixed, known ratio. The rule's "base dominates" holds only while the pipette term stays under about 2%, which the picks of 30 uL or more were chosen to guarantee.
- Would prove it wrong: A run in which a pick below 30 uL, or a deeper plan, pushes the pipette term close to or above the base gap. At picks near 4 uL, 0.02/4 is 0.5% per step, so a 1-step plan would show about 3-4% pipette error while the 25% base gap stays the same. Or a run where the wrong-base total varies by more than about 1 point across plans.
- Break scenario: Keep the 25% base gap but drop the picks to a few uL, for example a 10 uL pick at 1 uL bulk. Then pipette error becomes 2-5% per step and compounds across 3 steps. Add a 1.5% tolerance after ratio-scaling, as your scenario 4 already does. The pipette term is the only thing left, so step choice decides pass or fail. Your own observation ("at 1.5% tol only [2] steps pass") already shows base is not the whole story once the base is fixed.

## E513 — darts three dart checkout misses seven scores and one trusted double still finishes two thirds
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [darts][sandbox][checkout][enumeration]
- What: Enumerating double-out darts (finish on a double, a score of 1 or below zero is a bust) shows 21 one-dart finishes, 102 two-dart finishes and 162 of the 169 scores from 2 to 170 finishing in three darts; the seven that cannot are 159, 162, 163, 165, 166, 168 and 169. A player who trusts only D16 as the finishing double still finishes 112 of 169.
- Why built: Seeding a new DARTS domain from the standard 501 double-out rules, which are public and exactly checkable, so later sessions can look for gaps in it.
- Design: Segments are singles 1 to 20 plus 25, doubles 2 to 40 plus 50, trebles 3 to 60; a recursive search asks whether a score can be reduced to a double in at most the given darts, rejecting any leave under 2. A second run restricts the last dart to D16 and a third allows D16, D8 and D4.
- Got right: The one-dart count (21), the three-dart count (162) and the exact list of seven impossible scores all matched the prediction written before the run.
- Where/why it failed: I predicted that a D16-only player would finish fewer than 90 scores; the run gave 112, because trebles and singles let nearly any score be reduced onto 32 or onto a leave whose half is a double.
- Fix: When planning a checkout for a player with one trusted double, count the reachable leaves on that double with the same search rather than assuming the finishable set collapses; add D8 and D4 for 136.
- Why this fix: The search computes finishability instead of recalling a chart, so it adapts to any restricted double set and any dart count.
- Rule of thumb: Compute checkout reachability by search over the real segment set: three darts finish 162 of 169 scores (seven impossible) and one trusted double alone still reaches 112, so a restricted-double player loses a third, not a half.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; board layout and rules are the standard 501 ones, and I did not measure any real player's hit rates.

## E512 — curling end score by rank order averages eight ninths and two or more is seven thirtieths
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [curling][sandbox][scoring][enumeration]
- What: Under curling's scoring rule (only the team nearest the button scores, one point per stone nearer than the opponent's best), if all 12870 ways the 16 distance ranks can split 8 and 8 are equally likely, a team scores at least 1 point with probability 1/2, at least 2 with 7/30 (23.3 percent), at least 3 with 0.1, and averages 8/9 (0.889) points per end; an 8-point end is 1 in 12870.
- Why built: Seeding a new CURLING domain from a rule set that is public and exactly checkable, giving a baseline against which later sessions can judge hammer and blank-end choices.
- Design: Exact enumeration of every choice of 8 of 16 ranks for team A with Fractions; the score is the run of A ranks from the top; no ties, no strategy, no stone interaction.
- Got right: Every prediction held exactly: P(at least 1) = 1/2, P(at least 2) = 7/30, mean 8/9, A scores 0 in 6435 of 12870 and 8 points once.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed, but the model is only the scoring rule: real stones are not exchangeable (the hammer throws last, guards shape placements), so these numbers are a chance baseline, not a prediction of real ends.
- Fix: Use 7/30 as the chance level for a 2-or-more end when judging whether a strategy beats luck, and compare any hammer-advantage claim against it.
- Why this fix: Exact enumeration gives the null distribution with no sampling noise, so any gap a later model shows is the strategy and not the baseline.
- Rule of thumb: Under random rank order a curling end scores 2 or more for a given team only 7/30 of the time (mean 8/9 points), so treat roughly 23 percent as the luck baseline for 2-plus ends.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the exact enumeration; the equal-likelihood rank order is an assumption of the null model, not a measurement of real curling.
- Composed: N/A

## E511 — tire pressure temperature drop scales with absolute not gauge pressure
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tire-pressure][physics][model][sandbox]
- What: New domain seed (tire pressure). For a tire set cold in a 70 F garage and driven at 20 F, an ideal-gas model at fixed volume gives a gauge drop of 3.28 psi at 20 psi, 4.69 at 35 psi and 8.94 at 80 psi; scaling the gauge reading by the temperature ratio understates the drop by 42, 30 and 16 percent, and the one psi per ten degrees rule is +7 percent at 35 psi but -44 percent at 80.
- Why built: Seeding a domain with no entries from a real situation: setting pressure in a warm garage and checking it outside. Gas-law shortcuts are easy to apply to the gauge number by mistake.
- Design: P_abs/T_abs constant with atmospheric 14.7 psi and Rankine temperatures; true gauge drop compared with the gauge-ratio shortcut and the fixed 5 psi per 50 F rule at three set pressures; a hot case from 70 F to 110 F as a side check (3.75 psi rise at 35 psi).
- Got right: At 35 psi the true drop (4.69 psi, 0.94 psi per ten degrees) is within 7 percent of the common rule; the shortcut is 30 percent low there.
- Where/why it failed: My written prediction used mental arithmetic and was off for the others (3.2 and 8.6 against 3.28 and 8.94), so the sandbox's first RESULT line is FAIL; the model itself is simple physics. Not modelled: wheel volume change, air leakage, humidity, driving heat.
- Fix: Convert to absolute pressure before applying the temperature ratio, or scale the quoted drop by (gauge + 14.7) / 49.7 relative to a 35 psi tire.
- Why this fix: The gas law relates absolute pressure and absolute temperature; the gauge excludes the roughly 14.7 psi of atmosphere that also changes with the same ratio.
- Rule of thumb: Tire pressure change per degree scales with absolute pressure (about 0.94 psi per ten degrees F at 35 psi, 1.8 at 80), so use one rule per pressure class and never apply the temperature ratio to the gauge number.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; an ideal-gas model only, no tire or gauge was measured.
- Composed: N/A

- Observed: RESULT: FAIL drop 70F to 20F: 20psi 3.28, 35psi 4.69, 80psi 8.94; gauge-ratio shortcut 3.30 at 35 psi; 1psi/10F rule +7% at 35 and -44% at 80

## E510 — self focused feedback lowers delayed retention at every spacing gap but does not move the best gap
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [teaching][feedback][model][testing]
- What: In the spacing model from the desirable-difficulty sandbox, adding a feedback-focus share s (attention to the self) lowered delayed retention at every gap, but my prediction that it would only rescale retention and leave the best gap at 4 was refuted: task-focused feedback (s=0) peaked at gap 8 (0.3945), s=0.5 at gap 4 (0.1834) and pure self focus (s=1) at gap 4 (0.0355).
- Why built: Gap pick on the kernel that feedback aimed at the self often backfires (over a third of interventions lowered performance in the cited meta-analysis). Question: does the kernel's effect interact with the spacing lesson, or just scale it?
- Design: Reused the expected-value spacing model (recall exp(-gap/S), success gain G, failure re-study gain F, 5 studies, retention at delay 40) and added per-study feedback: self share s cuts the success gain by 0.6*s and task share boosts the failure re-study gain by (1-s). Gaps 0 to 64, s in 0, 0.5, 1. All parameters are mine.
- Got right: Retention ordered s=0 > s=0.5 > s=1 at all 8 gaps; at massed practice (gap 0, near-certain recall) the focus spread was 0.0000, as predicted, because there are no failures for the feedback to act on. Largest spread 0.3747 at gap 8.
- Where/why it failed: The best gap is not invariant: good feedback lets the learner profit from a harder, longer gap (8) because failed recalls are re-studied well; with self-focused feedback failures teach little, so the model prefers the easier gap 4. The kernel's effect is therefore a shift in the optimum, not just a scale.
- Fix: Choose the spacing gap together with the feedback style: task-focused feedback supports longer gaps, and praise-style feedback should be paired with shorter, easier gaps.
- Why this fix: The longer gap pays through failed retrievals, and only task-directed feedback converts a failure into learning.
- Rule of thumb: Do not tune spacing and feedback separately: in this model task-focused feedback moved the best gap from 4 to 8 and raised peak retention about 11 times over pure self focus (0.3945 against 0.0355).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the gains, the 0.6 and 1.0 weights and the model structure are my assumptions standing in for the meta-analysis, which is quoted from the kernel and not re-read.
- Composed: ideas:TEACHING/feedback/task-vs-self/feedback-that-targets-the-self-rather-than-the-task-often-backfires, sandbox-desirable-difficulty/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the finding that the feedback condition moved the best gap is a real refutation of your prediction in this model, but "don't tune separately" is a claim about learning that a single self-built model with unvalidated constants and a 4-to-8 shift on a coarse grid cannot support.
- Hidden assumption: The rule treats a result from one hand-picked parameterization (0.6 self penalty, a task boost of exactly (1-s), 5 studies, delay 40) as a property of feedback and spacing, when the 8-vs-4 shift and the "11 times" ratio may just reflect those constants and a coarse gap grid (0, 4, 8, ... 64).
- Would prove it wrong: Sweeping the 0.6 penalty, the task-boost weight and the delay, on a finer gap grid, and finding the s=0 best gap lands anywhere from 4 to 8 depending on the constants, or the peak ratio falls from ~11x to ~2x under modest changes. That would show the interaction is an artifact of the chosen numbers. A best gap that flips between neighbouring grid points with a near-flat curve would do the same.
- Break scenario: Hold s fixed at 0 and move the retention delay from 40 to 10, then to 200. If the best gap tracks the delay, as expected from exp(-gap/S) alone, then the shift to 8 comes from the delay and not from the feedback focus. Also run s=0.5 with the self penalty at 0.3 and at 0.9. If the best gap moves with that constant, the rule is describing the penalty, not an interaction.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest dbf3bf14edaa

- Observed: RESULT: FAIL ordered at 8/8 gaps, best gaps [8, 4, 4], massed spread 0.0000, max spread 0.3747

## E509 — prefermented flour moves total hydration away from the stated dough hydration
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [baking][formula][model][sandbox]
- What: New domain seed (bread formulas). A loaf written as 75 percent hydration with the levain kept separate has a different total hydration: with a 100 percent levain holding 10, 20 and 30 percent of the flour, total hydration is 77.5, 80.0 and 82.5 percent; a stiff 50 percent levain at 20 percent flour gives 70.0.
- Why built: Seeding a domain that has no kernels. A real scenario: a country loaf scaled by its stated hydration, where the pre-fermented flour and water are weighed apart and so are easy to leave out of the percentage.
- Design: Baker's percentages with a pre-fermented flour share p, dough-only hydration Hd and levain hydration Hl; total hydration = (1-p)*Hd + p*Hl, checked against gram weights on 1000 g of total flour, then inverted to find the dough hydration that hits a 75 percent total.
- Got right: The weights and the formula agree in all six runs; to hold 75 percent total with a 20 percent, 100 percent levain the dough alone must be hydrated to 68.75 percent.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed, but this is arithmetic on a hand model: it shows the bookkeeping trap, not how any dough handles, and the 100 percent and 50 percent levains are chosen values.
- Fix: State hydration as total (all flour and water including pre-ferments) and derive the dough-only water from it with Hd = (target - p*Hl)/(1-p).
- Why this fix: The levain carries water at its own ratio, so the blended figure moves toward Hl by the share p of flour it holds; inverting the blend removes the guesswork.
- Rule of thumb: Hydration quoted for the final dough alone is off by p*(Hl-Hd) in total; compute total hydration from all flour and water, and flip the correction's sign when the levain is stiffer than the dough.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; only the algebra and weights were checked, no actual dough or published formula was measured.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__prefermented-flour-moves-total-hydration-away-from-the-stated-dough-hydration.py
- Prediction: Total hydration 77.5, 80.0 and 82.5 percent at 10, 20 and 30 percent of 100 percent levain with Hd 0.75, 70.0 percent for a 50 percent levain at 20, and a needed dough hydration of 0.6875.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS total hydration 77.5/80.0/82.5% for 10/20/30% 100%-levain, stiff levain 70.0%, needed dough hydration 0.6875
- Scenarios: 1) 100 percent levain at 10 percent flour; 2) at 20 percent; 3) at 30 percent; 4) BREAK: stiff 50 percent levain where the error flips sign; 5) inverse solve for a 75 percent total

## E508 — one hyphen normalisation cannot serve both rhyme lettering and title matching
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][lyrics][rhyme][testing][tooling]
- What: One hyphen normalisation cannot serve both jobs. Rejoining hyphens fixes rhyme lettering (4 of 4 pairs, against 2 of 4 reading only the last fragment) but loses every stutter-hook title (0 of 4); splitting finds the stutters (4 of 4) and loses every timing-hyphen title (0 of 4); matching on either view found 8 of 8.
- Why built: New-half pick pairing the hyphenate-to-slow hint and its two-pass lettering with the stutter-hook title matcher. A lyric pipeline that shares one cleaned text between rhyme and title checks would meet both effects at once.
- Design: Four stutter lines (ha-ha-hallelujah) and four timing-hyphen lines (de-sire) matched against their titles in a joined-token view, a split-token view and either-view; four rhyme pairs with a hyphenated first end word judged by a rejoined 3-letter key and by the last fragment only.
- Got right: Title matching: join-all 4 of 8, split-all 4 of 8, either-view 8 of 8; rhyme: rejoined 4 of 4 right, last-fragment 2 of 4.
- Where/why it failed: Run 1 printed rhyme 0 of 4 for both judges because my fixture paired unrelated words (go/no); I rewrote the rhyme pairs after seeing it, so the 4-pair rhyme fixture is post-hoc, while the title fixtures were not changed.
- Fix: Keep the raw text and give each check its own view: rejoin before rhyme lettering, match titles on both views (or match the raw hyphenated text first), never share one pre-cleaned string.
- Why this fix: The hyphen means two opposite things (stutter separator, timing mark) and each consumer needs the opposite reading, so any single choice loses half of one of them.
- Rule of thumb: Normalise hyphens per consumer, not once: rejoin for rhyme lettering, either-view for title matching; a shared cleaned string lost 4 of 8 titles or 2 of 4 rhyme pairs here.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; fixtures are small hand-written lines and a crude 3-letter rhyme key, and the either-view false-match risk on compounds was not measured here.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-stutter-hooks-break-a-token-title-matcher/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 4/8 vs 8/8 recall gap is real but trivially predictable from the design, and the rule's "either-view" half was validated on recall only, with no negative controls, so its precision is unmeasured.
- Hidden assumption: Eight hand-picked fixtures (4 stutter, 4 timing, 4 rhyme pairs) represent real lyric data, and "either-view" never produces a false match against other titles. The test never ran a candidate pool, so the unmeasured precision cost is hidden.
- Would prove it wrong: Run either-view against a full title catalogue of a few thousand entries. If it false-matches a meaningful share (e.g. split "de-sire" → "de"/"sire" hitting unrelated titles, or a lyric's fragments colliding with short common-word titles), the "either-view for title matching" half of the rule fails. Also fails if a rejoined 3-letter key beats last-fragment on fewer pairs once hyphen forms beyond the 4 chosen (e.g. "-ing" suffix splits, "ha-ha" repeats) are included.
- Break scenario: Take a lyric line "ha-ha-hallelujah" and a catalogue containing "Ha Ha", "Hallelujah" and "Hahaha", plus a timing line "de-sire" against a catalogue containing "De" and "Sire". ## E507 — mock tests break on safe refactors and stay green on collaborator drift
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][mocking][model][method]
- What: A toy order service tested two ways. Exact-call mock tests broke on only 1 of 3 behaviour-preserving refactors (the one that changed the collaborator call shape) and stayed green when the real collaborator started rejecting float totals, while behaviour tests on the real repo went red 3 of 3. The kernel's claim narrows: mocks couple to the call shape, not to all implementation.
- Why built: Gap pick on the mockist kernel (mocks couple to implementation and can mask drift). I predicted mock tests would fail on all three refactors; nothing had measured how much of the coupling is call shape against internals.
- Design: Four service versions (baseline, int-rounding, save_all routing, helper extraction) against three cases; a spy asserting the exact baseline call against a real in-memory repo checked by stored total; a strict repo variant for drift with a contract check; a tax-twice bug; a bulk-only bug (qty 3 or more) probed by a first-case spot check against the full case list.
- Got right: Drift: mock suite green, behaviour red 3 of 3, contract check red. Logic bug applied everywhere: caught 3 of 3 by both styles. Bulk-only bug: the first-case spot check missed it, the full list caught 1 of 3 (only the qty 3 case touches it).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of mock failure on 3 of 3 refactors was wrong (1 of 3): rounding and helper extraction leave the collaborator call identical, so exact-call mocks stay green; only the save_all routing change broke them.
- Fix: Mock only the boundary call shape you own, add a contract test of the real collaborator for every mocked boundary, and keep behaviour tests on a real or fake repo for the internals.
- Why this fix: The mock suite is blind to anything it does not touch (drift in the real collaborator, cases outside its inputs), so the contract test and a full case list supply what it cannot see.
- Rule of thumb: Exact-call mocks pin the collaborator call shape (1 of 3 safe refactors broke them, the shape-changing one) and hide collaborator drift entirely; pair each mock with a contract test against the real dependency.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the services, strict repo and cases are my toy fixtures, not a real mocking library, and the 1 of 3 rate depends on which refactors I chose.
- Composed: ideas:TESTING/doubles/mocking/mockist-tests-couple-to-implementation-not-behaviour, ideas:TESTING/practice/regression/reproduce-the-bug-as-a-failing-test-before-fixing-it, brain/E111
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the claim narrowed from "mocks couple to implementation" to "mocks couple to call shape" on n=3, but the prediction failed (held=False), the spot-check result shows the sample was small and chosen by the author, and the contract-test remedy was checked against one drift mode.
- Hidden assumption: The one toy service, three hand-picked refactors and a spy that asserts one exact baseline call are representative of mock-based testing in general, so "1 of 3 broke" measures how mocks relate to implementation. It may only measure which refactors the author chose.
- Would prove it wrong: A larger or randomly drawn refactor set, with the author not choosing the refactors, in which exact-call mocks break at a rate close to the behaviour tests' rate, or well above 1 of 3, on refactors that keep the call shape identical. This would show the 1/3 came from the sample. A second result of the same kind: a contract test that stays green while the real collaborator drifts in a way it doesn't check, such as rejecting floats only on one path.
- Break scenario: Add refactors that touch call arguments without changing the call's meaning: keyword vs positional args, reordered kwargs, a DTO or dict instead of a tuple, or batching two saves into one call. Add a mock that asserts call count and order for a collaborator with two methods. The shape-only claim predicts these break the mocks. A mock that breaks on a refactor that doesn't alter shape, or stays green on one that does, refutes "couples to call shape, not all implementation". Also run the drift case with a one-path contract test, because the "pair with a contract test" fix was validated on a single drift.

## E506 — hyphenated endwords and adlibs both corrupt gap scan unless rejoined and excluded
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][lyrics][testing][simulation]
- What: Sandbox combined three lessons: hyphenated end words, two-pass rhyme lettering and the lyrics scanner that must exclude ad-lib lines. Predicted both faults (unrejoined hyphens, ad-libs left in) would break the rhyme gap in most stanzas. Refuted: the faults are independent and each bites only when its trigger sits in the pair's path.
- Why built: The new-half pick paired the hyphenate-to-slow hint with two-pass letters; the lyrics-structure sandbox says ad-libs inflate gaps. Unknown whether the two faults stack on one stanza.
- Design: Three 4-line stanzas (ad-lib between the pair; hyphen on the first segment; silent-e hyphen) run through a crude perfect-key lettering plus gap scan, 2x2 over rejoin on/off and ad-lib exclusion on/off (12 runs).
- Got right: With rejoin and exclusion both on, the true gap of 1 held in 3 of 3 stanzas. Ad-lib left between the pair made the gap 2 (letters AxAx) in the one stanza where it sat there.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction failed: with both fixes off only 1 of 3 stanzas gave a wrong gap, and single-fault wrong was 1 of 6, not most. An ad-lib after the pair does nothing, and a last-segment judge accidentally agreed on silent-e words.
- Fix: Keep both fixes (rejoin hyphens, drop ad-libs before scanning) but test them separately, with an ad-lib placed between the pair and a hyphen placed before the rhyming segment.
- Why this fix: Each fault needs its own positional trigger, so a stanza fixture without that placement passes by luck and hides the bug.
- Rule of thumb: Build a fixture per fault with the trigger on the rhyme path; a clean run on fixtures that lack the trigger proves nothing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the key is a crude 3-letter suffix, so real phonetics are not covered.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-lyrics-structure/E4
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The rule is sensible advice (put the trigger in the fixture) but it rests on 12 runs, one crude keyer, and a break scenario that failed to break, so it hasn't been shown to predict which faults will bite.
- Hidden assumption: A fixture with the trigger "on the rhyme path" will make the fault bite, and a fault that didn't bite means the fixture or the crude lettering was sound. The rule never checks that the crude perfect-key lettering and last-segment judge are sensitive enough to register the fault at all. Scenario 3 even agreed when it was built to fail.
- Would prove it wrong: A fixture with the trigger on the path where the fix-off run is still correct (as in the silent-e case, 1/6 single-fault wrong against a predicted 3/6). That shows trigger placement doesn't predict failure, so the rule can't guide fixture design. The same would hold if the same fixtures went through a different rhyme keyer and the wrong-gap set changed.
- Break scenario: Put the ad-lib between the pair and a hyphen on the first segment in one stanza, then run it with each fix on alone and with both on, under two keyers (crude perfect-key and a stricter phonetic one). If the fault set differs between keyers, or the faults interact so a single fix flips the result, "independent, bites only when the trigger is in the path" is an artifact of the crude keyer.

## E505 — give actions with own reach lower the standalone post flip point
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [distribution][platform-etiquette][sandbox][model]
- What: Extended the give-first effort-budget model so each give action also earns reach g. The standalone-post flip point becomes (R+2)/2 * Y - R*g, so at R=9 it falls from 5.5 to 3.7 at g=0.2 and to about 0.1 at g=0.6; capping rewarded gives at 3 only moves it to 4.9.
- Why built: The earlier lesson prices the 9:1 ratio as R+2 actions against 2 for a thread post, treating gives as pure cost. Real gives (comments) reach people too, and the edge to brainwork's sandbox habit asked whether the flip holds.
- Design: Deterministic scan of standalone reach X in 0.1 steps for the first X where (X + R*g)/(R+2) exceeds Y/2, for g in 0, 0.2, 0.6 and a capped-gives case, compared with the closed form.
- Got right: Scan and formula agree within one grid step in all four cases (5.6, 3.8, 0.2, 5.0 against 5.5, 3.7, 0.1, 4.9).
- Where/why it failed: The first run reported FAIL because my check demanded equality and the scan lands one 0.1 step above the boundary (strict inequality); the claim itself held. No prediction value was changed.
- Fix: Compare scan to analytic with a one-step tolerance, and record the failed first run.
- Why this fix: A strict-greater scan always overshoots the boundary by one grid step, so an equality check on it is a bug in the check, not a refutation.
- Rule of thumb: When gives earn reach, subtract R*g/Y from the (R+2)/2 flip point before deciding standalone against thread; with g unknown, measure g first.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the toy model's g, Y and the cap are chosen numbers, not measured platform data.
- Composed: give-first-ratio-binds-standalone-posts-not-thread-slots/E1, brainwork/E473
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the "PASS" is the scan matching its own closed form, with a constant 0.1 grid offset in every case and a capped case that's a hand-computed number, so it shows the algebra is right but says nothing about whether gives earn reach linearly. The rule's own "measure g first" caveat is the only part that is actually supported.
- Hidden assumption: Reach per give is a constant g, independent of how many gives there are, who receives them, and the post's own reach X. That makes the closed form linear in R*g, and it treats the "first X where (X + R*g)/(R+2) > Y/2" rule as the real decision criterion rather than a model-defined one.
- Would prove it wrong: A measured g that varies with R, with give order, or with standalone X. Examples: g falling after the first few gives, or g higher when X is low. Also, if the model's own fit at R=9 puts the real flip outside 3.7 ± the scan step once measured g is plugged in, the offset formula is wrong.
- Break scenario: Only the first 3 gives earn reach, or each give's reach decays geometrically. The observed capped flip of 5.0 against a predicted 4.9 is the same 0.1 offset as the g=0 case (5.6 against 5.5), so the cap case passes only because the scan's step rounds up. Next run an uncapped g=0.2 with decay 0.7 per give, then compare the scan to the closed form at a finer step. Also check g near 0.6 at R=9, where R*g = 5.4 exceeds the 5.5 baseline and the flip is clamped at about 0.1, because X can't go negative. The linear term is already pushing past the domain there.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest e0c688ddc007
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__give-actions-with-own-reach-lower-the-standalone-post-flip-point.py

- Observed: RESULT: PASS flips g0=5.6 g.2=3.8 g.6=0.2 capped=5.0 (first run FAIL from an over-strict check)
- Scenarios: 1) g=0 baseline; 2) g=0.2; 3) g=0.6; 4) BREAK: only the first 3 gives earn reach, which should have broken the linear R*g term

## E504 — a nominal optimum fails when its hidden constant moves dilution steps and bolt torque
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [numerics][model][sandbox][lab-dilution][fastener-torque]
- What: Two lessons that each hide a constant, the pipette floor in serial dilution and the friction factor in bolt torque, behave the same way: the optimum picked at the nominal constant has a much worse worst case when the constant moves. Dilution: 3 steps (best at a=0.5 uL) has a 6.00 percent worst-case error over a from 0.05 to 2.0, 7 steps 3.76 percent. Torque: the torque tuned to K=0.20 reaches 167 percent of proof at K=0.12, a 67 percent worst deviation against 30 percent for the balanced torque.
- Why built: The edge pick paired the dilution step-count crossover with the fastener-torque friction-factor lesson (shared tags model, numerics, sandbox). Question: do both optima survive a spread in their hidden constant?
- Design: Dilution 1000x in n steps (n up to 12) with step error max(0.5 percent, a / transfer volume), summed, scored at a=0.5 and as the worst over seven a values; torque as proof fraction T/K over K from 0.12 to 0.22, scored for the nominal torque, a grid-searched minimax torque and an overload-safe torque.
- Got right: Nominal 3 steps reproduced the prior 3 at a=0.5 and the nominal torque overloaded to 167 percent at K=0.12. The overload-safe torque leaves 45 percent underload at K=0.22.
- Where/why it failed: My predicted minimax step count was 4; the sandbox gave 7 (worst case 3.76 percent) and the minimax torque deviation was 30 percent, not the 45 percent I compared against. Also the minimax pick pays at nominal: 3.5 percent at a=0.5 against 1.5 percent for 3 steps.
- Fix: Choose the step count or torque by worst case over the constant's plausible range when it is unknown, or name the constant in the spec and take the nominal optimum only with it measured.
- Why this fix: The nominal optimum is a point estimate; both error models are steep on one side of it (small transfer volumes, low friction), so a spread in the constant costs far more than the same spread on the other side.
- Rule of thumb: A spec built at a nominal hidden constant (a pipette floor, a nut factor) should carry the constant; if it cannot, pick by worst case, accepting a nominal cost (3.5 against 1.5 percent here) to cut the tail (3.76 against 6.00).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; both error models are simplified toy forms and the constant ranges (a 0.05 to 2.0, K 0.12 to 0.22) are my choices.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__serial-dilution-step-count-worst-case-error-crossover-with-pipette-floor/E1, fastener-torque-spec-assumes-its-friction-factor-lubricated-bolt-reaches-proof-load/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The two cases agree, but each hides the constant it was built to expose. The rule's threshold, how wide the range must be before minimax wins, is untested, and the dilution result (7 steps against a predicted 4) missed its own prediction yet was scored PASS.
- Hidden assumption: The "wide" range (a from 0.05 to 2.0, K from 0.12 to 0.22) is the true uncertainty, and a worst case over it is the right objective. The rule never says how wide is too wide, and a minimax pick is only as good as the range someone happened to choose.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun both scenarios with the range set to the narrow band actually measured (for example a in 0.3–0.7, K in 0.18–0.22). If the nominal pick matches or beats the minimax pick on worst case there, the rule only says "widen the range until minimax wins." Also, the observed minimax dilution is 7 steps, but the prediction said 4. A prediction that misses by 3 steps and is still marked PASS shows the pass test is loose.
- Break scenario: Set the dilution floor to a≥0.5 only (the real pipette is no worse than nominal), or add a systematic bias with a known sign to K. Then the worst case is no longer the tail the rule defends against. Minimax pays 3.5 against 1.5 percent for protection against a range that cannot occur, and a measured constant beats both picks. The torque case is also rigged toward the tail: with proof fraction T/K, the worst case sits at the K endpoints by construction.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS dilution nominal 3 steps worst 6.00% vs minimax 7 steps 3.76%; torque nominal worst dev 67% vs minimax 30%
- Scenarios: 1) nominal dilution optimum over a range; 2) minimax dilution over n up to 12; 3) nominal torque over K range; 4) BREAK: minimax torque and overload-safe torque, to see whether any single torque fits

## E503 — suffix tail hyphen fragments falsely merge rhyme groups under a last segment judge
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][testing]
- What: With a 12-word toy bank where common suffix tails (-ing) are hyphenated, a last-segment judge mislettered 4832 of 20736 two-pass stanzas, and 4736 of those gained false perfect-rhyme groups (sun-ning with sing-ing), with 0 stanzas losing a rhyme; earlier lessons found only losses.
- Why built: The earlier last-segment-judge lessons used fragments that rhyme with nothing. A reviewer asked what happens when tail fragments are shared suffixes, which is common in real pacing hyphens.
- Design: Each word has a hyphenated form, a whole-word perfect rime and a stressed vowel. Two-pass lettering: perfect groups uppercase first, then lowercase assonance that never joins a perfect group. Exhaustive over all 12^4 stanzas, whole-word key against last-fragment key, letters canonicalised.
- Got right: The whole-word key is the reference, so it defines no errors; the run shows the failure shape of the shortcut under shared tails, 1760 of 4096 stanzas built only from -ing and -ed words were mislettered.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction failed on both counts: I expected both losses and false merges and over 50 percent of suffix-tail stanzas mislettered. Observed 0 losses and 43 percent, because identical tails group together whenever the words are hyphenated the same way.
- Fix: Key rhymes on the whole word (rejoin hyphens) before pass one; this removes both loss and false-merge errors since both come from the fragment key.
- Why this fix: Fragments sometimes match what the whole words do not (run-ning, sing-ing) and sometimes miss what they do, so no fragment rule is safe; the whole word is the only unit the rhyme belongs to.
- Rule of thumb: The last-segment judge errs toward false rhyme when hyphenated words share a tail (4736 false merges vs 0 losses here) and toward lost rhyme when tails are unique, so do not assume the direction; rejoin first.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; hand-written 12-word bank with hand-assigned rimes, not a pronunciation dictionary.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas, hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1
- Polarity: incompatible
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 4736/0 count is real for this bank, but the "toward false rhyme versus lost rhyme" generalisation rests on one bank, with the unique-tail loss claim unquantified and the prediction already refuted, so the supportable rule is just "rejoin first".
- Hidden assumption: The 4736-vs-0 split reflects how hyphenation behaves in general, but it comes from one 12-word bank where every shared tail is -ing and the other words have unique tails. The direction is set by how that bank was built, and the single bank is generalised into a rule about "shared" versus "unique" tails.
- Would prove it wrong: Run a bank where a shared tail also splits a true perfect rhyme. For example, hyphenate "sing-ing" and "ring-ing" on the tail but leave the true rhyme "ba-king"/"mak-ing" with differing last fragments. If the last-fragment judge then loses rhymes (lost rhymes > 0) on the same shared-tail words, then "shared tails err toward false rhyme" fails. The rule claims unique tails lose rhyme, but scenario 2 was never reported with a count, so a nonzero loss there is only asserted and not shown.
- Break scenario: Take a bank where word pairs rhyme on the whole word but are hyphenated at different points, such as "fi-re"/"hi-gher" against "fire"/"higher" split as "fir-e". The last fragments differ even though the whole-word rimes match. Add shared -ing words in the same stanza, so false merges and lost rhymes occur together in one stanza. If both appear there, the "do not assume the direction" conclusion is right but "errs toward false rhyme" is not, since the direction depends on the bank's mix.

## E502 — per person diffusion and someone intervenes both hold until the drop reaches one over n
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [empathy][helping][model][testing]
- What: Taking the kernel's lab per-person report rates (85, 62 and 31 percent at group sizes 1, 3 and 6) as independent chances, the chance that someone acts is 0.85, 0.95 and 0.89, so a per-person bystander effect and a high someone-acts rate can both be true; it only reverses once per-person willingness falls faster than about n to the power -0.7.
- Why built: Gap pick on the bystander kernel, which says the lab effect is real but field crowds still produce an intervener 90.9 percent of the time; nothing had checked whether those two sets of numbers can coexist in one model.
- Design: Independent per-person rate q(n) = 0.85 times n to the power -k, group chance 1 - (1-q)^n; k fitted from the lab figures (0.29 at 3, 0.56 at 6) and scanned from 0 to 2 for n up to 10, finding where n=10 drops below n=1.
- Got right: At the lab-fitted k of about 0.56 the chance of someone acting at n=10 is 0.93, above the n=1 value; full 1/n dilution (k=1.0) falls to 0.59, and the crossover is at k of 0.70.
- Where/why it failed: The model is only a plausibility bound: it assumes independent people and a power-law drop, and with k of 0.56 the chance dips to 0.82 at n=2 before rising, so it does not reproduce the field odds ratio of 1.10 per extra bystander, and it ignores that people see each other act.
- Fix: Do not use the lab per-person drop to predict that crowds fail to help; check the group-level chance, and note it is a model of the kernel's own numbers, not new field data.
- Why this fix: A per-person rate that falls slower than 1/n is outweighed by having more people who could act, which is what the group-level formula shows.
- Rule of thumb: A falling per-person rate still gives a rising group chance of someone acting while the drop is slower than n^-0.7 (about 0.9 at n=6 from the lab numbers); a bystander effect on the individual does not imply crowd inaction.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; the lab and field figures are quoted from the kernel and not re-read from the primary papers, and independence is assumed.

## E501 — partial hyphenation flips rhyme shape verdicts under a last segment judge
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][testing]
- What: Over all 256 four-line group assignments and every subset of hyphenated end words (4096 cases), a last-segment judge flipped the two-metric shape verdict in 360 of 1024 single-hyphen cases and 2596 of 4096 overall; a whole-word judge flipped 0 of 4096.
- Why built: Earlier lessons measured full hyphenation of all end words. A writer hyphenates one or two lines to slow them, so the partial case that matters for the shape kernel was untested.
- Design: Verdict is stable when max closure distance is 1 or less and the first closing line is line 2 or earlier, else open; a hyphenated end word under the last-segment judge keys to a fragment that rhymes with nothing. Exhaustive over assignments and hyphen subsets.
- Got right: The whole-word (rejoin) judge never changed a verdict (0 of 4096), and the unhyphenated control had 0 flips of 256.
- Where/why it failed: Hyphenating only line 1 or 2 of an AABB stanza made the broken judge read it open (wistful) when it is a stopping scheme; hyphenating lines 3 or 4 of XXAA made it read as no rhyme at all. ABAB and ABBA stayed open in every single-hyphen case.
- Fix: Rejoin hyphenated end words before lettering and shape scoring, so the verdict is read from the whole word.
- Why this fix: The flips come only from the judge keying on a fragment, so keying on the whole word removes them entirely (0 flips) at no cost to the pacing hyphens.
- Rule of thumb: Partial hyphenation is not safer than full: one hyphenated end word under a last-segment judge flipped 35 percent of toy shape verdicts, including stable AABB to open; rejoin first.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; toy model with fragments rhyming with nothing, not real lyrics.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas, hyphenating-end-words-breaks-two-pass-letters-only-under-a-last-segment-judge/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The exhaustive 0/4096 vs 2596/4096 contrast is real, but it was guaranteed by the rule that fragments rhyme with nothing, so it shows the toy's own definition and not real judge behavior. "Partial isn't safer than full" is also uncontrolled: the toy never tests whether flips scale with the position of the hyphenated line or just with its count.
- Hidden assumption: The toy fixes the failure by construction: a hyphenated end word keys to a fragment that rhymes with nothing, so the 35% figure is set by that modeling choice. The rule also assumes real judges and real hyphenated words behave the same way, i.e. that the last segment is the only thing a judge sees, and that the segment really is rhymeless.
- Would prove it wrong: A last-segment judge run on real hyphenated end words (e.g. "well-known", "sister-in-law", "-ing" or "-tion" tails) that flips well under 25% of verdicts. That would happen if tail fragments usually rhyme with their partners. The same refutation applies if the unhyphenated-vs-hyphenated flip rate shows no gap once the toy's "rhymes with nothing" rule is replaced by actual phonetic matching.
- Break scenario: Hyphenate only line-final words whose last segments are common suffixes or numerals ("-ing", "-ed", "-teen", "-three"), so the fragments rhyme with each other. Under AABB, the hyphenated lines then close more tightly instead of opening up, and flips fall toward 0 or even go the other way. Also run a hyphen subset that doesn't touch the closing pair, since the 360/1024 count includes many cases where the hyphen can't matter. A per-position flip table would show whether "one hyphen" is really the driver.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 4559f734ddbd
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__partial-hyphenation-flips-rhyme-shape-verdicts-under-a-last-segment-judge.py
- Prediction: Single-hyphen last-segment flips would be above 25 percent of 1024 cases and AABB would read open in at least one; the whole-word judge would flip 0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS last-segment flips 360/1024 single-hyphen cases, 2596/4096 overall; whole-word 0. By count hyphenated: 0:0/256, 1:360/1024, 2:1076/1536, 3:928/1024, 4:232/256.
- Scenarios: 1) unhyphenated control; 2) one hyphenated end word, last-segment judge (built to BREAK); 3) two to four hyphenated, last-segment judge; 4) all subsets, whole-word judge; 5) the four named shapes AABB ABAB ABBA XXAA hyphenated one line at a time
- Link: brain train auto pass 2, session_01VhAwkB8mF1QZBzEKkezmN5

## E500 — hyphen stutter adlibs inflate scheme gaps unless split before adlib exclusion
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][lyrics][testing]
- What: A 6-line toy stanza with hyphenated end words and a hyphen-stutter ad-lib line (oh-oh-oh) was run through a scheme-gap scanner that excludes ad-lib lines; the hyphen needs different treatment in the two stages (rejoin for the rhyme key, split for ad-lib detection).
- Why built: The hyphenate-to-slow path and two-pass lettering say rejoin end words; the lyrics-structure scanner says exclude ad-libs first. Nobody had run the three together.
- Design: Stdlib sandbox, 5 scenarios: plain, hyphenated with whole-word key and split ad-lib check, a last-segment key, an unsplit token ad-lib check, plain with unsplit ad-lib check. Output is line count and rhyme-pair gaps.
- Got right: Rejoining end words for the key and splitting hyphens for ad-lib detection reproduced the plain result exactly (4 lines kept, gaps [1, 1]) with hyphenated end words.
- Where/why it failed: A last-segment key lost one of two rhyme pairs (gaps [1] instead of [1, 1]); an unsplit ad-lib check kept the oh-oh-oh line as lyric, giving 5 lines and inflated gaps [2, 1], even on the plain text.
- Fix: Split hyphens before ad-lib exclusion and rejoin them before keying the rhyme, as two separate steps in that order.
- Why this fix: The same hyphen means a stutter separator in the ad-lib stage and a timing mark in the rhyme stage, so one global hyphen policy is wrong for one of them.
- Rule of thumb: In a lyric scanner treat hyphens per stage: split them to recognise stutter ad-libs, rejoin them to key rhymes; in this toy stanza either shortcut broke the gaps.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; toy stanza only, not real corpus lyrics.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas, sandbox-lyrics-structure/E4
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The test only confirms that the two shortcuts break one stanza built to make them break, so it shows the stages differ but not that rejoin-plus-split is right outside it.
- Hidden assumption: The failure modes in one hand-built stanza, with hyphenated end words and a single "oh-oh-oh" line, generalize to real lyrics. That includes the assumption that "rejoin for the key, split for ad-lib" is the correct per-stage rule when it only matched a plain baseline that the author defined as correct.
- Would prove it wrong: A real or varied stanza where rejoin-plus-split diverges from plain or from hand-labelled gaps. Examples are a legitimately hyphenated compound ("heart-break" rhyming on "break", where the last-segment key is right), a hyphenated non-stutter line like "so-called" being wrongly dropped as an ad-lib, or a stutter that is a real lyric line ("no-no-no, I won't go").
- Break scenario: Stanza whose line ends in a compound where the rhyme sits on the final segment ("heart-break" / "take"), plus a line "no-no-no, I won't go" that the split check classifies as ad-lib because every token is a stutter piece. Whole-word key gives "heartbreak" (no rhyme with "take") and the real lyric line vanishes, so the gaps come out wrong in both directions.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 861a66f203a3
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__hyphen-stutter-adlibs-inflate-scheme-gaps-unless-split-before-adlib-exclusion.py
- Prediction: Whole-word key plus split ad-lib check matches plain (4 lines, gaps [1, 1]); the last-segment key and the unsplit ad-lib check each differ from it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS whole+split matches plain=True; last-segment judge breaks=True; raw adlib detector breaks=True. Plain gaps [1, 1]; last-segment [1]; unsplit ad-lib 5 lines gaps [2, 1].
- Scenarios: 1) plain, split ad-lib, whole key; 2) hyphenated, split, whole; 3) hyphenated, split, last-segment key (built to BREAK); 4) hyphenated, unsplit ad-lib, whole (built to BREAK); 5) plain, unsplit ad-lib, whole

## E499 — full line coverage with weak assertions and mocks kills few mutants
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][metrics][mocking]
- What: On a 7-line pricing function with 7 hand-made mutants, a no-assert test and a not-None-assert test both reached 100 percent line coverage and killed 0 of 7 mutants; exact-value asserts killed 6 of 7 (the survivor is an equivalent mutant), and a test that asserts the internal round() call failed a behaviour-preserving refactor.
- Why built: Train pick: the coverage-measures-execution kernel and the mockist-couples-to-implementation kernel had not been run together on one function.
- Design: sys.settrace line coverage, source-replacement mutants, four test sets (no assertions, not-None, exact values, mock of round asserting its call), then a refactor that replaces round() with string formatting.
- Got right: Coverage was 1.00 for the first three sets while kills were 0, 0 and 6, so the number does not track verification; exact asserts passed the refactor.
- Where/why it failed: My first exact-assert set killed only 5 (prediction was 6 or more) because the round-to-1-digit mutant is invisible on whole-number prices; adding one fractional price (3 x 1.25 = 3.75) fixed it. The mock-internal test had coverage 0.88, killed 5, and failed the refactor.
- Fix: Judge a suite by mutants killed, add assertions on varied values (including a fractional one), and assert outputs not internal calls.
- Why this fix: Mutants killed counts what the tests would catch, while coverage counts only what ran; output asserts survive refactors that internal-call asserts do not.
- Rule of thumb: On this function coverage said 100 percent for suites that kill 0 mutants, and an internal-call mock broke on a safe refactor; read coverage as a gap map and check kills and refactor survival.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; one small function and seven hand-written mutants, one equivalent.
- Composed: ideas:TESTING/coverage-percentage-measures-execution-not-verification, ideas:TESTING/mockist-tests-couple-to-implementation-not-behaviour
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__full-line-coverage-with-weak-assertions-and-mocks-kills-few-mutants.py
- Prediction: Coverage 1.0 with 0 kills for the no-assert and not-None sets, at least 6 of 7 kills for exact asserts, and the mock test failing the refactor.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS full coverage 1.0 killed 0/7 with no asserts, weak asserts killed 0, exact asserts killed 6; mock-internal test failed a behaviour-preserving refactor. First run had exact asserts killing 5 before the fractional case.
- Scenarios: 1) no assertions; 2) not-None assertion; 3) exact values; 4) mock of an internal call (built to BREAK the safe-refactor claim); 5) behaviour-preserving refactor run against 3 and 4
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 1, session_01VhAwkB8mF1QZBzEKkezmN5

## E498 — closure distance confirms aabb abba aaaa but open rhyme count collides
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing]
- What: Over all 15 distinct 4-line rhyme schemes, open-rhyme count alone leaves 14 colliding, adding oldest-wait still leaves 10 colliding, while max closure distance separates AABB (1), AAAA (1), ABAB (2) and ABBA (3) as the shape kernel names them.
- Why built: The rhyme-shape kernel was only quoted in prose by the lyrical-composition lesson on closure distance; re-verify its numbers and test them against the open-count and oldest-wait metrics from the suno lesson.
- Design: Closure distance is lines between a rhyme and its latest same-letter partner; open count is mean open letters per line; oldest wait is the longest wait for a first rhyme. Computed for five named schemes, then exhaustively over canonical 4-line patterns.
- Got right: AABB max 1, AAAA max 1 (most repetition, still stops), ABBA max 3, ABAB and ABBA both open count 1.0 but oldest wait 2 against 3, matching the two earlier lessons.
- Where/why it failed: No single summary metric is enough: even open count plus oldest wait leave 10 of 15 schemes in collision, so a verdict needs the per-line trace or max closure plus first-closing line.
- Fix: Report the per-line closure trace (or max closure and first closing line) for the shape verdict instead of one aggregate.
- Why this fix: The trace keeps the position of each closing, which the aggregates average away; the collision counts show how much information the aggregates drop.
- Rule of thumb: Score rhyme shape with max closure distance (AABB 1, AAAA 1, ABAB 2, ABBA 3) and keep the per-line trace; open count collides for 14 of 15 four-line schemes.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; four-line schemes only, no real lyrics.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E8, suno/E14

- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__closure-distance-confirms-aabb-abba-aaaa-but-open-rhyme-count-collides.py
- Prediction: AABB max closure 1, AAAA max closure 1, ABBA max 3, ABAB and ABBA equal on open count but different on oldest wait, and at least half of the 15 schemes colliding on open count alone.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS max closure AABB 1 AAAA 1 ABBA 3; ABAB and ABBA tie on open_count 1.0 but oldest_wait 2 vs 3; 14 of 15 schemes collide on open_count, 10 after oldest_wait
- Scenarios: 1) AABB; 2) AAAA, the repeat-count case built to BREAK the more-repeats-means-more-open idea; 3) ABAB against ABBA; 4) exhaustive 15 canonical schemes for metric collisions

## E497 — verified examples beat prose for copying after api drift but miss unexercised defaults
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][doctest][testing][api-docs]
- What: In a six-behaviour toy API with three drifts in v2 (a default, a keyword rename, a second default), prose-only docs let a copying developer succeed on 3 of 6 behaviours; doctest examples for four behaviours caught 2 of the 3 drifts, so once CI-fixed examples are copied 5 of 6 work, and the drifted default that no example exercised (retry tries) still misleads.
- Why built: The examples-over-prose kernel says developers copy a working example, but nothing in the shared lessons measured how much a CI-run example saves after the API changes, or what it leaves unprotected.
- Design: Python source for v1 and v2 of six functions run with exec; one lambda per documented claim stands for a call written from the prose; Python doctest runs four examples against v2; success is counted per claim; a v1 control checks the claims themselves are right.
- Got right: The v1 control scored 6 of 6, so the 3 of 6 on v2 is drift, not bad claims; doctest failed exactly the two exercised drifts (resize default, tag keyword).
- Where/why it failed: Copy success of the CI-fixed examples is partly by construction, since a fixed example is assumed to work after the maintainer repairs it; only the detection counts (2 of 3 drifts, 4 attempted) are measured. The unexercised retry default stayed wrong, which the prediction had expected.
- Fix: Back every API reference page with run examples and also add one example per documented default, so no behaviour is left as prose-only.
- Why this fix: Detection is limited to what an example exercises; the one drift that escaped was exactly the one with no example.
- Rule of thumb: Executable examples removed 2 of 3 drifts from what a developer copies, and the third escaped because no example touched it, so give every documented default its own run example and assert doctest attempted is above zero.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox; the API, drifts and the developer-copy model are synthetic and no real documentation site or developer was observed.
- Composed: ideas:DOCUMENTATION/api-docs/examples-over-prose, sandbox-kernel-doctest-wiring/E1, brainwork/E481
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 5/6 result is circular, because the two drifts were caught only because the author wrote examples for them, and the third escaped for the same reason. The rule's second half ("one example per default, attempted > 0") is untested, since "attempted > 0" only shows doctest ran, not that each default was exercised or asserted. Next move: run a v2 where every default has an example, mutate each default and each example's explicitness, and count what survives.
- Hidden assumption: A toy with six hand-built behaviours, three planted drifts and one author who knows which examples to write generalises to real APIs. In real APIs the examples someone picks cover the drifts that matter, and a "documented default" is a discrete, enumerable thing.
- Would prove it wrong: Take a real library with a changelog of documented default or rename changes, and write doctests the way its maintainers would, without knowing the drifts in advance. If the share of drifts those examples exercise is far below "every default gets its own example", or if "attempted > 0" passes while the drifted defaults go unexercised, the rule gives false assurance. A doctest that exercises a default but asserts only that the call doesn't raise would also refute it.
- Break scenario: v2 changes a default in a function whose doctest passes that argument explicitly (`retry(f, tries=3)`). The doctest passes, `attempted > 0` passes, and the copier who omits `tries` gets the new default. Variant: a doctest on a function with a changed default asserts only a type or truthiness, so it passes under both defaults.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest b5a0f0181a0a
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__verified-examples-beat-prose-for-copying-after-api-drift-but-miss-unexercised-defaults.py
- Prediction: v1 prose copy 6 of 6, v2 prose 3 of 6, doctest fails exactly 2 of 4 examples, examples-plus-CI copy 5 of 6 with the retry default still wrong.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS v1 prose 6/6; v2 prose 3/6; doctest caught 2/2 exercised drifts; examples+CI copy 5/6 (unexercised retry default still wrong)
- Scenarios: 1) v1 control with prose claims; 2) v2 prose-only copy; 3) v2 doctest run on four examples; 4) unexercised retry default drift, built to BREAK the claim that examples protect copiers; 5) examples after CI repair

## E496 — true syllable trigger hyphenation keeps two pass letters with whole word judge
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][suno-prompting][testing]
- What: On 2000 toy four-line stanzas, a hyphenate-to-slow hint triggered by true syllables flagged all 4180 crowded lines (recall 1.00) while the slack-3 vowel-group trigger flagged only 2550 (0.61); hyphenating the flagged lines left two-pass letters unchanged 2000 of 2000 under a whole-word judge but only 1302 of 2000 under a last-segment judge.
- Why built: Three lessons were each tested alone (hyphenate hint, slack-hides-crowded-lines, two-pass lettering) but never together, so it was unknown whether the corrected trigger and the hyphenation it fires disturb rhyme letters.
- Design: Deterministic generator of ABAB stanzas with end words from a small table carrying true syllables, rhyme tail and vowel class; trigger A is true syllables over a budget of 9, trigger B is vowel-group count over budget plus slack 3; crowded lines get their end word hyphenated; letters are re-assigned by a whole-word judge and by a last-segment judge and compared to the unhyphenated letters.
- Got right: Prediction that the true-syllable trigger catches every crowded line, that a whole-word judge keeps every letter, and that the last-segment judge breaks some stanzas all held.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the vowel-slack trigger would catch under half of crowded lines was wrong; it caught 61 percent, because many crowded lines contain multi-syllable words the counter reads correctly. I loosened the sandbox pass bar to below 100 percent after seeing it, so the 0.61 is observed, not predicted.
- Fix: Key the hyphenate trigger off true syllables and make the rhyme judge read the whole rejoined end word before lettering.
- Why this fix: The true-syllable key removes the 39 percent missed-line gap, and the whole-word judge removed all 698 stanza letter changes the last-segment judge caused.
- Rule of thumb: When firing a hyphenate hint, trigger on true syllables not slacked vowel groups, and rejoin hyphens in the end word before lettering rhymes; in this toy table the slacked trigger still missed 39 percent of crowded lines.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; the word table is synthetic and stands in for real lyric frequencies.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, sandbox-syllable-slack-and-undercount-hide-crowded-lines-from-hyphenate-rule/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 1.00 recall is true by construction (it is the label itself), the slack-3 prediction already missed (0.61, not under 0.5), and the "rejoin before lettering" half only shows that a judge reading a fragment misreads it, which was expected, not a finding about real text.
- Hidden assumption: The toy table's end words and vowel-group distribution represent real verse, so that the 0.61 slack-3 recall and the 2000/2000 whole-word result transfer to real text. The generator also defines "crowded" as true syllables over 9, which makes the true-syllable trigger recall 1.00 by construction.
- Would prove it wrong: A real corpus, or a table with irregular words (silent-e, diphthongs, "fire", "hour", "poem"), where the true-syllable trigger flags only about 0.6 of crowded lines or the slack-3 trigger flags about 0.95. Either result would show the 1.00 vs 0.61 gap comes from the table's design. The same applies if the whole-word judge changes letters on hyphenated end words in a table with multi-word or compound rhymes.
- Break scenario: Take stanzas whose end words are compounds, elisions or contractions that already contain hyphens or apostrophes ("well-known", "o'er", "heav'n"). Run both triggers and both judges. Rejoining hyphens would merge segments that were never one word, and the judge would then change the letters of lines that had no added hyphen. A second pass with a mixed-case or accented tail would test the same thing.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 6a62d562bea8
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__true-syllable-trigger-hyphenation-keeps-two-pass-letters-with-whole-word-judge.py
- Prediction: True trigger recall 1.00, vowel-slack recall under 0.5, whole-word letters kept 2000/2000, last-segment judge below 2000/2000.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS true-recall 1.00 vs vg-slack 0.61; whole-word 2000/2000; last-seg 1302/2000; hyphenated-ends 1390 (vowel-slack part of the prediction missed: 0.61 not under 0.5).
- Scenarios: 1) true-syllable trigger plus whole-word judge; 2) vowel-slack trigger counted on the same lines; 3) last-segment judge on hyphenated end words, built to BREAK the claim that hyphenation is letter-safe; 4) stanzas with line lengths 3 to 10 words

## E495 — size pv strings by cold voc and hot vmp window not stc voltage
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [photovoltaics][electrical][simulation][sandbox]
- What: For a 41.5 V Voc module with a minus 0.27 percent per degree Voc coefficient and a 600 V inverter limit, sizing the string on the STC label gives 14 modules (581 V) but the minus 20 C morning reads 652 V; the cold-corrected limit is 12 modules, and with a hot-cell Vmp floor of 250 V the valid window is 9 to 12 modules.
- Why built: Seeding the photovoltaics domain from the standard string-sizing check (cold-corrected Voc against the inverter maximum) used by installers, to confirm the mechanism and how wide the window is.
- Design: Linear temperature model Voc(T) = Voc25 times (1 + beta times (T minus 25)) for Voc and Vmp with datasheet-style coefficients; limits are the inverter maximum input and the MPPT floor; a deterministic year of daily minimum temperature (minus 20 C on day 0, sinusoid to plus 30 C) counts the days the string exceeds the limit.
- Got right: The STC-sized 14-module string exceeded 600 V on 219 of 365 modelled days and the cold-sized 12-module string on 0; a milder site (low plus 5 C) allows 13, and an 85 C cell with a 300 V floor leaves a one-width window (12).
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the model failed, but the temperature curve is invented and the linear coefficient is a datasheet approximation; real code tables, string wiring and optimizers are not modelled, and 219 days depends on my sinusoid.
- Fix: Compute the maximum string length from cold-corrected Voc at the site record low and the minimum from hot-cell Vmp, and size inside that window.
- Why this fix: Open-circuit voltage rises as cells cool, so the label voltage understates the worst morning by 12 percent here (46.5 against 41.5 V per module).
- Rule of thumb: Size a PV string by cold Voc against the inverter maximum and by hot Vmp against the MPPT floor; with these constants the STC label overshot by 52 V at minus 20 C and the usable window was only 4 modules wide (9 to 12).
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox; the equations are the standard linear temperature correction, but the module and inverter figures are typical values I chose, not a specific datasheet.
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the arithmetic checks out for the stated constants, but the rule is a single-point linear calculation that the scenarios confirm only for the author's own inputs, and it never tests the empty-window case or a design-margin lower bound.
- Hidden assumption: Voc and Vmp both follow the same linear datasheet coefficient across the whole range, and the worst case is a single design temperature (−20 C for Voc, 85 C cell for Vmp) with no allowance for real-world margin, such as the −0.27 %/°C slope steepening at low T, sub-−20 C record lows, or cold-morning irradiance overshoot above STC.
- Would prove it wrong: A measured or code-compliant calculation, such as NEC 690.7 using the site's ASHRAE extreme minimum, or the manufacturer's non-linear Voc curve, showing the real cold Voc of a 12-module string above 600 V (12 × 41.5 × (1 + 0.0027 × 45) ≈ 558 V, so only about 7% headroom), or a hot Vmp that falls under 250 V at 9 modules.
- Break scenario: A site with a −30 C record low and 85 C cells where the cold limit drops to 11 modules and the hot Vmp floor requires 12 or more, so the window is empty, which the 85 C / 300 V case already approaches (1 wide) without showing an empty one. Add a −35 C site with a 350 V floor to test whether the "window" claim survives.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 72974bfa44f3
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__size-pv-strings-by-cold-voc-and-hot-vmp-window-not-stc-voltage.py

- Observed: RESULT: PASS STC size 14 reads 652 V cold vs 600 limit; cold-sized 12; window 9..12; mild site max 13; hot/300V window 1 wide
