## E494 — second resistor trim closes e series tolerance gaps within the same series
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [electronics][standards][simulation][method]
- What: On a 2000-point log grid over 10 to 100 ohm, every target an E12, E24 or E96 single value missed (26, 70 and 342 targets, 1.3, 3.5 and 17.1 percent) was reached within its series tolerance by one series or parallel pair of two same-series resistors, 100 percent in each, and even within a quarter of the tolerance; E6 had 0 misses.
- Why built: The tolerance-gap lesson says to trim with a second resistor but never tested that a pair actually closes the gap, or how far; this sandbox checks the closure per series.
- Design: Stock values over four decades per series (two significant figures, three for E96) with tolerances 20, 10, 5 and 1 percent; a target is missed if no stocked value is within tolerance; the pair set is every a+b and a*b/(a+b) with both parts at most 200 ohm; closure is checked at the full tolerance and at a quarter of it.
- Got right: Predicted the pair would close at least 99 percent of misses in every series; it closed 100 percent.
- Where/why it failed: Predicted the quarter-tolerance closure would fall below 100 percent for E96; it did not, so that half of the prediction was wrong and the pair gives much finer reach than assumed. My first pass criterion also wrongly demanded E6 misses, which I corrected after seeing E6 tile fully.
- Fix: Treat a second same-series resistor as the standard trim for any E12 and finer target; a third part is not needed within this 10 to 100 ohm range.
- Why this fix: The pair set grows quadratically with stock (hundreds of sums versus dozens of singles), so it fills every gap the single values leave.
- Rule of thumb: For targets in 10 to 100 ohm, one series or parallel partner from the same E-series closed all 438 single-value gaps across E12, E24 and E96, even at a quarter of tolerance; only E6 needs no trim.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; other decades and parts above 200 ohm were not tested.
- Composed: e-series-tolerance-bands-leave-gaps-from-e12-up-only-e6-tiles/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 100 percent closure is true only for nominal values on a 2000-point grid. It ignores the pair's own tolerance, so the "even at a quarter of tolerance" claim is vacuous in practice, and the prediction of E96 dropping below 100 percent was missed, which suggests the test was too easy rather than the rule too strong.
- Hidden assumption: A "hit" means the pair's nominal value lies within tolerance of the target, so the rule assumes the two parts' own tolerances, the 200 ohm cap, and the parts-count and cost of a second resistor don't matter. It also assumes the log grid of targets is representative of the targets anyone actually needs.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-running with the pair parts drawn from the same series' real tolerance bands (worst-case stack-up of a+b or a*b/(a+b)), or with a denser grid or exact E-series-adjacent targets, and finding closure below 100 percent. The same applies if a quarter-tolerance pass leaves E96 at 1 percent tolerance with any miss, or if the "miss" count changes when the target set shifts.
- Break scenario: Take E96 at 1 percent tolerance, quarter tolerance (0.25 percent), and score a pair as closed only if its worst-case range, with both parts at ±1 percent, still sits inside the target band. The pair's own tolerance already exceeds 0.25 percent, so closure should collapse. Check a range extended past 10 to 100 ohm, where the 200 ohm cap shrinks the pair set, and add the 10 to 100 ohm targets that fall between grid points.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 703ea300439d
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__second-resistor-trim-closes-e-series-tolerance-gaps-within-the-same-series.py
- Prediction: Pair closes at least 99 percent of single-value misses in E12, E24, E96; E96 closure at quarter tolerance drops below 100 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS E6 miss 0.0% closed 0%/0%; E12 1.3% closed 100%/100%; E24 3.5% 100%/100%; E96 17.1% 100%/100% (quarter-tolerance prediction missed).
- Scenarios: 1) E12 pairs; 2) E24 pairs; 3) E96 pairs; 4) E6 control with no misses; 5) quarter-tolerance closure, built to BREAK the claim and it held

## E493 — naive hyphenation heals hiatus undercount but overcounts silent e and keeps letters
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][syllables][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: On 28 hand-counted lyric words, naive vowel-group hyphenation fixed the vowel-group syllable counter on 5 words (fire, hire, desire, science, create) and broke it on 5 others (alone, stone, home, dome, late), leaving it exact on 15 of 28 before and after; hyphenating end words kept two-pass letters in 168 of 168 stanzas under a whole-word judge and 126 of 168 under a last-segment judge.
- Why built: The earlier lesson said true-break hyphens make the counter exact but that misplaced ones leave errors; this sandbox asks what a plain automatic hyphenate does when it is the thing feeding the counter, together with the lettering rule.
- Design: A vowel-group counter with silent-e removal, a naive hyphenator that closes a part after each vowel group, true syllable counts assigned by hand to 28 words, then 168 stanzas (three schemes over every ordered pair of rhyme groups) lettered before and after hyphenating end words by a whole-word key and a last-segment key.
- Got right: The letter result held as predicted: the whole-word judge is hyphen-proof and the last-segment judge is not (42 of 168 stanzas changed).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that naive hyphenation would raise the counter's exact count above plain was refuted: 15 to 15, with an equal five fixed and five broken. Words ending in a consonant plus silent e were split so the e became its own counted part, which broke words the plain counter had right.
- Fix: Do not rely on automatic hyphenation to correct the counter; hyphenate by a lexicon or true syllable breaks, keep the silent-e fix in the counter, and rejoin hyphens before lettering.
- Why this fix: The fixes and the breaks cancelled exactly here, and the lettering stayed safe only because the judge reads the whole word.
- Rule of thumb: Naive vowel-group hyphenation moved the syllable counter by net zero (5 fixed, 5 broken of 28) and made silent-e words worse, so take true syllable breaks from a lexicon; lettering stays safe only with a whole-word judge (168 of 168 against 126).
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox; the 28-word table and its syllable counts are hand-assigned, so the 15 of 28 figure is not a corpus rate.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1, hyphenating-hiatus-words-heals-a-vowel-group-syllable-counter/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — Net-zero on 28 words (5 fixed, 5 broken) is within noise and the sample is unrepresentative, and the lexicon advice and the whole-word-judge safety claim both rest on a judge definition the test itself chose.
- Hidden assumption: Hand-counted syllable truth on 28 chosen words, with silent-e and -ed/-es cases over-represented, generalizes to real lyric vocabulary, and the lexicon the rule recommends is more accurate than naive hyphenation. That recommendation was never tested here.
- Would prove it wrong: A random sample of a few hundred lyric words, not hand-picked ones, where the lexicon-based breaks leave the counter no better than naive hyphenation, or where the 5-fixed and 5-broken split shifts to a net gain once the sample is representative.
- Break scenario: Run both judges on stanzas whose end words are multi-syllable and share the last segment but differ in the stem (e.g. "desire" vs "entire", "create" vs "relate"). The last-segment judge would then merge groups that the whole-word judge keeps apart, and the 168/168 against 126/168 gap would look artifactual or reverse.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest cf66fc713679
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__naive-hyphenation-heals-hiatus-undercount-but-overcounts-silent-e-and-keeps-letters.py
- Prediction: Naive hyphenation raises the counter's exact words above the plain 15 of 28, and whole-word lettering stays at 168 of 168 while last-segment lettering drops.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS counter exact plain 15/28 -> hyphenated 15/28 (fixed 5, broken 5); letters kept whole 168/168 last-seg 126/168 (the counter-improves part of the prediction was refuted)

## E492 — multi signature imposition pairs sum locally not globally and greedy needs chain sizes
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [bookbinding][geometry][model][testing]
- What: In a multi-signature book plan, the folded-signature rule that facing pages sum to N+1 holds only inside each signature: one 8-page signature sums to 9 but three 8-page signatures in global page numbers sum to 9, 25 and 41; and a big-first greedy plan hit the minimum padding on all 199 page counts with chain sizes 32, 16, 8, 4 but was worse than a search on 131 of 199 with sizes 12 and 16.
- Why built: The imposition lesson and the signature-planning lesson were each verified alone; a real book needs both, so this checks whether the imposition rule survives being stacked across signatures and whether the plan stays minimal.
- Design: A function giving the sheet-face page pairs of an N-page fold-in-half signature, a greedy plan taking the biggest size first with a smallest-fitting final signature, a dynamic search for fewest blanks then fewest signatures, and a global pair sum that adds twice the page offset of each signature.
- Got right: The local sum was N+1 for every size tested (4, 8, 12, 16, 32), and chain-size greedy needed exactly (minus P) mod 4 blanks for every P from 1 to 199.
- Where/why it failed: The tempting global rule failed at once: the pair sum grows by 16 for every 8-page signature added, so a print script must impose per signature and offset the numbers. The non-chain comparison depends on my greedy tail rule, so 131 of 199 shows greedy is fragile there, not a precise rate.
- Fix: Impose each signature separately with its own N and page offset, check pair sums against 2 times offset plus N plus 1, and use a search rather than big-first greedy unless the sizes divide one another.
- Why this fix: The sum constant is a property of one folded sheet stack, and padding optimality is guaranteed by greedy only when each size divides the next larger.
- Rule of thumb: Check facing pairs per signature against 2 x offset + N + 1, never one global N+1; and plan signature sizes with a search unless they form a divisibility chain.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox; it models page numbers only, not paper grain, creep or real printing software.
- Composed: folded-signature-conjoint-leaves-pair-i-with-leaf-count-plus-one-minus-i/E1, brainwork/E324
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the per-signature formula is plainly correct but it's close to a tautology, and the greedy-vs-search half rests on one chain family and a single non-chain pair (12, 16), so "unless chain" is a conjecture, not a tested rule.
- Hidden assumption: Every signature is a fold-in-half stack of the same kind (one fold, sheets nested, page numbers contiguous per signature, no inserted blanks, tipped-in plates or cover wraps), so the global offset is always a clean multiple of the signature size. The "search beats greedy unless chain" half also assumes the objective is only fewest blanks, then fewest signatures. Binding cost, paper grain and press sheet imposition aren't in that objective.
- Would prove it wrong: Any mixed-size plan (e.g. 16+8+12) where the true sheet-face pairs don't match 2 x offset + N + 1 for some signature. Or a non-chain size set where greedy matches the search on every count, or a chain set where greedy is worse than the search on any count. The 199-count chain result was tested on one chain (32, 16, 8, 4), so a single miss elsewhere would refute the "unless chain" clause.
- Break scenario: Plan 20 pages as 12 + 8 with sizes {12, 8}, where 8 doesn't divide 12, so it isn't a chain. Check the pair sums (13 for the first signature, 2 x 12 + 9 = 33 for the second), then check whether greedy and search agree. Also try a chain like {24, 12, 4} with a page count that needs a stray blank, and confirm greedy's (minus P) mod 4 holds. Finally, test a case where the offset is odd, such as a 2-page insert before an 8-page signature, since the formula assumes the offset keeps recto/verso parity. Scenario 2 only stacks identical 8-page signatures, so it can't catch this.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 3160aa5f93e6
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__multi-signature-imposition-pairs-sum-locally-not-globally-and-greedy-needs-chain-sizes.py
- Prediction: Local sums equal N+1 for all sizes, global sums differ across signatures, chain-size greedy leaves (minus P) mod 4 blanks for all 199 page counts, and non-chain greedy is worse than a search on some counts.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS local sum constant per signature, global sums [9, 25, 41] over 3 signatures; greedy chain misses 0/199; non-chain greedy worse 131/199
- Scenarios: 1) local sums for five sizes; 2) three stacked 8-page signatures in global numbers, built to BREAK a global N+1 rule; 3) chain-size greedy over 199 page counts; 4) non-chain sizes 12 and 16 against a search

## E491 — drag pulls the best launch angle below 45 degrees and vacuum range overshoots
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [ballistics][physics][simulation][sandbox]
- What: A fourth-order integrator with quadratic drag found the range-maximising launch angle falling from 45.0 degrees in vacuum to 44.0 (k 0.002) and 41.0 (k 0.01) at 30 m/s, and to 36.5 degrees at 60 m/s with k 0.01, where the range was 117 m against 367 m for the vacuum formula.
- Why built: Seeding a ballistics domain from the textbook result that drag lowers the best launch angle, to see how much, and how badly the vacuum range formula overshoots once speed rises.
- Design: Acceleration is minus k times speed times velocity plus gravity; an RK4 step of 2 ms; range is interpolated at landing on flat ground; angles swept 20 to 60 degrees in half-degree steps for five speed and drag pairs; vacuum k=0 checked against v squared over g.
- Got right: The vacuum control hit 45.0 degrees and 91.7 m, matching the closed form; the best angle fell monotonically with drag and with speed at fixed k.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed, but k and the speeds are toy values, not a measured bullet or ball, and the flat-ground, no-wind, no-spin model leaves out lift and altitude density change.
- Fix: When a range matters, integrate with drag and search the angle instead of using 45 degrees or v squared over g.
- Why this fix: The drag term scales with speed squared, so it grows fastest on the fast, long flights where the vacuum formula is used most.
- Rule of thumb: With quadratic drag the best launch angle drops below 45 degrees as drag times speed grows (41.0 at k 0.01 and 30 m/s, 36.5 at 60 m/s) and the vacuum range overshoots 1.6 times at 30 m/s and 3.1 times at 60 m/s; integrate and search the angle.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox, whose vacuum case reproduces the closed form; real projectile drag coefficients were not measured.
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The numbers are plausible and the vacuum control passes, but the rule names the wrong control variable (k·v, not k·v²/g), and only five flat-ground pairs were tested, so the stated form is not demonstrated.
- Hidden assumption: Optimum angle depends only on the dimensionless drag k·v²/g, and the quadratic-drag model with constant k (no Reynolds-number dependence, no wind, no spin, no launch-height offset) stands in for real projectiles. The rule also assumes the 0.5° sweep and 2 ms step are fine enough that the 36.5, 41.0 and 44.0 values are real and not grid or integration artefacts.
- Would prove it wrong: A rerun with a 0.1° sweep and a 0.5 ms step that moves k 0.01 at 60 m/s by more than about 0.5°, or one that gives different angles for pairs sharing k·v²/g (for example k 0.0025 at 120 m/s against k 0.01 at 60 m/s). Either result would show the angle is not a clean monotone function of drag times speed, so "drag times speed" is the wrong variable (the dimensionless group is k·v²/g, and the rule writes it as k·v).
- Break scenario: Launch from 2 m height, or from a raised platform, at k 0.01 and 30 m/s: with a non-zero launch height the vacuum optimum is already below 45 degrees. The flat-ground "45 vacuum baseline" then no longer holds, and drag's share of the shift can't be separated from the height effect. A second probe is a very high speed at tiny k, such as 300 m/s at k 0.0001, where k·v is small but k·v²/g is large. The rule's "drag times speed" wording would predict a near-vacuum angle, and the true optimum would sit well below 45.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest b5496d1726b3
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__drag-pulls-the-best-launch-angle-below-45-degrees-and-vacuum-range-overshoots.py
- Prediction: Vacuum best is 45 degrees at 91.7 m; best angle falls with drag and speed; at k 0.01 and 30 m/s the range is under 70 percent of vacuum.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS vacuum best 45.0 deg matches v^2/g 91.7 m; drag k=0.002 44.0 deg, k=0.01 41.0 deg with range 56.2 of 91.7 m; at 60 m/s k=0.01 best 36.5 deg
- Scenarios: 1) vacuum control; 2) light drag k 0.002 at 30 m/s; 3) heavy drag k 0.01 at 30 m/s; 4) 60 m/s at k 0.002 and 0.01, built to BREAK the claim that the angle shift is small

## E490 — doctest attempted gate must exempt explanation pages in a diataxis doc set
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][doctest][testing][structure]
- What: In a seven-page doc set spanning the four diataxis quadrants, a per-file gate requiring doctest attempted above zero flagged 4 pages, 2 of them explanation pages that rightly carry no prompt examples; a quadrant-aware gate that exempts explanation flagged exactly the 2 real defects (a stale reference example and a how-to with no example).
- Why built: The doctest-wiring lesson says assert attempted is above zero per doc file, and the diataxis kernel says explanation is a different job from tutorials, how-tos and reference; combining them raises the question whether the gate fits all four.
- Design: Seven small pages as doctest text, run with Python doctest against two real functions; each page has a quadrant by path; two defects are planted (one failing example, one how-to with no example); gates compare attempted and failed counts per file, with and without the explanation exemption.
- Got right: Tutorial, how-to and reference pages attempted 2, 1 and 3 examples and passed; the stale page failed 1 of 1; the quadrant-aware gate matched the planted defects exactly.
- Where/why it failed: The naive per-file attempted gate cannot tell a prose-only explanation page from a how-to that forgot its example, so it either flags both or neither; the planted defects and page names are mine, so this shows the gate logic, not how often real doc sets do it.
- Fix: Apply the attempted-above-zero assertion by quadrant (required for tutorial, how-to and reference, exempt for explanation) and keep failures counted for all.
- Why this fix: Explanation pages have no runnable steps by design, so a zero count there is correct, while the same zero on a how-to is a defect.
- Rule of thumb: Gate doctest attempted above zero per diataxis quadrant: require it for tutorial, how-to and reference, exempt explanation; the flat per-file gate false-flagged 2 of 4 flagged pages.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox; it exercises the doctest-wiring and diataxis lessons and the examples-over-prose kernel only on a synthetic page set.
- Composed: ideas:DOCUMENTATION/diataxis, ideas:DOCUMENTATION/examples-over-prose, sandbox-kernel-doctest-wiring/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 2-of-4 false-flag result is true by construction, since the author planted the defects and chose which pages were explanations. It shows the exemption removes noise but never tests whether it hides defects in the exempt quadrant.
- Hidden assumption: Quadrant label is trustworthy and orthogonal to doctest need: a page's path-assigned quadrant matches its content, and explanation pages never need runnable examples (n=7, defects planted by the author, so the gate was tuned to the defects it catches).
- Would prove it wrong: An explanation page containing a stale prompt example (or a mislabeled how-to/reference sitting under the explanation path) passes the quadrant-aware gate with attempted=0 or untested failures hidden, while the flat gate would have flagged it; or on a real corpus the exemption lets through more true defects than it removes false flags.
- Break scenario: Put a how-to with no example under the explanation directory, and add an explanation page with a stale `>>> f(2)` example. If the failed-count check is applied to exempt pages, the stale example is caught. If exempt pages skip all checks, both defects pass silently. Scenario 3 only tests an unexempted how-to, so it never probes the exemption's blind spot.

## E489 — survey reach lead does not imply time share lead
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][survey][measurement]
- What: Modelled the docs-versus-Stack-Overflow survey lead (84% vs 80%, multi-select) to see what it supports. The lead is statistically solid at n=65000 but says only who is reached, not where most learning time goes; with plausible visit lengths Stack Overflow holds more minutes.
- Why built: brain train kernel listed the usage-data kernel as unapplied; its practical-consequence sentence reads a reach ranking as a primary learning surface, which a survey percentage alone cannot show.
- Design: Paired-proportion z for 84 vs 80 at n=65000 across answer correlations -0.5 to 0.9, and at n=1000 as the break. Then a 100-developer time model: docs visits split by the four diataxis types with different minutes and prose share, a copy-first reader who skips most prose, and Stack Overflow visits of 4 minutes.
- Got right: The headline lead is robust (min z 15.4 at n=65000, any correlation); at n=1000 it falls to z 2.33, marginal. Reach ranks docs first in every scenario.
- Where/why it failed: Time share did not follow reach. Docs got 1840 minutes reading everything and 1067 when copy-first readers skipped prose, against 1920 for Stack Overflow, so the first run's expected flip at the defaults never happened; only the break-even moved (3.83 to 2.22 minutes per Stack Overflow visit).
- Fix: Quote the survey as reach ("most-used"), and do not add "where most learning happens" unless time or task-completion data is available.
- Why this fix: The multi-select percentages overlap and carry no minutes, so any time-share conclusion is set by the unmeasured visit length and by how much prose readers skip.
- Rule of thumb: A multi-select usage lead (84% vs 80%) is a reach claim only; in the sandbox time share went to the 80% option (1920 vs 1067-1840 minutes) and copy-first reading cut docs break-even by 42%, so do not read it as where learning happens.

## E486 — hyphenated end words flip rhyme shape verdict under last segment judge
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][simulation][method]
- What: Ran hyphenated end words through a last-segment rhyme judge, then two-pass letters, then the closure-based stable/open shape verdict. The judge mislettered 55.0% of 4096 toy stanzas but changed the shape verdict in only 9.3%, and every change was open to stable (false closure).
- Why built: brain train edge paired the rhyme-shape kernel and the two-pass kernel with the last-segment-judge finding; the earlier entry measured only letter errors, not whether the shape verdict a song is steered by changes.
- Design: Eight end words with whole-word perfect and vowel keys and a hyphenated form whose last segment has its own key (river/tiger/mother/other collapse to the same segment). All 8^4 stanzas lettered two-pass (uppercase perfect groups first, lowercase assonance second), verdict stable only if max closure distance is 1 and no line is unresolved. Whole-word judge compared with last-segment judge; a break set of 256 stanzas uses only words whose last segment carries the whole rhyme.
- Got right: Predicted verdict flips far rarer than letter errors; got 380 of 4096 against 2254, and 0 differences on the safe-ending set, so the damage is tied to words whose earlier segment carries the rhyme.
- Where/why it failed: Predicted the flips would mostly be stable to open; observed 0 stable to open and 380 open to stable, because a false perfect match merges separate lines into one uppercase letter (AAbb became AAAA), which looks closed.
- Fix: Judge rhyme on the whole word with hyphens stripped before lettering, and treat a shape verdict of stable as unconfirmed when any end word was hyphenated.
- Why this fix: The error direction is toward false closure, so a stable verdict is the one a last-segment judge cannot be trusted for, and stripping hyphens removes the cause rather than counting its symptoms.
- Rule of thumb: With hyphenated end words a last-segment judge mislettered 2254 of 4096 stanzas but changed the stable/open shape verdict in only 380, all of them false closure (open read as stable), so strip hyphens before judging and distrust any stable verdict otherwise.

- Hidden assumption: The 8-word toy vocabulary and uniform 8^4 stanza sampling represent real hyphenated end words, so 9.3% flips, all open→stable, is a property of last-segment judging and not of how this word list was built (the river/tiger/mother/other collapse was chosen by the designer).
- Would prove it wrong: A run on a different or real hyphenated vocabulary (for example, words whose last segment has a different vowel from the whole word, or a list weighted by actual usage) that gives a flip rate well above 15%, or any stable→open flips. Another refutation would be a "strip hyphens" judge that still misses the shape verdict on stanzas where the whole-word key itself is wrong.

Run the same pass with stripped hyphens and with the last-segment judge. Then add stanzas where the last segment is a stub with no vowel match, such as "-ing" or "-ly". If any of these gives stable→open flips, or if stripping hyphens changes a verdict that the last-segment judge got right, the "strip hyphens and distrust stable" rule fails.

## E484 — versioned fills on a loop cache allocate after the check
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][invalidation][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of a 5-key loop over a size-5 LRU cache with late fills, invalidating writes and a toy generational GC, comparing unversioned fills, versioned fills that allocate before the version check and versioned fills that allocate after it, over 54 latency and write-period cells.
- Why built: The loop-sized-cache path says versioning fills fixes stale reads; I wanted to know whether the fix interacts with the GC cost that the cache-size sweep and garbage-collection kernel say decides cache sizing.
- Design: Per request tick, a miss queues one fill that arrives L ticks later carrying the database version it read; writes bump a key version and invalidate it. Each allocation advances a nursery counter (minor GC every 10 allocations promotes live entries), and a major GC runs when old garbage reaches 20. Latencies 1 to 12, write periods 0 and 3 to 17.
- Got right: Versioned fills (either allocation order) gave 0 stale reads in all 48 write cells while unversioned fills served stale reads in 21 of them, and with no writes all three policies were identical.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that allocating before the check would add GC work in every late-write cell was wrong: it changed allocations in 21 cells but GC work in only 13, because a dropped entry dies young and is never promoted; the cost is the earlier minor collections it triggers (largest gap 180 vs 140 at latency 1, write period 3).
- Fix: Do the version comparison before allocating the entry, so a rejected late fill costs nothing; versioning stays the fix for stale reads.
- Why this fix: Rejected fills never reach the old generation, so the only GC price of checking late is the extra nursery turns; checking first removes it entirely at no cost to correctness.
- Rule of thumb: Version late cache fills and compare before allocating; in this toy model that kept stale reads at 0 in 48 of 48 cells and the allocate-first order added GC work in 13 of 48, never in a cache with no writes.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the GC is a toy two-generation model, not a real runtime.
- Composed: ideas:PERFORMANCE/garbage-collection, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1, loop-sized-cache-with-writes-stays-size-5-but-late-fills-serve-stale-until-fills-are-versioned/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — 0 stale in 48/48 is near-tautological for a version check, while the allocate-order GC claim rests on 13/48 cells with one gap (180 vs 140) under hand-picked thresholds, 5 keys, and a prediction that already failed once.
- Hidden assumption: Fill-completion order and the fixed GC trigger (10 allocations, old garbage at 20) in a single-threaded toy are representative, so "extra GC work" from allocate-first transfers to real runtimes, and the version check alone, not the stale-read tally, is what drives the 0-stale result (the model may make versioned fills stale-free by construction).
- Would prove it wrong: A cell where versioned fills show nonzero stale reads (e.g., two fills for the same key in flight across a write, arriving out of order or a write landing between check and insert), or a rerun with nursery size 7 or 13 and a different old-garbage threshold where allocate-first GC gap is zero or flips sign in the same latency/write cells.
- Break scenario: Concurrent fills: allow multiple in-flight fills per key with variable latency (jitter, reordering) and a write between the version check and the cache insert, with a bigger key space than 5 so evictions interact, and nursery/major thresholds not aligned to the loop length.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 87ebdaf8e5bd
- Distinct from: loop-sized-cache-with-writes-stays-size-5-but-late-fills-serve-stale-until-fills-are-versioned/E1 shows versioning stops stale reads; this adds that the order of allocate and check changes GC work in some cells and that it ties without writes.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__versioned-fills-on-a-loop-cache-allocate-after-the-check.py
- Prediction: Before the first run I expected versioned fills to give 0 stale reads everywhere and allocate-before-check to cost extra GC work in every late-write cell; the first run (3 latencies by 3 write periods) already contradicted the second half, with a gap of 0 in all four cells.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS versioned fills gave 0 stale reads in all 48 write cells while unversioned went stale in 21; allocating before the check changed GC work in only 13 cells (largest gap 180 vs 140); no-write cells tie
- Scenarios: 1) unversioned fills; 2) versioned, allocate before the check; 3) versioned, allocate after the check; 4) BREAK: write period 0 (no writes) where all policies should tie

## E483 — hanoi bfs optimum vs formula and heuristic
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [hanoi][puzzles][algorithm][sandbox]
- What: Seeded the new HANOI domain: an exhaustive breadth-first search of the Tower of Hanoi state graph for 3 pegs (1 to 8 discs) and 4 pegs (1 to 7 discs), compared with 2^n - 1 and with the Frame-Stewart recursion.
- Why built: The new-domain pass needed a computable first kernel; the move count 2^n - 1 is usually quoted without its peg-count condition, so I checked where it stops holding.
- Design: A state is the peg of each disc; a disc moves if it has no smaller disc on top and none on the target peg. BFS from all-on-peg-0 gives distances; the optimum is the distance to all-on-the-last-peg, and the number of reached states is compared with pegs^n. The Frame-Stewart recursion is evaluated separately and compared cell by cell.
- Got right: BFS matched 2^n - 1 in all 8 three-peg sizes (255 at n=8), matched the recursion in all 7 four-peg sizes (25 at n=7), and reached all pegs^n states each time (for example 16384 at 4 pegs and 7 discs).
- Where/why it failed: Applying the three-peg formula to four pegs overstates the optimum from 3 discs on (7 vs 5, 15 vs 9, 31 vs 13, 63 vs 17, 127 vs 25); an earlier draft of my result line quoted 33 for n=7, which is the n=8 value, caught by reading the printed table.
- Fix: Key any Hanoi move count by both disc count and peg count, and generate par values from search for small sizes and from the recursion beyond them.
- Why this fix: The search and recursion agree on every searched size, while the closed form is wrong off its three-peg domain.
- Rule of thumb: 2^n - 1 is the Hanoi optimum for three pegs only; with four pegs the searched optimum was 25 at 7 discs against 127, so take the peg count as an input and check small cases by search.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox for the sizes searched (3 pegs to 8 discs, 4 pegs to 7 discs); larger sizes lie beyond what was searched.
- Composed: ideas:HANOI/move-counts/optimum-depends-on-peg-count, demo-disc/E39, sandbox-distance/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The finding that 2^n-1 fails for 4 pegs is solid and well tested, but the claim is narrow, the tested range is small, and it checks the implementation against itself (BFS vs a recursion written by the same author) without an independent reference such as OEIS A007664 or a 5-peg case.
- Hidden assumption: The Frame-Stewart recursion is the true 4-peg optimum for every n, yet it is only a conjecture. It was proved optimal for 4 pegs only in 2014 (Bousch), and the test confirms it only because BFS agrees up to n=7. The rule also assumes "take the peg count as input and check by search" scales, though BFS needs pegs^n states and so stops being feasible within a few more discs.
- Would prove it wrong: A BFS optimum that differs from Frame-Stewart at some 4-peg n (it is 25 at n=7, and the next values are 33 at n=8 and 41 at n=9). A BFS 3-peg optimum that differs from 2^n-1 at any n would also refute it. A case where the "overstates" claim fails would too: 3 discs on 4 pegs is 5 moves against 7, so the first overstated cell is n=3, as predicted. None of these appeared in the 1–7 range, which is a small window.
- Break scenario: Run the same code with a different target or start, such as discs starting spread over pegs, or the goal on a middle peg for 4 pegs, or 5 pegs at n=8. The rule says "2^n-1 is the three-peg optimum", but the harness only measures the all-on-peg-0 to all-on-last-peg case. Check whether the constraint "no smaller disc on top" is also enforced when the target peg is empty (an off-by-one in the move rule would still pass n≤3). Also run 5 pegs against Frame-Stewart with a deliberately swapped peg ordering, to see whether a symmetric bug hides behind the matching numbers.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 1527fe3fe98a
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__hanoi-bfs-optimum-vs-formula-and-heuristic.py
- Prediction: Before the first run I expected BFS to equal 2^n - 1 on three pegs, the Frame-Stewart numbers on four pegs, and every pegs^n state to be reachable, with the three-peg formula wrong for four pegs from 3 discs on.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS BFS matched 2^n-1 for 3 pegs (n=1..8) and the Frame-Stewart recursion for 4 pegs (n=1..7, optimum 25 at n=7); all pegs^n states reachable; applying the 3-peg formula to 4 pegs overstates the optimum at n=[3, 4, 5, 6, 7] (127 vs 25 at n=7)
- Scenarios: 1) three pegs, 1 to 8 discs; 2) four pegs, 1 to 7 discs against the recursion; 3) reachable-state count against pegs^n; 4) BREAK: the three-peg formula applied to four pegs

## E482 — front cut syllable budget keeps end word whole
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][sandbox][testing]
- What: Exhaustive sandbox (7 end words, 2401 four-line stanzas, budgets of 4 to 1 syllables) comparing a front-cut that never splits the end word with a naive front-cut by syllable count, scored by whether two-pass rhyme letters survive.
- Why built: The path pairs the two-pass lettering kernel with the shorten-from-the-front sandbox; earlier tests cut by words, so I tested a syllable budget where the cut can land inside a multi-syllable end word.
- Design: Toy lexicon with syllables, stressed index and stressed vowel; rhyme key is the stressed syllable to the end; pass one gives uppercase letters to identical keys, pass two lowercase to same-vowel leftovers; a lost stressed syllable makes the vowel unknown. Five one-syllable filler words precede each end word.
- Got right: The word-boundary cut kept the letters in 2401 of 2401 stanzas at every budget, and the naive cut also kept them all at budget 2 (2401 of 2401), so the front-cut idea holds well beyond the budgets previously tried.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the naive cut would already lose letters at budget 2 was wrong; it only broke at budget 1 (513 of 2401 kept, example cat cat tomorrow tomorrow read AAxx instead of AABB), because the damage needs the budget to be smaller than the end word's stressed tail.
- Fix: Cut from the front by syllables but never below the syllables from the end word's stressed syllable to its end; keep the end word whole when the budget is smaller.
- Why this fix: Every naive loss fell in stanzas containing an end word whose stressed tail exceeded the budget (1888 of 2320 such stanza-budget cases changed), and none outside them, so the stressed tail is the exact floor.
- Rule of thumb: When shortening a sung line from the front, the budget floor is the end word's stressed tail, not one word; below that floor the rhyme letters change, above it they did not in this toy lexicon.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox over a toy lexicon (real pronunciation, secondary stress and elision are outside the model).

- Hidden assumption: Real rhyme survival depends only on the stressed tail, and the toy lexicon's design (five one-syllable fillers, stress index and vowel stored per word, pass-two matching on vowel alone) is representative. Fillers can never carry the stressed syllable, and the budget floor is never above the end word's stressed tail except at budget 1. The rule's "floor" is therefore close to tautological: the scoring only reads the end word, so any cut that keeps it intact trivially passes.
- Would prove it wrong: A word-boundary cut that fails at a budget at or above the stressed-tail length. An example is a stanza where the end word is longer than the budget and can't be kept whole, so the cut either drops the stressed syllable or violates the budget. The observed 2401/2401 at budget 2 for the naive cut already contradicts the expectation that the floor is the cause. Naive cutting from the front keeps the tail of the line, so it only hurts when the budget drops below the tail length. That means the floor is the stressed tail only if the lexicon has stress-initial polysyllables, and the result doesn't show that it does.
- Break scenario: Add end words of 3-4 syllables with stress on the first syllable (like "ˈcarpenter" or "ˈmelody"), and add multi-syllable fillers. Run budgets 4 to 1 and report the word-boundary cut separately for budgets below the end word's length. Also run a variant with the stressed syllable in the middle. I expect the word-boundary cut to fail where the word is longer than the budget, and the naive cut to lose letters at the budget equal to the tail length minus one. If both cuts still pass, the lexicon is too gentle to test anything.

## E481 — docs drift doctest vs prose
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][doctest][api-drift]
- What: Sandbox of a two-version API (v2 renames a keyword argument and flips a default) with a tutorial doc made of executable examples, a one-example how-to, and a prose-only reference line, checked with the real stdlib doctest module.
- Why built: To test the doctest kernel (executable examples fail loudly), the examples-over-prose kernel (readers copy examples) and the diataxis split together, and find where wiring examples into a test stops protecting readers.
- Design: Load v1 and v2 of resize() as modules. Run the tutorial examples through doctest.DocTestRunner on each. A copy-first reader model executes only the example lines. A prose checker cannot execute anything. A break scenario uses a single example that never touches the flipped default.
- Got right: In sync (v1) there are 0 doctest failures; after the rename (v2) doctest reports 1 failure, exactly the example using the old kwarg; the copy-first reader also breaks on the stale tutorial, so loud failure is the right alarm for the reader who skips prose.
- Where/why it failed: The reference line still claims keep_ratio defaults to True and nothing flags it; the how-to example that avoids the changed argument passes with 0 failures although behaviour changed. Doctest only protects what the examples exercise.
- Fix: Treat doctest as protection for tutorial and how-to examples only, and give every changed or default-bearing parameter at least one example, or generate the reference text from the signature so it cannot drift on its own.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows the unprotected surface is exactly the prose claims and unexercised parameters, so coverage of parameters by examples (or generating reference from code) closes it, while more careful prose writing does not.
- Rule of thumb: Executable doc examples catch drift only on the parameters they exercise; reference prose and untouched defaults still rot silently, so cover each parameter with an example or generate the reference from the code.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the real-world prevalence of this drift pattern is not claimed.
- Composed: ideas:DOCUMENTATION/doctest, ideas:DOCUMENTATION/examples-over-prose, ideas:DOCUMENTATION/diataxis
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The finding that untouched defaults and prose rot silently is true, but it was built into the design, since the break example was written to avoid the default. The fix "cover each parameter with an example" is also insufficient, because an example only detects drift if its inputs distinguish the old behaviour from the new, and the sandbox never tested that.
- Hidden assumption: Drift is only dangerous where a doc example directly exercises the changed parameter, and the sandbox's hand-built v1/v2 and its three example types stand in for how real docs rot, so "one example per parameter" would suffice.
- Would prove it wrong: A doc with an example for every parameter, all passing on v2, where the reader still gets wrong behaviour. This happens when the example's output is the same under both defaults, or when a param interaction (new default × another arg) is changed and no example combines them. Also fatal: a v2 run where doctest fails for a reason other than drift, which would mean the "1 fail" was an artifact of the setup.
- Break scenario: Give the tutorial one example per parameter, including `resize(img, 100, 100)` with the flipped default, and write the expected output as `<Image 100x100>`. v2 flips `keep_aspect` from False to True and the output repr stays `<Image 100x100>` because the test image is square. The doctest passes on both versions, every parameter is "covered", and a user with a non-square image gets different output. Coverage by example is not coverage by behaviour.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 272bb200bb39
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__docs-drift-doctest-vs-prose.py
- Prediction: Before the first run I expected exactly 1 doctest failure on v2 (the renamed kwarg), 0 on v1, and 0 failures for the single-example how-to even though the default changed.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS doctest caught example drift (1 fails) and the copy-first reader breaks on stale docs, but reference prose is never checked and an example that avoids the changed default passes silently
- Scenarios: 1) docs and API in sync on v1; 2) API drifts to v2 with doctest wired; 3) copy-first reader on stale docs plus prose checker; 4) BREAK: one example that avoids the changed default passes while behaviour changed

## E480 — damage cap window where team fight and burst niche coexist
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [rpg][combat][balance][sandbox]
- What: Deterministic 3-versus-1 sandbox sweeping a percent-of-defender-max-HP damage cap fraction from 0.05 to 1.00 and finding the narrow range where the fight is contested, the burst skill still clears its 0.40 band, and the boss cannot kill a player in two hits.
- Why built: The composed-kernel pass joins two kernels that each fixed one side: the team-fight cap that must rise above the 1v1 value, and the burst-niche audit that says a low cap erases the skill's band. I wanted to know whether any cap satisfies both.
- Design: Three players (100 HP, one action each) against a 1000 HP boss; steady skill 100 per action, burst skill 400 every fourth turn; both capped at the fraction of the defender's max HP; boss hits the weakest player for 400 raw. Lineups: all steady, all burst, mixed. Constraints: contested (players lose 30% or more of total HP, or lose), burst clears 0.40, and a player is not dead in two boss hits.
- Got right: Each constraint alone is a half-line (contested from 0.30 up, niche from 0.40 up, two-hit-safe below 0.50) and together they leave caps 0.45 to 0.49, five of 96 grid points, so both earlier fixes are compatible but only barely.
- Where/why it failed: My first parameters (boss raw hit 90) never let the boss win at any cap and showed no window at all, and the break scenario of changing the boss raw hit to 60 left the window identical, so the window is set by the cap and by my own thresholds (30% HP loss, two-hit kill), not by boss damage.
- Fix: Treat the cap fraction as a value to compute from three explicit constraints, and state the thresholds that define contested and one-shot risk next to the number.
- Why this fix: The window moves with those thresholds, so a fixed default such as 0.20 or 0.50 either erases the niche (0.20) or lands on the two-hit-kill edge (0.50).
- Rule of thumb: A percent-HP cap fraction sits between the burst skill's band floor and the two-hit-kill ceiling; in this toy fight that was 0.45 to 0.49, so check both edges before copying a cap from a 1v1 fix.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the thresholds (30% loss, two hits, 0.40 band) are my definitions and the fight is a toy, not the real game.
- Composed: ideas:RPG/combat/team-fight-damage-cap-doesnt-generalize, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/damage-cap-can-erase-a-burst-skills-niche, brainwork/E296
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sweep is deterministic and the window is real in this one toy, but the boss-hit-60 break leaving the window unchanged suggests the upper edge isn't the two-hit-kill ceiling the rule claims, and nothing has been varied except that one parameter.
- Hidden assumption: The window's edges come from the toy's own constants (the 0.40 band and the 100 HP / 400-hit two-hit-kill ceiling), and a percent-of-defender-max-HP cap behaves the same when the defender's max HP, the burst multiplier or the team size changes. The "0.45 to 0.49" figure is then just those constants restated, not something the sweep found.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun the sweep with player HP 150 or 80, or with a burst of 300 or 600. If the window doesn't move to the values the two edge formulas predict, or if it stays at 0.45 to 0.49, then the edges aren't the band floor and the two-hit ceiling and the rule names the wrong mechanism. A window that is identical across all of those changes would refute it just as much.
- Break scenario: Change the boss target from "weakest player" to "random player", and scale the boss to 3000 HP with the players' damage scaled to match. The cap is a fraction of the defender's max HP, so the boss-side cap and the player-side cap now bind differently. Check that the contested, band and no-two-hit-kill constraints still land between the same two edges. Also check why boss hit 60 left the window unchanged: if 60 and 400 both give 0.45 to 0.49, the two-hit constraint probably isn't binding at the upper edge at all, and the "ceiling" label is unproven.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest b6a776708bcb

- Observed: RESULT: PASS fair team fight, burst niche and no two-hit kill coexist only for cap fractions (0.45, 0.49) (5 of 96 grid points) with boss hit 400; with boss hit 60 the window is [0.45, 0.46, 0.47, 0.48, 0.49]
- Scenarios: 1) all-steady lineup; 2) all-burst lineup; 3) mixed lineup; 4) BREAK: boss raw hit 60 instead of 400 to see if boss damage moves the window (it did not)

## E479 — billiards bank shot mirror unfold replays exactly but needs ball radius inset
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [billiards][geometry][sandbox][testing]
- What: Seeded the new BILLIARDS domain with a mirror-unfold bank-shot kernel and an exact-arithmetic sandbox replaying 840 one-cushion and 2520 two-cushion plans on a 100 by 50 table, plus a ball-radius break, a cushion-friction break and a float-tolerance check.
- Why built: The new-domain pass needed a first kernel from a scenario that can be computed; the reflect-the-target trick is commonly stated as exact, so I tested where it stops being exact.
- Design: Fractions for exact geometry; unfold the target across the last cushion first; replay the aimed ball step by step with wall reflections and measure closest approach and the cushions hit; repeat in a table inset by the ball radius; repeat with tangential retention below 1; repeat the two-cushion replay in floats.
- Got right: The unfolded aim reached the target in 840 of 840 and 2520 of 2520 plans, and unfolding on the inset box with radius 2.5 gave a miss of exactly 0, while unfolding on the nominal table missed by up to 4.85.
- Where/why it failed: The straight line reaches an image of the target but not always via the named cushions: the planned order held in 750 of 840 and 1500 of 2520 plans; 10% tangential loss per bounce moved 28 of 840 shots off by more than the radius; float replay hit exactly zero miss in only 1923 of 2520 two-cushion plans.
- Fix: Unfold on the ball-centre inset box, validate that the aim line crosses each planned cushion in order inside the table, treat the result as a first aim under friction, and compare misses with a tolerance rather than equality.
- Why this fix: Each fix matches a measured failure: the inset removed the 4.85 miss, the order check exposes the 90 and 1020 plans that go through other cushions, and the tolerance took float replays from 1923 to 2520 of 2520.
- Rule of thumb: Mirror-unfold a bank shot on the ball-centre inset box and verify the planned cushion order; the straight line alone can reach the target through different cushions, and cushion speed loss still needs a correction.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script on an idealised table (the model has no cloth, spin or throw).
- Composed: ideas:BILLIARDS/bank-shots/mirror-unfold-the-table, brainwork/E218, storyteller-perseus-mirror/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The finding that the unfolded line reaches the target through the wrong cushions in 90 of 840 and 1020 of 2520 plans is real and useful, but the rule's friction clause is untested advice. Its own "PASS" label also overstates a run where the planned order held in only 750/840 and 1500/2520.
- Hidden assumption: Planned cushion order is the thing that matters, and the exact-arithmetic, perfectly elastic, frictionless point-ball model transfers to a real table. The only verified correction is the ball-radius inset; friction and spin are asserted to "need a correction" but no correction was built or validated.
- Would prove it wrong: A run where the inset-box unfold with a verified cushion order still misses the target once tangential retention drops to 0.95 or 0.90, with an error larger than the ball's own radius and no single fixed aim offset closing it. Equally damning: any plan where the unfolded line passes the target via the wrong cushions and the "verify order" check never fires because it was only run on the sandbox's own replay.
- Break scenario: Three-cushion and corner-adjacent plans (840/2520 are one- and two-cushion only) in which the aimed path hits a corner or grazes a cushion at a near-zero angle. Add tangential retention 0.90 plus a float replay with a 1e-9 tolerance there. Exact unfolding gives one aim, the real replay hits a different cushion sequence, and the tolerance masks the mismatch as a pass.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 085cdb1b5375
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__billiards-bank-shot-mirror-unfold-replays-exactly-but-needs-ball-radius-inset.py

- Observed: RESULT: PASS unfolded aim reached the target in 840/840 one-cushion and 2520/2520 two-cushion plans, but with the PLANNED cushion order in only 750 and 1500; nominal-table aim missed by up to 4.85 with r=2.5 while inset unfolding missed by 0.0; float replay needed a tolerance (strict equality 1923/2520 vs 1e-9 tolerance 2520/2520)
- Scenarios: 1) one-cushion plans, exact; 2) two-cushion plans, exact; 3) BREAK: ball radius with nominal-table aim; 4) inset-box unfolding; 5) tangential retention 1.0, 0.99, 0.95, 0.90; 6) float replay, strict vs tolerance

## E478 — alloc order moves the cache vs no cache break even
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][gc][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic sandbox of a 5-key loop cache with late versioned fills, invalidating writes and a toy generational GC shows that whether a rejected late fill allocates before or after the version check moves the GC-cost break-even between a size-5 cache and no cache in 9 of 35 latency and write-period cells (up to 1.5 times), and never when there are no writes.
- Why built: The gap pass joined the GC-cost kernel, the cache-size sweep and a companion that found allocate-first costs extra GC work; the question was whether that extra work ever flips the cache-or-no-cache decision.
- Design: Cost is misses times 500 plus GC work times a pause price. Break-even pause is the saved miss cost of a size-5 cache divided by its GC work, found for latencies 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and write periods 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 13, 29 and for the no-write case, with both allocation orders; a second sweep over sizes 0 to 6 and pause prices 0.5 to 5000 looks for a partial cache beating both.
- Got right: With no writes the break-even is infinite for both orders (a size-5 cache never loses), and partial caches beat size 5 and no cache in 0 of 45 cells, which keeps the binary shape of the GC-cost lesson even with late fills.
- Where/why it failed: My first run at latency 3 showed the order changing nothing in any of four write periods, so my prediction that it would shift the break-even everywhere was wrong; the effect appears only in some cells (for example latency 5 and write period 6: 2755.6 allocating before the check vs 4133.3 after), and 4 of 45 size cells were exact ties with size 5, not wins.
- Fix: Check the version before allocating, then size the cache to the loop and decide cache versus no cache from the break-even pause computed with the allocate-after-check GC work.
- Why this fix: Allocating after the check raised the break-even pause in 9 cells, so the cache stays worthwhile at a higher pause price; in the other 26 write cells the order made no difference to the decision.
- Rule of thumb: Keep the loop-sized cache binary but compute the cache-versus-none break-even with the real fill order: allocate-before-check lowered it by up to a third in 9 of 35 write cells and never mattered without writes.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the generational GC, the 500 miss cost and the latencies are toy values.
- Composed: gc-cost-vs-loop-sized-cache/E1, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1, loop-sized-cache-with-writes-stays-size-5-but-late-fills-serve-stale-until-fills-are-versioned/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The order effect is real inside one fixed toy configuration, but the rule generalizes from one miss cost, one loop length and one GC model, the "a third" versus "x1.50" wording is inconsistent, and the break-even shifting does not show that the cache-or-none decision ever flips at a realistic pause price.
- Hidden assumption: The toy model's constants (miss cost 500, a 5-key loop, GC work counted as allocations, a fixed pause price per unit of work) stand in for a real cache, so a 9-of-35 shift in a break-even computed there carries over to real systems. The rule also assumes the "binary" framing (size 5 or none) is the decision that matters, and the sweep that supports it found 4 exact ties with size 5.
- Would prove it wrong: Perturb the miss cost (say 50 or 5000), the loop length, or the GC work weighting, and find that the 9 cells change count or move to different latency and write-period pairs. Or find that the "up to a third" lowering (rule) and "up to x1.50" (observed) describe the same ratio in opposite directions and one of them is miscomputed. Or find that in the 9 cells the optimal cache-or-none choice at realistic pause prices (not just the break-even point) is identical under both orders.
- Break scenario: Latency 3 with write period 7, with the loop length changed from 5 to 6 or 7 and the cache kept at size 5, so that the loop no longer fits and the "loop-sized" premise fails, then rerun both allocation orders. If the order effect appears or vanishes in different cells, the rule is an artifact of the 5-key/size-5 coincidence. Separately, the stated prediction ("differ in every write cell by at least 10%") was falsified at latency 3 (differed in none), which is the exact latency in scenario 1, so that scenario has nothing to say about the effect.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest c1b47c703928
- Distinct from: gc-cost-vs-loop-sized-cache/E1 gives the break-even for an immediate-fill loop cache; this finds that late versioned fills keep partial caches losing and that the order of allocation and check moves the break-even only when writes exist.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__alloc-order-moves-the-cache-vs-no-cache-break-even.py
- Prediction: Before the first run I expected the break-even pause to differ between the two orders in every write cell by at least 10%; at latency 3 it differed in none.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS allocation order moved the size-5 versus no-cache break-even pause in 9 of 35 (latency, write period) cells, by up to x1.50 when it moved, and never with no writes; partial caches strictly beat size 5 and no cache in 0 of 45 cells (4 exact ties with size 5)
- Scenarios: 1) latency 3 with write periods 0, 7, 13, 29; 2) the 35-cell latency by write-period grid with both orders; 3) BREAK: no writes, where the order must not matter; 4) sizes 0 to 6 across pause prices for partial-cache wins

## E477 — young generation size trades pause for throughput until the cache lifetime and heap ceiling decide
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][gc][sandbox]
- What: A toy generational collector with a cache whose entries live T ticks then get invalidated showed that growing the young generation raised the maximum minor pause every time (30, 40, 60, 100 for Y of 50, 100, 200, 400) but raised throughput only up to Y=200 when T=500, then dropped it (0.5435 to 0.4932), and overflowed the heap only at Y=700.
- Why built: The GC tuning kernel says the four goals trade against each other, the size-sweep entry says judge a size under a memory ceiling, and the invalidation kernel says cache entries die by a separate path; this puts a cache's invalidation lifetime into the GC trade-off to see whether the young-size knob still behaves as the kernel describes.
- Design: Stdlib copying-GC model. Each tick allocates 8 short-lived objects and 2 cache entries that die T ticks later. Minor GC when young holds Y objects (pause 20 plus survivors copied to old); full GC when old plus Y would exceed a heap of 1500 (pause 40 plus live old objects). Sweeps: T of 500, 100 and 5; Y of 50, 100, 200, 400, plus 600 and 700 at T=500. 20000 ticks, no randomness.
- Got right: Max minor pause rose with Y at T=500 (30, 40, 60, 100). At T=5, invalidation lands before the next collection and the pause stayed flat at 30 for every Y while throughput climbed from 0.62 to 0.93, so the pause-for-throughput trade disappeared. At T=100 throughput rose monotonically (0.61 to 0.78).
- Where/why it failed: Three of my first-run predictions failed. I expected throughput to keep rising with Y at T=500; it peaked at Y=200 because a bigger young generation leaves less old space and full collections went from 108 to 162. I expected a heap overflow at Y=400 and then at Y=600; there were none until Y=700, since live old data is about 880 not 1000. I expected promotion to fall with shorter T at T=100; it was identical to T=500 (all 40000 promoted) because lifetime exceeded the young window, and fell only at T=5.
- Fix: Sweep the young size against the real invalidation lifetime and the real heap ceiling together, and pick the interior throughput peak below the overflow point rather than the largest young generation.
- Why this fix: The pause rises monotonically while throughput peaks and then falls, so the largest young generation is worse on both axes at T=500 and the overflow comes from the ceiling, which only a sweep that includes the ceiling shows.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the best young size sat between the extremes (Y=200 of 50 to 400 at T=500) and invalidating cache entries before the next minor GC removed the pause cost entirely; sweep young size with the cache lifetime and the heap limit in the model, since throughput-only or pause-only tuning picks the wrong end.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox, RESULT: PASS on the third iteration after the first two runs refuted parts of my prediction. The pause and full-GC costs, 8 to 2 allocation mix and 1500 heap are assumed model constants, not a real JVM; real collectors with remembered sets or concurrent phases were not modelled.

- Picked-by: new-half

## E476 — write invalidation lowers the gc crossover of a loop sized cache in proportion to lost hits
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [caching][performance][gc][sandbox]
- What: Added write invalidation to the loop-sized LRU cache with a GC pause cost. The GC crossover (pause per live slot where no cache beats a size-5 cache) fell from 985.0 with no writes to 966.2, 887.0, 788.0 and 493.0 as a write after every 50th, 10th, 5th and 2nd read removed more hits, and under frequent writes a cache smaller than the loop became the best size.
- Why built: The GC-cost entry gave the crossover as miss savings divided by collections times slots and said sizes 1 to 4 are never best; the invalidation kernel says cache entries are also removed by a write path. Nobody had checked whether the binary answer and the crossover formula survive writes.
- Design: Stdlib LRU over 1000 reads cycling 5 items; after every W-th read a write deletes the item just read; cost is hits plus 100 per miss plus a pause of reads over 50 times pause times slots; sizes 0 to 8; crossover found by bisection on the pause; best size scanned for pause 0 to 1500 and W of 1 to 50.
- Got right: With no writes the crossover was 985.05 as in the GC-cost entry. With writes it followed savings over collections times slots computed from the simulated hits (887.04 at W=10 with 896 hits) and fell monotonically with write frequency. At W=1 the cache never hits and size 0 was best at pause 0.
- Where/why it failed: My first-run prediction that sizes 1 to 4 are never best was refuted: at W=2 size 3 was best and at W=3 and 4 size 4, because each write deletes the item just read, which shrinks the set the LRU has to hold, so the loop cliff moves to 4 and then 3. I also miscounted lost hits by one (predicted 895 hits and 886.05, observed 896 and 887.04). The best-size map for W=2 to 4 was written after seeing it; only W of 6 to 9 (best size 5) was a true forward prediction.
- Fix: When the model includes writes that delete the item just used, find the best size by scanning sizes under the real write pattern instead of assuming it equals the loop length, and recompute the GC crossover from the hits measured with writes.
- Why this fix: The crossover formula held exactly when fed measured hits, so the only moving part is the hit count, which the write pattern changes and the loop length alone does not predict.
- Rule of thumb: In the model, writes of the item just read lowered the GC crossover from 985 to 493 per slot (W=2) and moved the best cache size from the loop length 5 to 4 (W=3 or 4) and 3 (W=2); re-sweep size and crossover under the actual write pattern instead of reusing the no-write numbers.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox, RESULT: PASS on the second iteration. It is a hand-written cost model with abstract unit costs and a single write pattern (delete the item just read); real collectors, writes to other items and other policies were not run.
- Composed: local__gc-cost-vs-loop-sized-cache/E1, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1, ideas:PERFORMANCE/caching/invalidation/cache-invalidation-is-hard-because-reads-and-writes-race
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the one-sentence rule "re-sweep under the actual write pattern" is sound, but the specific numbers and the "smaller than the loop becomes best" shift are demonstrated for a single contrived delete-the-just-read pattern, and the first round's refuted prediction shows the mechanism wasn't understood before measuring.
- Hidden assumption: Misses scale with writes only because each write deletes the item just read, and a cyclic read pattern means that item is what the loop needs next time around. The rule also assumes the write pattern is periodic and aligned with the loop, which is a property of this toy workload. It further assumes a fixed 100-per-miss cost and a pause linear in slots, so the 493 and 985 figures are artifacts of those constants.
- Would prove it wrong: A run with writes that hit random or non-recent items (or W coprime to 5 with deletes of a different item) where the crossover does not fall monotonically with write rate, or where the best size stays at 5 despite frequent writes. Likewise, if changing the miss cost from 100 to 10 or 1000 moves the best size away from the "4 at W=3 or 4, 3 at W=2" pattern, the rule describes constants, not mechanism.
- Break scenario: Keep W=2 but delete a random item, or the item read one step earlier, instead of the one just read, then sweep size and crossover. In a Zipf-skewed or non-cyclic read stream the loop-length baseline of 5 does not even exist. If the "rule" survives only when the deleted key equals the just-read key in a 5-cycle, it is a restatement of the simulation.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 2e8f8f57b741
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__write-invalidation-lowers-the-gc-crossover-of-a-loop-sized-cache-in-proportion-to-lost-hits.py
- Prediction: Crossover 985 with no writes and falling with write frequency (W=10 predicted 886.05 from 895 hits); sizes 1 to 4 never best; at W=1 the cache is useless. Second round: best size 5 for W of 5 to 50 and 6 to 9, 4 for W of 3 to 4, 3 for W=2, 0 for W=1.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS crossover W0/50/10/5/2 = 985.0/966.2/887.0/788.0/493.0; best size by W: 50 to 5 gave 5, 4 and 3 gave 4, 2 gave 3, 1 gave 0; first round refuted sizes 1 to 4 never best and was off by one hit.
- Scenarios: 1) no writes against the GC-cost entry's 985; 2) write intervals 50, 10, 5, 2 for the crossover; 3) best-size scan over W of 1 to 50 and pause 0 to 1500; 4) BREAK: W=1 where every read is followed by deleting its item

## E475 — write invalidation and late fills on lru fifo loop and hot set caches
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [caching][performance][testing][sandbox]
- What: Added write invalidation and delayed fills to the LRU and FIFO cache simulators. A guard that drops a fill older than the latest invalidation cut stale reads from 10 to 0 on a trace where a write follows each read of one item, and cost 10 of the 86 apparent hits (76 left), the same under both policies.
- Why built: The eviction kernel says size the cache to the loop and the size-sweep entry judges sizes by cost, but both only ever read a cache that is never written. The invalidation kernel says the difficulty is ordering between the fill path and the invalidate path; nobody had run the two together.
- Design: Stdlib simulator with a backing store of versions, an OrderedDict LRU and a deque FIFO, writes that evict the key and record an invalidation version, and fills that land a set number of events after their miss. Traces: 100-read loop of 5 items, 20 rounds of three hot items plus one cold item, the loop with a write to item 0 every 10 reads, and a race trace with a write right after each read of item 0.
- Got right: Without writes the eviction kernel reproduced: 95 of 100 hits for both policies on the 5-loop in 5 slots, 0 for both in 4 slots, LRU 57 against FIFO 30 on the hot set. A write to item 0 every 10 reads dropped both policies to 86 hits, so policy stayed irrelevant on a loop.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that a fill delay of 0 would give 0 stale reads was wrong on the first run: it gave 10 stale reads for both policies, because the fill lands on the next event and the next event was the write. Only an atomic fill installed inside the read gave 0 stale without the guard. Also the unguarded cache's 86 hits include 10 stale hits, so its hit count overstates quality by that much.
- Fix: Judge a cache by stale reads as well as hits, and give the fill path an explicit ordering answer (version check or atomic install) before tuning size or policy.
- Why this fix: The guard removed all stale reads in the race trace under both policies, and the hit cost (86 to 76) is the true price that the unguarded number was hiding.
- Rule of thumb: In the traces tried, size and policy decided hits but not staleness; staleness came from fill-versus-invalidate ordering, so a delayed fill needs a version guard and the reported hit rate should exclude stale hits (86 apparent against 76 real here).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox, RESULT: PASS on the second iteration after the first run refuted my delay-0 prediction. It is a hand-written simulator with five keys and an assumed fill delay of 3 events, not a real cache or workload; multi-writer races were not run.
- Composed: ideas:CACHE-EVICTION/replacement-policy/lru-beats-fifo-on-a-hot-set-but-both-score-zero-on-a-loop-one-slot-too-big, ideas:PERFORMANCE/caching/invalidation/cache-invalidation-is-hard-because-reads-and-writes-race, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 10→0 result is real, but the rule's causal claim ("ordering, not size or policy") rests on one trace shape with one write pattern, and the delay-0 refutation shows the mechanism is misdiagnosed. Next move: rerun the break scenario and a size sweep, and fix the account of why delay 0 still goes stale before filing the rule.
- Hidden assumption: Staleness is purely a fill-versus-invalidate ordering effect, so the version guard is the whole fix. This ignores that the guard itself needs a correct, monotonic invalidation version, and it treats "10 stale reads" as a property of delayed fills when the observed delay-0 run (10 stale) shows the simulator's non-atomic miss/fill path, not delay, creates the race.
- Would prove it wrong: A guarded run with nonzero stale reads under any write pattern, or a trace where size or policy changes the stale count (e.g. a 3-slot cache that evicts a key between its read and its delayed fill). Also, "hits 86 → 76 real" differing between LRU and FIFO would contradict the "same under both policies" claim. The delay-0 result (10 stale, prediction refuted) already undercuts the stated mechanism: the rule says delay causes the race, and delay 0 reproduced it.
- Break scenario: Two writes to item 0 within one fill delay window (read, write, write, fill lands), with a small cache and interleaved cold-item reads, so a fill for an older miss lands after a newer fill for the same key. Then check that the guard compares against the latest invalidation version, not just the first one, and that a late fill can't overwrite a fresher one.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 2749da244cab
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__write-invalidation-and-late-fills-on-lru-fifo-loop-and-hot-set-caches.py
- Prediction: No-write numbers 95, 0, 57 and 30 reproduce; writes lower both policies equally; a delayed fill gives at least one stale read unguarded and 0 guarded; and a delay of 0 gives 0 stale reads (the break attempt).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS loop hits 95, hot LRU/FIFO 57/30, writes loop hits 86, stale unguarded 10/10 guarded 0/0; delay 0 gave 10 stale (prediction refuted), atomic fill gave 0.
- Scenarios: 1) loop of 5 in 5 and 4 slots, hot set in 4 slots, no writes; 2) loop with a periodic write to item 0; 3) race trace with fill delay 3, unguarded versus guarded; 4) BREAK: delay 0 and atomic fill, expecting the race to vanish

## E474 — two pass rhyme letters resolved first vs one pass and spelled key
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][verification]
- What: Rebuilt a rhyme-scheme labeller three ways on a hand-coded phoneme table (one-pass any-rhyme-counts, two-pass resolved-first, and a spelling-keyed grouping) and ran them on the fixtures behind suno-builder/E1 and E3, plus all 4096 four-line stanzas drawn from an 8-word pool.
- Why built: The kernel two-pass-letter-assignment was only quoted in prose by suno-builder/E1 and E3 and sandbox-lyrical-composition/E7; a link needs the claim re-run, not re-read. E1 and E3 disagree about whether a near-rhyme joins the uppercase group, so both readings needed a side-by-side run.
- Design: Words carry (vowel, coda, spelled vowel group). Relation is perfect (same vowel and coda), family (same vowel, both codas stops), assonance (vowel only). One-pass merges any relation into the first earlier match. Two-pass gives uppercase to perfect and family first, then lowercase to assonance among still-unlettered lines. A distinct-family variant gives the family word its own uppercase letter.
- Got right: Fixture sky/tone/mine/line gave ABAA one-pass (a stray assonance pair stole a letter from the real mine/line rhyme) and xxAA two-pass. Over 4096 stanzas one-pass let an assonance-only line share a symbol with a resolved line in 856 cases, two-pass in 0.
- Where/why it failed: truck/mud/blood/flood gives AAAA under both one-pass and two-pass with family counted as resolved, so the two-pass kernel as worded does not by itself separate a near-rhyme from a perfect group; only the distinct-family variant gave BAAA, matching E1's fix. The spelling-keyed grouping gave AABB on the same four words, reproducing E3's observation that spelling splits one spoken rhyme. The case built to break the claim (cat sky bad time, interleaved family and assonance pairs) did not break it: two-pass returned AaAa as predicted.
- Fix: Treat the kernel as proven for its stated mechanism (resolved before assonance, case carries lands versus open) and note that it needs a family-gets-its-own-letter rule to preserve the perfect-versus-family distinction. Key rhymes on pronunciation, not spelling.
- Why this fix: The 856 versus 0 count shows the ordering is what stops the stray steal, while the AAAA result shows ordering alone cannot show family versus perfect, and the AABB result shows the key source matters independently of ordering.
- Rule of thumb: Run resolved rhymes before assonance and key them on pronunciation; if the scheme must show perfect versus near, give near-rhymes their own letter, because ordering alone leaves them folded into the perfect group.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox, all scenarios printed expected values and the last line is RESULT: PASS. Whether writers find the distinct-letter output more legible is not tested here.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-tooling/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, suno-builder/E1, suno-builder/E3
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 0/4096 result is partly circular, because the author's own relation definition and 8-word pool set what counts as stray, and the "give near-rhymes their own letter" half of the rule was checked on one fixture (truck/mud/blood/flood) and never against chained relations.
- Hidden assumption: Pronunciation-keyed relation classes are transitive and sequence-independent (the first-earlier-match and uppercase-first passes assume this), and the hand-coded table plus the 8-word pool stand in for real lyrics, where family and assonance links can chain through shared vowels.
- Would prove it wrong: A stanza where two-pass assigns a lowercase assonance letter to a line that also has a family or perfect relation to a later line, or where the same line pair gets different labels depending on order. Stray-share would then be above 0 for two-pass, or the lowercase letters would split a group that one-pass kept together.
- Break scenario: Interleaved cat/sky/bad/time. Cat and bad share a vowel with stop codas (family), and sky and time share a vowel only (assonance). Check that two-pass gives Ab Ab (family A, assonance b) and not a stray merge. Then add a fifth line, "mat", which is perfect with cat but family with bad. Under two-pass, "bad" takes the uppercase A through its family link to cat, while "mat" and "cat" are perfect. The scheme can't show which relation put each line in A, so the distinct-family fix has to be run on this stanza too.
