## E473 — hyphenated line endings change rhyme letters unless the labeller rejoins the word
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][tooling]
- What: Ran a two-pass rhyme labeller on four stanzas written plain and with Suno-style hyphenated syllables (to-night, beau-ti-ful), reading each line's end word two ways: last hyphen fragment versus the rejoined word. The fragment reader created a false rhyme in one of four stanzas (xAxA became AAxA); the rejoining reader matched the plain scheme in all four.
- Why built: The hyphenate-to-slow kernel is advice about vocal timing, and the two-pass letter work is a labeller; nothing had tested whether the pacing trick corrupts the scheme the labeller reports on the same lyrics.
- Design: Hand-coded vowel/coda table, two-pass lettering (resolved first, then assonance). Stanza A hyphenates end words that still rhyme, B puts beau-ti-ful beside pull and full, C hyphenates re-sound and a-way, D has no hyphen at a line end and is a control. Each is lettered plain, hyphenated with the fragment reader, and hyphenated with the rejoining reader.
- Got right: Stanzas A, C and D were unchanged under the fragment reader because the last fragment happened to carry the same final rhyme as the whole word. Only the rejoining reader was identical to plain in every case, 0 of 4 mismatches against 1 of 4 for the fragment reader.
- Where/why it failed: Stanza B: the fragment ful maps to the vowel of full, so beau-ti-ful joined the pull/full group (AAxA) though beautiful is a different vowel from pull and was lettered x in the plain version. The break attempt (stanza D) cannot break anything because it has no hyphenated ending; it is a control, so the harm shows in one stanza of four, not four of four. The sample is hand-picked, not a corpus.
- Fix: In a lyric tool that accepts hyphenated pacing syllables, strip hyphens from the final whitespace token before looking up its pronunciation, and keep the hyphenated text only for display or for the prompt sent to the vocal model.
- Why this fix: The hyphens carry timing intent for the singer, not spelling of a different word. Rejoining restores the word the rhyme dictionary actually knows, and it was the only reader that matched plain in all four stanzas.
- Rule of thumb: When a pacing trick such as hyphenating syllables is added to lyrics, rejoin the hyphens before judging rhyme; a reader that takes the last fragment can fabricate a rhyme whenever that fragment is itself a word with a different vowel.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand with the saved deterministic sandbox, RESULT: PASS. The Suno rushing effect that motivates hyphenation comes from one community guide and was not tested here; only the labeller side was run.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/suno-prompting/hyphenate-words-to-slow-a-rushed-vocal-line, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-tooling/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, local__two-pass-rhyme-letters-never-merge-perfect-groups-but-hide-assonance-to-a-resolved-group-exhaustive-4-line-stanzas/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — one false rhyme in four stanzas, with the bait chosen by the author and a hand-coded table, shows only that the trick can fail, not that rejoining is the better default, and the rule is stated as if it were general.
- Hidden assumption: Rejoining is always the right reading, but it was only tested against hand-picked stanzas where the author's own table defines both "fragment" and "rhyme". Suno-style hyphens mark sung syllable breaks, not word boundaries. The rule also assumes that every line-end hyphenation is a single word split, and that the sung rhyme matches the written word.
- Would prove it wrong: A set of stanzas where rejoining produces a false or missed rhyme that the fragment reader or a human listener gets right. Examples include a hyphen joining two separate words (e.g. "go-on", "a-way" read as a phrase), or a stretched syllable that is sung to rhyme on the fragment ("beau-ti-FUL" sung as "full"). Also fatal: the fragment reader failing on a larger, unselected sample, or the 1/4 mismatch being an artifact of a table the author wrote after seeing beau-ti-ful.
- Break scenario: A stanza with a line-end compound or phrase hyphenated as two real words, such as "cold-heart" against "start" and "heart". Rejoining makes it "coldheart" (vowel and coda unknown to the table, so no match). The fragment reader gets "heart" right. Add a line ending in an unhyphenated "far" and a hyphenated "gui-tar" to test whether the rejoin reader tracks the stress-final vowel correctly.

## E472 — four to one ladder setback is a friction budget that fails on slick ground near the top rung
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ladder-safety][statics][testing][sandbox]
- What: Modelled the 4-to-1 ladder setback rule with exact-fraction statics and found it is a friction budget: at 4:1 with an 800 N climber on a 100 N ladder the ground needs coefficient 17/72 (0.2361) at the top rung, independent of ladder length, and a ground of 0.20 slips once the climber passes about 0.8376 of the way up.
- Why built: Seeding a new domain with a real scenario. The 4-to-1 rule is a proxy gauge (a ratio people can eyeball) for the real quantity (friction demand), so it tests the claim that a proxy needs its true readout beside it.
- Design: Fractions only, no randomness. Wall force from the moment balance about the base, ground friction needed equal to the wall normal force, no slip when that is at most the ground coefficient times the ground normal force. Sweeps: ladder length 3, 6, 9 m; climber position; wall friction 0.3; four climber and ladder weight pairs.
- Got right: Needed coefficient 0.2361 at 4:1 for every length; the fix at coefficient 0.20 is a lean of 1 to 4.72; wall friction 0.3 lowered the need by 0.41 percent, so a frictionless wall is a safe simplification.
- Where/why it failed: Two of my first-run results were wrong. The setback bisection had its branch reversed and returned 1:1, which I fixed in the code. And I predicted the need would stay within 0.03 of 0.2361 across loads; it spread by 0.0376 because a heavy 400 N ladder dropped it to 0.2083 while a 1500 N climber raised it to 0.2460, so one ratio is a bound, not a constant.
- Fix: Treat 4:1 as safe only when the ground grip is above about 0.25 for the loads tried, otherwise lean flatter by computing the setback from grip and expected top-rung load.
- Why this fix: The need is linear in the setback ratio and rises toward the top rung, so a flatter lean is the only lever once grip is below the budget, and the top-rung case is the worst case to size it on.
- Rule of thumb: Treat a setback ratio as a friction demand, not a safety guarantee: on a hand-written model 4:1 needed ground grip 0.236 to 0.246 at the top rung across loads, so surfaces near or below 0.25 need a flatter lean, found from the formula rather than from the ratio.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved exact-fraction sandbox, RESULT: PASS on the second iteration. It is a model of a rigid ladder with a frictionless or lightly rough wall; the grip values are assumed numbers, not measured surfaces, and tipping, flex and lateral loads were not modelled.
- Composed: ideas:ZEN/verification/finger-is-not-the-moon-proxy-gauge
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the arithmetic is exact, but it is a hand-written, single-model result, and its own spread prediction failed, so the rule of thumb (4:1 needs about 0.236 to 0.246) has no support beyond the idealised statics it came from.
- Hidden assumption: The model assumes a rigid ladder with exactly two contact points, a frictionless or mildly frictional wall, and a flat ground whose friction coefficient is known and constant. It also assumes the load sits at the centre of a rung, the ladder mass is uniform, and static equilibrium is the right test, so dynamic loading, foot-slide impulses, and surface contamination don't matter.
- Would prove it wrong: Physical slip tests where ladders on a measured surface (about 0.25) hold at 4:1 up to the top rung with loads outside the 800 N / 100 N pairs. Or the reverse: a ladder slips on a surface the formula calls safe. Either would show the friction demand is not the binding constraint. The model's own load sweep already refuted the "spread under 0.03" prediction, since the spread came out at 0.0376.

Check whether the static formula still shows margin, and whether wall-top contact, ladder flex or a soft footing breaks the two-point model before the ground slips.

## E471 — morse code needs its gaps because it is not prefix free
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [morse-code][coding][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of International Morse (dit 1 unit, dah 3, letter gap 3) counting how many letter sequences produce the same dit and dah string when the letter gaps are dropped, plus how many letter codes are prefixes of other letter codes.
- Why built: Seeds a Morse-code domain from the real International Morse table, to put numbers on why operators must time the gaps and why the code is not a prefix-free code like Huffman.
- Design: The 26-letter table, a dynamic-programming count of parses of a gap-free string, and a letter-pair prefix count; average letter duration uses a rough English frequency fixture.
- Got right: Counting parses by dynamic programming over code lengths 1 to 4, which is exact for the table.
- Where/why it failed: Without gaps SOS (...---...) parses 192 ways, PARIS 5304, HELP 2764, EEE 4 and ET 2, and 56 letter-code pairs have one code as the prefix of the other, so the dit-dah stream alone does not identify the message.
- Fix: Treat the timed gap as a third symbol of the alphabet and never transmit or store Morse as bare dits and dahs; if a gap-free form is needed, use a prefix-free code.
- Why this fix: The gap carries the letter boundary information that the prefix-violating table cannot, so removing it leaves hundreds of valid readings.
- Rule of thumb: Morse is not prefix-free (56 prefix pairs; SOS has 192 gap-free parses), so keep the letter gap as a symbol when storing or sending it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script against the standard letter table typed in from the ITU alphabet; the frequency fixture used for the average duration is approximate.
- Picked-by: new-domain
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the conclusion (keep the letter gap as a symbol) is sound and nearly tautological, but the PASS only confirms that the thresholds (>10, >1, ≥20) were cleared, and those thresholds are far below what any plausible implementation would produce, so it can't distinguish a correct counter from a sloppy one.
- Hidden assumption: Counting parses and prefix pairs (56, SOS = 192) shows that dropping the gap loses information. The rule assumes the real cost is ambiguity that a receiver would have to resolve, and that a gap-free stream is something people actually store or send. It also assumes the counts are right. I couldn't run the check here, so I haven't confirmed them.
- Would prove it wrong: Any recount that gives a different prefix-pair total (for example, not 56 once a letter is excluded from being its own prefix). A cheaper way to fail it would be a gap-free encoding that the same table decodes uniquely, because that would show the rule is about the missing gap and not about Morse.
- Break scenario: ET versus A. "·−" parses as E+T or as A, and nothing needs a long word. This is the scenario that matters, because it is already inside your own list of short strings (EEE, ET, TEA). It shows ambiguity from two letters, and also that the prefix-pair count and the parse count measure different things.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 15656878e597
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__morse-code-needs-its-gaps-because-it-is-not-prefix-free.py
- Prediction: SOS written without letter gaps has more than 10 distinct parses, EEE has more than 1, and at least 20 letter-code pairs are prefix pairs.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS SOS parses 192 ways and PARIS 5304 without letter gaps; 56 letter-code prefix pairs; average letter 6.1 units vs 19 for uniform dahs
- Scenarios: 1) SOS, PARIS, HELP gap-free parse counts; 2) EEE, ET and TEA short strings, built to BREAK the idea that ambiguity needs long words; 3) all-pairs prefix count over the 26 codes

## E470 — master keying multiplies the keys that open a pin tumbler lock
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [locksmithing][combinatorics][security][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of a five-chamber, six-depth pin-tumbler lock counting how many of the 7776 possible keys open it with no master pin, a master pin in two chambers, and a master pin in all five.
- Why built: Seeds a new locksmithing domain from a real scenario, apartment and office master-key systems, where adding one master pin per chamber is sold as free convenience and its security cost is rarely counted.
- Design: Each chamber allows its change depth, plus a second depth when it carries a master pin; a key opens the lock when every cut is in the allowed set; all 7776 keys are enumerated, and a sibling lock sharing the master cuts is checked for cross-opening.
- Got right: The counts are exact powers of two, 1, 4 and 32 openers, so each master-keyed chamber doubles the keys that open the lock.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing broke; the sibling lock, whose change cuts differ but whose master cuts share the same offset, still had 1 of its 32 keys open this lock, so a shared master offset leaks across locks.
- Fix: Count master-keyed chambers as a security budget: keep the number of master pins as low as the hierarchy needs, and vary the master offsets between sibling locks.
- Why this fix: Openers grow as two to the number of master-keyed chambers, so security falls geometrically with each added master pin while convenience gains are flat.
- Rule of thumb: Each master-keyed chamber doubles the keys that open a pin-tumbler lock (1, 4, 32 openers for 0, 2, 5 master chambers, of 7776 keys), so add master pins only where the hierarchy needs them.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the depth model and the chamber and depth counts are my own simplification of a real lock, not measured on hardware.
- Picked-by: new-domain
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 1/4/32 result is correct, but it follows from the model's definition and the sandbox never varies the allowed-depth count. The advice to "add master pins only where the hierarchy needs them" is also untested, since nothing in the run measures what the extra openers cost or whether they matter.
- Hidden assumption: Each master-keyed chamber adds exactly one new allowed depth, distinct from the change depth, and the chambers are independent. The 2^k count then follows from how the sandbox defines the allowed sets, so enumerating 7776 keys only confirms the arithmetic and doesn't test the rule against any real lock.
- Would prove it wrong: Any master-pin configuration where the opener count isn't 2^k. Examples are a chamber with two master pins (a grand-master tier) giving 3 allowed depths and a factor of 3, a master depth equal to the change depth giving no doubling, or a sibling-lock check showing more than the predicted cross-openers.
- Break scenario: Two chambers each carry a master pin and a grand-master pin (3 allowed depths each), with one chamber's master depth set equal to its change depth. Predicted by "doubling" this would be 4 openers. Enumeration would give 3×1 = 3, and with both chambers at 3 depths it would give 9.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest e72ec5585801
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__master-keying-multiplies-the-keys-that-open-a-pin-tumbler-lock.py
- Prediction: Openers are 1 with no master pin, 4 with master pins in two of five chambers, and 32 with master pins in all five.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS openers plain 1, master in 2 of 5 chambers 4, master in all 5 32 of 7776; sibling keys that cross-open 1 of 32
- Scenarios: 1) no master pins; 2) master pins in two chambers, built to BREAK a flat all-or-nothing reading; 3) master pins in all five; 4) sibling lock with the same master offset

## E469 — invalidation widens the sizes that earn hits under gc
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][gc][invalidation][sandbox]
- What: Full size sweep (0 to 61 slots) of an LRU cache on a 60-key loop of 600 accesses under a toy generational GC, with no invalidation and with one invalidation every 10 accesses, counting which sizes earn any hit and which hit-earning size has the lowest GC work.
- Why built: The loop-sized-cache GC lesson found only exact fit pays, and the earlier invalidation sandbox showed size 59 recovering with invalidation; the sweep tests whether invalidation moves the cheapest size, not only the one-short case.
- Design: Same toy GC as the invalidation sandbox (nursery of 10 allocations, major collection after 20 dead promoted entries); the sweep runs every size and reports hits, work and majors, keeping the cheapest size with at least one hit.
- Got right: Without invalidation only sizes 60 and 61 earned any hit (2 of 62), with the cheapest at exactly 60 for 60 work, matching the loop-cliff lesson.
- Where/why it failed: Invalidation widened the hit-earning sizes from 2 to 8 (54 to 61), for example size 58 went from 0 hits and 2490 work to 348 hits and 880 work, but the cheapest hit-earning size stayed at 60 and its work rose from 60 to 270, so partial caches get hits without getting cheaper than exact fit.
- Fix: When writes invalidate entries, a slightly undersized cache is no longer worthless, yet still size to the loop; do not pick a smaller cache on the strength of the recovered hits.
- Why this fix: The hole from each invalidation breaks the thrash only occasionally, so hits recover partially while promoted dead entries still feed major collections, which keeps exact fit the cheapest of the hit-earning sizes.
- Rule of thumb: In the toy GC, invalidation every 10 accesses let 8 of 62 sizes earn hits (up from 2) but the cheapest hit-earning size on a 60-loop stayed at 60, so keep sizing to the loop even when invalidation rescues smaller caches.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the GC thresholds and the invalidation schedule are my own fixtures, one loop length and one invalidation period only.
- Composed: gc-cost-vs-loop-sized-cache/E1, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — one cadence, one GC configuration and a "≥1 hit" bar support only "size 60 was cheapest here", and size 58 earning 348 hits at 880 work shows the margin is thin and the "keep sizing to the loop" advice is untested against other cadences.
- Hidden assumption: The rule assumes the toy GC's constants (10-allocation nursery, major after 20 dead promoted entries) and the invalidation period of 10 are representative, and that "cheapest" means lowest GC work with a hit count of at least 1. That makes the result a function of one cadence, one loop length and a one-hit threshold, not of invalidation as such.
- Would prove it wrong: A hit-earning size below 60 with lower GC work than size 60's 270. Size 58 already earns 348 hits at work 880, so the rule survives only because 880 exceeds 270. The same would hold if any of the 8 hit-earning sizes (size 30 is a spot check) beat 270, or if a different cadence, say every 5 or 20 accesses, moved the minimum off 60.
- Break scenario: Repeat the sweep with invalidation every 5, 20 and 30 accesses, then with nursery sizes 5 and 20 and a hit threshold of "at least 10% of accesses". If a small size such as 30 clears the threshold at work under 270, "keep sizing to the loop" is false. Also compare hits per unit of work. Size 60 is the cheapest earner, but that does not make it the best, and the rule never says what "cheapest" is being traded against.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 758dbc14f0a3
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__invalidation-widens-the-sizes-that-earn-hits-under-gc.py
- Prediction: Without invalidation only sizes 60 and 61 earn hits; with invalidation every 10 more sizes earn hits, the cheapest hit-earning size is still 60, and its work rises above the no-invalidation figure.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS sizes earning hits 2 -> 8; cheapest hit-earning size 60 (work 60) -> 60 (work 270); size 58 hits 0 -> 348, work 2490 -> 880
- Scenarios: 1) full 0 to 61 sweep, no invalidation; 2) the same sweep with invalidation every 10, built to BREAK the claim that only exact fit pays; 3) size 58 and 30 spot checks

## E468 — one pass rhyme letters flip the emotional shape label
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][sandbox]
- What: Exhaustive sandbox over all 1296 four-line stanzas built from six end words (two perfect pairs, one assonance-only word, one lone word) comparing the rhyme-scheme shape from one-pass lettering (any shared vowel rhymes) with two-pass lettering (perfect rhymes take the main letters), and the emotional motion each shape implies.
- Why built: The shape kernel says AABB and ABAB read stable while ABBA and an unrhymed first couplet read open; the two-pass kernel and its companion show one-pass lettering merges non-perfect lines, so the question was whether that merge changes the emotional reading, not just the label.
- Design: Words carry a vowel and a coda; perfect means both match, assonance means vowel only. Shapes map to stable, open or other per the shape kernel. Every stanza is labelled both ways and compared on shape and on emotion class.
- Got right: With a vocabulary of perfect rhymes only the two methods agreed on 256 of 256 stanzas, so the divergence comes from assonance and not from the lettering code itself.
- Where/why it failed: One-pass lettering gave a different shape on 896 of 1296 stanzas (69.1%) and a different emotion class on 456 (35.2%), for example cat cat cap cap read as AAAA instead of the stable AABB, so the stability claim would be judged on the wrong shape.
- Fix: Derive the shape that drives any emotional-motion advice from the two-pass perfect-rhyme letters and show assonance only as a separate lowercase layer.
- Why this fix: The emotion kernel is about resolved stopping points, and only perfect and family rhymes resolve, so a label that counts assonance as a rhyme misreads where the stanza stops.
- Rule of thumb: Compute the AABB/ABAB/ABBA shape from perfect-rhyme groups only; on this six-word fixture one-pass lettering changed the shape in 69% and the stable-versus-open reading in 35% of stanzas.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the six-word vocabulary and the emotion mapping are my own fixtures, not measured listener data.

- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the rule is true as arithmetic on this fixture, but the percentages describe how the fixture was built, not how often one-pass lettering misreads actual poems, and the prediction thresholds were set after the design was fixed.
- Hidden assumption: The 69% and 35% measure the real-world cost of one-pass lettering, but they are mostly set by the fixture: six words, with 4 of 6 in perfect pairs and 1 of 6 assonance-only. Uniform enumeration over 1296 stanzas also weights each word position equally, which no real poem does.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with a different assonance-to-perfect ratio, or on real stanzas weighted by actual end-word frequency. If shape divergence falls under 50% or emotion divergence under 30%, the rule is a fixture artifact and not a property of the lettering methods.
- Break scenario: Take a corpus where assonance-only words are rare, such as a stanza set drawn from the two perfect pairs plus the lone word, with the assonance word never used. One-pass and two-pass will agree on nearly every stanza, so the "69%" claim vanishes. The 256/256 perfect-only control already shows this: divergence needs the assonance word, so the rule is really "divergence ≈ share of stanzas containing it."

## E467 — invalidation under generational gc on a loop cache
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][gc][invalidation][sandbox]
- What: Toy generational GC (nursery of 10 allocations, major GC when 20 promoted entries have died) under an LRU cache on a 60-key loop of 600 accesses, sizes 0/30/59/60, with and without one invalidation every 10 accesses.
- Why built: The garbage-collection kernel and the cache sweep say a loop cache one slot short is the worst case; the invalidation companion had never been tested with them, so the question was what invalidation does to the GC bill.
- Design: Entries are young until a minor collection promotes the live ones; entries that die after promotion count as old garbage; a major pass costs old size plus garbage; work totals copy and major costs.
- Got right: Exactly-sized cache 60 without invalidation cost 60 work and 0 majors with 540 hits; size 59 without invalidation cost 2490 work and 27 majors with 0 hits, as the earlier lessons predicted.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction held, but the surprise is the direction for 59: invalidation every 10 cut its work from 2490 to 544 (majors 27 to 5) and gave 428 hits, because the invalidation holes stop the evict-the-next-needed-key thrash; meanwhile exactly-sized 60 got worse, 60 to 270 work and 2 majors, since every invalidated promoted entry becomes old garbage.
- Fix: Judge a loop cache by GC work and hits measured with the real invalidation rate rather than only the no-write sweep, since invalidation moves cost from the one-short cache to the exact-fit one.
- Why this fix: Invalidation both frees slots (helping a short cache) and kills promoted entries (feeding major collections), so the two effects pull the GC bill in opposite directions depending on how full the cache is.
- Rule of thumb: In this toy GC, invalidation raised exact-fit loop cache cost (60 to 270 work) yet cut one-short cache cost (2490 to 544), so measure GC work with invalidation included instead of trusting the write-free size sweep.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the toy GC thresholds are my own model, not a real runtime.
- Composed: ideas:PERFORMANCE/garbage-collection, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1, ideas:PERFORMANCE/invalidation
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the observed numbers match the prediction, but the evidence is one invalidation period and one set of GC constants, and the "measure with invalidation included" advice is sound while the specific cost ordering isn't established.
- Hidden assumption: The size-59 versus size-60 gap and the invalidation effect come from the GC model itself and would carry over to other workloads, but the one-short collapse is really LRU thrashing on a strict cyclic scan (hits59 = 0). The rule also assumes the invalidation schedule isn't what rescues size 59, and that the toy's cost constants (nursery of 10, major trigger of 20 dead promoted entries) aren't tuned to produce this ordering.
- Would prove it wrong: Size 59 with invalidation costing more than size 60 with invalidation, or the 60-versus-59 ordering flipping when the invalidation period moves from 10 to 7 or 13, or the nursery or major threshold changes from 10/20. Any of these would show the "invalidation cuts one-short cost" result is an artifact of the chosen parameters rather than a rule.
- Break scenario: Sweep invalidation period over 2 to 59 and nursery over 5 to 20, using the same 60-key loop at sizes 59 and 60. Include a period that never hits the entry about to be evicted, and a period of 60 or a multiple of it so the same keys are invalidated every lap. If 59 stays cheaper than 60 only at period 10, or work60 stays at 270 only at that setting, the rule is a single-point observation.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 6f615c5f712e
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__invalidation-under-generational-gc-on-a-loop-cache.py
- Prediction: Exact-fit size 60 costs more GC work with invalidation every 10 than without it (from 60), and size 59 without invalidation stays costlier than size 60 without it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS work60 no-inv 60, inv 270; work59 no-inv 2490, inv 544; majors59 27 to 5; hits59 0 to 428.
- Scenarios: 1) sizes 0, 30, 59, 60 with no invalidation; 2) the same with invalidation every 10, built to BREAK the claim that the one-short cache is always the worst; 3) 60 versus 59 compared on hits, work and majors.

## E466 — invalidation does not move the loop cliff
- Date: 2026-10-19
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching][invalidation][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of a 5-key cyclic loop (100 accesses) through LRU and FIFO caches of size 0, 4, 5, 6 with one key invalidated every 10 or every 2 accesses, to see whether invalidation changes the loop-size cliff.
- Why built: The kernel says size the cache to the loop, since one slot short scores zero for both policies; the companion performance/invalidation raised whether writes that evict entries leave that cliff where it is.
- Design: OrderedDict cache, deterministic round-robin invalidation victim, counts hits and invalidations that actually removed an entry.
- Got right: Size 5 and 6 agree for both policies (95 hits with no invalidation, 86 with 9 invalidations, 48 with 48), and each effective invalidation costs exactly one hit; size 0 stays 0.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction (size 4 stays at 0 hits at every invalidation rate) was wrong: LRU size 4 got 12 hits at every-10 and 39 at every-2, FIFO size 4 got 51 and 48, because an invalidation leaves a free slot so the next miss evicts nothing and the cyclic thrash is broken.
- Fix: Do not treat the loop cliff as fixed once entries get invalidated; measure hit rate with the real invalidation rate, and size to the loop plus the steady invalidation holes.
- Why this fix: The cliff is a property of a full cache evicting the next-needed key; holes from invalidation remove that eviction, so the effective capacity is higher than the slot count suggests.
- Rule of thumb: A one-slot-short loop cache is only at zero hits while nothing invalidates; in the tested round-robin runs (every 10 and every 2 accesses, 100 accesses) invalidation let it recover hits (LRU4 12 to 39, FIFO4 about 50), so benchmark with writes included before sizing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: ideas:CACHE-EVICTION/lru-beats-fifo-on-a-hot-set-but-both-score-zero-on-a-loop-one-slot-too-big, sandbox-cache-size-sweep-loop-cliff-and-ram-ceiling/E1, ideas:PERFORMANCE/invalidation
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the refuted prediction is real, but the rule generalizes from one deterministic round-robin schedule, and the advice to benchmark with writes is sound while the "recover hits" claim is unproven beyond it.
- Hidden assumption: Recovery is a general property of invalidation, when it likely depends on the specific round-robin victim order, the loop-to-interval phase (10 and 2 against a 5-loop), and the 100-access length, so one deterministic schedule is being read as a rule.
- Would prove it wrong: A run with random or loop-aligned victims (for example always invalidating the key that is about to be evicted, or the one just accessed) in which size 4 stays at 0 hits, or the FIFO4 and LRU4 hit counts shift sharply with the start offset or access count, would show the recovery is an artifact of the schedule.
- Break scenario: Size 4 on a 5-loop with the invalidation victim chosen as the key accessed next (or invalidating the just-accessed key every 2 accesses), compared against random victims over many seeds and over 100 versus 1000 accesses, to see whether hits stay at 0 or the 12 to 51 spread collapses.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-19 · digest 6885c885aa09
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-19__invalidation-does-not-move-the-loop-cliff.py
- Prediction: With one key invalidated every 10 or 2 accesses on a 5-loop, LRU and FIFO of size 4 stay at exactly 0 hits and size 5 loses one hit per invalidation.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL prediction refuted; lru4 hits 12 (every 10) and 39 (every 2), fifo4 51 and 48, lru5 86 and 48, size 5 loses exactly one hit per invalidation.
- Scenarios: 1) no invalidation, sizes 0/4/5/6; 2) invalidate every 10; 3) invalidate every 2, built to BREAK the cliff claim; 4) FIFO versus LRU at each.

## E465 — lossless cutoff stays worst gate only under jitter
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][input][state][testing]
- What: On a P15 W5 one-sided wave with 24 cycling lags and jitter J added to every seventh press, the lossless cutoff equalled the largest valid effective lag in all four cases (19, 19, 28, 32 for J 0, 2, 4, 8), but the gate-only invalid count at that cutoff was the maximum over cutoffs only for J 4 and 8 (135 and 133); at J 0 and 2 it was 95 and 94 against maxima of 135 and 137 reached at cutoffs 24 and 26.
- Why built: Join the lossless-is-worst rule and the one-sided cost formula with the jitter sweep to see whether jitter keeps the lossless cutoff the worst gate-only setting.
- Design: 600 ticks, one press per tick with nominal lag cycling 1..24, landing lag plus J on every 7th press; legal(t)=t mod 15 < 5; valid means legal at issue and at landing; invalid-exec means legal at issue and illegal at landing; scan cutoffs 0..39 for lost valid presses and for gate-only invalid executions. The sandbox also records the highest effective lag among invalid-exec presses and compares it with the cutoff where the gate-only count peaks.
- Got right: The lossless cutoff tracks the largest valid effective lag, so jitter moves it (19 to 28 to 32) exactly as the measured maximum valid lag moves, matching the jitter sweep lesson.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the lossless cutoff would be the worst gate-only cutoff in every case failed: at J 0 and 2 the lossless cutoff (19) sits below the lag range where invalid executions keep accumulating (maxima at 24 and 26), so it is not the worst; and the invalid counts of 95 and 94 were below my wrongly assumed 200 cap.
- Fix: Compute the highest effective lag that can land illegal and compare it to the lossless cutoff; the lossless point is the worst only if it is at or above it, otherwise a larger cutoff is worse.
- Why this fix: Gate-only invalid executions keep growing with the cutoff until every lag in the issued range is admitted, so whether the lossless cutoff is the maximum depends on where the lag range ends, not on the wave period or the jitter alone.
- Rule of thumb: Lossless cutoff equals the largest valid effective lag under jitter; the gate-only invalid count peaks at the highest effective lag that can land illegal (24, 26, 27, 31 for J 0, 2, 4, 8), so the lossless cutoff is the worst gate-only setting only when it is at or above that lag.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: lossless-cutoff-is-worst-without-validity/E1, sandbox-one-sided-formula-explains-gate-invalid-counts/E1, validity-cutoff-jitter-amplitude-sweep-sixth-angle/E1
- Picked-by: new-half

## E464 — hand kept cut list drifts off beat and flips the ranking
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model]
- What: A beat-cut list written by hand for a 120 BPM draft stays 100% on-beat at 120 BPM but only 10% at 128 and 30% at 140; with the clock-recut loss of 0.23 prorated by off-beat share, that flips the IPM times D1 winner from variant C (110.0, derived cuts) to variant A (100.0), while a 240 BPM variant, whose grid contains the old cuts, still lands 100% on-beat.
- Why built: Compose the derive-do-not-sync rule for two files that must agree with the trailer kernel's pick-the-music-first, cut-every-transition-to-a-beat structure and the IPM times D1 ranking, to see whether a stale hand-kept cut list can change which ad wins.
- Design: Python stdlib: ten cuts at beats 4 to 40; the hand list stores seconds computed once at 120 BPM; the derived list recomputes seconds from each variant's own BPM; on-beat means within one frame (1/30 s) of a beat; three variants at 120, 128, 140 BPM with base scores 100, 104, 110; score is base times one minus 0.23 times the off-beat share; a fourth case at 240 BPM tests where the stale list still works.
- Got right: Deriving cuts from the music removes the drift completely (1.0 on-beat everywhere) and keeps the true best variant on top, as the single-source rule predicts.
- Where/why it failed: The hand list looks fine for the draft it was written on and for tempos that are whole multiples of it (240 BPM), so a quick check at one tempo would pass it; the 0.23 loss, the base scores and the one-frame tolerance are assumed numbers, not measured ad data.
- Fix: Store cuts as beat numbers and compute seconds from the chosen track's tempo each time; verify on-beat share per variant before ranking.
- Why this fix: The beat number is the single source of truth and seconds are a pure function of tempo, so there is no second file to drift out of agreement.
- Rule of thumb: Keep cut points as beat numbers and derive seconds from each variant's tempo; a hand-copied seconds list is on-beat only at the tempo it was written for (and its multiples), and can flip the ranking.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: ideas:FILM/trailer-grammar/cold-open-three-acts-button-cut-to-the-beat, collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the rule itself (store beats, derive seconds) is sound, but the evidence is one synthetic penalty with a hand-picked 0.23 and 3 variants, so the winner flip says more about the scoring parameters than about the cut method.
- Hidden assumption: Beat-aligned cuts are what the score rewards, and a 0.23 loss prorated linearly by off-beat share is a realistic proxy. The rule never tests whether the hand list fails for reasons other than tempo mismatch, such as a cut chosen for a visual event rather than a beat.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-run with the loss at 0.05 or at a threshold step. If A still beats C, the flip comes from the base-score gaps (100/104/110) and not from the cut method. Or if a ±1-frame jitter on the derived cuts drops its on-beat share below the hand list's. Either would show the rule is an artifact of how "on-beat" and the penalty were defined.
- Break scenario: Use a 90 BPM variant (or 180, a multiple of 90 that is not a multiple of 120), with a hand list computed at 120. Beats at 90 BPM land every 0.667 s and the 120 list steps every 0.5 s, so only every third cut coincides. The "multiples" clause is then wrong in the other direction: it is true for integer multiples of 120 (240) and not for lower tempos like 60, where the 120 grid is a superset, not a subset. Also try the 128-BPM case with a one-frame tolerance, where 30 fps frame quantisation makes the share depend on rounding.

## E463 — fib linear scaling is generic to rotations offsets and fit anchor
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][input][state][testing]
- What: Across 25 window offsets, with the line fitted from the short horizon N 600 and tested at N 4800, the gate-only invalid count deviates by at most 10 presses on the golden-rotation word and 9 on a sqrt2-minus-1 rotation control, against 153 for a density-matched Bernoulli word, so the linear scaling is a property of rotation words generally, not of Fibonacci specifically.
- Why built: The companion lesson claimed linear scaling on a Fibonacci word, but its own check noted a single start offset, a self-anchored fit and no deterministic control; this run removes those three gaps and also rechecks the lossless-cutoff rule on the same word.
- Design: Rotation words built as floor((t+1)a)-floor(t a) for a=0.618 and a=0.414, plus one seeded Bernoulli word; invalid(L,N,s) counts t in [s,s+N) with legal at t-L and illegal at t; deviation is the absolute gap between the N 4800 count and 8 times the N 600 count at lags 55, 89 and 47 over 25 starts spaced 37 apart; a separate pass computes the smallest lossless cutoff for lags 3,8,21,55,89 with validity stacked.
- Got right: Lossless cutoff came out 89, equal to the largest lag with a valid press, on the Fibonacci word. The Bernoulli control separated by more than 10 times (94 to 153 versus 7 to 10).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of at most 3 presses deviation was wrong because fitting from N 600 multiplies the per-window discrepancy by 8; the observed 7 to 10 is about one press of window discrepancy. The Fibonacci-specific contrast failed: the sqrt2 rotation control scaled just as well (4 to 9).
- Fix: Treat bounded-discrepancy linear extrapolation as a property of any rotation word and use the rotation distance formula, keeping the per-lag scan for random legality.
- Why this fix: A rotation word has bounded discrepancy so counts over any window differ from rate times length by a constant, whatever the irrational slope; a random word's discrepancy grows like the square root of the window.
- Rule of thumb: Linear extrapolation of the gate-only invalid count holds for any irrational rotation word, at every tested offset and when fitted from a short run, so it is not Fibonacci-specific; random legality of equal density does not extrapolate.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: fibonacci-gate-invalid-count-scales-linearly-with-horizon-while-random-drifts/E1, age-cutoff-lossless-threshold-exceeds-period-p12/E1, lossless-cutoff-is-worst-without-validity/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — Two golden-class (bounded partial quotient) words at 10 and 9 deviation, with the pre-registered prediction failed, support "bounded-type rotation words", not "any irrational rotation word", and the "generally" claim is untested at the slopes where it would break.
- Hidden assumption: Small deviation of the N 4800 count from 8 times the N 600 count means the count is linear in N for any rotation word. That treats the sqrt2-minus-1 control as a different rotation word. It is one more word at an irrational, bounded-type slope, and a bound of 9 to 10 on a count of roughly several hundred is a bounded-discrepancy effect. The test also assumes "legal" is a fixed function of the word alone. It never says what the legality rule is. Under a different rule, rotation structure would not carry over.
- Would prove it wrong: A rotation word with a Liouville-like or very-well-approximable slope (large partial quotients), or a rational-adjacent slope such as a = 0.6180 + 1e-6, whose deviation at lags 55/89/47 grows with N instead of staying near 10. A Bernoulli-vs-rotation gap of 153 vs 10 also fails to separate "rotation" from "any low-discrepancy sequence", so a Kronecker or van der Corput word with the same density would produce the same pass.
- Break scenario: Run the same 25-offset, N 600 → 4800 fit on a = 0.6180 + 1e-6 or a continued fraction [0;1,1,1,200,...], and add an 8th-power horizon (N 600 → 38400). If the deviation scales with N or with the largest partial quotient, "any irrational rotation word" is false. Note too that the prediction was wrong on two of three parts, and the observed run printed FAIL. The sqrt2 control did not deviate more than Fibonacci by the stated criterion, and Fibonacci missed its 3-press bound (10 observed). The rule is therefore fitted after the fact to a failed prediction, and that is not confirmation.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-18 · digest c36efd667816
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-18__fib-linear-scaling-is-generic-to-rotations-offsets-and-fit-anchor.py

## E462 — comic engine variety cannot beat a fixed kit similarity floor
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model]
- What: In a 16-slot model of an 8-video fake-ad batch, giving every video its own comic engine (which fixes four slots: joke, script, voiceover, layout) lowers mean pairwise similarity from 0.875 to a floor of exactly 0.625 (10 of 16 kit slots), never below it, while rotating 3 kit assets as well reaches 0.451.
- Why built: Test whether varying the comic engine instead of the topic, the kernel's advice, is enough to keep a batch under a similarity flag line when the reusable kit stays fixed.
- Design: Python stdlib model: 10 kit slots, 2 topic slots that always differ, 4 engine-tied slots equal to the video's engine id; 8 videos with engines assigned round-robin over E in 1,2,4,8; k of 10 kit assets rotate through a pool of 6 variants by video index for k in 0,3,6; batch score is mean over all 28 pairs of the share of identical slots.
- Got right: Engine variety is real value: similarity falls monotonically with E (0.875, 0.732, 0.661, 0.625), and the fixed-kit floor of 0.625 matches the earlier template-similarity entry.
- Where/why it failed: The floor means no amount of engine variety gets a fixed-kit batch under the 0.5 flag line assumed in the template entry; the slot structure and the 0.5 line are assumptions of the model, not platform facts, and the 10-asset kit size comes from the source-checked list without measuring a real platform.
- Fix: Vary the comic engine and rotate at least 3 kit assets per video together; treat engine variety as covering only the engine-tied slots.
- Why this fix: Similarity counts slots, and the kit slots are untouched by the engine, so only kit rotation lowers the floor; with 3 rotated and 8 engines the batch reached 0.451.
- Rule of thumb: Varying the comic engine cannot lower batch similarity below the fixed-kit share of slots (0.625 here); to get under 0.5 also rotate 3 or more kit assets.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/ideation/vary-the-comic-engine-not-the-topic, fake-ad-kit-template-similarity/E1, fake-ad-kernel-source-check/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the rule is true by construction (floor = kit share, 10/16), and the 0.5 threshold and "3 or more assets" cutoff are properties of this toy's pool size and slot counts, not a finding that transfers to real batches.
- Hidden assumption: The 0.625 "floor" is an arithmetic artifact of the model's own construction (10 of 16 slots hard-coded as kit, 2 topic slots hard-coded as always differing, engines hard-coded to fix exactly 4 slots), so it says nothing about real fake-ad batches, where an engine may also change kit-like slots and the slot weights and counts are unmeasured.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-run with the engine-to-slot coupling widened (an engine ties 5 or 6 slots, some of them kit slots) or with equal-weight slots swapped for perceptual similarity on real rendered videos. If E=8 lands below 0.625 with kit rotation at 0, the "cannot go below" claim was only the 10/16 constant.
- Break scenario: Keep the 16 slots but make kit slots 8 and engine-tied slots 6, with topic at 2, and rotate 0 kit assets. The floor then becomes 0.5 by the same arithmetic, so "0.625" is not a property of engine variety. Also run 6 rotated kit assets with E=8 against a pool of 6 variants across 8 videos, since variants repeat by index (8 videos, 6 variants) and cap how low rotation can go.

## E461 — cache fill invalidate race needs version check
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][caching]
- What: Exhaustive model of one reader (read db, fill cache) racing one writer (write db, invalidate cache): of the 6 order-preserving interleavings exactly 1 (reader reads, writer writes and invalidates, then reader fills) leaves the cache permanently stale under a plain invalidate-on-write policy.
- Why built: To test the claim that cache invalidation is structurally hard because the fill path and invalidate path race, and to see which fix survives a loop-sized LRU and latency-ratio cost model.
- Design: Python stdlib script enumerates all interleavings of R1,R2 against W1,W2, runs a naive policy and a versioned-fill policy (reject a fill carrying an older version than the db), then runs a 5-key loop over a capacity-5 LRU with a write that skips invalidation, using a 500000 vs 100 miss/hit cost ratio, sweeping TTL.
- Got right: The race is real and narrow: only 1 of 6 orderings breaks, and version-checked fill removed it (0 of 6). The fill-after-invalidate case is exactly the kernel's mechanism.
- Where/why it failed: Plain invalidate-on-write is not sufficient, and the failure is rare enough (1/6 here, far rarer in practice) to hide from tests. TTL as the fallback heals staleness but is expensive: on the loop-sized cache stale reads fell 981 to 0 only at TTL 5, and cost rose from 2.6M to 500M units because every access became a miss.
- Fix: Version or sequence-number the fill so a stale fill is rejected; use a TTL only as a bounded-staleness safety net sized against miss cost.
- Why this fix: The version check closes the single bad ordering at the cost of one comparison, while TTL tuned to the loop length turns a loop-sized cache into no cache at all.
- Rule of thumb: Invalidate-on-write alone leaves a fill-after-invalidate ordering that stays stale forever; add a version check on fill, and treat TTL as a costly bounded-staleness fallback, not the primary fix.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: ideas:PERFORMANCE/caching/invalidation/cache-invalidation-is-hard-because-reads-and-writes-race, ideas:PERFORMANCE/hardware/latency-numbers, gc-cost-vs-loop-sized-cache/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The 1/6 versus 0/6 result is true but trivial for the one-reader, one-writer model, and the "TTL is costly" half rests on a cyclic workload that makes LRU pathological, so the rule overreaches until you add a second writer, an atomic-fill check and a non-cyclic workload.
- Hidden assumption: The model has only one reader, one writer and a single-version db, with the db read atomic and the fill unconditional. The cost ratio of 500000 vs 100 and the loop workload are also taken as representative, and "TTL costs more than it heals" is read off a capacity-5 LRU and a 5-key loop, which is the worst case for LRU.
- Would prove it wrong: A versioned-fill run that leaves any stale entry. That means a version check and the fill are not atomic (check-then-fill TOCTOU), or the version is read from a replica or cache that lags. Also wrong: a TTL sweep where TTL>=5 costs less than it heals once the access pattern is not a cyclic scan. The reported "981->0 for 2599500->500000000" shows TTL=5 equals the loop length, so every access is a miss, which is thrash, not a TTL effect.
- Break scenario: Two writers and two readers with a non-atomic check-then-fill. Reader A reads v1 and passes the version check, writer 2 bumps to v2 and invalidates, then A fills v1. The versioned policy ends permanently stale. Run the same sweep on a Zipf workload with a larger cache, where a TTL of 50 to 500 heals the lossy-invalidate staleness at a small miss-cost increase.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-18 · digest e6c64f0a6d5f
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-18__cache-fill-invalidate-race-needs-version-check.py
- Prediction: Predicted 1 of 6 interleavings stale for the naive policy, 0 for versioned, and TTL below the loop length to cost more than it heals.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS naive stale interleavings=1/6 versioned=0/6; TTL=5 cuts stale reads 981->0 at cost 2599500->500000000
- Scenarios: 1) naive policy over all 6 interleavings; 2) versioned policy over all 6; 3) BREAK attempt: lossy-invalidate loop workload with TTL none/50/10/5 on a capacity-5 LRU

## E460 — attention vs recurrence ops depth crossover at n equals d
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [machine-learning][performance][model]
- What: A counter-based model of one recurrent layer and one self-attention layer shows attention uses more multiply-adds than recurrence from n=d+1 on (17, 65, 257 for d=16, 64, 256), costing 64x at n=4096 and d=64, while the recurrent layer's sequential depth and token-to-token path grow as n (512 at n=512) against a constant 3 and 1 for attention.
- Why built: To apply the transformer kernel, whose headline is far lower training cost than recurrent systems, and find where its cost argument stops: the win is depth and parallelism, not fewer operations.
- Design: Python stdlib counter: the recurrent layer costs 2*d*d multiply-adds per step in a chain of n steps; the attention layer costs 2*n*n*d in three sequential stages; crossover found by scanning n up to 4096 for three widths; a Chinchilla-style budget C=6*N*D with D=20*N is computed to size the model and tokens at C=1e21.
- Got right: Attention buys parallel depth at an operation cost that grows as n squared; the crossover sits exactly where sequence length passes the width, and the compute-optimal split came out 20 tokens per parameter as set.
- Where/why it failed: The operation counts are closed-form formulas typed into the model, so the n=d crossover is derived by the model, not discovered by it; the BLEU and 3.5-day claims of the kernel were not tested at all, and I predicted the crossover at n=d while the strict comparison gives d+1.
- Fix: Judge an attention-versus-recurrence cost claim by comparing sequence length with width and by the hardware's parallel capacity, since fewer sequential steps do not mean fewer operations.
- Why this fix: Training time is set by operations divided by parallelism and by the critical path, and attention shortens the path at the price of extra operations once n exceeds d.
- Rule of thumb: Attention beats recurrence on training wall-clock by depth, not by operation count: past n equal to d it does more multiply-adds, so a cost win exists only while the hardware can absorb the extra work in parallel.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; numbers above are its printed output.
- Composed: ideas:MACHINE-LEARNING/architectures/transformer/attention-is-all-you-need-beat-prior-translation-sota-with-far-less-training-cost, ideas:MACHINE-LEARNING/scaling-laws/chinchilla/compute-optimal-70b-model-with-more-tokens-beat-280b-model-with-fewer
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the counts and depths are correct by construction, but the wall-clock conclusion is untested and depends on an unstated parallel-hardware premise, so the next move is to time both layers on real hardware at n=512 and n=4096.
- Hidden assumption: Wall-clock is set by sequential depth, so the rule assumes hardware parallelism is unlimited and that memory bandwidth, not multiply-adds, is never the bottleneck. The counter also treats attention's n×n score matrix as free to store and move, and it ignores batch size, which supplies the parallelism recurrence would otherwise lack.
- Would prove it wrong: Measured training step time at n=4096, d=64, batch fixed, where a fused-kernel recurrent layer (such as a scan or a cuDNN-style LSTM) matches or beats naive attention. The same result would appear if attention's step time scaled with n² as the MAC count predicts, instead of staying flat while depth stays at 3.
- Break scenario: A memory-bound regime: n=4096, d=64, large batch, no flash-style fusion. The n×n scores per head and batch element mean attention is limited by bandwidth and activation memory, not depth. The 64x extra MACs then show up almost directly as wall-clock, or as an out-of-memory error, and the rule's claim that depth wins stops being true. The "PASS" shows only that the counter agrees with its own formulas (2·n²·d against 2·n·d² is d+1 by algebra), not that wall-clock was measured.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-18 · digest fb662effd95e
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-18__attention-vs-recurrence-ops-depth-crossover-at-n-equals-d.py
- Prediction: Predicted attention exceeds recurrent multiply-adds at n=d for each width, recurrent depth equals n, attention depth stays constant, and at n=4096, d=64 attention costs about 64x; the crossover came out at d+1.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS attention macs overtake recurrent exactly at n=d+1 ({16: 17, 64: 65, 256: 257}); n=4096,d=64 attention costs 64x the macs but rnn depth is 1365x deeper
- Scenarios: 1) widths 16, 64, 256 crossover scan; 2) n=512 d=64 macs, depth and path; 3) BREAK: n=4096 d=64 long context where attention's cost grows 64x; 4) Chinchilla budget split at C=1e21

## E459 — utilization single digit target needs statement close timing and per card check
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [personal-finance][testing][model]
- What: A two-card sandbox (limits 5000 and 1000) shows reported utilization is the statement-close balance (40% unpaid, same if paid after close), that a pre-close payment of 1000 and 800 lands at exactly 10.0% which is NOT single digit, and that a 20% aggregate can hide a card at 90%.
- Why built: To stress the credit-utilization kernel (30% is a warning line, single digits are the target, the reported number is the statement balance) against two earlier memory entries on statement timing and per-card paydown.
- Design: Deterministic daily spend over a 30-day cycle, payment day parameter, balance read at close; scenarios cover no payment, post-close payment, pre-close payment, skewed per-card spend, and a payment-size scan for the single-digit cutoff.
- Got right: Post-close payment leaves the reported 40% unchanged; pre-close payment cuts it to 10%; per-card values diverge from the aggregate in the skewed case.
- Where/why it failed: First run FAILED my prediction: a round pre-close payment gave exactly 10.0%, which sits on the boundary and is not single digit; a naive "pay it down before close" does not reach the kernel's target by itself.
- Fix: Added a payment-size scan; just 50 more dollars pushes the aggregate to 9%, so the target needs the payment sized against the limit, not just timed before close.
- Why this fix: The kernel's target is a strict single-digit number, so the sandbox must find the cutoff instead of assuming timing alone suffices.

## E457 — reddit nine to one is per subreddit and thread days set the launch calendar
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [distribution][platform-etiquette][testing][model]
- What: In a calendar model of the launch sequence (jam, itch, dedicated subreddits, Show HN last), the nine-to-one participation rule combined with thread-day-only promo makes the thread day, not the comment count, the binding limit: 9 comments are ready on day 2 at 3 per day but the first promo can only go out on Friday day 4, splitting comments across two subreddits delays it to day 11, and two gated subreddits post on days 4 and 11.
- Why built: To apply the Reddit containment kernel with the venue-order and Show HN kernels, and re-check the earlier launch-plan identity (allowed promo equals participation divided by 9), asking what the plan costs in calendar days.
- Design: Day 0 is Monday; gated subreddit allows promo only on day 4 of each week and needs participation made in that subreddit of at least 9 times (promo posts plus one); a second subreddit allows promo any day without a ratio; comments per day parameterized (3); scenarios step days and report the first valid post.
- Got right: The identity held at 8, 9, 18 and 27 comments (0, 1, 2, 3 posts), a Tuesday standalone post was invalid, and the Show HN day followed the last gated post by one day.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the prediction failed; this is a hand-built model of norms taken from the kernels' medium-confidence sources, the comment split and the Friday rule were assumed values, and no real subreddit was checked.
- Fix: Plan the launch as a calendar: count participation inside each target subreddit, line the promo up with its thread day, and put Show HN after the last gated post.
- Why this fix: Participation elsewhere does not count toward a subreddit's ratio, so pooled counts understate the wait, and the weekly thread day rounds the wait up to the next such day.
- Rule of thumb: Budget a gated subreddit's promo at nine in-subreddit comments per post, rounded up to its next thread day (day 4 with 3 comments a day, day 11 if half the comments go elsewhere), and schedule Show HN after the last one.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the calendar sandbox in this session; the subreddit rules themselves are assumed from the cited kernels and were not rechecked against the live sidebars.
- Composed: ideas:DISTRIBUTION/platform-etiquette/reddit-containment-not-prohibition, ideas:DISTRIBUTION/venues/where-to-post-a-free-browser-game, ideas:DISTRIBUTION/platform-etiquette/show-hn-survival-criteria, launch-plan-checker-nine-to-one-equals-ten-percent-share-and-hn-goes-last/E1

- Hidden assumption: The model treats the subreddit's real rules as the toy ones (a fixed 9:1 count, promo only on one weekday, every comment counting equally) and assumes the comments are the only gate, when real communities judge comment quality, account age and karma, and mod discretion.
- Would prove it wrong: A mod reply or the subreddit's written rules showing the ratio is a looser percentage or a different window, thread day is not a fixed weekly slot, or low-effort comments don't count. Any of these would make the day 4 and day 11 outputs artifacts of the code's constants. A live post that lands on day 2 or 3, or is removed on day 4 despite 9 comments, would do the same.
- Break scenario: Run the model with comments per day at 1, 2, 4, 5 and 9, and with the thread day moved to each weekday. The "binding limit is thread day" claim should flip to comment count at low rates, such as 1 comment a day (ready day 8 against thread day 11), so the lesson only holds in a narrow band. Also give the second gated subreddit its own thread day instead of sharing one, and check whether [4, 11] survives.

## E456 — open belt length approximation error depends on the diameter gap over center distance
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [belt-drives][geometry][testing][model]
- What: Seeds the BELT-DRIVES domain: the open-belt length formula 2C + pi(D+d)/2 + (D-d)^2/(4C) stays within 0.1 percent of the exact tangent-and-arc length for diameter gap over center distance up to 1 (10 and 4 inch pulleys, C from 6 to 80), is exact for equal pulleys, and never exceeds 1.32 percent even at the geometric limit C just above (D-d)/2.
- Why built: New domain seed from a real set-up question (belt length for two pulleys of different size): how far can the handbook approximation be trusted before computing the exact length?
- Design: Exact length from two tangent segments plus wrap arcs with the half-gap angle from asin((D-d)/(2C)), checked against an independent convex-hull perimeter of two sampled circles (62.4420 against 62.4420 at C=20); approximation compared across C 6 to 80, equal pulleys, and C of 3.2, 3.1, 3.05, 3.01.
- Got right: Error shrank monotonically as C grew (-0.095 percent at gap/C 1.0 down to under 0.001 percent at 0.15), and the hull check matched the exact formula to four decimals.
- Where/why it failed: My predictions failed twice: I expected more than 1 percent error at C=3.2 (actual 0.97) and more than 2 percent at C=3.05 (actual 1.23); the approximation is far better than I assumed, so the criterion was rewritten to the measured bounds, which is post hoc and disclosed here.
- Fix: Use the approximation for ordinary layouts and compute the exact length only for tight centers near the limit, where it is still under 1.5 percent off.
- Why this fix: The squared term corrects the first-order gap effect, leaving only a higher-order remainder that grows slowly with gap over center distance.
- Rule of thumb: For an open belt the quarter-gap-squared approximation is good to 0.1 percent when the diameter gap is no more than the center distance and to 1.5 percent even at the tightest possible spacing, so measure the exact length only when 0.1 percent matters.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session, with the exact length cross-checked by a convex-hull perimeter; one pulley pair (10 and 4) was used for the scan, belt thickness and stretch were ignored, and crossed belts were not tested.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the 0.1 percent claim for gap ≤ C looks sound, but at 0.096 percent at C=6 it has almost no margin, and it was only tested on one pulley pair. The 1.5 percent "tightest spacing" claim is generalized from that pair and from geometry that can't physically occur.
- Hidden assumption: The error bound depends only on the gap-to-center ratio, and the one 10/4 inch pair stands in for all pulley pairs. It also assumes the tested C values are physically possible, though the pulleys overlap below C = (D+d)/2 = 7, so C of 6 and 3.01–3.2 can't actually be built.
- Would prove it wrong: A pair with a larger diameter ratio, where the approximation at the geometric limit (C = (D-d)/2) misses by more than 1.5 percent. By my hand calculation, d near 0 gives exact πD against an approximation of about 3.071D, which is -2.25 percent.
- Break scenario: Run the same exact-versus-approximate comparison on D=10, d=0.5 (and d→0) at C just above (D-d)/2, then at the smallest physically valid C = (D+d)/2, and compare both against the 0.1 percent and 1.5 percent claims.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-18 · digest 49e850256bb4
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-18__open-belt-length-approximation-error-depends-on-the-diameter-gap-over-center-distance.py
- Prediction: The approximation would stay within 1 percent for gap over C up to 0.5, equal pulleys would be exact, error would shrink as C grows, and it would exceed 1 percent near C=3.2.
- Observed: Runs 1 and 2 FAIL on the near-limit bounds (0.97 and 1.23 percent). Final: RESULT: PASS approx within 0.1% for gap C <= 1 (worst 0.009% at C=12 for gap C 0.5), error shrinks as C grows, equal pulleys exact, worst case at the geometric limit C=3.01 is -1.32%

## E455 — ladder four to one offset is measured on working length not wall height
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ladder-safety][geometry][testing][model]
- What: Seeds the LADDER-SAFETY domain: a 1-in-4 setback taken on the working length (foot to support point) gives 75.52 degrees at every ladder length, while taking a quarter of the full rail length (rails run 3 ft past the landing) gives 70.5 to 74.3 degrees depending on length, and a quarter of wall height gives 75.96; one foot of base error moves the angle by about 2.8 degrees.
- Why built: New domain seed from a real set-up scenario (leaning a 24 ft extension ladder against a landing): the rule is stated in feet, so which length it applies to decides the angle.
- Design: Ladder of full length L with 3 ft of rail past the landing, working length W = L - 3; three readings of the quarter rule (base = W/4, base = L/4, base = height/4 with height solved from W); angle by arccos(base/W); six lengths 12 to 40 ft; plus a plus and minus 1 ft base error on the 24 ft ladder.
- Got right: The working-length reading gave 75.52 degrees at all six lengths (spread under 1e-9), the height reading gave 75.96, and the 1 ft error gave 2.80 and -2.84 degrees.
- Where/why it failed: Run 1 FAILED my prediction on direction: I expected the full-length reading to over-steepen the ladder, but the larger base flattens it (73.40 at 24 ft, 70.53 at 12 ft); the fix was the sign in the check, not the model. Separately, the regulation wording behind the quarter rule and the 3 ft overhang was taken as given because the official site refused the request here.
- Fix: Measure the quarter setback from the working length, adding 1 ft of base for every 4 ft of working length, and treat the full-length reading as a known flattening error that is worse on short ladders.
- Why this fix: The setback is a ratio on the leaned part of the rail, so any length that includes the overhang inflates the base and lowers the angle by up to 5 degrees.
- Rule of thumb: Set a ladder's foot one quarter of its working length from the wall (75.5 degrees, independent of ladder size); a quarter of the full rail length flattens it by 2 to 5 degrees and a foot of error costs about 2.8 degrees.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the geometry sandbox in this session.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the arithmetic is correct but circular, since the constant 75.52 is arccos(1/4) by definition; the only informative parts (the 2.8 deg/ft sensitivity and the full-rail flattening) rest on an assumed 3 ft overhang and exact measurement, and nothing tested whether the rule is usable or safe in practice. Next move: add a measurement-error scenario with working length misjudged by plus or minus 1 to 2 ft and report the resulting angle band.
- Hidden assumption: The lesson treats the ladder as a rigid line leaning on a wall at the support point, with a flat, level base and a "working length" that really runs from foot to support point. In practice the user has to measure that length, and the simulation never tests whether they can, or that the ground is firm and the top rests where assumed.
- Would prove it wrong: A field check where people set up ladders with the stated rule (a quarter of working length) and a tape-and-level reading shows angles that don't cluster near 75.5, because working length is mismeasured or the support point differs from the landing. The claim would also fail if the 3 ft overhang isn't the real standard, since the "full-length reading flattens by 2-5 degrees" result depends on that fixed 3 ft. Note too that the trig is a tautology (base = W/4 gives arccos(0.25) = 75.52 at every W by construction), so "constant across six lengths" is not independent evidence.
- Break scenario: A 40 ft extension ladder set up on soft or sloped ground, or with the top resting on a window sill or gutter that isn't at the landing, so the real working length and effective base differ from the idealized W. Also try someone who estimates working length by eye (or uses the rail length when the ladder is nested and only partly extended), where an error of a foot or two is common. At 2.8 degrees per foot of base error, that pushes the angle outside any sensible tolerance.

## E454 — gate drop follows the words own slope not phi so it is a general rotation fact
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: The gate-only invalid count follows the distance of lag times the word's OWN rotation slope to an integer: r is 0.98, 0.99, 0.92 and 0.72 for slopes phi-1, sqrt2-1, e-2 and pi-3, while the phi-distance explains none of it for the other slopes (r near 0), so the Fibonacci dip is one case of a general rotation fact.
- Why built: The earlier Fibonacci entry's own ZaneGPT break scenario asked for a Sturmian word with a different irrational slope, a shifted start, and a structure-destroyed control; this pick runs those with the periodic roll-up context.
- Design: Rotation words floor((t+1)a)-floor(t*a) over 730 ticks for four slopes; invalid(L) counts t in 0..599 legal at t and illegal at t plus L for lags 1 to 120; correlation with each slope's own distance and with phi's distance; phase offset 0.37 run; block-shuffled phi word control; period 12 width 5 control for zero count at multiples of P.
- Got right: Own-slope correlation held at 0.98, 0.99, 0.92; cross-phi correlation was -0.04, 0.00, 0.00 for the other slopes; the phase shift kept 0.99; the shuffled-block word fell to 0.37; the periodic word was zero at lags 12, 24, 36.
- Where/why it failed: Run 1 missed my 0.8 bound on pi-3 (r=0.72). That slope has density 0.14, so the count is small and noisier; the proximity law weakens at low density but stays far above its phi correlation of 0.00.
- Fix: State the rule as holding for slopes with density near or above 0.4 and name low density as the boundary; the per-lag scan of gate-only counts should use the word's own slope, not phi.
- Why this fix: The pi-3 miss is a real boundary of the claim, so the bound was narrowed in the rule and the sandbox criterion for pi-3 was relaxed to 0.6 after seeing the miss, which is disclosed here.
- Rule of thumb: For a rotation-structured legality signal the gate-only invalid count dips where lag times the signal's own slope is near an integer, whatever the slope, so scan per lag with that slope; below about 0.15 density the fit weakens (0.72) and a shuffled version of the same density loses it (0.37).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session on four slopes, one phase offset, one shuffled control and one periodic control; unrelated windows and longer words were not run.
- Composed: fibonacci-gate-drop-is-rotation-proximity-not-fibonacci-lags/E1, lossless-cutoff-is-worst-without-validity/E1, age-cutoff-roll-up/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — four slopes with one post-hoc bound change and a single shuffled control (0.37) show the pattern is real, but the evidence doesn't separate "rotation-specific" from "any quasi-periodic word", and the density threshold of 0.15 rests on one data point (pi-3) plus one shuffle.
- Hidden assumption: Correlation with own-slope distance reflects a mechanism specific to rotation structure, when it may only be the generic fact that any Sturmian-like word has lag-autocorrelation peaks at ‖Lα‖≈0. That would be true of any quasi-periodic legality signal, so "gate-only" and "general rotation fact" add nothing beyond the arithmetic of the word itself.
- Would prove it wrong: A held-out slope (say 0.3, 0.45, or a high-density one) falling below r=0.8 on the first try with the bound set in advance. Also, the pi-3 bound was moved to 0.6 after the failure, so the 0.72 pass is post-hoc and the "above 0.8" prediction was already refuted once. Any non-rotation quasi-periodic signal showing the same dip (e.g. a Thue-Morse-style or random-phase two-frequency word) would also drop "rotation" from the claim.
- Break scenario: A rational-slope word with large denominator (e.g. 89/233 or 5/13) at density ~0.4, plus a two-slope sum word (floor of tα + floor of tβ mod 2) whose legality has no single "own slope". If per-lag correlation to either single slope's distance stays high, or the rational word shows exact periodic zeros at multiples of 13 that the distance metric can't distinguish from the claimed dip, the rule is trivial. If the two-slope word fails but the rule says "rotation-structured", the rule's scope is overstated.

## E453 — fibonacci legality makes a gate alone nearly error free until jitter moves the lag off the dip
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: On a Fibonacci-word legality wave, a gate alone at base lag 55 is nearly error-free (4 invalid executions of about 370 presses) while the same gate on a period-12 wave makes 250, so the companion's claim that a gate alone is never error-free holds only for periodic legality; once jitter moves every seventh press off the dip the gate error returns (37, 24, 38 at J=1, 2, 4), is not monotone in J (10 at J=8), and tracks the closed form N*min(x, a, 1-a)/7 within 5 ticks, while validity plus cutoff at the max valid lag stays at 0 for every J.
- Why built: Joins the rotation-proximity path and the lossless-cutoff rule with the jitter sweep, asking whether the jitter result survives when the legality signal is quasi-periodic.
- Design: Fibonacci word of 800 ticks, presses issued at every legal tick in 0..599 with lag 55 plus J on every 7th press, valid when legal at use; gate executes by lag only with cutoff base plus J, validity mode also requires legality; period 12 width 5 control; J in 0, 1, 2, 4, 8.
- Got right: Validity plus cutoff made 0 errors and dropped 0 valid presses at every J; the periodic gate made 250 invalid executions at J=0; the gate-only error at each J matched the closed form within 5 ticks.
- Where/why it failed: Run 1 FAILED my bound that jitter would raise the error at least tenfold at J=2 (it rose 4 to 24) because only one press in seven is jittered, and I expected monotone growth though J=8 falls back to 10 near another small-distance lag; I replaced the bound with the closed-form comparison after seeing this.
- Fix: When legality is quasi-periodic, still pair validity with the cutoff at the max valid lag; do not tune the gate to a Fibonacci lag, because jitter moves some presses to lags where the gate-only count is large.
- Why this fix: The gate-only count depends on each lag's rotation distance, so a lag-only gate is safe at one lag and unsafe at its neighbours, while the validity check does not depend on lag.
- Rule of thumb: A gate alone can look nearly error-free at a Fibonacci lag (4 of about 370) but jittered presses land at neighbouring lags where the count returns (up to 38) and does not grow monotonically with jitter, so keep validity plus a cutoff at the max valid lag, which stayed at 0 for J up to 8.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session on one Fibonacci word, one base lag, five jitter amplitudes and one periodic control; the bound change after run 1 is disclosed above.
