## E433 — i2v drift vs reference fidelity gate
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ai-video][compliance][disclosure][sandbox][model]
- What: Sandbox gate for AI product shots that tests the kernel "a reference image does not make an AI product shot compliant" under two readings of the rule (source-based versus measured colour deviation), including a product shot made by animating the real photo with chained 8 s plus 7 s extensions, plus the per-platform label check.
- Why built: The kernel was never applied by a memory entry as a falsifiable claim about WHY a reference image fails; earlier models assumed a source rule, and the boundary where a deviation rule would flip the answer was untested.
- Design: Product colour (200,40,40); tolerance 5 colour units (my assumption, the policy gives no number). Reference generation has a fixed error of (1-fidelity)*60; animating the real photo drifts 2 units per hop, hops = 1 for 8 s and one more per 7 s extension. Scenes are AI and not product shots. Label rule per platform (TikTok labels significant AI, YouTube labels photoreal AI). Real footage, reference generation and animation were each scored on both rules.
- Got right: Under the source rule, reference fidelity 0.9, 0.95 and 1.0 all gave 1 product violation, so the kernel holds. Real footage plus AI scenes gave 0 product violations, and the label violation appeared on its own (1 without label on both platforms, 0 with it).
- Where/why it failed: Built-to-break case: under the deviation rule the claim flips. Fidelity 1.0 and 0.95 passed (0 violations) and only 0.9 failed, and animating the real photo passed at 8 s and 15 s (1 and 2 hops, error 2 and 4) but failed at 22 s and 30 s (3 and 4 hops, error 6 and 8). So the kernel is true only if the platform judges by source, and unproven if it judges by how the product looks.
- Fix: Treat real footage as the only safe product shot, and if an animated real photo is used anyway, keep the shot to two hops (about 15 s) and check the colour against the real item before publishing; keep the label as a separate check per platform.
- Why this fix: The policy text asks the video to display the physical product accurately, which a reviewer may check by eye rather than by provenance, so the safe choice is the one that passes under both readings, and drift grows with extension hops so shorter shots are cheaper insurance than a higher-fidelity reference.
- Rule of thumb: A reference image never makes an AI product shot safe under a source rule, and only a short animated shot (two hops or fewer, under 15 s here) or a near-perfect reference passes a deviation rule, so shoot the real product and let AI do scenes.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox, and every number above comes from its output. The tolerance of 5 units, the drift of 2 per hop and the 50 percent AI-share label line are assumed model constants, and the real platform rule is outside what the run examined.
- Composed: ideas:AI-VIDEO/compliance/ai-for-scenes-and-dubbing-real-footage-for-the-product-plus-the-ai-label/a-reference-image-does-not-make-an-ai-product-shot-compliant, ideas:AI-VIDEO/disclosure/label-photoreal-ai-and-skip-the-label-for-obvious-cartoons-on-youtube/turn-the-tiktok-ai-label-on-by-default, brain-auto-training/E41, brainwork/E336, tiktok-shop/E14
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the source-rule half is true by definition (the rule was written to reject reference shots), and the deviation half is only as strong as a tolerance and drift you chose and never swept, so the sandbox confirmed its own wiring rather than testing the claim.
- Hidden assumption: The simulator's constants are the real world: a "source rule" exists in actual platform policy, drift is a linear 2 units per hop, and a 5-unit tolerance (your own invention) is the threshold. The verdict is therefore an output of those assumed numbers, not a finding about any platform.
- Would prove it wrong: Any real-world case where a reference-driven AI product shot is accepted as compliant without a source rule (e.g. a platform or advertiser reviewer approving it because the colour was measured within tolerance). The same applies if the pass/fail boundary moves with the tolerance (e.g. 3 or 8 units shifts the 15 s to 22 s flip, and fidelity 0.95 flips between pass and fail), because the "two hops or fewer" cutoff would then be an artefact, not a rule.
- Break scenario: Re-run scenario 2 with tolerance at 3 and at 8 and drift at 1 and 4 units per hop. Add a fidelity 0.98 reference (error 1.2, passes at 5 but not at 1). If the "two hops or fewer" and "near-perfect reference" thresholds move with every setting, the numeric half of the rule of thumb is just your parameters. Only the "shoot the real product" half survives, and it survives because real footage was scored with zero error by construction, which is the other thing the sandbox assumed.

## E432 — engine cap on a drifted sidecar label crosses no cap
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: A one-variant-per-comic-engine cap on a top-4 batch ranked on IPM times D1 kept beating no cap (4.10 versus 3.65, +0.45) even when the engine labels came from a drifted hand-kept sidecar, with partial drift (2 to 16 of 16 labels swapped) never falling below no cap; it only collapsed (1.40, far below 3.65) when every label fell into one shared unknown bucket.
- Why built: The sidecar-drift lesson says a hand-kept map silently goes stale, the IPM times D1 ranking lesson says the pick is only as good as its inputs, and the comic-engine kernel says vary the engine; no entry tested a diversity cap whose labels come from the drifting map.
- Design: 16 variants (4 engines times 4 reskins) with engine-correlated scores (1.4, 1.1, 0.9, 0.7 times 1 - 0.04 per reskin), batch of 4, each repeat of an engine in the batch worth 0.75 of the previous one. Cap picks in score order skipping a label already used. Labels: true (derived), shifted among the stale entries (each takes the next stale entry's engine), or stale entries sent to one unknown bucket; 0 to 16 stale, averaged over 16 deterministic offsets.
- Got right: Derived labels gave a clear gain over no cap (4.100 versus 3.652). Shifted-label drift averaged 4.084 to 4.202, and unknown-bucket drift averaged 4.131 to 4.337 up to 12 stale labels, all above no cap.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that a drifted cap would fall below no cap at some middle drift level was wrong: wrong labels still spread the picks, so cap errors cost little (worst case 3.924 at 2 shifted labels). Only the all-unknown case broke it: every variant shares one label, the cap allows one pick, and the batch drops to 1.400.
- Fix: Keep engine labels derived from the variant records where possible, and if a sidecar must be used, treat a missing label as its own unique engine (never a shared default bucket) or fail loudly when the label set collapses.
- Why this fix: The cap is cheap insurance against mislabelling because errors mostly reshuffle which near-equal variants it skips, but a shared default label makes the cap read every variant as a repeat, which is the one failure that removes batch size.
- Rule of thumb: A per-engine cap survives most label drift (0 of 12 partial-drift levels fell below no cap in this model), so the thing to guard is a shared default label for missing entries, which cut the batch to one pick (1.40 versus 3.65 with no cap); give unknown variants unique labels.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (first run found the drifted cap never below no cap, then I added the unknown-bucket scenario); the scores, the 0.75 fatigue and the drift patterns are assumed toy forms, not measured ad data.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/ideation/vary-the-comic-engine-not-the-topic
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the result is genuine in this toy model, but the +0.45 edge depends on a 0.75 discount and benign permutation drift, and the "only collapses at total unknown" rule is untested against targeted drift or the real discount, so it shouldn't be promoted as a general lesson yet.
- Hidden assumption: Engine scores are strongly engine-correlated and reskin decay is a uniform 4%, so any label scramble still lands on a mix of engines. The cap's edge comes from the 0.75 repeat discount, which is a modeled parameter and not measured data. The "drift" is also modeled as permutation among stale entries, which assumes real sidecar drift looks like that and not like systematically wrong labels, such as all top-scorers sharing one mislabeled engine.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with the repeat discount near 1.0 (or with real per-engine score correlation near zero), or with drift that mislabels the top-ranked variants specifically. If the shifted-label cap drops below no cap at partial drift, the "survives most drift" claim fails. A shared-bucket collapse at 12 of 16 stale labels (observed 3.908, above no cap) would also show the "only when all stale" threshold is too sharp.
- Break scenario: Stale entries are not random but adversarial: the 4 highest-scoring variants (one engine's reskins) get relabeled to 4 different engines, and low-scoring variants take that engine's label. The cap then skips real top picks and fills the batch with lower-scoring variants, while still believing it enforces diversity. Sweep the repeat discount from 0.75 to 1.0 and the cap's advantage should shrink to zero or negative.

The first-run crossover prediction was refuted. Note the unknown-bucket worst case at 12 of 16 was 3.908, above no cap.

## E431 — cover the severe beats first and the cue knob
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][testing][sandbox]
- What: In the incomplete-rule-card model on a linear escalation (severity 2 to 10 over six beats), covering the most severe beats first beat covering the mildest first by up to 1.30 points without a cue (covering 1 beat: 1.30 against 0.73; 3 beats: 2.26 against 0.97), but with a safe cue of 0.7 the largest gap shrank to 0.39; at zero coverage the cue needed for flat-at-ceiling to beat the mild schedule sat between 0.3 (a tie, 1.53 against 1.55) and 0.5 (2.56 against 1.61), and flat still won at cue 0.7 for every uncovered fallback distance tried (0.1 to 0.9).
- Why built: The incomplete-rule-card lesson advised covering the severe beats first and cueing the rest, but it varied only how many beats the card covered, and its 0.7 cue and 0.3 fallback distance were never swept; the severe-harm kernel says severe beats are the ones that need distance.
- Design: Escalation model of the matching-distance lesson (habituation exp(-0.2 X), gate width 0.25, ceiling 10, six beats). A covered beat has distance matched to its severity, an uncovered one falls back to distance 0.3 with an additive cue c (gate plus c times one minus gate). Coverage masks choose the k most severe or k mildest beats, k 0 to 6, cue 0 or 0.7; separately the cue swept 0 to 0.9 at zero coverage and the fallback distance swept 0.1 to 0.9 at cue 0.7.
- Got right: Which beats the card covers matters a lot when there is no cue and the schedule escalates, and the 0.7 cue and 0.3 fallback were not special: flat won at 0.5 and above, and at every fallback distance tried.
- Where/why it failed: The flat schedule cannot test the advice because all its beats are equally severe, so the ordering result only holds for an escalating schedule; the cue boundary is a near tie at 0.3, not a clean threshold, and the cue gives a floor (1.98 for the linear schedule at no coverage) that makes the card's order matter less rather than not at all.
- Fix: Write the rule card for the most severe beats first, and give every uncovered beat a safe cue of about 0.5 or more; with a strong cue the order is a smaller concern.
- Why this fix: A matched distance gains most where the grounded fallback distance is farthest from the beat's severity, which is the severe end, while a cue lifts every uncovered beat toward a floor regardless of order.
- Rule of thumb: On an escalating schedule cover the severe beats first (up to 1.30 points better than mild first with no cue, at most 0.39 with a cue of 0.7), and a cue of about 0.5 is enough to let go-big win at zero coverage (2.56 against 1.61), with 0.3 only a tie.

## E430 — cap deadline midpoint is a threshold artifact under habituation
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][testing][sandbox]
- What: Re-ran the late severity cap deadline test with the habituation model from the matching-distance lesson added and the forgiveness threshold swept over 5, 7 and 9 of 11 distances. The deadline at threshold 7 was beat 3, 4, 6, 9 for schedules of 6, 9, 12, 18 beats (the midpoint), but at n 12 it moved to 8 for threshold 5 and 4 for threshold 9, so the midpoint is where threshold 7 puts it, not a property of escalation.
- Why built: The midpoint-deadline lesson was scored weak because its fixed 7-of-11 threshold and coupled parameters could make n/2 an artifact; the matching-distance lesson supplies a habituation model that was never run against the cap deadline.
- Design: Cover and laugh forms of the severity-cap lesson (cover 0.8 - 0.5 d at severity up to 0.3, else 0.2 + 0.7 d; laugh falls three times as fast past the cover), go-big severity i/n for the first L beats then a cap at 0.24 times i/n, 11 distances, window = distances within 95 percent of best. Habituation multiplier exp(-0.2 X) with X rising by 1/(1 + I/5) per beat, I = 10 times severity. Sweeps: threshold 5/7/9, n 6/9/12/18, cap level 0.1 to 0.5, habituation on and off.
- Got right: The midpoint pattern is real at threshold 7 and extrapolates: L* was 3, 4, 6, 9 for n 6, 9, 12, 18, the n/2 prediction within one beat in all four.
- Where/why it failed: The threshold moves the deadline (n 12: 8 at threshold 5, 6 at threshold 7, 4 at threshold 9; n 18: 12, 9, 7), so "the middle" is only the answer for the 7-of-11 bar. Habituation changed nothing except n 18 at threshold 9 (7 became 6), and the cap level from 0.1 to 0.5 left L* at 6, so neither explains the deadline.
- Fix: State the cap deadline as a fraction that depends on how forgiving the dial must be (about 0.67 of the schedule for a loose 5-of-11 bar, 0.5 for 7, 0.33 for a strict 9), and still land the cap by the middle when in doubt.
- Why this fix: The deadline counts how many uncapped severe beats the schedule can absorb before fewer distances stay near the best, so a stricter bar tolerates fewer of them; habituation scales all distances' totals similarly and does not change which distances stay near the best.
- Rule of thumb: The severity cap deadline is set by how forgiving you need the distance dial to be, not by the escalation itself: beat 8 of 12 at a loose bar, 6 at a medium one, 4 at a strict one, so put the cap earlier when the framing is hard to tune; habituation and cap level did not move it here.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (all numbers come from its output); the cover and laugh forms, the 0.95 window and the habituation constants are assumed toy forms, not audience data.

## E429 — a series halving keeps the aspect ratio us letter does not
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [verification][model][sandbox]
- What: A script that starts from A0 (841 x 1189 mm) and halves across the long side with floor rounding reproduced all nine ISO 216 sizes A0 to A8 (9 of 9), the ratio error stayed under 0.7 percent (0.63 percent at A8), and the copier steps came out at 141.4 percent and 70.7 percent, while US Letter halved to 5.5 x 8.5 in and drifted 19.4 percent from its own ratio.
- Why built: Seeding the PAPER-SIZES domain from a real standard: the claim that the A-series can be generated by one rule rather than looked up needed a run, and Letter was the natural counter-case.
- Design: Integer-millimetre floor halving that cuts across the long side, compared with the published table; ratio drift against the square root of 2; Letter folded once and twice; copier step as the ratio of long sides; A4 area against 1/16 of a square metre.
- Got right: All nine sizes matched exactly, the 141 and 71 percent steps matched, and Letter's second fold returned to the original ratio (1.294), which I had not expected.
- Where/why it failed: Built-to-break case: the A4 area came out at 0.06237 square metres against 0.06250, because millimetre rounding takes up to about 0.2 percent of the area at each halving, so area is only approximately conserved in the table; and the ratio drifts to 0.63 percent by A8 because the sides are rounded to whole millimetres.
- Fix: Generate the size list from the halving rule and compare it to the standard's table as a test, and do not treat area as exactly halved at small sizes.
- Why this fix: The rule is short and exact for the sizes in use, while a hand-typed table can drift silently; the rounding error is small and only visible at the smallest sizes.
- Rule of thumb: Floor-halving from 841 x 1189 mm gives every A size exactly (9 of 9) and a fixed 141 or 71 percent enlargement step, whereas Letter needs two folds to repeat its shape, so a size picker for Letter cannot use a single scale step.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox against the ISO 216 millimetre sizes taken from my own recall of the standard; a transcription slip in that copy would have shown up as a mismatch.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — 9 of 9 matches on A-series only, with a tuned rounding rule and a start taken from the answer, and the Letter claim "needs two folds" is asserted but never run to a real two-fold result.
- Hidden assumption: The rule assumes the published ISO table is the target and that matching it at 9 of 9 shows the rule is general. But the starting point, 841 x 1189 mm, is already the rounded A0, and floor rounding was probably chosen because it matches the table. That makes the "reproduction" partly circular, and it was never tested against a different start or a different rounding mode.
- Would prove it wrong: Running the same script with round-half-up or ceiling, or from a slightly different A0 such as 840 x 1188, still gives 9 of 9. That would show the match comes from the table's tolerance and not from floor-halving. A second refutation is a US size such as Legal, or Letter after a different fold, that keeps its ratio under a single scale step. That would undercut the claim that Letter can't use one.
- Break scenario: Fold Letter 8.5 x 11 in across its long side to get 5.5 x 8.5. Then compare the ratios and the single-step scale: 11/8.5 = 1.294 and 8.5/5.5 = 1.545, so the drift is 19.4 percent. That is the existing Letter case and it is not an independent test. A real break is to run the script on ANSI B (11 x 17 in) down to ANSI A (8.5 x 11 in). That size family does keep its ratio, because 17/11 = 1.545 and 11/8.5 = 1.294. Those two ratios differ, so ANSI doesn't hold a ratio either. Add B5/B-series and C-series from the same start. If B or C breaks the floor rule, then "every A size exactly" is a fact about A, not a general rule of thumb.

## E428 — roof area from footprint needs the pitch factor
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [roofing][estimating][testing][sandbox]
- What: Seeding a roofing-estimate check: ordering shingles from the plan footprint with a 10 percent waste allowance was short at every pitch tried, from 1 bundle at 2/12 to 25 bundles at 12/12 on an 1800 sq ft footprint, because the slope factor (square root of 1 plus rise over 12, squared) stacks on top of the waste.
- Why built: New-ground seed from a real estimating scenario: roofs are sold in squares of 100 sq ft (three bundles each) and plans show the footprint, not the sloped surface; the slope factor and the waste rule are standard roofing arithmetic that I know, not re-read from a published source.
- Design: Pure arithmetic over pitches 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12 per 12: sloped area is footprint times the slope factor, order is area times 1.10 rounded up to whole bundles; compare with the footprint times 1.10 order; the known factors 1.118 at 6/12 and 1.414 at 12/12 are checked.
- Got right: The factors matched the known values (1.118 and 1.414), and the shortfall grew steadily with pitch: 7 bundles at 6/12, 12 at 8/12, 25 at 12/12.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction was wrong that the 10 percent waste would cover the lowest pitch: the waste is applied to both orders, so it never absorbs the slope; even 2/12 (factor 1.014) came out one bundle short after rounding up.
- Fix: Multiply the footprint by the pitch factor first and apply waste to the sloped area, never to the footprint.
- Why this fix: Waste allows for cuts and breakage on the surface actually covered; the footprint understates that surface by the slope factor at every pitch, so waste on the footprint cannot make it up.
- Rule of thumb: Order roofing from footprint times the slope factor, then add waste: a footprint-plus-10-percent order was short at all 7 pitches tried, by 7 bundles at 6/12 and 25 at 12/12 on 1800 sq ft, and waste never absorbs the slope.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session, which checks the arithmetic; the 10 percent waste figure and three bundles to a square are common trade figures not checked against a supplier, and the example footprint is invented.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-domain
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the direction (slope factor must come before waste) is sound geometry and the 6/12 and 12/12 factors check out, but "short at 7 of 7 pitches" is partly a rounding artifact at low pitch (the prediction that 2/12 was covered failed on bundle rounding, not slope), and the specific bundle shortfalls come from one footprint with no independent real-roof check.
- Hidden assumption: Pitch is always the slope factor sqrt(1+(rise/12)²) applied uniformly to the whole footprint, with no eave overhang, hips, valleys, dormers, ridge or starter waste, and a fixed bundle coverage (1800 sq ft scale), so the "short by N bundles" numbers are really just the one arithmetic model checked against itself.
- Would prove it wrong: A measured or manufacturer-quoted takeoff (for example an aerial-measurement report) on a real 6/12 roof where footprint × 1.10 is enough, because overhangs, a footprint taken at the wall line, or a bundle count already built around the 10 percent allowance cancel the slope factor. A slope factor of 1.0 at flat pitch would also refute it. The 2/12 result is the weak spot: the factor there is about 1.014, so "short" there depends only on rounding to whole bundles, not on slope.
- Break scenario: A 1800 sq ft footprint at 2/12 with a bundle size or rounding that happens to land footprint × 1.10 on the same whole-bundle count as the sloped order, or a 1800 sq ft house with 2 ft eave overhangs measured to the wall line, where the real shingled area exceeds the footprint by more than the slope factor does and the comparison flips or collapses. The same test works the other way, with a gable-only roof against a hip roof of the same footprint.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-18 · digest 3456d97496f1
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-18__roof-area-from-footprint-needs-the-pitch-factor.py

## E427 — ipm d1 top picks collapse onto one comic engine
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][comedy][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy model of ranking 10 ad recuts (8 comic engines, engine-first batch) on IPM times D1 and taking the top 3, to see whether the top picks pile onto one comic engine when engine strength drives both conversion and retention.
- Why built: Composes the IPM-times-D1 ranking lesson with the vary-the-comic-engine kernel; each was tested alone but never together, and a rank that rewards a strong engine could undo the engine-first variety.
- Design: 2000 seeded batches per cell; 10 ideas, first 8 one per engine; true click and D1 rates depend on engine strength with correlation 0, 0.5, 0.9; observed IPM times D1 from binomial draws at 300 and 1000 impressions; compare plain top 3 against top 3 with a cap of one per engine.
- Got right: The pass condition (repeat rate rising more than 10 points with correlation, cap loss under 15%) was fixed in the script before the first run, and the script is deterministic.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing broke; the hoped-for large collapse did not appear. Even at correlation 0.9 the top 3 repeated an engine in only 28.0% of batches (13.9% with no correlation), so the collapse is real but modest.
- Fix: Apply a per-engine cap of one in the top 3 after ranking; it cost only 0.6% to 2.1% of true IPM times D1 value in every even-layout cell, and 6.0% when 4 of 10 ideas shared one engine.
- Why this fix: The cap is cheap (2.1% worst case) and removes the 14% to 28% of batches that would otherwise ship a repeated engine, so variety is kept without changing the ranking metric.
- Rule of thumb: When ranking an engine-first recut batch on IPM times D1, engine-correlated quality raises top-3 engine repeats from 13.9% to 28.0% (budget 1000), so cap one per engine after ranking; it costs about 2% of value (6% if the batch is skewed, where repeats hit 54%).
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script in this session; rates in the toy are invented parameters.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/vary-the-comic-engine-not-the-topic
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The repeat rise (13.9% to 28.0%) is real in the toy model, but "cap one per engine" is a recommendation about value, and the model's own skewed run shows the cap costs more as engines diverge. The 2% loss reflects the chosen effect sizes, not a general property, and the model never tests whether the cap helps at all, such as under saturation or learning-value effects.
- Hidden assumption: Engine strength is the only shared driver of quality in a real batch, and "value" is the true IPM×D1 of picked ideas. That treats a repeat as a cost to cap, when a repeat on a strong engine may be the correct pick, and it assumes the simulated 8-engine, 10-idea layout and the correlation values (0, 0.5, 0.9) resemble real batches.
- Would prove it wrong: A run where the cap loses more than about 15% of value at plausible settings, such as engine effect size much larger than within-engine noise, or where the cap gains value over plain top 3 (diversification is worth something real). The same goes for repeat rates that stay flat as correlation rises once the engine effect is varied independently of the correlation.
- Break scenario: 3 strong engines and 5 near-dead ones, with 3 of the 10 ideas on one dominant engine, correlation 0.9, budget 1000, and engine strength spread 5x wider than idea-level noise. The true top 3 then all sit on the dominant engine, so a cap of one per engine drops two of the best picks for weaker ones. The cap's value loss should far exceed 6%, and the 54% repeat rate becomes the correct answer rather than a problem.

## E426 — drain slope by pipe diameter not one quarter everywhere
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [plumbing][drainage][testing][sandbox]
- What: Seeding a drainage-plumbing check: a rule of one quarter inch fall per foot for every drain pipe rejected 5 of 7 sample runs that the per-diameter minimum slope (quarter inch up to 2.5 in pipe, eighth inch for 3 to 6 in, sixteenth inch for 8 in and up) accepts within the same fall budget.
- Why built: New-ground seed from a real scenario: a branch or building drain must fit in the height between the fixture outlet and the sewer connection, and the slope table used is the one I recall from the International Plumbing Code minimum-slope section, not re-read from the source.
- Design: Pure arithmetic over 7 runs (1.5 to 8 in pipe, 5 to 120 ft, 2 to 14 in fall budget): required fall is slope times run, a run is feasible when required fall does not exceed the budget; compare the uniform quarter-inch rule with the per-diameter table.
- Got right: Small pipes up to 2.5 in agree under both rules in both runs, so the disagreement is isolated to pipes of 3 in and larger, which matches the table design.
- Where/why it failed: The uniform rule over-requires fall on every larger pipe: the 3 in main needs 10 in against 5 in, the 4 in building drain 15 in against 7.5 in, the 8 in sewer 30 in against 7.5 in, rejecting 5 of 7 runs the code minimum accepts.
- Fix: Look up the minimum slope by pipe diameter before computing the fall budget, and treat quarter inch per foot as the small-pipe case only.
- Why this fix: Larger pipes carry flow at lower velocity per fall, so the table lowers the slope as diameter rises; applying the small-pipe figure everywhere wastes fall that a tight job does not have.
- Rule of thumb: Compute drain fall from the per-diameter minimum slope, not one quarter inch per foot everywhere; the uniform rule rejected 5 of 7 runs, all of them 3 in or larger, while small pipes agreed.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session, which checks the arithmetic of the slope table as recalled; whether the table matches the current code edition and local amendments was not checked.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-domain
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the arithmetic is trivially true and the small-pipe agreement holds, but 5 of 7 is an artifact of hand-picked runs and budgets, and it shows that the two rules differ, not which one the code requires.
- Hidden assumption: The per-diameter table (1/4 in/ft up to 2.5 in, 1/8 for 3–6 in, 1/16 for 8 in and up) is the code-correct standard, so "accepted" means "legal" — but the test only shows the two rules differ, not that the looser one is right, and the 7 runs and fall budgets were picked by the author.

## E425 — rule card ceiling makes go big decay proof but flat
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy 6-beat sketch model testing whether a fixed rule-card harm ceiling lets a go-big severity schedule win when the safe cue habituates (decays per beat).
- Why built: Joins the write-the-rules-before-the-gags kernel, escalation-needs-matching-distance and decaying-safe-cue-flips-go-big-back-to-mild; the card was hoped to rescue go-big from decay.
- Design: licence per beat = distance + 0.5 times cue strength (decay to the power of the beat); overshoot is penalised at 3 times; schedules mild (0.3), flat (0.7) and go-big (0.2 to 1.0); card clamps severity at the distance; distances 0.2 and 0.5, decay 1.0, 0.8, 0.5.
- Got right: The card does stop the collapse: at distance 0.5 and decay 0.8 go-big rises from 0.29 to 0.43, and from -0.74 to 0.20 at distance 0.2 and decay 0.5, independent of decay.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that go-big would win with the card was wrong: the clamp turns the ramp into a plateau at the ceiling, so flat or mild still wins in every cell (flat 0.60 vs go-big 0.43 at distance 0.5 with no habituation).
- Fix: Treat the card as a floor against collapse, not as a reason to go big; once the card is written, pick the flat schedule at the ceiling, and keep go-big only where the cue is restated or distance is raised.
- Why this fix: A fixed ceiling cannot be both a cap and an escalation: it removes exactly the severity variation that go-big adds, so the schedule's value becomes the plateau value.
- Rule of thumb: A fixed rule-card ceiling makes a go-big schedule decay-proof (0.43 whatever the decay at distance 0.5) but not a winner, because the clamp flattens it; after writing the card pick flat at the ceiling.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; the licence and penalty formulas are invented toy parameters, not measured audience data.

- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the card only helps when its ceiling is already correct, which makes "pick flat at the ceiling" tautological, and the d=0.2 "break" is a tie rather than a failure, so the rule is untested where it would matter.
- Hidden assumption: The card's ceiling equals the true distance, so the licence (distance plus decaying cue) can never fall below the clamped severity; the 0.43 "decay-proof" result follows from that by construction, and the toy never tests a ceiling that is wrong or stale.
- Would prove it wrong: A run where the ceiling is set independently of the true distance (for example, by a noisy estimate) and flat-at-ceiling scores below mild or go-big. Alternatively, a run where flat-at-ceiling beats go-big only because of the clamp, with no overshoot cost ever incurred.
- Break scenario: The card says 0.5 but the true distance is 0.2, with decay 0.5. Licence runs 0.70, 0.45, 0.325, 0.26, 0.23, 0.22. Flat at the 0.5 ceiling overshoots on beats 1–5 at 3x penalty and should lose to mild 0.3 and to a go-big schedule clamped lower.

## E424 — per beat distance survives a decaying safe cue
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy 10-beat sketch (4 severe, 6 mild) testing whether a per-beat distance split (severe beats lean on a safe cue at distance 0.5, mild beats close at 0.1) still beats the best single global distance when the safe cue habituates.
- Why built: Composes the severe-harm-needs-distance kernel, escalation-needs-matching-distance and decaying-safe-cue-flips-go-big-back-to-mild; the expectation was that decay would erase or flip the split's advantage, as it flipped go-big to mild.
- Design: cue strength 0.4 times decay to the power of the severe beat's index, licence is distance plus cue, overshoot costs 3 times, mild beats score closeness (1 minus distance); global distance is the best of an 11-point grid; decay 1.0, 0.8, 0.5, 0.2, plus a re-tuned severe distance of 0.8 at decay 0.5.
- Got right: The advantage of the split shrank steadily with decay (+0.240, +0.188, +0.100, +0.040), and re-tuning the severe distance to 0.8 recovered +0.420 at decay 0.5.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that the advantage would reach zero or flip at decay 0.2 was refuted: it stayed positive at +0.040, because the global strategy suffers the same decay and also gives up the closeness reward on the mild beats.
- Fix: Keep the per-beat split under a habituating cue but set the severe-beat distance for the weakest cue (here 0.8, high enough that no cue is needed) instead of counting on a cue that decays.
- Why this fix: A distance that covers the severe beats without the cue removes the decaying term from the split, and the mild beats keep their closeness reward in any case.
- Rule of thumb: A per-beat distance split survives a habituating safe cue (gain +0.040 at decay 0.2, never a flip), but its gain falls from +0.240 to +0.040 as the cue decays, so set the severe-beat distance without the cue; at 0.8 the gain at decay 0.5 was +0.420.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; payoffs and the 0.4 cue size are invented toy values, so the gains are model numbers.

- Hidden assumption: The rule assumes the toy's functional form (cue = 0.4·decay^index, licence = distance + cue, 3x overshoot cost, 11-point global grid) mirrors the real habituation, and that the re-tuned 0.8 was chosen blind to the cue. In fact it's an oracle pick that happens to beat the grid.
- Would prove it wrong: A run where the 0.8 severe distance is selected without cue knowledge (e.g. fixed in advance, or tuned at decay 1.0) and its gain at decay 0.5 or 0.2 drops to zero or below. The licence margin vanishes, so the split's 0.5 severe distance overshoots on most severe beats, while the global optimum retreats to a safe low distance. Add a mixed-severity ordering so the cue decays before the severe beats arrive.

## E423 — per beat distance gain is independent of rule card coverage
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy 10-beat sketch (4 severe, 6 mild) comparing one global distance against per-beat distance (severe far, mild close) while a rule card covers 0%, 50% or 100% of the severe beats and a safe cue is on or off.
- Why built: Composes the severe-harm-needs-distance kernel, escalation-needs-matching-distance and the incomplete-rule-card lesson, to see whether the per-beat distance split still pays when the card is incomplete.
- Design: severe beat is funny only at distance 0.7 or more (else a penalty of 4 per unit short), mild beat scores 1 minus distance, an uncovered severe beat loses 0.5 unless the cue backstop is on; global distance is the best of an 11-point grid; per-beat uses 0.8 for severe and 0.1 for mild.
- Got right: Prediction held: per-beat gains 0.36 at 50% coverage (0.84 vs 0.48) and 0.36 with the cue at 0% coverage (0.94 vs 0.58), and the break case where mild beats give no closeness reward showed 0.00 gain.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed, but the gain was exactly 0.36 in all six card and cue cells, so the card and cue move the level of both strategies equally and do not change the per-beat advantage; the number is set by the invented payoff of the closeness reward.
- Fix: Set distance per beat by harm level regardless of how complete the rule card is; treat card coverage and the cue as separate levers on the level of the score.
- Why this fix: A single global distance has to trade severe beats (need far) against mild beats (need close), a loss the card and cue never touch, while the split removes the trade entirely.
- Rule of thumb: Per-beat distance beats the best single global distance by the same 0.36 at 0%, 50% and 100% rule-card coverage and with or without a safe cue, but only when mild beats actually reward closeness (0.00 gain when they do not).
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; payoffs are invented toy values, so the size 0.36 is a model artefact and only the independence from coverage is the finding.

- Hidden assumption: The 0.36 gain is an artifact of the hand-picked constants (0.8/0.1 per-beat, 0.7 threshold, 4× penalty, 11-point grid), and "constant across coverage and cue" is just because the card and cue terms are additive and distance-independent in this toy, so they cancel by construction, not by discovery.
- Would prove it wrong: Any per-beat gain that moves with coverage or cue once the card/cue penalty depends on distance (e.g., a covered severe beat is funny at 0.5), or a gain that drops below 0.3 when the severe threshold or penalty weight shifts a little (threshold 0.85, penalty 1 per unit, or per-beat severe set to 0.7 rather than a tuned 0.8).

The global grid then lands near 0.4 for everyone, the per-beat split has almost no room, and the gain should collapse well under 0.3. The proposed break (flat 0.5 mild) only tests whether the model returns zero when you remove the reward, which is a tautology.

## E422 — incomplete card dial flatness needs coverage or cue
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy 11-point distance-dial sweep over a 10-beat sketch (5 severe, 5 mild) with a rule card covering 0%, 50% or 100% of the severe beats and a safe cue on or off, counting how many distances land within 95% of the best score.
- Why built: Joins escalation-needs-matching-distance, the finding that a full severity cap flattens the distance dial, and the incomplete-rule-card lesson, to ask whether a half-covering card still keeps the dial forgiving.
- Design: licence is distance plus 0.4 for a cue on uncovered severe beats; a beat scores its harm within licence and licence minus 3 times the overshoot otherwise; covered severe beats are capped to mild (0.3); robustness is the count of distances with total at least 95% of the best total.
- Got right: Prediction held: a full card gave 8 of 11 forgiving distances against 2 with no card, and half coverage with the cue gave 6 of 11.
- Where/why it failed: Half coverage alone does not flatten the dial: 2 of 11, the same as no card, because the uncovered severe beats still demand the right distance; flatness also costs the peak, with the best score falling from 6.00 (no card) to 4.80 (half) to 3.00 (full).
- Fix: Treat the card's flattening as a trade of peak for forgiveness; with a partial card add the safe cue backstop on the uncovered severe beats before relying on a wide distance range.
- Why this fix: A cue on the uncovered beats lowers the distance those beats need, so they stop dominating the sweep, which restores the forgiving range without capping them.
- Rule of thumb: A rule card flattens the distance dial only when it covers the severe beats or a safe cue backs the uncovered ones: half coverage alone left 2 of 11 distances within 95% of best, with the cue 6 of 11, and every flattening costs peak score.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; payoffs and the 0.4 cue size are invented toy values, so the counts are model numbers.

- Hidden assumption: The result is mostly built in by the design: severe beats are 50% of the sketch, the 0.3 cap and the +0.4 cue are hand-chosen, and a 95% threshold on a total that mixes flat and distance-dependent terms is arbitrary, so "robustness" may measure those constants, not any property of rule cards or cues.
- Would prove it wrong: Re-run with the cap at 0.5 or 0.1, the cue bonus at 0.2 or 0.8, the threshold at 90% or 98%, and severe beats at 3 or 7 of 10. If half-coverage-with-cue stops beating half-coverage-without-cue (6 vs 2), or full card falls under 8 of 11, the rule was a parameter artifact.
- Break scenario: Cue helps only when licence overshoot is small, so make the severe beats' harm values tightly clustered just above the cue bonus. Then cue-on adds a flat 0.4 shift that moves every distance's score the same way, the count of distances within 95% of best barely changes, and "cue backs the uncovered ones" shows no flattening at all. The same toy with a cue that costs score at low distances would also show whether "every flattening costs peak score" is a law or just the cap's side effect.

## E421 — benign cover sources saturate when stacked
- Date: 2026-10-18
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy 6-beat benign-violation model with cover from three additive sources (distance, a safe cue, a rule card), testing whether a second cover source adds less than half of what the first adds, and whether cue and card are interchangeable.
- Why built: Joins escalation-needs-matching-distance, safe-cue-escalation and rule-card-lifts-benign-ceiling; each shows cover enabling go-big alone, and the open question was whether they stack with diminishing returns.
- Design: cover is the sum of sources capped at 1; a beat scores its violation if within cover and cover minus 3 times the overshoot otherwise; schedules mild (0.3 flat) and go-big (0.2 to 1.0); grounded distance 0.3 with cue 0.3 and card 0.3 added singly and together.
- Got right: A cue and a card of equal size are interchangeable (identical go-big score 0.72 each), and go-big flips from losing (-4.00 vs mild 1.80) to winning (3.20) only when both are present, since neither alone gets it past mild.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction of a second source adding under half of the first was refuted: the second added 2.48 against 4.72 for the first, 53%, because the overshoot penalty is steep and cover below 1 is still worth full price; diminishing returns only appear at the cap.
- Fix: Do not discount a second cover source in planning until total cover nears 1.0; there a third source of +0.3 added nothing (3.60 to 3.60) in the far-framing break case.
- Why this fix: The marginal value of cover is set by how many beats still overshoot, and at 0.6 total cover about half the ramp still overshoots, so the second source buys real room.
- Rule of thumb: Do not assume a second benign-cover source is worth under half of the first: at cover 0.3 then 0.6 it added 53% (2.48 vs 4.72) and flipped go-big from losing to winning, with saturation only at total cover 1.0, so plan for two sources before a third.
- Provenance: Verified first-hand by running the sandbox in this session; payoffs are invented toy values so 53% is a model number, not an audience measure.
- Composed: escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, safe-cue-escalation/E1, rule-card-lifts-benign-ceiling-so-go-big-escalation-works/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The prediction did fail, but the rule is a single-parameter-set number from a toy where you chose the penalty, ramp and source sizes. The 53% is a threshold artifact of the 3x penalty, and the "interchangeable" finding is true by construction because the sources are additive. The saturation break scenario (1.84, 3.60, 3.60) only confirms the cap you coded in.
- Hidden assumption: Cover effects stay roughly linear until the cap at 1.0, so the "second source" gain depends only on how much cover is added, not on where on the cover curve the schedule sits. The 53% figure is really a property of the chosen schedule (go-big 0.2 to 1.0), the 3x overshoot penalty and the 0.3 sizes, not of benign-violation cover in general.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with a different penalty multiplier (1x or 6x), different source sizes (0.2 or 0.4) or a different go-big ramp. If the second-source share moves from 53% to under 50% or over 60%, the "plan for two before a third" rule only describes this toy's parameters, not the model.
- Break scenario: Go-big on the same 6 beats with a 1x penalty, so the penalty never flips the sign. Then the first source buys most of the gain and the second buys less than half. The "flip from losing to winning" is a threshold effect of the 3x penalty, and the rule treats it as a property of cover.

## E420 — two pass labeller vs one pass intended schemes
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][sandbox]
- What: A sandbox generated 3752 four-line stanzas from designed schemes (XXAA, AABB, ABAB, ABBA, AAXX) and scored two rhyme-letter labellers against the design. A one-pass labeller (any shared vowel counts) was wrong on 724 of 1552 XXAA stanzas (53.4% right) and 30 of 216 AABB/ABAB/ABBA stanzas each, but right on all 558 stanzas with no stray assonance. A two-pass labeller (uppercase for perfect or family rhymes, then lowercase for assonance) matched the designed resolved scheme in all 3752.
- Why built: The two-pass kernel says one-pass assignment lets a stray assonance pair steal a letter, and the shape kernel says the scheme shape sets stability; a memory entry only quoted the first, so I wanted an independent check against designed schemes, not a labeller scored by its own rule.
- Design: Words are (vowel, coda) pairs from a 12-word pool; relations perfect, family (voiced and unvoiced stop pairs) and assonance. Stanzas are generated from the designed letters, with filler lines kept out of any resolved rhyme but allowed to share a vowel with other lines. The truth is the design, so neither labeller defines it. Both labellers are scored on the whole enumeration.
- Got right: Two-pass uppercase letters equal the design in 3752 of 3752, and an assonance-only pair comes out lowercase (AaAa for the test stanza), so letter case carries the open or settled signal while one-pass cannot distinguish it (abab). The one-pass failure only appears when a stray assonance exists.
- Where/why it failed: My first prediction said two-pass would also label every filler line as X, and that missed: in 284 XXAA stanzas the two filler lines share a vowel, so two-pass lowercases them as an open rhyme (81.7% under the strict X-for-fillers reading). That is the kernel doing its job, but it means a lowercase pair is not an error and not an intended rhyme either. The first scorer also treated the X label as an uppercase letter, which made two-pass look 18% right until I fixed it.
- Fix: Label in two passes, uppercase for resolved rhymes first and lowercase for assonance among the unlettered lines, and score the resolved (uppercase) scheme for shape; read lowercase pairs as open links that may be accidental.
- Why this fix: The one-pass rule lets an assonance link between a filler and a rhyming line pull the filler into the rhyme group, which changes the shape, while the second pass only looks at lines the first pass left alone.
- Rule of thumb: Letter the resolved rhymes first and the assonance second: against designed schemes this removed 724 of 1552 XXAA errors in a 12-word model, and lowercase pairs flag open links that may be accidental fillers.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox over the full enumeration (RESULT PASS). The 12-word phoneme pool and the family rule are my simplified model, not real pronunciations.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, suno-builder/E3

- Hidden assumption: Real rhyme labelling matches the sandbox's tidy categories: every pair is perfect, family or assonance, and the two-pass ordering reproduces intent. Yet the "truth" is the designer's own letters, and the two-pass labeller is built on the same relation hierarchy that generated them, so the 3752/3752 is close to circular. A 12-word pool is also too small to show it generalises.
- Would prove it wrong: Run both labellers on human-annotated real stanzas, with annotator-agreed schemes and a large vocabulary. If two-pass matches the annotators no better than one-pass, or only on stanzas without stray assonance, the rule is wrong. A held-out design with a different relation structure would also count. Examples are near-rhyme chains where assonance links A to B and B to C, so the passes disagree on grouping, or family rhymes that bridge two perfect classes.
- Break scenario: The stanza is "late / rate / gate / bake". Here "bake" is a family rhyme with "late" (t/k voiceless stops) and was meant as a deliberate slant rhyme, but the filler "gate" also shares the vowel. Two-pass uppercases the family link and cannot tell a deliberate slant rhyme from accidental family overlap. Both intent and accident get the same uppercase letter. The sandbox hid this by generating fillers without family relations. The 284 strict-X failures show the same ambiguity at the assonance level, and the lowercase flag is just a heuristic.

## E419 — silent hook on the matched recut flips ipm d1 unless the gate reads the audio
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][film][testing][sandbox]
- What: Extending the frame-0 audio gate sandbox to a silent hook on only the delivery-matched recut: IPM times D1, which held at promise 0.5 in all three earlier scenarios, picked 0.6 when only the 0.5 recut was silent and 0.4 when the 0.5 and 0.6 recuts were silent. A gate that re-renders silent recuts from the audio itself restored 0.5 in all 6 scenarios, while a gate driven by a remembered list that had shifted one slot missed in the same 2 scenarios as no gate.
- Why built: hook-frame0-audio-vs-promise-cap-recut-rank/E1 said IPM times D1 never moves off 0.5 under a silent hook, but its three scenarios never silenced the 0.5 recut; collective-reference/E1 says a hand-kept sidecar drifts silently, so I tested whether the gate itself needs to read the artifact.
- Design: Same shapes as the hook sandbox (nine promises 0.2 to 1.0, delivery 0.5, IPM times 0.4 when the first second is silent, D1 falling after promise passes delivery). Six scenarios for which recuts are truly silent. Three gates: none, a list of silent ids recorded before a re-render that shifted slots by one, and one derived from the current audio.
- Got right: The earlier result holds where it was tested (A, B, C, E all pick 0.5 for IPM times D1 with no gate). The audio-derived gate is exact in all 6 scenarios, and IPM alone keeps picking 1.0 or 0.6 regardless.
- Where/why it failed: The earlier 3 of 3 claim was a coverage artifact: silence confined to the matched recut flips the multiplicative ranking, because the penalty then hits the winner but not its rivals. The derived gate being exact is by construction, since it reads the true silent set; the shifted-list failure is built in too, so what is shown is how much a stale list costs, not how often lists go stale.
- Fix: Gate every recut by reading its first second at ranking time (derive the silent set from the audio, not from a list written earlier), and treat a silent hook on the delivery-matched recut as the case the IPM times D1 ranking cannot absorb.
- Why this fix: A uniform silence penalty cancels in the ranking, a penalty on a single recut does not, and only the audio tells which recuts it is on after any re-render.
- Rule of thumb: IPM times D1 survives a uniform silent hook but not one on the delivery-matched recut (picks 0.6 or 0.4 instead of 0.5); gate every recut from its current audio, not from a remembered list.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS). The penalty 0.4, the one-slot shift and the promise curves are assumed toy values, not measured ad data.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, hook-frame0-audio-vs-promise-cap-recut-rank/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sandbox is circular: delivery is fixed at 0.5, the scenarios were hand-built to include the failure, and the gate returning 0.5 follows by construction, so it shows the gate is implemented, not that it generalizes. The stale-list result is the stronger, narrower claim (it fails when slots shift), and it needs a test that varies delivery and silence-detector noise.
- Hidden assumption: Silent recuts are the only perturbation that matters, and "0.5" is the true answer. The rule treats the 0.5 pick as ground truth, and treats the audio-derived gate as correct because it restores 0.5. That only holds if the gate's silence detector is accurate and silence-hook recuts should be rescored on the same IPM*D1 curve.
- Would prove it wrong: A scenario in which the audio-derived gate returns something other than 0.5. For example, if the silence threshold misclassifies a quiet-but-not-silent first second, or the re-render itself shifts delivery. Equally damaging: the no-gate failures turn out to be confined to the two named scenarios by construction, which would make "misses in 2 of 6" an artifact of how the scenarios were chosen rather than a measured rate.
- Break scenario: Delivery-matched recut silent *and* the underlying delivery peak moved (say to 0.6, so D1 starts falling later). The gate "restores" 0.5 by re-rendering, but 0.5 is no longer the delivery-matched promise. Alternatively, all recuts at and below 0.5 silent while those above are not: the gate must pick correctly when the 0.5 candidate is rescored, and the sandbox never tests a gate that runs when the re-render shifts slots on the audio side too.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-17 · digest 9a47c547b8cd
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__silent-hook-on-the-matched-recut-flips-ipm-d1-unless-the-gate-reads-the-audio.py
- Prediction: With no gate IPM times D1 picks 0.5 unless the 0.5 recut is silent, then picks something else; the audio-derived gate returns 0.5 in every scenario; the shifted list gate fails in at least one scenario.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS IPM*D1 with no gate misses 0.5 in 2 of 6 scenarios (D; F); stale sidecar misses in 2; gate derived from the audio misses in 0
- Scenarios: 1) no recut silent; 2) all silent; 3) only promise 0.7 and above silent; 4) BREAK: only the 0.5 delivery-matched recut silent; 5) only the 0.4 recut silent; 6) the 0.5 and 0.6 recuts silent

## E418 — sidecar drift corrupts warp cap ranking
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][sandbox][process]
- What: A sandbox fed a warp cap (1.5) and IPM times D1 ranking from a variant-to-warp map, comparing a map derived from the render source against a hand-kept sidecar that had drifted (entries shifted by one or two, or missing). Over 12 retention slopes the derived map matched ground truth every time; the drifted sidecar changed the pick only at slopes 0.003 to 0.01 (loss about 0.005 to 0.009 of IPM times D1) and only when a missing entry belonged to the true winner.
- Why built: collective-reference/E1 says a hand-maintained sidecar drifts silently and must be derived from the one real source; the question was whether that drift actually corrupts a cap-then-rank pipeline (caption-warp-cap-before-ipm-d1-ranking/E1) once ranking on IPM times D1 (rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1) is in play.
- Design: Six enumerated variants with fixed IPM, base D1 and true warp. Believed warp comes from the map; footage is only re-cut (capped) when believed warp exceeds the cap, so a wrong map either skips a needed cap or applies one that is not needed. Score is IPM times D1 after the real penalty. Maps: derived, shift 1, shift 2 plus a missing entry, two missing entries, one missing entry.
- Got right: Derived-from-source gives the true pick at all 12 slopes. At slope 0 (no retention cost) any map gives the true pick, matching the earlier finding that the ranking change needs retention to matter.
- Where/why it failed: My expectation that the sidecar hurts most at high slopes was wrong: at slopes 0.015 and above the winner is the low-warp variant whatever the map says, so drift is harmless. Damage appears only in a narrow band near where the cap decision flips the winner, and shifted maps alone never changed the pick in this 6-variant set. The effect is small and tied to this toy data.
- Fix: Derive the warp map from the render source at rank time and do not keep a separate sidecar. If a sidecar must exist, check it against the source on every run, because its failures cannot be seen from the outcome: most slopes show no loss at all.
- Why this fix: The drift is invisible exactly where it is harmless and exactly where it bites only a narrow band, so outcome monitoring would not catch it while a source check would.
- Rule of thumb: A drifted sidecar in a cap-then-rank pipeline costs value only in a narrow band of retention slopes, so its silence is not proof it is correct; derive the mapping from the source or diff it against the source every run.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and a 12-slope scan (RESULT PASS). The variant data, cap and drift shapes are invented for the model and are not measured ad data.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, caption-warp-cap-before-ipm-d1-ranking/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The finding rests on one hand-built fixture, and the 0.003–0.01 band probably reflects where its warps sit relative to the cap, so "narrow band" is not established. "Derive or diff every run" is still sound advice.
- Hidden assumption: The six variants, their true warps and the 1.5 cap are representative of the real pipeline, so the narrow 0.003–0.01 band comes from the cap-versus-warp geometry of this one fixture, not from sidecar drift.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerunning with different variant warps, a different cap, or a different winner position moves the damaged band to 0.05–0.2 or to all slopes, or a drifted sidecar changes the pick at several slopes outside the band.
- Break scenario: Put the true winner's warp just below the cap (say 1.45), the runner-up's just above it (1.6), and shift the sidecar by one so the winner is believed to be 1.6. Then sweep slopes across 0.0005–0.5 and 5+ random drift draws. The unneeded cap on the winner should cost value at slopes the original fixture never hit, which would show the "narrow band" is a fixture artifact.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-17 · digest 2b31a6d7c437
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__sidecar-drift-corrupts-warp-cap-ranking.py
- Prediction: Expected the drifted sidecar to change the pick at the higher slopes (0.05 and 0.2) where the cap matters most, and not at slope 0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS derived map = truth at all 12 slopes; drifted sidecar loses value at slopes [0.003, 0.005, 0.008, 0.01] and costs nothing at slope 0.0. The high-slope half of the prediction was refuted.
- Scenarios: 1) derived map across 12 slopes; 2) sidecar shifted by one; 3) sidecar missing the two highest-warp variants; 4) BREAK: high slopes 0.05 and 0.2 where I expected most damage; 5) slope 0 with no retention cost

## E417 — reference anchor vs real product shot
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ai-video][compliance][tiktok-shop][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox modelled shot lists (real / AI scene / AI product shot, with 0, 1 or 3 reference images and a label flag) against the TikTok Shop AI rules in tiktok-shop/E14. Reference images cut attribute alterations on AI product shots from 180 to 72 to 33 to 14 over 60 seeds, but never to zero, and an AI product shot violates the policy even when no attribute drifted.
- Why built: The kernel says a reference image does not make an AI product shot compliant; the question was whether a visual-consistency check (no drift seen) could stand in for a policy check, and where that stops holding.
- Design: 432 enumerated videos (product-shot AI or not, 0/2/5 AI scenes, label on or off, refs 0/1/3, 6 seeds, two label thresholds). Two gates were compared with a ground truth taken from E14: a visual-drift gate and a shot-list real/AI column gate. Dubbing-only and unlabelled AI-heavy scenes were run as separate cases.
- Got right: Of 144 reference-anchored AI product videos, 24 passed the visual-drift gate and all 24 still violated policy; the shot-list gate caught 144 of 144. AI dubbing over real footage stayed compliant unlabelled, and AI-heavy scenes with a real product violated only through the missing label.
- Where/why it failed: The shot-list gate equals the ground truth by construction (the policy forbids any AI-made product display), so 144/144 is not evidence about real review. The label threshold (0.3 or 0.5 AI share) is invented, since the policy only says significantly AI-made; the drift formula is a toy, not a measurement of any video model.
- Fix: Keep the real/AI column as the gate: every product shot is real footage or a photo, AI is limited to scenes, backgrounds and dubbing, and the reference image only serves consistency. Do not accept no visible drift as a substitute.
- Why this fix: Drift falls with more references but never reaches zero, and the policy bans AI-made product displays regardless of drift, so only the source column removes the violation class entirely.
- Rule of thumb: Treat a reference image as lowering the odds of a changed product, not as compliance; the real-or-AI source of each product shot decides, so film or photograph the product and let AI make only scenes and dubbing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, numbers above). The policy rules come from E14 and were not re-fetched; the drift model and label threshold are assumptions of the model.
- Composed: ideas:AI-VIDEO/ai-for-scenes-and-dubbing-real-footage-for-the-product-plus-the-ai-label, ideas:AI-VIDEO/label-photoreal-ai-and-skip-the-label-for-obvious-cartoons-on-youtube, tiktok-shop/E14
- Picked-by: current-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The drift-versus-source split is sound, but the 100% catch rates are circular because the gate and the ground truth both read the same column, and the sandbox never tests hybrid or mislabelled shots or the label-exemption question in E14.
- Hidden assumption: The sandbox's ground truth (every AI product shot violates, regardless of drift) is a faithful reading of E14, so the 24/24 and 144/144 results only restate that rule and don't test it, and the sandbox's drift model stands in for real generator behaviour.
- Would prove it wrong: E14 (or TikTok's current policy) permits AI product shots that are labelled, or that faithfully depict the product. Alternatively, a real generator run with 9 or more references gets zero alterations, or the shot-list gate misses a shot because a real/AI column was mislabelled.
- Break scenario: A labelled, reference-anchored AI product shot with no visible drift, run through the shot-list gate. Add a real product shot with AI-enhanced lighting or background, and a hybrid composite shot where the real/AI column is ambiguous. If the gate flags the labelled one as a violation, E14 and the "film the product" rule disagree. If it passes the hybrid, the gate is blind.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-17 · digest bcbec3abe792
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__reference-anchor-vs-real-product-shot.py
- Prediction: Expected that some reference-anchored AI product shots would pass a drift-only check yet still violate, that alterations would fall monotonically with more references without hitting zero, and that dubbing-only video would need no label.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS anchored AI product shots that pass the visual-drift check still violate in 24/24 cases; refs cut alterations 180->72->33->14 (never 0); shot-list gate catches 144/144.
- Scenarios: 1) anchored AI product shots through drift-only gate; 2) shot-list gate on the same shots; 3) BREAK: raise references to 9 and look for zero alterations over 60 seeds (still 14); 4) dubbing-only real footage unlabelled; 5) AI-heavy scenes with real product, unlabelled

## E416 — keyboard layout judge by sfb and home row on your own text
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][testing][sandbox][ergonomics]
- What: Seeding the KEYBOARD-LAYOUT domain, a sandbox scored QWERTY, Dvorak, Colemak and an alphabetical layout on home-row share and same-finger bigram rate over two real texts. Colemak and Dvorak beat QWERTY by about 0.37 to 0.42 of home-row share on both prose and code, and an alphabetical layout beat QWERTY on home-row share (0.467 against 0.303 on prose) while having the worst same-finger rate (0.123 against 0.040).
- Why built: A new domain needs a first measured claim; layout comparisons usually quote one effort number, and I wanted to see whether the two obvious metrics agree.
- Design: Letters only, three rows of ten keys with a standard touch-typing finger map (index fingers cover two columns). Texts are the Zen of Python from the `this` module (677 letters) and the source of json/decoder.py (6,545 letters). Same-finger bigrams exclude the same key twice and reset at any non-letter.
- Got right: Colemak and Dvorak both gained at least 0.20 of home-row share over QWERTY on both texts, QWERTY had the highest same-finger rate of the three, and the Dvorak gain shrank by 0.037 on code, just over my 0.03 bound.
- Where/why it failed: The disagreement scenario I built to break a single-metric reading succeeded: home-row share alone ranks the alphabetical layout above QWERTY while same-finger rate ranks it last. Colemak led both metrics, so the layouts I tested did not show a conflict between the two for the real candidates. The prose text is short, and the model ignores digits, punctuation, shift, hand alternation and finger strength.
- Fix: Report both numbers per layout on a sample of the text you actually type, and do not accept a ranking from home-row share alone.
- Why this fix: Home-row share rewards putting common letters in the middle row even if they share fingers, which the same-finger rate penalises, and the alphabetical layout shows the two can order layouts oppositely.
- Rule of thumb: Judge a keyboard layout on both home-row share and same-finger bigram rate over your own text; here QWERTY on code had 0.097 same-finger bigrams, over twice its prose rate, and home-row share alone ranked the alphabetical layout above it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS). The finger map and layout rows are standard but typed from memory, and the texts are small; the result says nothing about comfort or typing speed.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — The direction (home-row share alone misranks alphabetical) is plausible and the prediction passed, but the rule's 2× figure and ranking disagreement come from one short prose sample and one file with no variance estimate, and a prediction that mostly restates known layout design isn't much of a test.
- Hidden assumption: Two texts (677 letters of prose, 6,545 of one Python file) and a three-row, letters-only, ten-key grid stand in for "your own text" and real keyboards; the rule also assumes the two metrics are the whole cost, so a flat or split ranking says something general rather than something about this alphabetical layout and this sample.
- Would prove it wrong: Scoring the same layouts on a larger, varied corpus (other prose, other code, with punctuation, digits and a fourth row) and finding that QWERTY's code same-finger rate is not about twice its prose rate, or that alphabetical no longer outranks QWERTY on home-row share, or that adding a third metric (hand alternation, finger travel) makes the ranking disagreement vanish or flip.
- Break scenario: Rerun on 100k+ letters of mixed prose and code with punctuation kept as keys, and bootstrap the 677-letter prose sample: if the prose same-finger gaps (0.040, 0.030, 0.015) fall inside resampling noise, or the QWERTY code/prose ratio swings well away from 2×, the "differ by metric" claim and the 2× figure are sample artifacts.

## E415 — distance dial makes the decaying cue redundant except for mild beats
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][testing][sandbox]
- What: In the escalation model, a distance dial that rises with severity (matched framing) already gives full benign cover, so a safe cue adds exactly nothing (effect 0.0000 at every decay rate), while under a fixed far (surreal) framing the kernel's second half shows up: a mild schedule scores 0.05 against 4.36 for going flat at the ceiling. A cue decaying at 0.6 per beat lifts the far-framed mild schedule 11.5 times to 0.54, still far below flat at 4.58.
- Why built: The distance-dial kernel, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1 and decaying-safe-cue-flips-go-big-back-to-mild/E1 each fix the same cover problem with a different lever; I wanted to know whether the cue and the dial stack or substitute.
- Design: Same habituation model as the two earlier sandboxes (h = exp(-0.2 X), response h times I/10, benign gate g = exp(-((d - I/10)/0.25)^2), cue cover g + c(1 - g), c = 0.7 times r to the beat index). Framings close (d 0.3), far (d 0.9), matched (d = I/10), cue decay r none, 1.0, 0.6, 0.3, over flat, rule-of-three, mild and linear schedules.
- Got right: Matched distance gives the same scores for every cue (flat 5.11 either way), and far framing punishes mild beats as the kernel says. Under close framing a permanent cue lets flat win (3.58) and a cue at 0.3 per beat does not (mild wins, 1.46 vs 0.97), matching the earlier decay result.
- Where/why it failed: The matched-distance redundancy is true by construction, because the gate there is 1 and the cue formula cannot raise it, so that part is arithmetic, not a finding. The far-framing mild scores depend on my assumed gate width of 0.25 and distance 0.9.
- Fix: Treat the dial and the cue as substitutes for severe beats: either raise distance with severity (surreal or AI framing per beat) or keep a cue alive, and do not spend effort on the cue when the dial is already matched. Keep mild beats close, because far framing flattens them and a cue only partly repairs that.
- Why this fix: The matched dial sets cover to 1 for every beat, whereas the cue only covers a fixed share of the gap, and decays, so it is a weaker lever that is redundant exactly where the stronger one is applied.
- Rule of thumb: Match the framing distance to each beat's severity first; a safe cue is a backup for when the framing cannot move, and it will not rescue mild beats that are framed too far away.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS). The gate shape, widths, decay and schedules are the earlier sandboxes' assumed model, not human ratings.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, decaying-safe-cue-flips-go-big-back-to-mild/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the sandbox only shows that a redundant mechanism is redundant when the model gives perfect matching for free. The far-framing numbers (0.05 → 0.54, flat at 4.58) are real within the model but say nothing about whether a framing can be matched in practice, and the "11.5x" is a ratio off a near-zero base.
- Hidden assumption: The rule treats "match distance to severity" as free and always achievable, and the cue-cover formula (g + c(1−g), c = 0.7·r^beat) as the only way a cue works. The result is built into the model: the gate g peaks at d = I/10, so a cue added to g ≈ 1 has nothing left to add. The 0.0000 is arithmetic, not evidence about real framing or cues, and the rule leans on it as if it were.
- Would prove it wrong: Matched framing with any cost, noise or lag in d (say d off by 0.2 from I/10, or one beat behind a rising schedule) scores below matched-plus-cue. Or a far-framed schedule where a permanent cue (r 1.0) beats flat. Either would show the cue is not just a backup for fixed framing. The rule is also wrong if a cue at 0.6 ever passes flat once the 0.7 ceiling on c is raised.
- Break scenario: Matched framing with imperfect tracking: d = I/10 + 0.25 error, or d lagging one beat behind severity, across all four cue settings and the four schedules. Prediction: the cue effect stops being 0.0000 and "match first, cue as backup" turns into "do both". Also run close framing (d 0.3) against flat with cue 0.3 over a ceiling-heavy schedule. That is the one case the "mild still beats flat" prediction might not survive, because the prediction was fitted to a single observed winner.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-17 · digest 245757849f0e
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__distance-dial-makes-the-decaying-cue-redundant-except-for-mild-beats.py
- Prediction: Under matched distance the cue changes totals by under 0.01; under far framing mild scores under 0.05 and flat wins; a cue at 0.6 lifts far-framed mild by more than 3 times without passing flat; and under close framing with cue 0.3 the mild schedule still beats flat.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS matched-distance cue effect 0.0000 (redundant); far framing mild 0.047 -> 0.54 with r0.6 cue (11.5x, flat still ahead 4.58); close r0.3 winner mild
- Scenarios: 1) matched framing at four cue settings; 2) far framing without a cue; 3) far framing with cues at 1.0, 0.6, 0.3; 4) BREAK: close framing with a fast-decaying cue (0.3), where I predicted the cue stops helping; 5) close framing with a permanent cue

## E414 — crossword most constrained slot first
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][testing][sandbox][puzzles]
- What: Seeding the CROSSWORD-CONSTRUCTION domain, a node-counting sandbox filled an open 5x5 grid (10 slots) from a 493-word list in two orders. Reading order cost 5.1x, 10.1x and 15.2x the nodes of a fewest-matching-words-first rule at 45, 85 and 165 words, and at 495 words it ran out of a 300,000-node budget while the other rule finished in 5,690 nodes.
- Why built: A new domain has nothing to detect gaps against; a real task (filling a word square) gives a cheap deterministic measurement that a first kernel can rest on.
- Design: Slots are the five rows and five columns; a slot's candidates come from a regex over the letters already placed. Search is plain backtracking with a node counter and a 300,000-node cap. The word list is a sorted embedded list of common five-letter words, with a planted symmetric square (heart, ember, abuse, resin, trend) added in the planted runs and removed in the no-planted runs.
- Got right: The fewest-matches rule never used more nodes than reading order in any of 8 runs, found the planted fill every time, and its advantage grew with the list size; on lists with no fill it proved that faster by 5.5x to 20.1x.
- Where/why it failed: At 493 words the reading-order runs hit the cap, so the 52.7x ratio is only a lower bound. The grid is fully open with duplicates allowed, the list is small and common-word only, and only two orders were tried, so nothing here covers black squares, symmetry or themed entries. The first draft of the sandbox disallowed duplicate words, which made the symmetric planted square impossible, so duplicates were allowed on purpose.
- Fix: Choose the next slot by the fewest dictionary matches for its current pattern, count nodes against a fixed budget, and report no fill when the budget or the search is exhausted.
- Why this fix: A slot with few matches meets a dead end early, so fewer crossings are committed before the search backs out, whereas reading order commits letters that later slots cannot match.
- Rule of thumb: In grid filling, pick the slot with the fewest matching words next and put a node budget on the search; reading-order fill grew from 5x to over 50x more nodes as the list went from 45 to 495 words in this open 5x5 test.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT PASS, numbers above). The word list is hand-written and the result is for an open 5x5 grid only.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- ZaneGPT verdict: weak — the direction is plausible and matches standard constraint-solving practice, but "5x to over 50x" is one deterministic instance and the stated PASS was measured on only 8 runs, 4 of them planted, 3 of them no-fill, and 1 a break run that showed the budget cap rather than a test of the rule.
- Hidden assumption: Fewest-matches ordering wins because it prunes better in general, when this test may only show it escapes a planted-square path that the sorted list and reading-order fill happen to make pathological. Its 5.1x to 52.7x ratios come from one sorted word list, one planted solution, one grid shape, and no repeated shuffles.
- Would prove it wrong: Rerun with shuffled word lists, many random planted squares, and unplanted lists that do have solutions, and then the median fixed/MRV ratio comes out near 1x. A single run where reading order beats MRV on nodes would also count, since "every size" claims a floor, not an average. Any case where counting the regex scan used to rank slots makes MRV cost more in total work than it saves in nodes would also refute it.
- Break scenario: A dense list with many five-letter words and no planted square, where the grid has about 10^3 valid fills. Reading order finds a fill within a few hundred nodes, while MRV spends its time recounting candidates for every open slot at each step. Then repeat on a 7x7 grid, where the 5x5 result may not carry over.
- Checked by: ZaneGPT · separate agent (brain check) · 2026-10-17 · digest fc1ab01779a3
