- Prediction: The fewest-matches rule uses fewer nodes than reading order at every list size and the ratio grows with list size; a list with no possible fill gives larger counts for both orders but the same ordering.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS MRV nodes <= fixed in all 8 runs; fixed/mrv ratio on planted grids [5.1, 10.1, 15.2, 52.7] grows with list size; fixed order exhausted its 300000-node budget on 2 full-list runs while MRV finished
- Scenarios: 1) planted fill at 45, 85, 165 and 495 words; 2) no planted fill at 40, 80, 160 words (exhaustive no-fill proof); 3) BREAK: full list where reading order might still keep up (it hit the budget instead)

## E413 — stale engine sidecar hides fatigue and flips reskin pick
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][comedy][model][sandbox]
- What: When the choice between reskinning the best comic engine and a diverse batch counts repeats through a hand-kept variant-to-engine sidecar, one missing reskin name already makes the stale count hide fatigue and wrongly pick reskin at 37 of 300 fatigue levels; with 2 of 8 missing it is 99 of 300.
- Why built: Edge pass (next path, since the first target was already drafted) joining the recut kernel, the lesson that reskinning the best engine beats a diverse batch only while fatigue is low, and the lesson that a hand-kept sidecar drifts silently.
- Design: Eight reskins of the best engine (strength 1.0, k-th repeat worth strength times one minus f to the k) against eight engines of strengths 1.0 down to 0.55. The believed reskin value treats names missing from the sidecar as fresh engines with no fatigue. Sidecar coverage 8, 7, 6, 4 and 0 of 8; fatigue swept 0 to 0.30 in 300 steps.
- Got right: Full coverage (or grouping by an engine field on each record) never mispicked; every wrong pick lay above the true break-even fatigue of 0.101 and always toward reskin, never away from it.
- Where/why it failed: I expected the error to grow steadily with staleness; it grew from 37 to 99 to 199 wrong levels as coverage fell from 7 to 6 to 4, then stopped at 199 for 4 and 0, because the believed value already beats the diverse batch at every fatigue level once about half the names are missing.
- Fix: Group repeats by an engine field carried on each variant record (derive the count) or fail when a variant name is absent from the map; never count a missing name as a new engine.
- Why this fix: A missing name is read as a fresh engine, which removes exactly the fatigue the rule depends on, and the error is invisible at low fatigue where both choices agree.
- Rule of thumb: Count engine repeats from a field on each variant, not a sidecar; one missing name of eight cost a wrong reskin pick over 37 of 300 fatigue levels, and half missing about doubled that.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the engine strengths and the 0.101 break-even are my own toy numbers, not the 3.4% of the earlier lesson, which used different strengths.
- Composed: ideas:GAME-ADS/iteration/concept-then-variants-ranked-on-ipm-times-early-retention/decompose-the-winner-and-recut, brainwork/E361, collective-reference/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Distinct from: sidecar-drift-flips-ipm-d1-winner-only-when-winner-renamed/E1 - this is the engine-repeat count behind the reskin-versus-diverse decision, with a coverage sweep, not an IPM-times-D1 winner flip.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__stale-engine-sidecar-hides-fatigue-and-flips-reskin-pick.py
- Prediction: Assumption: wrongness grows with how stale the sidecar is. Expected wrong picks only above the break-even fatigue and rising with missing names; the rising part held up to 4 of 8 missing and then flattened at 199 of 300, so the expectation was only partly right.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS stale sidecar over-picks reskin only above break-even f*=0.101: wrong fatigue values out of 300 = cover7 37, cover6 99, cover4 199, cover0 199, cover8 or derived 0; one missing name already costs max regret 0.080
- Scenarios: 1) full coverage; 2) 7 of 8 covered; 3) 6 of 8; 4) 4 of 8; 5) none covered (built to BREAK the rising-with-staleness expectation)

## E412 — sidecar d1 drift needs derived join for ipm d1 rank
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Ranking ad variants on IPM times D1 with D1 read from a hand-kept sidecar keyed by variant name silently picks the wrong variant whenever the true winner is renamed or recut; a join derived from the record holding IPM never errs.
- Why built: Kernel pass composing the IPM-times-D1 recut path with the sidecar-drift lesson from collective-reference, to see whether the drift matters for ad ranking.
- Design: Five variants with fixed IPM and D1; score by IPM x D1 from a sidecar dict vs from the joined record. Scenarios: no drift, rename a non-winner, rename the winner (built to break), default D1 of zero vs population mean, plus 400 randomized trials renaming one variant each.
- Got right: Renaming a non-winner left the pick unchanged, so drift is invisible in most spot checks; a key-diff check between ranked names and sidecar keys caught every rename.
- Where/why it failed: Winner renamed with a stale sidecar dropped it to a default D1 (zero or the mean) and the pick flipped in both default cases; 69 of 69 winner-renamed trials were wrong and 0 of the other 331.
- Fix: Derive D1 from the same record as IPM (one join) or fail loudly when ranked names and sidecar keys differ; never default a missing D1.
- Why this fix: The error only appears for the one variant that matters most, so only an explicit key check or a single source of truth can see it.
- Rule of thumb: In an IPM-times-D1 ranking, drift in a hand-kept D1 sidecar flips the pick only when the winner is renamed, so join D1 from the IPM record or assert the keys match.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the toy numbers are invented, not real ad data.
- Composed: ideas:GAME-ADS/concept-then-variants-ranked-on-ipm-times-early-retention, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, collective-reference/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Distinct from: sidecar-drift-flips-ipm-d1-winner-only-when-winner-renamed/E1 - adds the default-value comparison (zero vs mean) and the key-diff guard, with randomized trial counts.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__sidecar-d1-drift-needs-derived-join-for-ipm-d1-rank.py
- Prediction: Assumption: sidecar drift matters generally. Expected the pick to be wrong only when the winner is renamed (about 1 in 5 random trials), never for other renames, and derived join always right; a wrong pick on a non-winner rename would disprove it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS sidecar wrong only when winner renamed (69/69 winner trials, 69/400 overall); derived join 0 errors
- Scenarios: 1) no drift; 2) rename non-winner; 3) rename winner with default 0 and default mean (built to BREAK); 4) derived join after rename; 5) key-diff check; 6) 400 randomized trials
- Link: scheduled brain train auto pass 1; session_01SfPeSfBRAUqLBZr3G96y7j

## E411 — promise cap pre filter vs cue handicap in recut pick
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][film][model][sandbox]
- What: In 2000 seeded toy recut sheets, capping cold-open promise at delivery and ranking survivors on IPM did not protect the pick from hand-edited cue errors: it changed the pick less often (496 vs 714 sheets) but lost value against the remap truth in more sheets (960 vs 714), because the cap alone already disagreed with IPM times D1 in 606 sheets.
- Why built: Gap pass joining the cap-promise-at-delivery lesson, the IPM-times-D1 ranking lesson and the finding that hand-edited cue tables flipped a recut winner, to see whether the cap makes the pick robust to cue defects.
- Design: Six recuts per sheet with promise 0.2-1.0, hook 0.8-1.4, 0 to 4 cues off (each cuts IPM by 10%); the game delivers 0.5 and D1 falls 0.6 per unit of promise above it. Truth is the remap pick (no cues off) on IPM times D1; compared hand-edited picks under ranking A (IPM times D1) and ranking B (cap at delivery, then IPM). Deterministic generator, 2000 sheets.
- Got right: Ranking B did change the pick less often under hand edits (496 against 714 sheets), so a cap does shrink the field the defects can reorder.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that B would flip more often was wrong, but the robustness it suggested is false: B lost value in 960 sheets against 714 for A, since a cap-then-IPM pick drops high-hook recuts that IPM times D1 would have kept, and cue handicaps then pick among the survivors.
- Fix: Keep one-timeline remap and a cue check as the cue-sync guard, and rank on IPM times D1; use the promise cap only as a pre-recut check, not as a replacement for the second rank factor.
- Why this fix: The cap removes an axis the D1 term already prices, so it trades a lower flip count for a worse pick on both clean and hand-edited sheets.
- Rule of thumb: A promise cap with IPM-only ranking is not a cheaper guard against cue errors; it disagreed with IPM times D1 in 606 of 2000 clean sheets and lost value in 960 hand-edited ones, so keep remap and the D1 term.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the penalty per cue, promise and hook ranges and D1 slope are assumed toy values.
- Composed: cold-open-promise-matches-delivery/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, hand-edited-cue-tables-skew-recut-ranking-remap-does-not/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__promise-cap-pre-filter-vs-cue-handicap-in-recut-pick.py
- Prediction: Assumption: cue errors are independent of promise. Expected cap-then-IPM to change the pick more often than IPM times D1 under hand edits; refuted, it changed it less often (496 vs 714), though it lost value more often.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL hand-edited cues change the pick in 714/2000 sheets for IPM*D1 ranking and 496/2000 for cap-then-IPM; cap-then-IPM already disagrees with the IPM*D1 pick in 606/2000 sheets with remap
- Scenarios: 1) IPM times D1 ranking, remap vs hand edits; 2) cap-then-IPM ranking, remap vs hand edits; 3) cap-then-IPM vs IPM times D1 with remap only (built to BREAK the cap-as-guard idea)

## E410 — promise cap check needs derived from game link not any noun
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Capping a cold open's promise at what the game delivers works only if the check column counts promise by a link to a game mechanic; a column that counts any new noun treats decorative props as over-promise and keeps 0.84-0.88 of the best value, while the derived column keeps 1.00.
- Why built: Gap pass joining the cap-promise-at-delivery lesson with the earlier finding that an any-new-noun check column mislabels beats, to see whether the same column flaw hurts the promise cap.
- Design: Variants differ in mechanics shown (0-5), decorative nouns (0-4) and hook (1.0 or 1.2); the game delivers 2 mechanics; true value is IPM times a D1 that falls with mechanics beyond delivery. The cap is applied with a naive column (mechanics plus decorative nouns) or a derived column (mechanics only), then the top IPM survivor is picked. Four sheets: flat D1 with no decoration, linear, steep, and a cliff (built to break).
- Got right: On decorated sheets with a penalty, the derived column picked the true best (2 mechanics, most decoration) in all three; the naive column dropped every decorated variant and picked a plain one.
- Where/why it failed: With flat D1 and no decoration both columns kept only 0.62 of the best value because capping at delivery is wrong there (promise costs nothing), so the cap itself needs a penalty to exist.
- Fix: Define promise in the check column as elements derived from a game mechanic, and ignore decorative nouns; apply the cap only when D1 actually falls with the promise gap.
- Why this fix: Retention responds to unmet mechanics, not to props, so a column that cannot tell them apart penalises variants for something the game never fails to deliver.
- Rule of thumb: Cap cold-open promise at delivery only with a derived-from-game count of mechanics; an any-noun count cut value to 0.84-0.88 of best once decoration existed.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the constants and the split between mechanics and decoration are assumed toy values, not measured ad data.
- Composed: cold-open-promise-matches-delivery/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1
- Picked-by: new-half

- Prediction: Assumption: decorative nouns do not affect retention. Expected the naive column to land under 0.97 of the best value on every decorated sheet and the derived column at or above 0.97; a naive ratio of 0.97 or more would disprove it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS promise cap on any-noun column keeps 0.88/0.88/0.84 of the true-best value vs 1.00/1.00/1.00 for derived-from-game column on decorated sheets; identical with no decoration
- Scenarios: 1) flat D1, no decoration; 2) linear penalty with decoration; 3) steep penalty with decoration; 4) cliff penalty with heavy decoration (built to BREAK)
- Link: scheduled brain train auto pass 5; session_01SfPeSfBRAUqLBZr3G96y7j
- Audited: 2026-10-18 · fail · Read the entry and its stored sandbox, ran it (PASS, 0.88/0.88/0.84 versus 1.00 reproduced exactly). The model computes the picks, but the answer is partly built in: the true D1 depends only on mechanics beyond delivery, so the derived column is literally the variable the ground truth penalises, and decoration is given zero effect on retention by construction (the Prediction states this as an assumption, the Rule of thumb does not). I mutated the fixture so each decorative noun also lowers D1 by 0.02, 0.05 and 0.10 (linear penalty 0.06, same grid): the naive any-noun column then keeps 1.00 of best value while the derived column falls to 0.91, 0.57 and 0.19, so the ranking reverses. The Rule of thumb as written (cap only with a derived-from-game count) therefore covers more than was tested; it holds only when decoration is harmless to retention. ## E409 — monotone closeness cap misses mild harm up close
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: Under a two-sided dark-humor rule (severe harm needs distance, mild harm is funnier up close), a harm-ceiling card that only falls with victim closeness stayed safe (0 unsafe beats in 400 cases) but gave up 32% of the value a two-sided card kept (4302.7 vs 6307.2), losing most at distant, close victims (617.0 vs 1161.6).
- Why built: Kernel pass joining the severe-versus-mild harm kernel, the matched-distance escalation lesson and my earlier closeness-aware harm-ceiling card, to see whether the closeness term still holds when mild harm wants closeness.
- Design: Value per beat: severe harm (7 and up) is h times d over 10 and unsafe below distance 7; mild harm (3 or less) is h times closeness; middle harm needs distance 4. A six-beat go-big schedule is capped by no card, a monotone card (distance times one minus 0.6 closeness) or a two-sided card (severe gated by distance only). 400 seeded cases, four slices.
- Got right: Both cards had zero unsafe beats against 702 with no card, so a ceiling of either shape is enough for safety; the two-sided card won every slice on value.
- Where/why it failed: I expected the monotone card to leave unsafe beats at near, low-closeness cases; it did not, because in this model mild harm is never unsafe, only flat. The real cost of the monotone card was lost value: at far, close victims it capped severe beats the kernel says are funniest.
- Fix: Write the card as two clauses, severe harm gated by distance and mild harm scored by closeness, rather than one closeness-penalised ceiling.
- Why this fix: Closeness lowers tolerance for severe harm but raises it for mild harm, so a single monotone term gives up the case where both close and distant severe harm win.
- Rule of thumb: A single closeness-penalised harm ceiling is safe but cost 32% of the value once mild harm benefits from closeness; split the card into a severe-harm distance gate and a mild-harm closeness score.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the value functions and thresholds are assumed toy shapes following the cited kernel, not measured audience data.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/dark-humor/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, harm-ceiling-card-needs-closeness-term-to-escalate-safely
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__monotone-closeness-cap-misses-mild-harm-up-close.py
- Prediction: Assumption: closeness only lowers what a victim tolerates. Expected the monotone card to leave unsafe beats at near, low-closeness cases and to lose value at far, close ones; the first expectation was refuted (0 unsafe), the second held.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS both cards 0 unsafe; two-sided keeps score 6307.2 vs monotone 4302.7 (47% more); at far+close victims 1161.6 vs 617.0
- Scenarios: 1) no card; 2) monotone closeness card; 3) two-sided card; 4) slice of far, close victims (built to BREAK the monotone card); 5) slice of near victims

## E408 — hunting tooth pair spreads wear across gcd classes
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gear-trains][mechanics][model][sandbox]
- What: Meshing a gear pair tooth by tooth showed that the contact pairs number lcm(a,b) and a single chipped pinion tooth strikes only b divided by gcd(a,b) gear teeth: 40 of 40 for 17 and 40 teeth, 2 of 40 for 20 and 40, 7 of 42 for 18 and 42.
- Why built: Seed for the new gear-trains domain from a real design choice, picking tooth counts so wear spreads; no adjacent kernel in canon covers it, so this is isolated.
- Design: Step the mesh one tooth at a time (pinion tooth i mod a against gear tooth i mod b), stopping at the first repeated pair; count distinct pairs, the period, and the gear teeth met by pinion tooth 0. Six pairs, plus a fix case that adds one pinion tooth.
- Got right: Brute-force counts matched the formulas for all six pairs, including the near-hunting 18 and 42 (gcd 6); adding one tooth to 20 against 40 gave 21 against 40 with a chipped tooth meeting 40 of 40.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed in this model; the untested part is real wear, which I assumed follows contact count alone, ignoring load, lubrication and tooth stiffness.
- Fix: When wear evenness matters, choose a coprime tooth count rather than the exact ratio, shifting by one tooth if needed.
- Why this fix: Coprime counts are the only case where every pinion tooth meets every gear tooth, so a defect is shared instead of repeated on the same few mates.
- Rule of thumb: Pick tooth counts with gcd 1 so a chipped tooth meets every mate; with gcd g it meets only b/g of them (2 of 40 at 20 and 40).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; real wear is not modelled, so the wear benefit is an assumption from contact counts only.
- Composed: ideas:GEAR-TRAINS/tooth-counts/hunting-tooth-pair/pick-coprime-counts-so-a-chipped-tooth-meets-every-mate
- Picked-by: new-domain
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__hunting-tooth-pair-spreads-wear-across-gcd-classes.py
- Prediction: Assumption: wear follows contact count only. Expected 680 pairs and 40 of 40 gear teeth for 17 and 40, 40 pairs and 2 of 40 for 20 and 40, 126 pairs and 7 of 42 for 18 and 42; any brute count differing from lcm and b over gcd would disprove it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS brute-force meshing matches pairs = lcm(a,b) and chipped-tooth spread = b/gcd for 6 pairs; coprime 17/40 spreads over 40 of 40 gear teeth, 20/40 over 2; 20->21 against 40 restores 40 of 40
- Scenarios: 1) coprime pair 17 and 40; 2) equal-factor pair 20 and 40 (built to BREAK the even-wear assumption); 3) near-hunting 18 and 42; 4) 19/38, 21/22, 24/36; 5) one-tooth fix

## E407 — harm ceiling card needs closeness term to escalate safely
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][model][sandbox]
- What: A rule-card harm ceiling set to the framing's distance keeps a go-big escalation safe for distant victims (0 unsafe beats) but leaves 582 unsafe beats for close victims; a ceiling that also scales down with victim closeness removed all unsafe beats in the toy model.
- Why built: Edge pass composing the benign-violation kernel, the matched-distance escalation lesson and the write-the-rules-first kernel to answer the open question of whether a stated harm ceiling lets a sketch escalate safely to the framing's distance.
- Design: 300 seeded cases of framing distance 2-10 and victim closeness 0-1; true tolerance is distance times one minus 0.6 times closeness; a six-beat go-big schedule capped by three policies: none, ceiling at distance, ceiling at distance and closeness.
- Got right: The ceiling at distance alone had zero unsafe beats at closeness 0 (1745 funny score), so the card works when the victim is far; the no-card schedule had 1103 unsafe beats.
- Where/why it failed: Ceiling-only still had 942 unsafe beats, 582 of them at closeness 0.75 or more, because the card named distance but not who is hurt.
- Fix: Write the ceiling as a function of distance and victim closeness (the card should state who is hurt and how near), not distance alone.
- Why this fix: Tolerance falls as the audience identifies with the victim, so a distance-only cap is right only at one end of that range.
- Rule of thumb: A harm ceiling equal to the framing's distance escalates safely only for distant victims; add a closeness term, or close-victim beats still land as unsafe.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and reading its counts. The tolerance formula is an assumed toy model, so the closeness-aware cap matching it exactly is by construction.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__harm-ceiling-card-needs-closeness-term-to-escalate-safely.py
- Prediction: Assumption: distance is the only thing the ceiling needs. Expected ceiling-only to have zero unsafe beats for distant victims and more than zero for close ones; zero unsafe beats at close victims would have disproved it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS ceiling-only unsafe beats 942 (far victims 0, close victims 582); closeness-aware ceiling 0 unsafe; no-card 1103
- Scenarios: 1) no card; 2) ceiling at distance, distant victims; 3) ceiling at distance, close victims (built to BREAK); 4) ceiling at distance and closeness

## E406 — bookbinding imposition from fold simulation
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [bookbinding][imposition][model][sandbox]
- What: Simulating the folds of a sheet (right over left, bottom over top, mirroring each layer) and reading the stack top-down gives a valid page imposition for 8, 16 and 32 pages; the 16-page back came out 16 1 4 13 / 9 8 5 12, matching the standard octavo layout.
- Why built: Seed for the new bookbinding domain, from the real task of laying out a folded signature, replacing a memorised page-order table with a computation.
- Design: Grid of panels with a stack per cell; each fold mirrors the folded half, reverses its layer order and toggles face (and rotation for the vertical fold); the final stack read top-down assigns pages 2t+1 and 2t+2 to a layer's two faces. Checks: every page once, each leaf's two faces on one panel, and a page-N/page-1 pair adjacent.
- Got right: All pages appeared once at 8, 16 and 32 pages, leaf faces paired as odd and even on the same panel, and N+1 sum pairs appeared across creases (2 of 2, 4 of 6, 8 of 12 adjacent front pairs).

## E405 — two stage recut screen recovers ipm d1 gain
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic sandbox comparing one-stage IPM times D1 ranking of eight cold-open recuts against a two-stage screen (cheap IPM screen, then re-test of the top few at a larger budget).
- Why built: Train loop 2 pass 5 re-picked the film, rank-IPM-times-D1 and concept-then-variants triple; the earlier lesson said to confirm at two budgets, and this checks what a two-stage version buys per impression.
- Design: Eight recuts with promise 0 to 1, installs per impression 0.02 + 0.06 x promise, D1 falling 0.8 per unit of promise above a delivery of 0.4; 300 seeded runs; screen at 300 impressions each on IPM, then top 2 or top 4 re-tested at 3000 on IPM times D1.
- Got right: Two-stage with top 4 reached 98 percent of the best recut at 14400 impressions, the same as one-stage at 3000 each (98 percent) which costs 24000.
- Where/why it failed: Two-stage with top 2 reached only 96 percent at 8400 impressions, barely above one-stage at 300 each (95 percent at 2400), because an IPM-only screen tends to keep the high-promise recuts that D1 later penalises, so the gain is small here.
- Fix: Screen on IPM to prune, but re-test a wide enough top set (about half) on IPM times D1; do not shrink the confirmation set to 2.
- Why this fix: Top 4 recovers the full one-stage quality at about 60 percent of the cost, while top 2 saves more but gives little over the cheap single pass.
- Rule of thumb: In this toy model a two-stage recut test (IPM screen, then top half on IPM times D1) matches the large-budget pick at about 60 percent of its impressions (14400 vs 24000), while a top-2 confirmation barely beats a cheap one-stage pass.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the install and retention curves are my toy model, not real ad data.

## E404 — rule card ceiling must track a shifting distance
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][narrative][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox testing whether a rule card's harm ceiling, fixed at sketch start, still works when the framing distance shifts mid-sketch (rising 2 to 4, dropping 4 to 2).
- Why built: Train pass 2 re-picked the benign-violation, escalation-distance and rule-card triple; the first sandbox only held distance constant, so this edge probes a shifting distance.
- Design: Go-big severities 1,2,3,4,5,5 over 6 beats; a beat is funny iff 1<=severity<=distance at that beat; the card clamps severity to its ceiling, either fixed at the opening value or rewritten when the distance shifts.
- Got right: Rewriting the ceiling to track distance scored 17 on a rise and 12 on a drop with all 6 beats funny; steady distance 3 with ceiling 3 scored 15.
- Where/why it failed: A fixed ceiling of 2 under-used a rising distance (11 vs 17); a fixed ceiling of 4 on a dropping distance left only 3 of 6 beats funny (score 6 vs 12).
- Fix: Treat the card's ceiling as a function of the current framing distance and rewrite it at every reframe, not once at the start.
- Why this fix: Both failures come from the same stale ceiling, too low wastes headroom and too high breaks the benign half of benign-violation.
- Rule of thumb: In this model a rule card's harm ceiling must be re-derived whenever the framing distance shifts; a fixed opening ceiling loses headroom on a rise and funny beats on a drop.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the funny-beat rule is my own toy model, so real audiences are untested.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags
- Picked-by: new-half
- Distinct from: 2026-10-17 rule-card-ceiling-must-equal-framing-distance covers a constant distance and card order; this one finds the ceiling goes stale when distance shifts mid-sketch.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__rule-card-ceiling-must-track-a-shifting-distance.py
- Prediction: Assumed a static ceiling is enough; I expected rise static=2 to score about 11 vs 17 rewritten, and the drop case (the one built to break it) to lose funny beats with static=4.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS static ceiling under-uses a rising distance and breaks on a dropping one; rewriting tracks both; rise 11 vs 17, drop 6 (3 funny) vs 12 (6 funny).
- Scenarios: 1) rise static; 2) rise rewritten; 3) drop static (built to break it); 4) drop rewritten; 5) steady distance control

## E403 — rule card ceiling must equal framing distance

- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][narrative][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox composing benign-violation (a beat needs a violation and an ok-reason at once), escalation-needs-matching-distance, and the write-rules-first card, with the card's harm ceiling clamping a go-big severity schedule.
- Why built: Train pass 1 picked the benign-violation path plus its untested companion, the rule card, to see whether a stated harm ceiling lets a sketch escalate to the framing's distance safely.
- Design: 6 beats, go-big severities 1,2,3,4,5,5; a beat is funny iff 1<=severity<=distance and the frame precedes it; the card clamps severity to its ceiling. Distances 2,3,4; variants no card, mild, card=d first, card=d late, card=d+1.
- Got right: Card with ceiling equal to distance, written first, scored 11/15/18 at d=2/3/4 against 3/6/10 for uncarded go-big and a flat 10 for mild, with all 6 beats funny.

- Why this fix: The clamp only protects beats when ceiling <= distance, and the frame only counts for beats after it, so ceiling and order are both load-bearing.
- Rule of thumb: Within this toy model, set the rule card's harm ceiling equal to the framing distance and write it first; an over-high ceiling is as bad as no card.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the funny-beat rule is my own model, not measured audience data.

## E402 — rule card ceiling misestimate costs more high than low
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][narrative][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox testing what happens when the rule card's harm ceiling is a mis-estimate of the true framing distance, by error of minus 2 to plus 2.
- Why built: Train loop 2 pass 2 re-picked the benign-violation, escalation-distance and rule-card triple; earlier sandboxes assumed the card knew the distance exactly, so this probes an imperfect estimate.
- Design: Go-big severities 1,2,3,4,5,5; ceiling = true distance + error for true distances 2,3,4; a beat is funny iff 1 <= min(severity, ceiling) <= true distance; totals over the three distances.
- Got right: An exact ceiling made all 18 beats funny for a total score of 44.
- Where/why it failed: Underestimating by 1 still got 18 of 18 funny beats but a score of 32; underestimating by 2 scored 17 with 12 funny. Overestimating by 1 or 2 scored 19 with only 9 of 18 funny, because every beat above the true distance fails the benign half.
- Fix: When unsure of the framing distance, set the card ceiling at the low end of the estimate; a too-low ceiling loses headroom while a too-high one loses the joke.
- Why this fix: Underestimates cost score but keep each beat benign, whereas overestimates break beats outright (9 of 18 lost).
- Rule of thumb: Err low on a rule card's harm ceiling: one step under costs about 27 percent of score (44 to 32) while one step over costs about 57 percent (44 to 19) and half the funny beats.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the funny-beat rule is my own toy model.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags
- Picked-by: new-half
- Distinct from: 2026-10-17__rule-card-ceiling-must-equal-framing-distance/E1 assumes an exact ceiling; this one measures the asymmetric cost of a wrong ceiling.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__rule-card-ceiling-misestimate-costs-more-high-than-low.py
- Prediction: Assumed errors cost symmetrically-ish and that more overestimate is strictly worse; I expected over +1 below under -1 and +2 below +1. The strict +2 below +1 part was wrong (they tie at 19, saturated), the asymmetry held.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS exact ceiling scores 44; underestimating by 1 scores 32, overestimating by 1 scores 19
- Scenarios: 1) error -2; 2) error -1; 3) exact; 4) BREAK: error +1; 5) error +2; each over d=2,3,4
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 2; session_01PTu5uBJqYTUhgm91RqrjQ3

## E401 — ladder four to one rule sets reach and length
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [ladder-safety][geometry][sandbox]
- What: Seed of a ladder-safety domain: the 4-to-1 setting rule (one foot out per four feet of working height) is a single fixed angle, and it fixes the minimum ladder length for a given landing height.
- Why built: Train newdomain pass picked a domain absent from the kernel list; the real scenario is placing an extension ladder against a roof edge or landing.
- Design: Compute base-out = height/4, the angle as atan of 4, and the minimum ladder length as the hypotenuse of (height + 3 ft handhold extension) and base-out, for heights of 8, 12, 16 and 20 feet; test a 16 ft stock ladder against landings of 8 to 16 feet.
- Got right: The angle is 75.96 degrees at every height, because the rule fixes a ratio, so a protractor-style check does not depend on the job.
- Where/why it failed: The 3 ft extension makes the minimum length 11.18, 15.30, 19.42 and 23.54 ft for the four heights; a 16 ft stock ladder serves a landing only up to 12 ft and fails at 13, 14 and 16 ft, so the common instinct that a 16 ft ladder reaches a 16 ft roof is wrong.
- Fix: Pick the ladder from the landing height plus the 3 ft extension and the base-out hypotenuse, not from the landing height alone, then set the base out at one quarter of the working height.
- Why this fix: The required length is the hypotenuse of the extended height and the base-out, so it always exceeds the landing height by more than the 3 ft extension.
- Rule of thumb: Set a ladder at 75.96 degrees (1 out per 4 up) and size it as the hypotenuse of landing height plus 3 ft and height over 4; a 16 ft ladder safely serves only 12 ft landings.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the arithmetic sandbox; the 4-to-1 rule and 3 ft extension are commonly cited safety guidance I did not check against a standard.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__ladder-four-to-one-rule-sets-reach-and-length.py
- Prediction: Assumed pure arithmetic; I expected the angle constant at 75.96 degrees and a 16 ft ladder to fail at a 14 ft landing, and the 16 ft landing was the case built to break the common belief.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 4-to-1 is a fixed 75.96 degree angle at every height; a 16ft ladder serves a landing up to 12ft with a 3ft extension, not 16ft
- Scenarios: 1) 8 ft landing; 2) 12 ft landing; 3) 13 ft landing; 4) 14 ft landing; 5) BREAK: 16 ft landing on a 16 ft stock ladder

## E400 — drain fall accumulates over the run check joist depth
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: local/brainwork
- Tags: [plumbing][geometry][sandbox]
- What: Seed of a new plumbing domain: the total fall of a gravity drain is run times slope, so the run limit comes from the vertical room available at the far end, not from the pipe.
- Why built: Train newdomain pass picked plumbing, which had no kernel domain; the real scenario is routing a drain through a floor joist space with a code-style minimum fall of 1/4 inch per foot.
- Design: Compute total fall = run feet x slope for runs of 8, 20, 37, 38 and 40 feet against 9.25 inch and 5.5 inch voids, then try a flatter 1/8 inch per foot slope as the break case.
- Got right: Runs of 8, 20 and 37 feet fit a 9.25 inch void (2, 5 and 9.25 inches of fall), so the maximum run there is exactly 37 feet.
- Where/why it failed: A 38 foot run needs 9.5 inches and fails, a 40 foot run needs 10 inches and fails a 5.5 inch void, and the flat 1/8 inch slope fits 70 feet geometrically but breaks the minimum slope, so fit alone is not an acceptance test.
- Fix: Before routing, compute max run = available vertical room divided by the minimum slope, then add a vent, cleanout or re-route when the run exceeds it.
- Why this fix: The fall accumulates linearly with distance, so a check on room per foot catches the failure before the pipe is cut.
- Rule of thumb: Check run times minimum slope against the vertical room first (37 ft max in a 9.25 in void at 1/4 in per ft) and never recover a long run by flattening the slope.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the arithmetic sandbox; the 1/4 inch per foot figure is a commonly cited code value I did not check against a local code.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__drain-fall-accumulates-over-the-run-check-joist-depth.py
- Prediction: Assumed the limit is purely arithmetic; I expected 37 ft to fit and 38 ft to fail at 9.25 inches, and the 1/8 slope case (built to break the rule) to fit geometrically but to be invalid.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS max run in a 9.25in joist is 37ft at 1/4 in/ft; 38ft and any 40ft run in a 5.5in void fail; flatter slope fits but is below minimum
- Scenarios: 1) 8ft in 9.25in; 2) 20ft in 9.25in; 3) 37ft in 9.25in; 4) 38ft in 9.25in; 5) 40ft in 5.5in; 6) BREAK: 1/8 slope over 70ft

## E399 — age threshold best at tolerance fourth payload
- Date: 2026-09-30
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: Re-verified that the best age threshold equals the payload tolerance regardless of wrong-press weight, on a new tolerance (4 instead of 7) and two lag mixes (uniform and skewed).
- Why built: The asymmetric-wrong-press-cost result and the combined cost-step result each came from one sandbox; a new tolerance and lag distribution raise independence.
- Design: Deterministic cost model, no RNG: a press with lag L is good iff L is at most 4; gate at threshold t accepts iff L is at most t; cost = weight * wrong + lost, weights 0, 0.1, 1, 10, thresholds 0-12, lag counts uniform (10 each) or skewed (lag+1).
- Got right: The argmin was exactly t=4 for every positive weight under both mixes; at weight 0 thresholds 4-12 all tied at cost 0 while any lower threshold cost more.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing refuted; the weight only scaled the penalty of a wrong threshold (cost at t=12 was 8, 80, 800 for uniform weights 0.1, 1, 10).
- Fix: Set the age threshold at the payload tolerance, not from the wrong-press cost, and prefer dropping the filter when the tolerance is unknown.
- Why this fix: Each lag is decided independently, so the cost minimum lies at the tolerance boundary and the lag mix and weight cannot move it.
- Rule of thumb: Reweighting the lag histogram cannot move an age gate's optimum because each lag is judged on its own; uniform and skewed mixes both bottomed out at the tolerance, so measure the tolerance, not the traffic.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and observing the numbers below. The per-lag independence makes the argmin close to true by construction, so this confirms the earlier result on new parameters and does not test real input latency.
- Composed: local__age-cutoff-roll-up/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-09-30__age-threshold-best-at-tolerance-fourth-payload.py
- Prediction: Argmin threshold is 4 for weights 0.1, 1, 10 under both lag mixes; at weight 0 thresholds 4 through 12 tie at zero cost and lower thresholds cost more.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS argmin t==4 for w in 0.1/1/10 under both mixes; w=0 ties 4..12; uniform cost at t=12 was 8.0/80/800.
- Scenarios: 1) uniform lags, weights 0.1/1/10; 2) skewed lags, same weights; 3) weight 0 tie set; 4) threshold 12 accepting everything, built to break the optimum claim with a large wrong-press cost.

## E398 — age gate vs validity ramp dwell fourth angle
- Date: 2026-09-30
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: Re-verified from a ramp-dwell schedule (dwells 1..20, 1600 presses at ages 1-8) that no age gate threshold matches a validity guard: every threshold either executes stale presses or drops valid ones.
- Why built: The age-gate-versus-validity edges rested on square-wave and fallback sandboxes only; a ramp schedule is a fourth independent angle.
- Design: Deterministic model, no RNG: state changes at triangular-number ticks; a press is valid iff no change happened between sight and press; sweep age gate 0..8, count wrong (accepted but invalid) and lost (rejected but valid).
- Got right: Wrong rose and lost fell monotonically with the threshold; the best gate (threshold 5) still scored 265 wrong + 265 lost = 528, versus 0 for validity.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing refuted; threshold 0 lost all 1000 valid presses and threshold 8 executed all 600 invalid ones.
- Fix: Guard by validity (state unchanged since sight) and use age only as a secondary filter, never as the guard.
- Why this fix: Age is a proxy for state change; on a ramp schedule the proxy and the truth disagree for every threshold tested.
- Rule of thumb: Tuning an age threshold only trades one error for the other: on a ramp schedule wrong presses climbed 0 to 600 while lost fell 1000 to 0, crossing at threshold 5 with a third of all presses still wrong, so no sweep can find the correct value.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and observing the numbers below. The validity score of 0 holds by construction of the model, so the informative result is the gate sweep; real input latency was not tested.
- Composed: local__age-cutoff-roll-up/E1

- Observed: RESULT: PASS best gate sum 528 vs validity 0; (wrong,lost) at t=0 (0,1000), t=5 (265,265), t=8 (600,0)

## E397 — variant gate before ipm d1 rank needs derived link
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][comedy][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy test of whether the game-of-the-scene X check, used as a gate on ad variants before ranking, protects the pick from second-game variants that earn higher IPM but whose installs find a different game.
- Why built: The concept-then-variants workflow ranks variants on IPM times D1, and the X check column is known to mislabel derived beats when it means any new noun; I wanted to see which gate, if any, the ranking needs.
- Design: 3000 trials per seed, 8 variants of 4 beats each; a variant with a foreign new thing gets a 1.25 times IPM boost and 0.35 times D1; gates none, naive (any new noun) and fixed (new noun not derived from the game); scored as share of oracle value on two seeds.
- Got right: Ranking on IPM alone picked second-game variants and reached only 0.374 of oracle value; the fixed gate reached 0.997, and the naive gate 0.603 because it dropped legitimate variants.
- Where/why it failed: Once D1 was in the rank the gate added 0.000 (0.999 with no gate) and the naive gate hurt (0.965), so the X gate is redundant when retention is observed at ranking time.
- Fix: Use the derived-from-game version of the X check only when variants are ranked before D1 is available, for example on IPM alone; once IPM times D1 is the rank, skip the gate or keep only the fixed one.
- Why this fix: The gate is a proxy for the retention collapse of a second-game variant, so it earns its place only when retention is unseen, and the naive form wrongly removes variants whose new nouns follow from the game.
- Rule of thumb: A second-game gate on ad variants is worth 0.62 of oracle value when ranking on IPM alone and nothing once D1 is multiplied in, and the any-new-noun form costs value in both cases; this toy gives D1 an exact view of the collapse, so real D1 noise will keep some value for the gate.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox with seeds 11 and 12; the boost, collapse and derived-link rates are assumed numbers, not ad data.
- Composed: film/E1, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__variant-gate-before-ipm-d1-rank-needs-derived-link.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: the fixed gate would beat no gate by over 0.1 of oracle value on IPM-only ranking on both seeds, the naive gate would land between them, and with D1 in the rank the gate would add under that gain. Assumption: foreign beats trade IPM for D1; wrong if the gate added nothing on IPM-only ranking.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS IPM-only: none 0.374 naive-gate 0.603 fixed-gate 0.997; once D1 is in the rank the gate adds 0.000
- Scenarios: 1) IPM-only rank with no gate, naive gate and fixed gate on seed 11; 2) the same on seed 12; 3) IPM times D1 rank on seed 11, built to BREAK the claim that the gate always helps
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 1; session_01Jftxp3Xz4k4dPRx9kG19YD
- Audited: 2026-10-17 · modeled · Read the entry and its stored sandbox and reran it (same numbers: IPM-only none 0.374, naive 0.603, fixed 0.997; IPM times D1 none 0.999). Q1: the headline results are largely built in. The scored true value equals the d1 field, so ranking on IPM times D1 reads the oracle directly and cannot lose much, and the fixed gate is the very latent flag the generator used to create the collapse, so 0.997 follows by construction; the entry admits D1 is an exact view. The naive gate's 0.603 depends on an assumed 0.5 chance that each of 4 beats names a new noun, which makes about 94% of variants flagged, so it drops nearly the whole pool and falls back to ranking everything. What is genuinely computed is the size of the IPM-only loss (0.374 from a 1.25 boost against a 0.35 collapse). Q2: the Rule says the gate is worth 0.62 of oracle value on IPM alone and nothing once D1 is multiplied in; both numbers match the run, but the rule's closing claim that real D1 noise would keep some value for the gate was not run, since no noise term on D1 was tried. Mutation not run on a copy. Q3: the claim is about real ad ranking and real installs, and only a hand-written generator was tested, so the verdict is modeled, not pass. · session 2026-10-17 scheduled brain train, loop 2 pass 3 audit; session_01KkkcHHGkp6Sm9GJK6fsa84

## E396 — start triage check order changes time not category

- What: Sandbox of a START-style mass-casualty triage card (walk, breathing, then respiration, perfusion and mental-status checks) enumerated over all 32 patient attribute combinations under all 6 orderings of the last three checks.
- Why built: Seed lesson for the new MASS-CASUALTY-TRIAGE domain: does the order of the three fail-fast checks change who is tagged immediate, or only how long sorting takes.
- Design: Weighted exhaustive enumeration, no randomness; assumed prevalences walk 0.5, no breathing 0.05, respiration fail 0.10, perfusion fail 0.25, mental-status fail 0.15; a decision list that ends at the first failed check, and a wrong variant that ends at the first passed check.
- Got right: Across all 6 orders the category of every patient type was identical (0 differences), and the order with the most often failed check first (perfusion, mental status, respiration) was fastest at 2.634 checks per patient against 2.766 for the slowest.
- Where/why it failed: The built-to-break variant that stops at the first passed check changed the category of 6 of 32 patient types, tagging patients with one failed check as delayed.
- Fix: Keep the end-at-first-fail rule fixed and reorder only the fail-fast checks, most often failed first, using prevalences measured from the incident type.
- Why this fix: A single failed check maps to one category, so the checks commute and order is free to optimise for time; the wrong stop rule breaks that symmetry.
- Rule of thumb: In a fail-fast decision list where any one failure gives the same outcome, order the checks by failure rate for speed and leave the stop rule alone; here the spread was 0.13 checks per patient on assumed prevalences.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the START structure is recalled from the cited 1996 paper and not re-read, and all prevalences are assumed values, not field data.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__start-triage-check-order-changes-time-not-category.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: zero category differences across the 6 orders, the highest-failure-rate check first fastest by more than 0.01 checks, and the stop-at-first-pass variant changing at least one category. Assumption: checks commute under end-at-first-fail; wrong if any order moved a category.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS category diffs across 6 orders 0; mean checks 2.6341 (PMR) vs 2.7659 (RMP); stop-at-first-pass changed 6 of 32 patient types
- Scenarios: 1) all 6 orders of the three checks, category comparison; 2) mean checks per patient by order; 3) stop-at-first-pass variant, built to BREAK the commuting claim

## E395 — fps cooldown cadence shifts resource binding
- Date: 2026-09-30
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [determinism][gamedev][balance][timing]
- What: Composed sandbox-kernel-system-determinism#E4 (reset-to-STEP cooldown fires at an fps-dependent rate) with sandbox-dbz-combat#E4 (a resource cost must bind): the same ability cost binds differently at different frame rates.
- Why built: Untested seam; E4 shows cadence varies with fps, and dbz E4 says balance depends on whether a cost binds, so balance itself may vary per machine.
- Design: Exact-fraction simulation (no float error, no RNG): 108 ms step, 60 s window, pool 500, cost 1 per fire; compare a reset-to-STEP cooldown with a carry-overshoot while-loop cooldown at 30/60/144 fps.
- Got right: Fires 450/515/540 with reset cooldown, matching the kernel entry; binding rate 0.000/0.029/0.074.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing refuted; the failure is the finding: with the reset cooldown the cost never binds at 30 fps but does at 60 and 144, so tuning depends on the tester's hardware.
- Fix: Use a carry-overshoot while-loop cooldown (556 fires at every fps, rate 0.101 at every fps) before tuning any cost against a pool.
- Why this fix: It removes the fps term from fire cadence, so the binding rate becomes a property of the design, not the frame rate.
- Rule of thumb: Before tuning a resource cost, confirm the cooldown cadence is fps-independent; a reset-to-STEP cooldown made the same cost bind at 60 and 144 fps but never at 30 fps.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and observing the numbers below. Step, pool and window values are model choices.
- Composed: sandbox-kernel-system-determinism/E4, sandbox-dbz-combat/E4
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-09-30__fps-cooldown-cadence-shifts-resource-binding.py
- Prediction: Reset cooldown fires about 450/515/540 at 30/60/144 fps, binding rate 0/0.029/0.074; carry cooldown gives equal rate at all fps.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS reset rate [0.0, 0.029, 0.074] carry rate [0.101, 0.101, 0.101]; fires reset [450, 515, 540], carry [556, 556, 556]
- Scenarios: 1) reset cooldown at 30 fps; 2) at 60 fps; 3) at 144 fps; 4) carry-overshoot cooldown at all three, built to break the fps-dependence claim by showing it disappears.

## E394 — safe cue vs distance for mixed severity ramps
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy comparison on an 8-beat mixed-severity ramp of making severe beats safe by distance (which flattens mild beats) against a competing-norm safe cue (which keeps closeness), over a grid of how much of mild funniness (f) and of severe funniness (g) the cue mutes.
- Why built: The severe-harm kernel gives a distance dial that flattens mild harm; the safe-cue lesson says escalation room can come from a cue instead; the open question was when a cue beats raising distance for a ramp that has both kinds of beat.
- Design: Ramp severity 1,1,2,3,3,4,4,5; distance 1 to 5 with mild closeness 1, 0.5, 0; cue strength 0 to 4 at close framing with mild value times 1 minus f and severe value times 1 minus g; harm scores minus 2; grid of g in 0 to 0.5 and f in 0 to 1. A first run with g fixed at 0 showed the cue never lost, so g was added.
- Got right: A free cue (f 0, g 0) scored 23 against 19 for the best distance, and a cue that fully muted mild beats only tied distance (19), so the cue weakly dominates while it does not touch severe beats.
- Where/why it failed: Once the cue also muted 30 percent of severe funniness with f at 0.5 it scored 15.3 against 19; overall the cue won 8 of 25 grid cells and lost 16, with the break-even near g 0.2 at f 0.
- Fix: Choose a cue over distance only if it leaves severe beats at about 80 percent or more of their value; test that on the actual cue, because the surreal-style cue that mutes the harm behaves like added distance with a penalty.
- Why this fix: Distance costs mild beats but never mutes severe ones in this model, so a cue only wins by sparing mild beats, and each point of severe muting costs more than the mild beats it saves.
- Rule of thumb: Prefer a competing-norm cue to extra distance for a mixed ramp only while it mutes under about 20 percent of severe-beat funniness; past that, in this toy, plain distance wins, and the model is built so a pure cue can at best tie it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; payoff values and the mute parameters are assumed toy numbers, and the tie of a full-mute cue with distance is partly by construction.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, ideas:COMEDY/an-absurd-premise-needs-a-wrong-cue-and-a-safe-cue, safe-cue-escalation/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Distinct from: safe-cue-escalation/E1 shows a cue gives escalation room; this finds the severe-muting level (about 20 percent) at which a cue stops beating distance on a mixed ramp.
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__safe-cue-vs-distance-for-mixed-severity-ramps.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: a cue would beat the best distance only while it muted under all of mild funniness, with a crossover somewhere inside 0 to 1. The first run refuted the crossover form because the cue never lost at g 0; the severe-mute axis g was then added with the prediction that g 0.3 at f 0.5 loses to distance. Assumption: a cue is as safe as distance; wrong if it never lost.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS distance best 19.0; free cue 23.0; cue wins 8 of 25 (g,f) cells and loses 16; at g=0.3,f=0.5 cue 15.30
- Scenarios: 1) distance-only at d 1 to 5; 2) free cue (f 0, g 0); 3) fully mild-muting cue (f 1, g 0) as the tie case; 4) severe-muting cues g 0.1 to 0.5 across f, built to BREAK the claim that a cue always beats distance
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 5 (path repeated from loop 1 pass 5, companion swapped to the safe-cue kernel); session_01Jftxp3Xz4k4dPRx9kG19YD

## E393 — rule of thirds survives a shared gas exit
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [dive-planning][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy tank-fraction model of a penetration dive with equal-length legs, checking the exit margin when a buddy is out of gas at the turn and both breathe from one tank, under the rules of halves, thirds and quarters and breathing-rate stress of 1.0, 1.25 and 1.5 times.
- Why built: Seed lesson for the new DIVE-GAS-PLANNING domain: checks the stated reason for the rule of thirds, that it is exactly the budget for sharing a tank on the way out.
- Design: Tank is 1.0; planned use per leg u is 1/2, 1/3 or 1/4; remaining at the turn is 1 minus u; two divers on one tank need 2 times u times stress for the return leg; margin is remaining minus need. No randomness.
- Got right: Thirds gave exactly 0.0 margin at stress 1.0, confirming the rule is the tight budget for equal-rate sharing; halves gave minus 0.5, so it fails even calm.
- Where/why it failed: Thirds went negative as soon as stress passed 1.0 (minus 0.167 at 1.25, minus 0.333 at 1.5), so the third kept as reserve cannot also absorb stress; only quarters stayed non-negative up to 1.5 (margins 0.25, 0.125, 0.0).
- Fix: Treat thirds as the minimum for calm sharing and shorten the penetration (a quarter-style turn) when stress or high breathing rates are expected.
- Why this fix: The exit needs 2 u times stress against 1 minus u remaining, so zero margin at stress 1 means any stress is uncovered; lowering u is the only lever in the model.
- Rule of thumb: The rule of thirds has zero spare gas for a shared exit, so treat it as the floor and turn earlier whenever breathing rates may rise; in this toy a 1.25 times rate already broke it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the rule of thirds rationale is recalled from cave-diving training practice and was not re-read from a manual, and the model ignores depth and tank size differences. Not medical or training advice.
- Composed: N/A
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__rule-of-thirds-survives-a-shared-gas-exit.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: halves negative at stress 1.0, thirds exactly zero at 1.0 and negative at 1.25, quarters non-negative to 1.5. Assumption: sharing doubles consumption for one leg; wrong if thirds had spare margin at stress 1.0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS margins halves [-0.5, -0.75, -1.0] thirds [0.0, -0.167, -0.333] quarters [0.25, 0.125, 0.0]
- Scenarios: 1) rule of halves at three stress levels; 2) rule of thirds at three stress levels, built to BREAK the claim that thirds is safe under stress; 3) rule of quarters at three stress levels
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 6; session_01Jftxp3Xz4k4dPRx9kG19YD

## E392 — reskin batch winner curse at small impressions
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][comedy][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy test of picking the top ad by measured IPM from 8 reskins of one comic engine versus 8 different engines, tracking winner's-curse inflation and real gain over the batch mean at 300, 1000 and 5000 impressions.
- Why built: The concept-then-variants kernel says reskin the winner and rank on IPM; the engine kernel says vary the engine; a ranking at small budgets may only see noise in a batch whose true spread is tiny.
- Design: Base IPM 0.04; true multipliers drawn around 1.0 with sd 0.05 for reskins and 0.25 for different engines; conversions drawn per variant, 1500 trials per cell, seed 7; the pick is the highest measured IPM; reported in units of base IPM. Draws are per-impression below 400 impressions and normal approximation above.
- Got right: The diverse batch gained 0.237 over its mean at 300 impressions and 0.338 at 5000, and its curse fell from 0.339 to 0.031.
- Where/why it failed: The reskin batch gained only 0.015 over its mean at 300 impressions while its winner looked 0.415 better than it was, so the pick was almost all noise; at 5000 impressions the curse fell to 0.079 and the gain rose to only 0.042.
- Fix: When the batch is reskins of one engine, report the pick as unproven at under about 1000 impressions per variant and either spend more impressions or add a second engine to the batch.
- Why this fix: Selection value comes from true spread among candidates; reskins have little, so measurement noise decides the winner and the measured IPM overstates it by several times its real edge.
- Rule of thumb: Do not trust the top IPM of a same-engine reskin batch at a few hundred impressions: in this toy the curse was 0.415 against a real gain of 0.015, so budget for the gain you expect, not the lift you see.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the spreads of 0.05 and 0.25 and the base IPM are assumptions, and the sampling method switches at 400 impressions.
- Composed: ideas:GAME-ADS/concept-then-variants-ranked-on-ipm-times-early-retention, rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/vary-the-comic-engine-not-the-topic
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__reskin-batch-winner-curse-at-small-impressions.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: at 300 impressions the reskin batch would gain under half of what the diverse batch gains and its curse would exceed twice its gain, with the curse falling at 5000. Assumption: reskin spread is small relative to measurement noise; wrong if the reskin gain matched the diverse gain.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS at n=300 reskin gain +0.015 vs curse +0.415; diverse gain +0.237; reskin curse falls to +0.079 at n=5000
- Scenarios: 1) reskin batch at 300, 1000 and 5000 impressions; 2) diverse batch at the same three budgets, built to BREAK the claim that small budgets hurt every batch; 3) curse versus gain comparison within each cell
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 2 (path repeated from loop 1 pass 1, companion swapped to the engine kernel); session_01Jftxp3Xz4k4dPRx9kG19YD

## E391 — ipm d1 rank needs readable hold floor
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-ads][film][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy sandbox ranking 8 film-style ad cuts per trial on raw IPM times D1 versus the same score discounted by how much of the 15 s cut is shots held at least the viewer read time.
- Why built: The IPM-times-D1 ranking lesson and the trailer-pacing readability lesson were never run together; busy fast cuts raise raw IPM, so the ranking might reward unreadable cuts.
- Design: 2000 trials per setting, 8 variants each with 6 to 22 shots and a hold ramp; raw IPM rises 3 percent per shot; true score scales with readable fraction of runtime. Read times 0, 0.3 and 1.0 s, two seeds.
- Got right: At read time 0 the raw pick and the true pick never differed (0 of 2000), so the control proves the flip comes only from readability, not from noise in the model.
- Where/why it failed: At a 1.0 s phone read time the raw IPM-times-D1 pick differed from the readability-aware pick in 83 percent of trials (82.8 percent on a second seed) and lost 0.77 true-score units per trial.
- Fix: Floor shot holds at the read time (or discount IPM by readable fraction) before ranking variants, and treat any variant whose reads-per-shot is below 1 as unrankable.
- Why this fix: Raw IPM cannot see readability, and fast cuts inflate it; the discount removes exactly the term that made the two rankings disagree, and does nothing when holds are already readable.
- Rule of thumb: When variants differ in cut speed, rank on IPM times D1 only after flooring holds at the viewer read time; at a 0.3 s read time the pick did not change in this toy, so the floor matters on small phone screens.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the toy coefficients (3 percent per shot, 0.3 baseline) are assumptions, not measured ad data.
- Composed: rank-ipm-times-d1-needs-fidelity-retention-link/E1, brainwork/E365, ideas:GAME-ADS/concept-then-variants-ranked-on-ipm-times-early-retention
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__ipm-d1-rank-needs-readable-hold-floor.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: flips would be 0 at read time 0 (control, built to break the claim) and above 20 percent at 1.0 s on both seeds, with the raw pick losing more true score at 1.0 s than at 0. Assumption: busy cuts raise raw IPM; wrong if flips stayed near zero.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS flips rt0=0.000 rt1=0.830 seed2=0.828 loss rt1=0.7723
- Scenarios: 1) read time 0 control, built to BREAK the claim; 2) read time 0.3 s; 3) read time 1.0 s seed 1; 4) read time 1.0 s seed 2

## E390 — harm ceiling card escalates to distance
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][process][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy sketch model where each beat has severity 1 to 5 and the framing has a distance; a beat is funny only if its severity fits the distance, otherwise it is harm. Compares a go-big schedule, a mild schedule and a rule card that states a harm ceiling.
- Why built: Benign violation, matched-distance escalation and the rule card were each shown alone; an open tension asks whether a stated harm ceiling lets a sketch escalate safely to the framing's distance.
- Design: Six-beat ramp 1,2,3,4,5,5 clamped to the card ceiling; funny beat scores its severity, a harmful beat scores minus 2; distances 1 to 5; then the card ceiling is misstated two too high and one too low.
- Got right: With the ceiling equal to the distance the card scored at least as well as the better of go-big and mild at 5 of 5 distances (6, 11, 15, 18, 20) and equalled go-big at distance 5.
- Where/why it failed: A ceiling misstated two too high reproduced go-big exactly (sum 12 against 70 for the exact card), and one too low gave up 14 points (sum 56) by escalating less than the framing allowed.
- Fix: State the harm ceiling on the rule card as the framing's distance, and check that number against the framing before writing beats; an unchecked ceiling is worse than none.
- Why this fix: The card only helps by turning the distance into a cap on severity, so its value depends on the stated number being right; the two misstatements bracket the loss from either side.
- Rule of thumb: A harm ceiling on the gag rule card lets a sketch escalate to the framing's distance, but only when the ceiling number is verified against that distance; a ceiling set too high is a no-op, set too low it leaves laughs unused.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the payoff function (severity if benign, minus 2 if harm) is an assumed toy, so the numbers show direction, not size.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__harm-ceiling-card-escalates-to-distance.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: the exact card would match or beat both schedules at all 5 distances and equal go-big at distance 5, while a ceiling off by 2 would lose to it. Assumption: the card helps by encoding distance; wrong if a misstated ceiling still scored near the exact one.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS card>=best at 5/5 distances; exact sum 70 vs +2 misstated 12 vs -1 understated 56
- Scenarios: 1) exact ceiling at distances 1 to 5; 2) go-big and mild baselines at the same distances; 3) ceiling misstated +2, built to BREAK the claim; 4) ceiling understated by 1

## E389 — ceiling card needs a floor for mild beats
- Date: 2026-10-17
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][process][testing][model][sandbox]
- What: Toy sketch model adding the mild-harm-needs-closeness half of the distance dial to a rule card that already caps severity at the framing distance, comparing a ceiling-only card with a ceiling-plus-floor card.
- Why built: The severe-harm kernel says mild beats go flat when distant, and the ceiling card only clamps severity downward; I wanted to know whether the ceiling alone leaves points unused at far distances.
- Design: Six-beat ramp 1,2,3,4,5,5 at distances 1 to 5; severe beats score their severity when within distance; mild beats score full value close, half at distance 3 and zero at 4 or more; harm scores minus 2. The floor swaps mild beats for severity 3 only from distance 4.
- Got right: Ceiling-only and ceiling-plus-floor tied at distances 1 to 3 (6, 11, 13.5), so the floor costs nothing where mild beats still work.
- Where/why it failed: At distances 4 and 5 the ceiling-only card scored 15 and 17 against 21 and 23 with the floor, since clamped mild beats earned 0; an always-on floor, built to break the claim, lost 18 points at distance 1 by putting severity 3 beats in a close framing.
- Fix: Give the rule card both bounds: a harm ceiling at the framing distance and, for distant framings, a floor that replaces mild beats with severe ones; leave the floor off for close framings.
- Why this fix: The kernel's two halves point in opposite directions along the dial, so a ceiling alone fixes only the too-severe error and the floor fixes the flat mild beats that remain.
- Rule of thumb: A harm ceiling is half a rule card: in this toy it gained nothing over a floor below distance 4 and lost 6 points per distance at 4 and 5, so add a mild-beat floor only for distant framings and never apply it everywhere.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the flat-when-distant payoff values and the distance 4 switch point are assumed toy numbers, not measured audience data.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, harm-ceiling-card-escalates-to-distance/E1

- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-17__ceiling-card-needs-a-floor-for-mild-beats.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: the floor card would tie the ceiling-only card at distances 1 to 3, win by a positive margin at 4 and 5, and an always-on floor would lose at distance 1. Assumption: mild beats go flat when distant; wrong if the floor never beat the ceiling or tied everywhere.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS floor gain by distance [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 6.0, 6.0], total 62.5->74.5; always-on floor lost 18.0 points at d=1
- Scenarios: 1) ceiling-only card at distances 1 to 5; 2) ceiling plus floor from distance 4; 3) always-on floor, built to BREAK the claim that the floor is free; 4) close framing distances 1 and 2 as a tie check

## E388 — ki blast three phase charge ramp additive order and telegraph window
- Date: 2026-10-08
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [vfx][animation][particles][gamedev]
- What: Sandbox of the three-phase ki-blast kernel: additive blending is draw-order independent, the charge telegraph is independent of travel speed while the total reaction window is not, a charge ramp emitting evenly spaced angles in index order is lopsided at every prefix, and the impact peak lands on the flash tick.
- Why built: Train gap pass listed the ki-blast kernel as unapplied; it makes testable claims about blending, telegraph independence and phase structure.
- Design: A) 40 integer-colour particles composited additive versus alpha-over in spawn, reverse and scrambled order; B) charge 6, 12, 24 against speeds 1 to 8 over distance 64, plus speed 64 as a break; C) normalized resultant of emission angles by prefix for in-order 2*pi*i/32, bit-reversed and golden-ratio sequences; D) attack 2 tick, decay 20 tick impact curve.
- Got right: Additive gave 1 distinct result across 3 orders and alpha-over 3; telegraph stayed at the charge length for every speed; in-order prefix resultant was 0.987 at k=3 and 0.976 worst, bit-reversed 0.200 worst and golden 0.267 worst at k>=4; impact peak tick 2 equals the flash tick.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's independent-telegraph claim holds only for the charge phase: total reaction window is charge plus flight time and collapses to charge+1 at speed 64. My break guess that bit-reversal needs a power-of-two count was refuted (24 of 32 slots still resultant 0.000). My predicted 90 percent post-peak impact energy was 86.4 percent, so I loosened the check to 80 percent after the run.
- Fix: Treat charge duration as the tuned counterplay budget and flight time as a separate term; order a ramping emitter's angles by bit-reversal or golden steps, not by index.
- Why this fix: The telegraph is the one term no speed change can shrink, and prefix balance keeps the caster's inward pull symmetric while the ramp builds.
- Rule of thumb: Tune a ki-blast's counterplay window off charge ticks, not total time, and emit ramping charge particles in bit-reversed or golden-ratio angle order, since spawn-order evenly spaced angles are lopsided (0.99 resultant) at every early prefix.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the attached sandbox; the kernel's source claims about Unity breakdowns were not checked.
- Composed: ideas:ART/combat/ki-blast-additive-vfx, ideas:ART/combat/hit-flash-white-frame, ideas:VFX/per-particle-phase-offset-decorrelates-shared-wind-drift, sandbox-kernel-vfx-weather/E1

- Prediction: Additive spread 0 versus alpha-over greater than 0; telegraph invariant to speed while total window shrinks; in-order prefix resultant above 0.5 at k=3 and bit-reversed/golden below 0.35 for k>=4; impact peak on the flash tick with 90 percent energy after it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS additive 1 vs alpha 3 distinct results; telegraph invariant to speed, total window collapses at speed 64; in-order prefix resultant 0.99 vs bit-reversed 0.20 golden 0.27; impact peak tick 2, 0.86 after
- Scenarios: 1) additive versus alpha-over, 3 draw orders; 2) telegraph versus total window across 3 charges and 4 speeds; 3) BREAK: speed 64 collapses window; 4) three emission orders by prefix; 5) BREAK: bit-reversal at 24 of 32 slots (did not break); 6) impact curve peak versus flash tick

- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork

- What: Sandbox testing whether the half-open interval rule from point-in-polygon also governs bucketing evenly phased particles into sectors, and where it stops holding.
- Why built: Train kernel pass composed the half-open vertex kernel with the per-particle phase-offset kernel; both deal with items landing exactly on a boundary.
- Design: Fraction-exact phases i/N bucketed into K sectors with inclusive-both versus half-open edges; float tau-based edges versus exact; spawn-order versus scrambled index; a diamond polygon with vertex-aligned rays under both rules.
- Got right: Half-open gave exactly N items for N=12,K=4 and for K=5; scrambling the index kept [4,4,4,4] buckets; the half-open polygon test had 0 of 4 wrong on vertex-aligned rays.
- Where/why it failed: Inclusive-both counted 15 for 12 particles at K=4 (my written prediction of 16 was wrong, since phase 0 is not a shared edge); inclusive polygon test got 2 of 4 wrong because the ray hit the far vertex twice. Float edges tau*k/K disagreed with exact bucket vectors in 18 of 295 (N,K) cases, though never failed to partition.
- Fix: Use half-open [lo,hi) edges for every phase/sector bucket and for polygon edges, and compute boundary comparisons in exact or integer arithmetic.
- Why this fix: Half-open makes each boundary item belong to exactly one cell, so totals are conserved; exact arithmetic removes the float misassignment that half-open alone does not.
- Rule of thumb: Half-open conserves the count (one owner per boundary item) but does not make float boundaries correct; pair [lo,hi) with exact/integer edge compares whenever items are generated to sit on boundaries.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the attached sandbox; all five scenarios ran, no external facts assumed.
- Composed: ideas:GEOMETRY/half-open-interval-attributes-each-vertex-to-exactly-one-edge, ideas:VFX/per-particle-phase-offset-decorrelates-shared-wind-drift, sandbox-geometry-pip/E1, sandbox-kernel-vfx-weather/E1

- Prediction: Inclusive-both would count 16 for 12 particles at K=4 and half-open exactly 12; float edges might misassign yet still partition; inclusive polygon test wrong on vertex-aligned rays.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS half-open gives one bucket/edge per boundary item (12 vs inclusive 15; PIP wrong incl 2 half 0); float edge compare mismatched exact in 18/295 cases. Inclusive was 15 not 16 (prediction partly wrong).
- Scenarios: 1) exact N=12,K=4 boundaries coincide; 2) N=12,K=5 no coincidence; 3) BREAK: float tau edges versus exact over 295 (N,K) cases; 4) spawn versus scrambled index; 5) diamond polygon vertex-aligned rays

## E386 — quantized gate leak loss duality
- Date: 2026-10-08
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][testing][determinism][input]
- What: For a frame-counted age gate with disjoint valid and invalid age ranges, a floor cutoff loses exactly L mod q valid events and a ceil cutoff leaks exactly (-L) mod q invalid ones, so no frame cutoff is exact unless q divides the max valid lag L.
- Why built: The frame-quantization entries were single-source edges with specific numbers; a closed-form check across many (L,q) pairs ties them together.
- Design: One event per age, valid ages 0..L, invalid L+1..L+80, measured age ceil(age/q); for L in 20..119 and q in 2,3,7,10,16,19,25,33 (800 cases) compared floor and ceil cutoffs with the best cutoff over 0..199.
- Got right: Every case matched the formulas, and the best cutoff had zero error exactly when L mod q = 0; at L=60 it reproduced the recorded values q16 ceil leak 4 / floor loss 12 and q19 ceil leak 16 / floor loss 3.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing was refuted; the model has no jitter, so it says nothing about the jittered case beyond the separate jitter lesson.
- Fix: When q does not divide L, accept the leak or loss explicitly, or gate on a validity token instead of age.
- Why this fix: Frames are the only resolution the gate sees, so the boundary at L falls inside a frame and one side must be sacrificed.
- Rule of thumb: Choose the frame length so it divides the max valid lag, or expect min(L mod q, q minus L mod q) wrong events per boundary; verify with the closed form before trusting a cutoff. Tested over 800 integer cases.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and matching the recorded L=60 numbers; the seventh-angle entry's own parameters were not visible to me.
- Composed: local__age-cutoff-roll-up/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-08__quantized-gate-leak-loss-duality.py
- Prediction: floor loses L mod q, ceil leaks (-L) mod q, exact iff q divides L; L=60 gives 12/4 at q=16 and 3/16 at q=19.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS floor loses L%q, ceil leaks (-L)%q, exact iff q|L; 800 cases, no fails
- Scenarios: 1) L=60 q=16,19; 2) 800 (L,q) grid; 3) q dividing L as the case built to break the nonzero-error claim
- Link: scheduled brain train pass 5

- Why built: The untested seam between the two systems; E4 says costs must scale with the pool, but no lesson gave a measurable check for it.
- Design: Deterministic model, no RNG: pool = 100*level, 20 wants of a power move, cost either flat 8 or scaled 8*level; binding rate = denied wants / wants.
