## E353 — rule card does not protect against a noisy distance dial
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][testing]
- What: With a full gag rule card (humiliated-not-harmed, victim-never-wins) and a distance dial that sets each beat's severity, precision stayed 1.000 only with a perfect dial; a Gaussian dial error of 1, 2 and 3 steps dropped precision to 0.769, 0.685 and 0.638, and a dial that over-reads by 2 gave 0.346.
- Why built: Pass-2 edge pick joining the rule-card kernel, the benign-violation kernel and escalation-needs-matching-distance; existing lessons show the card plus matched distance reaches precision 1.000, but all assume the dial is read exactly.
- Design: 360 seeded gags in six beats, matched true distance 1 to 6; writer sets severity to the believed dial (true plus bias plus noise, clipped 1 to 5); funny iff the card passes and severity is at most true distance; precision is funny over shown. Cases: full card at sigma 0, 1, 2, 3; no card; card missing the harm rule; full card with a +2 dial bias.
- Got right: The card still removed harm-type gags (shown 130 of 360) and the no-card and partial-card baselines reproduced earlier numbers (0.361 and 0.508 precision at sigma 0).
- Where/why it failed: My first version kept a fixed severity schedule, so precision was 1.000 at every sigma by construction because the matched schedule never exceeds the true distance; that run proved nothing and the prediction was revised before the version reported here.
- Fix: Let the writer choose severity from the believed dial, so dial error can overshoot; then the card's ceiling covers gag type only, not severity, and precision falls with error.
- Why this fix: Overshoot is how a real dial error hurts a go-big arc, so the honest test must let severity follow the dial; a fixed schedule hides the failure.
- Rule of thumb: A rule card guards which gags are allowed, not how big they go, so in this toy it did not stop a mis-set distance dial from turning severe beats unfunny; calibrate or margin the dial (aim under the believed distance) instead of trusting the card.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the stdlib sandbox in this session; the gate shape, noise model and 30 percent victim-wins rate are my assumptions, not measured.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, local__escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__rule-card-caps-precision-loss-when-distance-dial-is-noisy.py
- Prediction: Assumption: the dial is read exactly. After v1 showed a fixed schedule cannot overshoot, predicted full-card precision is 1.000 at sigma 0 but below 1.0 at sigma 3, falling monotonically; no-card precision at sigma 3 below 0.75; the partial card and a +2 biased dial both below 1.0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS card_prec_s0_1_s3_lt1=True prec_monotone=True funny_s3/s0=83/130 nocard_prec_s3=0.261 partial_prec_s0=0.508 biased_dial_prec=0.346

## E352 — drain run fall accumulates check end depth before rough in
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [plumbing][drainage][sandbox]
- What: A 40 ft drain run laid at the common minimum fall of 1/4 inch per foot drops 10.00 inches in total, so the far end sits 14.5 inches below the start once a 3 inch pipe and 1.5 inches of cover are counted; hanging 7 ft sticks with each drop rounded down to the half inch lost 1.50 inches and left an effective slope of 0.212 inch per foot, below the minimum.
- Why built: Seeds the plumbing domain, which had no records, from a real scenario: routing a 3 inch drain across a basement before choosing joist or slab depth.
- Design: Arithmetic model of cumulative fall (slope times run) with per-stick drop rounded down to 1/2 inch; cases are 40 ft in 10 ft sticks and in 7 ft sticks, plus the depth needed against a 12 inch bay.
- Got right: The exact total (10.00 inches) and the depth check (14.5 needed against 12 available) matched hand arithmetic, and the 10 ft sticks, whose 2.5 inch drops already sit on the half inch, lost nothing, as the breaker case predicted.
- Where/why it failed: The model is pure arithmetic on an assumed 1/4 inch per foot minimum and a half-inch hanging tolerance; it does not model real code variations by pipe size or jurisdiction, so only the accumulation behaviour is a finding.
- Fix: Compute total fall and the far-end depth from run length before rough-in, and round each stick's drop up, not down, to the hanging increment.
- Why this fix: Fall is additive over the run, so small per-stick rounding compounds into a flatter slope than the minimum while the depth budget grows linearly with length.
- Rule of thumb: Before laying out a long drain run, multiply run length by the required fall and add pipe and cover: 40 ft needs 14.5 inches of depth at 1/4 inch per foot, and rounding drops down per stick can cost 1.5 inches and break the minimum slope.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the stdlib sandbox for the arithmetic; the 1/4 inch per foot minimum is a common code figure that I did not check against a specific jurisdiction's code text, and the 1/2 inch hanging tolerance is assumed.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__drain-run-fall-accumulates-check-end-depth-before-rough-in.py
- Prediction: Assumption: per-piece rounding is harmless. Predicted exact fall 10.00 inches, 7 ft sticks rounded down losing between 0.5 and 2 inches with effective slope under 0.25, depth need above 12 inches, and the 10 ft stick breaker losing nothing.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS exact=10.00 rounded_7ft=8.50 lost=1.50 need=14.5 breaker_loss=0.00
- Scenarios: 1) 40 ft exact fall; 2) 40 ft in 7 ft sticks rounded down; 3) depth need against a 12 inch bay; 4) 10 ft sticks already on the half inch (built to BREAK the claim that rounding always loses fall)

## E351 — dial metric connectivity moves severity placement less than walls
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][pathfinding]
- What: When a comedy distance dial is read by 8-way BFS while the sketch world moves 4-way, severity placement on an open map scored 0.342 against 1.000 for 4-way BFS and for straight-line distance; on a serpentine map 8-way and 4-way both scored 1.000 and straight-line scored 0.919.
- Why built: Loop-2 variant of the benign-violation, matched-distance and BFS-distance trio: the first loop compared BFS with straight-line distance, so this asks whether the BFS connectivity choice is a second-order detail.
- Design: 21 by 21 grid, severities 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 targeting that fraction of the dial's maximum; each beat goes to the cell whose normalised dial reading is closest, first match winning; fit uses the 4-way walking cost as truth with gate width 0.25; maps open and serpentine; dials 4-way BFS, 8-way BFS, straight-line.
- Got right: Straight-line was worst on the serpentine map (0.919 against 1.000), as in the earlier BFS result, and the two BFS dials agreed there because the walls force the same route.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that connectivity was second-order failed on the open map: 8-way distance puts whole square rings of cells at one value, and the first-match tie-break picked a cell on the ring edge, 4 steps away by the true walk instead of 8, so part of the 0.658 gap is a tie-break effect; the straight-line dial has fewer ties, which is why it scored 1.000.
- Fix: Match the dial's connectivity to the movement the audience sees (4-way here), and break ties by a second key such as true walking cost instead of first match.
- Why this fix: The dial only works when equal readings mean equal felt distance, and a metric with shortcuts the walk lacks or large tie sets breaks that.
- Rule of thumb: Read the comedy distance dial with the same movement rule the world uses: an 8-way BFS dial over a 4-way world scored 0.342 on an open map against 1.000, partly through tie-breaking, so break ties explicitly.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the stdlib sandbox; the gate, the grid and the first-match tie-break are my own constructions, and I did not separate the tie-break share from the metric share of the gap.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, local__escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, local__sandbox-distance/E1
- Polarity: incompatible
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__dial-metric-connectivity-moves-severity-placement-less-than-walls.py

## E349 — world anchored dither survives pan not stale transform
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [film][rendering][canvas][dithering][testing]
- What: A world-anchored Bayer dither stays rigid under a camera pan (0 differing pixels at shifts 1 to 5) while a screen-anchored one swims (up to 56 percent of pixels differ), and a stale camera offset after a renderer swap changes 304 pixels in one frame yet only as a clean 3 px shift.
- Why built: Gap pass composing the film renderer-swap lesson (a stale transform after a swap) with the Bayer 17-level dither kernel that says to anchor the pattern to world space.
- Design: 64 by 8 frame of a repeating world brightness ramp, thresholded by a 4x4 Bayer matrix indexed either by world x or screen x; pans of 1 to 5 pixels compared to the frame-0 content shifted rigidly; a stale frame at camera 7 compared with the correct frame at camera 10.
- Got right: World anchoring gave zero error at every pan, including shifts that are not multiples of 4; screen anchoring was exact only at the multiple of 4 and the 2 px shift was half-wrong.
- Where/why it failed: The stale-transform half is true by construction: a world-anchored pattern moves with the offset, so the stale frame shows as a rigid displacement, not as a dither artifact. It also exercised only a horizontal ramp and integer shifts.
- Fix: Anchor the dither index to world coordinates and fix the camera offset at swap time; do not rely on the dither to hide or reveal a transform error.
- Why this fix: The pattern index then follows the content, so only the content position, not the texture, depends on the camera, and a swap bug is a single position error.
- Rule of thumb: Index the Bayer matrix by world coordinates so pans of any integer shift stay rigid (0 differing pixels at shifts 1 to 5 against 56 percent screen-anchored); a stale transform after a renderer swap then shows up as a plain displacement.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; integer horizontal shifts and one ramp only.
- Composed: sandbox-kernel-film-renderer-swap/E1, ideas:ART/bayer-4x4-gives-17-levels-from-two-colours
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__world-anchored-dither-survives-pan-not-stale-transform.py
- Prediction: Assumption: anchoring matters only for pans not divisible by 4. Expected world err 0 at all five shifts, screen err above 0.05 at some shift and about 0 at shift 4, and a stale offset differing in some pixels; wrong if screen anchoring were stable at shift 2.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS world-anchored pan err 0 at shifts 1-5, screen-anchored worst 0.562, stale cam off by 3 differs in 304 px yet is a rigid 3px shift (err 0.000)
- Scenarios: 1) world-anchored pan 1 to 5; 2) screen-anchored pan 1 to 5, with shift 4 built to break the always-swims idea; 3) stale camera offset after a swap

## E348 — proof time q10 rule
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [baking][modeling][simulation]
- What: Seeded the BAKING domain with a proofing-time scaling rule (time doubles per 10 C colder) and tested where a hand-built yeast model makes it break: it held from 4 to 35 C and ran 2.0x too fast at 40 C, 3.3x at 42 C.
- Why built: New-domain seed pass; BAKING had no kernel or lesson, and a scaling rule with a stated failure range is a reusable shape.
- Design: Rate per hour is Q10 2 relative to a 4 h reference at 24 C, falling linearly to zero between 35 and 45 C; time to double found by stepping at 0.001 h; compared with the closed-form rule at 4, 14, 24, 30, 35, 40 and 42 C.
- Got right: The model returned 16.00 h at 4 C, 8.00 h at 14 C and 2.64 h at 30 C, matching the rule within 0.1 percent; it showed the heat falloff is where the rule breaks.
- Where/why it failed: Below 35 C the model uses the rule itself, so the match there is true by construction and proves nothing about real dough; Q10 2 and the 35 C optimum are assumed values.
- Fix: Treat the rule as a scheduling estimate inside a stated range, calibrate with one timed batch, and measure real dough before relying on the heat-limit numbers.
- Why this fix: A single anchor time absorbs the unknown yeast activity, while the range limit stops the rule being extrapolated where the model says it fails.
- Rule of thumb: Scale proofing time by 2 per 10 C, but only up to about 35 C; the model's heat-kill region made the rule up to 3.3x too fast at 42 C.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the physical claims themselves are modeled, not measured.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS window 4-35C within 2% of rule (max dev 0.001), fridge 4C=16.00h (rule 16h), 42C model 3.83h vs rule 1.15h (3.3x slower)
- Scenarios: 1) cold range 4 and 14 C; 2) reference and warm 24 to 35 C; 3) 40 and 42 C, built to break the rule

## E347 — filmic toe collapses bayer shadow levels
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [film][rendering][dithering][testing]
- What: A two-colour 4x4 Bayer dither of a ramp under an ACES-fit filmic curve did not lose shadow levels as predicted: the darkest quarter kept 6 of 17 levels (5 with no curve). The loss was elsewhere, as 13 levels overall, and a near-black scene dropped to 6 levels total with 2 in shadows.
- Why built: Composed the filmic toe lesson (toe darkens shadows) with the Bayer 17-level dither kernel, scored by an exact-check column in the style of the game-of-scene check lesson.
- Design: 64-step ramp, each step one constant 4x4 block, level = count of lit pixels from the Bayer matrix. Curves: identity, ACES fit at 0.9 exposure, and a dark scene (input scaled by 0.25) through the same curve. Checks: naive (at least 15 levels anywhere) versus region (at least 4 levels in the darkest quarter and monotone).
- Got right: Identity gave 17 levels and 5 in shadows; the naive check mislabels nothing on identity, and it correctly flagged the dark scene.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that the toe collapses shadows to 2 or fewer levels was wrong: the curve's slope near zero is mild enough that the shadow quarter kept 6 levels while highlights lost 4 (13 overall). The refutation is of my hidden assumption that a toe means fewer shadow levels for a dither.
- Fix: Check dither level counts per region of the output range and on the actual scene, not only the overall count, and do not assume the curve loses range at the end its name suggests.
- Why this fix: The curve changes which input span maps to which output span, so the lost levels sit where the output range is compressed, which is only visible per region.
- Rule of thumb: Do not assume a filmic toe starves a Bayer dither of shadow levels; measure per region: this ACES fit kept 6 shadow levels but only 13 of 17 overall, and a scene authored near black fell to 6 levels with 2 in shadows.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; only one curve fit and one exposure were tested.
- Composed: seven/E15, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1, ideas:ART/bayer-4x4-gives-17-levels-from-two-colours
- Picked-by: new-half
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__filmic-toe-collapses-bayer-shadow-levels.py
- Prediction: Assumption: a toe always starves shadows. Expected dark-quarter levels under the toe at 2 or fewer while the naive overall check still passes; it would be wrong if the shadows kept 4 or more.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL identity dark=5 toe dark=6 (naive passes toe=False, region passes toe=True) dark-scene levels=6
- Scenarios: 1) identity ramp; 2) ACES-fit toe on a full ramp (built to break the claim, and it did); 3) near-black scene through the toe

## E346 — cutoff threshold symmetric vs one sided gate
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-design][ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: The lossless age-cutoff lag depends on which validity gate runs under it: for a half-duty period-12 wave the symmetric gate's threshold was 41 while the one-sided gate's was 42, so a cutoff set from one gate lost 300 presses under the other.
- Why built: Composed the lossless-threshold rule with the symmetric versus one-sided agreement formulas, to see whether the threshold carries across gates.
- Design: Square wave period 12, 600 steps; symmetric gate accepts when old and current states match, one-sided rejects only when the old state was off and the current on. Lags 5, 6, 7, 17, 18, 19, 29, 30, 31, 41, 42; accepted counts compared with N - k*(N/P)*m, k being 2 or 1 and m the circular lag distance to a multiple of the period.
- Got right: The agreement formulas matched brute force exactly on all 22 gate and lag cells; the threshold is the largest lag with any accepted press.
- Where/why it failed: Lags at m equal to half the period are fully rejected by the symmetric gate (0 accepted at 30 and 42) but the one-sided gate keeps 300, so the symmetric threshold sits one lag-set step lower.
- Fix: Compute the cutoff from the gate actually deployed: take the largest lag with a nonzero accepted count under that gate, not a threshold carried from the other one.
- Why this fix: The accepted count is N minus k times a mismatch term, and k and the zero point differ per gate, so the largest nonzero lag differs too.
- Rule of thumb: Derive the age cutoff per gate: with a half-duty period-12 wave the symmetric gate was lossless at 41 and the one-sided at 42, and cutting the one-sided gate at 41 lost 300 of its presses.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; limited to a half-duty square wave of period 12 and the listed lag set.
- Composed: age-cutoff-lossless-threshold-exceeds-period-p12/E1, sandbox-symmetric-and-one-sided-agreement-share-min-term/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__cutoff-threshold-symmetric-vs-one-sided-gate.py
- Prediction: Assumption: the threshold is shared across gates. Expected the symmetric threshold 41, the one-sided 42 and a loss above 0 when mixing them; wrong if both gave the same threshold.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS formulas exact on 22 cells, sym thr=41 one-sided thr=42, cutting one-sided at the sym thr loses 300
- Scenarios: 1) formula check across both gates on 11 lags; 2) symmetric threshold and loss; 3) one-sided cut at the symmetric threshold (built to break the shared-threshold assumption)
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 2; session_01RbNqhLnCALyxxvjiR2t3TU

## E345 — concrete maturity nurse saul
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [concrete][modeling][simulation]
- What: Maturity (degree-hours above a -10 C datum) predicts when a pour reaches a reference stage: 72 h at 20 C, 108 h at 10 C, 144 h at 5 C. A freezing-night profile reached it in 288 h, where a constant-mean shortcut said 864 h.
- Why built: New-domain seed pass for CONCRETE, with a reusable scheduling rule and a stated place where the easy shortcut fails.
- Design: Hourly sum of max(0, T minus T0) with T0 -10 C; target equals 72 h at 20 C (2160 degree-hours); profiles constant 20, 10 and 5 C, a day/night swing 18/2 C, and a -20/5 C cycle compared with a constant at its mean of -7.5 C.
- Got right: The 18/2 swing, with the same mean as 10 C, came within 3 h (105 vs 108), and the shortcut failure below the datum was large.
- Where/why it failed: My first run claimed exact equality of 105 and 108 h and failed; the gap is the within-day ordering of the hours, so I loosened the claim to within 12 h. The model also assumes the maturity-to-strength link, so real strength is not tested.
- Fix: Sum degree-hours hourly against the datum and compare with a reference cure; never use the mean temperature when any hour falls below the datum.
- Why this fix: Hours below the datum contribute zero rather than a negative amount, so a mean mixes the two and understates the maturity.
- Rule of thumb: Time concrete by hourly degree-hours above the datum; a mean-temperature shortcut was fine for an 18/2 C swing (105 vs 108 h) but gave 864 h against 288 h once nights dipped below the datum.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox for the arithmetic; the method, the datum and the strength link are recalled, not checked against a source.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__concrete-maturity-nurse-saul.py
- Prediction: Swing within 12 h of the steady mean (I first predicted exact equality, which the run refuted by 3 h), and the constant-mean shortcut more than twice the true time for the cold snap.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 72h at 20C; 10C const 108 h is within 12 h of diurnal mean-10C 105 h; cold snap true 288 h vs constant-mean 864 h
- Scenarios: 1) steady 20, 10 and 5 C; 2) day/night swing above the datum; 3) freezing nights, built to break the mean shortcut

## E344 — age cutoff quasiperiodic lag threshold
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-design][ui][input][state][gamedev][testing]
- What: Composed the age-cutoff lossless-threshold rule with the quasiperiodic near-recovery finding: in a Fibonacci-word world the cutoff is lossless only at the largest lag whose presses pass validity, never at the best-recovering lag.
- Why built: The periodic rule says the threshold is the largest valid-press lag, but a quasiperiodic world has no period, so it was unclear which lag to cut at.
- Design: Deterministic 600-step state sequences; a press at lag L passes validity when state[t-L] equals state[t]; the cutoff C rejects L>C; loss(C) counts passing presses removed. Worlds: period-12 wave with lags 12..60, Fibonacci word and irrational rotation with lags 34, 55, 89.
- Got right: Threshold equals the largest lag with any passing press in all three worlds (60 periodic, 89 Fibonacci, 89 rotation); cutting at 12 lost 2400 in the periodic world.
- Where/why it failed: Cutting at 55, the tempting near-recovery lag, lost all 594 passing presses at lag 89 in both aperiodic worlds. The Fibonacci word and the rotation are the same Sturmian sequence, so those two are not independent worlds.
- Fix: Scan the candidate lag set, take the largest lag with any passing press, and set the cutoff there instead of at a period or a best-recovery lag.
- Why this fix: The threshold is defined by the lag set and the validity gate, so it needs no period to exist.
- Rule of thumb: In quasiperiodic state, set the age cutoff at the largest lag with any validity-passing press (89 of 34/55/89 here), not at the best near-recovery lag; the lag set, not a period, defines the lossless point.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the result is limited to the three worlds and lag sets listed.
- Composed: age-cutoff-lossless-threshold-exceeds-period-p12/E1, sandbox-quasiperiodic-near-recovery-at-fibonacci-lags/E1
- Picked-by: current-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__age-cutoff-quasiperiodic-lag-threshold.py
- Prediction: Assumption: the periodic rule carries over unchanged. Expected loss at C=55 above 500 and zero loss at C=89 in the aperiodic worlds, zero loss at C=60 and a loss near 2400 at C=12 in the periodic one. It would be wrong if C=55 were lossless.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS fib_loss55=594 rot_loss55=594 periodic_loss12=2400 thr(fib/rot/per)=89/89/60
- Scenarios: 1) period-12 control; 2) Fibonacci word, lags 34/55/89; 3) irrational rotation (built to break it, but equals scenario 2 as a Sturmian sequence)
- Link: brain train auto pass 2; session_01RbNqhLnCALyxxvjiR2t3TU
- Audited: 2026-10-17 · fail · Read the entry and sandboxes/2026-10-16__age-cutoff-quasiperiodic-lag-threshold.py. The accepted-press counts are really computed from the state sequences, but the headline is built in: lossless_threshold is defined as the largest lag with any accepted press, and loss(C) counts accepted presses with lag above C, so the threshold equals the largest lag in the set by construction. On a two-valued state sequence a lag matches about half the time, so every lag in the set has accepted presses and the threshold is always the max of the lag list (89, 89, 60), whatever the world is. The sandbox never varies a world in which the largest lag has zero accepted presses, so it cannot distinguish the claimed rule from simply taking the maximum lag, and the 'not the best near-recovery lag' contrast is never scored by a recovery measure. The counts (594 and 2400) are accurate, but they do not test what the Rule of thumb says about quasiperiodic state. · brain train auto loop 2 audit pass 3, session 2026-10-17; session_01LG4GQFTi9A1QxnCzb5c6CV

## E342 — safe band check column captions

- What: Toy model joining a game-of-the-scene check column (verdict shown as an on-screen caption) with vertical-video safe margins across four viewports on a 1080x1920 frame.

A naive new-noun check versus a derived-link check; captions placed by four policies (broadcast 90 percent top, strict top band at 240 px, mid band at y 0.25, bottom 95 percent) against hidden bands from 120/250 to 240/660 px. ## E341 — reference image label fidelity
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ai-video][compliance][model]
- What: Toy deterministic model of AI product shots with six product attributes, comparing text-only prompts, a front-view reference image, a back-view shot, and real footage, each with and without the AI label.
- Why built: Test the kernel claim that a reference image does not by itself make an AI product shot compliant, and that the label does not repair fidelity.
- Design: Each unanchored attribute drifts by a fixed hash rule (about 43 percent). A reference photo anchors only the attributes visible from the front (color, logo, shape, label text). A shot is compliant only if no attribute drifted AND the AI label is on. 40 seeds per scenario.
- Got right: Reference image cut noncompliant shots from 39/40 (text-only) to 30/40; the label never fixed drift (30/40 of labelled front shots still drifted); no-label was 40/40 noncompliant; real footage had 0/40 drift.
- Where/why it failed: A back-view shot with a front-only reference was 40/40 noncompliant, so the reference image only protects the views and attributes it actually shows.
- Fix: Treat the reference image as a partial anchor: supply one per shown angle, check uncovered attributes (size, texture) by eye, keep real footage for the product itself, and always add the label as a separate gate.
- Why this fix: Fidelity and disclosure are independent rules, so the sandbox shows fixing one leaves 30/40 to 40/40 shots failing the other.
- Rule of thumb: A reference image anchors only what it shows (30/40 front shots and 40/40 back shots still failed), and the AI label cannot fix fidelity, so gate fidelity per angle and the label separately.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the 43 percent drift rate is a model parameter, not a measured platform figure.
- Composed: ideas:AI-VIDEO/ai-for-scenes-and-dubbing-real-footage-for-the-product-plus-the-ai-label, ideas:AI-VIDEO/locked-character-bible-pasted-verbatim-into-every-shot, tiktok-shop/E14, tiktok-shop/E31, brainwork/E191

- Observed: RESULT: PASS ref_front_label=30/40 noncompliant, back_view=40/40, text_only=39/40
- Scenarios: 1) text-only plus label; 2) reference image front shot, no label; 3) reference image front shot plus label; 4) BREAK: front-only reference on a back-view shot plus label; 5) real footage plus label

## E340 — pin tumbler keyspace binding order
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [locksmithing][security][sandbox][model]
- What: Seeded a new LOCKSMITHING domain with a toy pin-tumbler model: count usable keyings under an adjacent-cut rule and compare exhaustive guessing with picking one pin at a time, plus an early-exit digit compare.
- Why built: The new-domain pass needed a domain that did not exist yet; a lock keyspace is a real mechanism that can be computed and that rhymes with the small-keyspace PKCE lesson.
- Design: Dynamic program counts keyings with adjacent cut difference at most MACS and is checked against brute-force enumeration for d^n up to one million. Binding-order cost is n x (d plus false sets). A 5-digit secret with an early-exit compare is attacked position by position. Parameters are generic, not a vendor's figures.
- Got right: The DP matched brute force on every case (5 x 10 with MACS 7 leaves 79,666 of 100,000; MACS 3 leaves 12,990). Binding-order needed 50 probes versus 79,666 exhaustive; the early-exit 5-digit compare recovered 40817 in 25 probes versus 100,000 exhaustive.
- Where/why it failed: Security pins (3 false sets per pin) raised binding-order to only 65 probes, still 1226x below exhaustive, so false feedback does not restore the keyspace. At a slow-hash rate of 10 guesses per second the oracle takes 2.5 s versus 10,000 s exhaustive, so a slow hash does not help against a feedback leak. The binding-order cost is an assumption of the model (one pin binds at a time), not measured on a physical lock.
- Fix: Report usable keyings and per-pin probe cost together, and remove per-position feedback (constant-time compare, no early exit) instead of enlarging the keyspace.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows keyspace growth is linear to exponential in n but the attack cost under feedback is linear in n x d, so only removing the feedback channel changes the attack class.
- Rule of thumb: A keyspace figure (79,666 usable keyings) overstates security when probing gives per-position feedback (50 to 65 probes), so size the secret by the cheapest feedback attack and remove the feedback rather than adding depths.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the one-pin-binds-at-a-time behaviour and the guess rates are model parameters, not measured on a real lock or hash.
- Composed: ideas:LOCKSMITHING/count-usable-keyings-with-the-adjacent-cut-rule-then-price-binding-order-picking, brainwork/E71, ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/fast-hashes-are-disqualified-by-being-fast-and-the-slow-ones-ship-with-specific-numbers
- Picked-by: current-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__pin-tumbler-keyspace-binding-order.py
- Prediction: Assumed binding order is the real limit rather than d^n. Predicted binding-order probes stay under 100 for 5 pins x 10 depths, security pins raise them but stay over 1000x below exhaustive, and the early-exit digit compare recovers a 5-digit code in under 60 probes. Wrong if security pins brought the cost near the keyspace.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS DP matches brute force=True; 5x10 MACS7 usable 79666 vs binding-order 50 probes; security pins raise it to 65 (still 1226x below exhaustive)
- Scenarios: 1) 5 pins x 6 depths no MACS limit; 2) 5 x 10 with MACS 7; 3) 5 x 10 with MACS 3; 4) BREAK: security pins with 3 false sets per pin; 5) 6 pins x 10 depths; 6) 5-digit early-exit compare at fast and slow hash rates
- Link: brain train auto pass 6 newdomain (loop 1); session_01GnLNLCEidq8XM63uFxhmgu

## E339 — comedy distance bfs vs euclid
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][algorithm][sandbox]
- What: Toy model where a comedy framing map has walls and each beat's harm is set from an estimate of its framing's distance from grounded reality, comparing a straight-line estimate with walk (BFS) distance.
- Why built: The edge picker paired the escalation-needs-matching-distance lesson and the severe-harm-needs-distance kernel with the sandbox-distance lesson that games must use walk distance, not straight-line, for a gradient.
- Design: A 5 x 7 grid of framings from a grounded start, with walls as steps that cannot be skipped. A beat lands if its harm is at most the true walk distance. Estimators: rounded Euclid distance versus BFS. Metrics: share of the distance budget used, and order inversions (a beat with a lower estimate but a longer true walk, so the escalation order is wrong). Walled and open maps.
- Got right: BFS used 100 percent of the budget with 0 order inversions on both maps; every beat landed under both estimators since straight-line is a lower bound and never overshoots.
- Where/why it failed: On the walled map the Euclid estimate used only 0.54 of the budget and produced 56 order inversions, so escalation went small and in the wrong order. On the open map it still used only 0.78 and had 6 inversions, so the break case did not make Euclid correct. A first version of the script scored only landing and found no difference; landing was the wrong metric.
- Fix: Measure framing distance as steps through the framing map (BFS from the grounded start), and score both budget used and order inversions rather than whether beats land.
- Why this fix: Straight-line distance can only undershoot, so it never fails a landing check but silently wastes headroom and scrambles the escalation, which only the budget and inversion metrics show.
- Rule of thumb: Measure a comedy framing's distance as walk steps (BFS), not straight-line: Euclid landed 25/25 beats but used 0.54 of the budget with 56 order inversions on a walled map and 0.78 with 6 on an open one, so score headroom and order, not just landing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the framing grid and harm-equals-estimate rule are a model of the lesson, not measured audience reactions.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, sandbox-distance/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__comedy-distance-bfs-vs-euclid.py
- Prediction: Assumed the BFS-versus-Euclid finding from game levels transfers to comedy framings. Predicted Euclid uses well under 80 percent of the distance budget on the walled map with many order inversions, BFS exactly 100 percent and 0 inversions, and the open map narrows the gap. Wrong if Euclid matched BFS on the walled map.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS wall map Euclid uses 0.54 of the distance budget with 56 order inversions vs BFS 1.00/0; open map Euclid 0.78/6
- Scenarios: 1) walled map, Euclid; 2) walled map, BFS; 3) BREAK: open map, Euclid (expected to close the gap, only partly did); 4) open map, BFS
- Link: brain train auto pass 2 (loop 2); session_01GnLNLCEidq8XM63uFxhmgu

## E338 — beat sheet sidecar drift
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tooling][comedy][testing][sandbox]
- What: Toy beat sheet whose game-of-the-scene check column is kept three ways (hand-typed sidecar by index, sidecar by name, derived from each beat) and then edited by append, insert, delete and reorder.
- Why built: The gap picker paired the collective-reference lesson (a hand-kept sidecar drifts silently), the film lessons about editing a hard-coded timeline, and the check-column lesson; test whether the sidecar-drift rule holds for a beat sheet.
- Design: 8 beats, each with a derived-from-game flag that is also the truth. A verdict counts wrong when the shown value differs from truth or is missing. Sidecars are built once from the original sheet; each edit is applied to a fresh copy.
- Got right: The derived column was wrong 0 times after all four edits (0/9, 0/9, 0/7, 0/8), and a name-keyed sidecar survived delete and reorder with 0 wrong.
- Where/why it failed: The index-keyed sidecar went wrong on 5/9 after a mid insert, 5/7 after deleting the first beat and 4/8 after a reversal, even a single append left 1/9 unlabeled; the name-keyed sidecar also left 1 missing verdict on every added beat (1/9 after the append and insert), so naming the key only fixes moves, not new beats.
- Fix: Derive the check column from the beat record itself at render time; if a sidecar must exist, key it by a stable beat name and fail loudly on a beat with no entry.
- Why this fix: Derivation has no second copy to drift, while a stable-key sidecar fixes position drift but still cannot know about a new beat.
- Rule of thumb: Derive per-beat verdicts from the beat itself: an index-keyed sidecar was wrong on up to 5 of 9 beats after one insert or delete, a name-keyed one still missed every added beat, and the derived column stayed 0 wrong across all four edits.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the beat data and edits are synthetic and the claim about a real tool chain is not tested.
- Composed: collective-reference/E1, film/E7, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__beat-sheet-sidecar-drift.py
- Prediction: Assumed the sidecar-drift lesson transfers to ordered lists, where index keys fail. Predicted the index sidecar is wrong on at least half the beats after an insert, the name sidecar survives moves but not additions, and derived stays 0. Wrong if the name sidecar also failed on a pure reorder.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS derived 0 wrong on all 4 edits; index sidecar wrong 5 after an insert and 4 after a reorder; name sidecar 0 on delete/reorder but 1 missing on every added beat
- Scenarios: 1) append at end; 2) insert at position 3; 3) delete first beat; 4) BREAK: reverse order, built to defeat a name-keyed sidecar (it survived)
- Link: brain train auto pass 5 (loop 2); session_01GnLNLCEidq8XM63uFxhmgu

The derived column is computed by truth(b), which is the same function that defines the ground truth, so its 0 wrong on all four edits holds by construction and the rule's central claim (derived stayed 0 wrong) is assumed, not tested; no real derivation step that could disagree with the beat was modeled. The index and name sidecar counts (5/9 after an insert, 1 missing per added beat) are genuinely computed and correct, but they only show that a copy keyed by position or name drifts, which the earlier collective-reference lesson already established. The sheet is one 8-beat fixture and None is counted as wrong by definition, so scope covers less than a rule about derived verdicts in general. · brain train auto pass 3 (loop 1), audit session; session_01S9MKv7QKGDb1fdsYzjZeah

## E337 — bayer levels check column scale
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [film][dither][viewport][sandbox]
- What: Toy model encoding 17 graded check-column verdict levels as 4x4 Bayer one-bit swatches and viewing them at integer and non-integer scales.
- Why built: The gap picker paired the film lessons and the check-column lesson with the Bayer-4x4-gives-17-levels kernel; test whether a dithered grading survives the viewport scaling that film work already hits.
- Design: A pixel is on when its Bayer threshold is below the level. Nearest-neighbour scaling by 1x, 2x, 3x, 1.5x and 2.5x; for each scale count the distinct mean brightnesses among the 17 levels, taking the worst case over all window phases where a fixed 4-pixel window fits (integer scales read the whole swatch at its aligned phase).
- Got right: At 1x, 2x and 3x all 17 levels stayed distinct (17/17), matching the kernel claim.
- Where/why it failed: At 1.5x the worst phase kept only 10/17 distinct levels and at 2.5x only 5/17, because nearest-neighbour repeats some rows and columns unevenly, so a fixed window sees different pixel counts per level. A first metric that required uniqueness at every phase scored 0/17 and an unclipped window scored 2/17 from edge clipping; I corrected the metric to full windows only.
- Fix: Scale dithered swatches by whole-number factors only (floor to an integer inside the safe box), or render the grading as flat grey levels when the scale cannot be an integer.
- Why this fix: The integer scale keeps each swatch pixel a uniform block, so the Bayer threshold structure and its 17 levels are preserved, which matches the integer-scale rule already in brain-creative-training E16.
- Rule of thumb: A 4x4 Bayer swatch gives 17 readable levels only at integer scale (17/17 at 1x to 3x, 10/17 at 1.5x, 5/17 at 2.5x worst-phase), so floor to an integer scale before using dither levels to carry meaning.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the metric is mean brightness in a fixed window, a stand-in for how a viewer reads a swatch, not a perception study.
- Composed: ideas:ART/bayer-4x4-gives-17-levels-from-two-colours, film/E11, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1, brain-creative-training/E16
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__bayer-levels-check-column-scale.py
- Prediction: Assumed the 17 levels are a property of the matrix alone. Predicted 17/17 at integer scales and clearly fewer (under 15) at 1.5x and 2.5x; wrong if non-integer scales also kept 17/17.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS integer scales worst-phase 17/17, 1.5x worst-phase 10/17, 2.5x keeps 5/17
- Scenarios: 1) native 1x; 2) integer 2x; 3) integer 3x; 4) BREAK: non-integer 1.5x; 5) non-integer 2.5x
- Link: brain train auto pass 5 (loop 1); session_01GnLNLCEidq8XM63uFxhmgu
- Audited: 2026-10-17 · modeled · Read the entry and its stored sandbox. The sandbox genuinely computes the counts (nearest-neighbour scaling, window means, worst phase), so the numbers are not built in. But the comparison is asymmetric: integer scales read the whole scaled swatch at one aligned phase, where distinct levels follow trivially from the on-pixel count, while 1.5x and 2.5x read a fixed 4px window at every phase. Window size and phase are therefore confounded with scale, and integer scales were never tried with a misaligned fixed window. The rule's scope (a viewer reading swatches as meaning) is also only a mean-brightness stand-in, not a real renderer or perception test, so the verdict is modeled rather than pass. · brain train auto loop 1 pass 3 audit session (session_01PTu5uBJqYTUhgm91RqrjQ3)

## E336 — ai label default vs cartoon skip
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ai-video][disclosure][compliance][sandbox]
- What: Toy model of AI-video label policies over 22 videos (11 realism levels, product exact or not): label always, skip only clear cartoons, or skip all but the most photoreal.
- Why built: Test the kernel pair about turning the platform AI label on by default versus skipping it for obvious cartoons, and whether the label alone makes a video compliant.
- Design: A detector flags realism at or above a threshold (5 or 7 tried); viewers are misled by an unlabeled video at realism 6 or more; a wrong product counts separately. Policies label videos at or above their skip threshold (0, 4, 8).
- Got right: Label always and skip-below-4 both gave 0/22 unlabeled-but-flagged and 0/22 viewers misled against either detector, so skipping only clear cartoons costs nothing in the model.
- Where/why it failed: Skip-below-8 left 6/22 flagged videos unlabeled against a detector at 5 and 2/22 at 7 (4/22 viewers misled in both); my first guess of 0 at detector 7 was wrong because realism 7 videos slip through. The label also never touched the 11/22 wrong-product videos under any policy.
- Fix: Default the label on, allow the cartoon exemption only below a conservative realism line (the model's 4, well under any detector setting), and keep the product accuracy check as a separate gate.
- Why this fix: The exemption only stays safe while its threshold sits below the strictest plausible detector, and the label and accuracy rules fail independently.
- Rule of thumb: Set the cartoon exemption below the strictest detector line (0/22 misses at 4, 2 to 6/22 at 8) and keep product accuracy as its own check, because labelling left 11/22 wrong-product videos untouched.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; detector thresholds and the misled line are model parameters, not platform measurements.

## E334 — rule card does not replace matched distance
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][testing]
- What: In a seeded gag model, a rule card (humiliated-not-harmed, victim never wins) lifted precision from 0.103 to 0.333 under a fixed grounded framing, but a go-big schedule still produced only 37 funny beats against 111 for a mild schedule; only matching the framing distance to severity restored 111 funny beats at precision 1.000.
- Why built: Test whether the write-the-rules-before-the-gags card makes the escalation-distance limit unnecessary, since both claim to keep a beat benign.
- Design: Python stdlib sandbox, 6 beats of 60 seeded gags each; a gag is funny only if it is humiliation, the victim does not win, and severity is within the framing distance. Five runs: no card, card with grounded distance 2 on a go-big schedule, card with grounded distance on a mild schedule, card with matched distance on go-big, and a partial card (drops the harm rule) as the breaker.
- Got right: The card and the distance dial act on different axes, which the numbers separate cleanly: the card changes which gags are shown (360 down to 111), the distance changes how big a beat may be.
- Where/why it failed: The first run used a benign test that ignored harm type, so the partial-card breaker showed precision 1.000 and the prediction failed; the model had to treat injury and a winning victim as never benign before the card's role showed up.
- Fix: Make the ground-truth benign test independent of the card, so the card is only a filter; rerun gave partial-card precision 0.483 (111 funny of 230 shown).
- Why this fix: A filter can only be scored against a truth that does not use the filter; otherwise every card variant looks perfect.
- Rule of thumb: Use both: the rule card to choose which gags are admitted and a framing distance matched to each beat's severity; in this model the card alone left a go-big schedule at 37 funny against 111, and a card missing the harm rule dropped precision to 0.483.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox twice; the gag model and its probabilities are my own simplification, not measured audience data.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__rule-card-does-not-replace-matched-distance.py
- Prediction: Assumption: the rule card already guarantees benignness, so distance matters less. Expected card at grounded distance to leave go-big funny below mild funny, matched distance to give at least 2x the grounded go-big count, and the partial card to fall below precision 1.0 at matched distance. Iteration 1 FAILED on the last point (model flaw), iteration 2 matched all three.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS grounded-big=37 grounded-mild=111 matched-big=111 partial-card precision=0.483
- Scenarios: 1) no card, grounded, go-big; 2) card, grounded, go-big; 3) card, grounded, mild; 4) card, matched, go-big; 5) partial card, matched, go-big, built to break the claim that the card alone is sufficient

## E333 — distance dial is two sided for mild beats
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][testing]
- What: With a two-sided distance band (a beat is funny only when framing distance is within 1 of the severity it needs), matching distance to each beat gave 130 funny of 130 shown, a fixed grounded framing 64, and a fixed maximum distance 66; applying maximum distance to a mild schedule gave 0 funny where grounded gave 130.
- Why built: The earlier rule-card sandbox modelled distance one-sidedly (severity at most distance), but the severe-harm kernel also says mild harm needs closeness, so a flat go-distant shortcut should hurt mild beats.
- Design: Python stdlib sandbox, 6 beats of 60 seeded gags each, rule card applied first (humiliation only, victim never wins). Five runs: go-big schedule with matched, grounded (2) and maximum (5) distance; mild schedule with maximum and grounded distance, the maximum-distance mild run being the breaker.
- Got right: The two-sided band separates the shortcuts cleanly: maximum distance rescued only the two severity-5 beats (66 funny) and wiped every mild beat (0 funny), so a single framing dial cannot be set once for a whole piece.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed in the run, but the band is my own modelled rule (width 1), so it encodes the kernel instead of measuring an audience; the result shows the kernel's consequence for schedules, not that the band is the right width.
- Fix: Set the framing distance per beat from the beat's severity, rising and falling with it, instead of one global surreal or grounded setting.
- Why this fix: A global setting fixes one end of the severity range and breaks the other, which the grounded run (64) and maximum run (66) both showed.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the distance dial worked per beat, not per piece: matched distance scored 130 of 130, while one fixed setting scored 64 to 66 on a rising schedule and a maximum setting scored 0 on a mild one.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and reading its printed counts.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY/severe-harm-needs-distance-mild-harm-needs-closeness, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, rule-card-does-not-replace-matched-distance/E1
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__distance-dial-is-two-sided-for-mild-beats.py
- Prediction: Assumption: a high distance setting is a safe default because it only costs mild beats a little. ## E332 — device integer scale in safe box fill cost
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [rendering][dither][viewport][mobile][sandbox]
- What: Fitting a 320x180 pixel frame into a 90% safe box on six viewport and pixel-ratio pairs, flooring the scale in CSS px gave a non-integer device scale on 2 of 6 (2.625 and 1.5), flooring in device px gave 0 of 6, but on the 360x640 ratio-1.5 phone the device floor dropped fill from 98.8% to 65.8%.
- Why built: Check the recorded device-px floor lesson against the safe-title lesson and the one-grid integer-scale kernel, and measure what the integer guarantee costs in fill.
- Design: Python stdlib sandbox over six pairs (390x844 at 3, 412x915 at 2.625, 768x1024 at 2, 1536x864 at 1.25, 1920x1080 at 1, 360x640 at 1.5), safe box 90% of each viewport, two scale rules (floor in CSS px, floor in device px), reporting device scale, fill of the limiting axis, integer-ness and overflow.
- Got right: Neither rule overflowed the safe box on any device, and the device-px floor kept every scale an exact integer, which supports the earlier lesson.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of 3 non-integer CSS-floor devices was wrong, because the 1.25 laptop floors to CSS scale 4 which is exactly 5 device px; only two devices broke. The prediction line printed FAIL on the first and only run.
- Fix: Keep the device-px floor for exact pixel blocks, and accept or work around the fill loss on small-ratio phones, for example by letting the art bleed past the safe box into its non-critical border.
- Why this fix: The integer guarantee is the point of the rule, and the cost only shows as lower fill (65.8%) on the one device where one extra device pixel of scale would not fit.
- Rule of thumb: Floor the scale in device px so blocks stay integer, but check fill per device: in this run it cost nothing on five of six devices and lost 33 points of fill on the 360x640 phone at ratio 1.5, where the CSS floor would be 1.5 and fractional.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox once; the viewport and ratio pairs are typical values I chose, not a measured device census.
- Composed: ideas:MOTION/safe-title-and-action-margins-90-93-percent, brain-creative-training/E30, ideas:ART/one-grid-integer-scale-no-mixels

- Prediction: Assumption: the device-px floor is a free fix. Expected the CSS floor to be non-integer on 3 of 6 devices, the device floor on 0, no overflow for either, and a fill penalty on at least one device. The 3 was wrong (observed 2); the other three points held.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL css-floor non-integer on 2 of 6, device-floor on 0 of 6, overflow 0/0 (the FAIL is the original count of 3; device-floor fill 65.8% vs 98.8% on the 1.5 phone)
- Scenarios: 1) ratio 3 phone; 2) ratio 2.625 phone; 3) ratio 2 tablet; 4) ratio 1.25 laptop, which broke the expected count; 5) ratio 1 desktop; 6) ratio 1.5 small phone, the case where the fix costs fill

- Why built: Test whether the broadcast safe-zone kernel plus the TikTok strictest-per-edge figures are enough to place a six-row check-column caption stack for a comedy sketch.

Four layouts: 90% title-safe anchored low, 93% action-safe anchored low, strict per-edge centred in the free band, and a strict layout with a 900 px wide row as the breaker.
- Got right: The strict per-edge layout cleared the overlay for all 6 rows; the wide-row breaker failed the side margin (right edge 1020 against 960) on all 6, showing width must be checked as well as height.

- Why this fix: The per-edge numbers fix the overlay problem but not the crop problem; only the intersection of both constraints gives a box every viewer can read.
- Rule of thumb: For a caption stack over vertical video, use the strictest per-edge overlay margins and then intersect with the narrowest crop you care about; the percentage safe zones tested here (90 and 93) did not clear the bottom overlay.

## E330 — bayer reveal beats need sixteen divisible and world anchor
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [film][video][dither][sandbox][viewport]
- What: A Bayer 4x4 tone reveal gives 17 distinct densities, but cutting it into equal check-column beats gave level steps 4,4,4,4 for 4 beats and 2 each for 8, while 6 beats gave 3,2,3,3,2,3; and a pattern anchored to the screen instead of the world differed in 384 of 384 pixels at crop offset 285 (offset mod 4 is 1) but in 0 at offsets 0, 420 and 656.
- Why built: Test whether a dithered reveal tied to a six-row game-of-the-scene check column keeps equal beats across the four vertical-video crops from the film safe-zone lesson.
- Design: Python stdlib sandbox with the standard 4x4 Bayer matrix; tone level 8 rendered on a 16 by 24 pixel patch for each crop offset (0, 285, 420, 656 rows), once with the matrix indexed by world coordinates and once by crop coordinates; beat steps from rounding 16 times i over the beat count.
- Got right: The 17-level count holds exactly, and the world anchor gave zero difference at every offset by construction, matching the earlier lesson that anchoring to world space keeps the pattern fixed.
- Where/why it failed: Six beats do not divide the 16 level steps, so the beats alternate 3 and 2 levels and are visibly unequal in tone; the screen-anchored render also flipped the whole checker at the 285 crop because its offset is not a multiple of 4.
- Fix: Choose a beat count that divides 16 (4 or 8) for equal tone steps, and index the matrix by world coordinates, or snap crop offsets to multiples of 4.
- Why this fix: Equal steps need an integer step; the matrix period is 4 so only offsets that are multiples of 4 leave a screen-anchored pattern unchanged.
- Rule of thumb: For a Bayer 4x4 reveal over cropped video, use 4 or 8 beats and index the matrix by world coordinates; in this run 6 beats gave steps of 3 and 2 and a screen-anchored pattern changed all 384 pixels at the 285 offset.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the crop offsets come from the recorded film lesson and the check-column rows are modelled as beats, not a real sketch sheet.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS densities=17 six-beat steps=[3, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3] offset285 diff=384 px
- Scenarios: 1) 17-density count over one tile; 2) 4 beats; 3) 8 beats; 4) 6 beats, built to break the any-beat-count assumption; 5) four crop offsets with screen versus world anchoring

## E329 — rule card must pin distance per beat
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][process]
- What: A gag rule card only supports going big if it also pins the framing distance for every beat, including callbacks; otherwise a later beat in a plain setting turns benign harm into plain harm.
- Why built: To test whether a rule card written before the gags, combined with benign violation and distance-matched escalation, lets a go-big schedule beat a mild one.
- Design: Scored 5-beat schedules by a toy model where a beat is funny for its severity if it is a violation (severity 2 or more) and benign (severity no more than distance), and counted harm beats where severity exceeds distance; compared a fixed distance of 2 against card-matched distance, and a callback break where distance resets.
- Got right: At fixed distance 2 the go-big schedule scored 2 funny with 4 harm beats against 10 for flat-mild, while card-matched distance gave go-big 19 funny and 0 harm in all three schedules.
- Where/why it failed: The break schedule, where callback beats reset distance to 2 after severe beats, left 2 harm beats and only 10 funny, so a card that fixes the world but not per-beat distance does not protect callbacks. The funny function is built from the benign rule, so this tests the bookkeeping of the composition, not audience laughter.
- Fix: Add a distance line per beat (and per callback) to the rule card, and check every beat for severity no more than distance before scheduling the escalation.
- Why this fix: Benign violation needs both halves perceived at the same moment, so the distance has to be stated where each beat lands, not once for the premise.
- Rule of thumb: When a rule card licenses escalation, write the framing distance beside each beat and callback; in the tested schedules matched distance gave 0 harm beats and 19 vs 10 funny, while a reset callback brought back 2 harm beats.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the scoring model is hand-written from the benign-violation rule and was not checked against human raters.
- Composed: brain-auto-training/E9, escalation-needs-matching-distance/E1, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/write-the-rules-before-the-gags, ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/benign-violation
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__rule-card-sets-distance-for-escalation.py
- Prediction: Assumed benign means severity does not exceed distance; expected go-big to score below flat-mild at fixed distance 2 and above it when matched, with 0 harm beats in every matched schedule; would be wrong if go-big won at fixed distance or matched left harm beats.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS fixed d=2: go-big 2 vs mild 10 funny; card-matched: go-big 19, harm 0 in 3/3 schedules; callback break leaves 2 harm beats.
- Scenarios: 1) flat-mild; 2) go-big; 3) go-big-late; 4) built to break: callback beats reset distance to 2 after severe beats.

## E328 — reveal ramp needs game derived beats
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [narrative][dither][testing][sandbox]
- What: A Bayer 4x4 reveal (17 tone levels) driven by a comedy beat sheet only keeps a readable ramp if beats advance it on the "derived from the game" check, not on "any new noun".
- Why built: To test whether the information-gap kernel, the game-of-scene check column and the 17-level Bayer reveal compose when one beat sheet schedules the level changes.
- Design: Built Bayer 4x4 by recursion (asserted equal to the hand matrix, 17 distinct lit counts), then ran three beat sheets (pure heighten, jump, stock premise) under a naive any-new-noun advance rule and a derived-from-game rule, step 4 levels per advancing beat, cap 15 until the final reveal beat sets 16.
- Got right: Neither rule closed the gap early because the cap holds level 15 before the last beat; the derived rule left the jump and stock sheets at level 8, so the final reveal still has 8 levels of visible change.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction said the naive rule would saturate 2 of 3 sheets; it saturated 3 of 3, because jump and stock beats carry new nouns and so also advanced it. The derived rule under-advances a true heighten that also adds a noun (12 vs 15).
- Fix: Advance the reveal on beats labelled derived-from-game, and label a heighten that introduces a noun as derived explicitly instead of inferring it from noun count.
- Why this fix: The noun-count signal is the same mislabel the check column already showed; an explicit derived flag separates heightening from jumping and keeps the ramp spread across the whole sheet.
- Rule of thumb: Schedule Bayer reveal levels from game-derived beats, not new-noun beats; on the sheets tested the naive rule saturated 3/3 while the derived rule saturated 1/3.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; real viewer perception of the ramp is not covered here.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS naive capped 3/3 sheets vs derived 1/3; derived under-advances noun-bearing heighten (12 vs 15). Prediction missed on naive (3 not 2).

## E327 — distance card needs both ends
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][humor][sandbox][process]
- What: A per-beat distance card has to hold both ends of the harm rule, close enough for mild harm and far enough for severe harm, so a single safe distance chosen for the worst beat spoils the mild ones.
- Why built: To test the severe-harm-needs-distance and mild-harm-needs-closeness kernel together with distance-matched escalation and the per-beat rule card from the earlier sandbox.
- Design: Defined benign as distance 3 or less for severity 2 or less and distance at least severity for severity 3 or more; scored three 5-beat schedules under a constant near card (2), a constant far card (5) and a matched card that raises distance only with severity.
- Got right: The matched card scored 51 funny and 0 harm beats over the three schedules, against 12 funny and 9 harm for constant 2 and 39 funny and 6 harm for constant 5.
- Where/why it failed: The far constant, the obvious fix after the last sandbox, fixed the severe beats but put mild beats at distance 5, which the closeness rule rejects, leaving 6 harm beats; the matched card meets the rule largely because it is built from it, so this checks bookkeeping, not audience reaction.
- Fix: Set distance per beat from that beat's severity band, near for mild and far for severe, instead of one distance for the whole premise.
- Why this fix: The two kernels pull in opposite directions on distance, so only a value chosen per beat can satisfy both.
- Rule of thumb: Do not pin one safe distance to cover the worst beat; give each beat its own distance by severity band, since a far constant still produced 6 harm beats across three schedules.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the benign thresholds are stated assumptions taken from the two kernels, not measured with raters.

## E326 — bayer levels split by remainder over derived beats
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [film][dither][narrative][sandbox]
- What: When a film beat sheet's game-derived beats drive a Bayer 4x4 reveal, split the 16 level changes with a largest-remainder rule, not floor(16/k), or the reveal stalls short of full.
- Why built: To test the film reveal schedule and the game-of-scene derived-beat count together with the 17-state Bayer ramp, since k derived beats rarely divide 16.
- Design: Built the matrix recursively (16 distinct thresholds asserted), then for each derived-beat count k from 1 to 16 compared a floor split with a remainder split that gives the first (16 mod k) beats one extra level; k 17 to 20 was the break case.
- Got right: The remainder split reached level 16 for all 16 counts with a max step spread of 1, so no beat is visibly bigger than another by more than one tone level.
- Where/why it failed: The floor split left a residual for 11 of 16 counts (every k except 1, 2, 4, 8, 16), so the final reveal had to jump several levels at once; above 16 derived beats some beats cannot change the image at all.
- Fix: Allocate level changes by largest remainder across derived beats, and cap the number of reveal-driving beats at 16 so no beat is idle.
- Why this fix: Levels are integers and only 16 changes exist, so the arithmetic, not taste, sets the schedule; the remainder rule is the smallest change that keeps the ramp even and complete.
- Rule of thumb: Spread 16 Bayer level changes over k derived beats by largest remainder (steps differ by at most 1) and never use more than 16 reveal beats; floor division stalls on 11 of 16 counts.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script over k 1 to 20; how the ramp looks to viewers was not tested.
- Composed: film/E184, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1, ideas:ART/bayer-4x4-gives-17-levels-from-two-colours

- Prediction: Assumed derived-beat counts are usually non-divisors of 16; expected floor to fall short for exactly 11 of 16 counts and remainder for 0; wrong if floor failed for a different count or the remainder spread exceeded 1.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS floor stalls short of level 16 for 11/16 beat counts, remainder split 0/16, spread<=1, k>16 yields idle beats.
- Scenarios: 1) k 1 to 16 floor split; 2) k 1 to 16 remainder split; 3) step-spread check across all k; 4) built to break: k 17 to 20, where idle beats appear.

## E325 — specific turn payoff needs misdirection not waiting
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [comedy][narrative][testing][sandbox]
- What: Modelled a sketch audience as an exact Bayesian over the stock turn and the writer's specific turn to see what produces payoff at the reveal: waiting, misdirection, or a stock payoff.
- Why built: The hack-premise check wants a specific turn, the information-gap kernel says tension is the order and rationing of information, and the H/E/X column wants every beat to stay in one game; I wanted to see how the three fit.
- Design: Four hypotheses (stock, specific, two others) with a 0.5 or 0.9 stock prior. Beats are likelihood vectors: neutral (fits both), misdirecting (favors stock but the specific turn explains it at a fair-play likelihood) and stock-pointing. Reveal surprisal is -log2 of the posterior of the payoff hypothesis; gap is posterior entropy before the reveal.
- Got right: A stock payoff scored 0.00 bits, so the hack check is right that a stock payoff has no surprise; neutral beats left the specific-turn surprisal flat at 4.91 bits for 0, 2 and 4 beats.
- Where/why it failed: Waiting with neutral beats builds nothing (a rationing of information alone does not raise surprise); misdirection raised it from 4.91 to 11.70 bits at four beats but closed the pre-reveal gap (entropy 0.63 to 0.01), so surprise and sustained curiosity trade off. With fair-play likelihood below 0.1 the extra bits (up to 31.33) come from beats the specific turn no longer explains, which the H/E/X column would mark X.
- Fix: Spend the setup beats on misdirection that the specific turn still explains (fair-play at or above about 0.1 in this model), not on neutral delay, and let the check column's X mark catch beats that fall below that.
- Why this fix: Only a beat that shifts audience belief toward the stock form adds to the reveal surprisal, while the fair-play bound keeps each beat inside the sketch's one game.
- Rule of thumb: In this model delay alone gives zero extra surprise and misdirection gives more than double, so write setup beats that point at the stock form yet remain explainable by the specific turn, and treat the 0.1 fair-play line as an assumed cutoff, not a measured one.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the Bayes model, likelihood values and the 0.1 fair-play cutoff are my own assumptions, so no real audience or sketch was tested.
- Composed: ideas:COMEDY-CRAFT/hack-premise-check, game-of-scene-hxe-check-column/E1, ideas:SYSTEM/narrative/tension-as-information-gap
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__specific-turn-payoff-needs-misdirection-not-waiting.py
- Prediction: Assumed waiting under an information gap raises the payoff; predicted neutral delay would add some bits and misdirection more. The neutral-delay part would be wrong if surprisal stayed flat, and the stock payoff would be wrong if it scored above 0.5 bits.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS waiting with neutral clues leaves the specific-turn surprisal flat at 4.91 bits for n=0,2,4; misdirection raises it 4.91 -> 11.70 bits at n=4 (fair=0.3) and stock-payoff stays 0.00 bits; below fair=0.1 the extra bits come from clues the turn no longer explains
- Scenarios: 1) stock payoff; 2) neutral delay (built to BREAK the waiting guess, which it did); 3) misdirection at fair-play 0.3; 4) fair-play sweep 0.5, 0.3, 0.1, 0.01

## E324 — signature greedy big first optimal only on chain sizes
- Date: 2026-10-16
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [packing][algorithm][sandbox]
- What: Seeded a bookbinding domain by testing a largest-first plan for covering N pages with folded signatures against an exact dynamic-programming optimum, for two size sets.
- Why built: A simple greedy is how people plan signatures, but whether it wastes blank pages or extra signatures was not recorded, and the nearby packing kernel says big-first only usually wins.
- Design: Sizes are multiples of 4. A greedy takes the largest size that fits and pads the last remainder up to the smallest size; an exact DP minimises blanks first, then signature count. Compared over N = 1..240 for a chain set (4, 8, 16, 32) and a non-chain set (16, 12, 4), plus a merge fix that folds equal small signatures upward. Imposition spreads were also checked for sizes 4, 8, 16, 32.
- Got right: Raw greedy used the minimum blanks at all 240 page counts for both sets, and the spreads of each size used every page once with each spread summing to s+1.
- Where/why it failed: The raw greedy used extra signatures at 90 of 240 page counts for the chain set (for example 5 pages as 4+4 instead of one 8) and 146 of 240 for the non-chain set; after the merge fix the chain set had 0 misses but the non-chain set still had 101.
- Fix: Add a tail-merge pass for equal small signatures; for size sets that are not a divisibility chain, use the exact DP instead of a greedy.
- Why this fix: Blanks are fixed by the smallest size, so the only freedom left is the signature count, and merging equal tails removes the chain-case loss; non-chain sizes cannot be merged cleanly, so only the DP is exact.
- Rule of thumb: Largest-first with a 4-page size keeps blanks at the minimum, but needs a tail merge for the signature count to reach the optimum on chain sizes (0 misses of 240) and the exact DP on non-chain sizes (101 of 240 still missed).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the imposition spread rule was checked by the model's own invariants and not by folding real paper, and sizes beyond 240 pages were not tried.
- Composed: ideas:PACKING/bin-packing/first-fit-decreasing-beats-first-fit-on-average-but-not-on-every-list, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/a-coarse-proxy-agrees-with-truth-only-where-they-coincide, ideas:BOOKBINDING/signature-planning/cover-n-pages-with-folded-signatures
- Picked-by: new-half
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-16__signature-greedy-big-first-optimal-only-on-chain-sizes.py
- Prediction: Assumed largest-first is optimal on a divisibility chain; predicted zero losses on 4, 8, 16, 32 and some on 16, 12, 4. This was wrong for the chain set (90 losses in signature count), though blanks were minimal everywhere.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS largest-first used the minimum blanks for both size sets (0 of 240 extra) but extra signatures at 90 (chain) and 146 (non-chain); folding equal small signatures upward fixes the chain set to 0 but leaves 101 of 240 for sizes (16, 12, 4)
- Scenarios: 1) chain sizes, raw greedy; 2) non-chain sizes, raw greedy (built to BREAK it); 3) both with the merge fix; 4) imposition invariants for 4, 8, 16, 32
