## E223 — zero allow history needs a benign canary
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [security][governance][testing][sandbox][design]
- What: Sandbox of a score-threshold gate showing that a zero-allow history over 20 messages is produced both by a calibrated gate fed all-risky traffic and by a hold-everything gate fed mixed traffic, and that replaying one known-benign canary separates them.
- Why built: The kernel says zero allows across a held history is its own signal and to tell a risky message from a miscalibrated gate; I wanted to find where the count alone stops being enough.
- Design: Gate allows below a risk score and holds at or above it; two gates (threshold 70, and threshold 0 that holds all); three deterministic 20-message histories (all risky, mixed, all benign); a benign canary at score 10 replayed through each gate; a binary-search prober against a gate whose hold response differs by score.
- Got right: The zero-allow count flagged the broken gate on the mixed and benign histories, and the canary separated calibrated from miscalibrated in 3 of 3 histories.
- Where/why it failed: On the all-risky history both gates showed zero allows, so the count was ambiguous in 1 of 3 histories. The prober also recovered the threshold (70) in 7 probes from the allow-versus-hold differences alone.
- Fix: Treat zero-allow as a trigger to replay a known-benign canary through the gate, and do not read the count alone; keep the hold response uniform so probing the gate reveals nothing about its threshold.
- Why this fix: The canary has a known right answer, so it tests the gate itself instead of the traffic; a uniform response removes the readout that the prober used.
- Rule of thumb: When a gate has allowed nothing, replay a benign canary before blaming the messages or the gate, and never let the hold response vary with the hidden threshold.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the identical-acknowledgement case is true by construction (the response ignores the score) and the gate is a one-threshold toy, so real gates with several signals were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SECURITY/governance-signal/zero-allow-across-a-held-history-is-its-own-signal, mirage/E5, collective/E14
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-14__zero-allow-history-needs-a-benign-canary.py
- Prediction: Zero-allow would be ambiguous in the all-risky history only, a benign canary would separate the two gates in 3 of 3 histories, and a binary-search prober would recover the threshold in 7 probes.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS zero-allow ambiguous in 1/3 histories (all-risky), canary separates 3/3, distinct hold leaks threshold in 7 probes, identical ack leaks none
- Scenarios: 1) all-risky history (built to BREAK the count-alone reading); 2) mixed history; 3) all-benign history; 4) prober against a distinct hold response
- Link: brain train auto pass 5, 2026-10-14; session_01Fej6hmi1TecJBFrsQdbvMU

## E222 — wfc restart rescues only satisfiable tilesets
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][gamedesign][procgen][testing][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of eager-propagation WFC without backtracking on all 560 three-tile sets (4-socket tiles, 4x4 grid), measuring which first-try contradictions a deterministic restart (up to 8 attempts) rescues.
- Why built: The earlier WFC lesson says keep restart after no-backtracking contradictions; I wanted to know how much restart actually buys and where it stops helping.
- Design: Tiles are (N,E,S,W) sockets in {0,1}; propagation runs to a fixpoint; the collapse choice is keyed by attempt number so restarts are deterministic; an exhaustive backtracking solver labels each unrescued set satisfiable or not.
- Got right: 409 of 560 sets completed on the first try, and restart rescued 37 of the 151 first-try failures.
- Where/why it failed: 104 of the 114 never-rescued sets have no valid 4x4 grid at all, so no number of restarts could help; 10 satisfiable sets were still lost within 8 restarts.
- Fix: Run an exhaustive or constraint pre-check (or cap restarts and report the set as unsatisfiable) before looping on restarts; keep a backtracking fallback for the rare satisfiable-but-lost sets.
- Why this fix: Restart only re-rolls collapse choices, so it cannot repair a tileset with no solution and wastes the whole budget; the pre-check is cheap on small grids.
- Rule of thumb: Treat restart as a rescue for unlucky collapse order only (about a quarter of failures here); cap it and pre-check satisfiability, because most persistent failures are unsatisfiable tilesets.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox over all 560 sets; the rescue ratio is specific to this tile model and 4x4 grid and was not tested at other sizes.
- Composed: ideas:PROCGEN/wave-function-collapse/eager-propagation-prevents-more-contradictions-than-tutorials-suggest, 2026-10-13__wfc-no-backtracking-contradicts-on-non-self-compatible-tilesets-and-completes-disconnected/E1, sandbox-procgen-wfc/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-14__wfc-restart-rescues-only-satisfiable-tilesets.py
- Prediction: Restart would rescue under half of first-try failures, and some never-rescued sets would be provably unsatisfiable.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS restart rescued 37/151; 104 unrescuable sets have no solution at all, 10 satisfiable ones still lost
- Scenarios: 1) first attempt over all 560 sets; 2) up to 8 deterministic restarts; 3) exhaustive solver on every unrescued set (built to BREAK the idea that restart always eventually works)
- Link: brain train auto pass 2, 2026-10-14; session_01Fej6hmi1TecJBFrsQdbvMU
- Audited: 2026-10-16 · pass · Read E222 and ran its stored sandbox, which reproduced 560 sets, 409 first-try completions, 37 of 151 failures rescued within 8 restarts, and 104 unsatisfiable plus 10 satisfiable never-rescued sets. The satisfiability label comes from a separate exhaustive backtracking solver rather than from the WFC run itself, so the claim that most persistent failures are unsatisfiable is computed, not assumed. The Rule of thumb ("about a quarter", cap and pre-check) matches the tested scope; the 4x4 grid, 4-socket model and eight deterministic attempts bound it, which the entry states, so this is a pass for that scope only. · scheduled brain train auto session, loop 2 audit pass; session_01K2o9Pz3SxQVCm2V4Z7ZhLe

## E221 — tides third constituent alternates spring heights
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tides][simulation][numerics][testing][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox adding an N2 constituent (12.658 h, amplitude 0.2 of M2) to the M2 plus S2 tide, measuring the spacing and height of successive spring peaks of the daily range over 240 days of hourly heights.
- Why built: The tides kernel says to derive the fortnight from the M2 and S2 periods; I wanted to find where that two-period picture stops describing the spring cycle.
- Design: Hourly sum of cosines with periods M2 12.4206 h, S2 12.0 h, N2 12.6583 h; the daily range is the maximum minus minimum over a 25 hour window sampled every 6 hours; spring peaks are local maxima of that range merged within 3 days; three runs: M2+S2, M2+S2+N2, M2+N2 without S2.
- Got right: The mean spring spacing was 14.75 d for M2+S2 and 14.78 d with N2 added, matching the 14.765 d M2/S2 beat, so the fortnight is robust to a third constituent.
- Where/why it failed: Adding N2 made successive spring peaks differ in height by up to 24.1 percent (0.000 for M2+S2), the 27.55 d perigean modulation, which the two-period derivation cannot show. Without S2 the peak counter reported 13.04 d, a spurious cycle (the same 13.0 d figure as brainwork/E213), not the 27.5 d N2 beat.
- Fix: Use the M2/S2 beat for the timing of springs but quote spring heights as a range across the N2 modulation, and confirm the cycle by removing a constituent rather than by counting peaks.
- Why this fix: The spacing and the height come from different beat pairs (M2/S2 and M2/N2), so one derived period cannot give both; removing S2 shows whether the fortnight is really from S2.
- Rule of thumb: Derive spring timing from M2/S2 (14.77 d, unchanged by N2) but expect alternate springs to differ by about a quarter with N2 at 0.2 of M2; peak counting without S2 gave a spurious 13.04 d.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox with fixed amplitudes; the amplitudes are chosen for the test and not taken from a real harbour, and only three constituents were run.
- Composed: ideas:TIDES/harmonic-prediction/spring-neap-is-the-m2-s2-beat-not-a-stored-cycle, sandbox-tides-fortnight-beat/E1, brainwork/E213
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-14__tides-third-constituent-alternates-spring-heights.py
- Prediction: Spring spacing would stay 14.77 +/- 0.4 d with or without N2, spring heights would differ by more than 10 percent with N2 and under 2 percent without, and removing S2 would lose the 14.77 d spacing.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS spring spacing 14.75 d (M2+S2), 14.78 d with N2; spring height step 0.000 vs 0.241; without S2 spacing 13.04 d
- Scenarios: 1) M2+S2; 2) M2+S2+N2; 3) M2+N2 without S2 (built to BREAK the fortnight claim)

## E220 — self demo proves only the path it exercises
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [presentation][credibility][pitch][sandbox][testing]
- What: Toy sandbox of a pitch that demos a slugify tool by running it live on the pitch's own text, across six versions where v4 and v5 regress on accented input only.
- Why built: The kernel says to pitch a tool by running it on its own creation; I wanted the boundary of how much that self-run actually proves.
- Design: Six versions of a slugify function; three evidence modes compared against ground truth: pasted output captured at v1, a live self-run on the pitch's own ASCII inputs, and a live self-run on wider inputs with accents.
- Got right: A live run on wide inputs tracked truth 6/6, while pasted output agreed with truth only 4/6 because it claimed success on the two regressed versions.
- Where/why it failed: The live self-run on the pitch's own ASCII text also agreed with truth only 4/6, because the pitch text never touches the accented path where v4 and v5 broke. It was first-party and fresh yet blind.
- Fix: Make the self-run input set include the inputs users have, not only the pitch's own text, and gate the build on that wider run.
- Why this fix: Freshness removes staleness but not coverage gaps; only widening the exercised inputs catches the regression, at the cost of a slightly less tidy demo.
- Rule of thumb: A self-run demo proves only the code paths the pitch text exercises; add a few adversarial inputs to the self-run and gate on them, or claim just what the run touched.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the toy tool is invented, so real-tool regression rates are not measured here.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS pasted 4/6, pitch-only self-run 4/6 (misses v4,v5), wide self-run 6/6
- Scenarios: 1) pasted output at v1; 2) live self-run on pitch inputs only (built to BREAK the kernel); 3) live self-run on wide inputs; 4) regression versions v4-v5 versus recovery at v6

## E219 — pythagorean comma wolf and meantone
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [temperament][music][numerics][sandbox][tuning]
- What: Seeds the keyboard-temperament domain: a sandbox computing the Pythagorean comma from stacked pure fifths, the wolf fifth left by keeping eleven pure fifths, the 12-TET fifth, and quarter-comma meantone with its pure major thirds and its larger wolf.
- Why built: Closing the circle of fifths is a real tuning problem with checkable cent values, and no Brain domain covered temperament.
- Design: Interval sizes computed in cents as 1200 times log2 of the frequency ratio; pure fifth 3/2; twelve fifths minus seven octaves gives the comma; wolf fifth equals seven octaves minus eleven stacked fifths; quarter-comma meantone fifth set so four fifths make two octaves plus a pure 5/4 third.
- Got right: The comma came out at 23.460 cents, the Pythagorean wolf fifth at 678.495 cents, the 12-TET fifth at 700.000 (each pure fifth flattened by 1.955), and the quarter-comma major third at 386.314 cents, equal to the pure 5/4.
- Where/why it failed: The assumption that tempering the fifths less leaves a smaller wolf broke: quarter-comma meantone, with fifths narrowed by 5.377 cents and pure thirds, has a wolf fifth of 737.637 cents, 35.68 cents from pure against 23.46 for the Pythagorean wolf, and the Pythagorean major third is 407.82 cents, 21.5 cents wide of pure.
- Fix: When choosing a temperament, compute both the stacked-third error and the wolf for each candidate and pick by which keys will be played; spread the comma (12-TET) only when every key must be usable.
- Why this fix: The circle must close by 23.46 cents, so the error has to go somewhere; making thirds pure moves more of it into one interval, and only a computation shows how much.
- Rule of thumb: The circle of fifths is 23.46 cents too long; whatever fifths you keep pure or thirds you make pure, the wolf absorbs the difference, and quarter-comma meantone's wolf (737.64 cents) is worse than Pythagorean (678.49).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox, which computes every number from frequency ratios; I did not look up a published table in this run, so agreement with the standard figures is from my own recall, and only three systems were tested.
- Composed: N/A
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-14__pythagorean-comma-wolf-and-meantone.py
- Prediction: Comma 23.46 cents, Pythagorean wolf 678.49, 12-TET fifth 700.00, quarter-comma third 386.31 and wolf about 737.64, with the quarter-comma wolf farther from pure than the Pythagorean one.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS comma 23.46c; Pythagorean wolf 678.49c (23.46 off pure); quarter-comma wolf 737.64c (35.68 off) though its thirds are pure
- Scenarios: 1) twelve pure fifths; 2) eleven pure fifths and a wolf; 3) equal temperament; 4) quarter-comma meantone (built to BREAK the smaller-tempering-smaller-wolf assumption)

## E218 — kawasaki float angles need integer lattice
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [origami][geometry][numerics][testing][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox testing flat-foldability of degree-4 origami vertices whose sector angles are decimal degrees on a 0.3 degree grid, comparing float equality, float reflection composition, a tiny tolerance, a grid-step tolerance and exact integer tenths of a degree.
- Why built: The origami lesson says to test with exact angles, and the game-loop lesson says to keep authoritative state on an integer lattice; I wanted to see whether float angles actually break the test in practice.
- Design: 358,801 vertices built as (a, b, 180-a, 180-b), all flat-foldable by construction; tests are float equality of the alternating sum to 180, float reflection-map identity modulo 360, a 1e-9 tolerance, and integer arithmetic in tenths of a degree; a perturbed set moves 0.3 degrees between two sectors to make non-foldable vertices.
- Got right: The integer tenths test and the 1e-9 tolerance each rejected 0 of 358,801 true vertices.
- Where/why it failed: Float equality on the alternating sum wrongly rejected 63,494 true vertices (17.7 percent), and the float reflection-map identity rejected 123,305 (34.4 percent) because accumulated crease angles pick up rounding error; a tolerance equal to the grid step then accepted all 358,801 perturbed non-foldable vertices, which is by construction because the perturbation equals the tolerance.
- Fix: Convert angles to integers of the smallest unit (tenths of a degree) before testing and use exact integer equality, or use a tolerance far below the grid step (1e-9) if angles must stay floats.
- Why this fix: Decimal degrees are not exact in binary floats, so equality fails by rounding noise in both directions, while an integer lattice makes equality exact and a tolerance well below the step cannot be confused with a real one-step error.
- Rule of thumb: For angle tests on a decimal grid, never use float equality (17.7 to 34.4 percent false rejects here) or a tolerance as wide as the grid step; use integers of the grid unit, or a tolerance orders of magnitude below it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. The rejection rates are specific to the 0.3 degree grid and the Python float; the perturbation result is true by construction, so only the rejection counts carry evidence, and other grids were not tested.
- Composed: 2026-10-13__origami-single-vertex-kawasaki-equals-reflection-composition-identity/E1, sandbox-combined-game-loop/E1, sandbox-anim/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-14__kawasaki-float-angles-need-integer-lattice.py
- Prediction: Float equality and float reflection identity would reject more than 10 percent of the true vertices, the 1e-9 tolerance and integer tenths would reject 0, and a grid-step tolerance would accept the perturbed vertices.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS float == rejects 63494/358801 foldable vertices, float reflection 123305/358801, 1e-9 tol and integer tenths 0; grid-step tolerance accepts 358801/358801 non-foldable
- Scenarios: 1) float equality on the alternating sum; 2) float reflection-map identity; 3) 1e-9 tolerance; 4) integer tenths exact; 5) grid-step tolerance on perturbed vertices (built to BREAK tolerance testing)

## E217 — ddmin on a flaky failure needs repeats
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [debugging][concurrency][testing][sandbox][heisenbug]
- What: Sandbox running delta-debugging (ddmin) over 16 preemption points whose true culprit is the pair {3,11}, with the failure shown on each run only with a set detection rate, to see how a flaky test corrupts minimisation.
- Why built: The heisenbug kernel says observation changes whether a bug appears, and the delta-debugging kernel assumes a test that gives the same verdict each time; I wanted to see what happens when both meet.
- Design: A test fails only if the subset contains both culprits and a deterministic low-discrepancy sequence says the failure shows; ddmin as the standard split-and-complement loop; 200 sequence offsets per setting; detection rates 1.0, 0.5 and 0.044 (the rare-preemption rate from sandbox-kernel-concurrency/E1), with 1, 20 or 68 runs per test.
- Got right: With a deterministic failure ddmin returned exactly {3,11} in 200 of 200 offsets, and with 20 or 68 runs per test at rate 0.044 it also returned exactly {3,11} in all 200.
- Where/why it failed: With one run per test, ddmin returned exactly the culprit in 100 percent at rate 1.0, 50.5 percent at rate 0.5 and 0 percent at rate 0.044; every miss was a non-minimal superset, never a smaller set, because a missed failure only makes ddmin keep more.
- Fix: Run each ddmin test several times (about 1/p runs, 68 at rate 0.044) and count it as failing if any run fails, or first raise the detection rate by widening the failure window.
- Why this fix: A flaky pass is a false negative, which ddmin reads as "this part is needed", so it silently inflates the answer; repeating until the detection odds are high removes that bias.
- Rule of thumb: Minimising a flaky failure with ddmin returns a bloated but still failing set; repeat each test about 1/p times before trusting that the result is minimal.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. Detection uses a deterministic low-discrepancy sequence, which spaces hits evenly, so the 20-run result is cleaner than random flakiness would give; the exact repeat count needed for random failures was not measured.
- Composed: ideas:DEBUGGING/concurrency/heisenbugs/heisenbugs-vanish-because-observation-changes-the-program, ideas:DEBUGGING/isolation/delta-debugging, sandbox-kernel-concurrency/E1

## E216 — change ringing plain course vs extent
- Date: 2026-10-14
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [change-ringing][permutation][sandbox][testing][algorithm]
- What: Seeds the change-ringing domain: a sandbox generating Plain Bob from place notation, showing a plain course can be a full extent on 4 bells but only a third of one on 5 bells, and that bobs must be placed deliberately to link courses.
- Why built: Change ringing (bell ringers sounding every permutation of n bells exactly once and returning to rounds) is a real tradition with checkable published counts, and no Brain domain covered it.
- Design: Place notation applied to a row tuple (cross swaps all pairs, digits are fixed places); Plain Bob Minimus as x14x14x14x12 with bob 14; Plain Bob Doubles as 5.1.5.1.5.1.5.1.5.125 with bob 145; call sets of lead indexes up to 12 enumerated up to size 6 (2509 sets) and each checked for 120 distinct rows ending in rounds.
- Got right: The Minimus plain course gave 24 distinct rows, the whole 4! extent, and the Doubles plain course gave 40 distinct rows returning to rounds, one third of 5! = 120.
- Where/why it failed: My assumption that any bob extends the course broke: a single bob at the first lead end produced 49 distinct rows over 600 changes and never came round, and only 4 of 2509 bob sets gave a true 120-row extent, the first being bobs at leads 0, 4 and 8.
- Fix: Verify an extent by counting distinct rows and checking the return to rounds, and choose bob positions by search or a known composition instead of adding bobs freely.
- Why this fix: A bob changes which coset of rows the next course visits, so only specific call patterns tile all 120 rows exactly once; counting rows catches a false extent that sounds plausible.
- Rule of thumb: A plain course does not guarantee an extent for odd or larger bell counts (40 of 120 on five bells); count distinct rows and the return to rounds, and treat bob placement as a search problem.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the Minimus 24-row and Doubles 40-row plain courses match the published figures I know, but I did not consult an external source during the run, and only 4 and 5 bells were tested.
- Composed: N/A

- Observed: RESULT: PASS Minimus course 24/24 distinct, Doubles plain course 40 of 120, one bob stays at 49 distinct rows, 4 of 2509 bob sets give a true 120-row extent
- Scenarios: 1) Minimus plain course; 2) Doubles plain course; 3) single bob (built to BREAK any-bob-extends); 4) enumeration of 2509 bob sets

## E215 — web mercator area inflation is sec squared and the 85 degree cutoff
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [cartography][geometry][numerics][testing][sandbox]
- What: Seeded the CARTOGRAPHY domain with a numerical check of Web Mercator distortion. A finite-difference Jacobian of the projection gave area scale 1.00 at the equator, 2.00 at 45 degrees, 4.00 at 60 degrees and 67.33 at 83 degrees, a square-tile cutoff at 85.0511 degrees, a Greenland-versus-equatorial inflation of 10.46x, and a 20-60 N band average of 1.833 against 1.704 from its midpoint latitude.
- Why built: The domain had no records at all, and a map's area distortion is a small real quantity that is easy to misstate.
- Design: stdlib, projection x = lon, y = ln tan(pi/4 + lat/2); area scale is the Jacobian determinant divided by cos(lat); the band average integrates 2000 latitude slabs. Scenarios: four latitudes, the cutoff, a Greenland-versus-equator pair, and the band-versus-midpoint comparison built to BREAK the single-factor shortcut.
- Got right: Scale values at 0, 45 and 60 degrees matched sec^2 exactly, and the cutoff matched 85.0511.
- Where/why it failed: Two things went wrong on the way. My first Jacobian mixed degrees and radians and returned about 0, which the 0.0 outputs exposed immediately. My prediction of 33.4x at 83 degrees was also wrong; sec^2(83) is 67.33. The single-factor shortcut for a band misses by 7.6 percent (1.833 vs 1.704).
- Fix: Compute area scale from the projection's Jacobian with matching units, and for regions spanning many degrees integrate the factor over the band.
- Why this fix: The Jacobian check does not depend on remembering the closed form, and the integral weights each latitude by the area it holds.
- Rule of thumb: Quote Mercator area inflation as sec^2 of latitude per band (2x at 45, 4x at 60, 67x at 83), integrate over wide regions because the midpoint was 7.6 percent low for 20-60 N, and keep square tiles inside 85.0511 degrees.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved sandbox (RESULT: PASS); no map data or external tile service was used. Isolated seed: no existing kernel or lesson was exercised.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__web-mercator-area-inflation-is-sec-squared-and-the-85-degree-cutoff.py
- Prediction: Area scale 1, 2, 4 and 33.4 at 0, 45, 60 and 83 degrees; cutoff 85.0511; Greenland about 10.5x; band average differing from the midpoint factor by more than 5 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS area_scale_0_45_60_83=[1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 67.33] cutoff=85.0511 greenland_vs_africa=10.46 band20_60=1.833 midpoint_factor=1.704 (the 83-degree prediction of 33.4 was my arithmetic slip; the script checks against sec^2)
- Scenarios: 1) four-latitude Jacobian; 2) tile cutoff; 3) Greenland versus equatorial region; 4) 20-60 N band versus midpoint, built to BREAK the single-factor shortcut

## E214 — ttc reaction tiers speed clamp boundary selector vs utility and vetoed brake
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [npc][ai][gamedev][state][testing][sandbox]
- What: Built the CARLA-style time-to-collision tier model (emergency under 5 m, hard brake under 3 s, soft reaction 3-6 s, none above) and pushed it to its edges. The kernel reproduces (stopped car with a hazard at 10 m stays silent; at 30 km/h it hard-brakes), but the max(1, closing/3.6) clamp makes ttc equal distance for any non-closing or slower-than-3.6 km/h hazard, so a lead pulling away still triggers the soft tier at exactly 5 to 6 m.
- Why built: The time-to-collision kernel, the behavior-trees-vs-goap kernel and the veto-blind-decision kernel had never been built against each other; the question was where the clamp misfires and whether tier choice or actuation is the weak seam.
- Design: stdlib, deterministic. Grid of 20 distances x 4 ego speeds x 5 obstacle speeds (400 cells). Two selectors over the same tiers: a 4-rule priority list and a utility argmax. A 40-tick stopping run at 30 km/h toward a static obstacle 12 m ahead, 0.5 s ticks, 4 m/s2 braking, with the brake actuator refusing for 0 or 3 ticks.
- Got right: Kernel cases reproduced (tiers 0, 2, 3, 2 for the four probes). The priority list and the utility argmax agreed on all 400 cells (0 mismatches), so the simple selector loses nothing here. Of 70 cells where the lead is not closing but a reaction fires, 56 come from the emergency distance rule by design and 14 from the clamp alone, all at d=5.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction put the clamp false positives up to 6 m with the honk tier; they only occur at d in [5,6) because the 5 m emergency rule takes everything closer. The prediction that an outcome-checking selector would re-tier and rescue the vetoed brake was also wrong: with a 3-tick brake veto the run collides at tick 2 (0 collisions with no veto, stops at tick 6), because 3 wasted ticks at 4.2 m per tick cost more distance than the stop needs. Correct tiering cannot recover time lost to a refused actuator.
- Fix: Use the signed closing speed for the soft tier (react only when closing speed is positive), and treat a refused brake as a first-class outcome that escalates immediately rather than waiting for the next tick to re-tier.
- Why this fix: The false positives come only from clamping a negative or tiny closing speed to 1 m/s, and the collision comes from the wasted ticks, not from the tier choice that the selector comparison showed to be identical across selectors.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the ttc tiers are safe to author as a plain priority list (0/400 mismatches against a utility argmax), but clamp-derived ttc reacted to non-closing hazards at 5-6 m, and a 3-tick vetoed brake turned a clean stop into a collision, so gate on positive closing speed and escalate on a refused actuator.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the model is hand-written with the kernel's formula and does not run CARLA, and the actuator veto is a modeled refusal, not a real vehicle API.
- Composed: ideas:NPC-SIM/vehicle-ai/time-to-collision-reaction-tiers, ideas:NPC-SIM/decision-making/behavior-trees-vs-goap-authoring-cost-not-power-ranking, ideas:NPC-SIM/decision-making/a-safe-commit-time-veto-can-still-blind-the-decision-layer
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__ttc-reaction-tiers-speed-clamp-boundary-selector-vs-utility-and-vetoed-brake.py
- Prediction: Kernel tiers reproduce; the clamp misfires on non-closing hazards up to 6 m; priority list and utility argmax agree on every cell; an outcome-checking selector rescues a vetoed brake.

## E213 — tides spring neap is the m2 s2 beat not a stored cycle
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [tides][simulation][numerics][testing][sandbox]
- What: Seeded the TIDES domain. A two-constituent tide (M2 12.4206 h, S2 12.0 h) produced a daily-range cycle of 14.86 d by peak counting (DFT 14.75 d) against the derived beat of 14.765 d, with range 2.92 at spring and 1.09 at neap against the formula's 2.92 and 1.08.
- Why built: The tides domain had no records at all; a harmonic sum is a small real scenario where a cycle appears without being stored.
- Design: Hourly-fraction (0.25 h) sum of cosines, daily range = max minus min per day; peak spacing and a Fourier scan of 2 to 50 day periods over 360 days; scenarios with swapped amplitudes, an added diurnal K1 term (23.9345 h, amplitude 0.8), and 2-day sampling.
- Got right: Spring and neap ranges matched 2*(A1+A2) and 2*(A1-A2); swapping the amplitudes left the period at 14.86 d and the range at 2.92 / 1.11.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that peak counting with K1 would stay near 14.8 d was wrong: it gave 13.00 d, because the diurnal term adds ripples to the daily range and moves its peak days, while the Fourier scan still found 14.75 d with and without K1. Peak counting at day resolution is the wrong instrument for mixed tides.
- Fix: Measure the cycle with a dominant-period scan over many cycles, and compare it to the derived 1/(1/T_S - 1/T_M).
- Why this fix: The scan integrates over all days and is insensitive to ripples that shift individual peak days.
- Rule of thumb: Derive the spring-neap fortnight from the two semidiurnal periods and read it back with a Fourier scan, because day-resolution peak counting drifted from 14.86 to 13.0 days when a diurnal term was added while the true period stayed 14.75.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the constituent periods are the standard published values and were typed in, and no real tide-gauge data was used. Isolated seed: no existing kernel or lesson was exercised.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__tides-spring-neap-is-the-m2-s2-beat-not-a-stored-cycle.py
- Prediction: Peak spacing within 0.1 d of 14.765 d, spring and neap ranges 2.92 and 1.08, unchanged period with swapped amplitudes and with an added K1 term.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS beat_pred=14.765 d measured=14.86 d range=2.92/1.09 swapped=14.86 d with_K1_peak_spacing=13.00 d dft_M2S2=14.75 d dft_with_K1=14.75 d (K1 range 4.08/2.06) sampled2d=14.67 d
- Scenarios: 1) M2+S2; 2) swapped amplitudes; 3) added K1 built to BREAK the peak-counting measurement; 4) 2-day sampling; 5) 360-day Fourier scan

## E212 — savings rate suppression vs fee drag vs start date compounding model
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [personal-finance][numerics][simulation][testing][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic compounding model puts three PERSONAL-FINANCE kernels on one scale. The SEC fee example reproduced at a $28,204 gap against "nearly $30,000", the Texas two-investor example reproduced within 0.5 percent ($398,298 and $184,816 against $400,290 and $185,740), and the trickle-down savings suppression (2.9 points of income) cost more than a 0.75-point fee at all three incomes, until the contribution rate reached 26 percent.
- Why built: The lifestyle-inflation kernel gives a savings-rate effect in percentage points of income and the expense-ratio kernel a fee effect in percentage points of return, with no comparison of which hurts more.
- Design: Annual model, 30 years at 4 percent growth for a saver contributing 8 percent of income at incomes 40k, 60k and 90k; suppression run at 8 minus 2.9 points with a 0.25 percent fee, fee run at 1.00 percent with the full 8 percent; a sweep of the contribution rate from 8 to 60 percent at 60k for the crossover; closed-form checks of the SEC lump sum and the Texas monthly-compounded annuities.
- Got right: Both published examples reproduced within tolerance, which validates the model arithmetic. Suppression cost 62,407 / 93,611 / 140,416 against fee cost 19,916 / 29,874 / 44,812 at the three incomes, a ratio near 3.1 at every income because both scale with income.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the two effects cross at 24 percent was close but off (measured 26 percent), and I expected the ratio to vary with income; it does not, so income level never decides which effect matters, only the contribution rate. The SEC gap is $28,204, not the "nearly $30,000" in the headline, so the kernel's rounded figure reads about 6 percent high under this model's annual compounding.
- Fix: Compare behavioral and fee effects in the same units (final wealth at the user's real contribution rate), and quote the model's own figure beside the published one.
- Why this fix: Percentage points of income and percentage points of return are not comparable until converted to final wealth, and the crossover shows the answer flips with the contribution rate rather than with income.
- Rule of thumb: In this 30-year 4 percent model, losing 2.9 points of savings rate cost about 3.1 times what a 0.75-point fee did for contribution rates up to 25 percent, flipping at 26 percent, so fix the savings rate before fee shopping unless you already save a quarter of income.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the published SEC and Texas figures were taken from the kernels, not re-fetched, and the model uses a flat 4 percent return with no taxes, inflation or income growth.

## E211 — lsystem bushy rule more segments smaller box holds at small angles only
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [procgen][lsystem][testing][sandbox]
- What: Re-ran the kernel claim that a "bushier" L-system rule (more F per rewrite) gives more segments but a smaller bounding box than the 3-F plant rule. With four bushy rules (one straight-trunk 8-F, three curling 7/9/11-F) over iterations 1-5 and angles 15-90 degrees, it never reproduced: bushy had more segments in all 14 comparisons but a LARGER bbox in all 14 (0/14 inverted).
- Why built: segment-count-and-spatial-spread-are-independent-axes was only evidenced by one rule pair; the sandbox tried to find where the inversion holds and where it breaks.
- Design: stdlib turtle interpreter, unit step, no RNG. Plant F[+F]F[-F]F vs bushy rules; metrics = segment count, bbox area, lit half-unit cells. Scenarios: 25deg iter1-5; angle sweep 15/25/45/60/90 at iter4 (built to break); plant width sweep 20-45deg; curling bushy variants at 25/45/90.
- Got right: Plant width sweep reproduced the angle-sensitivity kernel's numbers exactly (22.0 to 40.8, strictly monotonic). Measuring both axes separately still showed they are separable: at iter 5, 25deg, bushy had 10.5x the segments of plant but 14x the area, so the two axes scale at different rates. Plant lit cells grew 5.05x (962 to 4859) while segments grew 5x, so cell occupancy tracks segments when no viewport clips.
- Where/why it failed: The headline inversion (more segments yet smaller box) did not reproduce for any tested rule. Prediction (inversion at small angles, vanishing at large) was wrong; there was no inversion at any angle. The inversion in the kernel is therefore rule-specific, probably needing a rule whose extra turns curl back on themselves faster than F count extends reach.
- Fix: Narrow the rule: independence of the two axes holds in the sense of different growth rates, but "more branches per rewrite does not mean bigger" is not general. Always measure bbox for the actual rule instead of assuming the inversion.
- Why this fix: 0/14 comparisons across 4 distinct rules and 5 angles is enough to say the inversion is not a property of bushiness itself.
- Rule of thumb: Treat "more segments, smaller box" as a property of one specific rule pair, not of bushiness; in these 4 rules at 5 angles bushier meant both more segments and a bigger box, so measure the bbox of your own rule.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved sandbox run; the kernel's original bushy rule text was not available, so a different rule family was tested and nothing is claimed about that exact rule.
- Composed: ideas:PROCGEN/lsystem/segment-count-and-spatial-spread-are-independent-axes, ideas:PROCGEN/lsystem/angle-sensitivity-is-smooth-not-chaotic-for-self-similar-branching-rules, ideas:PROCGEN/lsystem/bounding-box-outpaces-segment-count, brainwork/E65

## E210 — healthy user bias reversal threshold stratification and proxy noise
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [statistics][confounding][simulation][testing][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic expected-value model of healthy-user bias with a harmful treatment (risk multiplier 1.29) reproduces the reversal in the confounding kernel: randomized RR 1.290, crude observational RR 0.820 at uptake 0.1 for the least healthy to 0.9 for the healthiest. The sign flips below 1.0 once the uptake spread across health exceeds 0.46, stratifying on the true health score recovers 1.283 (strata 1.244 to 1.285), and stratifying on a noisy proxy gives 1.009.
- Why built: The kernel states the reversal but not how strong self-selection must be to cause it or how much of it measured covariates can undo.
- Design: 100 health levels, 100 people each, baseline risk 0.20 falling to 0.02 with health, uptake linear in health, no RNG. Scenarios: randomized uptake; spread sweep 0 to 1; 10 strata on true health with Mantel-Haenszel pooling; 10 strata on a proxy off by 30 points (alternating sign); Bayes posterior of being in the healthier half given treated.
- Got right: Randomized RR equalled 1.29 exactly; the crude RR fell monotonically with spread (1.29, 0.975, 0.728 at spreads 0, 0.5, 1.0); every stratum on true health stayed above 1.24, a Simpson-style reversal against the crude 0.82; the posterior P(healthier half | treated) was 0.702 against a 0.5 prior.
- Where/why it failed: The noisy-proxy adjustment mostly failed: pooled RR 1.009, only 0.19 of the way from crude to truth, so adjusting for a mismeasured confounder can leave the study at apparent no effect while the real effect is 29 percent harm. My prediction only said it would land between crude and true, which it did, but I had expected it closer to the true value.
- Fix: Treat the crude-versus-randomized gap as the quantity to bound, state how well the confounder is measured, and prefer randomization or a validated measure of the selection variable over a coarse proxy.
- Why this fix: Stratifying on the true variable works exactly, while a proxy with error 30 on a 100-point scale removed under a fifth of the bias, so the quality of the measurement decides whether adjustment helps.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the reversal needed an uptake spread above 0.46 and exact stratification recovered 1.283 versus 0.82 crude, but a proxy off by 30 points recovered only 1.009, so adjust only for confounders you can measure well and otherwise randomize.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the saved deterministic sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the model is a hand-built linear risk and uptake model, not the WHI data, and the 1.29 multiplier is taken from the kernel.
- Composed: ideas:STATISTICS/correlation-vs-causation/confounding/whi-randomized-trial-reversed-observational-hrt-heart-disease-findings, ideas:STATISTICS/paradoxes/simpsons-paradox/berkeley-1973-admissions-reversed-when-broken-down-by-department, ideas:STATISTICS/base-rate-fallacy/bayesian-reasoning/gynecologists-only-21-percent-correctly-estimated-cancer-probability-from-positive-mammogram

## E208 — varroa wash cadence exposure vs wash count
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [beekeeping][projection][sandbox][model][sampling]
- What: A toy varroa monitoring model that pairs the doubling-time projection with a wash cadence (7, 14, 28 days) and counts days spent above the 3 per 100 threshold before action, against the number of washes spent.
- Why built: The beekeeping kernel and its memory (brainwork/E199) fix the projection method but say nothing about how often to wash; the tone-drift entry (proj/E1) argues checks should be justified by exposure, not by cost, so the same framing was tried on wash cadence.
- Design: Deterministic mites doubling every 30 days from 1.0 per 100 bees, threshold 3 per 100, readings quantised to a 300 bee wash (steps of 0.33). Modes: raw (act when a reading is at or over threshold) and proj (also act when a two-reading doubling-time fit says the threshold falls before the next wash). Scenarios also run shrinking bees and a 0.33 start.
- Got right: Raw threshold action with weekly washes leaves 1 exposure day over 8 washes, while 14 and 28 day cadences each leave 8 exposure days (5 and 3 washes). The projection mode brought exposure to 0 at every cadence, and the shrinking bee case crossed on day 41 as the kernel said.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that 28 day washes would be worse than 14 day ones was wrong: both gave 8 days because the wash days fell at the same place around the day 48 crossing. Projection at a 28 day cadence acted on day 28, 20 days before the true crossing, so exposure 0 was bought with an early, possibly unneeded treatment. In the shrinking bee case projection added nothing (exposure 1 for both).
- Fix: Report both exposure days and days of early action for each cadence, and treat the cadence result as depending on where wash days land relative to the crossing, not as a smooth trend.
- Why this fix: Exposure alone makes the projection look free; the early-action count shows its cost, which is the trade the exposure-not-cost rule in proj/E1 needs to be paired with.
- Rule of thumb: In this model weekly washes beat 14 or 28 day washes on exposure, and a doubling projection removes exposure but can act up to 20 days early on sparse washes, so log early-action days next to exposure days; model values only, not treatment advice.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; doubling time and threshold are model values quoted from the kernel and were not checked against any extension guidance.
- Composed: ideas:BEEKEEPING/varroa-monitoring/project-the-mite-count-by-doubling-time-not-a-straight-line, brainwork/E199, proj/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__varroa-wash-cadence-exposure-vs-wash-count.py
- Prediction: Weekly washes cut exposure days against 28 day washes at 4x the washes, projection triggers earlier than raw, and a 0.33 start might break the log fit.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS exposure days raw 7/14/28d = 1/8/8 (washes 8/5/3); proj at 14d exposure 0 vs raw 8; shrinking bees raw exposure 1; 0.33 start proj exposure 0 vs raw 2. Projection at 28d acted on day 28 against a true crossing on day 48.
- Scenarios: 1) cadence 7/14/28 raw vs proj at 1.0 start; 2) shrinking bees at 14d; 3) 0.33 start at 14d, built to break the log fit (it did not break it)
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E207 — seeded rng state words vs replay count and shared stream
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][state][testing][determinism][sandbox][model]
- What: Re-verification of the seeded-rng kernel's claims as sharpened by the-game-prologue/E1, with a break case the kernel only hints at: a cosmetic consumer drawing from the one shared stream.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel is only quoted in prose by the-game-prologue/E1; this run re-checks its three claims (state words restore in O(1) and exactly, canonical serialisation keeps the fingerprint stable) in a fresh implementation so the link can be declared.
- Design: A Python sfc32 with four 32-bit state words, a 250000-draw run saved either as the state words or as seed plus count, a 4-key state hashed over all 24 insertion orders with and without sorted keys, and a 60 step sim whose hit points depend on one stream while a particle effect draws 0, 3 or 10 numbers per step from either the same stream or a separate one.
- Got right: Loading the four state words took 0 draws and the next 1000 rolls matched the uninterrupted run, where seed plus count needed 250000 draws. Sorted-key hashing gave 1 hash over 24 orders against 24 for unsorted.
- Where/why it failed: The shared stream broke the fingerprint: the final hit points were -83, -67 and -50 for 0, 3 and 10 particle draws per step from identical seed and inputs, while a separate cosmetic stream gave -67 each time. The kernel says float-dependent physics stays out of the authoritative layer but does not say cosmetic rolls need their own stream. Also, Python dict keys do not reorder integer-like keys the way JavaScript does, so the 24-versus-1 result shows the hash risk generally, not the JS-specific reorder.
- Fix: Give cosmetic effects their own seeded stream and keep the authoritative stream's draw count a function of the sim alone.
- Why this fix: The split stream produced one fingerprint over all three particle counts, so the sim outcome no longer depends on how many cosmetic rolls were made.
- Rule of thumb: Save an RNG's state words, not a count, hash state with sorted keys, and give any cosmetic consumer its own stream, because one shared stream let particle count change the sim result (3 fingerprints versus 1); tested on one generator and one toy sim.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the toy sim and generator are my own, not the code from the-game-prologue.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/replay-fingerprint, the-game-prologue/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__seeded-rng-state-words-vs-replay-count-and-shared-stream.py
- Prediction: State-word load takes 0 draws and matches the next 1000 rolls, seed plus count takes 250000, plain hashing gives 24 hashes and canonical 1, and a shared cosmetic stream gives more than one fingerprint where a split one gives 1.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS state-word load 0 draws vs 250000 for seed+count; hashes plain 24 vs canonical 1; shared stream gave 3 fingerprints over particle counts, split stream 1
- Scenarios: 1) state words versus seed plus count at 250000 draws; 2) hash over 24 insertion orders, plain versus sorted keys; 3) shared versus split cosmetic stream over 0, 3, 10 draws per step, built to BREAK the one-stream rule
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E206 — rankpull layout inherits toposort tiebreak instability
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][graph][determinism][sandbox][model]
- What: A rank-pull force layout driven by toposort index inherits the toposort tie-break instability: the same 6 node graph lands in different positions depending on declaration order unless ties are broken by identity.
- Why built: The skilltree-formula entries showed toposort outputs are not unique under declaration order, and the rank-pull entry showed a layout can be tied to toposort rank; nobody had checked what the two do together.
- Design: Six nodes with two tied pairs (a/b and d/e) in a diamond shaped DAG, a one dimensional deterministic layout (rank pull 0.2 plus edge springs 0.02, 200 steps), run over all 720 declaration orders with declared-order versus lexicographic tie-break, plus a tie-free chain as the break case.
- Got right: Lexicographic tie-break gave exactly 1 layout over 720 orders (max node move 0.000); the tie-free chain gave 1 layout even with declared-order tie-break, so the instability needs ties and nothing else.
- Where/why it failed: My written numbers were too high. I predicted at least 3 layouts and a node move over 1 unit under declared-order tie-break; the run gave 2 layouts and a max move of 0.910, so the script printed RESULT: FAIL against those thresholds even though the mechanism held.
- Fix: Canonicalise the toposort tie-break (by node identity) before the rank feeds any layout force, and state the observed size of the effect rather than a guessed one.
- Why this fix: The layout is a pure function of the rank vector here, so making the rank vector canonical makes the layout canonical, as the lexicographic run showed.
- Rule of thumb: When a layout force reads toposort rank, canonicalise ties first; in this model the declared-order tie-break produced 2 layouts with a max move of 0.91 over 720 orders, lexicographic produced 1, and a tie-free graph needs no fix.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox over all 720 declaration orders; the size of the move depends on the toy spring constants and was not tuned.
- Composed: sandbox-combined-skilltree-formula/E2, sandbox-combined-skilltree-formula/E4, sandbox-rankpull-forcelayout/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__rankpull-layout-inherits-toposort-tiebreak-instability.py
- Prediction: At least 3 distinct layouts and a node move above 1 unit under declared-order tie-break, exactly 1 layout under lexicographic, 1 for a chain.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL rank-pull layout over 720 declaration orders: declared tie-break 2 layouts (max move 0.91), lexicographic 1, tie-free chain 1. Mechanism held, numeric thresholds missed.
- Scenarios: 1) declared-order tie-break over 720 orders; 2) lexicographic tie-break over 720 orders; 3) tie-free chain, built to BREAK the claim that declaration order alone destabilises the layout
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E205 — quilt seam allowance drift test strip
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [quilting][measurement][sandbox][model][correction]
- What: A toy model of seam allowance drift in a quilt row: how much a row of blocks comes up short when the real seam differs from the nominal one, and whether a one-time test strip correction removes it.
- Why built: To seed the QUILTING domain with a computed case, since a pattern card normally states a cut size and no way to catch a seam that is off by a sixteenth.
- Design: Row width is blocks times cut size minus two seam allowances per seam, cut at finished size plus 0.5 inch, 6 inch finished blocks. Cases: exact 1/4 inch seam, 1/16 wide and narrow seams at 4, 8 and 12 blocks, a four piece test strip recovering the seam, and an alternating wandering seam as the break case.
- Got right: Drift is exactly 0.125 inch per seam (1.375 inch at 12 blocks) and the test strip recovers the seam (0.3125) and removes the row error (residual 0.0000).
- Where/why it failed: The break case failed the correction: with seams alternating 1/16 wider and narrower, the strip of three seams over-read the seam (inferred 0.2708) and the corrected cut made a 12 block row 0.333 inch long where it had been 0.125 inch short.
- Fix: Treat the strip correction as valid only for a steady seam; sew and measure a second strip and compare the two inferred seams before changing the cut size.
- Why this fix: Agreement between two strips is evidence the seam is steady, which is the one assumption the correction needs and the one the wandering seam violated.
- Rule of thumb: Seam allowance error adds up per seam, so measure it on a test strip and cut to it, but a strip only fixes a steady seam; in this model a wandering seam got worse after one-strip correction (0.125 to 0.333 inch); the inference formula is the generating formula, so real fabric is untested.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the seam arithmetic and sizes are invented model values and no real fabric was sewn or measured.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__quilt-seam-allowance-drift-test-strip.py
- Prediction: A 12 block row sews 1.375 inch short at a seam 1/16 too wide, a four piece test strip recovers the seam within 0.01 inch and removes the error, and an alternating seam would make the correction add error.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 12-block row short by 1.375 in at seam 5/16, test strip infers 0.3125 and removes it (residual 0.0000); wandering seam drift -0.125 before and 0.333 after correction
- Scenarios: 1) exact, wide and narrow seams at 4, 8, 12 blocks; 2) four piece test strip correction on a steady wide seam; 3) alternating wandering seam, built to BREAK the correction (it did)
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E204 — fermentation end call needs temp corrected gravity
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [brewing][measurement][projection][sandbox][model]
- What: A toy fermentation model asks whether the call "two equal gravity readings means finished" needs temperature-corrected readings, and whether a log-slope projection of the finish day (the pattern from the varroa doubling-time entry) is better from corrected readings.
- Why built: The brewing kernel and brainwork/E196 show an uncorrected hot reading costs ABV points, but not whether the same error changes the finish call; the varroa entry shows a projection beats reading a quantised value at face value, so the two were tried together.
- Design: Gravity falls from 1.050 toward 1.010 with a 3 day time constant, readings quantised to 0.001 and shifted by a published-form temperature polynomial, with the sample cooling from 78 F to 62 F over 12 days (and a constant 60 F room as the break case). Compared the equal-readings call with and without correction, and a log(gravity minus final) projection from days 2, 4 and 6.
- Got right: At a constant 60 F corrected and uncorrected calls agree (both day 11), as the correction is about zero there. The corrected projection (day 12.5) landed closer to the true settle day (14) than the uncorrected one (11.3).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the corrected call would land within a day of the true settle day and the uncorrected one would be off by 2 or more days was wrong. Both equal-readings calls fired 3 to 4 days early (day 11 corrected, day 10 uncorrected) because the 0.001 quantisation hides an excess gravity of up to 0.0005 to 0.001, so the cooling-room correction moved the call by only one day.
- Fix: Do not call fermentation finished from two equal quantised readings; project the finish from the log of the excess over the target final gravity using corrected readings, and still expect it to run early.
- Why this fix: The projection used the whole decay shape and cut the error from 2.7 days to 1.5 days in this run; the equal-readings call is limited by quantisation, which no temperature correction can remove.
- Rule of thumb: In this model temperature correction shifted the finish call by one day while quantisation put it 3 to 4 days early, so correct for temperature and also project the finish from the decay, never trust two equal readings; model values only, one drift profile.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the correction polynomial is typed from a commonly published form and was not re-fetched, and the time constant and cooling profile are invented model values.
- Composed: ideas:BREWING/gravity-readings/correct-the-hydrometer-reading-for-sample-temperature-and-name-the-abv-formula, ideas:BEEKEEPING/varroa-monitoring/project-the-mite-count-by-doubling-time-not-a-straight-line, brainwork/E196, brainwork/E199
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__fermentation-end-call-needs-temp-corrected-gravity.py
- Prediction: Corrected equal-readings call within 1 day of the true settle day, uncorrected off by 2 or more days, corrected projection within 1 day, and corrected and uncorrected agree at a constant 60 F.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS cool-room call day corrected 11 vs uncorrected 10; const 60F agree=True; projected settle day corrected 12.5 vs uncorrected 11.3 vs true 14. The call-day predictions missed (both about 3 days early); the PASS reflects the constant-room agreement and the projection ordering only.
- Scenarios: 1) cooling room 78 to 62 F, corrected vs uncorrected equal-readings call; 2) constant 60 F room, built to BREAK the claim that correction matters (it did not); 3) log-slope projection from days 2, 4, 6, corrected vs uncorrected

## E203 — effect gated vs existence gated interactables softlock
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][quest][state][rpg][sandbox][model]
- What: A toy quest chain where one interactable is reused, run under three gating schemes over every early touch sequence: existence gating, effect gating that checks the current quest, and effect gating with an already-touched flag set on any touch.
- Why built: The effect-gated kernel names the already-used flag trap and the-game-prologue/E9 argues for existence gating; neither says how the two compare on the same chain, and the kernel is not yet applied by a memory entry.
- Design: Chain Q1 needs well 1, Q2 needs well 2, Q3 needs well 1 again. Prefix sequences are every touch sequence of length 1 to 6 over three wells (1092), then a perfect solver touches the needed well. Modes: existence (a well exists only while its quest is active), effect (any touch is allowed, only the needed well advances, others give a hint), flag (the same, but each well's touched flag is set on any touch and blocks its effect).
- Got right: Existence gating gave 0 soft-locks and 0 early hints, and effect gating on the current quest gave 0 soft-locks while 1050 of 1092 sequences drew a hint, so the discovery the kernel wants costs nothing in safety. The flag scheme soft-locked 1092 of 1092.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction was wrong on the flag scheme: I expected it to lock only prefixes that touched well 1 early, but a prefix that never touches well 1 (126 sequences) also locked, because the solver's own legitimate touch for Q1 sets the flag and Q3 then needs the same well again. So the flag is not an early-touch hazard, it is a permanent lock for any reused object. The script prints RESULT: FAIL for that reason.
- Fix: Gate the effect on the current quest state, never on a per-object has-fired or has-touched flag, whenever an object can serve more than one quest.
- Why this fix: Effect gating on the current quest locked 0 of 1092 sequences and the flag scheme locked all of them, with the same objects, chain and solver.
- Rule of thumb: With a reused interactable, existence gating and current-quest effect gating both gave 0 soft-locks in 1092 sequences (effect gating also showed hints in 1050), while a per-object touched flag locked every sequence, even a perfect player's; model of one three-quest chain.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox over all 1092 prefixes; the chain and the three modes are my own toy model, not the-game-prologue code.
- Composed: ideas:RPG/interactable/effect-gated-not-existence-gated, ideas:RPG/quest-design/existence-gating-solves-when-not-which, the-game-prologue/E9
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__effect-gated-vs-existence-gated-interactables-softlock.py
- Prediction: Existence gating 0 soft-locks and 0 hints, current-quest effect gating 0 soft-locks with hints, and the flag scheme soft-locking some prefixes but none that never touch well 1.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL soft-locks existence 0, effect(current quest) 0, touched-flag 1092 of 1092; early hints existence 0, effect 1050; flag mode clean when well1 untouched: False. The kernel's claim held; the last clause of my prediction failed.
- Scenarios: 1) existence gating over 1092 prefixes; 2) current-quest effect gating over the same; 3) touched-flag effect gating, built to BREAK the kernel's safety; 4) flag mode on the 126 prefixes that never touch well 1
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E202 — drain run cumulative fall vs joist depth
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [plumbing][measurement][sandbox][model][rounding]
- What: A toy fall budget for a horizontal drain under a floor: usable fall from the joist bay minus clearances, the longest run at a given slope, mixed slope sections, and the effect of rounding the fall up to whole-inch marks.
- Why built: To seed the PLUMBING domain with a computed case, since a layout often fixes the pipe route before anyone checks that the accumulated fall fits the joist bay.
- Design: Bay 9.25 inches, 1.5 inches above the pipe, outside diameter 3.5 inches, 0.75 inch below, giving 3.5 inches of usable fall; runs at 1/8, 1/4 and 1/2 inch per foot, one mixed run (10 feet at 1/4 plus 2 feet at 1/2), and a whole-inch rounding case as the break.
- Got right: Run limits were 14, 28 and 7 feet at 1/4, 1/8 and 1/2 inch per foot, and the mixed run used exactly 3.50 of 3.50 inches.
- Where/why it failed: Rounding each fall up to a whole inch overestimated by up to 0.75 inch and cut the accepted run from 14 feet to 12. Separately, this is straight arithmetic (fall equals slope times length), so the sandbox checks the bookkeeping and rounding only; the first draft prediction text was also muddled and was left as written.
- Fix: Carry the fall in fractions of an inch through the whole run and compare the sum, not each section rounded, to the usable depth.
- Why this fix: Whole-inch rounding turned an exactly fitting 14 foot run into a rejected one, so the check is only as good as its resolution.
- Rule of thumb: Budget total fall (slope times length, summed over sections) against the bay before routing, and do the sum unrounded; in this model rounding up to whole inches rejected a run that fit; slopes and clearances are model values, not code advice.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; no code, pipe or joist dimension was checked against a real standard.
- Composed: N/A
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__drain-run-cumulative-fall-vs-joist-depth.py
- Prediction: Usable fall 3.50 inches, limits 14, 28 and 7 feet at 1/4, 1/8 and 1/2 inch per foot, the mixed run fitting, and whole-inch rounding shortening the accepted run.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS run limit 14 ft at 1/4 in/ft (usable fall 3.50 in), 28 ft at 1/8, 7 ft at 1/2; 10 ft + 2 ft steep fall 3.50 in; whole-inch tape marks cut the limit to 12 ft with up to 0.75 in overestimate
- Scenarios: 1) limits at three slopes; 2) mixed slope sections; 3) whole-inch rounding, built to BREAK the exact-fit result (it did)
- Link: scheduled brain train session, 2026-10-13; session_01KgwUVJ8YiFpBjfevwrK7fS

## E201 — bounded assonance lettering vs closure distance blind spot
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lyrical-composition][rhyme-tooling][algorithm][testing][sandbox][model]
- What: Bounding the assonance pass of two-pass rhyme lettering stops four same-vowel lines collapsing to one letter, but the bounded output then matches a genuine assonance couplet scheme, so closure distance and letters alone cannot tell the two apart.
- Why built: The mush-boundary entry says a bounded assonance pass is needed, and brainwork/E159 says closure distance cannot separate assonance from perfect rhyme; nobody had run them together to see what the bounded fix leaves unseparated.
- Design: A 17 word toy lexicon of vowel and tail, pass 1 giving uppercase letters to perfect rhymes, pass 2 giving lowercase to unresolved same-vowel lines (unbounded: all join; bounded: each line joins at most one later line), closure distance as gaps between lines sharing a letter, and a resolved-pair count. Stanzas: perfect AABB, perfect ABAB, four same-vowel lines with four different tails, and a two-vowel stanza as the break case.
- Got right: The unbounded pass lettered the four same-vowel lines aaaa with closure [1,1,1]; the bounded pass gave aabb with closure [1,1], the same closure as perfect AABB, and the resolved-pair count (2 versus 0) separated them. The two-vowel stanza lettered abab with closure [2,2] either way.
- Where/why it failed: The bounded pass invents pairing structure: four lines that share only a vowel and have four different tails come out as aabb, indistinguishable by letters and closure from a stanza that really had two assonance couplets. My own scenario list also listed an assonance couplet stanza that used the same four words as the mush stanza, which is itself the finding, as the toy lexicon cannot say which pairs the author meant.
- Fix: Report resolved-pair count and distinct tail count beside letters and closure distance, and flag a bounded-assonance stanza with 0 resolved pairs as a possible mush rather than a scheme.
- Why this fix: Resolved pairs went 2 versus 0 and distinct tails 2 versus 4 between the perfect and the mush stanza, while closure and letters were identical after bounding.
- Rule of thumb: A bounded assonance pass fixes the collapse but makes mush look like a couplet scheme (aabb, closure [1,1] for both), so always print resolved pairs and distinct tails next to the letters; checked on a 17 word toy lexicon and five stanzas only.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the lexicon is hand typed and does not reflect real pronunciation.
- Composed: two-pass-rhyme-letters-assonance-mush-boundary-and-closure-distance/E1, brainwork/E159
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__bounded-assonance-lettering-vs-closure-distance-blind-spot.py
- Prediction: Unbounded mush letters aaaa with closure [1,1,1], bounded gives aabb with closure [1,1] equal to perfect AABB, resolved pairs 2 versus 0, and distinct tails separate the last two.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS unbounded mush aaaa closure [1, 1, 1]; bounded mush aabb closure [1, 1] equals perfect AABB closure [1, 1]; resolved pairs perfect 2 vs mush 0; distinct tails 2 vs 4
- Scenarios: 1) perfect AABB and ABAB; 2) four same-vowel different-tail lines, unbounded and bounded; 3) two-vowel stanza, built to BREAK the claim that bounding always yields aabb (it gave abab)

## E200 — wire gauge step rule and 240v drop vs ampacity pick
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [electrical][wire-sizing][voltage-drop][sandbox]
- What: Independent rebuild of the size-twice branch-circuit sheet with an added printed rule estimate beside the table value, and a 240 V case at the same wattage.
- Why built: The ampacity kernel had one origin sandbox; I wanted to check its 15 A at 100 ft numbers with my own script and test whether a halving-per-gauge-step rule or a higher voltage changes the picks.
- Design: Drop = 2 x amps x ohms per 1000 ft x feet / volts; table 3.07, 1.93, 1.21, 0.778, 0.491 ohm per 1000 ft and 15, 20, 30, 40, 55 A for 14 to 6 AWG; rule of 0.63 per two gauge steps; same 1800 W load at 120 V and 240 V.
- Got right: 14 AWG drops 7.67 to 7.68 percent, 12 AWG 4.83, 10 AWG 3.02 and 8 AWG 1.95 at 15 A and 100 ft, so the final pick is 8 AWG and 10 AWG misses the limit by a hair. The 0.63 cubed estimate gives 1.92 against 1.95 (1.3 percent off).
- Where/why it failed: My exact-value check at 7.68 failed on float rounding (7.675 prints as 7.67), so the check needed a tolerance. The step rule is only as good as the table: ratios run 0.627 to 0.643, so it is an estimate, not a substitute for the lookup.
- Fix: Print the rule estimate beside the table value and keep the table lookup as the pick; use a tolerance when comparing a rounded drop figure.
- Why this fix: The rule shows whether the lookup is plausible while the table carries the exact figure, so the two together catch a wrong row.
- Rule of thumb: Doubling the supply voltage at the same wattage quarters the percent drop (7.68 to 1.92 percent) and keeps 14 AWG at 100 ft, while at 120 V the same load needs 8 AWG; 10 AWG at 3.02 percent misses by 0.02, so re-check close calls with the table.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; table values typed from memory of the published copper figures and not re-fetched, 60 C column, no derating.
- Composed: ideas:ELECTRICAL-WIRING/branch-circuit/ampacity-sets-the-minimum-gauge-run-length-sets-the-real-one, brainwork/E186, ideas:DEAD-RECKONING/heading-error/one-in-sixty-rule-reads-low-below-thirty-degrees
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__wire-gauge-step-rule-and-240v-drop-vs-ampacity-pick.py
- Prediction: Final pick 8 AWG at 15 A and 100 ft, the 0.63 cubed rule within 3 percent of the table, and 240 V giving one quarter of the 120 V drop.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS ampacity pick 14, final pick 8 (7.67 to 1.95 percent); rule off by 1.3 percent; 240 V drop 1.92 percent keeps 14 AWG. First run FAIL only on the 7.68 rounding check.
- Scenarios: 1) 15 A at 100 ft, 120 V, all gauges; 2) rule estimate versus table; 3) BREAK: step ratio spread across the table; 4) same 1800 W at 240 V.

## E199 — varroa single count vs doubling time projection

- What: Sandbox seeding a beekeeping domain: varroa mite monitoring modelled with a 30 day doubling time, a 3 per 100 bee action threshold, a 300 bee wash and a shrinking autumn bee count.
- Why built: The domain had no records; a monitoring log is a checkable artifact and the straight-line projection habit is a common way to misjudge a doubling quantity.
- Design: Closed-form doubling model stepped by day; a straight-line projection from samples on day 0 and day 30; integer rounding for a 300 bee wash; a variant with 0.4 percent of bees lost per day.

- Rule of thumb: Project a doubling count with the doubling time (day 48 versus 60 by a straight line) and compare per-bee rates, not totals; assumed model values, not real hive data.

## E198 — spatial hash fixes missed pairs but not order dependent epsilon dedupe
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][gamedev][performance][testing]
- What: Sandbox combining the spatial hash cell-size precondition with the epsilon-compare lesson: a chain of five points spaced 0.9 epsilon apart, queried and deduplicated through a uniform hash at two cell sizes.
- Why built: The dog hash lesson says cell size must cover the query radius; the August-10 lesson says an epsilon compare is not an equivalence relation. Nobody had tested whether fixing the hash makes epsilon-based dedupe well defined.
- Design: Five collinear points, close means distance at most 1.0; brute-force pair set compared with 3x3-block hash pairs at cell 0.5 and 1.0; then keep-first greedy dedupe run in two insertion orders.
- Got right: Cell size equal to epsilon found all 4 close pairs, identical to brute force, while cell size 0.5 found only 1 of 4.
- Where/why it failed: Correct pair discovery did not make dedupe deterministic: keep-first dedupe left 3 survivors in index order and 2 in the scrambled order, because a close to b and b close to c does not make a close to c.
- Fix: Size cells to at least the query radius, and for dedupe define the result by a canonical order or by cell-snapped keys rather than by pairwise epsilon in arrival order.
- Why this fix: The hash precondition governs which neighbours are visible, while order dependence comes from the non-transitive relation itself, so the two defects need separate fixes.
- Rule of thumb: A hash sized to the query radius finds every close pair (4 of 4 versus 1 of 4 at half size) but pairwise-epsilon dedupe still keeps 3 or 2 points depending on arrival order, so canonicalise the order.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; five invented collinear points, one epsilon, two insertion orders only.
- Composed: local__sandbox-combined-dog-spatial-hash-cell-size-vs-rejection-radius/E1, pappydapimp69__dog/E13, pappydapimp69__august-10/E27
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__spatial-hash-fixes-missed-pairs-but-not-order-dependent-epsilon-dedupe.py
- Prediction: Cell 0.5 would miss some pairs, cell 1.0 would match brute force, and dedupe survivors would differ by insertion order (2 versus 3).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS brute=4 small-cell=1 eps-cell=4 survivors 3 vs 2 by insertion order.
- Scenarios: 1) BREAK: hash cell 0.5; 2) hash cell 1.0; 3) BREAK: greedy dedupe in index order versus scrambled order.
- Link: scheduled brain train session, loop 1 pass 2; session_01DiPNzPzfsHcE8oDezvZY3n

## E197 — link count vs authority weighted rank and independent link roots
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [seo][backlinks][ranking][sandbox][graph]
- What: Sandbox of the backlink-quality kernel on a 26 node link graph: target X with 12 links from a link farm against target Y with 2 links from authoritative hubs, scored by raw count, plain PageRank, trust-seeded PageRank and distinct link roots.
- Why built: The SEO kernel says link quality beats link count; the research kernel says count distinct roots, not repetitions; the attribution kernel says use a set of all roots when a source has two parents. Nobody had run them together on one graph.
- Design: Deterministic power iteration (damping 0.85, 200 iterations); farm pages have no inbound links; trust-seeded variant teleports only to the hubs and six independent sites; a variant lets one hub also link the farm; a root count over owner labels with one two-owner farm page.
- Got right: Distinct roots separated the targets cleanly: X has 1 root, Y has 2, and a two-owner page gives 2 roots with a set of all owners but 1 with a first-owner-only rule.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that plain PageRank would put Y above X was wrong: X scored 0.2585 against 0.1623 because 12 pages each pass on a teleport share. Trust-seeded rank fixed it (Y 0.2173 over X 0.1657), but one hub linking the farm flipped it back (X 0.2216 over Y 0.1164).
- Fix: Do not read link quality as an automatic property of PageRank-style scoring; seed trust from vetted sources, count distinct owner roots as a separate check, and treat any authoritative page that links into a cluster as a leak to audit.
- Why this fix: A farm with no inbound links is still rewarded by plain teleportation, while seeded trust only flows from approved sources, so a single approved source linking the farm transfers real rank.
- Rule of thumb: In this graph quality only beat count under trust-seeded scoring (Y 0.2173 over X 0.1657; plain rank had X 0.2585 over Y 0.1623) and one authority link into the farm erased it (X 0.2216 over Y 0.1164), so count owner roots (1 versus 2) too.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox on a hand-built graph; the real search engine's ranking lies outside what the run touched.
- Composed: ideas:SEO/backlinks/link-quality/link-quality-and-relevance-matter-more-than-link-count, ideas:RESEARCH/corroboration/trace-sources-to-independent-roots-not-a-repetition-count, ideas:SYSTEM/attribution/single-owner-rule-fixes-chain-double-counts-but-drops-a-root-at-a-join
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__link-count-vs-authority-weighted-rank-and-independent-link-roots.py
- Prediction: Raw count would rank X (12) above Y (2), plain PageRank would rank Y above X, a hub feeding the farm would flip it, roots would be 1 versus 2. The plain PageRank part came out wrong in the first run and the script now asserts the observed order.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS plain X 0.2585 over Y 0.1623; trust-seeded Y 0.2173 over X 0.1657; hub feed X 0.2216 over Y 0.1164; roots X1 Y2; two-owner roots 2 versus 1.
- Scenarios: 1) BREAK: plain PageRank on count 12 versus 2; 2) trust-seeded rank; 3) BREAK: one hub linking the farm; 4) distinct roots; 5) two-owner page with set versus first-owner rule.
- Link: scheduled brain train session, loop 1 pass 5; session_01DiPNzPzfsHcE8oDezvZY3n
