## E173 — nearest voicing greedy vs fixed and optimal across cadences parallel fifths
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [music][testing][model]
- What: A runtime greedy nearest-voicing rule (keep common tones, otherwise minimise total upper-voice movement to the next chord) was run on six C-major progressions built from the cadence kernel's types (authentic V-I, plagal IV-I, deceptive V-vi, half I-IV-V, a 14-chord mixed run, and a root-leap run), against a fixed root-position voicing and against an offline dynamic-programming optimum. Greedy never moved more than the fixed voicing and was strictly smaller in 4 of 6 (V-I 3 vs 9, V-vi 5 vs 7, mixed run 46 vs 70, root-leap run 28 vs 36), it kept every shared common tone in place, and it matched the offline optimum in all six. But it produced more bass-vs-upper parallel perfect 5ths/8ves than the fixed voicing in two cases (V-vi 2 vs 0; mixed run 6 vs 2).
- Why built: The nearest-voicing kernel claims smooth voice leading needs only the current voicing and the next chord's pitch classes, but it is silent on whether minimal movement also respects the first-species ban on parallel perfect intervals.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG. Voicings are one pitch per chord pitch class in MIDI 55-79; distance is summed absolute movement of sorted voices; bass is the chord root at 36+pc; parallels are counted when bass and an upper voice both move and the interval class stays 0 or 7.
- Got right: Total movement, common-tone retention and agreement with the dynamic-programming optimum all held across authentic, plagal, deceptive, half-cadence and longer runs.
- Where/why it failed: Minimal movement is not counterpoint-legal. Moving the upper voices least while the bass leaps by root made the same 5th or octave recur in V-vi and in the longer runs, so the movement-only search trades smoothness for parallel perfects.
- Fix: Add a penalty (or hard filter) for parallel 5ths/8ves between bass and each upper voice to the candidate-voicing cost; do not treat movement distance as the whole objective.
- Why this fix: The nearest-neighbour search already enumerates every candidate voicing, so a parallel-interval check costs nothing structural and addresses exactly the cases where the sandbox showed greedy worse than fixed.
- Rule of thumb: Greedy nearest-voicing matched the offline optimum on all 6 cadence progressions tested and kept all common tones, so lookahead is not needed for movement; but it needs a parallel-perfects penalty, since it produced more parallels than a fixed voicing in 2 of 6 cases. Tested only on triads in C major with root-only bass.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the parallel-interval rule is the textbook first-species rule as I implemented it, not checked against a notation tool.
- Composed: ideas:MUSIC/theory/common-tone-retention-and-nearest-voicing-for-runtime-unpredictable-chords, ideas:MUSIC/theory/cadence-types-are-phrase-punctuation-with-narrative-purpose, ideas:MUSIC/theory/species-counterpoint-is-graduated-constraint-training
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__nearest-voicing-greedy-vs-fixed-and-optimal-across-cadences-parallel-fifths.py
- Prediction: Greedy total movement is at most the fixed voicing's in every progression, common tones are always held, and greedy equals the offline optimum; a parallel-perfects count is expected to be no worse than fixed (built to break that).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS greedy<=fixed True strict 4/6 commontones-kept True suboptimal-vs-optimum []; parallels greedy/fixed V-vi 2/0, mixed run 6/2, root-leaps 4/4, half 0/2.
- Scenarios: 1) V-I; 2) IV-I; 3) V-vi; 4) I-IV-V; 5) 14-chord mixed run; 6) root-leap run (parallels check built to BREAK the kernel)
- Link: scheduled brain train session; session_01L8S9oqJa4aBbRJii1PPFmJ

## E172 — freelancer code ownership wfh conjunction assignment and unlicensed repo default
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [legal][testing][model]
- What: Three LEGAL kernels were encoded as predicates and run over a 48-case grid (3 work types x written x express-WFH-clause x signed-by-all x separate-assignment): the work-for-hire four-condition conjunction, the no-license-file default, and the claim-type statute of limitations. No software case ever qualified as work-for-hire (0 of 16), because software is outside the nine categories even with a fully signed agreement; ownership moved to the client only through a separate written assignment. So in the 8 of 16 software cases with no assignment, a client who publishes the code under MIT would be granting rights it does not own. For the deadline, a contract breach on 2024-02-29 has a 4-year limit of 2028-02-29 but 2026-02-28 under a mistaken 2-year rule, so a filing on 2027-06-01 is live under the right claim type and barred under the wrong one.
- Why built: The three kernels were each filed alone and never run together, so nobody knew whether a signed agreement, a public repo and a deadline lookup compose into one consistent rule for commissioned code.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG. Ownership is the conjunction for the nine categories, else the creator unless a written assignment exists; a licence grant is valid only if the grantor owns; the deadline uses a calendar year add with a Feb 29 fallback to Feb 28. The predicates restate the kernels' wording, so this tests how they compose, not the law.
- Got right: Software never became work-for-hire and a missing assignment decided ownership in all 16 software cases; the deadline gap between 2 and 4 years was reproduced.
- Where/why it failed: My first run printed RESULT: FAIL because I predicted 4 non-owner licence grants and the grid gives 8, a counting slip, since half of 16 software cases have no assignment; the model was right and the prediction wrong. The sandbox also cannot test real law, courts, or the discovery-rule tolling the deadline kernel mentions.
- Fix: For commissioned code get a signed written copyright assignment, not only a work-for-hire clause; do not publish it under any licence until that assignment exists; and look up the deadline by claim type before counting years.
- Why this fix: A work-for-hire clause cannot work for software under the nine-category rule, so the assignment is the only branch that moves ownership; and the licence and deadline checks both depend on knowing who owns it and which claim type applies.
- Rule of thumb: In a 48-case grid, commissioned software was work-for-hire in 0 of 16 cases and the client owned it only with a written assignment, so a public MIT repo of unassigned commissioned code grants rights the client lacks in 8 of 16 cases; the statute-of-limitations 2-year vs 4-year mix-up flips a live claim to barred. This restates the kernels' tests and is not legal advice.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS after correcting my own count); the legal rules are taken from the kernels' cited sources and were not re-checked here.
- Composed: ideas:LEGAL/intellectual-property/work-for-hire/a-freelancer-owns-their-work-by-default-not-the-client-who-paid-for-it, ideas:LEGAL/intellectual-property/open-source-licensing/no-license-file-means-all-rights-reserved-not-free-to-use, ideas:LEGAL/civil-procedure/statute-of-limitations/there-is-no-single-deadline-to-sue-it-depends-on-claim-type
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__freelancer-code-ownership-wfh-conjunction-assignment-and-unlicensed-repo-default.py
- Prediction: No software case is work-for-hire; ownership moves only with an assignment; 4 of 16 software cases would have a non-owner licence grant (wrong, it is 8 of 16); a 2-year rule bars a claim the 4-year rule keeps alive.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS software never WFH (0/16), only assignment moves ownership; non-owner MIT grants in 8/16 software scenarios; wrong-type deadline bars a live claim (first run FAIL on my miscount of 4).
- Scenarios: 1) software x all 16 flag combos; 2) translation and logo controls (translation can be WFH); 3) licence grant by non-owner in 16 software cases; 4) Feb 29 contract-breach deadline at 2 vs 4 years, built to BREAK the single-number rule

## E171 — f pattern scan window front loading vs plain rewrite readme five questions
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][testing][model]
- What: A toy scanner that reads only the first K words of the first L lines was run on three drafts of a README that must answer five questions (what, why, how to start, help, who). The front-loaded draft (answer word first) captured 3, 5, 3, 5 and 5 of 5 across the scan budgets, averaging 4.2; the buried draft (answer late in a preamble-led line) captured 0, 0, 0, 1 and 3, averaging 0.8. A shortened plain-language draft matched the front-loaded one except at the tightest budget (K=3, L=3), where one extra decorative title line cost an answer (2 of 5 vs 3 of 5).
- Why built: The scanning-behavior kernel says to front-load, the README kernel lists five questions every stranger asks, and the plain-language kernel says to write concisely, but nothing sized how they interact when the reader's scan budget is tight.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG. A scan budget is K words by L lines; an answer counts as seen only if its cue word is in the first K words of a line within the first L lines. Cue words are my own choice per draft, so the scanner is an assumed model of the F-pattern, not eye-tracking data.
- Got right: Front-loading beat burying at every budget tested and the gap shrank as K and L grew, reaching parity-ish only at 12 words by 6 lines.
- Where/why it failed: Shortening wording did not help once the answers already led the lines; the only thing that mattered was position, and a decorative opening line displaced an answer at the tightest budget. The result is built into the scan rule I chose, so it shows how the budget and order trade off, not that real readers scan this way.
- Fix: Put each of the five answers at the start of its own line, in order, with no title or decorative line ahead of them when the first screen is the budget; use concise wording to shorten lines only after that.
- Why this fix: Under a first-K-words rule only position decides what is seen, and every line above the answers spends scan budget.
- Rule of thumb: In a toy first-K-words, first-L-lines scanner, a README with each of five answers leading its line captured 4.2 of 5 on average against 0.8 for answers buried late in the line, and one non-answer line on top cost an answer at the tightest budget. The scanner is an assumption, not measured reader behaviour.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the scan rule and cue words are my own constructs, so the numbers describe the model, not real readers.
- Composed: ideas:DOCUMENTATION/readability/scanning-behavior/readers-scan-in-an-f-pattern-so-front-load-the-first-line, ideas:DOCUMENTATION/readme/essential-content/a-readme-answers-what-and-how-to-start-before-anything-else, ideas:DOCUMENTATION/plain-language/federal-mandate/plain-language-is-us-federal-law-not-just-a-style-preference
- Polarity: compatible

## E170 — ean13 weighted check digit catches all single errors but misses adjacent swaps differing by 5
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [barcodes][checksums][testing]
- What: The EAN-13 check digit (digits weighted 1 and 3 alternately, check = (10 - sum mod 10) mod 10) was run over 1000 deterministic 12-digit codes against an unweighted digit-sum check. Both caught every single-digit error (0 missed of 117,000). On adjacent swaps of unequal digits, EAN-13 missed 977 of 8,048 (12.1%), every one with a digit gap of exactly 5, while the unweighted sum missed all 8,030 of its swaps.
- Why built: Seeding a new BARCODES domain; the canon had checksum lessons for byte sums and CRCs but nothing on retail check digits or on what weighting buys.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG; codes are n x 999999937 for 1000 values of n below 10^12, so the set is fixed. Every digit of the 13-digit code was replaced by each other digit, and every adjacent unequal pair was swapped; a mutation counts as missed when the check digit still validates. The unweighted sum is the control.
- Got right: Weighting alone gave full single-digit detection and turned a total blind spot for swaps into a 12% one; the misses fell only where the two digits differ by 5, since weights 1 and 3 change the sum by 2 times the gap, and 2 x 5 = 10.
- Where/why it failed: A swap of two digits that differ by 5 passes validation unchanged, so the weighted check is not transposition-proof; the sandbox did not test non-adjacent swaps, jump transpositions, UPC-A, or other symbologies.
- Fix: Treat a valid EAN-13 check digit as strong evidence against typos but not against a swapped pair of digits differing by 5 (0/5, 1/6, 2/7, 3/8, 4/9); where swaps matter, add a second check such as a lookup against the product database.
- Why this fix: The check passes the swaps that the arithmetic cannot distinguish, so only independent information, not a stronger reading of the same digit, can catch them.
- Rule of thumb: EAN-13 caught 117,000 of 117,000 single-digit errors but missed 977 of 8,048 adjacent swaps (12%), all with a digit gap of 5; an unweighted digit sum missed every swap. Tested on adjacent swaps only.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS); the weights and check formula are the published EAN-13 rule as I implemented it, and I did not test them against real scanner data. No existing kernel is adjacent, so this entry is isolated apart from the loosely related checksum lessons.
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__ean13-weighted-check-digit-catches-all-single-errors-but-misses-adjacent-swaps-differing-by-5.py
- Prediction: Both checks catch all single-digit errors, the unweighted sum misses every swap, and EAN-13 misses about 10 to 14% of swaps, all with digit gap 5.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS EAN-13 missed 0/117000 single-digit errors and 977/8048 adjacent swaps, all with digit gap 5; unweighted sum missed 8030/8030 swaps
- Scenarios: 1) single-digit errors, EAN vs unweighted; 2) adjacent swaps, EAN; 3) adjacent swaps, unweighted control; 4) miss rate split by digit gap, built to BREAK the claim that weighting catches all swaps
- Link: scheduled brain train session; session_01L8S9oqJa4aBbRJii1PPFmJ

## E169 — braille unicode offset is dot bitmask and letter decades are dot3 dot6 shifts
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [braille][unicode][testing]
- What: Python's unicodedata names for all 256 characters in the Braille Patterns block (U+2800 to U+28FF) were parsed and compared with the formula codepoint = 0x2800 + sum of 2^(dot-1) over the raised dots. All 256 agreed, which gives 63 non-blank six-dot cells. Using the English braille letter table as I typed it, k to t equal a to j plus dot 3 and u, v, x, y, z equal a to e plus dots 3 and 6, with w (dots 2,4,5,6) as the only break.
- Why built: Seeding a BRAILLE domain; the canon had no entry on how braille cells map to code, which is checkable against a real source (the Unicode character names) instead of from memory.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG. For each of 256 codepoints the name's DOTS list is read, turned into a bitmask and compared with the codepoint offset. The letter-decade test builds each letter from its base letter and the added dots and compares it with the typed table, and a glyph built by the formula is checked to carry exactly the dots in its own Unicode name.
- Got right: The bitmask formula matched 256 of 256 names with dot 1 as the lowest bit, so a cell can be generated or decoded with one shift loop instead of a lookup table.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed in the check. The letter table is typed from memory of the published alphabet and was not compared with a source file, so the decade pattern is consistent with that table, not independently confirmed; contractions, numbers and the eight-dot extension were not touched.
- Fix: Generate braille characters from dot sets with the bitmask formula and keep the letter table as data checked against a published chart before use.
- Why this fix: The formula is verified against 256 real names while the letter table was not, so only the first can be trusted as code today.
- Rule of thumb: Unicode braille codepoint = U+2800 + the bitmask of raised dots (dot 1 is bit 0) held for all 256 cells; the letter decades (+dot 3, then +dots 3 and 6, except w) hold for my typed table but the table itself is unchecked.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): The bitmask formula was verified first-hand against Python's unicodedata names (RESULT: PASS). The letter table is assumed from memory and flagged above.
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__braille-unicode-offset-is-dot-bitmask-and-letter-decades-are-dot3-dot6-shifts.py
- Prediction: All 256 Unicode names agree with the bitmask formula; k-t and u-z follow the dot-3 and dots-3-and-6 shifts with w as the one exception.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS bitmask formula matched 256/256 Unicode names; k-t=+dot3 True, u-z=+dots3,6 True except w (True)
- Scenarios: 1) all 256 name-vs-formula checks; 2) letters k to t as a to j plus dot 3; 3) letters u, v, x, y, z as a to e plus dots 3 and 6; 4) w, built to BREAK the decade rule

## E168 — weighted astar plateau and alt ceiling
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [pathfinding][sandbox][tradeoff]
- What: Swept weighted A* weights 1 to 10 on three 48x48 4-connected maps (open, wall bars with gaps, scattered blocks) and compared against an ALT landmark heuristic, measuring expansions and path-cost ratio at every weight.
- Why built: To test whether the "measure both sides of a tradeoff curve" kernel's claim (speedup lives in a narrow low-weight band, not a smooth ramp) holds across map types, not just the maps it was synthesized from.
- Design: Deterministic grid maps with no RNG, Manhattan heuristic scaled by w, binary-heap A*; ALT used 4 corner landmarks with BFS distances and the triangle-inequality bound. Recorded expansions and cost/optimal for eight weights per map.
- Got right: On open and blocks maps the whole speedup arrives between w=1 and w=1.1 (expansions drop to 4-7 percent of w=1) and then the curve is flat out to w=10, so sweeping only w=2 vs w=1 would hide where the bend is. Cost penalty was 0 percent (open) and 4.3 percent (blocks) and also plateaus.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's shape claim is map dependent: on the wall-bars map the curve never bends at all (best case 0.75x expansions, 1.6 percent cost loss), because the heuristic is misleading at every weight. ALT with corner landmarks gave only 1955 vs 2011 expansions with equal cost, a marginal win on that map.
- Fix: Treat the sweep as per-map-class: measure a few representative maps and look for the knee on each; do not carry one knee weight across maps. On maze-like maps look at a better heuristic or hierarchy instead of a higher weight.
- Why this fix: A weight knee found on open terrain would lead to a false confidence on maze terrain where no weight helps; the sweep is cheap, so measuring each class costs less than mis-tuning.
- Rule of thumb: For weighted A*, sweep w from 1.0 in small steps on each map class; on the grids tested the whole gain sat at w<=1.1 on open and scattered maps and did not exist on a wall-and-gap map, so tune per map class.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script (grid sizes 48x48, 4-connected only); 8-directional grids and larger maps were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:PATHFINDING/general/measure-both-sides-of-a-tradeoff-curve-not-just-one-metric, ideas:PATHFINDING/hierarchical/alternatives-to-full-decomposition, ideas:PATHFINDING/uniform-diagonal-cost-changes-the-chosen-route-not-just-its-label
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__weighted-astar-curve-and-alt.py
- Prediction: Before running: expected expansions to fall mostly in w<=1.25 and then plateau on every map, with cost loss under 5 percent; expected ALT to cut expansions on the bars map by at least 10 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS knees={'open': 1.1, 'bars': None, 'blocks': 1.1} maxcost open 1.0, bars 1.02, blocks 1.04; ALT expansions 1955 vs 2011 with equal cost. The plateau prediction held; the ALT 10 percent prediction was wrong (only 2.8 percent).
- Scenarios: 1) open map; 2) scattered-blocks map; 3) wall-bars map built to BREAK the narrow-band claim; 4) ALT landmarks vs Manhattan on the bars map
- Link: brain train auto session 2026-10-13; session_011eTW7aDHC86vQjq7f9sRQG

## E167 — weighted astar octile grid knee and flat diagonal
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [pathfinding][sandbox][tradeoff]
- What: Settled an open question about whether the weighted-A* sweet spot and the flat-diagonal-cost routing difference carry over unchanged from a 4-connected grid to an 8-connected octile grid, using three 40x40 maps (open, wall bars with gaps, scattered blocks), no corner cutting, weights 1 to 5, and a flat-diagonal-cost variant.
- Why built: An open tension asked this directly, and the earlier sweep was 4-connected only.
- Design: Deterministic grids, no RNG. Octile heuristic (diagonal cost sqrt2) swept at w in 1, 1.1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 5, recording expansions and cost relative to the w=1 optimum. Then diagonal cost set to 1 and A* run with a Chebyshev heuristic (matching) versus the octile heuristic (over-estimating there).
- Got right: Scattered blocks kept a narrow knee: expansions fell from 435 to 146 at w=1.1 and 56 at w=1.25, with a 7.1 percent cost penalty from w=2 up. The open map showed no gain at all because the octile heuristic is already exact there (40 expansions at w=1). The wall-bars map was a gradual slope (1052 to 885 expansions, 16 percent) with at most 0.8 percent cost penalty.
- Where/why it failed: The 4-connected result that the gain always sits in a narrow low-weight band did not carry over unchanged: it is a property of the map class and heuristic quality, and an exact heuristic leaves nothing for weighting to save. Under flat diagonal cost the over-estimating octile heuristic returned the same optimal cost as the matching Chebyshev one on all three maps and expanded fewer nodes (63 versus 561 on blocks), but that is luck of these maps, not a guarantee.
- Fix: Do not reuse a 4-connected weight knee on an 8-connected grid; re-sweep on the target map class, and when diagonal cost is flat use the matching Chebyshev heuristic if optimality must be guaranteed.
- Why this fix: The sweep is cheap and the result changed shape across map classes, so a transferred number would have been right on one map class and meaningless on another.
- Rule of thumb: On an 8-connected grid, an exact octile heuristic leaves no room for weighting to help, so sweep weights only where plain A* expands far more than the path length, and keep the heuristic matched to the diagonal cost when optimality matters.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (40x40, three maps, no corner cutting); larger maps, other obstacle densities and real game maps were not tested. The first run had an assertion bug and was re-run after fixing it.
- Composed: ideas:PATHFINDING/general/measure-both-sides-of-a-tradeoff-curve-not-just-one-metric, ideas:PATHFINDING/uniform-diagonal-cost-changes-the-chosen-route-not-just-its-label
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__weighted-astar-octile-grid-sweep.py
- Prediction: Before running: the gain would again sit at w<=1.25 on open and scattered maps with under 5 percent cost penalty, and the octile heuristic under flat diagonal cost would change cost or expansions by over 10 percent. The open-map gain and the cost-change parts were wrong.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS halved_by_w1.25={'open': False, 'bars': False, 'blocks': True} max_cost_ratio={'open': 1.0, 'bars': 1.008, 'blocks': 1.071} flat_diag_octile_extra_cost=0 on all maps; flat_diag_expansion_ratio_octile_vs_cheb open 1.0, bars 0.97, blocks 0.11
- Scenarios: 1) open map; 2) wall-bars map; 3) scattered-blocks map; 4) flat diagonal cost with Chebyshev versus octile heuristic, built to BREAK the assumption that an over-estimating heuristic must change the answer

## E166 — rhyme letter assignment exhaustive enumeration
- Date: 2026-10-13
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][sandbox][exhaustive]
- What: Exhaustively enumerated all 1296 four-line stanzas over six end-sounds (two vowels times three codas) and compared a one-pass any-vowel-match rhyme-letter assigner with a two-pass assigner (uppercase for perfect rhymes, then lowercase for assonance among still-unlettered lines), plus closure distance for AABB, ABBA and AAAA.
- Why built: The two-pass letter-assignment kernel and the rhyme-scheme-shape kernel were each backed by a few hand-picked stanzas; this run asks how often the one-pass failure happens across the whole small state space and whether it can merge two schemes that sound different.
- Design: End-sounds are (vowel, coda) pairs, deterministic, no RNG. The truth scheme is the perfect-rhyme partition. One-pass keys letters by vowel only. Two-pass runs pass 1 on full (vowel, coda) matches and pass 2 on vowel-only matches among the rest. Closure distance is the largest gap between a line and its previous same-letter partner.
- Got right: One-pass mislabeled the perfect-rhyme scheme in 1164 of 1296 stanzas (90 percent), and it merged AABB and ABBA into one label when every line shares a vowel; two-pass kept them apart. Every line received exactly one letter in both approaches. Closure distances were 1, 3 and 1 for AABB, ABBA and AAAA, matching the earlier hand-picked results.
- Where/why it failed: The two-pass result (0 wrong) is true by construction on the uppercase letters, because pass 1 is the definition of the truth scheme, so the run confirms the mechanism and the size of the one-pass failure but does not test whether the two-pass lowercase pass is a good measure of perceived openness. The end-sound inventory is also tiny and hand-written, not real pronunciation data.
- Fix: Keep letter assignment in two passes with uppercase for resolved rhymes and lowercase for assonance, and judge the assigner by the share of stanzas it mislabels over an enumerated space, not by a few examples.
- Why this fix: When a single pass lets a shared vowel claim a letter, almost every stanza is affected (90 percent here), so the kernel's claim is the common case rather than an edge case; enumeration shows that cheaply.
- Rule of thumb: Test a rhyme-letter assigner by enumerating a small end-sound space, and treat uppercase as the resolved-rhyme claim; a one-pass vowel match mislabels most stanzas once codas vary.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; real pronunciation dictionaries, stanzas longer than four lines and sung (not written) rhyme were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E7, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E8
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-13__rhyme-two-pass-exhaustive-and-closure-distance.py
- Prediction: Before running: two-pass uppercase letters reproduce the perfect scheme in 1296 of 1296, one-pass mislabels at least 200, every line gets one letter, closure distance AABB 1, ABBA 3, AAAA 1, and one-pass merges AABB with ABBA when vowels are shared.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS stanzas=1296 onepass_wrong=1164 twopass_wrong=0 unlabeled=0 closure(AABB,ABBA,AAAA)=(1, 3, 1) onepass_merges_AABB_ABBA=True twopass_separates=True
- Scenarios: 1) all 1296 stanzas, one-pass vs two-pass; 2) AABB vs ABBA with a shared vowel and different codas, built to BREAK the one-pass assigner; 3) closure distance for AABB, ABBA and AAAA; 4) every line gets exactly one letter
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 1, 2026-10-13; session_011eTW7aDHC86vQjq7f9sRQG
- Audited: 2026-10-16 · pass · Read E166 and re-ran its stored sandbox, which printed the same RESULT line (1164 of 1296 one-pass mislabels, 0 for two-pass). The one-pass count is computed against a truth partition, not asserted, and the entry itself admits the two-pass 0 is true by construction because pass 1 defines the truth. The 90 percent figure depends on a uniform enumeration of six hand-made end-sounds, so it measures how often vowel-only matching disagrees with perfect rhyme in that space, not in real lyrics; the Rule of thumb (enumerate a small space, mislabels most stanzas once codas vary) stays inside that scope, so the claim is not wider than what was tested. · scheduled brain train run 2026-10-16 loop 2 audit pass 3; session_01LqkL6KzxrKDPe4qvy5sTwj

## E165 — random labels memorization vs holdout and smoothing
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ml][evaluation][testing][generalization]
- What: A deterministic 1-nearest-neighbour memorizer scored 100% train accuracy on hash-derived random labels and 0.49 on held-out data. On a noisy learnable rule it also scored 100% train but 0.84 held-out, and a 15-neighbour smoother raised held-out to 0.94 while fitting random labels only 0.57 on train.
- Why built: The random-labels kernel (high train accuracy is not evidence of learning) had no memory entry that applied it. brain/E116 already showed a holdout gap for search boosts, so this checks the same lesson on a model whose capacity can be dialled.
- Design: 200 train and 400 test points in a square from sha256 of (seed, index), no RNG. Labels were random, or sign of x+y with 10% flips (test truth clean). Models: k=1 and k=15 nearest neighbours; plus a 3-point single-quadrant training set like E116's 3-query list.
- Got right: Train accuracy was 1.00 for k=1 in every scenario, so it carried no information; the held-out set separated the cases (0.49 on noise, 0.84 on the rule). Smoothing did not rescue random labels (0.47 held-out).
- Where/why it failed: The 3-point training set also reached 1.00 train and 0.485 held-out, which is just the class share, because it only saw one region and one label. Only the k=15 smoother is an analogue of regularization; it is not dropout or a neural network, so the dropout kernel is touched only as the capacity-control idea.
- Fix: Report accuracy on held-out data that covers every class and region, and treat 100% train accuracy as a capacity check only. Give a capacity-control knob (here k) a chance to lower train accuracy and watch held-out.
- Why this fix: Train accuracy was 1.00 for the pure memorizer on noise and on signal alike, so only the held-out number changed between them.
- Rule of thumb: When a model hits 100% train accuracy, compare it with the same model on random labels: if it also hits 100% there, train accuracy proves nothing and only a held-out set covering every class tells you anything. Tested on a k-NN with 2 features, not on a neural net.
- Provenance (verified): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic stdlib sandbox (RESULT: PASS). Out of scope for this run: the paper's CIFAR-10 Inception result and any real network or real dropout.
- Composed: ideas:MACHINE-LEARNING/generalization/overfitting/neural-networks-fit-random-labels-to-100-percent-training-accuracy, ideas:MACHINE-LEARNING/regularization/dropout, brain/E116
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__random-labels-memorization-vs-holdout-and-smoothing.py
- Prediction: k=1 train 1.00 and held-out 0.45-0.55 on random labels; held-out 0.80-0.90 on the noisy rule; k=15 beats k=1 by at least 4 points on the rule and does not rescue random labels; 3-point set gives train 1.00 and held-out at most 0.60.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS random labels k1 train 1.00 test 0.49; noisy rule k1 test 0.84 -> k15 test 0.94; k15 random train 0.57 test 0.47; tiny-set train 1.00 test 0.48 (class share 0.48)
- Scenarios: 1) random labels k=1; 2) random labels k=15, built to BREAK the idea that smoothing helps everywhere; 3) noisy rule k=1; 4) noisy rule k=15; 5) 3-point single-region training set

## E164 — koan commentary elimination leak
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [zen][procgen][content][testing]
- What: Sandbox of the koan case / commentary / capping-verse shape as generated content. An irresolvable case stays irresolvable only while at least two candidate responses remain un-critiqued and the verse names none of them.
- Why built: The ZEN kernel says commentary evaluates wrong responses without confirming a right one. Nothing says how much commentary is too much, so I tested where the shape stops holding.
- Design: 8 candidate responses, a commentary set (critiqued responses), a verse string. A solver eliminates critiqued responses and also accepts a verse that names exactly one live candidate. Five scenarios, including a sweep of 0..8 critiqued.
- Got right: Canonical 5 of 8 critiqued leaves 3 live and stays open. The sweep is open for 0 to 6 critiqued and the answer leaks at exactly 7 (n-1), so the boundary is sharp.
- Where/why it failed: Critiquing 7 of 8 is thoroughness by the proxy (commentary count) but leaks the answer by elimination. A verse naming one live candidate leaks it too. A plan of 5 critiques passed, but after an alias-merge step the finished commentary held 7 and leaked.
- Fix: Validate irresolvability on the finished artefact: count live candidates after all merges, and scan the verse for candidate words. Require at least 2 live and no candidate named.
- Why this fix: The finished text is what the player sees. The plan-level check passed in scenario 4 while the finished text failed.
- Rule of thumb: A commentary that critiques all but one response solves the koan by elimination; cap critiques at n-2 and validate the finished text, not the plan.
- Provenance (verified): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic stdlib sandbox, 5 of 5 checks passed. Not tested: real koan corpora or human solvers.

## E161 — adaptive allocation negative bias exact enumeration
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [regret][experimentation][statistics][testing]
- What: Exact enumeration of every outcome of a 12-pull two-arm Bernoulli test shows greedy adaptive allocation biases both arm sample means downward (-0.065 and -0.088 at p=0.6/0.4; -0.087 and -0.104 at 0.5/0.5), while fixed alternating allocation has bias exactly 0. Greedy halves the pulls spent on the worse arm (3.93 vs 6.00) but the worse arm's mean squared error rises from 0.040 to 0.072.
- Why built: The REGRET kernel says minimising regret during a test biases the estimate you ran the test to get, and notes the magnitude was not verified. No memory entry had applied it, so I measured the size and where it stops.
- Design: Python with Fractions, no RNG, depth-first over all 2^12 outcome sequences with exact probabilities. Policies: alternate, and greedy (2 pulls each, then the higher running mean, ties to arm 0). Conditioned on the arm having at least one pull. Also the in-test mean of the apparent winner, and a 6-pull fresh holdout of the chosen arm.
- Got right: Bias was negative for both arms and for equal arms; the fixed design was exactly unbiased; greedy paid less cumulative regret, which is why anyone uses it.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's wording that every favoured arm is understated is only half the picture: the apparent winner's in-test mean is still overstated (+0.045 greedy, +0.071 fixed) because picking the max of two noisy means selects upward noise, so two opposite biases coexist and neither is the same as the arm-mean bias. Thompson sampling and larger T were not run.
- Fix: When the deliverable is an effect estimate, use a fixed-horizon design, or re-estimate the chosen arm on a fresh fixed holdout sample (exactly unbiased in the run); do not read arm means or the winner's lift off the adaptive dashboard.
- Why this fix: The holdout is drawn without regard to the earlier outcomes, so its mean has expectation p; the adaptive and winner-selected numbers do not.
- Rule of thumb: An adaptive test buys lower cumulative regret by biasing every arm mean downward and raising the worse arm's error; re-measure the chosen arm on a fresh fixed sample before publishing a lift. Exact for 12-pull two-arm greedy only; not Thompson, not other horizons.
- Provenance (verified): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic exact-enumeration sandbox (RESULT: PASS). Out of scope for this run: Thompson sampling, the theorem's conditions, bias at other horizons, and the log-regret floor in the cumulative-versus-simple regret kernel, which the run touches only through the cumulative-regret versus estimation-error trade.
- Composed: ideas:REGRET/experimentation/minimising-regret-during-a-test-biases-the-estimate-you-took-the-test-to-get, ideas:REGRET/bandits/cumulative-regret-has-a-logarithmic-floor-but-simple-regret-does-not, brain/E116
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__adaptive-allocation-negative-bias-exact-enumeration.py
- Prediction: Fixed bias exactly 0; greedy bias negative for both arms at p=0.6/0.4 and 0.5/0.5; greedy has fewer worse-arm pulls but higher worse-arm error; the winner's in-test mean is overstated (positive) under both designs; a fresh holdout re-estimate has bias exactly 0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS greedy arm means biased low (-0.0653, -0.0885 at p=.6/.4; -0.0870, -0.1043 at .5/.5) vs fixed 0; worse-arm pulls 3.93 vs 6.00; MSE arm1 0.0724 vs 0.0400; winner in-test overstatement +0.0445 (greedy) +0.0706 (fixed); holdout bias 0
- Scenarios: 1) fixed alternate p=0.6/0.4; 2) fixed p=0.5/0.5; 3) greedy p=0.6/0.4; 4) greedy p=0.5/0.5; 5) BREAK: winner-selected in-test mean, which goes the opposite way; 6) fresh holdout re-estimate

## E160 — tour linear spine vs fork edit drift switch identity truthful engine and hidden step autoplay
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ux][onboarding][state][sandbox]
- What: A five-step tour (link, query, graph, mine, sync) driven by a small real state machine with an early local-or-full mode choice was built two ways, as one linear spine with conditional copy and as a fork of per-mode tours, and scored on screen count, edit drift, mid-tour mode switch, truthfulness of the failure text, and whether an auto-play with a hidden extra step can be detected from final state.
- Why built: The early-binary-choice kernel says to implement the persisted choice as conditional copy on one spine rather than a structural fork; its siblings say the reader should drive the system by hand first and that a demo should run a real engine instead of canned output. Each part was asserted from sources but never run together.
- Design: Deterministic, no RNG. The engine returns the real result of each step for the mode (the local sync says nothing was pushed; the graph step needs full mode). Spine screens are built from the engine's result plus a mode badge. Fork tours are 2^k lists in which the local one omits the graph step. Edit drift is the number of fork screens left stale when 3 shared steps are edited in the primary tour only. A fake-error variant replaces the local sync text. Auto-play adds a hidden extra sync after mine.
- Got right: The spine showed all 10 mode-by-step screens with engine-true text (10 of 10), while a scripted fake hard error on the local sync mismatched the engine on 1 cell. Editing 3 shared steps left 3, 9 and 21 stale screens in the fork for k=1, 2, 3 choices and 0 in the spine. A trace comparison caught the hidden extra step in both modes.
- Where/why it failed: Two of five predictions missed. The fork at k=1 has fewer screens than the spine (9 against 10), so the kernel's testing-surface argument is about edit drift, not screen count. A positional mode switch mis-lands on 2 positions (mine against graph, sync against mine) with a third position (the last full step) having no local counterpart, not the 3 mismatches I predicted. And final-state comparison missed the hidden extra sync in both modes (state identical in local and in full), because the hidden step was idempotent, so I wrongly expected full mode to differ.
- Fix: Build the tour as one spine over a real engine, show the blocked graph step with a one-tap switch instead of omitting it, edit copy in one place, and verify an auto-play against the manual drive by comparing the step trace, not only the final state.
- Why this fix: Edit drift grew as 2^k minus 1 times the edited steps in the fork and was 0 in the spine, the omitted step shifted every later position in a switch, and the trace comparison was the only check that saw the hidden step, since final states matched in both modes.
- Rule of thumb: Choose the one-spine tour for its edit drift and switch identity, not for fewer screens: a fork left 3, 9 and 21 stale screens after editing 3 steps (k=1, 2, 3) against 0 for the spine, and an auto-play with an idempotent hidden sync had identical final state to the manual drive in both modes, so compare step traces to prove no hidden step.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: FAIL 3/5 predictions held; both misses are reported above); this is a synthetic five-step engine, and the kernel's behavioural claims (reactance, completion past five steps) were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:UX/interaction-pattern/make-an-early-binary-choice-ripple-through-later-steps-without-punishing, ideas:UX/explorable-explanations/let-the-user-drive-the-system-by-hand-before-automating, ideas:UX/demo-craft/make-a-product-demo-genuinely-live-with-an-in-page-engine-over-a-real-data-snapshot
- Polarity: compatible

- Observed: RESULT: FAIL 3/5 predictions held; fork screens 9 vs spine 10; stale {1: 3, 2: 9, 3: 21}; positional mismatches 2 vs 0; spine truthful 10/10, fake mismatches 1; hidden-sync state equal local True full True, trace equal local False full False. P3 and P5 missed.

## E159 — rhyme two pass case separates landed from open closure distance cannot
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][tooling][sandbox]
- What: A mini lexicon (vowel plus coda, families for nasals, stops and sibilants) was used to label five four-line stanzas with the two-pass letter assigner (uppercase for resolved rhymes, lowercase for assonance) and a single-pass vowel-only assigner, then to measure closure distance (index gap to the most recent same-letter partner). An AABB stanza with perfect rhymes and one with assonance-only rhymes had identical closure distance (2 pairs, mean 1.0) but different two-pass letters, AABB against aabb.
- Why built: Two kernels were sandboxed separately: the two-pass assigner keeps schemes legible, and rhyme scheme shape sets emotional motion, which an earlier entry operationalized as closure distance. Their combination was never run: does distance alone see the open-versus-landed difference the case of the letter carries?
- Design: Deterministic table of 16 words, no RNG. Pass one gives uppercase letters to words that resolve (same vowel and coda, or coda in one family) with another line; pass two gives lowercase letters to remaining lines that share a vowel; unmatched lines are X. The single-pass control letters any vowel match. Closure pairs are read from the letters; resolved pairs are those with uppercase letters. Stanzas: AABB perfect, AABB assonance-only, ABBA, a stray-assonance stanza (night, name, day, way) and a mixed stanza.
- Got right: Distance alone could not separate landing from open: both AABB stanzas gave 2 pairs at mean 1.0 while two-pass letters gave AABB with 2 resolved pairs and aabb with 0. ABBA kept its outer pair at distance 3 (distances 1 and 3). The mixed stanza read AAbb with 1 resolved and 1 open pair, where distance-only counts 2 pairs. On the stray stanza two-pass gave XXAA with 1 resolved pair while single-pass gave ABBB.
- Where/why it failed: One prediction missed and one bug was found on the first run. I predicted the single-pass assigner would report 3 pairs on the stray stanza; it reports 2 (ABBB), still twice the true 1, so the inflation is real but smaller than I wrote. My first two-pass code never let a later assonant line join an earlier lowercase letter and printed aXbX for the assonance-only stanza, which would have hidden the open-versus-landed contrast; fixing it changed that stanza to aabb.
- Fix: Measure rhyme scheme motion with letters that carry case, and report resolved pairs next to closure distance: distance says how far apart partners are, case says whether the pair lands. Write a case check on the assonance-only stanza so a letter assigner that fails to chain lowercase partners fails loudly.
- Why this fix: The two metrics vary independently in this run: distance was identical for aabb and AABB while resolved pairs were 0 versus 2, so neither alone can express stable-versus-wistful, and the case check catches the chaining bug that distance could not.
- Rule of thumb: Do not use closure distance alone to judge a rhyme scheme's stability: AABB with perfect rhymes and AABB with assonance-only rhymes both give 2 pairs at mean distance 1.0, while two-pass letters separate them (AABB with 2 resolved pairs against aabb with 0); this used a 16-word hand lexicon on five four-line stanzas.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: FAIL 4/5 predictions held; the P4 pair-count miss and the fixed pass-two bug are reported above); phoneme data are a hand-written lexicon, not a pronunciation dictionary, and no real songs were scored.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-tooling/two-pass-letter-assignment-keeps-schemes-legible, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E7, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E8
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__rhyme-two-pass-case-separates-landed-from-open-closure-distance-cannot.py
- Prediction: Closure distance is identical for perfect and assonance-only AABB (2 pairs, mean 1.0) while two-pass letters differ by case; ABBA keeps distances 1 and 3; the stray-assonance stanza gives XXAA with 1 resolved pair under two-pass and 3 pairs under single-pass; the mixed stanza reads AAbb.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL 4/5 predictions held; aabb perfect AABB vs assonance aabb (distance-only both mean 1.0); abba ABBA dists [1, 3]; stray two-pass XXAA pairs 1 vs single-pass ABBB pairs 2; mixed AAbb. P4 missed on the single-pass count (2, not 3).
- Scenarios: 1) AABB perfect; 2) AABB assonance-only, built to BREAK distance-only measurement; 3) ABBA outer pair; 4) stray assonance stanza against the single-pass assigner, built to BREAK the single-pass assigner; 5) mixed AAbb stanza

## E158 — lore power level load bearing vs decoupled combat layer lie rate vs upset rate
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedesign][balance][power-scaling][sandbox]
- What: A 24-fighter roster with lore power levels from 1e3 to 1e9 was clashed under four combat layers: the lore number used directly (A), fully decoupled hash-derived combat values (B), combat values derived monotonically from the display (D), and D with a fraction f of low-lore specialists given the top combat value. Upset rate (lore-weaker side wins) was read per lore-ratio band next to the lie rate (pairs where the displayed order contradicts combat order).
- Why built: The power-scaling kernel says never make the lore number load-bearing for combat and keep a separately tuned combat layer so lower-number characters can win; the clash-window entry brainwork/E76 bounds when a weaker side can overturn a stronger one, so the two should be checked together for what decoupling costs the display.
- Design: Deterministic, no RNG: clash strength is combat value times (5 + m) with the mash count m enumerated over 1..10 for both sides, ties to the defender, as in E76; hash-derived values use an integer hash of the fighter index. Bands are lore ratio under 10, 10 to 1000, over 1000. The notation check formats lore numbers as K/M/B labels and compares text sort with numeric sort, taken from the idle-game notation kernel.
- Got right: With the lore number load-bearing (A) the upset rate was 0.000 in the 10-1000 and over-1000 bands (window bound (5+10)/(5+1)=2.5). Fully decoupled values gave upset 0.472 in the far band but a lie rate of 0.500. Text-sorting the labels misordered them (90K versus 120M), so the display must sort by the parsed value.
- Where/why it failed: Two of five pre-registered predictions missed. I predicted the derived monotone layer would give 0 far-band upsets; it gave 0.061 with lie rate 0, because its combat values span 50 to 142 (ratio 2.84, above the 2.5 window bound), so the kernel's decoupling is not the only way to get upsets. And buying far-band upsets by specialists costs display honesty at about 1.3 to 1.6 upset per lie: f=0.1 gave upset 0.246 at lie 0.152, f=0.25 gave 0.486 at 0.370.
- Fix: Do not read the kernel as all-or-nothing decoupling: first set the combat-value spread relative to the clash window, ratio above (5+M)/(5+1), which gives some upsets with zero lie rate, and only then add bounded decoupling, with the lie rate printed next to the upset rate so the display cost is visible.
- Why this fix: The window ratio alone moved far-band upsets from 0 to 0.061 at lie rate 0, while every specialist added bought upsets at an almost proportional lie rate, so the cheap lever is the combat spread and the expensive one is breaking the displayed order.
- Rule of thumb: A lore power number can stay honest and still allow upsets if the combat layer's value spread exceeds (5+M)/(5+1) for mash range M (derived layer: far-band upset 0.061, lie 0); fully decoupling it reaches 0.47 upset but contradicts the displayed order in 50% of pairs, so treat the lie rate as the price of each extra upset and sort labels by parsed value.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: FAIL 3/5 predictions held; the two misses are reported above); the roster, hash and clash form are synthetic, borrowed from E76, and no real game's numbers were used.
- Composed: ideas:UI-UX/power-scaling/canon-inconsistency/narrative-vs-stat, brainwork/E76, ideas:UI-UX/power-scaling/number-notation/idle-games

## E157 — condorcet exact dp vs brute force and seeded sfc32 sampling power
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [social-choice][condorcet][testing][sandbox]
- What: The exact margin-vector DP for the 3-candidate no-Condorcet-winner probability was cross-checked against brute-force enumeration of all 6^n profiles for n=1..7, and a seeded sfc32 sampler of 20000 elections was compared with the exact value at n=3 and n=31 to see when sampling can tell the exact figure from Guilbaud's 8.774% limit.
- Why built: The kernel says to use the exact DP and quote 8.77% only for large odd electorates; the earlier entry verified it against published numbers only, never against an independent enumeration, and a team might reach for sampling instead of the DP.
- Design: Pure Python with Fractions. The DP adds one of 6 sign vectors per voter to a margin state; brute force loops itertools.product over 6 rankings per voter and tallies the same margins. The sampler uses sfc32 with a fixed seed, saves its four state words after 1000 draws and restores them (the state-word discipline of the seeded-rng entry), then draws 20000 elections at n=3 and n=31 and compares z-scores with the exact value and with 0.08774.
- Got right: DP and brute force matched exactly (as Fractions) for n=1..7. Odd n gave cycle = no-winner = 5.556% (n=3), 7.502% (n=7), 8.499% (n=31), 8.635% (n=61), all under 8.774%. Even n gave 66.7% (n=2), 55.6% (n=4), 29.1% (n=30) no strict winner against at most 3.30% true cycles. Restoring the four state words reproduced the next 100 draws.
- Where/why it failed: The sampling shortcut fails at the size where the limit is usually quoted: at n=31 the 20000-election estimate was 8.55% with standard error 0.20%, z=-1.13 against 8.774%, so it cannot separate the exact 8.499% from the limit, while at n=3 (5.56%) z=-19.8 rejects the limit easily.
- Fix: Use the exact DP for any stated cycle frequency, and treat a sample only as a sanity check whose error bar must be shown: distinguishing 8.5% from 8.77% at 1 sigma-level needs roughly 100000 or more elections per electorate size.
- Why this fix: The DP is exact and costs seconds up to n=61 while sampling error at p near 0.085 shrinks only as 1/sqrt(trials), so the small gap below the limit stays inside the noise unless the sample is made very large.
- Rule of thumb: Quote Guilbaud's 8.77% only for large odd electorates and get the exact value from the margin-vector DP: it matched brute force at n=1..7, and a 20000-election seeded sample at n=31 (se 0.20%) could not reject 8.774% although the exact value is 8.499%.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS); brute force covers only n up to 7, larger n rely on the DP agreeing there and on the published values.
- Composed: ideas:SOCIAL-CHOICE/condorcet/exact-margin-vector-dp, sandbox-kernel-social-choice/E1, brainwork/E44
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__condorcet-exact-dp-vs-brute-force-and-seeded-sfc32-sampling-power.py
- Prediction: DP equals brute force at n=1..7; odd-n values stay under 8.774%; a 20000-election sample matches the exact value within 3 se at n=3 and n=31 but rejects 8.774% only at n=3, not at n=31.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS dp==brute n1-7; odd cycles<8.774; even n30 nocw 29.1%; sfc32 20000-sample n=31 z_limit=-1.13 not rejectable. n=3 z_limit=-19.80.
- Scenarios: 1) DP vs brute force n=1..7; 2) odd n=3,7,31,61 vs published and the limit; 3) even n=2,4,30 tie mass; 4) sfc32 sample at n=3 (rejects limit); 5) sfc32 sample at n=31, built to BREAK the sampling shortcut; 6) state-word save/restore of 100 draws

## E156 — age cutoff 2lag bytearray or vs first cover dict base 3011 p8 p10 and third flat at 3p reverifies 3001 and 3011
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][state][model]
- What: The bytearray-OR cover rule and the first-cover dict rule for the two-lag shadow count were run side by side at base 3011 on P8 and P10, which neither source entry covered, and the lag range was extended past 2P for P5 and P6 (to 3P) and P5 (to 4P). Both rules agreed everywhere and the period average was flat at N=P and N=2P for P8 (8, 18) and P10 (15, 65/2), but it was also flat at N=3P for P5 (42/5) and P6 (27/2) and at N=4P for P5 (58/5).
- Why built: The two source entries each reported flats at N=P and N=2P and no flat at 2P+1 or 2P+2, so a reader could take 'two flats' as the rule; this checks that on two new periods and asks whether the flats stop at 2P.
- Design: Python with Fractions, no RNG. Landing times per lag from the synthetic cutoff model; dict rule streams events into a first-cover dict; bytes rule builds a bytearray bitmap per lag and tests whether the OR equals the earlier map; a sizes-only rule is the wrong-rule control. Averages are over the P residues of base 3011. Cells run: P8 and P10 at N in {P-1,P,2P-1,2P,2P+1}; P5 and P6 at 3P-1,3P,3P+1; P5 at 4P-1,4P,4P+1.
- Got right: Dict and bytes rules agreed on all 21 cells, the sizes-only rule differed, and every flat was followed by a move one lag later (P8 at 2P+1 gave 151/8, P10 gave 167/5, P5 at 3P+1 gave 46/5, P6 gave 43/3, P5 at 4P+1 gave 62/5).
- Where/why it failed: The prediction written before the first run was wrong: it expected the average to keep moving at N=3P for P5 and P6, treating the flats as a P-and-2P pattern. All three extension cells were flat, so the earlier entries' wording 'flat at N=P and N=2P' describes the range they tested, not a limit.
- Fix: State the pattern as flat at N equal to a multiple of P (checked k=1,2 on P8 and P10, k=1,2,3 on P5 and P6, k=4 on P5) and quote the tested range; revise the prediction instead of the assertion only after recording the miss, as the sandbox docstring does.
- Why this fix: The extension cells show the flat recurring at each multiple tried while the lag after it still moves the average, so a bound at 2P would be wrong for P5 and P6, and the claim stays tied to what was run.
- Rule of thumb: Do not cite the 2-lag flat as limited to N=P and N=2P: in this synthetic model the dict and bytearray-OR rules both gave flats at every multiple of P tried (P5 to 4P, P6 to 3P, P8 and P10 to 2P) with a move at +1; it is untested beyond 4P and outside P5-P12.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS after the recorded revision); the cutoff model is the synthetic one inherited from the two source entries, not field data, and multiples beyond 4P were not run.

## E155 — first flush is per storm so small storm climates lose far more
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design]
- What: Applied the rain-barrel kernel (gallons = roof sq ft x inches x 0.623, about a 10 percent haircut
  for gutter loss and first flush) with the passive-harvesting kernel (overflow is slowed and sunk) and
  brainwork E105 (3 inches of mulch cut drip water 47 percent) in one season model.
- Why built: The kernel was never applied, and its 10 percent haircut treats first-flush diversion as a
  share of rain when a diverter takes a fixed depth from every storm.
- Design: Deterministic 120-day season, 1000 sq ft roof, 6 inches total rain as 0.15 in every 3 days
  (drizzle) or 0.75 in every 15 days (monsoon). Diverter 0.5 mm (clean roof) or 2 mm (dirty), gutter
  loss 5 percent. A 150 sq ft bed needing 1 in a week, mulched at E105's 226/424. Barrels 55 to 440 gal.
- Got right: The formula is exact (623 gal per inch on 1000 sq ft). Mulch let a 110 gal barrel meet all of
  the monsoon demand that a bare bed needed 220 gal for. A 220 gal barrel overflowed 53 percent of the
  monsoon catch, so the passive sink is part of the design, not an extra.
- Where/why it failed: The 10 percent haircut is climate-bound: the dirty-roof diverter plus gutter loss
  took 55 percent of drizzle-climate rain (clean roof 17 percent), and only 7.5 to 15 percent in the
  monsoon climate. My 10 to 15 percent band for the clean monsoon case was itself too high (7.5).
- Fix: Compute the diverter loss per storm (diverter depth over typical storm depth), not as a flat share;
  in small-storm climates use the clean-roof diverter size or clean the roof, and plan a rain garden or
  swale for the overflow from the first storm that fills the barrel.
- Why this fix: The diverter's volume is fixed per event, so its share scales with how many storms the
  rain arrives in, which the per-inch formula cannot see.
- Rule of thumb: First flush is a fixed depth per storm, not 10 percent: a 2 mm diverter took 55 percent
  of a 0.15 in-storm season and 7.5 to 15 percent of a 0.75 in one; size the loss per storm.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox in this entry (RESULT FAIL 4/5 of my
  predictions; numbers copied from the run). Storm series and demand are assumed, not local data.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/water/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, ideas:GARDEN/water/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, pappydapimp69__brainwork/E105

- Prediction: the formula gives 623; dirty diverter plus gutter loss takes over 30 percent in drizzle; clean
  loss stays 10 to 15 percent in monsoon; a mulched half-size barrel meets at least the bare full barrel's
  share; a 220 gal barrel overflows over half the monsoon catch.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL 4/5; loss share drizzle dirty 0.55 clean 0.17, monsoon dirty 0.15 clean 0.07;
  monsoon met bare220 1.00 mulched110 1.00; overflow@220 0.53

## E154 — two pass rhyme letters and scheme shape stops
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [songwriting][rhyme][testing][model]
- What: Sandbox with a 22-word hand lexicon that labels rhyme schemes in one pass versus the kernel's two passes (uppercase for perfect and family rhymes first, lowercase assonance second) and counts the stopping points of each scheme shape.
- Why built: Two songwriting kernels were only quoted in prose by sandbox-lyrical-composition/E7 and E8; this exercises both against one fixture to declare the link.
- Design: Words carry a vowel nucleus and a coda; perfect means same nucleus and coda, family means same nucleus with codas in one class (nasal or stop), assonance means nucleus only. Stanzas AABB, ABAB, ABBA, XXAA, a stray-assonance stanza (town, night, mine, line) and an assonance-only stanza (night, road, mine, home). Stopping points are adjacent lines sharing an uppercase letter.
- Got right: One pass read the stray stanza as XAAA because night grabbed mine and line, while two passes returned XXAA; an assonance-only stanza read ABAB in one pass and abab in two, so case carries the open versus landed distinction; stops came out AABB 2, ABAB 0, ABBA 1, XXAA 1, matching the shape kernel's stable-to-open ordering.
- Where/why it failed: My first fixture had no stray assonance mate for the XXAA line and its assonance-only pair turned out to be a family rhyme (stone and home share a nasal class), so the first run showed no difference between the labelers and a FAIL; the fixture was corrected and the prediction unchanged. The mislabel needs a stray line whose vowel matches an already resolved pair.
- Fix: Label resolved rhymes first and assonance second, show case in the output, and count stopping points only on uppercase adjacent pairs.
- Why this fix: The mislabel appeared only when an assonance-only line shared a vowel with a resolved pair, and the second pass cannot claim lines the first pass already lettered.
- Rule of thumb: Letter resolved rhymes before assonance (XAAA became XXAA here), and count stopping points on uppercase adjacent pairs only; test the labeler with a stray line sharing a vowel with a resolved pair (22-word hand lexicon).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the lexicon and its coda classes are hand-made approximations of English pronunciation, and the emotional effect of a shape was not measured, only its stopping-point count.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS two-pass labels XXAA=XXAA stray one-pass=XAAA two-pass=XXAA assonance-only one-pass=ABAB two-pass=abab stops AABB/ABAB/ABBA/XXAA=2/0/1/1
- Scenarios: 1) AABB, ABAB, ABBA with no stray assonance, both labelers agree; 2) XXAA with no stray; 3) stray assonance line beside a perfect pair, built to BREAK the one-pass labeler; 4) assonance-only stanza; 5) stopping-point count per shape.

- Audited: 2026-10-15 · pass · Read the entry and its stored sandbox (2026-10-12__two-pass-rhyme-letters-and-scheme-shape-stops.py). The labels are computed, not built in: one_pass and two_pass derive letters from the lexicon through rel(), and the stray stanza really does come out XAAA in one pass and XXAA in two because night is assonance-only with mine and line, which are a perfect pair. The Rule's claim about letting resolved rhymes claim lines before assonance is therefore tested by a case built to break it. Limits I found: the stopping-point counts (AABB 2, ABAB 0, ABBA 1, XXAA 1) follow almost by definition from counting adjacent equal uppercase letters, so they check the counter rather than a finding, and the mislabel is shown on one stray stanza over a 22-word lexicon with hand-made coda classes, so it is not a measured rate on real lyrics. ## E153 — seeded rng state words vs count replay and fingerprint
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][state][testing][determinism]
- What: Python sfc32 sandbox re-verifying the seeded-RNG kernel and the replay-fingerprint kernel together: state-word save versus seed-and-count save, lockstep clients, an ambient clock source, and raw versus sorted-key state hashing.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel was only quoted in prose by the-game-prologue/E1; this declares the link after an independent rebuild in a different language and generator implementation.
- Design: sfc32 with four 32-bit state words; restore by loading the words or by replaying count rolls (count 200000); two lockstep clients over 10000 rolls; a 1000-roll sim that restores at roll 500 with and without an ambient counter-clock term mixed in; a 1000-roll fingerprint hash; two dicts with different insertion order hashed raw and with sorted keys.
- Got right: State-word restore replayed 0 rolls against 200000 for the seed-and-count restore, and the next five rolls were identical; lockstep clients stayed equal over 10000 rolls; the seeded sim's save and load round trip matched the uninterrupted run.
- Where/why it failed: The ambient-source sim did not round trip (fingerprint differed), and the raw insertion-order serializer hashed two equal states differently, which both confirm the kernel's tell rather than refuting it; no scenario contradicted the kernel.
- Fix: Keep every roll on one RNG whose four state words are saved, take ambient clocks and random calls out of the authoritative sim, and hash state through a sorted-key serializer.
- Why this fix: Each break was removed only by one of those three disciplines, and the fingerprint over 1000 rolls caught the ambient version while passing the seeded one.
- Rule of thumb: Save the generator's state words, not seed plus count (0 versus 200000 replayed rolls), and fingerprint 1000 rolls with sorted keys to catch ambient sources (assumed Python sfc32, not the JS runtime).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run in Python; the JavaScript integer-key reordering and cross-browser Math drift in the original entry were not run here.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/replay-fingerprint, the-game-prologue/E1
- Polarity: compatible

- Prediction: State-word restore replays 0 rolls and count restore 200000 with the same next five rolls; the ambient sim diverges after restore and the 1000-roll fingerprint catches it; raw key order hashes differently from sorted.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS restore words=4 ints/0 rolls vs count=200000 rolls, next5 equal, lockstep 10000, seeded roundtrip True vs ambient False, raw-key-order hash equal=False canonical=True
- Scenarios: 1) state-word versus count restore; 2) two lockstep clients over 10000 rolls; 3) seeded sim round trip at roll 500; 4) BREAK: ambient clock mixed into rolls; 5) BREAK: raw versus sorted-key hashing.

## E152 — rain garden sizing drain time by soil

- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork

- What: Sandbox of the roof/6 (clay) and roof/8 (sand) rain-garden sizing rule with 6 in ponding, checking whether each soil drains a 1 in and 3 in storm within 48 h, and what a 55 gal barrel does to ponding depth.
- Why built: The passive-harvesting kernel gives sizing divisors but no drain-time check; a basin that holds water past 48 h is a failure mode the divisor alone hides.
- Design: 1000 sq ft roof, runoff = area x rain x 0.623; garden area = roof / divisor; ponded depth capped at 6 in; drain hours = ponded depth / infiltration rate (assumed sand 2.0, loam 0.5, clay 0.1, compacted clay 0.03 in/h).

A 55 gal barrel took off 0.53 in of ponding on a 167 sq ft garden, not the under 0.1 in predicted.

- Rule of thumb: Rain-garden divisor sizing is not enough on clay: check ponded depth divided by infiltration rate stays under 48 h, or cap ponding depth near 3 in (assumed constants).

## E150 — rain garden sizing divisor drawdown and soil class misread
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][soil][model]
- What: A minute-step model of the rain-garden sizing rule (roof area divided by 6 on clay, by 8 on sand, 6 in ponding, 1000 sq ft roof, 3 hour storms). Both divisors captured a 1 in storm fully, but at 3 in the clay garden overflowed 65 percent and the sand garden 50 percent, so the divisor is a one-inch-storm rule, not a soil-adjusted safety margin. A full 6 in pond drained in 60 h on clay (past a 48 h standing-water limit) and 3 h on sand, and a jar-test texture misread turned a loam into a sandy clay with a drawdown estimate 3.3 times too long.
- Why built: The passive-harvesting kernel gives the divisor and the swale figures but no memory entry had applied it; brainwork E132 had said one 3 in storm overflows a roof/6 rain garden and a rain barrel alike, and the soil-jar entry E1 had shown the jar-timing misread, so I wanted to see whether the divisor holds across storm size and across the soil class that a home texture test would give.
- Design: Stdlib-only deterministic model with 1 minute steps: roof runoff spread evenly over the storm, garden stores pond depth times area, infiltrates at an assumed rate (sand 2.0, loam 0.5, sandy clay 0.15, clay 0.1 in/h) and overflows the rest. Divisors 6 (clay), 8 (sand) and 7 (loam, interpolated by me) at 1, 2 and 3 in storms. A reduced USDA texture classifier is applied to the true loam (40/40/20) and to the soil-jar E1 misread readout (47.6/7.7/44.6) to compare drawdown estimates.
- Got right: Roof/6 on clay captured a 1 in storm with 0 percent overflow and a full pond needed 60 h to drain, so the kernel's divisor is fine for capture but needs a shallower pond or an underdrain on clay; the roof/6 garden overflowed 65 percent in a 3 in storm, matching E132's direction. The soil-jar misread classified as sandy clay against a true loam and made the drawdown estimate 40 h versus 12 h (x3.3).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the sand roof/8 garden would overflow under 10 percent of a 3 in storm was wrong, it overflowed 50 percent: the divisor shrinks the sand garden by a quarter, so its storage is smaller even though it drains in 3 h, and the faster infiltration only recovers part of that over a 3 h storm. The drawdown trend is as the kernel implies, the capture trend is not. The infiltration rates, the 3 h storm shape and the interpolated loam divisor are assumed, and nothing was modelled for compaction, ponding-depth limits or the swale figures.
- Fix: When applying the kernel, size the garden to the design storm and not only to the divisor: check overflow at the storm you care about, and check the full-pond drain time (ponding depth over infiltration rate) against a 48 h limit; on clay either lower the pond depth or add an underdrain. Read soil class by a jar test taken at 2 hours for silt, as soil-jar E1 corrected, before choosing the divisor.
- Why this fix: Capture is storage plus infiltration during the storm, so a smaller sand garden loses storage faster than faster infiltration gains it once the storm is longer than a few hours, while drawdown depends only on pond depth over rate; the two can point in opposite directions, so each needs its own check.
- Rule of thumb: Treat the roof/6 to roof/8 rain-garden divisor as a roughly one-inch-storm capture rule and check pond drain time separately: in this model both divisors overflowed 50 to 65 percent at 3 in, a clay pond took 60 h to drain while sand took 3 h, and a jar-test misread of loam as sandy clay inflated the drain estimate x3.3. Rates and storm shape are assumed, so the sizes are illustrative.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS after the corrected claim for the sand case, original prediction refuted and disclosed above); overflow percentages, drain hours and the texture classes are observed output. Infiltration rates, storm shape, 100 percent roof runoff and the loam divisor of 7 are assumed parameters.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, brainwork/E132, 2026-10-09__home-soil-jar-test-stokes-timing-and-leaf-triage-order/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__rain-garden-sizing-divisor-drawdown-and-soil-class-misread.py
- Prediction: Roof/6 on clay captures 1 in fully but its full pond needs 48 h or more; the same garden overflows at least 40 percent of a 3 in storm; roof/8 on sand overflows under 10 percent of a 3 in storm and drains in under 6 h; the jar-test misread classifies loam as sandy clay with a drawdown estimate at least 3 times too long.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS original sand 3in under 10pct overflow refuted; roof/6 clay: 1in overflow 0.0%, 3in 65.0%, full pond drains 60 h; roof/8 sand 3in overflow 50.0%, pond 3.0 h; jar misread sandy clay vs true loam drain x3.3
- Scenarios: 1) clay at roof/6 with 1, 2 and 3 in storms; 2) sand at roof/8 with the same storms (built to BREAK the divisor trend, and it did on capture); 3) loam at roof/7; 4) full-pond drawdown on clay versus sand; 5) texture classification of the true loam versus the jar-misread readout

## E149 — fennel allelopathy radius 3 to 10 ft small garden placement
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][pest-control][design][model]
- What: A grid model of the companion-planting kernel's fennel case (inhibits tomatoes, beans and peas within 3 to 10 ft). With tomatoes every 2 ft and one fennel plant at a plot corner, the share inside a hard radius rose from 1 to 20 percent in a 20 ft plot and from 4 to 80 percent in a 10 ft plot as the radius went from 3 to 10 ft, a factor of about 20 either way. Placing the fennel 10 ft outside the plot edge left 0 percent in all three plot sizes, and a smooth exposure decay cut the expected loss to 0.22 of the hard-radius count.
- Why built: The companion kernel lists fennel as the negative-allelopathy case with a 3 to 10 ft radius but gives no placement advice; brainwork E104 had modelled coverage as a smooth dose curve for marigolds and E130 had put fennel in a claim-ranking graph, and neither asked how the wide radius range turns into a layout decision.
- Design: Stdlib-only deterministic grid arithmetic. Plots of 10, 20 and 40 ft with plants every 2 ft; fennel at the plot corner or 3 or 10 ft outside the edge midpoint; radii 3, 6 and 10 ft. Hard model counts plants within the radius; smooth model (the E104 style dose curve) uses exposure exp(-d/L) with L set so exposure is 5 percent at the radius, and reports the mean exposure as expected loss.
- Got right: A separation equal to the largest stated radius removed all exposure in every plot (a rule that does not depend on which radius is true), and the smooth model's expected loss at R=10 was 0.22 of the hard count in a 20 ft plot, so the hard-radius count overstates a dose-response loss.
- Where/why it failed: Two predictions were wrong. I expected over 60 percent of a 20 ft plot inside a 10 ft radius and 100 percent of a 10 ft plot; a corner fennel only reaches a quarter disc of the grid, which gave 20 and 80 percent, so I had forgotten the geometry before running. The unit effect is that the unknown radius, not the plot, dominates the answer. The grid, the plant pitch, the 5 percent decay choice and a single fennel plant are assumed, and no root-growth, soil or species data were used.
- Fix: When applying the kernel, convert the 3 to 10 ft range into a placement rule that does not need the radius: keep fennel about 10 ft from vegetable beds, or grow it in a container with its roots contained, and do not try to squeeze it into a small bed on the strength of the 3 ft end of the range.
- Why this fix: The affected share scales with the area of the disc, which goes with the radius squared, so a range of 3 to 10 ft spans a factor of about 11 in area and about 20 here after edge effects; a separation equal to the largest radius is the only position that is safe whichever radius is true.
- Rule of thumb: Treat the fennel 3 to 10 ft range as a placement problem: in this grid model the affected share changed about 20x between the two ends (1 to 20 percent in a 20 ft plot), a 10 ft separation cleared every plot size, and a smooth decay cut the expected loss to about a fifth of the hard-radius count. Layout and decay are assumed, so the shares are illustrative.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS after the corrected claims; the two wrong predictions are disclosed above); the shares and ratios are observed output. Plot sizes, plant pitch, the 5 percent decay point and the single fennel plant are assumed parameters.
