## E148 — drip lateral friction uniformity pressure 25 vs 60 psi
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A Hazen-Williams lateral-line model of the drip kernel's spec (25 psi, 1 gph emitters at 12 in on 0.6 in tube). Distribution uniformity (lowest over mean emitter flow) was 0.998 at 100 ft, 0.948 at 300 ft and 0.890 at 400 ft; 60 psi inlet gave 0.951 and 0.896, so higher pressure does not repair a long run, and it cut the emitters a 5 gpm zone supports from 300 to 193.
- Why built: The drip kernel says regulate to 20-25 psi and space emitters 12-18 in, and brainwork E112 modelled pressure only as an emitter-flow law (sqrt of pressure) and listed line friction and compensating emitters as not modelled. I wanted to see how long a lateral the spec supports.
- Design: Stdlib-only deterministic march from the far end of the lateral back to the inlet, with Hazen-Williams friction (C=150, 0.6 in ID) summed per 12 in segment and a bisection on far-end pressure to hit the inlet pressure. Emitters are plain orifice (1 gph at 25 psi, sqrt law as in E112) or pressure-compensating (flat above 10 psi). Lengths 50 to 400 ft at 25 and 60 psi. The drip efficiency of 0.92 from E105 is multiplied by the uniformity to get an effective figure.
- Got right: Raising the inlet to 60 psi moved the 300 ft uniformity by 0.003 (0.948 to 0.951), as predicted, because friction grows nearly as fast as head. Compensating emitters held uniformity 1.000 on every run whose far end stayed at or above 10 psi, and failed at 400 ft on 25 psi (far end 6.3 psi, uniformity 0.871) while 60 psi rescued them (1.000). The effective efficiency 0.92 times 0.948 is 0.872 at 300 ft.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that uniformity falls below 0.90 by 300 ft was wrong: it was 0.948 at 300 ft and crossed 0.90 only between 300 and 400 ft. The first run was also wrong for a unit reason, a coefficient that gives psi per foot was divided by 100 again, which hid all friction and gave uniformity 1.000 everywhere; a check of 5 gpm in 0.6 in tube against roughly 10 psi per 100 ft caught it. Tube diameter, C and the orifice law are assumed, and real emitters have manufacturing variation and clogging that this model lacks.
- Fix: When applying the kernel, treat 12 in spacing at 25 psi as good to roughly 300 ft of 0.6 in tube and break longer runs into separate laterals or feed them from the middle; do not raise pressure to fix a long run (it barely moves uniformity and shrinks the emitters per zone x1.55), and use compensating emitters only if the far end still sees 10 psi.
- Why this fix: Friction loss scales with flow to the 1.85 power while emitter flow scales with the square root of pressure, so raising pressure raises the lost fraction of head almost as much as the head itself, leaving uniformity unchanged; shortening the run or a middle feed cuts the flow that each segment must carry.
- Rule of thumb: Check lateral length before pressure: in this model 25 psi with 1 gph emitters at 12 in stayed above 0.94 uniformity to 300 ft and fell to 0.89 at 400 ft, 60 psi changed that by under 0.01 while costing a third of the emitters per zone, and only compensating emitters on a high-pressure feed held 400 ft. Pipe constants are assumed, so the 300 ft figure is illustrative.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS after the corrections described above); the uniformity, pressure and emitter counts are observed output. Tube diameter, Hazen-Williams C and the orifice law are assumed parameters, not measured hardware.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E112, brainwork/E105
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__drip-lateral-friction-uniformity-pressure-25-vs-60-psi.py
- Prediction: Uniformity at or above 0.90 at 100 ft and below 0.90 by 300 ft at 25 psi; 60 psi within 0.05 of 25 psi at 300 ft; compensating emitters at or above 0.97 wherever the far end is at or above 10 psi and failing at a long 25 psi run; effective efficiency 0.92 times uniformity below 0.92.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS original 300ft threshold refuted; DU 100ft 0.998 300ft 0.948 400ft 0.890 at 25psi, 400ft 0.896 at 60psi; compensating 400ft DU 0.871 (25psi, p_end 6.3) vs 1.000 (60psi); zone 300->193 emitters; eff at 300ft 0.872
- Scenarios: 1) plain emitters at 25 psi, 50 to 400 ft; 2) plain emitters at 60 psi (built to BREAK the idea that pressure fixes a long run); 3) compensating emitters at 25 psi; 4) compensating emitters at 60 psi; 5) zone emitter count at 25 versus 60 psi; 6) the unit-bug first run, which showed uniformity 1.000 everywhere and was discarded

## E147 — mulch ring clearance volume and drip emitter placement with decay topup
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][soil][design][model]
- What: A geometry sandbox of a mulch ring around a mature tree showed the 12 in trunk clearance costs only 5.6 percent of the mulch volume at 3 in depth, while a volcano of the same volume peaks at 9.1 in (3.0 times the layer) at the trunk. The same clearance wastes 44 percent of a 6 in radius per-plant bed.
- Why built: The mulch kernel gives a depth and a stem clearance but nobody had costed the clearance or checked it against where the drip kernel puts emitters; brainwork E105 and E113 gave depth and decay behaviour to combine with it.
- Design: Ring volume pi (R squared minus clearance squared) times depth for a 6 ft radius bed round a 6 in trunk radius; a cone solver for the volcano depth; dripline emitter distance outside the clearance edge for canopy radii 4 to 10 ft; 25 percent yearly depth loss for the top-up; and a small-bed case built to break the cheap-clearance claim.
- Got right: Clearance is cheap on a mature tree bed (3.1 percent at 8 in, 5.6 percent at 12 in), the volcano is 3.0 times the layer depth, and dripline emitters sat at least 2.5 ft outside a 12 in clearance edge on every tested canopy, so the mulch and drip kernels never collide.
- Where/why it failed: Three of my predictions were wrong: the 12 in saving was 5.6 percent not under 5, the 2 year top-up was 1.31 in not 1.7, and the 2 ft seedling bed wasted 2.8 percent not 11. Only the 0.5 ft per-plant bed broke the cheap-clearance claim, at 44.4 percent. The sandbox RESULT line prints FAIL because of those misses.
- Fix: Treat clearance as nearly free on tree-sized beds and as a real cost only when the bed radius approaches the clearance; plan the top-up from a depth-decay rate instead of a fixed annual volume.
- Why this fix: The volume ratio depends on the clearance squared over the radius squared, so it is negligible for large beds and dominant for tiny ones, which the two bed sizes confirmed.
- Rule of thumb: Keep the full stem clearance on tree beds because it costs about 3 to 6 percent of the mulch, and never pile mulch against a trunk (the same volume reaches 3 times the depth there); on single-plant beds near the clearance size the rule eats most of the mulch, so size the bed up. Toy geometry with an assumed 25 percent yearly decay.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and reading its output. The 25 percent decay rate, 6 in trunk radius and circular beds are assumed, not measured.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/mulch-benefits-and-stem-clearance-rule, ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E105, brainwork/E113
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__mulch-ring-clearance-volume-and-drip-emitter-placement-with-decay-topup.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: 12 in clearance saves under 5 percent of mulch volume on a 6 ft radius bed, the volcano reaches 3 times the depth, dripline emitters stay outside the clearance, a 3 in layer needs about 1.7 in top-up over 2 years, and a 2 ft seedling bed wastes about 11 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL 12in clearance saves-volume 5.6%, volcano 9.1in, topup 1.31in, small-bed waste 44.4%. The volcano and emitter placement predictions held; the 5 percent, 1.7 in and 11 percent numbers did not.
- Scenarios: 1) mature tree ring at 8 in and 12 in clearance; 2) volcano of equal volume; 3) dripline emitters at four canopy radii; 4) three year depth decay and top-up; 5) BREAK: 2 ft seedling bed and a 0.5 ft per-plant bed with 4 in clearance.

## E146 — marigold cover year rotation vs interplant nematode yield over eight seasons
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][pest-control][model]
- What: An eight-season rotation model of a root-knot nematode pool showed a sacrificed marigold cover-crop season every third year gave mean tomato yield 0.58 against 0.19 for tomato every year and 0.20 for a 10 percent marigold interplant. Cover every second year was worse (0.46), until the kill strength was halved, which flipped the ranking.
- Why built: The companion-planting kernel says the marigold nematode effect needs a full-season soil-occupying cover crop, and brainwork E104 modelled only one season's coverage curve; nobody had asked whether giving up a growing season for the cover crop pays back over several seasons.
- Design: Pool relative units starting at 2, tomato season multiplies the pool by 6 up to a cap of 50, yield 1 over (1 plus pool over 5); a cover season applies the E104-form coverage kill at 95 percent coverage (0.006 of control) and yields nothing; an interplant at 10 percent coverage costs 10 percent yield. The kill coefficient 0.0473 was calibrated so the model reproduces the E104 curve (0.765, 0.585, 0.260, 0.067, 0.006). Four plans, plus a halved-kill case built to break the ranking and a weak-multiplier case.
- Got right: All five predictions held: tomato-only 0.194, interplant 0.197, cover 1-in-3 0.579, cover 1-in-2 0.463, and the halved-kill case flipped the order (0.312 against 0.431). The interplant barely helped because the pool still grows at 6 times 0.585 per season.
- Where/why it failed: The weak-multiplier case (multiplier 2) was an unplanned finding that cuts against the simple story: the 10 percent interplant reached 0.530 against 0.288 for tomato-only, because at a low growth rate a 41 percent cut per season is enough to hold the pool down. The multiplier, yield curve, cap and the 10 percent yield cost are assumed, not field data, and the kill coefficient was fitted to the earlier toy rather than to trials.
- Fix: Judge a cover-crop recommendation by pool growth per season and the yield sacrificed, not by the single-season suppression figure; use a rotation with a cover year when the pest multiplies fast, and treat an interplant as enough only when the multiplier is near 2 or lower.
- Why this fix: The same single-season kill produced opposite rankings depending on the multiplier and kill strength, so the decision depends on pool growth against suppression, not the suppression alone.
- Rule of thumb: In this toy a full cover-crop season every third year beat both tomato-only and a 10 percent interplant when the pest multiplies about 6 times per season, but a weaker kill favoured cover every second year and a slow-growing pest favoured the interplant, so size the rotation from the pest growth rate and the kill actually achieved. Assumed parameters only; three rules of ranking were tested at three parameter settings.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and reading every printed number. The pest multiplier, the yield function, the yield cost of interplanting and the kill coefficient (fitted to a prior toy, not to data) are assumed.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/companion-planting-claim-taxonomy, brainwork/E104
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__marigold-cover-year-rotation-vs-interplant-nematode-yield-over-eight-seasons.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: tomato-only mean yield under 0.2; cover 1-in-3 best of the four plans; cover 1-in-2 worse than 1-in-3; interplant within 0.05 of tomato-only; and with the kill halved cover 1-in-3 falls below cover 1-in-2.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 5/5 predictions held. Means: tomato-only 0.194, interplant 0.197, cover 1-in-3 0.579, cover 1-in-2 0.463; halved kill: 0.312 against 0.431; multiplier 2: interplant 0.530, cover 1-in-3 0.655, tomato-only 0.288.
- Scenarios: 1) four plans at multiplier 6 and full kill; 2) BREAK: kill halved; 3) multiplier 2 with full kill; 4) reproduction of the E104 coverage curve as a calibration check.

## E145 — drip emitter spacing wetted bulb bridging by soil texture and root zone loss
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][soil][model]
- What: A wetted-bulb model of the drip kernel's 12 to 18 in emitter spacing found that 1 gph bridges an 18 in spacing in 0.85 to 1.12 hours across sand, loam and clay, but that sand sends 20 percent of the bulb below a 12 in root zone at 2 hours and 40 percent at 6 hours while loam and clay send 0 and 8 percent or less. Only 2 of 5 written predictions held.
- Why built: The drip kernel gives emitter flow and spacing without saying what soil they assume, and the jar-test entry gives the soil texture classes; nobody had tested whether the same spacing bridges a continuous wet strip in every texture.
- Design: Half-ellipsoid bulb with horizontal radius a = (3 V lam / (2 pi theta))^(1/3), V = flow times hours. Soil constants are assumed, not measured: usable storage theta 0.08, 0.17, 0.18 and lateral to vertical spread lam 0.6, 1.0, 1.4 for sand, loam and clay. Checks: bridge time for 18 in at 1 gph and 12 in at 0.5 gph, share of the bulb deeper than 12 in, and a mulch run-time test.
- Got right: At 0.5 gph for 1 hour the radius stayed under 9 in in all soils (7.5, 6.9, 7.5 in), so 18 in spacing leaves gaps; at 1 gph for 2 hours every soil reached at least 6 in (11.8, 10.9, 12.0 in), so 12 in spacing is continuous.
- Where/why it failed: Three predictions failed. The sand deep-loss share was 20 percent at 2 hours not above 40 (it reached 40 percent only at 6 hours); the bridge-time spread across soils was 32 percent not under 15 (loam slowest at 1.12 h against 0.85 and 0.88); and the mulch prediction was built wrongly: the need factor 0.58 multiplied the run time so the bridge time rose 72 percent. A bulb depends only on applied volume, so mulch cannot shorten bridging, it only stretches the interval between runs (1.72 times). The soil constants are assumed, so the soil ranking is a property of those numbers, not of real sand and clay.
- Fix: Size run time per emitter from the target bulb radius for the soil, not from the kernel's flat spacing; cap run length in sandy soil so the bulb stays inside the root zone, and take mulch's benefit as longer intervals between runs rather than shorter runs.
- Why this fix: Radius grows with the cube root of volume while sand's low storage and shallow lateral spread push the bulb downward, so a time that bridges the strip in sand also starts losing water below the roots, which is a different limit from the one that sets spacing in clay.
- Rule of thumb: In this toy 1 gph bridged 18 in spacing within about 1.1 hours in all three textures but 0.5 gph for 1 hour never did, and sand began losing water below 12 in after 2 hours (40 percent at 6 hours); run short pulses in sandy soil and lengthen the interval, not the run time, under mulch. Constants are assumed and only three textures were run.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox and reading its printed output. The storage and spread constants for the three soils, the half-ellipsoid bulb shape and the 12 in root zone are assumed, not measured, and the jar-test class names were used only as labels.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, ideas:GARDEN/mulch-benefits-and-stem-clearance-rule, 2026-10-09__home-soil-jar-test-stokes-timing-and-leaf-triage-order/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__drip-emitter-spacing-wetted-bulb-bridging-by-soil-texture-and-root-zone-loss.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: 0.5 gph for 1 hour leaves a dry gap at 18 in in all soils; 1 gph for 2 hours bridges 12 in in all; sand's below-root-zone share exceeds 40 percent against under 25 for loam and clay; loam is slowest to bridge with all soils within 15 percent; and mulch shortens the 18 in bridge time by about 42 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL 2/5 predictions held. Radii 7.5, 6.9, 7.5 in (0.5 gph, 1 h) and 11.8, 10.9, 12.0 in (1 gph, 2 h); sand deep share 20 percent at 2 h and 40 percent at 6 h; bridge times 0.88, 1.12, 0.85 h; mulch test inverted (plus 72 percent, labelled post-hoc).
- Scenarios: 1) 0.5 gph 1 h at three textures; 2) 1 gph 2 h at 12 in spacing; 3) below-root-zone share at 2 h and 6 h; 4) bridge time across soils at 1 gph and 18 in; 5) BREAK: mulch need factor applied to run time (built wrongly, the failure is reported).

## E144 — swale spacing upper bound from trench capacity and storm depth
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][soil][model]
- What: A trench-capacity model of the water-harvesting kernel's swale (18 in deep, 4 ft wide, 0.279 m3 or 74 gal per metre) found the kernel's 2 m minimum spacing never overflowed up to a 150 mm storm, but the missing upper bound is 11.1 m at 50 mm, 5.6 m at 100 mm and 3.7 m at 150 mm; a 10 m spacing at 100 mm overflowed 44.3 percent.
- Why built: The kernel gives swale dimensions and a spacing of at least 2 m but no maximum, and earlier garden entries tested rain gardens and barrels rather than how far apart swales can be placed.
- Design: Per metre of swale, inflow = spacing x storm x 0.5 runoff coefficient against V-shaped trench capacity plus one hour of clay infiltration at 5 mm/h; bisection for the largest overflow-free spacing; a gallon cross-check with the rain-barrel kernel's 0.623 gal per sqft per inch; a 25 percent slope reducing usable depth; and the 3 in storm from brainwork E132.
- Got right: The spacing bounds, the 44 percent overflow at 10 m, the under 10 percent effect of clay infiltration (2.2 percent) and the barrel-kernel conversion (0.06 percent error) all matched the prediction, and a 3 in storm (76.2 mm) bound of 7.3 m means a 5 m swale spacing held the storm that overflowed a barrel and a roof/6 rain garden in E132.
- Where/why it failed: My slope prediction was wrong: a 25 percent slope left 67 percent of flat capacity, not under 50 percent, because my hand arithmetic doubled the depth loss across the 1.22 m width; the sandbox RESULT line is FAIL for that reason.
- Fix: Add a maximum spacing to the swale rule: spacing times design storm times runoff coefficient must stay under about 0.28 m3 per metre, so quote the design storm with the spacing, and derate capacity by roughly a third on a 25 percent slope.
- Why this fix: Overflow depends on how much catchment each metre of trench serves, which grows linearly with spacing, so a minimum spacing alone cannot prevent it.
- Rule of thumb: Treat the 2 m swale spacing as a minimum only: for a 100 mm storm keep it under about 5.6 m (11 m at 50 mm, 3.7 m at 150 mm) and expect about a third less capacity on a 25 percent slope (assumed runoff coefficient 0.5 and V-shaped section, illustrative).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; trench shape, runoff coefficient, infiltration rate and the slope derating are assumed constants, and the E132 comparison was added after the first run.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, brainwork/E132
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__swale-spacing-upper-bound-from-trench-capacity-and-storm-depth.py
- Prediction: Overflow-free spacing about 11, 5.6 and 3.7 m at 50, 100 and 150 mm, 2 m spacing never overflowing up to 150 mm, 10 m at 100 mm overflowing about 44 percent, clay infiltration shifting the bound under 10 percent, conversion agreeing within 1 percent, and a 25 percent slope leaving under half the capacity (the last part came out wrong).
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL bounds 11.1/5.6/3.7 m at 50/100/150 mm; 10 m at 100 mm overflows 44%; slope 25% keeps 67% of capacity; conv err 0.06%; 3 in storm bound 7.3 m

## E143 — sfc32 state save vs seed count replay and substreams
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][state][testing][determinism]
- What: A stdlib sfc32 sandbox confirmed that saving the four state words restores in zero replay draws and stays exact after an uncounted draw, while a seed-plus-count save cost 50000 replay draws and diverged after one draw outside the counter.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel is only quoted in prose by the-game-prologue/E1; this declares the link by exercising the kernel's state-words advice, E1's canonical hash, and the shared-stream ordinal-space kernel together.
- Design: sfc32 with a 12-draw warmup; scenarios for state-word versus seed-count restore at 50000 draws, an uncounted draw, insertion-order JSON hash versus sorted-key canonical hash with a NaN guard, removal of one of four entities from a shared stream versus per-entity substreams, and substreams keyed by name versus by list index.
- Got right: State words restored the next 1000 draws exactly; canonical hashes matched across key orders while plain JSON hashes differed; NaN threw loudly; removing an entity flipped 8 of 8 downstream combat rolls on a shared stream and 0 with named substreams.
- Where/why it failed: Substreams keyed by list index were not stable: after removing one entity the per-entity rolls of later entities changed, so the substream fix needs stable names, not positions.
- Fix: Store the full sfc32 state words in the world state, hash with a canonical sorted-key serializer that rejects non-finite values, and give each RNG-consuming concern a substream keyed by a stable name, never an index.
- Why this fix: The state words capture the entire generator, so any draw outside a counter cannot desync a load; a name survives removal and reorder while a position does not.
- Rule of thumb: Save the generator state words, not a seed-plus-count (50000 replay draws, and wrong after one uncounted draw), and key RNG substreams by stable name; an index key re-creates the shared-stream shift it was meant to remove (small toy world, 11 checks).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; entity names, counts and the sfc32 seeding routine are my own fixture, and E1 itself was read, not re-run in its original JavaScript.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/a-shared-rng-stream-is-an-ordinal-space-address-it-symbolically, the-game-prologue/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__sfc32-state-save-vs-seed-count-replay-and-substreams.py
- Prediction: State words exact with 0 replay cost; seed-count exact but cost 50000 and diverging after an uncounted draw; JSON hashes differ by key order while canonical hashes match; shared-stream removal flips some of 8 rolls and named substreams none; index-keyed substreams shift again.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 12/11 checks held; replay cost 50000 vs 0; shared-stream flips 8/8; name-keyed stable=True index-keyed stable=False
- Scenarios: 1) state-word versus seed-count restore at 50000 draws; 2) uncounted draw (built to BREAK seed-count); 3) key-order hash and NaN guard; 4) entity removal on shared stream versus named substreams; 5) index-keyed substreams (built to BREAK the substream fix)

## E142 — rain garden vs barrel back to back storms
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][soil][model]
- What: An hourly toy model of a 1000 sqft roof sending 1 inch bursts to a 55 gal barrel (0.5 gal/hr draw) versus a ponding rain garden sized roof/6 (clay, 0.1 in/hr) or roof/8 (sand, 2 in/hr) with 6 in ponding.
- Why built: The water-harvesting kernel says slow, spread and sink beats storing; earlier entries tested single storms only, so this tests storms arriving back to back where only drain-down restores capacity.
- Design: Hourly loop; inflow = rain x roof x 0.623 gal; barrel overflows above 55 gal; garden overflows above area x 6 in ponding and drains at area x infiltration rate. Scenarios: one 1 in burst, three 1 in bursts 1 h apart, three bursts 48 h apart, each on clay and sand.
- Got right: Clay garden took a lone 1 in burst with 0 percent overflow while the barrel lost 91.2 percent; with 48 h gaps clay overflow fell from 65.5 to 13.3 percent, so spacing between storms is what refills the garden.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that the sand /8 garden would stay under 5 percent overflow failed: it lost 25 percent of a single 1 in burst (468 gal ponding cap, ~156 gal/hr infiltration) and 58.3 percent when bursts were 1 h apart; sand at 48 h gaps also kept 25 percent, because the burst outruns infiltration.
- Fix: Size by ponding volume against the design storm intensity, not only by area ratio; for sandy soil keep the /6 area (or deepen ponding) so burst volume fits, and treat infiltration rate as the refill term between storms.
- Why this fix: The sand garden's smaller area gives less ponding volume, and fast infiltration only helps over hours, so the per-burst overflow is set by volume, not soil speed.
- Rule of thumb: Rain-garden area ratios hold for one storm; for clustered storms check ponding volume against the burst and the gap against drain-down, and expect a barrel to overflow nearly all of a 1 in event regardless.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; infiltration rates, ponding depth and draw rate are assumed constants, illustrative only.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, brainwork/E115, brainwork/E132

- Prediction: Clay overflow under 5 percent on one burst and over 40 percent on tight bursts, 48 h gaps lower than tight, and sand under 5 percent on tight bursts (the last part came out wrong).

## E141 — drip lateral length friction and slope vs emitter uniformity
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A friction-loss model of one drip lateral (1/2 in tube, 0.6 in ID, Hazen-Williams C=150, emitter flow proportional to the square root of pressure) found the drip kernel's 25 psi and 12 in spacing safe at 100 ft (end emitter at 99.1 percent of the first) but only 68.4 percent at 400 ft, with a 10 ft rise costing 10 percent at the end.
- Why built: The drip kernel gives pressure, flow and spacing specs but no run length, and brainwork E112 and E137 cover pressure lift and the 4 gpm ceiling without friction along the lateral.
- Design: Backward sweep from the end emitter summing cumulative flow friction per segment plus 0.433 psi per foot of rise, bisection on end pressure to hit the inlet pressure; six cases: 1 gph at 12 in at 25 and 60 psi for 100 and 400 ft, a 10 ft rise over 100 ft, and 0.5 gph at 18 in over 400 ft.
- Got right: The 60 psi inlet lifted first-emitter flow by 1.55 times (matching E112) without improving uniformity (69.8 versus 68.4 percent at 400 ft), and 0.5 gph at 18 in held 94.2 percent over 400 ft; all six predictions held.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing in the model failed, but the 400 ft case pulls 5.12 gpm at 25 psi, above the 4 gpm supply ceiling in E137, so the water source limits the run before friction does for 1 gph emitters at 12 in.
- Fix: Add a lateral length limit to the kernel specs: cap runs where end flow stays above 90 percent of the first emitter, and split a long bed into zones, since both friction and the gpm ceiling bind before the 25 psi regulator advice does.
- Why this fix: Regulating the inlet fixes pressure at the tap, not along the tube; friction scales with cumulative flow, so halving emitter flow and doubling spacing cuts the drop far more than raising pressure.
- Rule of thumb: A drip regulator does not guarantee even emitters: at 1 gph per foot the 400 ft run lost 31.6 percent at the end while 100 ft lost 0.9, so cap lateral length by end-flow uniformity and the supply gpm before trusting the 25 psi spec (assumed tube and emitter constants).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; tube diameter, roughness and the square-root emitter law are assumed values, and no real emitter curve was used.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E112, brainwork/E137
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__drip-lateral-length-friction-and-slope-vs-emitter-uniformity.py
- Prediction: 100 ft at 25 psi keeps end over 95 percent, 400 ft falls under 90, 60 psi lifts first flow 1.5 to 1.6 times with a smaller relative drop, a 10 ft rise ends under 92 percent, and 0.5 gph at 18 in holds up better than 1 gph at 12 in.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS end/first 100ft 99.1% 400ft 68.4% 60psi400ft 69.8% rise10 90.1% half-gph400ft 94.2% flow60/25 1.55; 400 ft total 5.12 gpm.

## E140 — swale grade error shrinks storage and barrel offload to meet storm
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A geometric model of a 30 ft by 4 ft by 18 in swale with a grade error along its length. Storage fell from 1346 gal when level to 90 percent at 1 percent grade, 50 percent at 5, 25 percent at 10 and 12.5 percent at 20, so "on contour" is a capacity requirement and not only a tidiness one.
- Why built: The passive-harvesting kernel says a swale must be level and on contour but gave no tolerance. The rain-barrel kernel and the rain garden overflow entry supply the storm volume it has to take.
- Design: Water pools at the low end, so depth at distance x is the trench depth minus grade times x. Storage is integrated over 3000 slices and checked against the closed form when level. Storm runoff is a 1000 sq ft roof times inches times 0.623. A 55 gal barrel takes its volume first, then the maximum storm held is capacity over roof gallons per inch.
- Got right: Level storage matched the closed form (1346 gal). A level swale held a 2.16 in storm of roof runoff, 2 percent grade held 1.73 in and 5 percent held 1.08 in.
- Where/why it failed: At 10 percent grade the swale held 0.54 in of roof runoff, and adding a 55 gal barrel only raised that to 0.63 in, so a small barrel cannot rescue a badly graded trench. The model has pure geometry with no infiltration during the storm, a flat bottom and a full wedge, so real tolerance would be looser when soil drains.
- Fix: Treat grade error as a sizing input: check the trench with a level over its length, and where it runs off by more than about 2 percent either add check dams every few feet to cut each pool's wedge or size capacity at the graded fraction.
- Why this fix: The sweep shows capacity falls steeply and nearly in proportion to 1/grade once the wedge is shorter than the trench; breaking the trench into cells is what keeps the wedge short.
- Rule of thumb: Swale storage falls to about half at a 5 percent grade error over 30 ft with 18 in depth (wedge length depth/grade), so verify level end to end and do not count on a barrel to make up the lost volume. Pure-geometry model without infiltration, one trench size.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. Trench size, flat bottom and absence of infiltration during the storm are assumed; check dams were not modeled.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, brainwork/E132
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__swale-grade-error-shrinks-storage-and-barrel-offload-to-meet-storm.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: 1 percent grade would keep over 85 percent, 5 percent about half, a level swale would hold more than 2 in of roof runoff, and a 55 gal barrel would not bring a 10 percent grade swale to a 1 in storm.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS level swale 1346 gal holds 2.16 in; 1% grade keeps 90%, 5% keeps 50%, 10% holds only 0.54 in even with a 55 gal barrel (0.63)
- Scenarios: 1) grade sweep 0 to 20 percent against the closed form 2) maximum storm held at 0, 2, 5 and 10 percent grade 3) same with a 55 gal barrel upstream, built to BREAK the idea that a barrel compensates

## E139 — seeded rng state words vs seed count and shared stream desync
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][state][testing][determinism]
- What: A stdlib sfc32 sandbox checked the seeded-RNG kernel. Saving the four state words restored in 0 draws against 500 for a seed-and-count replay, both gave identical next rolls, and a replay fingerprint caught a one-step leaked change. One shared stream broke lockstep as soon as a single cosmetic roll was added on one client.
- Why built: The seeded-RNG kernel was only quoted in prose by a single entry. This declares the link by exercising it together with the replay-fingerprint kernel and that entry's canonical-hash lesson.
- Design: sfc32 with integer-only math; a 500-step walk, a save of the state words, and 1000 following rolls compared three ways. Same-seed, other-seed and leaky runs hashed with sorted-key JSON. Two lockstep clients differing by one cosmetic roll every fifth step, with a shared stream against a separate cosmetic stream. Insertion-order against sorted-key hashing of equal states.
- Got right: State-word restore and seed-and-count replay matched exactly, replay cost 500 draws against 0. The fingerprint separated same-seed (equal), other seed and the leaky run. Insertion-ordered JSON hashed two equal states differently while sorted keys matched.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's single stream does not hold once any non-authoritative roll shares it: one cosmetic draw every fifth step shifted every later sim roll and the clients ended at different positions. Splitting a cosmetic stream (separate seed) fixed it. Cross-runtime float behaviour, the kernel's other claim, was not tested because the sandbox uses integers only.
- Fix: Keep one seeded stream for the authoritative sim, give every cosmetic or client-local effect its own stream, save all state words, and hash with canonical key order.
- Why this fix: The shared against split comparison changes only which stream the cosmetic roll draws from, and shows the sim result then does not depend on it.
- Rule of thumb: One stream is right for the sim and wrong for anything cosmetic: a single extra draw from the shared stream desyncs lockstep, so give effects their own seeded stream, save the state words, and fingerprint with sorted keys. Integer sfc32 in Python, one script, two clients.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. Browser runtime float differences and real multiplayer transport were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/replay-fingerprint, the-game-prologue/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__seeded-rng-state-words-vs-seed-count-and-shared-stream-desync.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: state restore equal with 0 draws against 500 for replay, fingerprint different for a one-step leak, and a shared stream desynced by one cosmetic roll while a split stream stays equal.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS state-word restore 0 draws vs replay 500, fingerprint catches leak, shared stream desyncs on 1 cosmetic roll (split streams fix), sorted-key hash needed
- Scenarios: 1) state words against seed and count after 500 steps 2) same seed, other seed and leaky run fingerprints 3) shared against split cosmetic stream, built to BREAK the one-stream rule 4) insertion-order against sorted-key hashing

## E138 — mulch depth widens stem clearance needed and drip emitter offset
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][soil][water][model]
- What: A toy wicking model of how much stem clearance a mulch layer needs. Wetness at the stem decays as exp(-gap/lam) with lam proportional to mulch depth, so the clearance that keeps the stem dry grew almost one-for-one with depth: 1.1 in at 1 in of mulch, 3.2 in at 3 in, 4.2 in at 4 in, 8.3 in at 8 in.
- Why built: To test whether the fixed 2 to 4 in stem-clearance band in the mulch kernel holds at every depth, against the drip emitter placement kernel and the earlier clearance and saving entries.
- Design: Assumed lam of 0.45 in per inch of depth, a wet threshold of 0.10, drip every second day for 120 days, clearance swept in 0.1 in steps for the smallest value giving zero wet stem days, with the emitter at the stem ring (offset 0) or 4 in out. Water saving modeled as 1 - exp(-0.55 x depth).
- Got right: The 2 to 4 in band was enough at 2 and 3 in of mulch (2.1 and 3.2 in needed). A 4 in emitter offset removed the need for any clearance at 3 in depth (0.0) and cut it to 0.2 at 4 in. Saving flattened as in the earlier mulch entry: 89 percent at 4 in against 99 percent at 8 in.
- Where/why it failed: The band is not depth-independent. At 4 in of mulch with the emitter at the ring 4.2 in was needed, just over the band, and at 6 and 8 in it needed 6.3 and 8.3 in, so the kernel's fixed 2 to 4 in is wrong for deep mulch. Wicking length, the threshold and the saving constant are assumed, not measured.
- Fix: State clearance as a function of depth (about one inch of clearance per inch of mulch at the ring) or move the emitter 4 in out, rather than quoting a fixed band alongside a deep-mulch saving.
- Why this fix: The depth sweep isolates depth as the driver, and the offset scenario shows the emitter kernel's placement removes the dependence.
- Rule of thumb: Clearance should scale with mulch depth (about 1 in per inch in this model) unless emitters sit 4 in or more from the stem; the 2 to 4 in band holds only for mulch up to about 3 in. Toy model with assumed constants, one wicking form.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. The wicking length, threshold and saving constant are assumed parameters, not measured.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/mulch-benefits-and-stem-clearance-rule, ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E105, brainwork/E118
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__mulch-depth-widens-stem-clearance-needed-and-drip-emitter-offset.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: the 2 to 4 in band would cover depths 2 to 4 in, 8 in mulch would need more than 3 in, and a 4 in emitter offset would zero the need at 3 in. The 4 in depth landing just outside the band (4.2) was not predicted.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL min clearance by depth(offset0) [(1, 1.1), (2, 2.1), (3, 3.2), (4, 4.2), (6, 6.3), (8, 8.3)]; offset4 3in=0.0; saving 4in=0.89 8in=0.99
- Scenarios: 1) clearance sweep at depths 1 to 8 in with emitter at ring 2) same with emitter 4 in out 3) 8 in mulch against a fixed 3 in clearance, built to BREAK the band 4) saving curve 4 against 8 in

## E137 — drip zone grouping by need and supply gpm ceiling with mulch runtime
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A toy drip-zoning model with lettuce, tomatoes and fruit trees showed that one shared valve gave a worst-case 105 percent delivery mismatch, while one zone per need class gave 0 percent. The supply ceiling only bound at 481 half-gallon-per-hour emitters on a 4 gpm spigot, so need grouping, not the flow ceiling, was the binding constraint at garden scale.
- Why built: The drip kernel says to group plants with similar water needs into separate zones and keep total zone flow within supply, and it had no memory entry applying it. The mulch kernel and the earlier emitter-spacing entry gave the run-time cut to combine with it.
- Design: Three plant classes (20 lettuce at 1 gal a week with one 0.5 gph emitter, 10 tomatoes at 7 gal with two 1 gph emitters, 3 trees at 35 gal with four 2 gph emitters). A valve has one compromise run time (total need over total flow). Zone gph checked against a 240 gph supply, the lettuce count that breaks it found by search, and needs scaled by 0.58 for mulch.
- Got right: Mixed zone worst mismatch 1.05 against exactly 0 grouped; zone flows were 54 gph mixed and 10, 20 and 24 grouped, all within supply; mulch cut total weekly run time from 9.9 to 5.7 h (42 percent) and left grouping exact.
- Where/why it failed: The 0 percent grouped result is exact by construction because each zone has one need class, so it shows the direction but not a real tolerance. Supply never constrained the base garden, so the kernel's flow-ceiling advice is only relevant for large plantings. Pressure loss along laterals was not modeled (see the lateral friction entry), nor soil, so the 105 percent is about this mix only.
- Fix: Treat zoning by need as the first design step and the GPM ceiling as a check that matters only past a few hundred emitters; recompute run times per zone when mulch is added rather than scaling one shared valve.
- Why this fix: The mixed against grouped comparison isolates the compromise run time as the source of mismatch, and the ceiling search shows how far the garden was from the flow limit.
- Rule of thumb: Mixed-need beds on one valve over- or under-watered some plants by about 100 percent here, so zone by need first and check GPM second; mulch shortens every zone's run time by the same fraction without changing the grouping result. Toy model with assumed plant needs and a 4 gpm spigot.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. Plant needs, emitter counts, the 4 gpm supply and the 0.58 mulch factor are assumed, not measured.

## E136 — swale level tolerance grade along trench drains the storage
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][model]
- What: A numerical model of the passive-harvesting kernel's contour swale (18 in deep, 4 ft wide, 30 m long) shows that "level" is a tolerance of well under 1 percent: a trench floor with 0.5 percent grade holds 84 percent of the level capacity, 1 percent holds 67, 2 percent 38 and 3 percent 25, because water pools as a wedge at the low end. At 3 percent the top 14.8 m of the trench is dry.
- Why built: The kernel says on-contour and level, and E115 found the 8-12x swale gain only above 50 mm storms, but neither said how far from level a real trench can be before the storage that makes the gain disappears.
- Design: Python stdlib, no RNG: step the trench floor in 3000 slices with a flat water surface set by the low-end rim, sum depth times width; then chain a 6 m wide contributing strip at runoff coefficient 0.5, converting to gallons with the rain-barrel kernel's 0.623 gal per sq ft per inch, against storms of 25, 50 and 100 mm.
- Got right: The capacity fractions for 0.5, 1 and 2 percent grade fell within my written tolerances (0.84, 0.67, 0.38 against predicted 0.84, 0.67, 0.34), the metric and gallon conversions agreed (1188 against 1189 gal for 50 mm), and a 100 mm storm (9.0 m3) overflowed the 2 percent swale (6.4 m3) but not the level one (16.7 m3).
- Where/why it failed: My written line that a grade of 1.5 percent leaves the upper half of the trench dry was wrong: dry length is zero until grade times length exceeds the 0.457 m depth, so 1.5 percent leaves 0 m dry and 3 percent leaves 14.8 m. I also did not predict that a 3 percent trench already overflows at 50 mm.
- Fix: Check the trench floor with a level or A-frame along its whole length and keep grade under about 0.5 percent over 30 m, or break a long swale into short level cells with check berms.
- Why this fix: Usable storage falls linearly with grade times length over twice the depth, so shortening the cell has the same effect as flattening the grade.
- Rule of thumb: In this model a swale loses a third of its storage at 1 percent floor grade over 30 m, so the kernel's level requirement is a sub-1-percent tolerance, and the swale only matters for storms near its capacity; a small storm (25 mm) is held at any grade tested.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the runoff coefficient (0.5), strip width (6 m) and the flat rectangular trench cross-section are assumed, and infiltration during the storm is ignored so capacity is a lower bound for porous soil.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, brainwork/E115
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__swale-level-tolerance-grade-along-trench-drains-the-storage.py
- Prediction: Capacity fraction about 84, 67 and 34 percent at 0.5, 1 and 2 percent grade over 30 m; a 50 mm storm (4.5 m3) fits the 2 percent swale and a 100 mm storm (9 m3) overflows it but not the level one.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS capacity vs grade 0.5% 0.84 1% 0.67 2% 0.38 3% 0.25; 100 mm storm 9.0 m3 overflows the 2% swale (6.4) but not the level one (16.7)
- Scenarios: 1) capacity fraction at grade 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 percent; 2) dry length at 1.5 and 3 percent; 3) storms of 25, 50 and 100 mm against grades 0, 1, 2 and 3 percent, with 3 percent at 50 mm built to BREAK the tolerance

## E135 — rain barrel gravity drip pressure and overflow to rain garden
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: Chaining the rain-barrel, drip and rain-garden kernels as roof to barrel to gravity drip, with overflow to a roof/6 rain garden, showed a barrel on a 2 ft stand gives 0.87 psi against the drip kernel's 20 psi (about 46 ft of head), so a non-compensating emitter runs at about 21 percent of nominal and a 55 gal barrel takes 33 h to drain instead of 6.9 h. A 0.5 in storm on a 1000 sq ft roof is 311 gal, the barrel absorbs 55, and the 256 gal overflow ponds 2.47 in on the 167 sq ft garden; at 2 in the garden ponds 11.5 in despite the barrel.
- Why built: No memory entry had applied the three kernels as one chain; earlier entries tested each pair, never the pressure gap between a barrel and the drip pressure spec.
- Design: Python arithmetic with fixed constants: 0.623 gal per sq ft per inch, 0.433 psi per ft, 1000 sq ft roof, 55 gal barrel, 16 emitters at 0.5 gph, flow proportional to the square root of pressure, rain garden area roof/6, storms of 0.1, 0.5, 1 and 2 in, a 3 in ponding design depth.
- Got right: The square-root scaling reproduces the recorded x1.55 flow at 60 versus 25 psi (1.549), the barrel fills at 0.088 in of rain, and the overflow-to-garden arithmetic matched my written prediction.
- Where/why it failed: The drip kernel's 20-25 psi is a regulated-spigot spec and cannot be met by a barrel at any practical stand height, so the kernels do not compose into a gravity drip system without a pump or a very tall stand. Also the barrel does not rescue the rain garden: with no barrel the 0.5 in storm ponds exactly 3.0 in and with the barrel 2.47 in, and no storm tested moved the garden from over to under the 3 in design depth.
- Fix: Treat the barrel as a hand-watering or low-flow soaker source, or add a pump, and size the rain garden for the full roof runoff without crediting the barrel for storms above about 0.1 in.
- Why this fix: The head table shows pressure scales with height only, so gravity cannot reach the spec, and the storm table shows a 55 gal barrel is only 0.088 in of roof rainfall.
- Rule of thumb: In this model a gravity-fed barrel delivers about 1 psi per 2.3 ft of head, so drip emitters designed for 20 psi need a pump or roughly 46 ft of head, and a small barrel buys almost nothing against the rain-garden sizing storm.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the emitter exponent of 0.5 (non-compensating) and the 3 in design depth are assumed, and pressure-compensating emitters would stop regulating below their minimum pressure rather than slow down, which this model does not capture.

## E134 — mulch depth damps daily soil temperature not seasonal and thins with decay
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][soil][model]
- What: A 1-D heat-conduction model of mulch over soil showed the mulch kernel's temperature moderation does not saturate at 4 in the way the recorded water saving does. The daily swing 5 cm into the soil fell from 6.38 C bare to 1.06 C at 2 in, 0.50 C at 4 in and 0.13 C at 8 in, and a 4 in layer also cut the annual swing there by 31.7 percent (14.65 to 10.01 C). A layer decayed from 4 to 2 in doubled the daily swing (2.1x).
- Why built: The mulch kernel claims 2-4 in moderates soil temperature, and brainwork/E105 found water saving flat past 4 in and E113 found wood chips thin below 2 in by month 24; nothing had tested whether temperature behaves the same way.
- Design: Python stdlib implicit finite-volume model, mulch conductivity 0.12 W/mK and heat capacity 0.6e6 J/m3K over soil at 1.0 and 2.0e6, harmonic-mean conductances, sinusoidal air temperature (10 C daily amplitude, 15 C annual), amplitude read 5 cm below the soil surface in the last of several cycles, depths 0 to 8 in.
- Got right: Amplitude fell monotonically with depth, and the decay case (2 in versus 4 in) landed at 2.1x, inside my 1.5-3.5x prediction.
- Where/why it failed: Several written predictions missed. I computed the soil damping length wrongly (it is about 12 cm, not 3.7 cm), so bare amplitude was 6.4 C not 2.6 C. Returns from 4 to 8 in were 0.38 C, not under 0.3 C, so temperature keeps improving past 4 in where water saving did not. The annual cut was 32 percent, not under 15 percent, so the claim is not only about daily swings.
- Fix: Quote mulch temperature benefit as a depth-dependent amplitude reduction per cycle length, and do not reuse the 4 in plateau from the water-saving result for temperature.
- Why this fix: The model separates the two benefits: water saving flattened past 4 in in E105 while the daily soil temperature swing kept falling by about 4x from 4 to 8 in.
- Rule of thumb: In this toy, extra mulch depth past 4 in still damps temperature swings (daily 0.50 to 0.13 C at 5 cm), so the 2-4 in range is a water and stem-safety optimum, not a temperature one; and a layer decayed to 2 in loses half the damping.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the material properties are assumed round values for wood chips and moist soil, not measured, and no moisture or evaporation coupling is modelled.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/mulch-benefits-and-stem-clearance-rule, brainwork/E105, brainwork/E113
- Polarity: incompatible

## E133 — age cutoff 2lag flat at p and 2p first cover dict vs bigint andnot base 211 p7 p10 reverifies 3001 and 8101
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][state][model]
- What: The first-cover dictionary rule (base 3001) and the big-integer and-not rule (base 8101, there in Ruby) were run in one Python harness at a new base 211 on P7 and P10. They agreed on every period average (P7: 38/7 at N=7 and 88/7 at N=14; P10: 15 at N=10 and 65/2 at N=20) and both were flat exactly at N=P and N=2P with a rise at 2P+1 (P10: 167/5).
- Why built: To test whether the flat at N=P and 2P depends on how cover is computed (dictionary versus bit mask) or on the moduli the source entries used, by crossing the two rules on moduli neither had.
- Design: Landing ticks per lag from the shadow model; the dictionary rule streams events and records the first lag that reaches a tick; the and-not rule builds one integer bit mask per lag and treats b as adding cover iff mb & ~ma is non-zero; a rule using mb & ma is the wrong-rule control and base 0 the base control; averages over the P start residues.
- Got right: Both rules agreed at all 10 (P, N) cells, the P10 values equal the 15 and 65/2 recorded from other implementations at other bases, the base-0 control differed at N=P, and the wrong and-rule differed, so agreement is not from a rule that ignores cover.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing failed on the claim. The Ruby entry was not re-run in Ruby; Python big integers stand in for Ruby Bignum, so the language-specific behavior of the source is not exercised.
- Fix: When citing the flat result, say it holds across the dictionary and bit-mask cover rules on P5-P12 in Python (with Ruby covered only by its own source entry).
- Why this fix: The cross-check separates the cover rule from the language and from the base, and only the first two were varied here.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the flat at N=P and N=2P held for dictionary and bit-mask cover rules on P7 and P10 at base 211 (4 flats, 0 exceptions); treat it as rule- and base-independent over P5-P12, not beyond.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the cutoff model is the synthetic one inherited from the source entries and the Ruby behavior was not run here.

## E132 — rain barrel sizing vs storm pattern mulch demand and rain garden overflow
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][soil][model]
- What: A 60-day roof-to-barrel-to-drip model with a 1000 sq ft roof and 200 sq ft bed. The flat 10 percent haircut on the roof-area formula held for few large storms (loss 6.2 percent for 2 storms of 1.5 in, 8.7 for 6 of 0.5 in) but failed for many small ones (12.5 percent at 12 storms, 23.7 percent at 30 storms of 0.1 in) because the first-flush volume is charged per event, not per inch.
- Why built: To test the rain-barrel sizing kernel against the drip and mulch demand from the mulch entry, and against the passive rain-garden kernel as the place overflow goes.
- Design: Gross gallons are roof area times inches times 0.623. Each storm loses a fixed first-flush volume (0.5 L per square meter of roof, about 12.3 gal) and 5 percent gutter loss, the rest fills the barrel up to its size and the excess overflows. The bed draws the drip total from the mulch entry (424 mm bare, 226 mm under 3 inches of mulch, spread evenly over 60 days). Overflow goes to a rain garden of roof area divided by 6 (or 8) sq ft with 6 inches of ponding. Storm patterns all total 3 inches.
- Got right: The formula and the diverter figure are consistent: net water was 1752, 1706, 1636 and 1426 gal against a 1682 gal claim. Barrel coverage of demand at 165 gal was 48 percent bare and 89 percent mulched, and the smallest barrel reaching 90 percent of the 1100 gal result was 275 gal bare against 175 gal mulched.
- Where/why it failed: The flat 10 percent haircut is wrong for frequent small storms, where the per-event diverter lost 368 gal and net was 24 percent below gross. Mulch cut the barrel needed by about 36 percent, not by half as the 47 percent demand cut might suggest, since storage is also limited by storm timing. A single 3 inch storm defeated both stores: a 55 gal barrel overflowed 1709 gal and the roof/6 rain garden held only 623, leaving 1086 gal unhandled (1241 with roof/8). Rain on the bed and evaporation from the barrel were not modeled.
- Fix: Size the barrel from storm count as well as annual inches: charge the diverter volume per event, use the flat haircut only where storms are few and large, and treat the barrel and the rain garden as a chain, since a barrel sized only to demand leaves most of a big storm for the garden to absorb.
- Why this fix: The sweep over storm count at fixed total rainfall isolates the per-event charge as the cause, and the single-storm scenario shows overflow routing is a sizing problem of its own.
- Rule of thumb: Net harvest equals gross minus a per-event diverter volume, so the 10 percent haircut only holds for storms above roughly 0.5 in; reduce demand first (mulch) because it shrinks the barrel needed by about a third, and size the rain garden for the overflow of the design storm. Dry-spell model with assumed rates, one roof geometry, and a coded evenly spaced rain schedule.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox. Diverter volume, gutter loss, pond depth and the even demand spread are assumed parameters taken from the kernels and the mulch entry, not measured.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, brainwork/E105
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__rain-barrel-sizing-vs-storm-pattern-mulch-demand-and-rain-garden-overflow.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: the 10 percent haircut would hold for 2 to 6 storms and exceed 15 percent loss at 30 small storms; mulch would raise coverage of a 165 gal barrel; a single 3 inch storm would leave over 1000 gal unhandled with a 55 gal barrel.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS haircut loss% by storm count [(2, 6.2), (6, 8.7), (12, 12.5), (30, 23.7)]; coverage 165gal bare 48% mulch 89%; 3in single storm unhandled 1086 gal; barrel needed bare 275 mulch 175. All five checks passed on the first run; the predicted mulch halving of barrel size was not made, the observed ratio is 0.64.
- Scenarios: 1) same 3 in total as 2, 6, 12 and 30 storms 2) barrel 55 to 1100 gal, bare against mulched demand 3) one 3 in storm with rain garden roof/6 and roof/8, built to BREAK the barrel-sizing story 4) first flush on against off at 30 storms of 0.1 in 5) smallest barrel reaching 90 percent of full coverage, bare against mulched

## E131 — drip lateral friction uniformity vs regulator and emitter count
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A Hazen-Williams friction model of a half-inch poly drip lateral with emitters every 12 in and flow scaling with the square root of pressure. Inlet pressure barely changed evenness: the longest run holding min/max emitter flow at 90 percent or better was 230 emitters at 25 psi, 236 at 60 psi and 225 at 10 psi for 1.0 gph emitters. What changed with pressure was the flow budget: a 5 gpm zone supports 300 such emitters at 25 psi but 193 at 60 psi, so past about 193 emitters the zone budget binds before evenness does.
- Why built: The drip kernel says to regulate a spigot down to 20 to 25 psi and to keep zone flow within supply, and the spacing and pressure entry modeled flow against pressure but not friction along the pipe, so it was unclear whether regulation protects evenness or only the flow budget.
- Design: Stdlib deterministic model. Lateral ID 0.600 in, C=140, one emitter per foot, rated 0.5, 1.0 or 2.0 gph at 25 psi with q = q0 times sqrt(P/25). Pressures and flows are solved by fixed-point iteration from the inlet along the pipe; evenness is min flow over max flow. Compared inlets 10, 25 and 60 psi, a 5 gpm zone budget and a pressure-compensating (flat flow) emitter.
- Got right: Larger emitters shortened the even run (361, 230, 147 emitters for 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 gph at 25 psi) so the kernel's 0.5 to 1.0 gph advice stretches the run; a compensating emitter held evenness at 1.000 over 500 emitters; at 100 emitters evenness was 0.990 at both 25 and 60 psi.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that high inlet pressure would make evenness clearly better was true only by a hair (0.9905 against 0.9898 at 100 emitters, 236 against 230 emitters at the 90 percent limit), and low pressure hurt only slightly, so evenness is almost insensitive to inlet pressure in the 10 to 60 psi range here. The limit is set by emitter flow and pipe size. At 300 emitters, the 25 psi budget count, evenness falls to 0.81, so the flow budget and the evenness limit are different caps and the budget count is not safe on its own. Elevation change, clogging, emitter manufacturing variation and real emitter curves are not modeled, and the sqrt law is an orifice approximation.
- Fix: When applying the kernel, check a lateral against two caps, flow budget at the actual pressure and evenness from friction, and take the smaller; regulate to 20 to 25 psi for hardware and flow-budget reasons, not to improve evenness, and cut lateral length or use compensating emitters when the evenness cap is the lower one.
- Why this fix: The sweep shows the budget cap scales with the inverse of head flow while the evenness cap hardly moves with inlet pressure, so the two caps cross, and which one binds depends on emitter size and pressure.
- Rule of thumb: Size a drip zone by the smaller of the flow budget and the friction evenness limit: at 1.0 gph on half-inch tube the evenness limit is about 230 emitters whatever the inlet pressure, while the 5 gpm budget is 300 at 25 psi but 193 at 60 psi. Tested for one tube size, flat ground and an assumed square-root emitter law.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; counts and evenness values are observed output. The friction formula constants are standard Hazen-Williams values for smooth poly, but tube diameter, C, spacing and the sqrt exponent are assumed parameters, and no emitter was measured.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E112, brainwork/E105
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__drip-lateral-friction-uniformity-vs-regulator-and-emitter-count.py
- Prediction: Before the first run: the 90 percent evenness run would exceed 100 emitters at 25 psi with 1.0 gph and shrink with bigger emitters; 60 psi would cut the 5 gpm budget count and give better evenness than 25 psi; 10 psi would give a shorter run; a compensating emitter would remove the length limit.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS max emitters 25psi q1.0=230, 60psi q1.0=236, 10psi=225; budget 5gpm 25psi=300 60psi=193; uniformity n=100 25psi 0.990 60psi 0.990; flags (True, True, True, True). The directions held but the pressure effect on evenness was under 1 percent, far smaller than the budget effect.
- Scenarios: 1) emitter rating 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 gph at 25 and 60 psi 2) 5 gpm zone budget at 25 against 60 psi 3) 100 and 300 emitters on one lateral 4) inlet 10 psi, built to BREAK the claim that pressure drives evenness 5) pressure-compensating emitter at 500 emitters

## E130 — companion claims repetition count vs independent roots citation graph
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][pest-control][research][model]
- What: On a hand-built page graph of the four companion-planting claims, ranking by how many pages repeat a claim puts basil-against-hornworm first (12 pages) while counting independent trial roots puts it last (0), with marigold-nematodes first (2 trial roots from 3 pages). Uncited verbatim copies break the graph count: fennel showed 7 apparent roots by citation links alone and 2 after merging verbatim text by three-word shingle similarity.
- Why built: The companion-planting kernel says repeated is not tested, and the research kernel says to trace to independent roots, but neither had been checked against the other or against the earlier companion-planting entry whose mechanisms were set by construction.
- Design: Stdlib deterministic model. Pages carry a claim, a citation list, a kind (trial or site), text and an author. Repetition count is pages per claim; roots are pages that cite no other page of the claim; genuine roots are trial roots merged by author; a second pass merges unlinked copies with shingle Jaccard of 0.9 or more. Basil is one book quote copied across 12 linked pages, marigold has two independent trials and an extension summary, allium one trial and three citing copies, fennel one trial, one citing page and six uncited copies.
- Got right: Ranking by repetition gave basil, fennel, allium, marigold, and ranking by trial roots gave marigold, allium, fennel, basil, a full reversal at the ends; the citation-link count alone was enough for basil (one root, no trial), and merging two marigold trials by one shared author reduced them from 2 to 1.
- Where/why it failed: The citation graph alone over-counts roots when copies carry no links (fennel 7 against 2), so it needs the text-similarity merge, and that merge is only valid for near-verbatim copies, since paraphrases would slip through. The graph is hand-built with my chosen counts of pages, so the ranking reversal follows from the construction; what the run tests is that the two counting rules diverge, and where the graph rule needs repair. No real web pages or trial records were used.
- Fix: When grading a companion claim, count independent trial sources (merged by author and by verbatim text) next to its mechanism bucket and do not rank claims by how often they are repeated.
- Why this fix: The run separates three counts that a repetition tally conflates: pages, citation-graph roots and genuine trial roots, and shows the order of claims depends on which is used.
- Rule of thumb: Rank a companion-planting claim by independent trial roots, not by page count, and merge uncited verbatim copies before counting roots, because citation links alone can overstate the roots (7 against 2). A synthetic graph built by me, not a measurement of the real web.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; counts are observed output. The graph topology, page counts and similarity threshold are assumed inputs that I chose to mirror the kernel's description.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/companion-planting-claim-taxonomy, ideas:RESEARCH/trace-sources-to-independent-roots-not-a-repetition-count, brainwork/E104

## E127 — seeded rng state words restore cost and hidden cache breaks exact resume
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [determinism][state][testing][model]
- What: Saving the RNG's four state words restored in 4 word copies at 10, 1000 and 100000 draws, versus replaying exactly n rolls for seed plus count, with identical states; but a gaussian roller that caches its second value lost that value on a words-only restore and diverged on the next 6 draws.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel says to save full state words so load is O(1), and the-game-prologue/E1 found the seed-and-count form replays count rolls; neither tested whether the words are the whole state.
- Design: Python sfc32 generator; restore compared by roll count (no timing); an integer resume over 10 draws; a Box-Muller-style pair roller with a cached spare saved mid-pair with words only, words plus spare, and replayed by call count; plus a 20-tick shared stream versus split streams with an extra consumer on even ticks (assumed constants).
- Got right: Words-only restore was exact for plain integer rolls and equal to the replay result at every n; shared stream changed 14 of 20 ticks with an extra consumer, split streams 0.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction that seed plus call count would also fail was wrong: replaying the same number of gaussian calls restored the spare and matched. Only the words-only save broke, because the cached spare lives outside the four words.
- Fix: Treat the saved RNG state as the words plus every cache a wrapper holds (spare gaussian, buffered bits), or keep wrappers stateless by always drawing both values and discarding one.
- Why this fix: Saving words plus spare made the 6 post-load draws match exactly, and a stateless wrapper removes the second hidden location entirely.
- Rule of thumb: In this model, state words give an O(1) exact restore only for a bare generator; any wrapper that caches a derived value must save that cache with the words or the first post-load draw can diverge.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the generator, cache scheme and tick counts are assumed model constants, not a production engine.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/seeded-rng, the-game-prologue/E1, seeded-rng-save-load-vs-shared-stream-coupling/E1

- Observed: RESULT: PASS state words O(1) restore exact; hidden spare cache lost words-only (exact=False), fixed with spare; shared stream 14/20 vs split 0/20. Seed plus gaussian-call-count replay was exact (prediction missed).
- Scenarios: 1) restore at n=10, 1000, 100000; 2) integer resume after 50 draws; 3) gaussian with pending spare, words-only built to BREAK it, words plus spare, call-count replay; 4) shared versus split streams with an extra consumer

## E126 — mulch decay topup cadence and flare clearance vs drip ring
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][soil][water][model]
- What: Running the mulch kernel's depth and clearance numbers through time in a model: organic mulch at 4 in fell below the 2 in floor after 2.0 years and 3 in after 1.0 year with no top-up, stone never did but released 0 organic matter, and a mulch ring fixed 8 in from a trunk centre had 2 in of clearance from the root flare at year 0 and 0 in by year 4.
- Why built: The mulch kernel states depth 2-4 in and clearance 3-5 in or 8-12 in as static numbers, and E105 tested clearance only with fixed geometry; nothing modelled decay of the layer or growth of the trunk.
- Design: Python arithmetic model with assumed constants: organic decay 1.0 in per year, stone 0, release 0.04 lb per sq ft per inch decayed, 36 in bed radius, trunk radius 6 in growing 0.5 in per year, top-up to 3 in below 2 in, a dump-on-top policy against a raked-back policy, and a dripline ring at 24 in.
- Got right: Top-up cadence is (starting depth minus 2) divided by decay rate; 5 years of organic mulch on 28 sq ft needed 4 top-ups and released 5.7 lb of organic matter while stone needed none and released none; the 24 in dripline ring sat outside every clearance even with the year-8 flare.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's clearance numbers silently stop holding if the ring is placed once from trunk centre: the 8 in ring closed on the flare by year 4 and the 10 in ring by year 8. Dumping top-up mulch against the stem gave 120 wet days a season versus 0 when raked back, so top-up is where the clearance rule is usually broken.
- Fix: Treat depth and clearance as maintained quantities: top up on the interval (depth minus 2) over decay, rake the ring back at every top-up, and re-measure clearance from the flare edge as the trunk grows.
- Why this fix: The model shows three separate ways a static rule decays (layer thins, top-up buries the stem, flare grows into a fixed ring) and only a recurring re-measure from the flare handles all three.
- Rule of thumb: In this model organic mulch needs topping up every (depth minus 2) over decay years and each top-up must re-establish the flare clearance, because depth and clearance numbers are only true on the day they are set.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; most outputs are arithmetic on assumed constants (decay rate, growth rate, wet-day season), so it checks the kernel's logic over time and is not a field measurement.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/mulch-benefits-and-stem-clearance-rule, ideas:GARDEN/drip-irrigation-efficiency-plus-design-specs, brainwork/E105
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__mulch-decay-topup-cadence-and-flare-clearance-vs-drip-ring.py
- Prediction: A 4 in layer lasts 2.0 years and a 3 in layer 1.0 year; stone needs no top-up and adds 0 organic matter; dumping against the stem gives wet days while raking back gives 0; an 8 in ring from trunk centre closes on the flare by year 4; the 24 in dripline ring stays outside every clearance.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 4 in lasts 2.0 yr, 3 in 1.0 yr; stone 0 OM; dump=wet 120 d vs rake 0; 8 in center ring is 0 in from flare at yr4
- Scenarios: 1) years to the 2 in floor for 2.5, 3, 4 in and stone; 2) five-year top-up bed organic versus stone; 3) dump versus rake-back top-up wet days, built to BREAK the clearance rule; 4) fixed ring of 8, 10 and 12 in against flare growth to year 8; 5) dripline ring against clearance plus flare

## E125 — jar test timing misread picks wrong rain garden divisor
- Date: 2026-10-12
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][soil][water][measurement][model]
- What: Chaining the jar-test readout into rain-garden sizing in a Stokes model: reading silt at the kernel's 3 minutes mislabelled 2 of 4 true textures (a 40/40/20 loam and a 20/60/20 silt-loam both read as clay, 45 and 63 percent), which moves the divisor from 8 to 6 and makes a 1000 sq ft drainage garden 167 sq ft instead of 125, 33 percent too large; reading silt at 2 hours labelled all four correctly.
- Why built: The jar-test kernel gives timings and the passive-harvesting kernel gives a clay-or-sandy divisor; soil-jar E1 showed the timings misread silt but nothing followed that error into a sizing decision.
- Design: Python Stokes settling (density 2650, 20 C, 10 cm fill, log-uniform sizes per class, clay floor 0.2 um); texture read from the layer heights at a sand mark, a silt mark and a 48 hour total; a class rule (clay at 35 percent or more, sandy at 50 percent sand or more, else loam) picks divisor 6 for clay and 8 otherwise; assumed infiltration of 50, 13 and 5 mm per hour and 6 in ponding for drain times.
- Got right: The sandy soil read sandy at both marks, so the error is specific to silt-rich soils; the loam read 46/10/45 at 3 minutes, consistent with the 47.6/7.7/44.6 in soil-jar E1; the 2 hour mark corrected all four textures; drain times 11.7 h for loam and 30.5 h for clay, both inside 48 h.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's 3 minute silt mark is not just a texture error: it flips the sizing class for loam and silt-loam, so the garden is built a third too large and its drain time is predicted at 30.5 h instead of 11.7 h.
- Fix: Take the silt mark at about 2 hours before choosing the divisor, or test infiltration directly with a filled hole, and treat the class as a rough label near the 35 percent clay boundary.
- Why this fix: The 2 hour mark corrected every tested texture, and it removes the dependency on a reading the model shows is not complete at 3 minutes.
- Rule of thumb: In this model a rain-garden divisor chosen from a 3-minute jar silt mark treats loam as clay and oversizes by 33 percent; read silt at about 2 hours first, because the soil class is only as good as the settling clock behind it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the particle distributions, class thresholds, infiltration rates and ponding depth are assumed model constants, and four textures is a small set, not a field survey.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/cheap-home-soil-diagnostics, ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, 2026-10-09__home-soil-jar-test-stokes-timing-and-leaf-triage-order/E1
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-12__jar-test-timing-misread-picks-wrong-rain-garden-divisor.py
- Prediction: The 3 minute read labels a true loam as clay and picks divisor 6; sandy still reads sandy; wrong divisor oversizes by 33 percent; a 2 hour silt read labels every tested texture correctly.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 3-min read mislabels 2/4 textures, 2h read 0/4; wrong divisor sizes area 33% off; drain loam 11.7 h clay 30.5 h
- Scenarios: 1) true loam at 3 minutes versus 2 hours; 2) sandy soil, built to show where the kernel timing still works; 3) clayey soil; 4) silt-loam, built to BREAK the 3 minute mark; 5) divisor area comparison and drain times

## E124 — swale chain spacing cascade and roof overflow feed
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [garden][water][design][model]
- What: A 5-swale contour chain (0.28 m3 per metre each, 6 h storm, runoff 0.8) absorbed a 100 mm storm completely at 2 m spacing on both sand and clay and on sand at 6 m, but on clay at 6 m it spilled 0.85 m3 per metre, and the swale-to-flat infiltration gain never reached 8 to 12x: it was 0.8 to 1.0 on sand at every storm and peaked at 5.2 on clay at 200 and 400 mm. A roof overflow of 650 gal onto the top swale lifted clay 4 m spill from 0.05 to 0.30 m3 per metre and no chain length up to 39 swales cleared it.
- Why built: The passive-harvesting kernel quotes 8 to 12x swale infiltration, 2 m minimum spacing and a slope cap but gives no chain behaviour, and the rain-barrel kernel stops at the overflow; I wanted to see how spacing, soil and a roof feed interact down a slope.
- Design: Python per-metre model with a cascade (each swale takes inflow up to its volume plus soil infiltration over 6 h on a 1 m base; overflow passes downhill), sand 50 and clay 5 mm/h, spacings 2, 4 and 6 m, storms 10 to 400 mm, a flat-strip comparison where the strip can soak only its own infiltration rate, and the barrel sandbox's 650 gal overflow as extra input (all constants assumed, no RNG).
- Got right: Spacing mattered as the kernel's minimum implies, a 2 m chain absorbed 100 mm on both soils, and the big-storm-only gain matches the earlier rain-garden finding that the swale gain appears only above about 50 mm.
- Where/why it failed: Three predictions broke: clay at 2 m did not spill at 100 mm, sand at 6 m did not spill, and no storm put the gain in the 8 to 12x band (best 5.2 on clay). On sand the gain was below 1 because the flat strip already soaks everything. The chain-length fix for the roof feed also failed: when per-swale catchment (0.32 m3 at 4 m) exceeds per-swale capacity (0.31), each added swale adds its own overflow.
- Fix: Quote the swale gain only with soil and storm (clay, 100 mm and up, up to 5x here), size spacing so each swale's own catchment is under its volume plus infiltration, and send roof overflow to its own sink or a wider spacing, not down the chain.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows the cascade only clears while per-swale catchment is below per-swale capacity; past that point adding swales moves the spill and never removes it, and the gain exists only where infiltration is the limiting step.
- Rule of thumb: Do not quote swale gain as 8 to 12x without soil and storm: in this model it was under 1x on sand and at most 5.2x on clay, and a chain never clears an overflow once per-swale catchment exceeds per-swale capacity, so more swales will not absorb a roof feed.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox, which printed RESULT: FAIL for the refuted parts; storm duration, runoff coefficient, base width, soil rates and the flat-strip definition are assumed model constants and the 8 to 12x figure of the kernel was not tested against field data.
- Composed: ideas:GARDEN/passive-landscape-water-harvesting, ideas:GARDEN/rain-barrel-sizing-plus-first-flush-diverter, brainwork/E115
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__swale-chain-spacing-cascade-and-roof-overflow-feed.py
- Prediction: A 5-swale chain absorbs 100 mm on sand but not clay at 2 m, sand spills at 6 m and 100 mm, the swale gain lands in 8 to 12x for some storm, and adding roof overflow makes clay spill, curable by a longer chain.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL sand2m100mm spill 0.00, clay2m100mm spill 0.00, sand6m100mm spill 0.00, ratios in 8-12x [], roof feed chain needs None swales. Roof overflow raised clay 4 m spill from 0.05 to 0.30.
- Scenarios: 1) spacing 2, 4, 6 m by sand and clay at 25, 50, 100 mm; 2) swale to flat ratio for 10 to 400 mm storms on both soils, built to BREAK the 8 to 12x figure; 3) 650 gal roof overflow on the top swale of a clay 4 m chain; 4) chain lengths 1 to 39 for the roof feed
