## E101 — viewer built pond parameters must reach dynamics narration adapt and vdc spread
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [simulation][narration][onboarding][testing]
- What: A deterministic toy pond sandbox that applies the viewer-builds-the-world kernel: six build configurations (volume, plant count, floater coverage) feed an oxygen model, the same six are run with the volume ignored by the dynamics, a fixed and a state-gated narration line about coverage are counted for falsehood, and van der Corput placement is compared with hash pool order for even spread.
- Why built: The onboarding kernel claims the built parameters must reach the dynamics and that downstream narration must adapt, and its sibling claims van der Corput keeps a drawn count readable as a proportion. None had a first-hand build, so I measured each claim and tried to find where it stops holding.
- Design: Oxygen rises with plants times unshaded surface and falls with a base cost plus a nutrient term that is the fixed load divided by pond volume. Scenarios: wired versus volume-ignored dynamics; one extra plant at small versus large volume; fixed line saying coverage is a fifth versus a line emitted only when live coverage is within 0.05 of a fifth; max gap of the first N items on a ring for N from 2 to 32.
- Got right: Wired, the minimum oxygen spans -190.5 to 70.0 across the six configs; with volume ignored, 4-volume and 12-volume ponds with the same plants and coverage tie exactly (27.6 and 27.6) while wired they were -85.5 and 65.3. One extra plant moved minimum oxygen 41.99 in the small pond and 20.44 in the large one. The fixed coverage line is false in 5 of 6 configs and the gated line was never false (emitted once). Van der Corput had a max gap no larger than hash order at all 31 values of N.
- Where/why it failed: My first tuning clipped oxygen at zero, so every small pond collapsed to 0.0 and the extra-plant effect read 0.00 versus 20.44, hiding the sensitivity the kernel describes. Metrics that saturate at a failure floor cannot show how much a choice matters in the failing region; I had to measure the unclipped oxygen debt. I built no case that breaks the van der Corput claim, so its 31 of 31 only says it held on this ring metric.
- Fix: Wire every viewer-set parameter into the dynamics and check by tying test (set the parameter, change nothing else, outcome must move); measure sensitivity on an unclipped quantity; gate each narration line that mentions a viewer-set number on the live value; use bit-reversed positions for any first-N pool the viewer grows.
- Why this fix: The volume-ignored run and the unclipped-measure rerun are both direct measurements that the failure modes are real, and the gated line removed the false statements the fixed line produced.
- Rule of thumb: A viewer-built parameter only counts if changing it alone moves the outcome (4-volume versus 12-volume tied at 27.6 when ignored, -85.5 versus 65.3 wired), measure its effect on an unclipped value because a failure floor hides the swing (0.00 versus 41.99), and gate numeric narration on live state.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; all numbers are its output. The oxygen model, constants and the 0.05 gate are my own toy choices, not the pond film, and the van der Corput check was only a max-gap comparison on a ring.
- Composed: ideas:SIMULATION/onboarding/let-the-viewer-build-the-initial-conditions, ideas:SIMULATION/rendering/low-discrepancy-subset-so-a-count-reads-as-a-proportion, ideas:NARRATION/adaptive-copy/branch-on-the-claim-not-on-a-correlate
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__viewer-built-pond-parameters-must-reach-dynamics-narration-adapt-and-vdc-spread.py
- Prediction: Wired outcomes differ across the six configs with the minimal pond failing and the generous one surviving; one extra plant moves the small pond more than the large one; ignoring volume ties configs sharing plants and coverage; the fixed narration line is false in at least 5 of 6; van der Corput max gap is no larger than hash order at every N.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS wired min-O2 -190.5..70.0 vs unwired tie; extra plant 41.99(small) vs 20.44(big); fixed narration false 5/6 gated 0; vdC no-worse in 31/31 N
- Scenarios: 1) six build configs wired; 2) same configs with volume ignored (built to BREAK the wiring); 3) one extra plant small versus large pond; 4) fixed versus gated coverage narration; 5) van der Corput versus hash order for N 2 to 32

## E100 — scrub seek needs counter rng not per entity stream when roll count varies
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [determinism][gamedesign][state][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox composing the scrub-needs-constant-roll-count lesson with the per-entity-random-stream lesson: four entities random-walk, and one extra roll is consumed only when hp is low, so roll count is state-dependent. It compares a shared stream, per-entity streams and a counter-style hash RNG on seeking and on isolation.
- Why built: Per-entity streams were adopted to stop unrelated changes perturbing a fight, and the scrub lesson says seeking needs a constant roll count. I wanted to know whether per-entity streams alone make scrubbing safe when the count varies, or whether a different RNG shape is needed.
- Design: Hash-derived draws (seed, entity, tick, slot) stand in for a counter RNG. Scenarios: replay control, how often the low branch fires, a naive seek that assumes one draw per tick on a per-entity stream (built to BREAK the constant-count assumption), a rule tweak on entity 0 under a shared stream versus the counter RNG, and counter seek versus full replay at T=1, 13, 40, 60.
- Got right: Per-entity streams keep entities isolated, and the counter RNG gives addressable draws: tweaking entity 0's rule changed 0 of 3 other entities, while the shared stream changed 3 of 3. A counter-RNG seek matched full replay at all four tested ticks for all four entities.
- Where/why it failed: Per-entity streams do not fix seeking: the naive constant-count seek was wrong for 1 of 4 entities, the one that hit the low branch (5 low-branch ticks over 60), so the other three looked fine and the bug hid. The counter seek still replays state (hp) tick by tick; only the draws became addressable, not the state.
- Fix: When roll count depends on state, give each draw an address (seed, entity, tick, slot) rather than a position in a stream, and still replay or checkpoint the state. Keep the constant-roll-count rule only where streams stay sequential.
- Why this fix: Addressable draws remove the coupling between how many rolls an earlier tick took and which value a later tick sees, which is what breaks both seek and cross-entity isolation.
- Rule of thumb: A per-entity stream isolates entities but does not make seeking safe when the roll count varies with state; use addressed draws (hash of seed, entity, tick, slot) and test the seek on an entity that actually takes the extra-roll branch (1 of 4 mismatched here).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; numbers above are its output. A sha256 hash stands in for a counter RNG, and the walk rules are toy rules I chose, so the effect sizes are illustrative only.
- Composed: sandbox-combined-scrub-vs-roll-count/E1, brainwork/E14
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__scrub-seek-needs-counter-rng-not-per-entity-stream-when-roll-count-varies.py
- Prediction: Naive constant-count seek on a per-entity stream fails for at least one entity that reaches the low branch; a shared stream leaks a rule tweak to the other entities while a counter RNG leaks to none; the counter seek equals replay.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS naive constant-count seek wrong for 1/4 entities; shared stream leaks rule change to 3/3 others, counter RNG to 0; counter seek matches replay
- Scenarios: 1) replay determinism control; 2) low-branch frequency (5 ticks); 3) naive constant-count seek on per-entity streams (built to BREAK); 4) shared stream rule tweak isolation; 5) counter RNG rule tweak isolation; 6) counter seek versus replay at four ticks
- Link: brain train auto loop 1 pass 2; session_01MWSgVSo3kzvSufZC4PAqmL
- Cited-by: 2026-10-14 · projects/pappydapimp69__brainwork.md#E253 · compatible · sandboxes/2026-10-14__live-emit-skip-desyncs-shared-rng-snapshot-and-addressed-draws-contain-it.py · observed RESULT: PASS skipped_first_emit=[0, 1, 3, 4] shared_diffs=4/5 addressed_diffs=1/5 nounsub_diffs=0,0 · brain train auto loop 2 pass 2; session_015vYTjNJNEjDvnZgWaJaTSv

## E99 — per axis deadzone and per axis clamp compound angle error uniform ops keep direction
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [input][ui][gamedev][algorithm][testing]
- What: A deterministic 2D-vector sandbox that chains a deadzone stage and a clamp-to-box stage and measures the direction error each combination adds, testing whether the per-axis deadzone lesson and the per-axis marker clamp lesson compound when both are present.
- Why built: Both lessons say a per-axis operation on a 2D vector bends its direction and a uniform or radial one keeps it. A stick driving an off-screen marker uses both stages, so I wanted to know whether the errors add up and whether the stage order matters.
- Design: Vector at 360 angles and a chosen radius; deadzone 0.2 either per-axis or radial; clamp to a box either per-axis or by one uniform scale; square and 16:9 boxes; then a sweep of 7 radii by 5 boxes in both stage orders, counting angles where the composed error exceeds the worse single stage.
- Got right: Radial deadzone plus uniform clamp kept direction exactly (0.00 deg) in both box shapes. Per-axis alone bent it: clamp up to 15.25 deg and deadzone 36.5 deg at radius 0.25 with 64 of 360 directions dead. The per-axis clamp error is symmetric about 45 degrees for a square box (gap 0.00) and not for 16:9 (gap 15.22 deg).
- Where/why it failed: My prediction of compounding was refuted three ways: at radius 0.35 in a 0.3 box the composed error equalled the larger single error at all 360 angles, with no compounding and no cancelling; the clamp-then-deadzone order did no worse; and across 35 cases (11800 samples) the composed error never exceeded the worse single stage. Once the per-axis deadzone zeroes a component the vector lies on an axis and the clamp cannot bend it further, and where nothing is zeroed only the clamp acts.
- Fix: Do not budget for stacked angle errors, but do not expect a one-stage fix to help either: the composed error equals the worse stage, so in the 17 of 35 cases where both stages were active, fixing only the weaker stage changes nothing. Replace both stages with their radial or uniform forms together, and test a 16:9 box as well as a square one.
- Why this fix: The error is set by whichever stage acts at that angle, so the worst stage is the number to chase and a square-only test hides the aspect-dependent asymmetry.
- Rule of thumb: Per-axis deadzone and per-axis clamp errors do not compound (0 of 11800 samples worse than the worse stage, either order), so fixing the weaker stage alone changes nothing; make both radial or uniform, then check a non-square box because the square one is symmetric and hides the skew.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT: PASS on the third iteration after two refuted predictions). It is a hand-written 2D model with a deadzone of 0.2 and toy boxes, not a real gamepad API or camera projection.
- Composed: sandbox-offscreen-marker-projection/E1, brainwork/E48
- Polarity: incompatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__per-axis-deadzone-and-per-axis-clamp-compound-angle-error-uniform-ops-keep-direction.py
- Prediction: Uniform stages give 0.00 degrees; each per-axis stage alone exceeds 5 degrees; the two per-axis stages together compound beyond either alone with some cancelling angles; square box symmetric and 16:9 not. Revised after refutations: reversing the order compounds (also refuted), then the sweep claim that composed never exceeds the worse stage.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS uniform stages 0.00 deg; per-axis clamp max 15.2; dz->clamp composed 34.5 equals worst single 34.5 at all 360 angles; no compounding in 11800 samples across both orders
- Scenarios: 1) uniform plus uniform on square and 16:9; 2) per-axis deadzone alone at radius 0.25; 3) both per-axis at radius 0.35 in a 0.3 box (built to BREAK, compounding refuted); 4) stage order swapped; 5) sweep of 7 radii by 5 boxes in both orders; 6) symmetry about 45 degrees square versus 16:9
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 2 (edge); session_01MWSgVSo3kzvSufZC4PAqmL

## E98 — checkable lie filter costs no draws and bias sets how guessable the lie is
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][narrative-systems][determinism][testing]
- What: A deterministic sandbox of the speaker pick for a false roster line in a six-actor party that follows a walking lead, comparing a uniform pick with a pick biased to a checkable speaker (out of earshot or gone) implemented as a filter over an order already shuffled by hash draws.
- Why built: The unreliable-narrator kernel says to bias the lie toward a checkable speaker at no extra randomness, with a fallback to the merely eerie version. I wanted to measure the claims it makes (more checkable lies, no extra draws, a fallback share) and find what the bias costs.
- Design: Actors sit at formation distances plus stragglers lagging in walk phases and a rare gone state; checkable means over 20 m or gone. Draw counts are tallied per pick. A player heuristic flags any line spoken by a checkable actor as a lie; its precision is measured against truthful lines drawn uniformly. Bias settings 0, 50, 80 and 100 percent over 60 sessions of 40 steps; a break case biases the truthful lines the same way.
- Got right: Checkable lies rose from 0.40 at no bias to 0.90 at full bias, and draws per lie stayed at 6 for every bias level, so the filter really costs no extra randomness. A fallback was needed in 10 percent of lies at full bias, so the merely-eerie branch actually runs.
- Where/why it failed: Checkability is itself a tell: the player heuristic's precision rose from 0.50 to 0.70 as bias went up, so a stronger bias makes the lie easier to guess without checking anything. It stayed below 1.00 only because truthful lines also come from checkable speakers 40 percent of the time in this world; when the truthful lines were biased the same way, the heuristic fell back to 0.50.
- Fix: Keep the bias moderate and bias truthful lines toward the same speakers sometimes, so that being checkable is not evidence of a lie; test the fallback share and the heuristic precision as rates, not just that the filter works once.
- Why this fix: The draw counts show the bias is free, so the only cost left is guessability, and the break case shows decoy truths remove that cost.
- Rule of thumb: A checkable-speaker filter costs no extra random draws (6 per lie at every bias) and lifts checkable lies from 0.40 to 0.90, but it also lifts a guess-by-speaker heuristic from 0.50 to 0.70 precision, so pair it with truthful lines from the same kind of speaker.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; numbers are its output. The party motion, 20 m threshold, base checkable share of about 0.40 and the guessing heuristic are my own toy assumptions, not the game's, and no human player was involved.
- Composed: ideas:gamedev/narrative-systems/lie-in-the-voice-of-someone-who-could-not-have-said-it, ideas:testing/verification/mechanism-tests-and-rate-tests-are-different-axes, sandbox-combined-scrub-vs-roll-count/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__checkable-lie-filter-costs-no-draws-and-bias-sets-how-guessable-the-lie-is.py
- Prediction: Checkable share rises monotonically with bias; draws per lie are identical across bias levels; fallback is a non-zero minority; the speaker heuristic's precision rises with bias but stays under 1.0; biasing truthful lines the same way drops it to the base rate.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS checkable lies 0.40->0.90 as bias 0->100%, draws/lie constant at 6, fallback 0.10, heuristic precision 0.50->0.70 (not 1.0), falls to 0.50 if truthful lines share the bias
- Scenarios: 1) bias 0 percent; 2) bias 50; 3) bias 80; 4) bias 100 with a rate measured over 2400 picks each; 5) truthful lines biased the same way (built to BREAK the guessing heuristic)

## E97 — apology forgiveness request weakest top set unstable repair gated by deal zone
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [negotiation][regret][sandbox][apology]
- What: A deterministic sandbox that re-computes the apology-component rankings quoted in the kernel (Study 1 six means, Study 2 four means), then checks which parts of the advice survive across studies, and gates the repair offer on a bargaining deal zone and on the situation still being repairable.
- Why built: The kernel says to own the harm and offer repair and never lead with a forgiveness request, but admits the ordering of the strong components moved between studies. I wanted to see which part of the advice is stable and where the repair advice stops applying.
- Design: Study means are plain constants copied from the kernel. Six scenarios: S1 rank, S2 quoted means vs the S1 forgiveness mean, top-three SET from S1 evaluated on S2 means (built to break), a compose rule that drops the forgiveness request, a repair value gated by deal-zone width (ceiling minus BATNA) and repairability, and a no-zone case showing acknowledgement keeps its value.
- Got right: Forgiveness request is the minimum in Study 1 (2.68) and every quoted Study 2 mean sits above it. Acknowledgement plus repair stays in the top three in both studies, so that core rule is robust.
- Where/why it failed: The top-three SET is not stable: the S1 set (ack, repair, explanation) scores 3.22 on S2 means while the S2 set (ack, repair, repentance) scores 3.51, so choosing the combination by Study 1 rank loses to Study 2 rank. Study 2 does not quote a forgiveness-request mean, so "weakest in both" is only partly checkable here.
- Fix: State the rule as a stable core (own it, offer concrete repair, never open with a forgiveness request) and treat the third component as open. Gate the repair offer: with no deal zone or a closed relationship it is worth nothing in the model, while acknowledgement keeps its full value.
- Why this fix: It keeps only what held across both studies and the break case, and the gate reuses the bargaining finding that a missed deal only matters if a deal exists, plus the opportunity principle that regret and repair live where correction is still possible.
- Rule of thumb: Apology advice that survives both studies is only own-it plus offer-repair plus never lead with asking forgiveness; pick the third component by context, and do not offer repair where no deal zone or repair path exists (model: repair 6.83 open vs 3.49 gated).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run: the rankings, set-instability numbers and gate outputs. The gate itself is a modelling assumption I imposed, and the study means come from the kernel quote, not from the paper.
- Composed: ideas:REGRET/asking-for-forgiveness-is-the-weakest-part-of-an-apology-and-the-only-stable-finding-across-studies, ideas:REGRET/regret-concentrates-where-repair-is-still-possible-not-where-loss-was-greatest, sandbox-negotiation-batna/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__apology-forgiveness-request-weakest-top-set-unstable-repair-gated-by-deal-zone.py
- Prediction: Forgiveness request ranks last in Study 1; the Study 1 top-three set scores lower on Study 2 means than the Study 2 top-three set; repair value drops to zero with no deal zone while acknowledgement is unchanged.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS apology: forgive weakest S1, top-set differs S1 vs S2 (3.22<3.51), ack+repair core robust, repair worth 0 without deal zone or repairability (open 6.83 vs 3.49)
- Scenarios: 1) Study 1 rank; 2) Study 2 quoted means vs forgiveness mean; 3) S1 top-three set scored on S2 means (built to BREAK set stability); 4) compose rule without forgiveness request; 5) repair gated by deal zone and repairability; 6) no-zone case where acknowledgement survives

## E96 — adaptive copy cause gate is exact only when cause is sole driver
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [narration][testing][state][proxy]
- What: A deterministic pond-state grid (plants, surface mat, temperature, predator) where the copy asserts that the pond has gone quiet on one branch and that it is busy on the other, gated three ways: on a proxy (mat exists), on the cause (bed failing) and on the exact asserted predicate (fish inactive), in three worlds that differ in what else drives fish activity.
- Why built: The adaptive-copy kernel says branch on the claim, not on a correlate, and an open tension asks whether gating on the cause is enough or the exact predicate is needed. The sandbox counts false lines per gate over every cell instead of arguing it.
- Design: Oxygen is a function of plants and mat; fish are active when oxygen is at least 60. World A: oxygen is the only driver. World B adds cold water that makes fish sluggish. World C adds a predator that makes them hide. The false-line count is measured against the true activity in each cell. Scenario A2 aligns the cause threshold with the claim threshold.
- Got right: The proxy gate was wrong in 4 of 10, 9 of 20 and 19 of 40 cells in worlds A, B and C. The cause gate beat the proxy in A and B and tied it in C (19 of 40), and it never said quiet wrongly. It always erred in the other direction, telling a quiet pond it was busy, so the healthy-branch line was the one that lied.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction said the cause gate would be exact in world A; it was wrong in 1 of 10 cells, because the failing threshold (oxygen under 50) and the claim threshold (activity needs 60) leave a band where the bed is not failing yet the fish are quiet. With the threshold aligned (A2) it had 0 false lines. In worlds B and C the cause gate had 7 of 20 and 19 of 40 false lines, since temperature and predators drive the asserted state outside the cause. The exact gate scores 0 by construction because it reads the asserted predicate itself.
- Fix: Gate each line on the predicate that line asserts, computed from live state; use a cause gate only when the cause is the sole driver of that predicate and its threshold equals the claim's, and say so in the code beside the gate. Give the healthy branch its own claim and its own gate too.
- Why this fix: The false-line counts show the error moving to whichever branch makes a claim the gate does not read, so every claimed sentence needs its own predicate.
- Rule of thumb: Branch on the predicate the sentence asserts; a cause gate was exact only where one cause drove the state and its threshold matched the claim (0 of 10 false, 1 of 10 with a 50 against 60 mismatch), and 7 of 20 and 19 of 40 false once temperature or predators were added.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; counts above are its output. The pond physics, thresholds and drivers are toy assumptions I chose, and the exact gate being 0 is true by construction, so the result supports the ordering of gates, not real pond numbers.
- Composed: ideas:NARRATION/adaptive-copy/branch-on-the-claim-not-on-a-correlate, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/a-coarse-proxy-agrees-with-truth-only-where-they-coincide, ideas:ZEN/verification/finger-is-not-the-moon-proxy-gauge
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__adaptive-copy-cause-gate-is-exact-only-when-cause-is-sole-driver.py
- Prediction: Cause gate has 0 false lines in world A and more than 0 in B; exact has 0 everywhere; proxy is worst; cause is worse in C than in B. (First run missed: cause had 1 false line in A because of mismatched thresholds.)
- Observed: RESULT: PASS cause gate false 1/10 in A (0 when threshold aligned, A2=0), but 7/20 false in B and 19/40 in C; proxy 4/10, 9/20, 19/40; exact 0 everywhere
- Scenarios: 1) world A oxygen only; 2) world B plus cold water (built to BREAK the cause gate); 3) world C plus predator; 4) A2 threshold aligned to claim threshold

## E95 — wason positive test strategy vs hidden rule superset boundary
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][bias][debugging][verification]
- What: Modelled Wason's 2-4-6 rule discovery as deterministic hypothesis elimination: a learner holds the narrowest rule consistent with its data, five hidden rules (step of two, even ascending, any arithmetic progression, ascending, non-descending) on a 14-value grid, and four testing strategies (positive-only, naive smallest violator, near-miss violator, alternating positive and near-miss) with 10 tests each.
- Why built: To check the kernel that confirmation-seeking tests produce mounting yes answers without evidence, and to find where seeking disconfirmation stops being enough.
- Design: Rules are predicates over triples; the learner re-picks the narrowest consistent rule after every answer; candidate tests are taken in a fixed enumeration order; a property-style search lists the smallest triple on which the held rule and the hidden rule disagree.
- Got right: With hidden rule ascending, positive-only testing got 9 yes answers and still announced the step-of-two rule, and the smallest disagreement triple (1, 2, 3) can only be reached by a negative test, since every positive test of the held rule passes under both rules.
- Where/why it failed: My first prediction, that any negative test strategy finds the rule, was refuted: naive smallest-violator negative tests (such as 1-1-1) are rejected by both rules and failed for ascending, any arithmetic progression and even ascending. Even near-miss tests found only 2 of the 4 wider hidden rules within 10 tests (ascending and non-descending, not the progression or even rules). Positive-only testing was correct whenever the hidden rule was not wider than the held one (step of two, even ascending).
- Fix: Choose disconfirming tests as near misses of the current hypothesis (violators nearest to what it accepts), alternate them with confirming tests, and budget enough tests for each plausible wider rule.
- Why this fix: Near-miss plus positive alternation found ascending and non-descending where positive-only did not, and the near-miss ordering is what separates a useful disconfirming test from a vacuous one.
- Rule of thumb: Positive-only testing is safe only when the true rule is not wider than your hypothesis, and a negative test that both rules reject teaches nothing, so pick near misses; here that gave wrong announcements on 3 of 5 hidden rules for positive-only, 3 of 5 for naive negative and 2 of 5 for near-miss, and 10 tests were not enough for every wider rule.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the learner is a mechanical model, so human rates such as the roughly 20 percent first-announcement success in the source are not tested.
- Composed: ideas:DECISION-MAKING/cognitive-bias/confirmation-bias/wason-2-4-6-rule-discovery-task, ideas:DEBUGGING/cognitive-bias/confirmation-bias/confirmation-bias-makes-a-hypothesis-hard-to-abandon, ideas:TESTING/property-based/generation-and-shrinking/property-based-tests-search-for-a-counterexample-and-shrink-it
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__wason-positive-test-strategy-vs-hidden-rule-superset-boundary.py
- Prediction: With hidden rule ascending, positive-only testing ends on the step-of-two rule with nearly all yes answers, while negative testing finds the rule.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS hidden=asc: positive-only announced step2 after 9 yes of 10, naive negative failed, near-miss and alternating found it; positive-only correct only for even ascending and step of two; smallest negative-test counterexample (1, 2, 3)
- Scenarios: 1) hidden ascending, four strategies; 2) hidden non-descending; 3) hidden narrower or equal (step of two, even ascending); 4) BREAK: naive negative tests and near-miss on the progression and even rules; 5) smallest-disagreement counterexample search

## E94 — mechanism test vs rate test party sighting sandbox
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][verification][rng][sandbox]
- What: Built a deterministic model of a party-sighting event (roll with probability P, fires only if the party is inside the lead's field of view, party chases a formation slot derived from the lead's yaw) and ran a stubbed-roll mechanism test, rate tests under four stated player-behaviour models, a bug matrix, and an A/B of two builds.
- Why built: To check whether the kernel that mechanism tests and rate tests are different axes holds in a model, and where it stops holding.
- Design: Party position, FOV cone test and a per-tick roll; models: spin in place, straight walk, walk-stop-turn every 20 ticks, same every 200 ticks. Expected fires are computed as visible ticks times P, so no RNG is needed for the rate result; the A/B uses a fixed-seed LCG versus a (tick, purpose) keyed hash.
- Got right: The mechanism test (roll stubbed to 0, party hand-placed ahead) passed at P=1e-12, a rate at which the feature never fires. Spin-in-place and straight walking gave 0 of 2000 visible ticks, walk-stop-turn gave 199 and 19 at periods 20 and 200.
- Where/why it failed: The rate answer is only as good as the behaviour model: a 10x change in turn cadence moved sightings 10.5x. Neither test caught a FOV narrowed to 10 degrees, since the turn-around still produced visible ticks. The sign-flipped visibility bug was caught only by the mechanism test, and a 1000x-low or shipped 1/4096 rate only by the rate test.
- Fix: Keep both tests, write the behaviour model in the rate test as a named assumption, and compare builds with keyed draws (tick, purpose) or a fixed scenario instead of two full same-seed runs.
- Why this fix: With a shared stream, build B with one extra draw per tick fired on 9 ticks and A on 6, sharing none; keyed by (tick, purpose) both fired on the same 11 ticks.
- Rule of thumb: A stubbed-roll mechanism test cannot see a rate bug and a rate test cannot see a logic bug (here each caught bugs the other missed), and the rate figure moves 10x with the assumed player cadence, so state that cadence in the test; in this model (4 behaviour models, 5 bug variants, 2 A/B builds) uncontrolled same-seed A/B comparison measured nothing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox script; the model is a simplification and real gameplay cadence is assumed, not measured.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS spin visible=0, wstw-20=199, wstw-200=19, mech passes at P=1e-12, shared-stream A/B diverges (6 vs 9), keyed identical=True

## E93 — managed language sandbox escape vs capability allowlist stage freeze
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [modding][security][sandbox][testing]
- What: Built a Python analog (a managed language) of a mod loader and ran escape attempts against four isolation designs: stripped-builtins eval, a syntax allowlist, a data-only verb allowlist, and a data-only allowlist with argument schemas and a frozen verb table. The spawn capability was a recorder, so nothing hostile was executed; the only real OS call was os.getpid().
- Why built: To check whether the kernel that a memory-safe managed language is not a sandbox holds in a model, and which additions make a capability allowlist actually hold.
- Design: S1 eval with empty builtins reaching the os module through the object-subclass walk; S2 an AST validator rejecting underscore names and attributes; S3 mods as data steps interpreted against a verb allowlist; S4 break: an allowlisted verb (run_script) takes an arbitrary argument; S5 break: a later mod rebinds the allowlisted verb log to run_script (last loaded wins) while the table is still mutable.
- Got right: S1 reached os.getpid() with no builtins at all. The AST validator blocked the same payload. Data-only mods rejected 5 of 5 hostile steps and loaded the benign one with 0 spawns once arguments were schema-checked and the verb table frozen.
- Where/why it failed: The syntax filter still passed a format string that walks dunder attributes (it leaked class names, information only, not execution). A verb-name allowlist alone let run_script take an arbitrary command string, the Process.Start analog, and a later mod rebinding log to run_script spawned it through an allowlisted name.
- Fix: Treat the allowlist as verbs plus per-verb argument schemas, and freeze the verb table after the settings stage so the data-stage patch pass can add content but not rebind capabilities.
- Why this fix: With schemas and a frozen table all 8 checks held, and each break scenario leaked until exactly its own control was added; the language never provided the boundary.
- Rule of thumb: A restricted language subset is not the sandbox: 1 of 1 stripped-builtins evals reached the OS, and even a data-only allowlist leaked in 2 of 2 break cases until arguments were schema-checked and the verb table frozen before mods patch each other.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; Python stands in for .NET, so the escape route differs and only the structural claim is tested. The first run's S1 payload used a class absent from this interpreter and failed, so it was corrected and rerun with the same claim.
- Composed: ideas:MODDING/security/managed-language-is-not-a-sandbox/process-start-shell-execute-escape, ideas:MODDING/data-architecture/three-stage-load-lifecycle/settings-data-runtime-separation, ideas:MODDING/conflict-resolution/last-loaded-record-wins/engine-simplicity-vs-community-tooling-tradeoff
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__managed-language-sandbox-escape-vs-capability-allowlist-stage-freeze.py
- Prediction: Stripped-builtins eval reaches the OS, a name-only allowlist leaks through an allowlisted verb, a last-loaded rebind leaks until the table is frozen, and arg schemas plus freeze stop everything.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS language-only restriction escaped (S1), syntax filter leaked via format (S2), verb allowlist alone leaked (S4), rebind leaked until table frozen (S5); arg schema + frozen table stopped all 8 of 8
- Scenarios: 1) stripped-builtins eval escape; 2) AST validator plus format-string bypass; 3) data-only mods, 5 hostile plus 1 benign; 4) BREAK: allowlisted verb with an unconstrained argument; 5) BREAK: later mod rebinds an allowlisted verb before the table is frozen

## E92 — estimate buffer fails under shared delay and order effect artifact
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [time-management][estimation][bias][testing]
- What: Two exact, deterministic models of time-management claims: (A) project totals as sums of per-task durations with a shared delay factor and a per-switch cost, compared against sum-of-medians, sum-of-worst-cases and outside-view estimates; (B) a parole-style session in which every ruling follows case merit with no fatigue, but favorable rulings take longer and a clerk fits the next case that still finishes before the break.
- Why built: To test two TIME-MANAGEMENT kernels that no memory entry had built on: that even worst-case estimates underestimate, and that an order effect in rulings can be a scheduling artifact instead of fatigue.
- Design: A: per-task duration 1, 2 or 4 days with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2; shared factor 1, 1.5, 2.5 with probabilities 0.6, 0.3, 0.1; half a day per task switch; n of 1, 3, 6 and 12 tasks, exact convolution. B: golden-ratio case pattern (about half favorable), 60-minute sessions, durations 12 for favorable and 4 for unfavorable, compared with equal durations and a ratio sweep.
- Got right: Sum-of-medians finished on time with probability 0.125 at 3 tasks, 0.016 at 6 and 0.000 at 12, so the typical-case plan fails. Under independence a sum of per-task worst cases was safe (1.000), but with a shared delay and switching it finished on time only 0.874 to 0.890 of the time at every n. In B the favorable rate fell from 0.72 early in a session to 0.04 late with no fatigue in the model, and equal durations gave 0.50 and 0.50.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel's claim that worst-case estimates underestimate only appeared once delays were shared; independent worst cases were generous and the half-day switch cost added only about 3 to 4 points of overrun. My first run of B had a flat control that was not flat (0.20 vs 0.60) because a 10-periodic case pattern aliased with the session length, which was fixed with a golden-ratio pattern and 100 sessions.
- Fix: Estimate the whole project from totals of similar past projects (the reference class, which sat near the middle at 0.597 to 0.631) instead of summing padded per-task worst cases, and before reading a within-session decline as fatigue, check whether decision duration drives who gets scheduled late.
- Why this fix: The per-task buffer fails because delays are shared across tasks, so padding each task cannot reach the tail, while a past-totals estimate carries the shared factor automatically; the ratio sweep (early vs late 0.5 vs 0.5, 0.61 vs 0.30, 0.72 vs 0.04 at duration ratios 1, 2, 3) shows the artifact grows with how much longer favorable rulings take.
- Rule of thumb: Summed per-task worst cases are safe only when delays are independent (1.000 at 12 tasks) and drop to about 0.88 under one shared delay factor, so use totals from similar past projects; a late-in-session decline in favorable rulings (0.72 to 0.04) appears with zero fatigue whenever favorable rulings take longer, and vanishes with equal durations.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox with exact fractions; the distributions and the shared factor are chosen by me, so the probabilities are illustrative and the human effect sizes in the sources are not tested.
- Composed: ideas:TIME-MANAGEMENT/planning-fallacy/estimation-bias/even-worst-case-estimates-underestimate-how-long-things-take, ideas:TIME-MANAGEMENT/decision-fatigue/replication-crisis/ego-depletion-failed-a-23-lab-replication-and-the-parole-study-has-a-rival-explanation, ideas:TIME-MANAGEMENT/multitasking/switch-cost/switching-tasks-costs-time-even-when-the-switch-is-fully-predictable
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__estimate-buffer-fails-under-shared-delay-and-order-effect-artifact.py
- Prediction: Sum-of-medians finishes under 50 percent for 3 or more tasks, independent worst-case sums are near 1, shared delay plus switching pulls the worst-case sum below 95 percent, an outside-view total sits near 50 percent, and the within-session decline appears with unequal durations and vanishes with equal ones.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS A: sum-of-medians finish prob 0.016 at n=6; independent worst-case sum 1.000 at n=12 but shared delay plus switching 0.884; B: favorable rate early 0.72 -> late 0.04 with no fatigue, vanishes with equal durations (0.50 vs 0.50); checks 7/7
- Scenarios: 1) sum of medians at four project sizes; 2) sum of worst cases with independent delays; 3) BREAK: worst cases with a shared delay factor and switch cost; 4) outside-view total; 5) session fitting with unequal durations; 6) control with equal durations; 7) duration ratio sweep 1, 2, 3

## E91 — bm25 whole doc vs chunk overlap inverted index
- Date: 2026-10-11
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [search][chunking][bm25][testing]
- What: Deterministic stdlib sandbox: an inverted index (term to posting dict) scored with BM25 (k1=1.2, b=0.75) over 4 docs of 14 sentences, where every doc holds all the query words and only the adjacent-sentence pairing differs. Compared whole-doc vs chunk size 1/2/3/4/8, with and without overlap.
- Why built: To test the chunking bias-variance kernel on a lexical index, composing the inverted-index and BM25 length-normalisation kernels with the earlier tf-idf chunk sweep (E34).
- Design: 16 queries of two words (a_j, b_k) whose answer is a single doc. Chunk score is the max over a doc's chunks. A first, easier corpus with unique rare needle words gave MRR 1.0 for every setting and was discarded as non-discriminating.
- Got right: Whole-doc MRR 0.521 and b=0 vs b=0.75 identical (length normalisation cannot help when all docs have equal length and all terms). Size 2 with overlap 1 reached MRR 1.000 (the pair span is 2 sentences).
- Where/why it failed: Without overlap, pairs straddling a chunk boundary are lost (size 2 ov0 = 0.646, size 4 ov0 = 0.844). Overlap is not monotone good: size 3 ov1 = 0.938 and size 4 ov1 = 0.812, because larger overlapped windows re-admit wrong pairings. Size 1 equals whole-doc (0.521) since a single sentence never holds both words.
- Fix: Set chunk size to the answer span and overlap to span-1, then sweep size and overlap together on a labeled query set instead of using a fixed 10-20 percent default.
- Why this fix: The only configuration where every answer pair fits whole inside some chunk and no chunk is wide enough to hold a wrong pairing is size equal to span with overlap span-1.
- Rule of thumb: For lexical BM25, whole-doc and too-small chunks both score at chance when disambiguation needs adjacent-sentence co-occurrence; chunk to the answer span with overlap one less, and sweep, since extra size or overlap past that point lowers MRR (1.00 to 0.94 to 0.81).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; numbers are exact and deterministic. Not tested: dense embeddings, real text.
- Composed: ideas:SEARCH/vector/chunking-is-a-bias-variance-tradeoff, ideas:SEARCH/lexical/inverted-index-is-the-foundational-structure, ideas:SEARCH/lexical/bm25-two-knobs-tf-saturation-and-length-normalization, brainwork/E34
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-11__bm25-whole-doc-vs-chunk-overlap-inverted-index.py
- Prediction: Whole-doc MRR near 0.5, size 2 ov0 below 1.0 from boundary straddles, size 2 ov1 exactly 1.0.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS whole=0.52; chunk2 ov0=0.65; chunk2 ov1=1.00; chunk3 ov1=0.94; chunk4 ov1=0.81
- Scenarios: 1) whole-doc with b=0.75 and b=0; 2) chunk sizes 1,2,3,4,8 with no overlap; 3) sizes 2,3,4 with overlap 1 (size 4 built to BREAK the more-overlap-is-better idea)

## E90 — why comment stale sandbox
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [documentation][testing][process]
- What: Sandbox that generates real Python config source with six constants, writes either a restating comment or a rationale comment above each, then mutates the code and audits comment staleness with a tokenize/ast checker.
- Why built: The kernel DOCUMENTATION/code-comments/why-not-what says a comment that restates the code adds nothing and can go stale; I wanted to find where that holds and where it stops.
- Design: Six constants, two comment styles, three mutations (value-only refactor, premise-only change with identical values, both). Ground truth stale count is compared with what a mechanical number-matching checker flags.
- Got right: Restating comments went stale 6/6 on a value change and the checker caught all 6; rationale comments stayed correct 0/6 stale on a value change, so the kernel holds for value drift.
- Where/why it failed: Built to BREAK the claim: when only the premise changed and values stayed identical, 6/6 rationale comments were wrong yet the checker flagged 0, while restating comments were fine. Why-comments are not immune to staleness; their staleness is just invisible to tooling.
- Fix: Treat why-comments as cheap to keep through refactors but not free: tie each to a checkable premise (a test, assertion or linked doc) so premise drift fails somewhere, instead of trusting the comment style alone.
- Why this fix: The checker only sees literals it can compare, matching the doctest result that only wired-in claims are caught, and the spec-repo result that cross-repo claims drift silently without a failing signal.
- Rule of thumb: Prefer why-comments to restating ones because value changes cannot stale them, but know their staleness on premise change is undetectable by tooling; pin the premise to a test or dated note. Tested on 3 scenarios with 6 constants each, not on prose-heavy comments.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the checker, mutations and counts are all from the run. Whether real teams' why-comments drift at this rate is not measured.
- Composed: ideas:DOCUMENTATION/code-comments/why-not-what, sandbox-kernel-doctest-wiring/E1, ideas/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__why-comment-stale-sandbox.py
- Prediction: Value-only: restating comments 6/6 stale and caught, rationale comments 0/6 stale. Premise-only: rationale comments 6/6 stale with checker catching 0.

## E89 — silence is evidence only against window audience and baseline
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [humor][measurement][negotiation]
- What: Exact-fraction Bayes sandbox that prices a missing laugh, and a counterpart's silence after an offer, as a likelihood ratio under different audience sizes, response windows, correlation, unknown crowd type and baseline reply speed.
- Why built: The kernel on silence as evidence says a missing laugh is strong only with a long enough window, many independent chances and a baseline from earlier repeats; the negotiation silence kernel treats a pause as pressure. I wanted to see which conditions carry the weight.
- Design: Prior failed 1/2, a 1/100 politeness-laugh floor. Silence probability if the joke worked is (1 - r*c)^n for n independent listeners with response rate r and window coverage c; if failed it is (1-e)^n. Cases: 40 listeners, 2 listeners, one text reader, a short window, a fully correlated room, an unknown crowd type updated on earlier answered repeats, and a negotiation pause of 6 seconds against a reject hazard of 1/2 per second.
- Got right: 40 listeners gave P(failed given silence) 0.99947, 2 listeners 0.593, text 0.510, so room size sets how much a silence says. Unknown crowd type went from 0.790 with no earlier answered repeats to 0.949 after three, so the baseline matters. The same 6 second pause read as reject at exactly 0.50 when the counterpart's usual reply hazard was 1/2 and 0.029 when it was 1/10.
- Where/why it failed: Two of my predictions were wrong. The big-room figure was lower than the 0.9999 I wrote because the politeness floor caps it. Built to BREAK the kernel's window condition: with a window covering only 1/3 of the tail, 40 listeners still gave 0.914, so many independent chances compensate for a short window and the three conditions are not each necessary. The other break: 40 fully correlated listeners behave as one draw and gave 0.547.
- Fix: Compute the silence as a likelihood ratio from the room's effective independent count, window coverage and the audience's own observed baseline, instead of reading it against zero or by headcount alone.
- Why this fix: The ratio only depends on how likely silence would be if the joke had worked, which collapses toward 1 when listeners are few, correlated, or unlikely to respond in the window; the baseline decides what counts as unusual.
- Rule of thumb: Judge a silence by its likelihood ratio: effective independent listeners times response chance in the window, against the observed baseline; 40 independent listeners gave 0.99947 but 40 fully correlated gave 0.547, and the same pause flipped from 0.50 to 0.029 with the counterpart's baseline. Toy model with assumed parameters, not field data.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox with exact Fractions; every posterior is computed in the run. All rates, floors and hazards are assumed parameters, not measured from real audiences or negotiators.
- Composed: ideas:HUMOR-STYLES/measurement/silence-as-evidence, ideas:NEGOTIATION/tactics/silence, sandbox-self-directed-humor-dose-response/E1
- Polarity: compatible

## E88 — n plus one lazy property vs batch vs join latency thresholds
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [performance][database][testing]
- What: Sandbox on in-memory sqlite comparing a lazy per-author property in a loop, an IN-batch with an optional key cap, and a JOIN, counting the select statements each really issues and converting counts to latency at a simulated 2 ms round trip.
- Why built: The kernel says N+1 hides inside a loop that looks innocent; I wanted the counts, the point where it crosses a perceived-latency line, and where the usual fixes stop being equivalent.
- Design: N of 10, 100, 500 authors with 3 books each. Queries are counted with a sqlite trace callback, not assumed. Latency is queries times 2 ms, an arithmetic stand-in, not measured wall time. Thresholds used are 100 ms for feels instant and 1000 ms for loses flow.
- Got right: Naive issued exactly 1+N queries (11, 101, 501), batch 2, join 1, and all three returned identical results. At N=500 naive costs about 1002 ms, past the 1000 ms line, while batch and join stay near 4 ms and 2 ms.
- Where/why it failed: Built to BREAK the fixes. An INNER JOIN silently dropped the 6 childless authors of 30 that batch kept, so the one-query fix changes the answer; a LEFT JOIN matches batch. A 100-key cap turned the batch into 6 queries, the same shape as the DataLoader cap result. At zero round trip the naive version looked fast yet still issued 501 queries.
- Fix: Count queries per request as the invariant, not wall time on a local database; fix with a batched IN lookup or a LEFT JOIN, never an inner join when parents may lack children.
- Why this fix: Query count scales with N regardless of environment, while latency depends on the round trip, so a local fast test hides the problem that production's network exposes.
- Rule of thumb: Assert a query-count budget in tests, because in-process databases make N+1 invisible by time; batch with IN or LEFT JOIN and expect 1 + ceil(N/cap) queries if keys are capped. Tested on sqlite with one-to-many only, latency simulated.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; query counts and result equality are measured. The latency figures are arithmetic from an assumed 2 ms round trip, not a real network measurement.
- Composed: ideas:PERFORMANCE/database/n-plus-one, ideas:PERFORMANCE/perceived-performance/response-time-thresholds, sandbox-kernel-api-design/E3
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__n-plus-one-lazy-property-vs-batch-vs-join-latency-thresholds.py
- Prediction: Naive 1+N queries (501 at N=500), batch 2, join 1; naive crosses 1000 ms at N=500 with a 2 ms round trip; inner join drops childless authors; cap 100 gives 6 queries; zero round trip leaves naive at 501 queries.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS N=500 naive 501 queries ~1002ms vs batch 2 / join 1; zero-RTT naive still 501 queries; inner join dropped 6; cap100 -> 6
- Scenarios: 1) N=10,100,500 naive vs batch vs join; 2) zero round trip (BREAK: time hides the bug); 3) inner join with childless authors (BREAK: fix changes results); 4) key cap of 100

## E87 — bbox overlap necessary not sufficient exact sat grid
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [geometry][visibility][testing]
- What: Exact-arithmetic sandbox that compares cheap visibility tests against a ground-truth separating-axis overlap test for 6936 thin rotated bars against a square frame, plus a two-tile edge-ownership check.
- Why built: The kernel says bounding-box overlap is necessary but not sufficient for a visible artifact; I wanted the size of the gap and to see which other cheap tests fail in which direction.
- Design: Bars are rectangles built from integer direction vectors with Fraction centres, half-lengths 1/2, 3/2, 4 and thin half-width 1/8, so no float error. Ground truth is SAT on the closed frame. Tests compared: bbox overlap, any-vertex-inside, and a centre-only fit like the per-item min(halfW/|x|, halfH/|y|) form in the camera clamp entry. Separately, two adjacent tiles sharing the edge x=1 are checked under inclusive, exclusive and half-open ranges.
- Got right: bbox overlap had 0 false negatives, confirming necessary; it also had 1392 false positives out of 3452 hits (40.3%), so not sufficient. Half-open ranges gave the shared edge exactly one owner (1), inclusive gave 2 and exclusive 0.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction was wrong in one place: I expected the centre-only test to also wrongly accept bars, but a centre inside the frame is inside the bar, so it had 0 false positives and 1460 false negatives; it is sufficient but not necessary. The any-vertex test also missed 1318 true overlaps (long bars piercing the frame with all corners outside).
- Fix: Use bbox overlap only as a cheap reject, then confirm with an exact test such as SAT; do not accept a vertex or centre test as a visibility check for long thin shapes; use half-open ranges when a boundary point must belong to exactly one region.
- Why this fix: Each cheap test errs in one direction (bbox lets false overlaps through, vertex and centre tests drop real overlaps), so combining a reject filter with an exact confirm removes both errors at low cost.
- Rule of thumb: Treat bbox overlap as a reject-only filter (0 misses, 40.3% false hits on thin diagonal bars) and confirm with an exact test; vertex-in-frame and centre-fit tests miss real overlaps on long shapes (1318 and 1460 of 2060 true). Tested on one square frame and rectangles only.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox with exact Fractions; all counts above are from the run. Only rectangular bars and a square frame were tested, and the camera-clamp entry itself was not rerun, only its centre-fit form.
- Composed: ideas:GEOMETRY/visibility/verify-piercing-geometry, ideas:GEOMETRY/point-in-polygon/half-open-interval-attributes-each-vertex-to-exactly-one-edge, sandbox-kernel-motion-camera/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__bbox-overlap-necessary-not-sufficient-exact-sat-grid.py
- Prediction: bbox has 0 false negatives and over 10% false positives; vertex-in-frame misses some true overlaps; centre-fit errs in both directions (this last part was wrong); shared tile edge claimed 2 times inclusive, 0 exclusive, 1 half-open.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 6936 bars: bbox false-neg 0, false-pos 1392/3452 (40.3%); vertex-in-frame misses 1318 true overlaps; centre-fit misses 1460 and wrongly accepts 0; shared edge claimed {'incl': 2, 'excl': 0, 'half': 1}
- Scenarios: 1) bbox vs SAT on 6936 bars; 2) vertex-in-frame vs SAT (BREAK: long bars piercing with corners outside); 3) centre-fit vs SAT; 4) shared-edge ownership under three range rules

## E86 — style card replace per slot never append
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ai-video][prompting][sandbox][testing]
- What: A deterministic prompt-composer sandbox built the three AI-video kernels together: the six-block shot formula with audio separate, per-style cards (UGC, demo, premium) filling the slots, and a shorter image-to-video form. It found that cards can be mixed slot by slot but must replace, not append, values within a slot.
- Why built: Three AI-VIDEO kernels were never applied by a memory entry; I wanted to see whether "same structure, different slot values" survives mixing cards and where a lint has to sit.
- Design: Compose function with fixed block order, three cards of slot values taken from the kernels' vocabulary, an author-written conflict table (handheld versus rigged camera moves, shallow versus deep focus, available versus shaped light, ambient versus scored audio), and a one-action lint. Cases: whole cards, 81 slot-by-slot mixes, appended-value merges of card pairs, an image-to-video form, and a two-verb action.
- Got right: All three whole cards composed in the identical block order with zero conflicts. Appending two cards' values into each slot conflicted for 3 of 3 card pairs. The image-to-video form had 4 blocks with no style or context block, so its structure is deliberately different. A two-verb action filled a slot but the one-action lint caught it.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that fewer than half of the 81 slot-by-slot mixes would be lint-clean was refuted: all 81 were clean, because the vocabulary conflicts sit inside a slot (two camera moves) rather than across slots. The conflict table is mine, not measured on a video model, so cross-slot taste clashes are untested.

- Rule of thumb: Treat a style card as slot values that replace, not stack: in this test mixing cards slot by slot never produced a lexical conflict, but appending two cards produced one every time, and a full form still allowed a two-verb action.

## E85 — postgres default isolation anomalies on real server
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [database][transactions][postgres][sandbox][testing]
- What: Ran the isolation-levels kernel against a real scratch PostgreSQL 16 server with interleaved sessions, and confirmed that its default level lets a write-skew and a skipped-row paging bug through, while two cheaper fixes exist.
- Why built: The kernel was sourced from the Postgres docs table only and no memory entry had built against it; I wanted to see the anomalies happen, not read them, and to find which fix is the smallest.
- Design: Python started a throwaway server with initdb on a unix socket (the approach from garden/E5) and drove separate psql processes one statement at a time. Scenarios: on-call write skew at read committed, repeatable read and serializable; a non-repeatable read; the same skew with a row lock; and OFFSET paging with a delete between pages (the August-10 E29 failure) in separate statements versus one repeatable-read transaction.
- Got right: The default was read committed. Write skew left 0 doctors on call at both read committed and repeatable read, and serializable aborted the second commit with a serialization error, leaving 1. The re-read changed under read committed (true then false) and held under repeatable read. Paging per statement missed row 6 after a delete before the cursor; one repeatable-read transaction missed nothing.
- Where/why it failed: Two harness slips of mine, not claim failures: the first row-lock query used an aggregate, which Postgres rejects, and my pass condition looked for an error code that quiet psql output does not print. Both were fixed and the run repeated.
- Fix: For a check-then-write race, prefer locking the rows read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), which kept 1 doctor on call at read committed because the second session re-read after the first committed; use serializable plus a retry on the serialization error when the rows to lock are not known up front; for paging, read all pages in one repeatable-read transaction or use keyset.
- Why this fix: Repeatable read did not stop write skew here, so raising to it only fixes the non-repeatable read and paging cases; the lock or serializable level addresses the actual dependency between the two transactions.
- Rule of thumb: Check the active isolation level before trusting a transaction to prevent a race: on Postgres 16 defaults, check-then-write skew gets through at read committed and at repeatable read, and only a row lock or serializable (with retry) stopped it in this test.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox against a real PostgreSQL 16 scratch server; scope is one two-row table, two sessions and one deterministic interleaving per case; no other engines or versions.
- Composed: ideas:DATABASE-DESIGN/transactions/isolation-levels/read-committed-not-serializable-is-what-most-apps-actually-run-on, garden/E5, august-10/E29
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__postgres-isolation-levels-real-server.py
- Prediction: Default read committed; on-call count 0 at read committed and repeatable read, 1 with a serialization error at serializable; non-repeatable read at read committed only; a row lock keeps at least 1 at read committed; per-statement OFFSET paging misses a row while one repeatable-read transaction misses none.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS default=read committed; on-call left RC=0 RR=0 SER=1 RC+FOR UPDATE=1; nonrepeatable RC=('t', 'f') RR=('t', 't'); offset-page rows missed RC=[6] RR-txn=[]
- Scenarios: 1) write skew at read committed, repeatable read and serializable; 2) non-repeatable read at two levels; 3) BREAK: row lock at read committed as a fix without raising the level; 4) BREAK: OFFSET paging with a delete between pages, per statement versus one repeatable-read transaction
- Link: brain train auto loop 2 pass 1; session_01AA8Uvte5UTxtoXrEfFp3KE

## E84 — grapheme cap needs order and byte budget
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [text][unicode][sandbox][testing]
- What: Applied the kernel that a length cap must cut on grapheme boundaries, using real Node v22 Intl.Segmenter, and pushed it to its edges: a transform applied after the cap, and a UTF-8 byte budget.
- Why built: No memory entry had built against this kernel's cap rule together with the case-mapping kernel; I wanted to know where "cap on graphemes" alone stops being enough.
- Design: A Python harness runs a JavaScript snippet in Node. S1 trims three flags by code units, code points and graphemes. S2 caps "straßen-café" at 6 graphemes before and after toUpperCase, and checks Turkish dotted capital I lowercasing. S3 caps ten family emoji at 10 graphemes, then tries a 100-byte and a 90-byte budget with a raw byte slice versus a grapheme-boundary walk.
- Got right: The kernel held: the code-unit cut left a lone surrogate, the grapheme cut returned exactly the three flags. Turkish İ lowercase added one code point but no grapheme, so a grapheme cap is stable under that mapping.
- Where/why it failed: Two edges the kernel does not cover. Capping at 6 before uppercasing gave 7 graphemes (ß becomes SS), so the cap was violated; capping after gave 6. Ten family emoji are 10 graphemes but 250 bytes, so a grapheme cap does not bound storage. My own prediction was also wrong once: a raw 100-byte slice happened to be clean because 100 is exactly 4 x 25-byte emoji; at 90 bytes it produced a replacement character.
- Fix: Apply any length-changing transform first and cap last, and for a byte limit walk graphemes accumulating encoded length instead of slicing bytes (the 100-byte walk kept 4 graphemes, 100 bytes, no corruption).
- Why this fix: The cap must be measured in the unit the limit is expressed in, on the final string, and cut only at boundaries; the walk satisfies both without re-validating.
- Rule of thumb: Cut on grapheme boundaries, but cap after case or normalization changes and measure bytes when the limit is bytes; a clean raw byte slice can be luck of alignment, so test it at an offset that is not a multiple of the character size.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox in real Node v22 (English segmenter only; no other locales or Node versions run; only Python-side orchestration is stdlib).
- Composed: ideas:TEXT/unicode/truncate-on-grapheme-boundaries-not-code-units, ideas:TEXT/case/case-mapping-is-locale-dependent-and-not-one-to-one, sandbox-kernel-text-unicode/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__grapheme-cap-order-and-byte-budget.py
- Prediction: Code-unit cut malformed and grapheme cut exactly 3 flags; cap-before-uppercase exceeds 6 graphemes while cap-after does not; a raw 100-byte slice of ten family emoji corrupts. The last part came out wrong (clean at 100, corrupt at 90).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS flags: code-unit cut well-formed=False, grapheme cut=3 flags; cap-before-upper 7 graphemes vs cap-after 6; cap10 family=250 bytes, byte-bounded=100 bytes/4 graphemes
- Scenarios: 1) three flags cut by code units, code points, graphemes; 2) BREAK: cap before versus after toUpperCase on straßen-café, plus Turkish İ; 3) BREAK: ten family emoji under a grapheme cap and under 100- and 90-byte budgets

## E83 — dubbing third rewrite share is rate ratio dependent
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [localization][dubbing][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic sandbox re-tested the dubbing kernel's claim that about a third of Spanish lines need rewriting after speed-up. It used a 12-pair EN/ES SHOT/DIALOGUE/SFX script and swept the speech rates.
- Why built: The kernel's one-third figure came from 22 pairs at one fixed pair of rates. I wanted to know whether the share is a stable property of EN-to-ES dubbing or an artifact of the line set and rates.
- Design: Dialogue was extracted by regex from the quoted block only, and shot and SFX lines were diffed byte-identical across languages. Syllables were counted by heuristic, then required speed-up = ES time / EN time. Rate pairs were EN/ES 6.2/7.7, 6.8/7.7, 5.5/7.7, and equal 6.2/6.2 as the case built to break it.
- Got right: Quoted-dialogue isolation worked mechanically, since the non-dialogue text was identical in both versions. In every scenario most lines needed more than a 1.10x speed-up, so speed-up alone never fixed the set.
- Where/why it failed: The prediction (3 to 5 of 12 lines over 1.25x) failed. At base rates 7 of 12 (58%) were over 1.25x, ES syllables were 1.71x EN (kernel had 1.55x), and the share ranged from 42% to 92% across the rate sweep.
- Fix: Treat "about a third" as one dataset's number. Measure the over-1.25x share on your own script using the syllable ratio and the two speech rates, then plan rewrites for that share.
- Why this fix: The over-threshold share moves with the ES/EN rate ratio and the line set's syllable growth, so a fixed fraction does not transfer. The per-line needed-speed-up column in the kernel is the part that does.
- Rule of thumb: The qualitative rule (speed-up fixes only a small residual, so rewrite the longest lines) held in all 4 rate scenarios here, but the one-third figure did not; compute the share per script.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox (author-written 12 lines, heuristic syllable counter, human speech rates). Scope is limited to human speech rates; AI-voice pacing and tool stretch limits were out of scope.

## E82 — tts pinned per chunk settings fix drift but not tag stacking or stitch context
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [audio][state][testing][pipeline]
- What: A stateless text-to-speech model run over a twelve-chunk document, comparing first-call-only settings, stitching context alone, and identical settings pinned on every chunk, with a gold-reference diff per chunk, plus tag stacking and a high style slider as break cases.
- Why built: The per-request style kernel and the stacking-averages kernel are both unapplied; the claim that pinning is the whole fix and that stitching context is not a style channel had never been run.
- Design: Hand-written model where output depends only on the request (settings, tags), stitching context only sets a boundary-smoothing flag, stacked tags average their valence, and style above 0.75 or more than three tags sets an instability flag; a gold read per voice flags any differing chunk.
- Got right: First-call-only drifted 11 of 12 chunks; stitching context without pinned settings also drifted 11; pinned settings drifted 0; the gold diff caught every drifted chunk.
- Where/why it failed: Pinning did not cover stacking: an excited tag next to a sorrowful tag in a pinned chunk averaged to valence 0.0 and was flagged; style 0.9 flagged unstable while 0.6 did not. The model is hand-written, so the numbers show the logic of the pipeline and say nothing about any real service.
- Fix: Send an identical settings payload on every chunk request, keep contradictory tags in separate chunks, keep the slider at or below 0.75, and gate each chunk with a gold-reference diff.
- Why this fix: Pinning removes the only source of drift in a stateless request, and the gold diff is what notices the cases pinning cannot fix.
- Rule of thumb: In a stateless per-request synth, drift is cured by pinning settings per chunk and by nothing else; stitching context gave 11 drifted chunks anyway, and pinned chunks still need a gold diff because stacking and high sliders fail through averaging.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox below, a model of the API behaviour described in the kernels.
- Composed: ideas:VOICE/consistency/style-is-per-request-not-session-state, ideas:VOICE/performance/known-brittleness-averaging-and-non-parallel-transfer, ideas:VOICE/qa/gold-standard-clip-plus-asr-diff

- Prediction: First-call-only 11 drifted, stitching-only 11, pinned 0, stacked tags valence 0.0 and flagged, slider 0.9 unstable and 0.6 not.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS drifted first_only=11 stitch_only=11 pinned=0; stack valence=0.0 flagged=True; unstable@0.9=True @0.6=False
- Scenarios: 1) first-call-only settings; 2) stitching context without pinned settings; 3) pinned every chunk; 4) stacked contradictory tags in a pinned chunk, built to break the pinning-fixes-all claim; 5) slider 0.9 versus 0.6

## E81 — real git shows title is first paragraph joined body hidden from oneline and blame summary
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [git][tooling][documentation][testing]
- What: Real git 2.43 in a temporary repository, checking which tools show only a commit title (log oneline, format-patch Subject, blame summary), where the body surfaces, and what git counts as the title when the first paragraph spans several lines.
- Why built: The commit-message kernel claims the title is used throughout git and that it should be 50 characters; the blame and gitignore kernels were unapplied and the claims were quoted from docs, never run.
- Design: Subprocess calls to the real git binary with fixed dates and no global config; one commit with a short title and a two-line body, one commit whose first paragraph runs three lines with no blank line, a gitignored build directory; compared log, format-patch, blame porcelain and ls-files output.
- Got right: Oneline showed only the 23-character title and hid the body; the body came back through the body format; format-patch put the title alone in Subject with the body below; blame summary was the title; the ignored build file stayed out of ls-files while the source was tracked.
- Where/why it failed: The 50-character rule is not enforced: the three-line first paragraph was joined by spaces into a 108-character subject for the log format, while blame summary kept only the first physical line, so the two tools disagree on what the title is.
- Fix: Put a blank line directly after one short line, and never rely on wrapped first paragraphs; read the full message, not only the blame summary, before changing a line.
- Why this fix: The blank line is the only thing git itself uses to split title from body, so it is the part worth enforcing rather than the length.
- Rule of thumb: Git defines the title as the first paragraph, not the first line: a wrapped opening paragraph became a 108-character subject in log and format-patch terms but a one-line summary in blame, so enforce the blank line after one short line.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox below against the real git binary, version 2.43.0.
- Composed: ideas:VERSION-CONTROL/git/commit-messages/a-commit-message-is-two-parts-a-50-char-title-and-a-body, ideas:VERSION-CONTROL/git/git-blame/blame-finds-why-a-line-exists-not-who-to-blame-for-it, ideas:VERSION-CONTROL/repo-hygiene/gitignore/gitignore-generated-files-because-committing-them-lies-about-source
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__real-git-shows-title-is-first-paragraph-joined-body-hidden-from-oneline-and-blame-summary.py
- Prediction: Oneline, Subject and blame summary show only the title and the body only via the body format; a three-line first paragraph joins into a subject over 50 characters; blame summary equals the title; the ignored file is not tracked.

## E80 — disjoint world chrome by derived cap beats zorder hit testing reverifies brain 29 dark goblin 8 brain 33

- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][input][state][gamedev][debugging]
- What: Grid model of a full-bleed world with a chrome band over its bottom four rows, testing whether capping the world above the chrome stops misrouted clicks where z-order hit-testing cannot, and what breaks the cap.
- Why built: The kernel on constraining the world so chrome cannot overlap it was only applied once; its claim that the failure presents as a state bug and that a fixed cap is enough was never stress-tested against a resize.
- Design: 20 rows by 10 columns, chrome from row 16, every cell clicked as a world-aimed click; counted clicks routed to chrome, scene steps advanced, and a framework-style hit test that ignores container scale against my own four-comparison containment test.
- Got right: Overlap gave 40 misrouted clicks and 41 scene steps (40 stray plus one timer step); a cap at row 15 gave 0 and 1; the own containment test had no wrong cells while the scale-blind test missed 107.
- Where/why it failed: A hardcoded cap broke when the chrome grew to row 14 (20 misroutes returned); only a cap derived from the chrome top (chrome_top minus one) stayed at 0.
- Fix: Derive the world bound from the chrome geometry at layout time instead of storing a constant, and keep containment tests in your own code.
- Why this fix: The disjointness is then an invariant of one number rather than a coincidence of two independent constants.
- Rule of thumb: Make world and chrome disjoint by computing the world limit from the chrome rect; a literal cap passes until the chrome moves, and the symptom is extra scene advances, not a visible overlap.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox named below; real browsers and pointer-events were not run, only the grid model.

## E79 — cvd naive rgby worst pair and no universal four color palette with fixed text floor and clamp
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [accessibility][color][testing][gamedev]
- What: Machado 2009 colour-vision-deficiency matrices applied in linear RGB with redmean distance, testing the naive red/green/blue/yellow player set, an orange/sky-blue swap, and an exhaustive search of all four-colour subsets of a 24-colour pool for a single palette safe across all three deficiency types; plus the text-floor and camera-clamp numbers from the sibling kernels.
- Why built: The colour kernel says no single four-colour swap is safe across protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia, so presets per type are needed; its figures were from one run of one swap and nobody had searched for a universal palette.
- Design: Matrices at severity 1.0 on linearised sRGB, back to sRGB, worst pair by redmean per type; subsets enumerated exhaustively (10626 palettes), recording the best palette per type and the best worst-case over all three; split-screen text 32px to 16px against the 26px floor; two players 80 units apart with padding 1.2 at 16:9 against a clamp of 10.
- Got right: Naive worst pair was green against yellow under protanopia (30, deuteranopia 78, tritanopia 303 for green against blue); the swap raised protan to 226 and deuteranopia to 181 but dropped tritanopia from 303 to 193; the text halved to 16px, under the 26px floor; framing needed an orthographic size of 27.0 against a clamp of 10.
- Where/why it failed: The strong reading of the kernel failed: a single palette from the pool kept every pair at distance 314 or more under all three types, above every worst case of the naive set; per-type presets beat it only by 52 (protanopia), 10 (deuteranopia) and 95 (tritanopia). My numbers also differ from the kernel's (protan 30, not 58; deuteranopia moved 78 to 181, not flat), which points to a different colour space step or constants, so the exact figures are method-dependent.
- Fix: Pick palettes by exhaustive worst-case search over all three types instead of hand swaps, expect a universal four-colour set to exist, and use per-type presets as a modest extra margin plus shape or number pairing rather than as the only remedy.
- Why this fix: The search shows a hand-chosen swap fails on one type while a searched set meets all three, so the lesson is about how the palette is chosen, not that none exists.
- Rule of thumb: Do not conclude that no one palette suits all colour-vision types from a single hand swap; an exhaustive four-colour search over a 24-colour pool found one with worst-case distance 314 across all three types, so search the palette and keep per-type presets as extra margin only.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox below, with the published matrices typed from memory of the paper and the pool of 24 hues limited to two brightness levels.
