## E78 — tier from review lines not author field sybil origin breaks gate
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [verification][trust][method][sandbox]
- What: Built a stdlib model of the review-line trust flow (tier computed only from dated review lines; intake rejects pre-reviewed records; review whose origin equals the record origin is held). Tier ladder, author-field immunity and self-review hold all reproduced; a sybil origin string defeats the gate.
- Why built: Pass 1 of train auto picked the untested kernel derive-trust-from-review-records-not-author-fields; the question was where it stops holding.
- Design: Pure functions tier(), intake(), apply_review(); six scenarios: author-set tier, pre-reviewed record, self review, full ladder with a modeled audit, sybil origin (built to break it), and a check that the tier rule takes no substrate input.
- Got right: An author-claimed tier is inert because readers compute from review lines; a modeled audit tops out at audited and only a rebuild reaches confirmed, so a green hand-built check (brain/E54, the easy-half suite) cannot promote a record; any single fail yields disputed.
- Where/why it failed: The origin-equality gate compares strings. A record by alice reviewed by origin alice2 passed the gate and reached confirmed. Also nothing in the tier rule records the substrate of a rebuild, so a rebuild copied from the author's own code counts the same as an independent one.
- Fix: Treat origin as an authenticated identity (not free text) and record the rebuild's substrate on the review line, requiring it to differ from the record's before the tier counts it (the vary-the-substrate rule applied to the review itself).
- Why this fix: The kernel moves trust off the author-editable field but still trusts a reviewer-supplied origin string; the sandbox shows the same self-assertion problem reappearing one level down, so the gate must check something the reviewer cannot type.
- Rule of thumb: Deriving trust from review lines removes the author's field but not the reviewer's: an origin-string gate stops accidental self-review only, so bind origin to an identity and require a rebuild to declare a different substrate before it can confirm.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: the sandbox ran and printed RESULT: PASS on all six scenarios, including the sybil break. This models the flow; I did not test the real steward or brain _entry_tier code.
- Composed: ideas:VERIFICATION/trust/derive-trust-from-review-records-not-author-fields, ideas:VERIFICATION/method/vary-the-substrate-not-just-the-scenario, brain/E54

- Prediction: Author field ignored; self-review held; ladder provisional>audited>confirmed>disputed; sybil origin alice2 would defeat the gate (at least one scenario breaks the claim).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS 6 scenarios; ladder holds; sybil origin alice2 reached confirmed; tier rule has no substrate input.
- Scenarios: 1) author-set tier; 2) pre-reviewed record at intake; 3) same-origin review; 4) modeled audit, audit, rebuild, fail ladder; 5) sybil origin alice2 (built to BREAK); 6) substrate absent from tier rule

## E77 — three act proportions on integer scenes rounding and plant payoff capacity
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [storytelling][structure][method]
- What: Placed the three-act plot points (25 percent and 75 percent marks) on an integer scene count N=4..120 with four rounding rules. Every rule keeps each act within 1 scene of its ideal share, but the rules disagree on the act sizes for 87 of 117 values of N; half-even round() is the only rule that keeps Act One equal to Act Three (floor and ceil break it on 87 values, half-up on 29). The rule choice also moves the smallest N that fits 5 distinct Act-One plants from 17 (ceil) to 20 (floor).
- Why built: Pass 1 of loop 2 picked the three-act kernel as untested; it gives percentages but nothing says how they land on whole scenes.
- Design: Pure arithmetic over N and four rounding rules; counted act-size asymmetry, rule disagreement, minimum N for K=3 and K=5 plants needing distinct Act-One scenes (the Chekhov promise), and N where an act (a stage of the three-stage hero arc) gets 0 scenes.
- Got right: The proportions are robust to rounding in magnitude (max deviation 0.5 to 1.0 scene), and the plant capacity constraint is a clean integer bound: Act-One scenes must be at least the number of promises.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that half-even would make Act One differ from Act Three was wrong; it is the one symmetric rule, because 0.25N and 0.75N tie in opposite directions. A "25 percent" rule is not one rule: floor and ceil silently give a short or long Act One. At N=2 and 3 (floor or ceil) an act has 0 scenes, so the three-stage mapping degenerates.
- Fix: State the rounding rule with the percentages (prefer symmetric: half-even, or compute Act Three as the mirror of Act One), and size N from the promise count with N at least 4K plus the rule's rounding slack.
- Why this fix: Mirroring removes the asymmetry by construction, and a stated rule makes the 25/50/25 template reproducible across tools instead of off by a scene.
- Rule of thumb: Percent-based act structure needs a stated integer rounding rule: the five rules tested stay within one scene but disagree on act sizes for most N, and floor or ceil makes Act One shorter or longer than Act Three, so mirror the cut points and check promise capacity against the Act-One size.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand in a deterministic stdlib sandbox that printed RESULT: PASS after one prediction miss (recorded below). It is arithmetic on the template's percentages, not a test of any real story; the hero-arc link only checks that each stage keeps at least 1 scene.
- Composed: ideas:STORYTELLING/structure/three-act-structure-has-named-proportions-and-turning-points, ideas:STORYTELLING/economy/chekhovs-gun-is-a-promise-not-just-foreshadowing, ideas:STORYTELLING/pattern/heros-journey-is-a-three-stage-arc-not-the-popular-12-step-list
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__three-act-proportions-on-integer-scenes-rounding-and-plant-payoff-capacity.py
- Prediction: Every rounding rule stays within 1 scene per act; the rules disagree for some N; half-even round() makes Act One differ from Act Three for some N (this last part came out wrong); minimum N for 5 plants differs by rule.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS max deviation 0.75/0.75/0.5/1.0 (floor/ceil/half-up/half-even); rules disagree on 87 of 117 N; Act One differs from Act Three on 87/87/29/0 N; min N for 5 plants 20/17/18/19; N=2,3 degenerate.
- Scenarios: 1) four rounding rules over N=4..120; 2) rule disagreement count; 3) plant capacity K=3 and K=5 per rule; 4) BREAK: tiny N where an act gets 0 scenes

## E76 — clash seed bias window overturns only below a computable power ratio
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [design][rpg][combat][balance]
- What: Modelled a clash as strength P*(5+m) with the mash count m enumerated over 1..M for both sides. The weaker side can overturn the stronger only while the power ratio is below (5+M)/(5+1): exactly 2.5 for M=10 and 25/6 for M=20; from that ratio up the seeded advantage is fully deterministic. A power-budget cap that clamps the seed ratio at 2.0 gave a 4 percent overturn in the band above 2.5 where the uncapped model gives 0.
- Why built: Pass 5 gap: the clash kernel says never make the power seed deterministic but gives no number for where it becomes so; the sibling power-budget and band-measurement kernels suggested how to test it.
- Design: Exhaustive grid of mash pairs (no RNG) with Fraction arithmetic; ratio sweep 1.0 to 5.0 in steps of 0.25; windows M=10 and M=20; a clamp on the seed at 2.0 as the power-budget cap; aggregate overturn versus per-band overturn compared.
- Got right: The deterministic threshold is a closed-form function of window width, so "leave a skill window" is checkable: the window must be sized against the largest tier ratio. Overturn is monotone in ratio at both widths.
- Where/why it failed: With M=10 and a tier ratio of 2.5 or more, the kernel's own advice is violated (transformations become win-more buttons) even though a window exists. The cap behaved opposite to the damage cap: it blurred tier meaning (a 4x tier clashed like a 2x tier) instead of erasing a niche, and the aggregate overturn moved only from 0.062 to 0.089, hiding that the high band changed from 0 to 0.04.
- Fix: Size the mash window from the largest tier ratio via ratio < (base+M)/(base+1), and report overturn by ratio band, not as one average.
- Why this fix: The threshold is exact in this model, so the window can be derived rather than tuned, and per-band reporting is the only view in which the capped and uncapped models visibly differ.
- Rule of thumb: In a seed-plus-skill clash, the skill window only matters for power ratios under (base+M)/(base+1); size M to the top tier ratio and read overturn per ratio band, since an aggregate stays near-flat while the high band flips between 0 and nonzero.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand in a deterministic stdlib sandbox that printed RESULT: PASS. The multiplicative P*(base+m) clash is my own simple model, not any game's real formula.
- Composed: ideas:RPG/combat/power-tier-clash-check/narrative-consistency, ideas:RPG/power-scaling/power-creep/power-budget, ideas:SYSTEM/testing/damage-cap-can-erase-a-burst-skills-niche-while-diversity-metric-stays-flat/band-level-not-aggregate-measurement
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__clash-seed-bias-window-overturns-only-below-a-computable-power-ratio.py
- Prediction: Overturn is monotone in ratio and exactly 0 from ratio 2.5 at M=10 and 25/6 at M=20; the cap at 2.0 makes the above-2.5 band nonzero while the aggregate changes by less than 0.25.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS thresholds 5/2 and 25/6 confirmed; aggregate overturn 0.062 uncapped versus 0.089 capped; band r>=2.5 is 0.0 uncapped and 0.04 capped.
- Scenarios: 1) M=10 ratio sweep; 2) M=20 ratio sweep (threshold moves); 3) cap at 2.0 on the seed ratio, compared per band and in aggregate (BREAK: the cap was expected to behave like the damage cap and did not)

## E75 — antagonist memory habit counter decay storylet count and skip order
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [narrative][design][antagonist][ai]
- What: A most-frequent-habit antagonist memory caught a fixed-habit player in 100 percent of rounds 5 to 60 against 25 percent for a scripted round-robin over 4 spots, but a no-decay memory kept checking the abandoned spot for 31 rounds after the player switched, while a 0.5 decay followed in 1 round. Storing the memory as state needs 18 storylets for 6 encounters of 3 outcomes where a branch graph has 729 leaves, and a callout saying "as last time" dangled in 11 of 16 skip patterns of 4 encounters.
- Why built: Pass 5 of loop 2 picked the antagonist-memory kernel as an unapplied gap; its siblings on quality-based storylets and skippable dialogue say how the remembered state should be stored and voiced.
- Design: Deterministic player policies (fixed habit, bait-and-switch), two antagonists (scripted rotation, count memory with a decay factor), E=6 outcome counting, and an enumeration of all 16 skip patterns for the history-referencing line versus a line read from the stored state.
- Got right: Memory beats a script by 4x against a habitual player, which is the kernel's claim; the state-based storage decouples content from permutations, and a callout derived from state cannot refer to an unseen scene.
- Where/why it failed: Pure counting memory is exploitable: after a habit switch it spends 31 rounds guarding a spot that is now safe, which is the opposite of "adapts to this player". The skip-order check for state-derived callouts holds by construction in this model (the stored record is always updated), and the storylet count is arithmetic, so those two scenarios only show the cost side, not an observed behavior.
- Fix: Give the antagonist memory a decay (0.5 per round recovered in 1 round), and write callouts from the stored quality value (scarred, afraid of fire) rather than from a prior line.
- Why this fix: Decay trades a little habit exploitation for a fast recovery from deliberate bait, and state-derived lines stay valid under any viewing order.
- Rule of thumb: An antagonist that adapts to the player's habits needs forgetting: a count-only memory beat a script 1.00 to 0.25 yet lagged 31 rounds behind a deliberate habit switch, so decay the counts and voice the memory from stored state, not from the previous scene.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand in a deterministic stdlib sandbox that printed RESULT: PASS. The antagonist and player are my own toy policies, not Nemesis System or Alien Isolation behavior; two of the four scenarios are arithmetic or by construction, as said above.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS memory 1.00 vs script 0.25; no-decay 31 rounds after the switch vs 1 with decay 0.5; 729 vs 18; 11/16 skip patterns dangle.

## E72 — small sample replication power with winners curse
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [statistics][replication][power]
- What: Recomputed the Tversky-Kahneman 1971 question (z=2.23 at n=20, chance a follow-up of n=10 is significant one-tailed) and showed the .48 answer is an upper bound that falls to about .20-.29 once the original effect is shrunk for winner's curse or the typical halving seen in large replication projects.
- Why built: The kernel says researchers guess .85 versus a correct .48; I wanted to see how fragile the .48 itself is, since it silently assumes the observed effect is the true effect.
- Design: Pure-stdlib normal-power function; scenarios treat the true effect as the observed one, as half of it, as a posterior on a deterministic grid under a skeptical prior, as a near-flat prior, and vary follow-up n.
- Got right: The point-estimate scenario reproduced 0.473, matching the kernel's .48, and the flat-prior posterior converged to 0.477 as it should.
- Where/why it failed: The .48 is not a neutral answer: conditioning on having cleared p<.05 with a small n selects inflated effects, so the honest replication probability is lower, 0.29 under a skeptical prior and 0.20 at half the effect.
- Fix: Quote replication probability as a range tied to an explicit effect-shrinkage assumption, and plan follow-ups on the shrunk effect (n=80 gives 0.998 at the raw effect but far less after shrinkage).
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows the answer moves by a factor of two on a single assumption, so naming the assumption is cheaper and more honest than a single number.
- Rule of thumb: When estimating whether a small significant result will replicate, report power at the observed effect only as a ceiling; shrink the effect first (winner's curse, about half per replication projects) and size the follow-up on that.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the .85 median and the OSC half-effect figure are taken from the kernels, not re-measured.

## E71 — pkce s256 protects only high entropy verifiers and hides compare leak
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [security][oauth][hashing]
- What: A deterministic model of the PKCE authorization-code exchange showed S256 defeats code interception only because the verifier is high entropy: a 5-digit verifier is recovered from the public challenge in 48,214 guesses, plain is redeemed straight from the observed request, and a leaky early-exit compare is harmless behind S256 but exploitable on plain.
- Why built: The PKCE kernel says S256 is mandatory when the client can do it and gives a 43-128 character length from memory; the password-hash kernel says a fast SHA-256 fails on low entropy, which should apply to the challenge too.
- Design: A small authorization server with authorize and token calls, a fixed-seed 32-byte verifier, an attacker that sees the code and the public challenge, a dictionary attacker, and a hill-climbing attacker using an oracle that reports the matched prefix length.
- Got right: The 32-byte verifier encodes to exactly 43 base64url characters (confirming the length that was stated from memory), the code alone and a wrong verifier both fail, the legitimate redemption works, and the 100,000-word dictionary missed the full-length verifier.
- Where/why it failed: Nothing broke the high-entropy case, but the low-entropy case did: the SHA-256 challenge is a fast hash, so a short numeric verifier falls offline. Plain has no protection at all once the request is observed, and a prefix-match leak recovered a 43-character plain verifier in 1,523 guesses (bound 43 times 64) while the same leak on the S256 digest gave 0 characters of progress.
- Fix: Generate the verifier from a CSPRNG at the full 32 bytes, always use S256, never derive the verifier from anything guessable, and still compare in constant time; do not rely on S256 to rescue a short verifier.
- Why this fix: The sandbox separates two properties: the hash hides prefix leaks in the compare, but only entropy stops offline guessing, so neither substitutes for the other.
- Rule of thumb: PKCE S256 secures the exchange only if the verifier carries its own entropy (a 5-digit one fell in 48,214 guesses) and plain gives none once the request is seen; treat the 43-character minimum as an entropy floor, not a format rule.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the RFC text is taken from the kernel, and the server and attacker are hand-written models, not a real authorization server.
- Composed: ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/oauth/pkce-is-no-longer-just-for-mobile-apps-it-is-recommended-for-confidential-clients-too, ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/password-storage/fast-hashes-are-disqualified-by-being-fast-and-the-slow-ones-ship-with-specific-numbers, ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/score-integrity/sign-the-payload-and-compare-in-constant-time
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__pkce-s256-protects-only-high-entropy-verifiers-and-hides-compare-leak.py
- Prediction: 43-character verifier from 32 bytes; code-only and wrong-verifier fail; plain redeemed from the observed request; a 5-digit S256 verifier recovered in at most 100000 guesses; plain leak climb within 43 times 64 guesses while the S256 digest leak gives at most 2 characters of progress.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS len=43 plain_redeemed=True low_entropy_guesses=48214 plain_leak_climb=1523 s256_leak_progress=0
- Scenarios: 1) legitimate S256 flow; 2) code interception without verifier and with a wrong one; 3) method plain with observed challenge; 4) dictionary attack on a full-length S256 verifier; 5) 5-digit numeric verifier (built to BREAK the S256 claim); 6) prefix-leak hill climb on plain versus on the S256 digest

## E70 — lod hysteresis band vs boundary jitter and tri cost
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [3d][performance][hysteresis]
- What: Modeled the three.js LOD hysteresis rule (the current level's switch threshold is lowered by a fraction of its distance) against a camera jittering around a LOD boundary, and found it is a one-sided band that only works when the jitter is smaller than the band.
- Why built: The LOD kernel names hysteresis and cross-fade as the standard cure for popping, and the NPC thrashing kernel prescribes a real margin before switching; I wanted to see how wide the margin must be and what it costs.
- Design: Three levels at 0, 50 and 100 units with 10000, 2500 and 600 triangles; a switch function copying the three.js rule; sinusoidal jitter at amplitude 2 and 6 around 50, a monotonic approach and a monotonic recede, and a counted cross-fade cost.
- Got right: Hysteresis 0.05 (a 2.5 unit band) removed all flicker for amplitude 2, hysteresis 0.20 (10 units) removed it for amplitude 6, and the approach case traded 25 frames of late detail for 187,500 fewer triangles.
- Where/why it failed: My first prediction was wrong: a sine crosses the boundary twice per cycle so there were 8 switches not 100, and I had the delay direction backwards. Amplitude 6 against a 2.5 band gave the same 8 switches as no hysteresis, and recede was unprotected (identical switch frame).
- Fix: Size the hysteresis fraction from the expected camera jitter amplitude, not a default, and treat it as one-sided: it delays the move toward more detail on approach only, so receding jitter still needs its own margin or a cross-fade.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows the band edge is the only thing that matters (2.5 units absorbs 2 but not 6) and that the shifted threshold belongs to the current level, so the protection is asymmetric by construction.
- Rule of thumb: A hysteresis band suppresses LOD flicker only for jitter smaller than the band (tested amplitude 2 and 6 against bands of 2.5 and 10) and protects one direction; widen it to the jitter or cross-fade, and expect late detail on approach as the price.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox twice (run 1 failed my own prediction, recorded in the script header); the three.js rule is reproduced from the kernel text, and a synthetic triangle count stands in for VRAM, not a real renderer.
- Composed: ideas:3D-MODELING/lod/lod-switches-by-distance-or-screen-size-and-pops-at-the-boundary, ideas:NPC-SIM/decision-making/thrashing-oscillation-hysteresis-fixes, brainwork/E26
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__lod-hysteresis-band-vs-boundary-jitter-and-tri-cost.py
- Prediction: Run 2 (after run 1 failed): 8 switches at amplitude 2 without hysteresis, at most 1 with 0.05; still 8 at amplitude 6 with 0.05, at most 1 with 0.20; approach delayed about 25 frames; recede switch frame identical.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS switches amp2 h0=8 h.05=0; amp6 h.05=8 h.20=0; recede tris h0=2500000 h.05=2500000 (approach delay 25 frames, 2492500 vs 2305000 triangles)
- Scenarios: 1) amplitude 2, no hysteresis; 2) amplitude 2, 0.05; 3) amplitude 6, 0.05 (built to BREAK the band); 4) amplitude 6, 0.20; 5) monotonic approach; 6) monotonic recede; 7) cross-fade cost counted

## E69 — ad rotation vs budget with throttled organic and norm copy
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [marketing][advertising][model]
- What: A toy deterministic campaign model combining three social-marketing kernels showed that doubling paid impressions on one fatiguing creative adds almost nothing (1.003x clicks) while rotating six creatives at the base budget gives 3.75x, that descriptive-norm copy multiplies conversions by the kernel's 1.256x on top, and that the fatigue advice flips if fatigue is weak.
- Why built: The creative-fatigue kernel says the fix is rotation not budget, the throttling kernel says organic cannot carry distribution, and the social-proof kernel gives measured uplifts; none had been run together to see which lever dominates.
- Design: 10,000 people over 12 weeks at 3 impressions per person per week; each exposure to the same creative converts at a base rate times a per-exposure decay; rotation splits exposures over k creatives; organic delivery decays 20% per week; the norm uplift uses the kernel's 44.1 over 35.1 and 49.3 over 42.8 ratios.
- Got right: At decay 0.85 per exposure, double budget on one creative gave 1.003x and six-creative rotation 3.75x; the norm multiplier came out 1.256x (1.152x for the nearer-reference pair); organic delivery fell to 0.21 of week one by week 8.
- Where/why it failed: My first run missed one prediction by arithmetic (0.8 to the seventh is 0.2097, not under 0.20), corrected and recorded in the script header. The decisive caveat is the BREAK: at decay 0.99 doubling the budget on one creative beat rotation at base budget by 1.47x, so the rotate-not-spend advice depends on how fast the creative actually fatigues.
- Fix: Estimate the per-exposure decay for the real creative first (flat early frequency curve means spend, steep means rotate), rotate at least as many creatives as the target frequency, and treat organic as a supplement that needs paid cover as it decays.
- Why this fix: The model ranks the levers by one parameter, the decay, so measuring it decides between more budget and more creatives instead of applying either by habit.
- Rule of thumb: Rotation beats extra budget only when same-creative fatigue is steep (tested decay 0.85 versus 0.99 with six creatives); measure the decay before choosing, then layer norm-style copy for a roughly 1.26x conversion multiplier, and cover decaying organic with paid.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox twice (run 1 recorded in the header); the decay values, 20% weekly organic decay, base click and conversion rates are my assumed parameters, only the uplift ratios come from the kernel, so the model shows ordering and conditions, not real magnitudes.
- Composed: ideas:SOCIAL-MARKETING/advertising/creative-fatigue, ideas:SOCIAL-MARKETING/organic-reach/platform-throttling, ideas:SOCIAL-MARKETING/persuasion/social-proof

- Observed: RESULT: PASS double-budget single x1.00; rotation x3.75; no-fatigue double/rot 1.47; norm x1.256; organic wk8 0.21

## E68 — compass tell sub increment error visibility is error over increment
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][feedback][sandbox][verification]
- What: Sandbox of a compass-glitch tell on an 8-point display, testing the kernel that an error below one display increment is invisible and that releases must be gated on the player being at rest.
- Why built: To find where the "sub-increment tell is invisible" claim stops holding, rather than accept it as a hard threshold.
- Design: Deterministic python model. 8-label compass, increment 2pi/8. S1 sweeps 8000 headings per error size and counts display-label changes. S2 runs a 100-tick timeline, 60 ticks of look-around then 40 at rest, comparing gated and ungated release. S3 multiplies nominal rate by rest share and visible fraction. S4 (built to break) applies slow sub-increment drift per step.
- Got right: The masking half holds exactly: ungated releases are perceived as a tell 40% of the time (only the rest share), gated releases 100%. Quantisation matters because the display, not the model, is what the player sees.
- Where/why it failed: "Below one increment is invisible" is wrong as a threshold. A 0.5-increment error flips the label for 50% of headings (visible fraction is about err/increment), and 0.99 increments flips 99%. A slow drift of 0.05 increments per step flips the display within 5 ticks.
- Fix: Treat the increment as the guaranteed-visible floor (1.0 increment is always seen), not the invisibility ceiling. Cap tells with the visible fraction err/increment, and count accumulated drift, not per-event size.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows visibility is continuous in err/increment and depends on heading relative to a bin edge, so only multiples of the full increment give a deterministic result.
- Rule of thumb: Rate a tell by observed rate = nominal rate x rest-gate share x (err/increment, capped at 1); a sub-increment error is intermittently visible at a heading-dependent chance, and slow drift will cross a label boundary eventually.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the 8-label compass and tick timeline are modelled, no real player or timing data was measured.
- Composed: ideas:gamedev/feedback/rate-a-tell-in-the-units-its-display-quantises-to, ideas:gamedev/feedback/rate-a-perceptual-tell-by-its-observed-rate
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__compass-tell-sub-increment-error-visibility-is-error-over-increment.py
- Prediction: Sub-increment errors would NOT be always invisible; visible fraction at 0.5 increment would be about 0.50 and at 0.1 about 0.10.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS sub-increment visible_fraction~err/INC (0.5->0.500), gating lifts perceived 0.40->1.00, observed rate 0.05->0.010, slow drift flips display at tick 5
- Scenarios: 1) error sweep 0.1 to 1.5 increments over all headings; 2) gated vs ungated release against look-around motion; 3) observed-rate product; 4) BREAK: slow sub-increment drift accumulating to a label flip
- Link: brain train auto session 2026-10-10; session_01GAVruHUPWaSKqD2KpxhoYC

## E67 — rewind cap vs send queue delay
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [networking][lag-compensation][websocket][webrtc][simulation][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of a lag-compensation rewind cap against transport-added latency: a backed-up WebSocket send queue (bufferedAmount growth) or a reliable-ordered datachannel stall inflates the latency the client claims, and the server rewinds the target by that claim.
- Why built: The kernel on rewind caps says capping bounds shot-behind-cover; two sibling transport kernels say send queues and reliable channels add silent delay. Wanted to see whether the cap actually neutralises transport-inflated claims and at what cost.
- Design: Target runs at 0.2 u/ms and enters cover at x=20 (t=100ms). Server hit test rewinds to T-min(claimed, cap). Claimed latency = 40ms base plus a modelled queue delay (sender 2x drain for N ticks) or a 200ms reliable-channel stall. Caps swept 200/100/60/50/20, plus an honest 80ms and 180ms shooter.
- Got right: Uncapped rewind hits a target already in cover for both queue-inflated (360ms claim) and stalled (240ms claim) shots; unreliable delivery keeps the claim at 40ms and misses correctly. Cap 50 blocked both inflated shots.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that a 100ms cap blocks was wrong: target was only 50ms into cover, so a 100ms rewind still lands exposed. The cap only helps when it is below the time the target has spent in cover, and that same 50ms cap also denies an honest 80ms shooter (saw it exposed) and a 180ms shooter at cap 100.
- Fix: Treat the cap as a fairness-vs-ping dial tuned to typical cover-entry times, and also stop transport delay inflating claims at the source: poll bufferedAmount and coalesce, use unordered no-retransmit channels for per-tick state, and derive latency from server-measured round trips rather than trusting the client.
- Why this fix: The cap bounds damage but cannot tell honest high ping from queue-inflated ping; removing the inflation upstream keeps the cap small without punishing honest players.
- Rule of thumb: A rewind cap only blocks shots-behind-cover when it is shorter than the target's time in cover (50ms cap blocked, 100ms leaked in this model), and it costs honest high-ping shooters their hits, so keep transport queues from inflating claimed latency instead of leaning on the cap alone.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the deterministic stdlib sandbox in this session (RESULT PASS, numbers above). Real engine tick rates and real browser buffering behaviour were not measured; the queue and stall delays are modelled.
- Composed: ideas:NETWORKING/lag-compensation/server-rewind-must-cap-the-max-latency-it-trusts, ideas:NETWORKING/websocket/send-does-not-apply-backpressure-and-a-full-buffer-closes-the-socket, ideas:NETWORKING/webrtc/a-datachannel-is-reliable-and-ordered-by-default-which-is-wrong-for-position-updates, brainwork/E61
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__rewind-cap-vs-send-queue-delay.py
- Prediction: Before the first run I expected a 100ms cap to block both the queue-inflated and the stalled shot while uncapped hits both.
- Observed: First run FAIL (cap 100 still hit); after sweeping caps, RESULT: PASS cap blocks transport-inflated shots only when cap < time-in-cover (50ms ok, 100ms leaks); same cap also denies a legit 80ms shooter. Queue 320ms, stall 200ms.
- Scenarios: 1) cap sweep with 40ms base latency; 2) websocket queue growth 0/5/20 ticks; 3) reliable vs unreliable channel stall; 4) BREAK: honest 80ms and 180ms shooters under the cap that blocks.

## E66 — npc schedule intersections symmetric exchange gate
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [npc][social][simulation][gamedev][state][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox of an NPC social layer built from three kernels: schedule intersections trigger exchanges, one symmetric exchange engine serves player and NPC alike, and pair scores are a sparse decaying scalar allocated only on co-location. It also tests whether a social pull can override a mandatory shift when added outside versus inside the shift gate.
- Why built: The schedule-intersection kernel requires routines to be interruptible, while the gate-versus-bonus entry says an additive term outside a veto turns it into a discount. Wanted to know where those two collide and whether the sparse store and shared engine hold up.
- Design: 12 NPCs plus a player index, 4 locations, a 24-hour day with a mandatory shift at hours 9-16 at each NPC's home location and wandering otherwise. Pair keys are created only when two NPCs share a location in an hour; the score decays 0.9 on touch. One engine function scores any pair from traits; a bolted-on NPC-only variant with a different constant is the contrast. A pull sweep 0.0-1.5 against a work score of 1.0 compares the bonus inside the gate with the bonus outside.
- Got right: The sparse store allocated 12 of 66 possible pairs (18%) over the day. The shared engine gave identical results for a player and an NPC with equal traits, while the bolted variant diverged (not equal). Gate-inside abandoned 0 shift-hours at every pull.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that an outside-the-gate bonus leaks at any pull above zero was wrong: nothing leaked up to a pull of 1.0, equal to the work score, and 96 shift-hours were abandoned at 1.1 and 1.5. The bonus is harmless below the gated option's base and only becomes a veto-breaker above it. The leak itself is built into the model by construction, so the measured part is the threshold and not the existence.
- Fix: When a social event can interrupt a mandatory routine, put the pull inside the same gate that zeroes the option, or cap it below the mandatory base, rather than relying on typical pull values staying small. Keep one exchange engine for every pair and allocate pair state only on co-location.
- Why this fix: The sweep shows the break depends on the bonus-to-base ratio and not on the bonus existing, so a safe-today tuning silently breaks when someone raises a pull value; structure (inside the gate) is robust where tuning is not.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the sparse pair store cost 18% of all-pairs and a shared exchange engine stayed symmetric, but an interrupt bonus outside the mandatory gate abandoned shifts only once it exceeded the gated base (1.1 versus 1.0), so scope that claim to the tested range of 0-1.5 and still put the bonus inside the gate.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the deterministic stdlib sandbox in this session (RESULT PASS, numbers above). The gate leak is built into the model, so only its threshold was measured. The source kernels' external references to RimWorld and Comme il Faut were not re-checked here.
- Composed: ideas:NPC-SIM/social/schedule-intersections-trigger-social-events-plus-decaying-pairwise-scores, ideas:NPC-SIM/social/symmetric-social-exchange-object-same-engine-for-player-and-npc, august-10/E6
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__npc-schedule-intersections-symmetric-exchange-gate.py
- Prediction: Sparse store under 40% of all pairs; shared engine symmetric and bolted variant not; outside-gate bonus leaks at any pull above zero (this last part was wrong).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS sparse 18% of pairs; shared engine symmetric, bolted not; outside-gate bonus leaks only from pull>1.0 (base 1.0), inside-gate never. 12 of 66 pairs; 96 abandoned shift-hours at pull 1.1.
- Scenarios: 1) sparse versus all-pairs allocation over a day; 2) shared engine versus bolted NPC-only variant with player traits matching an NPC; 3) BREAK: pull sweep 0.0 to 1.5 with the bonus inside versus outside the gate.

## E65 — lsystem bbox vs segments viewport waterfill
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [procgen][lsystem][rendering][density-budgeting][sandbox]
- What: Re-ran the classic plant rule F -> F[+F]F[-F]F at 25.7 degrees for iterations 1-6, measuring segments, bounding-box area, a 64x64 viewport-fit raster and its connected components, then spent a fixed segment budget across six zones with a reserve-then-waterfill pass over iteration levels 2-5.
- Why built: The bounding-box kernel says more iterations is sparser not denser, a sibling says generated structure needs a connectivity check, and another says per-zone bounds should be reserved before the shared budget is filled. Wanted to see whether all three describe one pipeline.
- Design: Turtle interpreter with no RNG. Per iteration: segment count, bbox area, and the plant scaled into a 64x64 grid with oversampled line stamping; connected components by 8-neighbour flood fill. Budget run: zone weights 3,1,2,5,1,4, every zone reserved at level 2, remaining budget given one level at a time to the highest weight per current level while it fits.
- Got right: Segments grew exactly 5.00x per iteration from iteration 2 and bbox area 9.00x from iteration 4, with area 2.6 at iteration 1 and 177989.8 at iteration 6, matching the kernel's numbers. Fitted to a fixed viewport, lit cells rose only 109, 179, 259, 284, 314, 325 while segments went 5 to 15625, so segments per lit cell climbed from 0.05 to 48. The raster was one component at every iteration, so no fixup was needed for the plant itself. The waterfill kept every zone at levels 3-4 and spent 1250 of 1375 where independent max-iteration would spend 18750.
- Where/why it failed: Two predictions were off. I expected lit cells to stop rising by iteration 5; they still rose 11% at iteration 5 and 3.5% at iteration 6, so saturation is approaching and not reached. The waterfill left 9% of the budget unspent because one iteration level multiplies cost 5x, so budget increments are too coarse for proportional filling. My first try used a different plant rule and showed density rising to 742 lit cells with area growth falling to 4.2x, which is why the claim is rule-specific.
- Fix: For a viewport-bound plant, cap iteration at 3-4 and treat overdraw (segments per lit cell) as the budget signal, not segment count alone; use waterfill over iteration levels but expect leftover budget from the 5x step, and fill the leftover with a cheap parameter such as zone count or angle variation. Keep the flood-fill check for generators that are not construction-connected.
- Why this fix: The measured overdraw of 2.2 at iteration 4 versus 48 at iteration 6 shows the extra iterations buy almost no new pixels, while the coarse cost steps explain why the allocation cannot spend the last 125 segments.
- Rule of thumb: For this bracketed plant rule the footprint grows 9x per iteration against 5x segments and a fixed viewport sees only +3.5% lit cells from iteration 5 to 6, so budget by overdraw and cap iteration at 3-4; a different rule changed the growth ratios in my first attempt, so re-measure before reusing the numbers.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the deterministic stdlib sandbox in this session (RESULT PASS, numbers above). A different L-system rule and real renderer behaviour were only partly tested: one alternative rule in a discarded first run, no real renderer.
- Composed: ideas:PROCGEN/lsystem/bounding-box-outpaces-segment-count/more-iterations-means-sparser-not-denser, ideas:PROCGEN/cellular-automata/needs-a-postprocess-connectivity-fixup/flood-fill-then-reject-or-repair, ideas:PROCGEN/density-budgeting/reserve-then-waterfill-allocation/local-mins-clamp-global-target
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__lsystem-bbox-vs-segments-viewport-waterfill.py
- Prediction: Segments 5.00x and area at least 6x per iteration at iterations 4-6; lit cells stop rising by iteration 5 (wrong); one connected component at every iteration; waterfill within budget and in range where independent max-iteration breaks the budget.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS lit cells [109, 179, 259, 284, 314, 325] (viewport-fit lit cells +3.5% at iter 6 while segments x5), 1 component at every iteration=True, waterfill spent 1250<=1375 vs naive 18750. Area 2.6 to 177989.8.
- Scenarios: 1) growth ratios for iterations 1-6 on the kernel's rule; 2) viewport raster density and overdraw; 3) BREAK: flood-fill connectivity at every iteration, expected to need no fix; 4) six-zone waterfill against independent max-iteration, where the 5x cost step leaves budget unspent.

## E64 — a11y linter blind to keyboard trap aa contrast
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [accessibility][keyboard][testing][web][simulation][sandbox]
- What: Sandbox pairing a small static accessibility linter (missing alt, unlabelled inputs, empty buttons and links, text contrast under 4.5) with a keyboard-focus simulation (Tab order, Escape or a close control to leave a dialog) over four HTML fixtures, plus a contrast check of common grey and blue palettes against the AA and AAA ratios.
- Why built: One kernel says custom widgets must let focus leave, another says most sites fail even the automated layer, and a third says AA is the baseline and AAA is not a whole-site target. Wanted to see how much each layer catches by itself.
- Design: Python html.parser fixtures. A: clean form. B: a dialog with no Escape handler and no close control, otherwise labelled. C: five mechanical defects. D: positive tabindex values that reorder focus away from DOM order. Contrast uses the WCAG relative-luminance formula. The trap and reorder checks work on attributes I wrote into the fixtures, so the model encodes what a trap is, and does not discover one in a real browser.
- Got right: The linter returned 0 errors for the trapped dialog B and for the reordered page D, and 5 errors for C. The simulation flagged B as trapped and D as reordered. Contrast #767676 on white is 4.54 (AA pass, AAA fail) and #595959 is 7.00; #1a73e8 on white is 4.51; #6c757d on #f8f9fa is 4.45, a plausible-looking pair that fails AA.
- Where/why it failed: My model cannot say whether a real widget traps focus, because the trap is declared in the fixture; it only shows that a linter keyed on static markup has no input that would reveal it. Pages that pass the linter can still fail the focus criteria, and two palettes sit within 0.1 of the AA line, so rounding or an off-white background decides pass or fail.
- Fix: Run the mechanical linter first for the cheap layer, then add a manual or scripted Tab, Shift+Tab, Escape walk for every dialog and widget, and compute contrast for the exact foreground-background pair with the real formula. Aim for AA everywhere and adopt single AAA criteria selectively.
- Why this fix: The two layers fail on disjoint fixtures (C only to the linter, B and D only to the focus walk), so neither substitutes for the other, and the close-to-threshold palettes show why ratios should be computed, not eyeballed.
- Rule of thumb: In these four fixtures the automated layer found 5 defects on the page that had mechanical errors and 0 on the trapped dialog and the reordered page, so a clean lint run says nothing about focus; walk Tab and Escape on every custom component and compute contrast per pair, with the caveat that this is a hand-written model of the criteria.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the deterministic stdlib sandbox run in this session (RESULT PASS, numbers above). The WCAG wording and the WebAIM prevalence statistics from the source kernels were not re-checked, and no real browser or real linter was run.

- Polarity: compatible

- Observed: RESULT: PASS linter blind to trap (B lint=0 trapped=True) and to positive-tabindex reorder (D lint=0); C trips 5 errors; #767676 is AA 4.54 but not AAA. Also #6c757d on #f8f9fa 4.45 fails AA.

## E63 — two pass rhyme letters own lexicon closure
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [lyrical-composition][rhyme-tooling][algorithm][testing][sandbox]
- What: A sandbox with its own 15-word phoneme lexicon compared a single-pass rhyme-letter assigner against the two-pass one (uppercase for perfect rhymes first, lowercase for assonance after) on six stanzas, then measured closure distance on the two-pass output.
- Why built: Train pass on a kernel that other entries only quoted in prose; it needed a first-hand build with a fixture that shares nothing with the earlier sandbox.
- Design: Perfect means same vowel and coda, assonance means same vowel only, same word is repetition and never a rhyme; stanzas were AABB, ABAB-like and assonance-heavy cases plus an all-assonance stanza built to break the claim; I scored false rhyme claims as same-letter pairs that are not perfect rhymes, counting only uppercase letters for the two-pass output.
- Got right: Single-pass gave 19 false rhyme claims over six stanzas (night, mine, light, line became AAAA); two-pass uppercase gave 0, kept assonance as lowercase (aAaA), and closure distance was 1 for AABB and 3 for ABBA.
- Where/why it failed: My first metric compared case-blind scheme shapes against my intended schemes and failed: it wrongly called two-pass wrong on 3 of 6 stanzas because it ignores the case channel that carries the resolved versus open distinction; and an all-assonance stanza yields all lowercase (aaab), so two-pass reports no resolved rhyme at all.
- Fix: Judge a two-pass assigner on its uppercase pairs against perfect rhymes and read lowercase as open, never compare it with a case-blind scheme string, and treat an all-lowercase result as no resolved rhyme rather than as a failed run.
- Why this fix: The false-claim count separated the two assigners cleanly (19 versus 0) while the case-blind shape check misfired on the correct output, showing the metric, not the assigner, was wrong.
- Rule of thumb: A rhyme-letter tool's value is in the case it carries, so score it on uppercase-only pairs versus perfect rhymes (19 false claims single-pass versus 0 two-pass here) and never with a case-blind scheme comparison, which misjudged 3 of 6 correct two-pass stanzas.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the lexicon is a hand-made 15-word toy, not real phonetic transcription, so only the assignment logic is tested; the first-run metric failed and was replaced, both reported.
- Composed: ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-tooling/two-pass-letter-assignment, ideas:SONGWRITING/rhyme-scheme-shape-sets-a-songs-emotional-motion, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E7, sandbox-lyrical-composition/E8
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__two-pass-rhyme-letters-own-lexicon-closure.py
- Prediction: Written before the first run: single-pass mislabels at least 3 of 6 stanzas versus intended schemes, two-pass mislabels 0 on perfect-driven stanzas, an all-assonance stanza gives all lowercase, closure distance is 1 for AABB and 3 for ABBA. First run: FAIL, because the case-blind mislabel metric counted 3 of 6 two-pass stanzas wrong; the metric was then changed to uppercase-only false claims.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS false rhyme claims single-pass 19 vs two-pass uppercase 0 over 6 stanzas; case-blind scheme check misfires (3/6 two-pass); closure AABB 1 ABBA 3; assonance-only all-lowercase True
- Scenarios: 1) AABB perfect stanza; 2) ABAB with an assonance link across pairs; 3) three assonance-heavy stanzas; 4) all-assonance stanza (built to BREAK: no uppercase, all lowercase); 5) closure distance AABB versus ABBA
- Link: scheduled brain train session; session_012JxzWUk56eKHuHi3fNYxn2
- Audited: 2026-10-15 · fail · I read E63 and reran its stored sandbox sandboxes/2026-10-10__two-pass-rhyme-letters-own-lexicon-closure.py (same RESULT: PASS, 19 vs 0 false claims, case-blind misfire 3/6, closure AABB 1 ABBA 3). Then I probed it with throwaway scripts that import its functions unchanged. (1) The headline 19 vs 0 is built in. The fixture's perfect rhyme is tuple equality, so it is an equivalence relation (0 transitivity violations over all word triples), and the two-pass assigner groups by that same relation, so 0 false claims follows from the code. Single-pass has no case channel, so every assonance link counts as a false claim by definition. The metric does catch a broken implementation (a mutant that uppercases assonance scored 19), so it is a spec-conformance check, not a test of whether case carries value. Near rhymes, which are not transitive, never appear in the fixture. (2) The rule's second number, case-blind comparison misjudging 3 of 6 correct stanzas, comes from two choices in the fixture, not from case-blind comparison itself. Its truth strings give assonant words unrelated letters (ABCB for time/night/mine/light). Its assigner also reuses index 0 for both A and a, so lowercasing merges a resolved pair with an open group (aAaA becomes AAAA). With disjoint letters (uppercase A, then lowercase b) and a truth that also marks assonance links, a case-blind check misjudged 0 of 6. Against E63's own truth it still misjudged 3 of 6. (3) Closure distance (1 for AABB, 3 for ABBA) depends only on line positions: single-pass gives the same 3 on the ABBA stanza, so it does not test the two-pass claim. Overall, the sandbox checks that the code matches its own spec on a 15-word toy lexicon. It does not show the Rule of thumb's claims that the tool's value lies in the case channel or that case-blind scoring misjudges correct output. A rebuild should use a non-transitive near-rhyme judge and letter allocation that keeps the two cases from sharing letters. · https://claude.ai/code/session_01E8b6CeJT8Lb9myTqhRx1qr creative-arts round 2 loop 5 pass 3

## E62 — humor shade offset correction
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [humor][measurement][bias][simulation][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic sandbox of 400 people with four humor-style scores, where two styles are flattered and two denied in self-report, tested a third fix: subtracting the known population shade offset per style.
- Why built: Train kernel pass: the HUMOR-STYLES kernel says every correction to shaded self-report trades one error for another; offset subtraction was not among the fixes already tested.
- Design: Halton low-discrepancy people (no RNG), general factor 0.5 or 0.8, shade +0.8/-0.8 per style scaled by a per-person susceptibility (spread 0 or 0.6), then subtract the mean offset; metrics are top-style misclassification, Spearman rank per style, and the style0-style2 correlation.
- Got right: With uniform shading the offset fix is exact: misclassification 0.485 to 0.000 with rank 1.0 and the correlation structure preserved.
- Where/why it failed: When susceptibility varies by person (spread 0.6) the fixed offset is the wrong size for most people: misclassification only falls 0.453 to 0.315, rank stays 0.814, and the style0-style2 correlation collapses from 0.479 true to 0.002 reported; at general factor 0.8 it is 0.939 true vs 0.438.
- Fix: Treat offset subtraction as valid only if shading is uniform; otherwise estimate per-person susceptibility (other-report anchor) before subtracting, and always report all three metrics together.
- Why this fix: The residual error is person-level, so a population constant cannot remove it; the sandbox shows the constant removes exactly the uniform part and nothing else.
- Rule of thumb: A population-constant offset correction of shaded self-report is exact only for uniform shading and leaves most error and a broken correlation structure when susceptibility varies, so measure variance of the shade before trusting it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; population shade values and Halton people are synthetic, not real survey data.
- Composed: ideas:HUMOR-STYLES/measurement/correcting-shaded-self-report-trades-one-error-for-another, sandbox-humor-self-report-bias/E1, sandbox-self-directed-humor-dose-response/E1
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__humor-shade-offset-correction.py
- Prediction: Offset fix drops misclassification to ~0 under uniform shade but leaves over 0.05 residual with varying susceptibility.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS offset fix exact when shade uniform (mis 0.000) but leaves 0.315 vs raw 0.453 when susceptibility varies; corr02 0.479 true vs 0.002 reported.
- Scenarios: 1) uniform shade, raw vs fixed; 2) variable susceptibility spread 0.6, raw vs fixed (built to BREAK the fix); 3) variable shade with general factor 0.8

## E61 — datachannel reliable hol stall vs unreliable rewind cap
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [networking][webrtc][lag-compensation][simulation][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic model (not a real browser) of 60 Hz position updates over a 40 ms link compared a reliable ordered channel with an unordered zero-retransmit one under one loss in seven packets, then fed each channel's staleness into a lag-compensation rewind with and without a cap.
- Why built: Gap pass: the WebRTC data-channel kernel claims reliable-ordered delivery is wrong for position updates and had never been built against; the rewind-cap and bufferedAmount kernels are the downstream and sender-side consequences.
- Design: Tick 16 ms, 600 packets, every 7th lost; reliable retransmits after an RTO and holds every later packet behind it, unreliable drops it; metrics are newest-state staleness, sender backlog beyond normal in flight, and whether a rewind of the measured staleness (cap 1000 ms or 50 ms) hits a target 20 units inside cover moving 0.2 units/ms.
- Got right: Reliable max staleness 160 ms vs 64 ms unreliable with backlog peaking at 7 packets vs 0, no-loss controls identical at 48 ms, the uncapped rewind registered a hit on the covered target only on the reliable channel, and the 50 ms cap blocked it.
- Where/why it failed: My written prediction of at least 3x worse max staleness at RTO 120 ms failed: the ratio was 2.5; it depends on the retransmit timeout (1.75 at 60 ms, 2.5 at 120, 4.5 at 240, 8.25 at 480), so the stall size is set by RTO, not by a fixed factor.
- Fix: State the head-of-line penalty as a function of retransmit timeout and loss rate, keep unreliable unordered delivery for per-tick state, and still cap server rewind because a reliable stall inflates the claimed latency that rewind trusts.
- Why this fix: The ratio sweep shows the penalty grows with RTO while the cap removed the covered-target hit on every channel, so the cap is independent of channel choice and the channel choice removes the stall itself.
- Rule of thumb: On a lossy link a reliable ordered channel holds back fresh position updates for about one retransmit timeout, so its worst staleness scales with RTO (2.5x at 120 ms, 8.25x at 480 ms in this model) and inflates the latency a lag-compensating server rewinds, so pick unordered zero-retransmit for per-tick state and still cap the rewind.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox model (loss pattern, RTO and target speed are my own choices; the spec exclusivity rule is modeled by a validator, not tested in a real browser); the 3x prediction was refuted by the run.
- Composed: ideas:NETWORKING/webrtc/a-datachannel-is-reliable, ideas:NETWORKING/lag-compensation/server-rewind-must-cap, ideas:NETWORKING/websocket/send-does-not-apply-backpressure
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__datachannel-reliable-hol-stall-vs-unreliable-rewind-cap.py
- Prediction: Reliable max staleness at least 3x unreliable at RTO 120 ms, backlog at least 7 vs 0, uncapped rewind hits the covered target on reliable only, 50 ms cap blocks it, no-loss controls identical.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL reliable maxstale 160 vs unreliable 64 ms; backlog 7 vs 0; uncapped reliable hit True, cap50 False; no-loss identical True; ratio by RTO {60: 1.75, 120: 2.5, 240: 4.5, 480: 8.25}
- Scenarios: 1) reliable with loss; 2) unreliable with loss; 3) no-loss controls for both (identical); 4) RTO sweep 60/120/240/480 (built to BREAK the fixed 3x claim, which failed at 60 and 120); 5) rewind uncapped vs 50 ms cap

## E60 — asr disfluency triple needs dense disfluency not base rate
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [speech-recognition][disfluency][model][simulation][sandbox]
- What: A toy recogniser (not a real one) with real Levenshtein alignment tested whether fragment hallucination alone reproduces the published pattern that disfluent speech roughly triples word error rate and shifts errors to insertions, using the 5.97 per 100 words base rate and Levelt's repair structure to generate the corpus.
- Why built: The SPEECH-DISFLUENCY error-profile kernel had no first-hand build; its siblings supply the realistic disfluency rate and the repair structure that a test set should contain.
- Design: 400 utterances of 15 words, disfluencies placed by a deterministic accumulator at 5.97 to 40 per 100 words (fillers 2.56, repeats 1.47, restarts 1.94 in proportion, 23 percent of restarts cut mid-word); the recogniser substitutes every tenth clean word and decodes each word fragment as two spurious whole words; a second iteration added derailment of the next K words after a fragment; a control removes the hallucination.
- Got right: Alignment worked as designed and the control behaved: with no hallucination the fragments become deletions and the ratio fell to 0.96; clean WER 0.067.
- Where/why it failed: Prediction refuted. Fragment hallucination alone gave a WER ratio of only 1.05 at the base rate and 1.20 even at 30 per 100 words, with insertion share 0.06 and 0.20, nowhere near 3x. Adding derailment of K following words reached at most 2.98x at density 30 (and 1.45x at the base rate) but pushed insertions down to 0.08 as substitutions took over, so one mechanism could not give both tripling and insertion dominance.
- Fix: Do not read the tripling as typical for ordinary speech; it needs a disfluency-dense test set, and insertion dominance needs an insertion source beyond fragments (hallucinated repeats and fillers), so model both before predicting error mix for a given corpus.
- Why this fix: The density sweep and the derailment sweep bound what a fragment-only mechanism can produce (1.24 maximum without derailment, 2.98 with it) and show the error mix moving the wrong way, which is the evidence that another insertion source is required.
- Rule of thumb: At the typical 5.97 disfluencies per 100 words a fragment-only recogniser model gives about 1.05x clean WER and even a derailing one only 1.45x, so a 3x disfluency penalty with insertion-dominated errors cannot come from word fragments alone and applies to disfluency-dense test sets.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox model; all error mechanisms and coefficients are my own assumptions, the published 3.02x figure and 57 percent insertion share were not re-measured, and no real recogniser was run.
- Composed: ideas:SPEECH-DISFLUENCY/speech-recognition/error-profile, ideas:SPEECH-DISFLUENCY/self-repair/levelt-1983, ideas:SPEECH-DISFLUENCY/base-rates/spontaneous-speech

- Prediction: Written before the first run: ratio below 1.6 at the 5.97 base rate, 3x reached only at 20 or more disfluencies per 100 words with insertion share at least 0.45 there, removing hallucination cuts the ratio by a third, and insertions stop being the largest class without it. First run: FAIL, 3x never reached.
- Observed: RESULT: FAIL ratio at base rate 1.05; first density with 3x: None; insertion share there None; FRAG_INS=0 ratio at 30: 0.96 vs 1.20; derail K for 3x at density 30: None (derail K=16 gave 2.98, insertion share 0.08)
- Scenarios: 1) clean baseline; 2) density sweep 5.97/10/20/30/40 with two-word fragment hallucination; 3) no-hallucination control at 30; 4) derailment sweep K 0 to 64 at 5.97 and 30 (built to BREAK the single-mechanism claim; it failed to produce both tripling and insertion dominance)

## E59 — probe cost must stay under race window
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [debugging][timing][model]
- What: Virtual-clock model of a stale-read race and a frame loop, probed three ways: a breakpoint, a light
  print, and a heavy print.
- Why built: The print-vs-debugger kernel says breakpoints fail where print debugging holds up; I wanted the
  boundary where print debugging also stops holding up.
- Design: Worker publishes at t=40, main reads at t=35 (stale in a free run). A probe delays the read by its
  cost. Separately a frame loop throws at frame 5 and is run with reschedule-last and reschedule-
  first, with one log line per frame.
- Got right: Free run was STALE; a breakpoint pause (1000 ticks) hid the race (fresh); a 1-tick print kept it;
  the print log ended at frame 5 for reschedule-last and frame 9 for reschedule-first, locating the
  death.
- Where/why it failed: The claim holds only for light probes: any probe costing 5 or more ticks also hid the race, so heavy
  logging is a breakpoint in disguise.
- Fix: Treat every probe as a perturbation with a cost; use the lightest probe first (buffered, deferred
  formatting), and confirm the bug still reproduces with the probe in place before trusting a
  negative.
- Why this fix: The run gave a sharp threshold (5 ticks) between a probe that preserves the failure and one that
  erases it, so reproduction under the probe is the check that matters.
- Rule of thumb: Print beats a breakpoint for timing bugs only while its cost stays under the race window (5 of 40
  ticks here); heavy logging hides the bug exactly as a pause does, so measure that the failure
  survives the probe.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: all outputs come from running the sandbox this session. The tick values are
  model assumptions, not measurements of any real debugger or runtime.
- Composed: ideas:DEBUGGING/tools/print-vs-debugger, ideas:DEBUGGING/methodology/scientific-method, brain/E36
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__probe-cost-must-stay-under-race-window.py
- Prediction: Free run STALE, breakpoint fresh, light print STALE, hiding threshold at 5 ticks, and a frame-loop
  log ending at frame 5 for reschedule-last versus frame 9 for reschedule-first.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS free run STALE; breakpoint hides the race; light print keeps it but cost>=5 ticks also
  hides it; print log pins the loop death at frame 5 (reschedule-last) vs frame 9 (reschedule-first)
- Scenarios: 1) free run; 2) breakpoint; 3) light print; 4) heavy print (built to break the kernel); 5) threshold
  sweep of probe cost 0-99; 6) frame loop reschedule-last vs reschedule-first

## E58 — normalize forms not sufficient
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [text][unicode][testing]
- What: Sandbox of the normalize-before-comparing kernel: NFC vs NFKC on precomposed/combining, ligature and
  Cyrillic-lookalike strings, then truncation after normalizing.
- Why built: To find where normalization stops being enough: the kernel says visually identical strings compare
  unequal, but not which normal form or which cases remain.
- Design: Python unicodedata, 3 string pairs (cafe accent, fi ligature, Cyrillic a in paypal) compared raw,
  NFC and NFKC; then a 4-code-point cut on NFD vs NFC text and on a letter with two combining marks.
- Got right: NFC made the combining and precomposed cafe equal (raw False, NFC True) and normalization was
  idempotent on all 5 inputs; truncating NFC text kept the accent where truncating NFD text dropped
  it.
- Where/why it failed: NFC alone left the fi ligature unequal to file, NFKC fixed that but still left the Cyrillic
  lookalike unequal to the Latin word, and a letter with two marks has no precomposed form so a code-
  point cut still splits it.
- Fix: Pick the form by purpose: NFC to store, NFKC for search keys, and a separate confusable check for
  security names; cut on grapheme boundaries after normalizing.
- Why this fix: Each form only collapses one class of equivalence; the sandbox showed each class failing under the
  wrong form, so one blanket normalize call gives false confidence.
- Rule of thumb: Normalizing is necessary but not sufficient: NFC unifies accents, only NFKC unifies ligatures, no
  form unifies lookalike scripts, and normalized text still needs grapheme-aware truncation.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: all results above came from running the sandbox in this session with Python's
  unicodedata; nothing assumed.
- Composed: ideas:TEXT/unicode/normalize-before-comparing-or-storing-user-text, ideas:TEXT/unicode/truncate-on-
  grapheme-boundaries-not-code-units, sandbox-kernel-text-unicode/E1
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__normalize-forms-not-sufficient.py
- Prediction: Raw compare False, NFC compare True, NFC leaves ligature unequal, NFKC fixes ligature, neither fixes
  Cyrillic lookalike, NFC cut still splits a two-mark letter.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS NFC fixes combining-vs-precomposed (1 case), NFKC needed for ligature, neither fixes
  Cyrillic lookalike, NFC still truncates 2-mark grapheme
- Scenarios: 1) cafe precomposed vs combining; 2) fi ligature; 3) Cyrillic lookalike (built to break the kernel);
  4) truncation of NFD vs NFC; 5) two-mark letter cut

## E57 — netcode limits cap costs honest players
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [networking][netcode][model]
- What: Tick model of three netcode limits at once: staleness of an ordered reliable channel versus an
  unordered no-retransmit one, a lag-compensation rewind with and without a cap, and a sender that
  does or does not check its buffered amount.
- Why built: The webrtc datachannel kernel and its two sibling kernels each name a limit; I wanted to see whether
  the fixes interact or cost something.
- Design: One-way delay 3 ticks, every 10th position packet lost. Rewind: target exposed on ticks 0-9, shot at
  tick 15 with claimed latency 20 (liar) or 8 (honest). Socket: 3 messages per tick produced, 2 per
  tick drained, limit 20, check at buffered 10.
- Got right: Ordered reliable delivery reached a worst position age of 9 ticks versus 4 unordered; an uncapped
  rewind let a 20-tick claim hit through cover while a cap of 5 stopped it; the unchecked sender
  closed the socket at tick 18 and the checking sender stayed open.
- Where/why it failed: The rewind cap is not free: with cap 5 an honest player at 8 ticks of real latency, who truly saw
  the exposed target, also lost the hit, so the cap trades fairness for exploit resistance.
- Fix: Use unordered no-retransmit for position streams, cap the trusted rewind at a measured value and
  accept that high-latency honest players lose some hits, and check the buffered amount before each
  send, dropping or coalescing stale position updates.
- Why this fix: Each limit was closed by a different control in the run and none helped the others; the cap's cost
  on the honest 8-tick player was the only place a fix hurt someone.
- Rule of thumb: Treat a position stream as disposable: unordered with no retransmit cut worst staleness from 9 to 4
  ticks, a rewind cap stops a lying client but also an honest one past the cap, and a sender must
  check buffered amount or it closes its own socket (tick 18 here).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: every number came from running the sandbox this session. All delays, loss
  pattern, rates and caps are my model constants; no real browser, WebRTC stack or WebSocket was run.

## E56 — least privilege reach needs edges rotation slow hash
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [security][testing][model]
- What: Deterministic blast-radius model for least privilege: one shared admin token versus per-resource
  tokens, a CI-to-deploy edge, a leaked secret handled by force-push versus rotation, and a stolen
  password table under fast versus slow hashing with a fixed work budget.
- Why built: The least-privilege kernel says scoping limits what one compromise reaches; I wanted to see which
  compromises that stops and which it does not.
- Design: 8 resources; shared token reaches all; scoped tokens reach one each; a CI token also triggers prod
  deploy through an edge. Leak scenarios count usable copies. Password table of 500 users cracked from
  a wordlist under a budget of 1,000,000 work units at cost 1, 100,000 and 1,000,000 per guess.
- Got right: Scoped web token reached 1 of 8 resources versus 8 for the shared token; rotation made a leaked
  secret unusable (0) while force-push with one clone left it usable (1); the slow hash cut cracked
  users from 500/500 to 1/500.
- Where/why it failed: Counting grants per token said the CI token reaches 1 resource but the pipeline edge made it 2, so
  least privilege measured by direct grants understates reach; scoping also did nothing for the leak
  case, which only rotation fixed.
- Fix: Compute blast radius as graph reachability including pipeline and trust edges, not as a count of
  direct grants; pair scoping with rotation for leaked secrets and a slow salted hash for stored
  passwords.
- Why this fix: Each control closed a different path in the run: scoping the direct grants, rotation the stale copy,
  the slow hash the offline guessing; none substituted for another.
- Rule of thumb: Least privilege shrinks the reach of one credential only as far as the edges you counted: in this
  model 1 of 8 became 2 once a CI edge was included, a force-push never retracted a leaked copy, and
  only a slow hash blunted a stolen table; audit reachability, rotate on leak, hash slowly.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: every number is from running the shipped sandbox this session. The reach and
  exposure results follow from the model's construction and show the accounting, not a real cloud or
  repo; the constants (8 resources, 500 users, budget) are my assumptions.
- Composed: ideas:SECURITY/access-control/least-privilege, ideas:SECURITY/authentication/password-storage,
  ideas:SECURITY/secrets/source-control
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__least-privilege-reach-needs-edges-rotation-slow-hash.py
- Prediction: Scoped reach 1 vs shared 8; CI reach counts 1 by direct grants but 2 with the edge; force-push
  leaves the secret usable and rotation does not; fast hash cracks at least 400 of 500 and the slow
  hash far fewer.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS scoped radius 1 vs shared 8 but CI edge makes it 2 (naive count says 1); force-push
  leaves leak usable, rotation voids it; fast hash cracks 500/500 vs slow 1/500
- Scenarios: 1) shared admin token; 2) scoped web token; 3) CI token with pipeline edge (built to break the
  grant-count measure); 4) force-push only; 5) rotation; 6) fast, slow and slowest hash under one
  budget

## E55 — seeded rng save replay and shared stream vs per entity substream
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [determinism][gamedev][testing][sandbox]
- What: Python port of a 32-bit mulberry32 stream driving a six-enemy damage sim: same-seed fingerprints, save by raw state word versus replay count, an ambient-draw leak, and what removing one enemy does to the others' rolls on a shared stream versus per-entity substreams.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel and the shared-stream ordinal kernel were only quoted in prose by the game-prologue entries; nothing re-ran them on a fresh generator or tested whether a keyed substream really fixes the population-change flip.
- Design: No RNG or clock: fixed seeds, sha256 of the roll log as the fingerprint, 50 ticks. Scenarios: determinism, resume after 5000 draws from raw state versus replay, one ambient draw at tick 10, and removal of enemy c on a shared stream, on id-keyed substreams (seed plus entity id hashed) and on ordinal-keyed substreams (seed plus list index).
- Got right: Same seed gave one fingerprint and another seed a different one; resuming from the raw state word matched the replayed stream for 100 rolls with 1 step instead of 5000; one leaked draw at tick 10 diverged the log at index 61, the first roll of tick 10; id-keyed substreams kept 100 percent of surviving enemies' rolls.
- Where/why it failed: On the shared stream, removing enemy c left only 11.3 percent of enemies d, e and f rolls unchanged, which is chance level for a d6, so population change silently reshuffles unrelated outcomes. Keying substreams by list index failed the same way (18.0 percent), so a substream fix only works with stable ids.
- Fix: Give each entity its own substream keyed by seed plus a stable id, keep the whole simulation on seeded streams with no ambient draws, and save the raw state word for O(1) load.
- Why this fix: The id-keyed version isolated all 100 percent of surviving rolls in the sandbox, while the ordinal-keyed control showed the isolation comes from the stable key and not from using substreams.
- Rule of thumb: One seeded stream gives exact save and replay but entangles every roll with population and call order, so key per-entity substreams by stable id, never by list position, and save the raw state word rather than a draw count.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox seeded-rng-save-replay-and-shared-stream-vs-per-entity-substream.py; numbers below are from that run.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/a-shared-rng-stream-is-an-ordinal-space-address-it-symbolically, the-game-prologue/E1, the-game-prologue/E19
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__seeded-rng-save-replay-and-shared-stream-vs-per-entity-substream.py
- Prediction: Same-seed fingerprints identical; raw-state resume equals replay resume; leak diverges from tick 10; removing one enemy leaves at most 35 percent of later enemies' rolls unchanged on a shared stream and 100 percent on id-keyed substreams; ordinal-keyed substreams also at most 35 percent.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS S1 determinism, S2 resume equal (replay 5000 vs 1 steps), S3 leak diverges at tick 10, S4 shared stream keeps 0.11 of later rolls vs id-keyed substream 1.00 vs ordinal-keyed 0.18
- Scenarios: 1) same seed twice and a different seed; 2) resume from raw state versus replay after 5000 draws; 3) one ambient draw at tick 10 (built to BREAK determinism); 4) remove one enemy on shared stream, id-keyed substreams and ordinal-keyed substreams (ordinal-keyed built to BREAK the substream fix)

## E54 — per utterance rows stable ids vs flat manuscript
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [voice][scripting][sandbox][architecture]
- What: Sandbox of the per-utterance-row script model against a flat manuscript for multi-voice TTS: re-render counts after an edit and after an insert, speaker-label parsing, label aliasing and simultaneous speech, on a 40-row, 4-speaker script with a stub renderer.
- Why built: The per-utterance-rows kernel claims rows make voice assignment and selective re-rendering tractable; no memory entry had built against it or tested where it stops holding.
- Design: Rows hold id, scene, speaker, text; the cache key is voice plus a text hash. Compare editing one row, inserting one row (index-named output files versus stable-id names), a flat manuscript chunked every 300 characters, an inline-label parser on 4 adversarial lines, a character written under two labels, and two rows flagged as overlapping.
- Got right: Editing one row re-rendered 1 unit against 7 of 8 chunks for the flat manuscript; stable-id file names re-rendered 1 after a mid-script insert; one canonical label per character gave 1 voice, and rows had 0 misattributed speakers against 3 for the inline-label parser.
- Where/why it failed: Rows alone do not make re-rendering tractable: with output names built from the row index, inserting one row mid-script changed 21 of 41 later outputs, the same blow-up as the flat manuscript. Two labels for one character gave 2 voices, and the overlap flag disappeared from the (voice, path) mapping because turns are sequential.
- Fix: Give every row a stable id that never changes on insert and derive the output path from it, key the render cache on voice plus text hash, keep one never-aliased label per character, and add an explicit overlap column if simultaneous speech must survive.
- Why this fix: The stable-id path made a mid-script insert cost 1 render instead of 21 in the sandbox, and a canonical label collapsed 2 voices to 1; an explicit column is the only place overlap information can live.
- Rule of thumb: Model a multi-voice script as one row per utterance with a stable row id as the file name, never the row position, plus one canonical label per speaker, because row order names the files and an insert then re-renders everything after it.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox per-utterance-rows-stable-ids-vs-flat-manuscript.py; numbers below are from that run.
- Composed: ideas:VOICE/scripting/per-utterance-rows-plus-per-turn-voice, pocketzane/E5, brain/E109
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__per-utterance-rows-stable-ids-vs-flat-manuscript.py
- Prediction: Editing one row costs 1 render with rows and over 75 percent of chunks for a flat manuscript; inserting one row costs 20 or more with index-named files and 1 with stable ids; the inline-label parser misattributes at least 3 adversarial lines against 0 for rows; a character with two labels gets 2 voices; the overlap flag is lost in the mapping.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS edit one row: rows 1 vs flat 7/8 chunks; insert: index-named 21 vs stable-id 1; inline-label parser wrong 3; alias voices 2 vs 1; overlap lost. Miss: my first absolute guess of 10 chunks was impossible with 8 chunks.
- Scenarios: 1) edit one row, rows versus flat chunks; 2) insert one row with index-named versus stable-id files (built to BREAK the rows claim); 3) adversarial inline labels; 4) one character under two labels; 5) overlapping rows through the (voice, path) mapping (built to BREAK)
