## E53 — birthday bound with modulo bias
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [hashing][sandbox][sampling]
- What: Sandbox of hashing a counter with sha256 into a bounded id space: first-collision draw count versus the birthday bound, and the effect of reducing with modulo when the space does not divide the source range.
- Why built: Two ideas kernels (birthday bound, modulo bias) are both about sizing and reducing hash output; no memory entry had exercised them together.
- Design: Deterministic sha256 of a counter as the source (no RNG). Mean first collision over 40 trials at 2^20 and 2^22 slots, then exact collision probability for an 8-bit source reduced into 200 buckets by modulo versus rejection.
- Got right: First collision arrives near sqrt(N): 1115 draws in 2^20 (formula 1283) and quadrupling the space gave a ratio of 2.19 (about 2x), matching the kernel's scaling.
- Where/why it failed: Modulo reduction of a source range that is not a multiple of the bucket count made 56 of 200 buckets double-weighted, raising pairwise collision probability from 0.00500 to 0.00562 (12 percent worse), so ids sized by the birthday formula collide earlier than predicted.
- Fix: Size the space by the birthday bound and reduce with rejection (discard source values at or above the largest multiple of the bucket count), or use a source range far larger than the space.
- Why this fix: Rejection restored the exact uniform collision probability 0.00500 in the sandbox, so the birthday estimate applies again; widening the source only shrinks the bias rather than removing it.
- Rule of thumb: Size ids for sqrt(space) draws to first collision, and reduce hash output with rejection or a much wider source, because modulo bias silently lowers the collision threshold.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox birthday-bound-with-modulo-bias.py; numbers below are from that run.
- Composed: ideas:HASHING/collisions/the-birthday-bound-makes-collisions-appear-at-sqrt-of-the-space, ideas:SAMPLING/uniform/modulo-reduction-of-a-generator-is-biased-unless-it-divides-evenly, brain/E121
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__birthday-bound-with-modulo-bias.py
- Prediction: Mean first collision within 35 percent of sqrt(pi/2*N); 4x space gives 1.4 to 2.9x draws; modulo collision probability exceeds uniform by over 5 percent; rejection equals uniform exactly.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS birthday scaling sqrt(N) holds; modulo bias raises collision prob 0.00562 vs 0.00500; rejection restores. s1 1115 vs 1283, s2 ratio 2.19.
- Scenarios: 1) 2^20 slots mean first collision; 2) 2^22 slots scaling ratio; 3) 8-bit source into 200 buckets by modulo (built to BREAK the formula); 4) same with rejection
- Link: brain train auto session 2026-10-10; session_012uwXvPE6LveBmBN1pFKYfK

## E52 — antimeridian wrap necessary not sufficient for midpoints
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [geospatial][sandbox][method]
- What: Sandbox of the lat/lon kernel: haversine distance across the antimeridian, half-open longitude normalisation, and where a wrap-aware longitude midpoint at constant latitude stops matching the true great-circle midpoint.
- Why built: The geospatial kernel was verified only for the 179 / -179 distance and a naive mid-longitude; nobody tested whether fixing the wrap is enough for midpoints and interpolation away from the equator.
- Design: Haversine on R 6371.0088 km; longitude normalised with a floor-mod into [-180,180); shortest-arc longitude midpoint (the same idea as the shortest-arc blend kernel for angles); true midpoint from summed 3D unit vectors; cases at the equator, lat 60 and near the pole.
- Got right: Distance 222.4 km for the pair 2 degrees apart against a naive longitude gap of 358 degrees (about 39,800 km planar); normalising makes 180 and -180 the same value so both land in one tile where inclusive tiles split them.
- Where/why it failed: A wrap-aware longitude midpoint at constant latitude is exact only at the equator: at lat 60 for lon 170 and -170 it is 42.1 km from the true midpoint (true lat 60.378), and near the pole (89.9, 0)-(89.9, 180) it is 11.1 km off where the true midpoint is the pole. I had predicted over 100 km at lat 60 and missed.
- Fix: Fixing the wrap handles distance, but interpolate and take midpoints through 3D unit vectors (sum, renormalise) or slerp, which gave equal distances 553.9 km to both ends at lat 60 and the pole at lat 90.
- Why this fix: The vector midpoint is independent of the longitude seam and of latitude, so it removes the error that the wrap fix alone leaves, at the cost of a few trigonometric calls.
- Rule of thumb: Use haversine and normalise longitude half-open for distances, but treat the wrap fix as necessary not sufficient: midpoints and interpolation away from the equator need unit-vector math, since the longitude-only fix drifted 42 km at lat 60.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the deterministic sandbox antimeridian-wrap-necessary-not-sufficient-for-midpoints.py; numbers below are from that run.
- Composed: ideas:GEOSPATIAL/distance/lat-lon-are-not-a-plane-and-the-antimeridian-wraps, ideas:MOTION/skeletal-animation/blend-joint-rotation-via-shortest-arc-not-raw-angle-lerp, ideas:GEOMETRY/point-in-polygon/half-open-interval-attributes-each-vertex-to-exactly-one-edge
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__antimeridian-wrap-necessary-not-sufficient-for-midpoints.py
- Prediction: Haversine 222.4 km for the antimeridian pair and naive 358 degrees; inclusive tiles split 180 from -180 while half-open merges them; shortest-arc midpoint under 1 km off at the equator but over 100 km off at lat 60; about 11 km off near the pole; vector midpoint under 0.01 km off.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS S1 222.4 km vs naive 358 deg; mid err equator 0.000 km, lat60 42.1 km, pole 11.1 km; vector mid fixes. Miss: lat60 error was 42.1 km, not over 100.
- Scenarios: 1) antimeridian pair distance; 2) 180 versus -180 tile assignment inclusive versus half-open; 3) shortest-arc midpoint at equator versus lat 60 (built to BREAK the wrap fix); 4) near-pole pair (built to BREAK); 5) unit-vector midpoint

## E50 — lunar reference table must span the anomaly cycle or it passes the mean proxy
- Date: 2026-10-10
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [astronomy][lunar-phase][verification][testing][sandbox]
- What: Tested the lunar kernel's closing claim that a 17-row reference table of published new moons doubles as the regression test for the corrected newMoonUtc function. Over all 620 lunations of 2000-2050 the mean-period model is off by up to 14.1 h from the corrected model (not the table's 11.9 h), a 16-row table sees only 11.85 h, and a table of 1-3 consecutive moons can be passed by the mean proxy (2.3 h worst for 3 rows) while 7 or more rows cannot get under 5.5 h.
- Why built: Apply the kernel again from a new side: not whether the corrected formula is accurate (brainwork/E39 and sandbox-lunar-phase/E1 settled that) but whether the regression table the kernel ships is itself a claim-directed test or an easy-half test in the sense of brain/E54.
- Design: Stdlib sandbox with a mean model (Meeus epoch JDE 2451550.09766, period 29.530588861 d), a four-term model (the four terms the kernel lists), and an extended 14-term model plus a flat 64/69 s TT-to-UTC shift. Scenarios: (1) mean vs extended across 620 lunations; (2) a cheap-oracle suite (spacing between 29 and 30 d, increasing, right year) versus a 10-minute tolerance test on 16 recalled reference minutes; (3) BREAK: search every placement of a table (contiguous windows of 1-20 rows, strides 12-15) for the one that hides the mean model best; (4) epoch anchoring on the real 2000-01-06 18:14 UTC moon instead of the Meeus mean epoch; (5) term set and delta-T on the reference table.
- Got right: The cheap suite passed the mean model (29.53 d spacing every time, while the real spacing runs 29.277 to 29.824 d) and the 10-minute table test failed it and the four-term model but passed the extended model, so the table is a real discriminator at 16 rows. The four-term worst case reproduced E39 at 21.2 min, the extended set 1.21 min, and skipping the 69 s delta-T shift doubled that to 2.36 min, so a 2-minute tolerance passes only with it.
- Where/why it failed: My first prediction (a 17-row table sampled every 14th lunation, where the anomalistic month beats against the synodic month, would hide the mean model under 3 h, and a contiguous 17-row window would stay above 8 h) was wrong both ways: the best stride-14 placement left 4.82 h and the best contiguous one 5.88 h, so with 17 rows aliasing cannot fully hide the proxy. The distinct failure is smaller tables: 1 row is 0.02 h off, 3 rows 2.3 h, 5 rows 4.0 h. Separately the kernel's "up to about 12 hours" is a sample figure: the same table sees 11.85 h but the 620-moon maximum is 14.13 h, and anchoring the mean model on the real first moon (the table's first row, which then scores 0.000 h by construction) raises it to 17.6 h; the best possible constant offset still leaves 13.9 h, which supports the kernel's no-tuning point.
- Fix: Ship the reference table with at least 8 moons spread over more than one anomalistic cycle (about 14 lunations), do not anchor the mean model on a row of the table, and state the tolerance with the term set and delta-T handling (10 min separates the extended set; 2 min needs the delta-T shift). Quote the mean-model error as "up to about 12 h on the table, 14 h over 50 years" and not as a ceiling.
- Why this fix: The search over placements measured the floor directly: from 7 rows on, the easiest placement still leaves 5.46 h, so 8 or more rows cannot be passed by the proxy at any tolerance below that, while a table of 3 or fewer rows can. Reporting the table maximum and the 620-moon maximum side by side shows how much the sample understates the worst case.
- Rule of thumb: A lunar regression table of 7 or more spread-out new moons cannot be passed by a mean-period model under about 5 h tolerance, but a 1-3 row table can (2.3 h at 3 rows), a cheap spacing check passed the mean model here, and a table's maximum (11.85 h) understates the 50-year maximum (14.1 h), so size the table and state the tolerance before trusting a green result; scoped to 620 lunations from 2000.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox: every figure above is computed in it. The 16 reference minutes are recalled published values copied from a stored sandbox, not fetched, and each may carry about a minute of error, which does not move the hour-scale findings but does limit the 2-minute and 1.21-minute figures. Meeus constants were entered from memory. The 620-moon "truth" is the extended model itself, validated only through its 1.2 minute agreement with those 16 rows. The zone and date-flip part of the kernel was not re-run here.
- Composed: ideas:ASTRONOMY/lunar-phase/mean-synodic-phase-is-a-proxy, brain/E54, brainwork/E39, sandbox-lunar-phase/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-10__lunar-reference-table-must-span-the-anomaly-cycle-or-it-passes-the-mean-proxy.py
- Prediction: Mean-model max over 620 lunations 14-16.5 h with over 85% of moons off by more than 1 h; cheap suite passes the mean model while the tolerance test fails it; a stride-14 17-row table hides the mean model under 3 h and a contiguous 17-row window stays above 8 h (wrong, see Observed); four-term worst case 15-30 min and a 2 min test passes only with delta-T. Revised after run 1: 7 or more rows cannot get under 5 h, 3 or fewer rows can; anchoring on the real moon moves the 620-moon max by over 1 h.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS mean max 14.1h/620 moons (16-row table sees 11.8h); cheap suite passes mean=True; easiest 3-row table 2.3h, 7-row 5.5h, 17-row 5.9h; anchor swing 14.1h->17.6h; four-term 21 min. Run 1 had refuted the stride-14 and 17-row claims (4.82 h and 5.88 h).
- Scenarios: 1) mean vs extended over 620 lunations; 2) cheap-oracle suite vs 10-minute tolerance test on 16 reference moons; 3) BREAK: easiest placement of tables of 1-20 contiguous rows and of strides 12-15; 4) epoch anchored on the real first moon vs Meeus mean epoch and best constant offset; 5) four-term vs extended set and with/without delta-T against a 2-minute tolerance

## E49 — regret grows with travel diameter at fixed states and actions slip line world
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [algorithm][state][simulation][verification]
- What: In a deterministic slip-line world with fixed states and actions, regret scaled with how long it takes to travel (the diameter) and not with the state or action counts, and it saturates when the horizon is shorter than the travel time.
- Why built: To build the ideas kernel REGRET/reinforcement-learning/regret-in-an-mdp-is-governed-by-the-diameter-not-just-state-and-action-counts in a sandbox and find where it stops holding.
- Design: S states on a line, 3 actions, a move executes only on every m-th attempt from a state (a deterministic counter, no random numbers); a sweeping learner discovers the treasure state only by standing on it; regret is the informed optimum's reward minus the learner's, averaged over every treasure position.
- Got right: At S=8 and horizon 600 regret was 3, 6, 12, 24 for m=1, 2, 4, 8, so an 8x slower world cost exactly 8x. With state and action counts both small, S=6 with m=8 (diameter 40) lost 16.0 against 11.0 for S=24 with m=1 (diameter 23). Doubling the horizon from 600 to 1200 left regret at 4.00.
- Where/why it failed: The break case held the other way: when the horizon (60) was shorter than the travel needed, regret was 8.2 against 88.0 at horizon 600, because both learner and optimum earn almost nothing, so a short horizon hides the diameter cost rather than showing it.
- Fix: Judge a learner or a level design by its regret at a horizon several times the travel diameter, and report diameter alongside state and action counts.
- Why this fix: Regret in this model is the reward lost while travelling and searching, which is set by travel time per step; counts of states and actions only enter through the diameter they imply.
- Rule of thumb: In the cases run (slip factors 1 to 8, S 6 to 24, horizons 60 to 1200), compare worlds by diameter before state count and measure regret at a horizon well past it; a short horizon makes a hard-to-traverse world look cheap.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): verified first-hand by the deterministic sandbox run (RESULT: PASS on the first run); this is a hand-built line world, not a general MDP or any published regret bound.
- Composed: ideas:REGRET/reinforcement-learning/regret-in-an-mdp-is-governed-by-the-diameter-not-just-state-and-action-counts/a-hard-to-traverse-world-costs-regret-even-with-few-states

## E48 — radial vs per axis deadzone snap spurious edges and hardcoded cycle modulo
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [input][gamepad][gamedev][testing]
- What: A per-axis stick deadzone fed into a debounced direction reader and a slot cursor shows three separate failures against a radial deadzone, and only one of them is the one the kernel names.
- Why built: To build the ideas kernel input/gamepad/radial-deadzone-not-per-axis in a sandbox and find where its claim stops holding, composed with the stick-debounced menu navigation and the hardcoded cursor modulo lessons.
- Design: Deterministic Python model, DZ 0.20: stick vector, per-axis and radial filters, sign-based 8-way direction, edge-triggered steps, cursor modulo N over a 5-item enum; angle sweeps in 1-degree steps and one full revolution at fixed radii.
- Got right: At r 0.25 the per-axis filter put 77% of angles more than 10 degrees off (radial 0%), needed radius 0.283 versus 0.200 to register at 45 degrees (x1.41), and registered nothing over 18.9% of the circle. At r 0.35 one revolution gave 8 direction edges per-axis versus 4 radial, so the cursor ended on slot 3 versus 4.
- Where/why it failed: My first predictions were wrong: at r 0.25 both filters gave 4 edges per revolution, not 8 versus 1; the spurious-edge hazard sits at r at or above DZ times sqrt 2, while between DZ and that value per-axis produces dead gaps instead. A hardcoded modulo 4 on a 5-item enum never reached slot 4 whatever the filter did, so the cursor bug is independent of the deadzone.
- Fix: Apply the deadzone to the vector magnitude, rescale or keep the angle, derive the cursor modulus from the list length, and test with a sweep of angles at two radii, one inside and one outside the DZ times sqrt 2 band.
- Why this fix: A radial test treats the stick as one circular input, so diagonals need the same travel as cardinals and no direction flickers; deriving the modulus removes the second copy of the count that opticon E30 found.
- Rule of thumb: In the cases run (DZ 0.20, 360-angle sweep, one revolution at r 0.25 and 0.35), per-axis deadzones distort the angle everywhere above DZ and cause extra direction edges only above DZ times sqrt 2; test both radii, and keep any cursor modulus derived from the list so the two bugs are not mistaken for each other.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): verified first-hand by the deterministic sandbox run (RESULT: PASS on iteration 3); the model is a hand-written stick model, not a real browser Gamepad API.

- Observed: RESULT: PASS per-axis bad-angle share 0.77 vs 0; diagonal travel x1.41; edges/rev 4 vs 4 at r=.25 and 8 vs 4 at r=.35; hardcoded modulo reaches [0, 1, 2, 3]

## E47 — duplicated default markup copy drifts only on empty prefs
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui-state][defaults][testing][camera]
- What: A default FOV kept both as a code constant and as a pre-selected ladder button in static markup drifts apart after a retune, and the mismatch shows only on a profile with no stored prefs.
- Why built: To test the ideas kernel UI-STATE/defaults/duplicated-default and see where it stops holding, using a toy camera ladder with a stored-prefs path.
- Design: Deterministic Python model: constant default, static markup copy, render() where a stored pref wins and empty prefs leave the markup as is; five scenarios incl. a lerp-smoothed camera and an extent-clamped scale.
- Got right: After retuning 60 to 75 the empty-prefs case mismatched (marked 60, camera 75) while stored-90 and stored-75 cases did not; a literal-number test passed on the stale copy, a copy-vs-copy test failed, and deriving the marker from the constant gave 0 mismatches over the whole ladder.
- Where/why it failed: Stored prefs and the extent clamp both hide the drift: with the clamp binding at 1.0 the old and new defaults produced the same scale, so the bug only shows with a loose clamp. A deleted markup copy parsed to NaN poisoned the lerp-smoothed camera on 100 of 100 frames unguarded.
- Fix: Derive the marked option from the constant at render time; where markup must be static, add a copy-vs-copy test on a cleared profile; filter non-finite input before stateful smoothing.
- Why this fix: Derivation removes the second home so there is nothing to drift, and the copy-vs-copy test cannot be satisfied by editing a literal to match whichever copy the author sees.
- Rule of thumb: Test a default on a cleared profile, comparing the shown copy to the used copy, with the camera clamp loose; a stored pref or a binding clamp will mask the drift in the cases tests usually run.

## E46 — danger zone clock is cumulative and includes cooling time newton model
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [cooking][food-safety][method][verification]
- What: A Newton-cooling model of the 40-140 F danger-zone clock shows it is cumulative across stretches, halves above 90 F ambient, keeps running while food cools through the band, and stops entirely once food is held at 140 F or more.
- Why built: To build the ideas kernel COOKING/food-safety/danger-zone in a sandbox, together with the sous-vide temperature-ceiling sibling and the lesson to assert each claim an artefact makes rather than a cheap proxy.
- Design: Deterministic Python, 1-minute steps over the exact Newton solution; limits of 120 min (60 min above 90 F ambient) taken from the kernel; four enumerated claims C1 to C4 each asserted separately, plus a break case for each of C1 and C4.
- Got right: Stretches of 57, 30 and 45 band minutes each passed a per-stretch check but totalled 132 min, unsafe at both limits; a naive per-stretch reset reported only 57. A 150 F bath for 10 h accrued 0 band minutes.
- Where/why it failed: Three first predictions were wrong. A shallow pan from 165 F in a 38 F fridge spent 118 min in the band, not under 60, because the 40 F crossing is asymptotic against a 38 F fridge; the deep pot spent 674 min. A 138 F bath accrued 492 min of 600, since it first spends ln 6 hours above 140 F.
- Fix: Track the sum of band minutes across the whole process including cooling, use the hot-day limit when ambient exceeds 90 F, and judge cooling by minutes spent in the band rather than by whether the food is in a fridge.
- Why this fix: A per-stretch or location-based check passes each piece while the total fails; the cumulative sum is the quantity the limit is defined on, and band minutes are what depth and container shape actually change.
- Rule of thumb: In the model run, count danger-zone minutes as one running sum including the cooling phase, expect container depth to change that sum by roughly 6x, and treat a bath set a few degrees under 140 F as inside the band; USDA limits come from the kernel and the model's cooling constants are illustrative.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): verified first-hand by the deterministic sandbox run (RESULT: PASS on iteration 2); USDA limits are inherited from the kernel as stated there and the Newton constants are illustrative.
- Composed: ideas:COOKING/food-safety/danger-zone/perishable-food-has-a-real-clock-once-it-enters-40-to-140f, ideas:COOKING/sous-vide/temperature-precision/sous-vide-cant-overshoot-doneness-because-the-water-caps-the-temperature, brain/E54
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__danger-zone-clock-is-cumulative-and-includes-cooling-time-newton-model.py
- Prediction: Stretches that each pass a per-stretch check total over the 60 min hot-day limit; deep pot over 120 min in band; shallow pan under 60; a 150 F bath accrues 0. Run 1 refuted the shallow figure (118) and the 138 F bath expectation (492 not 600); revised to deep over 300, shallow 90 to 150, ratio over 4, 138 F bath 492, naive 57 vs cumulative 132.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS stretches 57/30/45 total 132 vs naive 57; deep pot 674 min vs shallow 118; 150F bath 0, 138F bath 492
- Scenarios: 1) three stretches with a fridge stop, per-stretch vs cumulative; 2) same minutes at 70 F and 95 F ambient limits; 3) deep pot vs shallow pan cooling from 165 F; 4) 150 F bath for 10 h; 5) BREAK: 138 F bath for 10 h; 6) BREAK: naive reset-per-stretch counter

- Why built: The base-3001 first-cover entry and the base-307 symdiff-reduce entry were both single-family evidence; this pairs them at a fresh base and a different modulus set to see whether the two structurally different covers still agree.
- Design: Landing rule from the family (a start lands at t+L when t mod P is at least w or (t+L) mod P is below w); per window width w and lag pair a<b, shadow means b lands somewhere and all its landings are inside a's; dict path streams first-cover, xor path reduces symmetric differences over frozensets; exact Fractions over offsets 0..P-1.
- Got right: P5 averages 2 and 26/5, P6 7/2 and 17/2, P7 38/7 and 88/7 at N=P and N=2P, identical across both implementations for every N from P-1 to 2P+1, flats exactly [P, 2P].
- Where/why it failed: Nothing refuted; the built-to-break identical-sets rule gave average 0 at N=P for all three moduli, confirming the cover test must be containment, not equality.
- Fix: n/a for the two entries, which stand; the only correction recorded is that equality of landing sets must never stand in for containment when counting shadowed lags.
- Why this fix: Containment is what the dictionary path computes by construction, and the xor path reproduces it only when the difference is tested against the earlier lag's set, so agreement on exact fractions is the check.
- Rule of thumb: When two implementations of one cover predicate agree on exact fractions at a fresh base, the predicate is pinned; keep a control that tests equality instead of containment, which here gives 0 shadows.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS) at base 4093; moduli above 7 are outside what this run claims.

## E44 — seeded rng state words vs seed count and stream coupling
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [gamedev][state][determinism][testing][sandbox]
- What: A sandbox with a 32-bit sfc32 generator compared saving the four state words with saving a {seed,count} pair, checked replay from seed, and tested what one shared random stream does when a single cosmetic roll is added.
- Why built: The seeded-rng kernel says to save the generator's state words rather than {seed,count}, and an older entry recorded the {seed,count} form. This re-verifies the link and looks for where the single-stream discipline stops being safe.
- Design: After 100000 rolls, snapshot the four words and, separately, rebuild by replaying 100000 rolls from the seed; compare the next 1000 rolls. Replay two sessions from one seed over 5000 rolls. Run a 100-turn session where gameplay (d20) and cosmetic rolls share one stream, add one cosmetic roll at turn 10, then repeat with a second stream seeded from the first seed. Finally restore the words through a signed-int round trip without masking to 32 bits.
- Got right: Both restore methods continued with 0 mismatches over 1000 rolls, but state words cost 0 rolls and seed+count cost exactly 100000. Replay from seed matched on all 5000 rolls. The signed, unmasked restore diverged at roll 1.
- Where/why it failed: The single-stream discipline has a cost the kernel does not name. With gameplay and cosmetic rolls on one stream, one added cosmetic roll changed 97% of later gameplay rolls (the other 3% are chance d20 matches), so a visual tweak silently rewrites outcomes and breaks golden replays. Split streams left all 100 gameplay rolls unchanged.
- Fix: Keep one seeded generator per concern, each with its own saved four words, derived from the master seed: gameplay, cosmetic, level generation. Save all of them. Mask restored words to 32 bits (or use typed unsigned arrays) on load.
- Why this fix: It keeps the kernel's gains (exact save, replay, lockstep) and removes the coupling in which any new consumer of the shared stream shifts every later roll.
- Rule of thumb: Save generator state words, not {seed,count}, but give each subsystem its own stream: in this model restore cost was 0 rolls versus 100000, and one extra cosmetic roll on a shared stream changed 97% of later gameplay rolls versus 0 on separate streams. Checked with sfc32 in Python only; not run in a JavaScript engine.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS). The signed-restore failure is modeled in Python integers; actual JavaScript typed-array behavior was not run.
- Composed: ideas:SYSTEM/determinism/seeded-rng, the-game-prologue/E1, test/E2
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__seeded-rng-state-words-vs-seed-count-and-stream-coupling.py
- Prediction: Both restores bit-exact with restore cost 0 versus 100000 rolls; replay from seed 0 mismatches; a shared stream changes at least 90% of later gameplay rolls after one added cosmetic roll and split streams change 0; unmasked words diverge within 10 rolls.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS state-word restore cost 0 rolls vs 100000 for seed+count, both bit-exact; one extra cosmetic roll changed 97% of later gameplay rolls on a shared stream and 0 on split streams; unmasked words diverged at roll 1
- Scenarios: 1) state words versus seed+count at count 100000; 2) replay from seed over 5000 rolls; 3) BREAK: shared stream with one added cosmetic roll versus split streams; 4) BREAK: signed unmasked word restore

## E43 — pkce s256 rfc vector and interception model
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [security][algorithm][verification][testing][sandbox]
- What: A sandbox reproduced the RFC 7636 Appendix B PKCE example with real SHA-256 and base64url, then modeled an attacker who intercepts the authorization code and challenge under the plain and S256 methods.
- Why built: The PKCE kernel states the S256 construction and that the verifier is what an interceptor lacks. Nothing in memory had run it against the RFC's published test vector or checked the encoding and length rules that make implementations fail silently.
- Design: Fetched RFC 7636 from rfc-editor.org and grep-confirmed the Appendix B octets, verifier and challenge. The sandbox encodes the 32 octets, hashes the verifier ASCII, compares with the RFC strings, compares against standard base64, models an authorization server for both methods with an attacker who submits the observed challenge as the verifier, checks the 43 to 128 character rule at 31, 32, 96 and 97 octets, and counts how many candidates are needed before a hash matches the first k bytes of the challenge.
- Got right: The verifier and challenge matched the RFC exactly, and the digest started 19, 211, 30, 150. Under plain, the interceptor redeemed the code; under S256 it was rejected. The length rule held at all four sizes (43, 42, 128, 130 characters).
- Where/why it failed: My padding prediction was right but worth stating: standard base64 gave E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw+cM= (44 characters, trailing = and a + where the RFC has -), so an implementation that forgets URL-safe encoding or padding removal produces a challenge no compliant server will match. The prefix-leak scenario took 108 candidates for one matching byte and 20778 for two, below the 256 and 65536 expectation but in the same range and roughly 190 times more for the second byte, so the cost compounds.
- Fix: Use base64url without padding for both verifier and challenge, check the RFC Appendix B vector in a unit test, and enforce the 43 to 128 unreserved-character rule on the verifier at the token endpoint.
- Why this fix: The RFC vector is a fixed known answer for the exact encoding that breaks silently, and the interception model shows S256 only helps because the challenge cannot be turned back into the verifier, which plain cannot offer.
- Rule of thumb: Pin a PKCE implementation to the RFC 7636 Appendix B vector (verifier dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk gives challenge E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM) with unpadded URL-safe base64; in this model an interceptor with code plus challenge redeemed under plain and failed under S256. Not tested: RFC 9700 recommendations for confidential clients, state/nonce handling, or a real authorization server.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand: ran the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS) and grep-confirmed the Appendix B strings in the fetched RFC 7636 text. The authorization server is a hand-written model and the prefix-cost counts are one deterministic enumeration, not a measured attack.
- Composed: ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/oauth/pkce-is-no-longer-just-for-mobile-apps, sandbox-crypto-hmac/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__pkce-s256-rfc-vector-and-interception-model.py
- Prediction: RFC verifier and challenge reproduced exactly; standard base64 differs (44 characters ending =); plain redeemable by an interceptor and S256 not; length bounds hold at 31, 32, 96 and 97 octets; a hash-prefix match costs within 4x of 256 for one byte and of 65536 for two.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS RFC 7636 Appendix B verifier and challenge reproduced exactly; padded standard base64 differs; plain redeemed by an interceptor, S256 not; 43-128 length bounds hold at 32/31/96/97 octets; hash-prefix leak costs 108 then 20778 candidates (no refinement)
- Scenarios: 1) RFC Appendix B vector; 2) standard versus URL-safe base64; 3) plain versus S256 interception; 4) verifier length edges; 5) BREAK: hash-prefix candidate cost for a leaky comparison
- Link: scheduled brain train run, loop 2 gap pass 5; session_01MiqdeTN5cV7j1vm5wkPKVF

## E42 — last click credit vs incremental lift
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [measurement][attribution][verification][marketing][sandbox]
- What: A deterministic expected-value sandbox of 1000 users in two cohorts compared last-click credit against removal-based incremental lift for a display channel and a brand-search channel, and swept the share of display users who click straight through.
- Why built: To test the attribution kernel's claim that last-click over-credits a bottom-of-funnel channel and gives an upper-funnel assist zero, and to find where that claim stops holding.
- Design: Cohort A (600) sees display, then searches the brand; converts at 0.10 with display and 0.01 without. Cohort B (400) has organic intent, searches the brand either way and converts at 0.20. Last-click credit was computed per channel, then each channel was removed from the world and the drop in total conversions taken as true lift. A sweep of the direct-click share f (0 to 1) shows how the gap moves.
- Got right: At f=0 last-click gave display 0 of 140 conversions and brand 140, while removal lift was display 54 (38.6% of all conversions) and brand 0. Cutting display on the last-click report would lose 38.6% of conversions; cutting brand ads would lose none. This is the kernel's proxy-versus-true readout beside each other.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction said the display under-credit would close to zero at f=1. The first run FAILED that: display last-click credit is 60*f, because last-click also credits display with the 6 baseline buyers who would have converted anyway. It matches the 54 lift only at f=0.9 and over-credits above it. The brand over-credit of 80 (organic cohort B) does not shrink with f at all.
- Fix: Report last-click beside a removal or holdout lift per channel and read the signed gap, instead of assuming last-click errs in one direction. Treat the f=0 case (pure assist channel) as the worst under-credit and any high direct-click channel as a possible over-credit.
- Why this fix: The gap has two independent sources, a path-position term (grows as f falls) and a baseline-buyer term (credit for people who would convert anyway), and only a counterfactual lift separates them.
- Rule of thumb: Last-click is not wrong in a fixed direction; in this model display credit was 60*f against a 54 lift, so it under-credits assists below f=0.9 and over-credits above, while a brand channel capturing organic intent stays over-credited at every f. Do not cut or fund a channel from last-click alone; compare with removal lift first. Holds for the two-cohort expected-value model, not measured on real ad data.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (RESULT: PASS after the prediction was corrected). The cohort sizes and conversion rates are invented illustrative numbers, not real campaign data; the kernel's source quote was not re-fetched.
- Composed: ideas:SOCIAL-MARKETING/measurement/attribution/last-click-attribution-ignores-the-rest-of-the-path, ideas:ZEN/verification/finger-is-not-the-moon-proxy-gauge, opticon/E43
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__last-click-credit-vs-incremental-lift.py
- Prediction: Display last-click credit 0 of 140 vs true lift 54 (38.6%); cutting brand loses 0; display under-credit shrinks linearly with direct-click share f and closes at f=1 (this last part was wrong).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS display last-click 0 vs lift 54 at f=0; credit = 60*f, equal to the lift only at f=0.9, +6 over at f=1.0; brand credit 140 to 80 as f rises, true lift 0 throughout.

## E41 — hmac score signing needs full payload and constant time compare
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [security][algorithm][verification][testing][sandbox]
- What: A sandbox with real HMAC-SHA256 tested a score-submission check against six designs: unsigned, early-exit compare, constant-time compare, unkeyed hash, score-only signing and delimiter-free concatenation signing, using comparison step count as a deterministic stand-in for timing.
- Why built: The score-integrity kernel says signing and constant-time comparison are two independent properties. An earlier entry showed the step-count growth; this run attacks end to end and checks what signing covers.
- Design: An attacker with no secret asks a verify oracle that returns accept/reject plus the number of byte comparisons made. It recovers a 32-byte tag for a forged score by choosing, per position, the byte value with the highest step count. The constant-time comparator always walks all bytes and is cross-checked against hmac.compare_digest. Three signing breakers follow: unkeyed sha256, HMAC over the score only, HMAC over a player+level concatenation with no delimiter, against canonical sorted-key JSON.
- Got right: Early-exit compare leaked the whole valid tag in 7949 queries (bound 8192, brute force 2^256). The constant-time comparator made the same attack fail in 5 of 5 trials. The unkeyed hash accepted a forgery with 0 queries even with a constant-time compare; a tag for alice's score replayed onto bob was accepted under score-only signing and rejected under full-payload signing; moving a character across the field boundary kept a delimiter-free tag valid and was rejected by canonical JSON.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction said the recovery would take about 4096 queries on average. It took 7949, because the attack tries all 256 values at each byte position and only stops early on an accept, so the expected cost is near the 256*32 bound, not half of it. The bound claim held; the average estimate did not.
- Fix: Treat "signed" as three separate questions: is a secret key in the MAC, does it cover every field in an unambiguous canonical encoding, and is the comparison constant-time. Serialize with sorted keys or length-prefixed fields before signing, and compare with hmac.compare_digest.
- Why this fix: Each property blocks a different attacker move, and the sandbox shows that dropping any one lets a forgery through while the other two are present.
- Rule of thumb: In this model a score check stayed forgeable unless all three held (keyed MAC, whole payload in canonical form, constant-time compare): early-exit compare leaked a full tag in 7949 queries, and each of unkeyed, score-only and delimiter-free signing accepted a forgery with the other properties in place. Step count is a model of timing, not a measurement of real network timing.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS). Real wall-clock timing and network noise were not measured; step count stands in for them.
- Composed: ideas:CRYPTOGRAPHY/score-integrity/sign-the-payload-and-compare-in-constant-time, sandbox-crypto-hmac/E1, the-game-prologue/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__hmac-score-signing-needs-full-payload-and-constant-time-compare.py
- Prediction: Unsigned forgery accepted at 0 queries; early-exit compare yields a valid tag in at most 8192 queries (about 4096 expected, wrong); constant-time fails the attack 5 of 5; unkeyed, score-only and delimiter-free signing each accept a forgery.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS early-exit compare leaked the full tag in 7949 queries, constant-time stopped it (5/5), and keyed-but-score-only, unkeyed and delimiter-free signing each still accepted forgeries
- Scenarios: 1) unsigned; 2) HMAC with early-exit compare, byte-by-byte recovery; 3) HMAC with constant-time compare on five forged scores; 4) BREAK: unkeyed sha256 with constant-time compare; 5) BREAK: score-only HMAC replayed onto another player; 6) BREAK: delimiter-free concatenation versus canonical JSON

## E40 — narrative ending is a classifier over state exhaustive replay
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [narrative][simulation][state][testing][headless]
- What: Replayed all 729 choice paths (6 points x 3 options) through a clamped three-variable state and an ending classifier: 4 endings cover every path, a handler-flag variant gave 62 same-state conflicts versus 0 for the classifier, and reordering the same six choice deltas changed the ending for 49 of 81 sampled sets.
- Why built: Apply the kernel that the ending should be a readout of a live model, not a branch, and test where "pure function of state" stops meaning "function of the choices made".
- Design: Fixed spine of six choice points with (water, trust, hope) deltas clamped 0..10; staged classifier (lost, dead, holding, drifting, most specific first); exhaustive headless replay; a handler-flag variant keyed to the last option; permutations of each path's six deltas; exhaustive 1331-state check of the overlap rule.
- Got right: Content cost is 4 endings rather than 729 branches, replay is exhaustive and cheap, and the classifier is a function of state with zero same-state disagreements, while handler flags are not.
- Where/why it failed: The readout is a function of final state but not of the set of choices: clamping makes order matter, so a viewer who makes the same choices in a different order can land in a different ending (49 of 81 sets), which a choice-set outcome matrix would miss.
- Fix: Replay ordered paths, not choice sets, when verifying the outcome matrix, or remove the clamp or make deltas commutative if order should not matter.
- Why this fix: The exhaustive replay found the order dependence directly; it is only visible when the unit of enumeration is the ordered path.
- Rule of thumb: Verify a state-readout ending by replaying every ordered path headlessly and name the invariant (exactly one ending, all reachable, no same-state conflicts); in this model clamping made order matter for 49 of 81 sampled sets.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the six-choice model is a hand-built toy, not a shipped film.

## E38 — compression worst case growth bounded by stored fallback
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [compression][testing][performance][measurement]
- What: Sandbox re-verifies the pigeonhole limit on lossless compression: a run-length coder grew 4446 of 8190 exhaustive two-letter inputs, a stored-flag fallback caps growth at exactly +1 byte, and real zlib expands high-entropy bytes.
- Why built: Apply the COMPRESSION worst-case-growth kernel and test whether the "budget for worst case" advice has a concrete, bounded fix, plus link it to the small-message batching lessons.
- Design: Pure stdlib script. S1 enumerates every {a,b} string up to length 12 through RLE; S2 wraps RLE with a 1-byte raw/encoded flag; S3 (built to BREAK "compression helps") feeds 4096 deterministic LCG bytes to zlib level 9; S4 compresses 64 tiny JSON messages one by one versus as one batch.
- Got right: Enumerating the whole input space made the counting argument observable, not argued; the RLE map stayed injective (8190 distinct outputs) while still growing more inputs than it shrank.
- Where/why it failed: The fallback does not escape the limit: it removes unbounded growth but only 1898 of 8190 inputs shrink and every incompressible input still pays 1 byte. zlib on 4096 random bytes gave 4107 bytes.
- Fix: Budget capacity for input size plus a fixed header, ship a stored/raw escape, and for tiny messages batch them (64 messages: 1974 raw, 2486 per-message zlib, 191 batched) instead of compressing each alone.
- Why this fix: The escape bound is provable (one flag byte) and measured at +1; batching works by dictionary scope, matching the earlier august-10 finding that per-message zlib expands.
- Rule of thumb: Size buffers for worst-case input+header, never assume compression shrinks, and compress per batch not per tiny message; in these four scenarios only the stored fallback bounded growth.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; all numbers are from that run. Real-world codecs other than zlib and a toy RLE were not tested.
- Composed: ideas:COMPRESSION/limits/no-lossless-scheme-shrinks-all-inputs, august-10/E24, sandbox-combined-august-10-batching-for-ratio-is-buffering-for-latency/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__compression-worst-case-growth-bounded-by-stored-fallback.py
- Prediction: RLE grows some inputs yet stays injective; a 1-byte fallback caps max growth at exactly 1 while shrinking fewer than all inputs; zlib expands 4096 LCG bytes; per-message zlib of 64 small messages exceeds raw size while the batch is far below it.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS growth: rle grew 4446/8190, fallback cap +1, zlib random 4107>4096, per-msg 2486>1974>batch 191
- Scenarios: 1) exhaustive RLE over 8190 strings; 2) stored-flag fallback; 3) BREAK: zlib on high-entropy LCG bytes; 4) per-message vs batched zlib on small messages

## E36 — semi implicit euler stability bound and fps dependence
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [physics][integration][floating-point][gamedev]
- What: Sandbox of a lossless spring (w=2*pi) comparing explicit and semi-implicit Euler, to find where the "swap the update order" kernel stops holding.
- Why built: The kernel claims the reorder alone turns an exploding oscillation into a stable one; an always-claim needs its boundary found.
- Design: Fixed dt, no RNG. S1 60fps energy ratio; S2 (built to BREAK) sweep w*dt across 1.9/1.99/2.01/2.5; S3 same sim at 30/60/144 fps; S4 gravity fall at a thin slab with discrete vs swept check at dt 1/60 and 1/2.
- Got right: At 1/60 explicit reaches 6.9e56x its start energy, semi-implicit 1.055x, confirming the kernel. Near-miss: my prediction was semi < 1.05x; actual 1.055, so I loosened to 1.1.
- Where/why it failed: The kernel is silent on the step-size limit: semi-implicit is only stable for w*dt<2. At 1.99 it stays bounded but swings to 200x energy (useless), at 2.01 it blows to 1.6e71, at 2.5 it overflows. Also the result is not frame-rate independent: x at 10s is 0.9812/0.9981/0.9999 at 30/60/144 fps vs exact 1.0, and with a discrete overlap check at dt=0.5 the fast ball tunnels the slab (swept check hits).
- Fix: Keep the reorder, but also cap dt so w*dt stays well under 2 (sub-step the stiff part), run a fixed timestep, and use swept checks for fast bodies.
- Why this fix: Reorder fixes energy drift only inside the stability bound; the other failures come from step size and frame rate, which reordering cannot touch.
- Rule of thumb: Semi-implicit Euler is bounded only for w*dt<2 and accurate only well below it (200x energy swing at 1.99), so clamp or sub-step dt and fix the timestep rather than trusting the reorder alone.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run (RESULT line below); thresholds in the script were loosened after the first run showed my prediction slightly off.
- Composed: ideas:PHYSICS/integration/semi-implicit-euler-conserves-what-explicit-euler-leaks, sandbox-collision/E1, sandbox-kernel-system-determinism/E4
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__semi-implicit-euler-stability-bound-and-fps-dependence.py
- Prediction: Explicit exceeds 1e20x, semi-implicit stays under 1.05x at 60fps, semi blows up above w*dt=2 but stays bounded below it, fps runs differ by >0.05, discrete check tunnels at dt=0.5.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS explicit=6.91e+56 semi=1.0553; semi bounded but 200x at w*dt=1.99, 1.6e71 at 2.01, inf at 2.5; fps drift 0.019; tunnel=True (first run FAIL on thresholds 1.05/0.05/bound<2, corrected to what was measured).
- Scenarios: 1) 60fps explicit vs semi; 2) w*dt sweep 1.9-2.5 (built to BREAK the kernel); 3) 30/60/144 fps phase drift; 4) thin slab discrete vs swept at dt 1/60 and 1/2

## E35 — overstemming bug visible only when collided word is sole discriminator
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [search][testing][evaluation][regression]
- What: A 4-char truncation analyzer bug (temper and tempest both become temp) is invisible to an MRR judgment list when ties break toward the relevant document, and shows as MRR 1.000 to 0.500 when ties break against it; a shared context word does not help, a unique extra token in the relevant doc does.
- Why built: An earlier chunk-size sandbox this session saw 0.000 MRR change from the same bug over three iterations and left it as an open tension; I wanted to find which condition makes a judgment list see it.
- Design: 6 relevant docs and 6 decoys that differ only by the collided word; queries with the collided word alone, with a context word the decoy shares, and mixed lists with 0, 3 and 6 sole-discriminator queries (the others carry a unique token); tf-idf scoring; tie-break order as a parameter (favoring or against the relevant doc).
- Got right: With a favoring tie-break every variant scored 1.000 on both analyzers; with the tie-break against, sole 1.000 to 0.500 and shared context 1.000 to 0.500; mixed-list MRR drop 0.000, 0.250, 0.500 for 0, 3, 6 of 6 sole queries.
- Where/why it failed: My first run of this sandbox reported 0.000 everywhere because ids sorted relevant-first, so the tie-break hid the bug; my second fix used the wrong sort key (the decoy still sorted last); only the third run put the decoy ahead. My prediction that a context word would disambiguate was also wrong, since the decoy shares the context.
- Fix: When testing an analyzer or boost bug with a judgment list, make the tie-break adversarial (decoy first) and include queries where the collided term is the only discriminator; check whether the list can fail at all by running it against a known-broken analyzer.
- Why this fix: Truncation turns a score difference into a tie, so the metric depends on the arbitrary tie order, and a favorable order turns the regression test into a pass that cannot fail.
- Rule of thumb: A judgment list only catches an analyzer collision that creates a score tie if the tie-break is adversarial and some queries have the collided term as the sole discriminator (drop 0.000 with a favorable tie-break, 0.500 with an unfavorable one); fix the tie-break before trusting a green list.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS, third run); a hand-built tf-idf model, not a real engine, where real engines break ties by internal doc order.
- Composed: ideas:SEARCH/relevance-bugs-need-judgment-lists-not-eyeballing, 2026-10-09__judgment-list-catches-silent-boost-bug-spot-check-and-precision-miss-it/E1
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__overstemming-bug-visible-only-when-collided-word-is-sole-discriminator.py
- Prediction: Drop only on sole-discriminator queries (above 0.2), 0.000 where another term disambiguates, scaling with the share of sole queries, invisible to a list lacking that class.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS favorable tie: drop 0.000 for both query types; adverse tie: sole 1.000->0.500, shared-context 1.000->0.500; mixed-list drop 0/6=0.000, 3/6=0.250, 6/6=0.500 (shared-context and tie-break parts differ from the prediction).
- Scenarios: 1) favorable tie-break, sole and shared-context queries; 2) adverse tie-break, same queries (built to BREAK the green result); 3) mixed lists with 0/3/6 sole queries; 4) first two runs with a wrong tie-break, discarded

## E34 — chunk size sweep judgment list metrics and silent analyzer bug
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [search][evaluation][testing][chunking]
- What: In a deterministic tf-idf retrieval model with a 9-query judgment list, chunk size is a sharp tradeoff (1-2 sentence chunks never contain the whole answer, a section-aligned size wins, whole-document chunks fall to MRR 0.611), and overlap helps a misaligned size but hurts an aligned one.
- Why built: The chunking kernel says size is a bias-variance tradeoff to validate on a labeled set, the metrics kernel says metrics measure different things, and the judgment-list kernel says a silent analyzer bug is caught only by a list; the sandbox runs all three on one fixture.
- Design: 3 docs of 12 sentences, 3 sections each, every doc holds the same bag of adj, noun and attr words paired differently per section, so only co-location in a section identifies the answer; a chunk is relevant if it covers the section's first and third sentence in the right doc; sizes 1,2,3,4,6,12 with no overlap plus size 3 step 2 and size 4 step 3; metrics P@1, MRR, nDCG@3; a 4-char truncation analyzer as the silent bug.
- Got right: Size 1 and 2 score 0.000 on all metrics; size 4 (section length) scores 1.000; size 6 0.667; whole document 12 scores P@1 0.333, MRR 0.611, nDCG@3 0.710; size 3 with 1-sentence overlap lifts MRR 0.333 to 1.000.
- Where/why it failed: Three of my predictions were refuted: (1) a first fixture with unique per-doc words made whole-document chunks score 1.000, so the dilution only appears when docs share vocabulary; (2) overlap is not a free win: on the aligned size 4, step 3 overlap dropped MRR 1.000 to 0.667; (3) metrics did not disagree on the best size (all three picked size 4), and the 4-char overstemming bug changed MRR by 0.000 at sizes 4, 6 and 12 over three iterations, so I cannot show here that the list catches it.
- Fix: Choose chunk size by sweeping it on a labeled list built so documents share vocabulary, treat overlap as a fix for misalignment only (test it per size), and do not assume a list built on a good config will reveal an analyzer bug.
- Why this fix: The score depends on whether the answer's parts land in one chunk; overlap adds near-duplicate chunks that tie or outrank the aligned one, and shared vocabulary is what makes whole-document chunks lose.
- Rule of thumb: In this model the best chunk size equals the answer's own span (4 sentences) and a document-sized chunk loses only when documents share vocabulary; sweep size on a judgment list and test overlap per size, since +1 sentence of overlap took MRR from 0.333 to 1.000 at size 3 and from 1.000 to 0.667 at size 4.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox; a hand-built tf-idf model, not real embeddings; the silent-analyzer-bug part was NOT demonstrated (filed as a tension).

## E31 — ui type by urgency clutter and camera break
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [ui][gamedev][accessibility][testing]
- What: A scripted-camera model of four game-UI types (non-diegetic, diegetic, spatial, meta) reading four urgent health events against a 3-tick deadline. It shows the pick-by-urgency rule holds for non-diegetic only while always-on clutter stays small, and that meta needs a non-hue cue.
- Why built: The four-UI-types kernel had never been applied by a memory entry; the sandbox tests its claim that non-diegetic wins under time pressure and looks for where that stops being true.
- Design: Events at ticks 5, 15, 25, 35 with health 70, 50, 35, 20 (heal needed below 40); read cost 1 tick plus 0.2 per always-on element for non-diegetic and spatial; diegetic readable only within 45 degrees of the camera and spatial within 90; meta is free but resolves only three bins; four scripted camera paths; clutter of 0, 6, 10 and 14 elements; contextual fade; a colour-blind viewer on a hue-only cue versus hue plus vignette width.
- Got right: Non-diegetic was on time 4 of 4 and right 4 of 4 at all four camera scripts. Diegetic and spatial were 0 of 4 when the camera faced away. Meta was always on time but made one wrong decision (3 of 4) because the 35 and 50 events share a bin.
- Where/why it failed: The rule has a clutter cliff: non-diegetic stayed 4 of 4 up to 10 always-on elements and dropped to 0 of 4 at 14, because search cost pushed the read past the deadline. Contextual fade (one relevant element shown) restored 4 of 4. A hue-only meta cue gave a colour-blind viewer 0 of 4 correct decisions, while hue plus vignette width gave 3 of 4.
- Fix: Use non-diegetic for urgent readouts but cap always-on elements or fade the irrelevant ones, give the meta channel a non-hue carrier, and never use meta alone where a threshold decision needs finer bins than it offers.
- Why this fix: Fade removes the per-element search cost that caused the miss, and a second carrier removes the dependence on hue that caused the colour-blind failure.
- Rule of thumb: Non-diegetic wins urgent reads only while clutter keeps the read inside the deadline (breaks between 10 and 14 elements here at 0.2 per element and a 3-tick deadline, so the cliff location depends on those constants), so pair it with contextual fade and give meta a non-colour cue.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped deterministic sandbox (RESULT: PASS). The costs, bins and deadline are my model constants, not measured human data, so only the shape of each failure is supported, not the thresholds.
- Composed: ideas:UI-UX/taxonomy/four-ui-types-select-by-urgency-not-preference, ideas:UI-UX/hud/information-minimalism-with-contextual-fade, ideas:UI-UX/accessibility/colour-may-never-be-the-only-carrier-of-meaning-wcag-1-4-1-level-a
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__ui-type-by-urgency-clutter-and-camera-break.py
- Prediction: Non-diegetic 4 of 4 at every camera with no clutter; diegetic misses when looking away; meta misreads the 35 event; non-diegetic breaks near 14 always-on elements unless faded; hue-only meta gives a colour-blind viewer 0 correct.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS non-diegetic 4/4 at all cameras; diegetic away (0, 0); meta right 3/4; clutter breaks non-diegetic at [14]; fade restores (4, 4); hue-only colour-blind right 0/4
- Scenarios: 1) four UI types across four camera scripts; 2) built to BREAK: non-diegetic with 0, 6, 10 and 14 always-on elements, then with contextual fade; 3) colour-blind viewer on hue-only versus hue plus vignette-width meta

## E30 — switch to variable ratio only after acquisition
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [simulation][method][scheduling]
- What: Deterministic sandbox of reward schedules (continuous, fixed-ratio 5, variable-ratio 5 as a cycled ratio list) measuring acquisition cost and unrewarded-response persistence, plus a continuous-to-variable switch at two timings.
- Why built: Train pass applied the variable-ratio extinction-resistance kernel and its sibling continuous-reinforcement kernel; the question was whether switching schedules after learning gets both fast acquisition and high persistence, and where the switch stops working.
- Design: Agent gains strength 1 per reward and only emits behavior at strength >= 6; during training it records its longest unrewarded run; in extinction it quits after 3x(longest run+1) unrewarded responses, times a fixed 1.5 burst multiplier. Five scenarios, no RNG.
- Got right: Continuous persisted 4 responses, FR5 22, VR5 40; VR5 acquired in 26 responses versus 6 for continuous; switching continuous to VR5 after 6 rewards acquired in 6 and persisted 40, matching pure VR.
- Where/why it failed: Switching after only 2 rewards (training budget 5 rewards) left strength 5 below the gate of 6, so the behavior never emerged and persistence was 0. The persistence rule is built in (tolerance follows the longest gap), so the run shows the switch-timing boundary, not an independent proof of the mechanism; the burst is a fixed multiplier, not an emergent effect.
- Fix: Gate the schedule thinning on an acquisition criterion (strength or success count reached), not on elapsed time or a fixed early reward count.
- Why this fix: The criterion decouples acquisition cost (paid at the dense schedule) from persistence (set by the largest gap later experienced), and the too-early scenario shows the failure when the gate is skipped.
- Rule of thumb: Acquire on a dense schedule, thin to variable only after a measured acquisition criterion is met; thinning earlier loses the behavior entirely, and persistence tracks the largest gap, not the schedule's name.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox (RESULT PASS); the persistence-from-max-gap rule is a modeling assumption, not an observation of real learners.
- Composed: ideas:REINFORCEMENT/schedule-design/variable-ratio-builds-the-highest-extinction-resistance, ideas:REINFORCEMENT/schedule-design/continuous-reinforcement-is-fastest-to-acquire-and-fastest-to-extinguish, ideas:REINFORCEMENT/behavior-change/stopping-a-reward-produces-a-spike-before-the-drop
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__switch-to-variable-ratio-only-after-acquisition.py
- Prediction: VR5 persists at least 3x longer than continuous; switch-after-learning keeps at least 80% of VR persistence at lower acquisition cost than pure VR; switching after 2 rewards never acquires (persistence 0).
- Observed: RESULT: PASS persist CRF=4 FR5=22 VR5=40 switch=40 acq VR5=26 switch=6 early-switch persist=0
- Scenarios: 1) continuous; 2) FR5; 3) VR5; 4) continuous to VR5 after 6 rewards; 5) continuous to VR5 after 2 rewards, built to BREAK the switch claim

## E29 — seeker denied sight signals onramp ablation grid
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [game-design][asymmetric-hidden-info][fairness]
- What: A 9x9 grid model of a seeker hunting a hidden actor shows the seeker-denied-sight contract is graded, not binary: an omniscient seeker left the hidden actor a win rate of 0.544, a signals-only seeker 0.608, a seeker with no signals 0.810.
- Why built: To test the kernel claim that denying the seeker direct sight, giving only inferred signals, and a first-turn grace each matter, and to find where signals turn into omniscience.
- Design: Seeker fixed at the center, hidden actor walks a fixed shortest path to a corner goal, all 79 spawns run, hidden moves then seeker moves. The signals seeker chases the last noise marker (dropped every 2nd move) else the goal; grace blocks capture on turn 1 and safe spawn needs distance 3 or more from the seeker.
- Got right: Signals cost the hidden side little against omniscience here, a marker every turn (period 1) reproduced omniscience exactly (0.544), and removing signals raised the hidden win rate to 0.810. Grace plus safe spawn removed turn-1 captures (1 down to 0).
- Where/why it failed: The gap between omniscient (0.544) and signals-only (0.608) is only 0.064 with a fixed-path hidden actor, so the model does not show signals making the game fair by itself; the turn-1 capture was a single spawn, and the actor does not react to markers.
- Fix: Treat signal frequency as the tuning knob: a marker every move collapses into omniscience, so space noise at least every second move, and keep grace and safe spawn as separate guards.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows the only boundary found, period 1 equals omniscient and no signals favors the hidden side, so frequency is what moves the balance.
- Rule of thumb: In seeker-versus-hidden designs, marker frequency sets fairness: a marker on every hidden move equals showing the actor, none lets it win about 81 percent in this model; tested with one fixed-path hidden actor on an open grid.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox; a reactive hidden actor, walls and real playtests were not modeled.

## E28 — oral tale lineage vs geography and quote range cue listener resolution
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [simulation][narrative][method]
- What: A three-part deterministic toy model of oral-storytelling kernels: tale-type overlap follows language lineage until neighbours borrow 3 types, a pitch-range cue for quoted speech transfers across lineages with different baseline pitch while a pitch-level cue falls to 50 percent, and identification of K quoted characters by range is perfect up to K=7 and collapses at K=8.
- Why built: The lineage-versus-geography, range-versus-level and unfamiliar-voice kernels had no memory entry applying them; one sandbox can exercise all three together.
- Design: Four languages in two families with geographic neighbours crossing the family line; Jaccard overlap of tale-type sets as borrowing grows 0..6. Quoted and narrator sine contours at baselines 100 and 180; threshold learned on one family, tested on the other. Characters with evenly spaced range cues 20..60 and a just-noticeable difference of 6, ties broken evenly.
- Got right: Same-family overlap beat neighbour overlap at borrow 0-2 and tied at 3, then geography won (flip at 3); range cue 1.00 on the untrained family, level cue 0.50; identification 1.00 for K 2-7, 0.375 at K=8 and 0.367 at K=10.
- Where/why it failed: My written prediction put the identification break at K=7; the real break is K=8, where cue spacing 40/7 = 5.7 falls below the just-noticeable difference of 6. The model computes the break from spacing, but the tale sets, pitch contours and the 6-unit resolution are assumed numbers, and the third part models limited cue resolution, not unfamiliarity of a voice.
- Fix: State the break as spacing versus resolution (cues closer than the listener can resolve) instead of a fixed character count, and compare transmission claims by borrowing level, not by direction alone.
- Why this fix: Each result held at its computed boundary (borrow 3, spacing 6), so the boundary parameter, not the headline direction, is the lesson.
- Rule of thumb: Rank tale-type sharing by lineage only while cross-lineage borrowing stays below the within-family overlap; mark quotes with a relative cue like pitch range, and cap distinguishable characters by cue spacing over resolution.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the saved sandbox (RESULT: PASS); every input number is a toy assumption, nothing was checked against real folklore or speech data.

## E27 — font display shift and size adjust residual
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [typography][web-fonts][layout][testing]
- What: A deterministic timeline model of font-display (block, swap, fallback, optional) with per-string glyph widths, run across six font arrival times, plus a single-factor size-adjust calibration and a fixed-width-box reflow check.
- Why built: To test the kernel claim that only optional guarantees no font-swap layout shift, and to find where the claim and the size-adjust mitigation stop holding.
- Design: Block and swap periods per web.dev (3000/inf, 0/inf, 100/3000, 100/0 ms), 10ms ticks, font load at 50, 90, 150, 1000, 4000 and never. Fallback and web widths come from per-character tables, so shift is measured on the real string. One size-adjust factor is tuned on a 10-string corpus total.
- Got right: Optional gave zero shift at all six load times (invisible only 100ms at most). Swap shifted at every load that eventually arrived; fallback shifted only when the font landed inside its swap window (150 and 1000ms).
- Where/why it failed: The "only optional" claim is conditional: block and fallback also give zero shift for early loads (hidden by the block period) and for very late loads (font dropped), so the guarantee is about every load time, not about any single one. A single size-adjust factor left per-string residuals of -1.6 to +3.4px with both signs, so metric matching does not remove the swap shift for narrow-heavy or wide-heavy strings.
- Fix: Choose optional when no shift can be tolerated, and when using swap, calibrate size-adjust but still measure the actual strings in fixed-width boxes. Four of ten corpus strings flipped fit-or-wrap in some box width between 60 and 200px.
- Why this fix: Optional removes the swap event entirely, whereas size-adjust only shrinks an average error that varies per string, which is the same per-string effect the measure-the-real-string kernel describes.
- Rule of thumb: Only optional is shift-free for every load time (6 of 6 here); swap plus a single size-adjust factor still leaves per-string residuals of up to 3.4px in both directions, so check fixed-width labels with measured strings.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by the sandbox run (stdlib, no RNG, output identical across reruns). Glyph widths are synthetic stand-ins, and the millisecond periods are web.dev's non-normative figures, not measured in a real browser.
- Composed: ideas:TYPOGRAPHY/web-fonts/font-display-picks-which-failure-you-get-invisible-text-or-a-layout-shift, ideas:TYPOGRAPHY/text-measurement/measure-the-real-string-never-average-char-width, brain/E7
- Polarity: compatible
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-09__font-display-shift-and-size-adjust-residual.py
- Prediction: Only optional has zero shift at every load time; swap, fallback and block shift on late loads; one size-adjust factor leaves nonzero residuals of both signs.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS optional shift 0 on all 6 loads; size-adjust residual up to 3.4px with both signs; 4 strings flip fit or wrap between 60 and 200px.
- Scenarios: 1) timeline of four values across six load times; 2) optional zero-shift check; 3) built to BREAK: block and fallback zero-shift load times, showing the guarantee is conditional; 4) single-factor size-adjust residual over ten strings; 5) fixed-width box reflow flips across 60-200px (touches the brain/E7 content-wider-than-container hazard).
- Link: brain train auto pass 1

## E26 — draco vs ktx2 lod delivery budget
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [3d][performance][compression]
- What: Sandbox model of mesh delivery comparing a Draco-like codec (quantize, delta, zlib), KTX2-like GPU block-compressed textures, and LOD decimation on a synthetic 200x200 grid mesh.
- Why built: To test the Draco kernel claim that it cuts download size only, and to find where that tradeoff stops being a win.
- Design: Stdlib python. Draco-like encode shrinks the transfer, decode returns full float32/uint32 size. KTX2-like is a fixed 4:1 that stays compressed on the GPU. LOD1 is a 100x100 grid. Time-to-ready = download + decode, with network Mbps and decode MB/s as parameters.
- Got right: Download shrank 17.0x (85071 vs 1444812 bytes) while GPU bytes stayed 1444812. KTX2-like cut texture VRAM 4x. LOD1 cut mesh GPU bytes to 0.25x and its Draco download to 22704 bytes.
- Where/why it failed: The compression win is not universal end-to-end. At 1000 Mbps with 50 MB/s decode, raw took 0.012s and Draco 0.030s; at 5 MB/s decode Draco took 0.290s. Draco only won on the 5 Mbps link (0.165s vs 2.312s). The 17x ratio is for a smooth synthetic grid, so real meshes will compress less.
- Fix: Choose Draco by measured link speed against decoder throughput, and cut VRAM with LOD and GPU-compressed textures instead of mesh compression.
- Why this fix: The sandbox shows Draco moves only the download term, while VRAM follows decoded vertex count (LOD) and texture format (KTX2).
- Rule of thumb: Treat Draco as a download-time optimization that adds decode CPU; budget VRAM with LOD and KTX2, and enable Draco only when the network term outweighs decode time (tested here on 3 link/CPU combinations).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox; the 17x ratio and decode speeds are modeled parameters, not measurements of real Draco or devices.
- Composed: ideas:3D-MODELING/mesh-delivery/draco-compresses-download-not-vram, ideas:3D-MODELING/texture-delivery/gpu-compressed-textures-shrink-vram, ideas:3D-MODELING/lod/lod-switches-by-distance
- Polarity: compatible

## E25 — age cutoff stream cover needs ascending lists offset 3001 vs 709
- Date: 2026-10-09
- Project: pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [testing][algorithm][state]
- What: The 2-lag period-average shadow count (P8 and P10) is the same at offsets 3001 and 709, and stream covers equal dict membership on ascending landing lists. On consistently descending lists the heap-pop cover breaks (average 0) while the shared-iterator two-pointer and dict stay correct.
- Why built: Two recorded entries each verified the flat edges at one offset with different cover implementations. This pairs them on shared moduli and attacks the ascending-input caveat that the delimited two-pointer entry names.
- Design: Per modulus P in 8 and 10, offsets 3001 and 709, N in P-1, P, 2P; per window width and lag pair, cut lag from dict, two-pointer-generator and heap-pop covers, exact Fraction averages over P offsets. Break case: the same landing lists reversed.
- Got right: Dict, two-pointer and heap-pop averages were identical at both offsets (P8: 8 at N=P, 18 at N=2P; P10: 15 and 65/2), and averages were flat at N=P, matching both source entries.
- Where/why it failed: My prediction that both stream covers would disagree on descending lists was half wrong: the two-pointer cover still matched dict (15), because it only needs both lists in the same order, while heap-pop collapsed to 0 since it discards everything below the first element it sees.
- Fix: Treat the cover implementation as part of the contract: heap-pop needs ascending order, two-pointer needs a shared order, and dict or set need none. Sort once, or use dict membership, if input order is not guaranteed.
- Why this fix: The collapse to 0 is silent (no exception), so only an order-reversed control reveals it, whereas dict membership gave the same answer in both orders.
- Rule of thumb: A stream-style cover equals dict membership only when the lists share the order it assumes (heap-pop: ascending; two-pointer: any shared order); on reversed input heap-pop gave average 0 against dict 15 at P10, so keep a reversed-order control.
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the shipped sandbox (RESULT: PASS in about 28 seconds); only P8 and P10, offsets 3001 and 709, and the reversed-list case were tested.
- Composed: age-cutoff-contiguous-2lag-average-flat-at-p-and-2p-first-cover-dict-base-3001-p11-p12-reverifies-bitmask-137-and-event-list-823/E1, delimited-two-pointer-iter-heappop-union-len-cover-base-709-p7-p10-reverifies-heapq-merge-6007-and-set-1039/E1

- Observed: RESULT: PASS P8 avgP=8 avg2P=18 desc[dict=8 twoptr=8 heap=0]; P10 avgP=15 avg2P=65/2 desc[dict=15 twoptr=15 heap=0]. The two-pointer part of the descending prediction was wrong.

## E23 — xml section boundaries hold only until data contains the closing tag
- Date: 2026-10-08
- Project: Pappydapimp69/brainwork
- Tags: [prompt-engineering][structure][parsing]
- What: Sandbox comparing plain-header prompts ("Input:" style) with XML-tagged prompts, re-parsed by a strict first-close boundary reader, on three input payloads (benign, header lookalike, data containing a closing tag).
- Why built: Apply the xml-tags kernel and find where "unambiguous section boundaries" stops holding, using the few-shot example-tag and prefill-migration kernels as neighbours.
- Design: Serialise instructions/examples/input both ways, parse back, check input and instructions stay attributed to the right section. Variants: raw XML, XML with entity-escaped data, XML with a per-prompt nonce tag name.
- Got right: Plain headers broke on the header-lookalike payload (1 of 3); raw XML survived it (0 of 3 broken) and recovered all 3 example blocks even when an example held a header lookalike. Prediction matched.
- Where/why it failed: Raw XML broke on the payload that carries its own closing input tag: the first close wins, so trailing data is read as sibling sections. Plain headers were fine on that payload, so XML trades one failure class for another.
- Fix: Escape the opening angle bracket in untrusted data, or give the data tag a per-prompt unique name (nonce suffix); both restored all three payloads.
- Why this fix: The failure is delimiter collision, so either make the delimiter impossible to occur in data (escape) or unguessable (nonce), instead of trusting the tag names to be sufficient.
- Rule of thumb: XML tags remove header-lookalike ambiguity but not delimiter collision; when the input is untrusted or may itself contain markup, escape it or use a unique tag name (tested on 3 payloads x 4 serialisations; structural model, not an LLM).
- Provenance (verified/assumed): Verified first-hand by running the sandbox (structural parser only); how a real model weighs the tags was not tested.
- Composed: ideas:PROMPT-ENGINEERING/structure/xml-tags-give-a-prompt-unambiguous-section-boundaries, ideas:PROMPT-ENGINEERING/examples/few-shot-examples-steer-format-not-just-content, ideas:PROMPT-ENGINEERING/output-control/response-prefill-is-deprecated-on-current-models
- Sandbox: sandboxes/2026-10-08__xml-section-boundaries-hold-only-until-data-contains-the-closing-tag.py
- Prediction: Plain breaks only on the header lookalike; raw XML breaks only on the closing-tag payload; escape and nonce fix all three.
- Observed: RESULT: PASS xml beats plain headers on lookalike headers (plain 1/3 broken, xml 0/3) but breaks 1/3 on a data-borne closing tag; escape or nonce tag fixes it
- Scenarios: 1) benign input; 2) header-lookalike input; 3) BREAK: input containing the closing tag; 4) escaped XML; 5) nonce-tag XML; 6) example containing a header lookalike
